Marc Marquez wins Malaysian MotoGP, extends championship lead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:32:10 UTC
00:32:10 KST

Halis Sunnetci
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
Defending MotoGP world champion Marc Marquez won the Malaysian Grand Prix on Sunday, securing his seventh victory of the season and extending his championship lead to 44 points.
The Ducati Lenovo rider completed the 20-lap race at the 5.54-kilometer Sepang International Circuit in 40 minutes and 14.236 seconds, claiming his third Malaysian Grand Prix victory and first since 2018.
Spain’s Pedro Acosta of Red Bull KTM Factory Racing finished second, 4.172 seconds behind Marquez, while his younger brother Alex Marquez of BK8 Gresini Racing took third, 5.955 seconds behind.
Marquez, who started second on the grid, overtook pole-sitter Alex at the opening corner. His younger brother briefly regained the lead before running wide, allowing the Ducati rider to move back ahead and control the remainder of the race.
The victory, his 80th in the premier class, lifted Marquez to 399 championship points, 44 ahead of second-placed Jorge Martin, who missed the Malaysian Grand Prix due to a wrist injury sustained at the Australian Grand Prix.
Martin’s Aprilia Racing teammate Marco Bezzecchi finished sixth, 11.259 seconds behind Marquez, and remained third in the championship standings with 332 points.
Acosta followed in fourth place with 295 points, while Japan’s Ai Ogura was fifth with 278.
Marquez will have his first opportunity to clinch his eighth MotoGP world title at the Qatar Grand Prix on Nov. 8, with two rounds remaining after the event.

Transcript: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 1, 2026
The following is the full transcript of the interview with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 1, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: All right. So, Governor, you're campaigning for re-election, and you're also trying to help some of these Democrats get elected to Congress. According to our CBS polling, 57% of likely voters believe Democrats have not offered a clear plan for what they would do if they do win control of Congress. What is it that Democrats are running for, or is it simply in opposition to President Trump?
GOV. JOSH SHAPIRO: Well, certainly for me, it's not about opposition to Trump. I'm running as a GSD Democrat—a Get Stuff Done Democrat. I think what people have seen in my leadership here in Pennsylvania is someone who listens, who goes back to the Capitol, and then delivers, executes for the people of Pennsylvania, and I'm working hard to elect these members of or these challengers to the members of Congress here in Pennsylvania who run on a similar platform, common sense things, making sure people have access to health care, making sure that there is actually accountability in Washington D.C. so that the corruption doesn't take money out of people's pockets here and enrich the folks in D.C. Those are just two examples of the kinds of things I see from our challengers here in Congress. And as I crisscross this Commonwealth, what they're seeing from me is a Democrat who understands how to win, but more importantly, understands how to deliver for them. And that's what these candidates are running on.
MARGARET BRENNAN: How optimistic are you that you're going to be able to take four seats I think you've said?
GOV. SHAPIRO: I mean, look. Right now, it seems like there might even be five competitive congressional districts here in Pennsylvania. Obviously, four have received the most attention. I think we're seemingly ahead in at least three of them. But look, I never pay much attention to these polls. I think it's all a jump ball, and the most important thing is to do what we're doing on this bus: show up everywhere, talk to people, let them know what's at stake, how important it is to not just re-elect their governor, but that we can finally have a check on Donald Trump's chaos, cruelty, and corruption in Washington D.C. If they get out and vote for their candidate for Congress.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And they're still going to have to work with a Republican president for those next two years when they get there. If they get there.
GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah. But there'll be a check on his corruption, and hopefully have real leverage to roll back the Medicaid cuts, to roll back the SNAP cuts, to make sure that there's real responsibility and accountability in Washington D.C. Something we have not had when Republicans have had a trifecta there.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Let me ask you about what's going to happen here in this state in terms of administering the election. Homeland Security claimed earlier this year that as many as 14,576 non-citizens could be registered to vote here. Has the federal government provided enough information to you–
[STOP DOWN]
MARGARET BRENNAN: So Homeland Security said that in this state there are as many as 14,576 non citizens that could be registered to vote in Pennsylvania. Did they provide information to back up that claim? And what did your own investigation find?
GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah, could is the operative word. As soon as we received that from the federal government, we immediately responded and said, "Look, if you have information of illegal voters who are on our rolls, we want that information because we don't want them casting a ballot here in Pennsylvania." I'm very serious about it. Look, I'm the former chief law enforcement officer of this Commonwealth. I have prosecuted election fraud cases. I don't want anyone voting who's not a legal eligible voter–
MARGARET BRENNAN: Did they back that up?
GOV. SHAPIRO: And of course, of course, when we responded to the Trump administration, they provided no backup. So it was a press release designed to get some attention for their false narrative. Listen, the first appointment I made when I was elected governor was the Secretary of State. That's the person that administers elections here in the state. A Republican named Al Schmidt. I chose him, even though I'm a Democrat, because I think the administration of elections should be nonpartisan. Al Schmidt, in his career of running elections, has done more to root out corruption than anything that's ever been done in the Trump administration. We take that very, very seriously, and the Trump administration has never provided a shred of evidence to suggest that there are people on our rolls who are ineligible. If they have it, I want it, and we will act on it immediately.
MARGARET BRENNAN: A recent CBS investigation found Pennsylvania was one of the states where Homeland Security has been going door to door. They've been knocking on doors and asking about the immigration status of people who live there. What can you tell us about what DHS has been doing here? And did the administration coordinate with you as governor in any way?
GOV. SHAPIRO: No. And I want to make very very clearly the Pennsylvania State Police does not do DHS's work for them. Does not do ICE's work for them. We do not ask immigration status. In fact, when ICE came here and tried to bully their way into building two massive detention centers here in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, one in Berks County, one in Schuylkill County, I fought back and won and drove those detention centers out of Pennsylvania.
MARGARET BRENNAN: How many non-citizen voters did you find?
GOV. SHAPIRO: Well, what they said was that there were, whatever the number was, over a thousand people. So we said, great, tell us who they are, so we can check their status. They never told us who they were, and so it is impossible for us to be able to check the people that they claim to have identified. I will tell you, we've got very, very strict guardrails in place, led by Secretary Schmidt, constantly making sure that the people who are on our voter rolls are legal, eligible voters. And if we find that someone is not, if a mistake was made in a county where someone was registering, as an example, we immediately get on that. We work with prosecutors to ensure that they are not in a position to cast a ballot. As I said, I was the chief law enforcement officer of this Commonwealth. I prosecuted election fraud. It was a handful of cases. By the way, some were Republican, some were Democrat. None of it impacted any elections. But still, we can't allow that to happen here in our Commonwealth. And what I would ask of the Trump administration is, instead of sending me a press release, send me actual evidence, actual data, and we will review it promptly.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you did speak recently with Philadelphia Inquirer's editorial board, and you told them that you think President Trump and his allies are going to try and stop votes from being counted.
GOV SHAPIRO: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You also said you expect Speaker Johnson to make efforts to delay seating new members if Republicans lose the majority. Why are you raising these concerns now? And do you think at all that you might be undermining faith?
GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah. Well, respectfully, I was answering their question as to whether or not I thought the Trump administration would take steps to try and undermine our elections. So just to offer some context to that, and I did issue those answers, and I'll tell you why. Because I have lived through this before with the Trump administration. Back in 2020, I was the attorney general, and Trump lost the election here in Pennsylvania and tried to undermine the counting of the vote. In fact, he and his enablers sued me 43 different times to try and throw out the votes of certain Pennsylvanians. Heck, even my opponent went to court to throw out the votes of people in Bucks County. I won every single one of those cases. Went 43 and 0, Trump went 0 and 43. And so we are prepared should they try to do that again this time. In fact, we put together a task force more than a year ago when Trump began to hint at the idea that he would once again take that tack. So we are prepared in the courtroom. Should they go forward and try and undermine the right to vote. Now, more recently, we've seen further evidence of this president trying to undermine the right to vote in signing that bogus executive order, trying to make it so people here in Pennsylvania and across America couldn't vote by mail. I sued him. I won, and we protected the right to vote. So again, this was A) in response to a question, and B) based on a history of dealing with a guy who is constantly trying to undermine the right to vote here in our Commonwealth.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So I want to ask about you. Brian Fitzpatrick, who represents Bucks County, Republican here in Pennsylvania, describes you as a good man, a friend. He said you're smart, competent. He said he thinks you're going to run for president. And Senator Chris Coons, who was just here earlier, of Delaware said a Democrat. If you win Pennsylvania, you win the whole presidency. It's a good argument for you as a candidate. It's a Republican, It's a Democrat speculating. Are they wrong to speculate like that?
GOV. SHAPIRO: Well, I wouldn't be focused on speculating. I'd be focused on these midterms, which is all I'm focused on. You know, we talked here today not just about my re-election, but the fact that I'm working hard to elect four more Democrats to Congress to tilt the balance of power, take the gavel away from Mike Johnson, working hard to win a trifecta here in Harrisburg, something that hasn't been done since 1992. We have some gerrymandered state senate districts, but I'm hopeful that we're going to be able to get that done this time. So my focus has only been on these midterms, both getting myself reelected, but importantly providing a check on this president, a check to his his chaos, his cruelty, and his corruption, and to show that here in Pennsylvania, when you run on a GSD Democratic platform, that you can win up and down the ballot.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you are close to winning re-election. You said you're focused on the midterms, but how soon after you're going to make a call on your own presidential run?
GOV. SHAPIRO: I appreciate the confidence you have, or Brian has, or Chris has, but the reality is—
MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm just talking about the polls.
GOV. SHAPIRO: I always run like I'm 20 points behind. I'm running through the tape. I'm on this bus for 10 days, crisscrossing this Commonwealth. I showed up in a district yesterday that I think Donald Trump won with about 80% of the vote in the last presidential election. I take absolutely nothing for granted. I'm competing everywhere for the support of certainly Democrats, but Republicans and Independents as well.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you're laying out an agenda that would require some time to achieve.
GOV. SHAPIRO: I'm not sure I follow your question.
MARGARET BRENNAN: If you win re-election in this position now to be governor, to get everything done you want to get done, do you have to serve the whole term?
GOV. SHAPIRO: Well, I'm going to focus on getting done what I've pledged to get done here, and continuing to listen, see, and do, and make a lot of good things happen for the people of Pennsylvania as their governor.
MARGARET BRENNAN: People like me are just going to continue to ask you.
GOV. SHAPIRO: Well, and you're welcome to ask. And look, I'm humbled that you would ask that question. I'm humbled by the responses the senator and the representative gave you. But the only thing I'm focused on is here in Pennsylvania, winning up and down the ballot.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So when you spoke to the editorial board recently, you said six people were recently charged in the past nine months. They reported as making terroristic threats or ethnic intimidation against you or your family. You've said it has—it's weighed on you.
GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: What did you mean by that?
GOV. SHAPIRO: You know, a year and a half ago, my family and I finished celebrating our Passover Seder with the community. And you know someone broke into the governor's residence, threw Molotov cocktails throughout the home, destroyed about a third of the residence, and was running through the residence with a metal hammer that he said he was going to use to beat me to death when he found me. And he's behind bars now for the next 50 years. But since that time, even more people have threatened me and my wife, our family. Threatened us based on how I worship, and it weighs on you, certainly, to know that there are people out there trying to do you harm. But I would also tell you, it motivates me to keep doing what I do to not let the bad guys win, to not let those—
MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean, you look at this campaign right now, some of the rhetoric in states out now- Ohio, in Michigan, it's downright hateful.
GOV. SHAPIRO: It's dangerous. It's dangerous. It's hateful.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean, how do you get rid of that? How do you lower that?
GOV. SHAPIRO: I think what you do is- is try and lead by example, as we all here- as we are trying to do here, as I am trying to do here. Try and bring back kindness in the face of the cruelty that we see from this president. I've got profound differences from the person I'm running against, from the president and others, but I don't think engaging in cruelty is the answer. I think it makes everyone less safe. But what I was saying in response to your question a moment ago, it weighs on me, but- but it doesn't control me. In fact, my family and I met before, you know, we decided to run for re-election, and everybody agreed, can't let the bad guys win. We've got to keep going forward. You got to stand up against the hate. You got to lead by example, and you got to try and bring some decency back to this country.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I want to get to some of the politics here in Pennsylvania in a moment, but I want to ask you quickly about what is happening in Alaska. The Justice Department has now issued subpoenas to people believed to be connected to what the New York Times reported was the Democratic effort to stack Alaska's Senate ballot with candidates to siphon off votes. I know you must have been following this story. The Democratic candidate said she had no knowledge of the scheme. What do you think this does to election integrity, and do you think that this undermines Democrats' argument that they are the party trying to protect election integrity?
GOV. SHAPIRO: I've been focused, obviously, a lot more on Pennsylvania than Alaska, but what we're seeing from Trump is not super different from what we have seen from him here in Pennsylvania- trying to prejudge an outcome, file a bunch of lawsuits to silence the voices of the voters before they've had their say, and he's already showing that he is going to go to court should the result not be what he wants. Because what Trump doesn't like is when someone thinks different than you, or votes different than you, or has a different perspective than you- he tries to go to court to silence those voices.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But in terms of what has been reported by the New York Times, as one Democrat said to me, "may not be illegal, but it looks like dirty pool." Does it look like "dirty pool" to you? I mean, if you saw something like that in this state, you were an attorney general.
GOV. SHAPIRO: I- yeah, well--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Would you try to prosecute?
GOV. SHAPIRO: You're asking- respectfully, I think you're asking two different questions. Is there something illegal here, or is there something that seems sort of political?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
GOV. SHAPIRO: I don't know enough to be able to weigh in on this, but what I do know is that- to weigh in with any new information- I want to be clear, happy to answer your question. But what is clear to me is that Donald Trump tries to use the Justice Department to silence people who disagree with him, to try and silence the voices of those who might make a different choice in the ballot box than he would want.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But I can't imagine you condone these kind of tactics on the Democratic side.
GOV. SHAPIRO: I'm not engaged in it, I'm focused on these races here in Pennsylvania.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Let's talk about Pennsylvania. This state is in the midst of one of the worst measles outbreaks the United States has seen in three decades. In this county, a school here had to close for a day earlier this month--
GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: --because of a confirmed case of measles. This is highly transmissible. How do you get this under control?
GOV. SHAPIRO: We've got five deaths in Pennsylvania. 1,500 people sickened by measles, a disease that was eliminated in the year 2000 in the United States of America, and it's come roaring back, largely because of vaccine misinformation and disinformation promoted by quack conspiracy theorist RFK, who Donald Trump has now put in charge of our nation's healthcare system. Now, here in Pennsylvania, I believe in making sure people have access to the information, that there is vaccines available to them, it is a personal choice if they wish to get it. But what is critically important is that they hear from an actual medical provider, an actual medical expert, not RFK, who can explain that the MMR vaccine, that's the measles vaccine, is highly effective, and the best way to protect yourself against this measles outbreak. Make no mistake; you can draw a straight line between the nonsense that RFK has been spewing for years and now his work as the leading public health official in this country, and people getting sick here in my state and across the country. How do we get control of it--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
GOV. SHAPIRO: --now, it's the second part of your question. You do what we're doing here in the Commonwealth, bringing all of our healthcare partners together, and working to provide actual medical information to people in our Commonwealth, and making sure they get access to the vaccine, and encouraging them to take it. Now, here's some data for you. Typically, our Department of Health, working with our healthcare partners, would vaccinate around 25,000 people a month. Since the measles outbreak and my encouragement, and Dr. Bogen, our health secretary's encouragement to get vaccinated, we're now up to 55,000 vaccines being administered a month. So, Pennsylvanians are doing what we do best: coming together, looking out for our neighbors, and trusting science- something RFK continually tries to undermine.
[STOP DOWN]
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you clashed with HHS Secretary Kennedy in September, pretty publicly. You had a back and forth over what happened, what was driving the measles problem in the state. The CDC now recognizes three measles-associated deaths. That's fewer than the five--
GOV. SHAPIRO: Right.
MARGARET BRENNAN: --that your state health department has seen. You just accepted CDC help. Do you have any regrets about how you handled this?
GOV. SHAPIRO: No, and respectfully, that's not accurate. First, RFK denied that anyone died here in Pennsylvania. Literally poked his finger in the eye of these families here in Pennsylvania.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, he disputed deaths due to the measles or--
GOV. SHAPIRO: No, first he said- respectfully, first he said I fabricated it. First he said I lied about it, which we didn't. We know these people died. It's been confirmed not just by our state health department, but also by independent coroners. Then they tried to play games with the number of deaths, and you correctly point out that he's only acknowledged three of those deaths. As it relates to working with CDC, we've had people embedded here from CDC in our state Department of Health before the measles outbreak, and we did accept one additional person that they were asking us to accept.
MARGARET BRENNAN: An Intelligence Service Officer, right?
GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah, one- one person to help with tracking. By the way, this isn't like they're sending 1000 people here to vaccinate folks. It was one additional person, and we gladly accepted them and CDC had been here for, you know, again prior to this outbreak. The fact that RFK claims that we're lying about this, he's doing that because it doesn't fit his narrative. Remember, he's the guy who went to Lancaster, the epicenter of this outbreak, and said, "You don't need the vaccine. Just take a bunch of chicken soup, and you'll be fine."
MARGARET BRENNAN: You're talking about before he was HHS Secretary?
GOV. SHAPIRO: This guy- this guy is not fit to be the head of public health in this country. He's not a health expert. He's not a doctor, and he preaches fabricated--
[STOP DOWN]
GOV. SHAPIRO: Look, he is not qualified to serve as America's top public health official. He is not a health expert, and he is constantly undermining public health here in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania and across the country. He's unfit to lead. Donald Trump should remove him, and that will help all of us do a better job of beating this disease that was eliminated in the United States back in the year 2000, but has come roaring back sadly because of his vaccine misinformation and disinformation campaign.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But do you worry at all that the degree to which this has now become a political fight or the politicization of health will make it that much harder--
GOV. SHAPIRO: To be clear--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --for you to persuade people to go get the shot, that are so--
GOV. SHAPIRO: Not at all. Not at all. RFK politicized this. RFK is playing games with this. And in fact, if you look at the work we're doing here in Pennsylvania, it's working. We went from vaccinating about 25,000 people a month to over 55,000 people a month because people trust actual public health experts here in Pennsylvania, not the nonsense that is being spewed by RFK Jr.

Saudi-led coalition launches operation to ‘neutralize’ Houthi military resources in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:29:33 UTC
00:29:33 KST

Mohammed Al Ragawi and Rania Abushamala
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
The Saudi-led coalition said Sunday that it had carried out a military operation to “neutralize vital resources” used by the Houthi group to support its war effort and strengthen its military capabilities, particularly ballistic missiles and drones.
Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said in a statement that the operation took place Sunday morning following continued Houthi attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
The coalition’s joint forces command had monitored the Houthis’ “continued use of vital resources to support their war effort and bolster their military capabilities, especially ballistic missiles and drones,” he said.
Al-Maliki said the continued attacks posed a direct threat to civilian lives and the safety of civilian infrastructure.
The operation sought to “neutralize” resources used by the group to carry out repeated attacks and threaten the security of Saudi Arabia and Yemen, as well as shipping lanes in the southern Red Sea, he added.
The statement did not identify the targeted locations or specify the nature of the resources it said had been neutralized. It also provided no details on casualties or material damage.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
Since Oct. 5, Yemeni government forces have launched Operation “Dawn of Yemen” to restore state institutions from Houthi control and retake the capital, Sanaa.
Military escalation between government forces and the Houthis resumed in July, killing and wounding thousands and displacing more than a quarter of a million people, according to UN reports.
The escalation ended a period of relative calm that had prevailed in Yemen since April 2022, while the humanitarian crisis has worsened amid continued fighting and displacement.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

News
Bulgaria to seek €2 billion from the EU over attacks on ships in the Black Sea
Sunday 1 November 2026 16:25
Sunday, 1 November 2026, 16:25
PHOTO Gerb Party/BTA
Font size
Nine countries could receive additional financial assistance from the EU during the next programming period to offset losses incurred as a result of the war in Ukraine. Bulgaria will seek EUR 2 billion in compensation for attacks on merchant vessels in the country's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
This became clear following a visit to Varna by a delegation of Members of the European Parliament, which included Andrey Novakov and Emil Radev, as well as fellow MEPs from Germany, Austria and Poland. The funding earmarked for Bulgaria for the 2028–2034 period amounts to EUR 22.3 billion.
“Bulgaria should receive more funding to compensate farmers, transport operators, the tourism sector and everyone else suffering from a war they did not start”, Andrey Novakov said.
The purpose of the European Parliament delegation's visit to Varna was to gain first-hand insight into the situation in the Black Sea region following drone attacks on merchant vessels, BTA reported.

Ukraine calls allowing return of Russian ice hockey teams to world championships ‘unacceptable’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:27:02 UTC
00:27:02 KST

Kanyshai Butun
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
Ukraine’s foreign minister on Sunday called the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport to allow Russian ice hockey teams to return to the world championships “unacceptable.”
“By letting Russian hockey back, CAS is staining the ice with Ukrainian blood,” Andrii Sybiha wrote on US social media platform X.
Sybiha stressed that Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities continue and argued that the return of Russian teams would give Moscow the international legitimacy it seeks.
“Russia has not stopped its war. It has not stopped killing Ukrainians. It has not stopped its relentless attacks on our cities. So what exactly has changed to justify the return of its national ice hockey teams to international competition?” he said.
Sybiha urged the international sporting community and Ukraine's partners to oppose Russia's return to international competitions, saying there can be “no business as usual” as long as the war continues.
He also called on governments to deny Russian players entry to their territories, adding that Russia's actions must have consequences, including in international sport.
“This shameful decision must be reversed,” he said.
On Friday, the CAS overturned a ban on Russian teams, ruling that the arguments put forth by the sport's global governing body to justify their suspension, including “safety, security and other concerns,” are “not supported by sufficient evidence.”
The decision followed an appeal by the Russian Ice Hockey Federation against the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), which barred Russian teams from competitions following the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022.
In July, the IIHF extended the restrictions through the 2026-27 season, citing concerns about the safety of competition participants.
The IIHF maintained that its restrictions were necessary to protect participants and safeguard the integrity of its competitions.
“While the IIHF respects the authority of CAS and will act in accordance with its ruling, the outcome does not remove the concerns that informed its assessments,” the federation said.

Iran inflicted at least $5 billion in damage on US military bases: WSJ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:26:07 UTC
00:26:07 KST

Iran inflicted at least $5 billion in damage on US military bases: WSJ
Iranian missile and drone strikes have inflicted at least $5 billion in damage on U.S. military bases across the Middle East, according to a sweeping Wall Street Journal investigation that offers the fullest public picture yet of what the war on Iran has cost American forces in the region.
The Journal's analysis, drawing on satellite imagery, Iranian military statements and interviews with U.S. officials, identified 274 damaged structures at 24 installations with an American military presence during the war's first six months.
The investigation found that Iran increasingly targeted buildings where American troops live and sleep, showing an improved ability to sequence attacks and strike with greater precision.
While the Pentagon has priced the damage to bases at a minimum of $5 billion, according to U.S. officials familiar with the matter cited by The Journal, a separate person briefed on the cost said the figure could reach as high as $15 billion.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies, which reviewed the Journal's findings on damaged buildings, estimated that reconstruction alone would top $4 billion, a figure that excludes replacing the equipment and systems housed inside.
Those repairs come on top of the war's overall cost, which stood at $47.1 billion as of Oct. 16, according to a document viewed by The Journal.
According to an Associated Press analysis, Iran's strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East focused on early-warning systems before hitting aircraft and buildings, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage.
The AP independently verified damage to American targets using satellite imagery from multiple providers and spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or have firsthand knowledge of what was hit. The AP found that, through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment.
The Journal also said the human toll has also mounted. More than 20 U.S. service members have died in activity related to the war since it began on Feb. 28, according to Defense Department data, and more than 400 were wounded before a temporary ceasefire collapsed in July. After that, the government stopped publishing casualty figures specific to the conflict.

After inconclusive elections, Israeli opposition seeks control of Knesset
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:25:55 UTC
00:25:55 KST

Zein Khalil and Rania Abushamala
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
The Israeli opposition is seeking to take control of the Knesset (Israel’s parliament) by replacing the Knesset speaker and advancing legislation targeting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, local media reported on Sunday.
Preliminary results from Tuesday's parliamentary elections gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, against 48 for the opposition and 19 for Arab parties.
Neither bloc has so far secured the minimum 61 seats needed to form a government.
Walla news website, citing unnamed sources, said opposition leaders are planning a four-way meeting at the home of opposition leader Yair Lapid, who heads the Yesh Atid party.
In addition to Lapid, the meeting will also bring in Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, Avigdor Lieberman of Yisrael Beiteinu and Yair Golan of the Democrats.
The meeting is intended to develop a joint plan to translate the election results into political power inside the Knesset, the outlet said.
The meeting will be held ahead of consultations scheduled to begin on Nov. 4 at the residence of President Isaac Herzog to determine who will be given the first mandate to try to form a government.
Opposition sources told Walla that Eisenkot has decided to accept the first mandate to form a government.
Shifting balance of power
According to Walla, another key date for opposition leaders is Nov. 10, when newly elected Knesset members are scheduled to take the oath of office.
The opposition plans to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, a move that could give it control over parliamentary business and allow it to try to pass legislation during the six weeks before the deadline for forming a government passes.
The opposition leaders are expected to discuss a consensus candidate for the post. Names being considered include Eisenkot, Lapid and Oded Forer of Yisrael Beiteinu.
The opposition also wants to advance a bill to establish an official commission of inquiry into the events of Oct. 7, 2023, Walla said.
The Israeli army has launched a deadly war on the Gaza Strip on Oct. 8, 2023, killing more than 74,000 people, injuring over 175,000 others and leaving the entire enclave into ruins.
The opposition also seeks to pass a bill that would bar anyone facing a criminal indictment from forming a government, even before a conviction.
Netanyahu, 76, is on trial on corruption charges, including bribery, fraud and breach of trust. He could face prison if convicted.
Opposition leaders believe that replacing the Knesset speaker could be an important first step toward shifting the political balance of power, even as negotiations to form a government continue, Walla said.
But carrying out the plan will require opposition leaders to agree on a candidate and secure enough votes to elect their candidate.
Eisenkot has repeatedly said he would not join a government with Netanyahu, even under a power-sharing arrangement in which they would rotate as prime minister.
Netanyahu has led a coalition of far-right parties since late 2022, widely described as the most right-wing government in Israel's history.
He has also been sought by the International Criminal Court since 2024 on accusations of of war crimes and crimes against humanity related to the war in Gaza.

Burnham ‘open’ to UK slavery apology, but not reparations: Why now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:24:08 UTC
00:24:08 KST

Burnham ‘open’ to UK slavery apology, but not reparations: Why now?
The UK PM’s statement comes as Commonwealth nations meet in Antigua and Barbuda.
The United Kingdom’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said his country is open to apologising for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade but ruled out reparations, which campaigners have for years called for.
Burnham wrote in an opinion article in The Guardian on Friday that Britain would also work on debt restructuring for the poorest countries, marking an historic turn in London’s stance.
The move comes ahead of a four-day summit starting Sunday of the 50-plus Commonwealth nations formerly colonised by Britain. The UK’s King Charles, who arrived in the Caribbean last week, is hosting the leaders in St John’s, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda.
“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” Burnham wrote, in what amounted to a personal apology.
Caribbean nations that have more forcefully demanded reparations in recent years said they expect more from Britain, while opposition Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has criticised Burnham’s move as “navel-gazing”.
Here’s what we know:
What was Britain’s role in slavery?
Transatlantic slavery lasted between the 16th and 19th centuries and saw some 12 million enslaved Africans torn from their homes and forcibly transported on ships to the Americas with the help of local warlords. Enslaved people were sold on plantations and as domestic workers, and their labour produced goods that built wealth in Europe.
Britain and Portugal accounted for about 70 percent of all Africans exported to the Americas, while France, Spain and the Netherlands also traded in significant numbers of enslaved people. Britain alone transported 3.1 million Africans to British colonies in the Caribbean, the Americas and other countries, according to its national archives. Only 2.7 million arrived, as many perished in treacherous sea journeys.
British abolitionists began campaigning against slavery in 1787, particularly in cities like Manchester. In 1807, Parliament passed the Slave Trade Act, essentially banning new enslavement. More than three decades later, in 1834, Britain banned slavery in its entirety, although the practice continued for several years.
Amid calls for accountability in 2006, then-Prime Minister Tony Blair expressed “deep sorrow” for Britain’s role in the slave trade, but fell short of apologising or speaking about reparations.
Why now?
Burnham’s apology came during Britain’s Black History Month and as the Commonwealth is meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.
In his article, the British prime minister said London wants to keep diplomatic and trade ties with its Commonwealth allies.
“In an increasingly divided and dangerous world, our family of nations in the Commonwealth is vital to our interests,” he wrote, adding that Britain “can seize opportunities for trade and economic collaboration”.
Britain will allow the most vulnerable countries to repay their debts over a longer period, he added, with former Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, who spearheaded the UK’s 1991 initiative to reduce debt for poorer countries, leading the charge.
What is the debate regarding apologies and reparations?
Since 2013, the Caribbean Community and Common Market (CARICOM) has called on Western countries involved to acknowledge their role and institute monetary reparations for slavery.
In recent years, those calls have grown louder, led by Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley.
Ghana, where around 10-15 percent of enslaved people were transferred from, has also played a major role and pushed a historic resolution at the United Nations in March that saw 123 countries vote to declare trafficking of enslaved Africans the gravest crime against humanity. All European nations abstained while the United States, Israel and Argentina voted against the measure.
Campaigners argue that there is a legal and moral case for financial payment and debt cancellations for the centuries of damage caused by enslavement. Those damages, they say, are evident in the structural inequalities that continue to plague countries where human capital was stolen from and those in the Caribbean that faced genocides after Europeans arrived.
They also point to the loss of lives, the erasure of cultures, the looting of artefacts in the colonial era that followed, and ongoing economic disparities and development challenges that see those nations struggle to access international financial institutions.
In June, Mottley announced a 19-point manifesto at a conference in Ghana, as Caribbean and African countries increasingly align to more strongly push their case. It called for a “full and formal apology”, monetary compensation from nations, but also institutions, including corporations and churches. It also called for technology transfer, education and healthcare funding, debt relief and economic development. The plan revised an earlier CARICOM 10-point plan.
“We live in a world today where people call out people for everything, for misogyny, for sexual assault, for all kinds of behaviour. But yet we have not found the moral courage to state unanimously across humanity that this grave crime against humanity that persisted for centuries ought to be declared so by all,” Mottley said at the conference.
Why are European nations not keen on reparations?
European nations, including Britain, argue that those crimes were committed long ago and that, as such, their people should not pay for them. Some also point to the role of local African chiefs who worked with the Europeans to kidnap and enslave people.
“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” Burnham wrote in The Guardian.
Instead, he said, the UK was “offering a structured dialogue” with those affected and debt restructuring.
France recognised slavery as a crime against humanity in 2001. In May, French President Emmanuel Macron said Paris should look into reparations, but did not make clear proposals.
In 2022, the Netherlands apologised for its role.
The Church of England, whose clergy also owned enslaved people, set up a fund of 100 million British pounds ($134mn) to cater to affected communities and to conduct further research into slavery’s legacies.
What are the reactions?
In a statement, Saint Lucia’s Prime Minister Philip J Pierre, who currently chairs CARICOM, said the organisation rejects the argument that Britain of today cannot be held responsible for slavery.
“Reparatory justice has never been about individual guilt. It is about the responsibility of states and institutions — and that responsibility does not expire with the passing of generations,” he said. Without repair, PM Burnham’s apology was “incomplete”, he added.
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama said he welcomed Burnham’s statement with “caution” and reiterated the need for a formal apology, targeted investments in several sectors, and an international commitment to “dismantle systemic racism and Afrophobia”.
Denis O’Brien, founder of the advocacy group The Repair Campaign, also said London “must stop obfuscating and give a full and formal apology now”.
The UK’s opposition Conservative Party leader Badenoch kicked against the move entirely in a post on X, and asked whether the descendants of African rulers involved would also be asked for reparations.
“There is no reason British taxpayers today should be held financially responsible for things that happened generations before any of us were born,” she said.
“Labour are already spending too much on Britain’s welfare state, now is not the time for Andy Burnham to be providing global welfare.”
Meanwhile, Bell Ribeiro-Addy, chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Afrikan Reparations, which endorses compensation, welcomed Burnham’s steps but said action was still “lacking”.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 2,100 Troops, 259 Vehicles, and 16 Artillery Systems in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 2,100 troops and hundreds of pieces of military equipment over the past 24 hours, bringing its total personnel losses since the start of the full-scale invasion to approximately 1,590,270, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on November 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff, Russia lost another tank, bringing its cumulative losses to 12,451, while two additional armored combat vehicles raised the total to 25,622.
Russian artillery losses increased by 16 systems, reaching 51,755, while two additional multiple-launch rocket systems brought the cumulative figure to 2,249. Air defense system losses remained unchanged at 1,730.
Ukraine also reported nine additional ground robotic systems destroyed, bringing the cumulative figure to 3,054. Another 944 operational-tactical UAVs were recorded as lost, pushing the total to 591,605.
Russian aviation losses remained unchanged at 452 aircraft and 356 helicopters. Cruise missile losses stayed at 5,140, while naval losses remained at 35 ships and boats and two submarines.
Another 259 vehicles and fuel tankers were recorded as lost over the latest reporting period, raising the cumulative figure to 168,739. Special equipment losses increased by one unit to 4,861. Fighting intensified across the front, with 264 combat engagements recorded over the past 24 hours, according to the General Staff’s morning operational update.
The heaviest fighting occurred in the Pokrovsk direction, where Ukrainian forces repelled 55 Russian attacks. Russian troops attempted to advance near Serhiivka, Molodetske, and Novopavlivka, as well as toward several other settlements.
Ukrainian forces also repelled 17 attacks in the Kostiantynivka direction, 13 in the Southern Slobozhanshchyna direction, and 10 in the Lyman direction. Nine additional Russian assaults were reported in the Huliaipole direction, while Ukrainian defenders repelled seven attacks in the Northern Slobozhanshchyna direction.
No Russian assault operations were recorded in the Kupiansk direction, while the situation in the Volyn and Polissia directions remained largely unchanged, with no signs of Russian offensive groupings being formed.
Earlier, on October 31, Ukrainian Neptune missiles and attack drones struck Russia’s Kamensky Combine rocket fuel plant in the Rostov region, setting a warehouse ablaze and damaging four production workshops. The facility produces solid rocket propellant for Russia’s Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems.

Protestors loot shops in Frankfurt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:17:00 UTC
00:17:00 KST

Protestors loot shops in Frankfurt
320,000 hold protests in France as police arrest 770
Protestors looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.
Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannons to disperse protesters who were targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles, BBC said on its website.
Thousands joined demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organized by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.
The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.
On Sunday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild newspaper that overnight police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris" in recent weeks and called for "harsh punishments" for rioters and looters.
Overnight, a large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.
Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organizers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.
Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".
She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favor of a fairer distribution of the burden."
On Saturday night Frankfurt police said "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre and that special police units had been deployed.
The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said.
Officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect. People also broke into other shops, stealing items like trainers.
Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended.
"We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard.
Police said the situation calmed down overnight into Sunday in the city.
Similar instances took place in other German cities.
In Cologne, police said officers were attacked near the main train station, with bottles thrown and a bicycle launched.
A smaller demonstration in the evening in Berlin - following larger protests in the day - resulted in 27 police officers being injured, and up to 56 people temporarily detained, Berlin police said.
In Hamburg, people dressed in black set off fireworks and set barricades on fire, with public broadcaster NDR reporting that 120 people were arrested.
The protests in Germany took place on the same day as other large-scale demonstrations in Europe.
In France, more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful protests in cities across the country, demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially in the education sector.
Thousands of police officers were deployed across the country, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests across France during the demonstrations on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said a police officer had been injured by a molotov cocktail and French prosecutors later launched an attempted murder probe.
Police in Paris said several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles.
French protest organizers, the Gilet Jaune, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".
France suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off.
Protests also took place in Italy, with some clashes between police and demonstrators in Rome and Turin.
In Portugal, police moved to clear a new tent camp that had been assembled after thousands marched to protest against a rental bill that they argue could worsen a housing crisis in the country, where house prices have more than doubled over the past decade.
Mostly young protesters have recently taken to the streets in a swathe of European nations: France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania.
While the specific demands vary from country to country, the protesters have largely focused on cost-of-living issues, such as access to housing, the quality of education and cuts to public services.

Marta Shahbazi had been on her way to collect the 2026 José Luis Gómez-Skarmeta prize for her "outstanding contributions to the study of the early stages of human development."
A researcher at the University of Cambridge has been named as one of at least 69 victims of a deadly train crash in Spain earlier this week.
Marta Shahbazi had been travelling to receive a prize for scientific excellence from the Spanish Society of Developmental Biology when the train she was on collided with another service near Urda in the province of Toledo on Wednesday.
Shahbazi was a group leader at the Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) and an affiliate assistant professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute.
In a statement, the LMB said it was "deeply saddened by the tragic death of our colleague Marta Shahbazi, Group Leader in the Cell Biology Division."
"Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist. Her death is a profound shock and a huge loss. Our thoughts are with her family, friends and colleagues at this extremely difficult time," it added.
News of her death was confirmed by the CiMUS research centre in Santiago de Compostela, which called her a "brilliant young researcher."
"The CiMUS community would like to express its support and deepest sympathies to our dear PI María José Alonso, following the death of her niece, Marta Shahbazi, in the railway accident that occurred on 28 October," the centre said in a post on social media.
Shahbazi had been due to arrive in El Rompido, Huelva, to collect the 2026 José Luis Gómez-Skarmeta prize for her "outstanding contributions to the study of the early stages of human development."
According to the Society of Developmental Biology, her research focused on "understanding how the human embryo organises itself during early development and how cells make decisions that determine their fate," while her laboratory work centred on embryonic implantation.
The train collision occurred when a high-speed Renfe service slammed into a stationary Iryo train outside of Urda, south of the Spanish capital Madrid.

Midterms reopen debate over dominance of wealth in US politics

Midterms reopen debate over dominance of wealth in US politics
American democracy is drifting away from principle of ‘one person, one vote’ to a system of ‘one dollar, one vote’
TEHRAN – Campaign spending during the current U.S. midterm election cycle has become the subject of intense political and media debate.
It has brought back into focus a fundamental dilemma facing the United States. How can political equality among the public be preserved when a small group of wealthy individuals enjoys extraordinary financial power to fund election campaigns and shape public debate?
While this is hardly a new issue, it has taken on sharper dimensions in 2026 amid soaring campaign expenditures and the growing influence of major donors and special interest groups.
Approximately $8.9 billion was spent on the 2022 midterms. Approximately $11.2 billion for the 2024 presidential election and a projected $11.6 billion for the 2026 midterms.
Donald Trump’s presence on the political scene has played a particularly striking role in highlighting this contradiction.
Having entered the presidential race in 2015, attacking the influence of major donors and presenting his personal wealth as a guarantee of his political independence, Trump went on to benefit, in the 2024 election, from massive financial backing provided by several billionaires and political action committees, most notably those associated with Elon Musk.
The 2026 midterm elections have since witnessed record levels of spending, both during the primary season and in the campaigns leading up to the election.
An investigation published by The New York Times revealed that at least $1 billion in funds linked to donors whose identities remain undisclosed had flowed into the 2026 elections.
The newspaper reported that tens of millions of dollars from unknown sources had been used in efforts to influence Democratic primary contests, particularly in Michigan and Minnesota.
Michigan offered a striking picture of the unprecedented escalation in campaign spending, with expenditures on political advertising exceeding $850 million over the election cycle. Notably, Abdul El-Sayed secured the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate despite being significantly outspent by his rival, Haley Stevens, who received substantial backing from outside funding groups, most prominently the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).
Further evidence of the concentration of campaign financing emerged in a Washington Post report revealing that the 50 largest donors and lobby groups contributed approximately $2.77 billion during the current election cycle. Elon Musk alone accounted for around $446 million, most of which went to political action committees supporting Republican candidates.
The controversy, however, has extended beyond the sheer volume and sources of campaign money to questions about the effectiveness of regulatory oversight.
The Brennan Center for Justice has raised concerns about the Federal Election Commission’s declining ability to carry out some of its core responsibilities, after the agency spent more than a year without the quorum required to make certain official decisions.
The center warned that this situation heightens the risks associated with opaque campaign financing, particularly as spending on digital advertising and social media influencers continues to expand, areas that do not always fall under the same disclosure and oversight requirements as traditional media.
The current elections have therefore exposed a debate that goes beyond record-breaking campaign expenditures.
At its heart lies a more fundamental question: how freely can political parties and voters choose their representatives when wealthy individuals and corporations possess enormous financial resources with which to influence the electoral process?
This dilemma was explored earlier by legal scholars who offer a critical examination of the American democratic experience, focusing on the contradictions between the principles underpinning the country’s political system and the way those principles are put into practice.
Among the central issues examined are economic and social inequality, the influence of money and private interests, equality in the political process, the role of constitutional and judicial institutions, and the gap between America’s proclaimed democratic values and its conduct on the international stage.
Specifically addressing campaign finance, criticism has been aimed at the U.S. Supreme Court’s 1976 decision overturning key restrictions on campaign spending because they violated the constitutional protection of freedom of speech. That ruling became one of the legal foundations of the campaign finance system that operates in the United States today.
Many critics argue that the distinction between political contributions and campaign expenditures opened the door for wealthy individuals, corporations, and lobbying groups to exercise disproportionate political influence, thereby threatening the principle of equality on which a supposedly democratic society is based.
The arguments closely echo warnings voiced by prominent American thinkers, writers, and politicians who represent a broad intellectual and political current that views the growing influence of money as a genuine threat to the electoral process and to the principle of political equality.
Among the most prominent is Nobel Prize-winning economist Joseph Stiglitz, who has drawn a direct connection between wealth inequality and disparities in political influence.
He has warned that American democracy is drifting away from the principle of “one person, one vote” and moving closer to a system of “one dollar, one vote.” In Stiglitz’s analysis, wealth and political power reinforce one another in a self-perpetuating cycle: wealth enables its holders to influence legislation and public policy, while those very laws and policies, in turn, help consolidate their fortunes and political influence.
Along similar lines, a widely cited academic study by researchers concluded that economic elites and business-oriented interest groups exercise considerable influence over American policymaking, while ordinary citizens have little independent influence on political outcomes.
Studies have sparked widespread debate about whether the political system genuinely reflects the will of the majority or instead grants economic elites influence far beyond their share of the electorate.
These warnings and academic findings have emerged against the backdrop of a lengthy judicial and legislative trajectory that has progressively expanded the scope for unlimited political spending, building on the foundations established by the Supreme Court’s 1976 ruling.
Since 2010, a series of Supreme Court rulings, beginning with Citizens United v. FEC, has dismantled campaign finance restrictions, granting lobby groups, wealthy individuals, and political parties greater freedom to spend money on elections. The result is a system that increasingly treats political spending as constitutionally protected free speech rather than a force to be regulated.
U.S. politics has become a system where money speaks louder than votes, and wealth, not the majority, ultimately decides who rules.

An “inspiring” University of Cambridge scientist died in the Spanish train collision on Wednesday that killed at least 69 people.
Dr Marta Shahbazi, an affiliate associate professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute and a group leader at the city’s Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB), was travelling on one of the trains involved in the crash near Urda in Toledo province.
The LMB said the mother of two had recently won the Spanish Society of Developmental Biology’s scientific excellence prize. She had been due to be presented with the award during its conference in El Rompido, Andalucía.
In a LinkedIn post, the LMB said it was deeply saddened by her death, which was “a profound shock and a huge loss”, adding: “Martha was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies.”
It said she was a role model who had written eloquently about balancing her family and career, describing herself as a “mother scientist”.
Dr Roser Vento-Tormo, a group leader at the Wellcome Sanger Institute outside Cambridge, wrote: “Marta Shahbazi was a beautiful person: a close collaborator, a treasured friend, and an inspiration to me both as a scientist and as a mother.
“As a scientist, we shared so many dreams. We co-supervised two students together, and I cannot describe how much joy it was to work alongside her. Some of our work will still be published in the coming months, and anyone who reads it will feel the passion she poured into everything she did …
 
“My thoughts are with her family. Anyone who knew Marta could see how deeply they were a unit, and how much they meant to her.”
The Center for Research in Molecular Medicine and Chronic Diseases (CiMUS), based in Santiago de Compostela, Spain, paid tribute to Shahbazi as “a brilliant young researcher”.
The disaster was Spain’s second high-speed rail crash this year. Both collisions occurred on the line between the central city of Madrid, Spain’s capital, and Seville, in the Andalucía region in the south of the country.
Three days of national mourning were observed from Thursday. The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, described the incident as a “tragedy” and has promised an investigation.

‘Some photos imprint upon us’: How our Saturday magazine puts together special issues about world-changing photographs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:00:14 UTC
00:00:14 KST

Can photographs still exert power in an age when millions of pictures are taken and shared every minute, and when a viewer’s first response is to question whether an image is even real?
Every few months, a team of editors on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine puts together a special photography package in print and digital formats. It features photographs that don’t just stop the scroll, they have also prompted the rewriting of history books. They are the kind of images that have changed the world in some way or radically shifted people’s perceptions.
Each issue has a particular theme. Earlier this month, the magazine featured photographs that have changed how we view masculinity – from a 1950 portrait of Marlon Brando in a white T-shirt to a paparazzi shot of David Beckham in a sarong and a bare-chested Vladimir Putin on horseback. Previous issues have focused on photographs that have reshaped sport, forced people to confront the reality of the climate crisis and upended the world of fashion.
Beyond the impact each image had back when it first came out, they still feel powerful and affecting today – reminding us how great photography can command a kind of reverence and stillness in the viewer. “Working on these issues, you realise that there’s something about the power of the images that’s elemental,” says Rebecca Liu, a commissioning editor on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine. “Some photos imprint upon us before we even can think about them. They just immediately hit our bloodstream.”
The first special issue featured protest images that have prompted social or political change. It was initially conceived as a one-off feature in 2022 amid protests in the US that year against the overturning of Roe v Wade and demonstrations against police brutality. But the feature resonated so strongly with readers that it spawned an occasional series.
That regularity means the process of putting the issues together is now fine-tuned, though not without its own drama and headaches. “Sometimes on the day of going to print we’re waiting on two or three final things to be confirmed,” says Rebecca. “It’s a massive act of organisation and coordination and a real collective effort with a lot of moving parts.”
Selecting which pictures to include involves tapping the collective minds of picture editors and journalists on the magazine and across the Guardian. Different colleagues will have different criteria. How to weigh up a photograph’s social or political impact against its technical importance to the medium? Should it be an image that, in itself, has changed the world or a photograph of a world-shifting moment?
“Everyone working on the magazine has a different take on it,” says Louis Siroy, the magazine’s deputy picture editor. “Some editors will ask how a particular photograph shaped society; what does it mean? Whereas I might be asking what are the important photographs or photographers that fit into that theme or category.”
For example, the first special issue about protest photography didn’t just include the famous image of a protestor standing in front of a tank in Tiananmen Square, it also included a less famous but equally powerful photograph of a boy sitting on the shoulders of relatives above the sea of soldiers’ helmets. Taken by the photographer Dario Mitidieri, the image was suggested by Louis. “That to me is a great photograph, and I was trying to bring something that wasn’t necessarily the image people are familiar with,” he says. “Hopefully these selections inspire people to value and appreciate the breadth and power of great photographs.”
By drawing on colleagues’ different perspectives and experience, each special issue sheds unique light on its theme. “So while the selection can’t possibly be comprehensive and definitive, it’s still authoritative,” says Rebecca.
Other images included in the initial protest photography issue include the famous picture of US athletes John Carlos and Tommie Smith raising their fists in a black power salute during a medal ceremony at the 1968 Olympics. There are also several photographs of protesters facing off against riot police or soldiers, including a powerful image of a young girl in Santiago, Chile, during a 2016 demonstration marking the anniversary of the country’s 1973 military coup.
One of the most time-consuming challenges involves obtaining the rights to publish the images. “Some of the greatest challenges involve finding the right copyright holder for some lesser-known photographs,” says Caroline Hunter, the magazine’s picture editor.
Even well-known photographs can present hurdles. “Sometimes you have to get permission from the subject of the photo as well as from the photographer, particularly when it comes to photos of celebrities or fashion,” explains Louis. “It can get really hard to track down the person you need. For instance, the masculinity special featured a famous second world war photo of a US aeroplane gunner that was taken by the photographer Horace Bristol, who is now deceased. It took some time to contact the photographer’s son Henri in California and explain the context in which we wanted to use the photo. And even when dealing with well-known photographers, it still involves negotiating the rights for editorial use rather than commercial use.”
Another challenge that can arise is the quality of the photographs. “We have to ensure the image is large enough or good enough quality to reproduce, especially for very old images that previously existed only as prints,” says Caroline. “Works by famous and art photographers often have specific rules around usage, so it’s important to ensure that we keep within their guidelines. We had a really good response from photographers after our recent photo special marking America at 250. I think this was because there were so many great, iconic images from seminal photographers.”
The team also has to decide the best layout for the print and digital editions – which images to give prominence to, how they might best fit together, and the range of black-and-white and colour images. Maggie Murphy, the magazine’s art director, experiments with different layouts, sometimes on a screen, sometimes with printouts strewn across the desks.
As well as the images, a huge amount of work goes into the words. Each special issue includes a short guest-written essay, and each photograph has an extended caption about that particular picture’s significance or backstory.
The journalists who are commissioned to write these captions undertake extensive research. For example, the masculinity issue includes a famous 1970 advertisement depicting a pregnant man, for which the journalist tracked down the original campaign’s photographer, who is now 98. “I encourage original interviews and research wherever possible,” says Rebecca. “We want the words to illuminate something about the picture and for people to learn things. That’s not something you necessarily have to do for a 150-word caption, but we want to do it because the editorial component is so important to us at the Guardian.”
Researching the captions also reveals something about the nature of photography. “It really shows the importance of not just taking an image at face value,” says Rebecca. “I’m always surprised by what you discover when you look into things. You might find a complicated backstory behind the person who is photographed – perhaps their ambivalence about being pictured, for instance.”
The same applies to the thought that goes into the introductory essays. The novelist Anne Enright wrote perceptively about how women are captured on camera, for better or for worse, in her introduction to an issue that featured photographs that have changed the way society sees women. “As you look at a Kardashian selfie, consider how many rules had to be broken to get her to this moment of self-commodification,” writes Enright.
The masculinity issue contains an accompanying essay by the poet and novelist Luke Kennard, who reflects on how the images seem to capture extremes of masculinity, with little in between: “To judge from our media, one would think we were either waifs or muscle-men… Even the bang average is barely represented.”
Rebecca noticed that gap in representation back when the team was initially selecting which photographs to include in the issue. “I remember thinking, where are the other male bodies? It was difficult to find any – at least with the quality and artistry that we look for in these stories. You’d Google the words ‘dad bod’ and you’d just get screenshots of Seth Rogen and grainy paparazzi shots of celebrities on the beach.”
The team is very mindful of the power of images to subtly reinforce or subvert people’s preconceptions. “Working on these issues makes us reflect on how much we subconsciously absorb images,” says Rebecca. “And how they feed into our imaginations.”
