Study finds a specific emotional route from feeling humanized to political compromise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:00:03 UTC
00:00:03 KST

When voters believe their political rivals see them as full human beings rather than mindless brutes, they become more willing to negotiate, compromise, and work across party lines. New research published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin suggests this effect works mainly by reducing feelings of disgust toward the opposing party, and that it is especially relevant when people feel political divisions threaten the fabric of society.
In many Western democracies, political disagreements have increasingly become personal and moral clashes. Psychologists call this affective polarization, the tendency of partisans to distrust and dislike members of the opposing party, not merely disagree with their policies. Rather than seeing opponents as fellow citizens, partisans often view them as morally corrupt or even less than human.
Part of this hostility may stem from meta-perceptions, or beliefs about how one’s own group is viewed by outsiders. Partisans often experience meta-dehumanization, the belief that the other party sees them as subhuman, irrational, or animalistic. A 2020 study of American political partisans found that Democrats and Republicans both substantially overestimated how much the other side disliked and dehumanized them, and these exaggerated beliefs predicted stronger support for spiteful actions that harm democratic norms.
Feeling dehumanized can set off a cycle of retaliation. A 2016 series of studies on intergroup conflict indicated that people who feel dehumanized by a rival group tend to dehumanize that group in return and support aggressive policies against it.
The reverse belief, known as meta-humanization, may help repair relations between groups. In a 2021 study of Muslims and non-Muslims in Canada and the United Kingdom, the same two researchers behind the new paper found that perceiving the other group as seeing one’s own group as fully human reduced prejudice and encouraged friendly contact, even when tensions were high. But a 2024 study in post-conflict Kosovo found that feeling humanized by former adversaries did not reliably make people more willing to negotiate with them, suggesting the effect may depend on how immediate and threatening the division feels.
Less is known about how feeling humanized changes people’s emotions toward their opponents. Moral emotions shape how people treat other groups. Anger typically stems from perceived injustice and sparks confrontation, disgust is tied to a sense of moral contamination and motivates avoidance, and empathy encourages perspective-taking and care.
To examine which of these emotions explains the benefits of meta-humanization, and how they interact with fears that society is fracturing, the researchers conducted five experiments with a total of 1,541 participants in the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada. The work was led by Melissa Pavetich, an assistant professor at Heriot-Watt University in Dubai and a member of the SOCIAL Impact Lab, together with Sofia Stathi of the University of Greenwich.
“A lot of research on polarization focuses on what partisans think of each other,” Pavetich told PsyPost. “We were interested in a different question: what people believe the other side thinks of them.”
“We wanted to know whether that belief matters in politics, and if so, why,” she said. “In particular, we wanted to identify the emotional route that links it to whether people are willing to reconcile.”
Across all five experiments, the researchers statistically controlled for frequency of out-partisan contact on a 1-to-5 scale, accounting for how often participants already encountered members of the rival party in everyday life. The first study, conducted in February 2021 via the online platform Prolific, included 353 British adults (average age 36, 61.1 percent female, 79.9 percent White), split between Conservative Party supporters (52.0 percent) and Labour Party supporters (48.0 percent).
Participants were randomly assigned to read fictional social media posts, styled as messages from Twitter (now X), supposedly written by supporters of the rival party. In the meta-dehumanization condition, the posts referred to the participant’s party as “animals and brutes lacking in self-control,” whereas in the meta-humanization condition, the posts described them as “sophisticated.”
After reading the posts, the British participants rated their feelings and attitudes on 7-point scales, where higher numbers meant stronger agreement or intensity. Both Labour and Conservative supporters who read the humanizing posts reported lower anger, lower disgust, weaker intentions to hurt or humiliate opponents, and greater comfort with close social contact, such as having a doctor from the opposing party.
Among Labour supporters, those in the meta-humanization group reported lower disgust (an average of 2.14 vs. 3.21 in the meta-dehumanization group), lower anger (1.94 vs. 2.61), lower hostility (2.05 vs. 2.55), and less desire for social distance (3.50 vs. 3.75). Conservative supporters showed a similar pattern when comparing the humanizing and dehumanizing conditions for disgust (1.68 vs. 3.09), hostility (1.82 vs. 2.32), and social distance (2.77 vs. 3.05), alongside a pronounced drop in anger (1.64 vs. 2.77).
Because the first experiment did not include a baseline control group or a measure of empathy, the authors designed Study 2a to add both elements while testing how moral emotions connect to broader political reconciliation and whether perceived threat to social cohesion alters the process. Threat to social cohesion refers to the worry that political divisions are eroding shared community values, mutual trust, and collective belonging. The remaining four experiments were preregistered on the Open Science Framework, with materials and data posted publicly.
Conducted one week before the 2024 U.S. presidential election, Study 2a recruited 301 American Republicans (average age 47, 63.8 percent female, 83.1 percent White) through Prolific. Participants first rated their perceived threat to social cohesion on a 7-point scale, reacting to statements such as “The values in our society have gone seriously off track,” and were then randomly assigned to read humanizing X posts from Democrats, dehumanizing X posts from Democrats, or no posts at all in a control group.
They next rated their anger, disgust, and empathy toward Democrats on 7-point scales, and evaluated how civilized and evolved they considered Democrats to be on a slider from 0 to 10. Finally, they completed 7-point scales measuring affective polarization and four conciliatory attitudes: support for cross-party negotiation, willingness to compromise, support for bipartisan teamwork, and openness to future contact with Democrats.
Republicans who read humanizing posts felt much more humanized by Democrats (an average of 5.31 out of 7) than those in the control group (3.91) or the dehumanizing group (1.52). Statistical modeling indicated that feeling humanized by Democrats lowered Republicans’ disgust, which in turn led them to view Democrats as more human and civilized, predicting lower affective polarization and higher support for negotiation, compromise, teamwork, and contact. This indirect pathway held across all outcomes under moderate perceived threat to social cohesion, compared to both the meta-dehumanization and control groups, and extended to high threat for several outcomes. The pathways through anger and empathy were not statistically significant.
Study 2b mirrored this setup in the same pre-election context in the United States, examining 302 American Democrats (average age 46, 66.6 percent female, 79.9 percent White) reading fictional posts attributed to Republicans. Democrats in the meta-humanization group scored an average of 5.73 out of 7 on feeling humanized by Republicans, compared to 3.43 in the control group and 1.70 in the meta-dehumanization group.
Just as with Republicans, disgust was the sole emotion that linked meta-humanization to viewing the opposing party as human and adopting more conciliatory attitudes. This chain reaction through reduced disgust held most consistently under moderate perceived threat to social cohesion, where it predicted lower affective polarization and greater support for negotiation, compromise, and contact compared to both other conditions (and teamwork compared to the control group), while extending to low threat for several conciliatory outcomes when compared to the meta-dehumanization condition and to high threat when compared to the control condition. The pathways through anger and empathy were not statistically significant.
To test whether these patterns held outside the intense atmosphere of a U.S. presidential election, the researchers replicated the experiment in Canada using Qualtrics Panel. Study 3a surveyed 310 supporters of the Conservative Party of Canada (average age 46, 55.4 percent male, 73.1 percent White), evaluating their reactions to supporters of the rival Liberal Party. Canadian Conservatives who read humanizing posts felt more humanized by Liberals (an average of 4.55 out of 7) than those in the control group (3.81) or the dehumanizing group (2.92).
Consistent with the American findings, feeling humanized reduced disgust and increased how human Canadian Conservatives viewed Liberals to be, which in turn predicted more conciliatory attitudes. This indirect effect emerged under moderate threat to social cohesion for conciliatory outcomes such as compromise and teamwork and extended across all outcomes, including reduced affective polarization, when perceived threat was high. The pathways via anger and empathy were not statistically significant.
Study 3b completed the series by surveying 300 supporters of the Liberal Party of Canada (average age 49, 51.5 percent male, 71.1 percent White) regarding their attitudes toward Canadian Conservatives. Liberals in the meta-humanization condition reported feeling more humanized by Conservatives (an average of 4.64 out of 7) than those in the control group (3.91) or the meta-dehumanization group (2.64).
Among Canadian Liberals who reported low to moderate threat to social cohesion, feeling humanized by Conservatives again reduced disgust and increased outgroup humanization, predicting lower affective polarization and stronger support for negotiation, compromise, teamwork, and contact compared to both other conditions. Uniquely in this fifth experiment, heightened empathy also served as a parallel bridge toward reconciliation alongside reduced disgust, though only when comparing the meta-humanization group to the control group under low to moderate threat.
Taken together, the five experiments suggest that learning one’s political group is respected as human promotes compromise mainly by disarming disgust rather than by soothing anger or sparking empathy. Because disgust functions as a psychological barrier that motivates people to avoid perceived moral contamination, lowering disgust removes a major obstacle to treating political opponents as fellow citizens worthy of dialogue.
“How we think the other side sees us shapes how we treat them,” Pavetich explained. Across the five studies, she said, “when people feel seen as human, they feel less moral disgust toward the other side, and that makes room for reconciliation.”
“I expected empathy to do much of the work, since it’s so often discussed as the path to bridging divides,” Pavetich noted. “Instead, disgust stood out as the main pathway. This suggests that reducing a negative moral reaction may matter more than building positive feelings.”
The researchers also noted a difference in how perceived threat operated across political camps: the pathway through reduced disgust was most consistent at moderate threat across groups, extending to high threat among conservative participants and to low threat among liberal and Democratic participants. The authors suggest that because conservative voters are often particularly attuned to threat cues, seeing goodwill from the opposing party when threat is elevated may be especially reassuring to them or create a psychological tension that resolves by warming toward the outgroup.
As a competing explanation, the authors note that low threat may simply allow people to feel safe and open enough to benefit from humanizing messages, whereas high threat can push people into a defensive posture that blocks reconciliation.
“We were also interested to find that these processes were strongest when people saw a moderate level of threat to social cohesion,” Pavetich said. “Feeling some stake in the conflict seems to make how you’re perceived matter more.”
“The effects were small to moderate,” Pavetich added. “Effects like this won’t erase partisan hostility on their own. They were consistent across countries and outcomes, though, and they come from people’s beliefs about the other side.”
“That matters because those beliefs are often inaccurate and can potentially be corrected,” she said. “Small shifts in how people think they’re seen could add up across many everyday political interactions.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Although the researchers experimentally manipulated the social media posts that participants read, participants’ emotional reactions, their humanization of the opposing party, and their willingness to compromise were all measured at the same time through survey questions, meaning the study cannot prove that a drop in disgust directly causes someone to become more open to political negotiation.
“These findings don’t mean people should simply be told ‘the other side sees you as human’ whether or not it’s true,” Pavetich cautioned. “Meta-perceptions work best when they reflect genuine signals from the other group.”
“Perceived threat was measured as an existing attitude rather than manipulated experimentally, so we’re more cautious about interpreting its role,” she added. “Finally, humanization was measured with a widely used but debated scale, the Ascent of Man scale. Future work using a range of measures would strengthen the conclusions.”
In addition, the experiments took place in three Western nations where politics largely revolves around two dominant rival parties, meaning the findings might not apply to countries with multi-party coalitions or entrenched violent conflicts where partisans have little desire to reconcile. Future work could test whether combining humanizing messages with face-to-face collaborative problem-solving helps partisans build lasting trust across the political aisle.
“One direction I’m especially keen to pursue is the role of disgust itself,” Pavetich said. “Disgust is closely tied to how people judge right and wrong, so I want to understand why it emerged as the key pathway here. Does it reflect seeing the other side as morally contaminated or as violating core values? And can that response be reduced directly?”
“Alongside this, I’m examining how intergroup contact interacts with meta-humanization,” she added. “We’re testing whether the quality and type of contact, both face-to-face and through media, strengthens the benefits of feeling humanized. I also plan to extend this work beyond Western two-party systems to multi-party contexts and regions that are underrepresented in this research.”
“I’d love readers to remember that polarization isn’t only about disagreement over issues,” Pavetich concluded. “It’s also about feeling looked down on. Signs that we see the other side as fully human, even when we disagree strongly, may do more to lower the temperature than winning the argument.”
The study, “Bridging the Political Divide: Meta-Humanization and Moral Emotions Shape Partisan Reconciliation,” was authored by Melissa Pavetich and Sofia Stathi.

‘I’ve Developed Thirst for Life’ – Wounded Ukrainian Veteran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Serhiy Hrachov has already bought the wedding rings. They are waiting for the moment when he and the woman he divorced can marry again. Between their separation and that decision lie five battlefield injuries, more than 30 operations and a struggle to recover his sense of purpose. The Ukrainian veteran who once feared becoming a burden to his family now speaks enthusiastically about their future. “I love my family, my family loves me, and I’m doing something I really enjoy,” he tells me.
It is a remarkable place to have reached. Serhiy is one of hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians facing the task of rebuilding their lives after military service. Many return from some of the war’s deadliest battles carrying physical and psychological wounds, trying to recover a sense of normality and find their place again.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine’s government estimates that veterans and their families will number five to six million once the war is over. For many, the support they need will extend far beyond physical rehabilitation. It will mean overcoming isolation, feeling understood even by those closest to them, and finding a renewed sense of purpose in civilian life.
Listening to Serhiy, I am reminded that courage can be required long after a soldier’s last battle. Now 40, he was born in Pavlohrad, a mining town in Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk region. He attended the National Mining University, where he met his future wife. They married after graduating and have two children.
Drones and Neptune Missiles Strike Kamensky Rocket Fuel Plant
Before the full-scale invasion, their relationship had broken down. Hrachov worked in Germany during 2021, returning to Ukraine in January 2022. Reports of Russian atrocities in Bucha and Irpin convinced him that he must fight. He imagined looking into his daughter’s eyes and explaining that he had been too frightened to defend her.
“I couldn’t see how I could do anything else.”
Twice, the army rejected him because he lacked military experience. On his third attempt, he was accepted. After basic training in July 2022, he joined the 53rd Separate Mechanised Brigade, named after Volodymyr Monomakh. He had been assured that further training would follow with his brigade. Instead, he says, he was in Bakhmut the next day.
Imagining war and experiencing it proved very different. “Everyone thought of themselves as heroes, as fearless,” he recalls. “But imagining it is one thing. Finding yourself right in the middle of it is another.”
His first injury came when shrapnel broke fingers on his hand. After a month of treatment he returned. Further mortar fragments struck his leg, then his side and arm. Some still remain in his body.
Each return became more frightening. He knew his luck could not hold indefinitely. After his third injury, he approached his commander and admitted that he could no longer cope.
The officer was surprised. Serhiy had proved himself and was regarded as fearless. He, however, challenges the comfortable idea that brave men feel no fear. Hrachov felt it keenly and continued to serve as his injuries were insufficient to secure his discharge.
He says it took about six months to accept that he might not survive. “When you understand that tomorrow might never come for you, and you come to terms with that, it becomes a little easier.” By then, he was commanding a unit. Responsibility for his men proved harder to bear than fear for himself.
On the Avdiivka front, an explosion left him severely concussed. A young comrade sitting nearby was killed. Serhiy had selected the men accompanying him to that position. He knows someone else might have died had he chosen differently. That knowledge still haunts him.
“I still dream about him.”
On March 20, 2023, a tank round struck the wall behind Serhiy as he watched the perimeter from an abandoned farm. His right arm and leg were almost severed. It took two hours to reach the first stabilization point.
He thought he would die. Yet he remembers the pain of his earlier smaller injuries more clearly than those hours with his limbs hanging by skin and tendons. Adrenaline, he believes, carried him through.
Evacuated through Karlivka and Pokrovsk to intensive care in Dnipro, he faced 18 months of treatment and rehabilitation. Surgery in Germany gave him an artificial elbow joint.
When his former wife and children visited him in hospital, he did not know whether his arm and leg could be saved. He told her they were divorced and she owed him nothing. She and the children should live their own life. He did not want to become a burden.
Her answer was firm: he was being foolish, and she did not want to hear such talk again.
For the first six months of rehabilitation, Serhiy thought constantly about returning to his unit. He felt he had left something unfinished. Military life, for all its dangers, offered clarity: an order, a task, men who depended on one another. Outside it he faced uncertainty and misunderstanding.
After his discharge in August 2024 he withdrew. There was alcohol. He did not want to leave home or see anyone. “It feels as though your body has returned, but your soul has stayed there.”
He worried about his injuries, employment and the future. He questioned why he had survived when others had died.
Eventually, he began seeking help through veterans’ activities and retreats. An announcement from Dnipro’s veterans’ policy department introduced him to Future Reclaimed, a British-Ukrainian program addressing moral injury. Initially, sitting in a circle reminded him of a religious gatherings or an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting. But over three days, he noticed that he and the other participants were beginning to feel better. He returned, then trained as a facilitator.
“Every time you give it a name, it becomes a little easier,” he says of discussing painful experiences. Veterans lead the sessions for fellow veterans, with a psychologist present should anyone need support. Nobody is compelled to speak.
Some have remained silent for years, fearing that their experiences will distress their families or change how loved ones see them. One participant told Serhiy that, for the first time in two years, he felt as though he was back among his own unit.
The connections continue afterwards. Participants remain in contact, and some have even started businesses together.
Serhiy now travels helping other veterans with Future Reclaimed across Ukraine delivering the program. His prescription for better veterans’ support is practical: start in hospital. “Someone should explain the assistance available to these veterans immediately and maintain contact, helping each wounded soldier find a way forward,” he says. Serhiy speaks from experience where he spent months lost and uncertain before discovering opportunities that already existed.
Asked what Britain could offer, he suggests funding, specialist treatment and rehabilitation, alongside visits that give veterans a chance to experience life beyond war.
His own recovery includes competitive rowing. He captains Dnipro’s veterans’ team, which recently won a Ukrainian competition in Odesa and, he says, finished second at a European championship in Greece last year. Finding money to attend competitions remains difficult. The team now pays its own way.
He has also begun a master’s degree in public administration.
His family remains in western Ukraine, where the children attend school in person and enjoy their activities. His son plays guitar, his daughter plays volleyball. Serhiy is reluctant to disrupt the childhood they have recovered in safer areas of Ukraine. He visits whenever possible, and continues to plan a second wedding with the woman who is both his former and future wife.
People sometimes look at his injuries and express pity. He wishes they understood how he feels now. “I’m genuinely enjoying life more than I ever have,” he says. “I’ve developed a thirst for life.”
He speaks of rediscovering his family, reassessing his priorities and finding work that gives him satisfaction. None of this erases what happened to him or the comrades he remembers. It shows what can become possible with support, companionship and the opportunity to contribute.
Serhiy Hrachov volunteered to protect his family and country. Today, helping other veterans rebuild their lives, he continues that service. His plans for the future carry as much meaning and valor as the wounds he carries.
Lord Ashcroft KCMG PC is an international businessman, philanthropist, author and pollster. For more information on his work, visit lordashcroft.com. Follow him on X/Facebook @LordAshcroft.

RAF Chinooks Take to Sea with HMS Queen Elizabeth on Exercise Hathi Pol
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:00:00 GMT
00:00:00 KST

Royal Air Force Chinook crews and support personnel embarked on HMS Queen Elizabeth (QNLZ) to undertake Exercise Hathi Pol, a key maritime aviation training activity that sustains critical operational capability for future global missions.
Led by 27 Squadron, with support from personnel from 7 Squadron, the exercise saw two RAF Chinook helicopters and 80 personnel operating from the Royal Navy's flagship in the Western Mediterranean and Eastern Atlantic region.
The training focused on delivering Deck Landing Qualification (DLQ) and Embarked Aviation Qualification (EAQ) training, enabling aircrew to gain or revalidate the specialist qualifications required to operate safely and effectively from maritime platforms.
The exercise provided valuable opportunities for engineers and support personnel to develop and maintain the unique skills needed to sustain aviation operations at sea, strengthening the RAF's ability to deploy rapidly alongside our partner services wherever required.
Operating a large support helicopter from a moving aircraft carrier presents a distinct challenge, demanding close integration between RAF and Royal Navy personnel. Through joint planning, flying and engineering activity, the exercise enhances interoperability between the Services and reinforces the UK's ability to project air power from the maritime domain.
Memorably, Ex Hathi Pol coincided with the (221st) anniversary of the Battle of Trafalgar. On 21 October, QNLZ was sailing approximately 100 miles west of Cape Trafalgar, close to the waters where Nelson secured his famous and final victory in 1805.
"27 Sqn’s deployment on Ex Hathi Pol marked a significant milestone for both the Sqn and HMS Queen Elizabeth. Chinooks from 27 Sqn were the first embarked aviation to operate from QNLZ in over two years, providing an important opportunity for aircrew and Ship’s Company to work together and refresh their embarked maritime experience.
Departing the familiar training areas of the English Channel, QNLZ sailed south towards  Gibraltar. During the passage, Chinook aircraft were dispatched ashore to embark the essential equipment required to support at-sea replenishment from a UAS, the first fixed-wing aircraft operated by the ship since her return to sea." 
Squadron Leader Grahame, Deputy Officer Commanding 27 Sqn RAF Odiham
Detachment Commander on Ex Hathi Pol
The recent embarked training contributes directly to maintaining Defence readiness for a range of future operations, including Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief missions, Non-Combatant Evacuation Operations and wider contingency tasks around the world.
The activity reflects the RAF commitment to maintaining a Warfighting Ready force, investing in its people and strengthening the UK's integrated Defence capability through close collaboration with the Royal Navy.
By training in the maritime environment, Chinook crews gain experience operating from sea-based platforms, extending the flexibility and reach of the UK's heavy-lift helicopter force.
The exercise reaffirms the RAF remain ready to respond to emerging crises and support operations across the globe, demonstrating the value of a highly trained, adaptable and integrated Joint Force capable of delivering effect wherever and whenever required.

Russia's FSB says minor detained over park attack threat after US tip-off
Nov 1 - Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) said on Sunday that a Russian minor had been detained over a threat to carry out a terrorist attack in a Moscow park following a tip-off from the United States, news agency Interfax reported.
On Saturday, the FSB said it had received information from the US through established partner channels about preparations for an attack in Moscow and was taking appropriate measures.
The minor had posted photographs of himself on TikTok wearing tactical clothing and a balaclava, holding an object that looked like an automatic weapon, as well as photographs taken at Moscow's Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve with the caption: "I found a place," Interfax cited the FSB as saying.
"We are grateful to the American side for providing the information," the security service was quoted as saying in its statement.
It said officials searching the minor's home found the clothes and accessories seen in the social media posts, while his phone showed a subscription to a neo-Nazi channel on the app Telegram and “a significant number of searches concerning terrorist attacks, mass killings and other acts of violence,” according to Interfax.
Russia's Investigative Committee is considering what legal or procedural action to take, the FSB said.
Tsaritsyno, a palace museum and park complex in southern Moscow, was temporarily closed on Saturday following the US tip-off. REUTERS

Belgium Delivers First Tripartite-Class Minehunter to Bulgaria – Ukraine Operates the Same Type of Vessel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:54:56 UTC
23:54:56 KST

Belgium has transferred the BNS Bellis, a Tripartite-class minehunter, to the Bulgarian Navy.
Naval News reported the handover, citing Belgium’s Ministry of Defense.
The BNS Bellis is the first of four Belgian Tripartite-class minehunters scheduled for transfer to Bulgaria.
The handover ceremony took place on October 30, 2026, at the Zeebrugge Naval Base in Belgium. Following the flag change, the vessel was given a new name: Briz.
The transfer is part of a trilateral Memorandum of Understanding between Belgium, the Netherlands, and Bulgaria. Under the agreement, Bulgaria is set to receive a total of seven minehunters: four from Belgium and three from the Netherlands.
Belgium and the Netherlands are gradually retiring their Tripartite-class minehunters and replacing them with newer vessels under the Replacement Mine Counter Measures (rMCM) program.
The transfer also benefits Ukraine. Under the agreement, Bulgaria will help train Ukrainian crews operating Tripartite-class minehunters.
This will allow the countries to share operational experience with Tripartite-class vessels and strengthen cooperation between their navies in the Black Sea region.
Furthermore, amid recent developments and increasingly frequent Russian attacks on civilian vessels near Bulgaria, the minehunters could also be used to protect territorial waters and conduct patrols in open waters.
A joint mine countermeasures task group comprising Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey will monitor the security of underwater cables, gas pipelines and other critical subsea infrastructure in the Black Sea.
In addition to searching for naval mines, the task force will also monitor and help protect underwater infrastructure.
In June 2025, Belgium and the Netherlands transferred two Tripartite-class minehunters to Ukraine: the former BNS Narcis and HNLMS Vlaardingen, which were renamed Mariupol and Melitopol, respectively. A third vessel, the former HNLMS Makkum, joined them later.
Displacement: 550–605 tonnes, depending on the variant.
Length: 51.5 m.
Beam: 8.96 m.
Draught: 3.6–3.8 m.
Hull: Fiberglass-reinforced plastic (FRP), with a low magnetic signature to reduce the risk of triggering magnetic mines.
Propulsion system: One Werkspoor-Wärtsilä diesel engine rated at approximately 1,900 hp, two electrically driven active rudders, and a bow thruster.
Maximum speed: 15 knots (approximately 28 km/h).
Range: Approximately 3,000 nautical miles at 12 knots.
Crew: 30–45 personnel, depending on the variant.
Sonar equipment: Hull-mounted sonar to detect and classify naval mines.
Mine countermeasures equipment: PAP 104 remotely operated underwater vehicles (ROVs) for mine inspection and neutralization.
Additional equipment: Mine detection and identification systems, diving equipment, and a decompression chamber.
Small arms: Up to three 12.7 mm machine guns, depending on the national configuration.

Serbians mark railway disaster that led to rise of victorious student movement
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:54:05 CET
23:54:05 KST

By Fedja Grulovic
NOVI SAD, Serbia, Nov 1 (Reuters) - Tens of thousands of people gathered at a Serbian railway station on Sunday to mark the anniversary of a deadly roof collapse that gave rise to the protest movement that toppled longtime President Aleksandar Vucic in an election a week ago.
Crowds converged from across the city of Novi Sad on the main train station, where the concrete awning crashed down shortly before noon on November 1, 2024, killing 16 people.
Mourners observed 16 minutes of silence before laying wreaths, flowers and candles near the site.
“On a personal, emotional, and social level, I hope for a collective healing,” said Zorana Sijan Oborina, a student supporter.
The disaster, which struck at a station renovated under a China-backed high-speed rail project, ignited Serbia’s massive nationwide anti-corruption protest movement, culminating in last week’s election victory by a student-led bloc.
Protesters saw the collapse as symptomatic of corruption under Vucic. The protests forced resignations, including that of the construction minister, a government reshuffle and eventually snap elections.
Prosecutors indicted 13 people over the collapse, but pretrial proceedings have stalled. The defendants denied any wrongdoing.
“I hope we have finally realised that we shouldn’t wait … years to change what is bad, especially when it costs human lives,” said Jelena Trajkovic, 32, an academic from Novi Sad.
On October 25, the Student List, a group that includes academics, professionals, farmers, actors and activists chosen by student assemblies, secured 141 seats in the 250-member parliament, according to a preliminary tally. Final results are due in coming days and not expected to change the outcome.
Vucic, standing as the candidate for prime minister from his SNS party at the end of his presidential term, acknowledged defeat and left office. A presidential election is expected before the end of the year.
(Reporting by Fedja Grulovic and Jana SimovicWriting by Aleksandar VasovicEditing by Peter Graff)

Somali piracy resurges as Iranian vessel seized carrying 23 crew
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:54:00 UTC
23:54:00 KST

Somali piracy resurges as Iranian vessel seized carrying 23 crew
Maritime security monitors warned that the ship could become a floating base for further attacks
Somali pirates have seized an Iranian fishing vessel carrying 23 people, the European Union’s Maritime Security Centre Indian Ocean (MSCIO) said, warning that the ship was approaching a commercial shipping lane and could become a floating base for further attacks.
The Azini was hijacked on Thursday between the coastal towns of Bandar Bayla and Hafun in northeastern Somalia, a maritime security officer with the Puntland Maritime Police Force said on Sunday.
The officer said that 12 pirates seized the vessel, which was carrying 21 Iranian crew members and two Somali security guards. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn’t authorised to speak with the media.

France launches ‘attempted murder’ probe after petrol bomb attack on security forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:53:00 UTC
23:53:00 KST

France launches ‘attempted murder’ probe after petrol bomb attack on security forces
- France has opened an attempted murder probe after petrol bombs hit security forces during Paris protests against rising living costs.
- Prosecutors said around 15 gendarmes and police were targeted; one officer suffered burns, and no suspect has been arrested.
- More than 770 people were arrested nationwide, while shop damage was lower than before, though retailers fear harm before the holiday season.
AI generated
PARIS – France has launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at security forces during a weekend protest in Paris, prosecutors told AFP on Nov 1.
On Oct 31, clashes erupted in the capital and some other cities after hundreds of thousands of people staged a third weekend of protests against soaring living costs.
The Paris police prefecture said that several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles, including a Molotov cocktail. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has decried an “extraordinary” level of violence from some rioters.
“Explosive devices were thrown at around 15 gendarmes as well as police officers,” the prosecutor’s office said on Nov 1.
Gendarmes are military police officers who are part of the French armed forces.
Prosecutors said an investigation had been opened for “attempted murder of persons vested with public authority”.
Dramatic images, including AFP photos and video, showed a homemade incendiary device exploding at the feet of a security officer in eastern Paris, engulfing his lower body in flames.
An assessment of the injured was ongoing, prosecutors said, adding that the reported injuries include second-degree burns.
Initial complaints were expected to be filed on Nov 1.
The gendarme struck by the Molotov cocktail told French television of the burns he suffered, describing “skin that stings” and a “rain” of projectiles thrown at his unit.
Fewer shops damaged
No suspects “have been arrested at this stage in connection with the incident”, the prosecutor’s office said, adding that investigators were working to identify those responsible.
Far-right leader Marine le Pen said those responsible for the firebomb attack must be “punished with the utmost severity”, in a post on X, describing images of the officer in flames as “unbearable”.
More than 770 people were arrested during weekend protests in France, the Interior Ministry said on Nov 1. It added that there had been “no major incidents” late on Oct 31.
The number of shops damaged on the sidelines of the Oct 31 protests was significantly lower than during previous weekends, with some 20 businesses affected, according to France’s Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).
But CCI France voiced concern about the impact of the protests on retail activity ahead of the year-end holiday season, a peak period for businesses. AFP

Third man sent to prison after stealing sound systems from murdered Nova festival victim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:51:01 UTC
23:51:01 KST

The Beersheba Magistrate’s Court sentenced San Lucian Tevel on Sunday to 28 months in prison for helping steal two high-value sound systems from the Nova music festival massacre site just two days after the Hamas-led October 7 attack three years ago.
The systems belonged to a company co-owned by Matan Lior and his business partner, Amitai Rahum. Lior was murdered at the festival after helping evacuate festival-goers under fire.
Judge Amir Doron also fined Tevel NIS 10,000 and ordered him to pay NIS 20,000 in compensation to Lior’s parents and NIS 10,000 to Rahum. The court ordered the forfeiture of Tevel’s vehicle, which was used in the offenses. Time already served in detention in the case will be deducted from his prison term.
Tevel pleaded guilty under an amended indictment to two counts of aiding aggravated theft. His sentence followed those of the other two men involved, Ram Shahin and Daniel Hasson, who were sentenced by the same court on October 7, the third anniversary of the Hamas-led massacre attack.
In Sunday’s judgment, Doron found that Tevel had provided logistical support without which the criminal plan could not have been carried out. He rented a trailer, gave Shahin his vehicle and connected those involved, knowing the circumstances surrounding the thefts.
The judge said Tevel’s active assistance bordered on full participation in the offenses.
Tevel received a more lenient sentence than co-others involved
Doron nevertheless took account of Tevel’s admission and his post-traumatic stress disorder, placing his sentence at the bottom of the 28-to-36-month range the court set for his conduct. The judge said his condition did not justify a sentence below that range.
Tevel also received suspended prison terms of 12 months and six months, applicable to specified further property or fraud offenses committed within three years of his release.
“Behind every hearing and every postponement is a bereaved family, forced to gather its strength and confront again what was done to their son’s property after he was murdered,” Lior’s father, Ofer, said in a statement released Sunday.
“Nothing will bring Matan back. We fought so that those who harmed what he left behind would be held accountable, and to preserve his dignity and memory.”
The Nova Tribe Community Association said: “Over the years, we have stood alongside the Lior family in its struggle to make Matan’s voice heard and demand justice. Matan worked to save lives, and while his family was contending with its terrible loss, some chose to steal his life’s work. We will continue to stand alongside the family after the legal proceedings end and work to preserve the memory and dignity of Matan and all those murdered.”
Two other men charged with theft, deception, concealment
Shahin, whom the court described as the driving force behind the scheme, was sentenced last month to seven years in prison, less time already served in detention. He was also fined NIS 60,000 and ordered to pay NIS 75,000 to Lior’s parents and NIS 25,000 to Rahum.
The court found that Shahin arranged for a truck driver to collect the first sound system while falsely claiming that he was retrieving equipment belonging to his missing friend.
After a tracking device on a generator alerted police and officers seized the truck and equipment, Shahin falsely presented himself as Lior’s business partner and persuaded a police investigator to release the truck. The second sound system was subsequently taken from the festival site.
Shahin argued that he had initially intended to safeguard the equipment and return it to its owners. The court rejected that account, finding that his repeated acts of deception and concealment established his intention to permanently deprive the owners of the systems.
Hasson, whose role the court found was more limited, pleaded guilty under an amended indictment after some witnesses had testified. He tried to sell the stolen equipment while falsely presenting himself as its owner.
He was sentenced to three years and four months in prison, less time already served in detention, and fined NIS 30,000. The court also ordered him to pay NIS 40,000 to Lior’s parents and NIS 15,000 to Rahum.

Daniel Silva's newest novel 'Ransom' proves to be a superb and timely spy thriller - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:50:53 UTC
23:50:53 KST

Followers of superb thriller writer Daniel Silva have relished the 25 novels he has produced since 2000, featuring his Israeli spy hero, Gabriel Allon.
The series began with The Kill Artist. Allon, raised on a kibbutz by Holocaust-survivor parents, is studying art in Jerusalem. In 1972, veteran spymaster Ari Shamron recruits him to hunt down those responsible for the murder of Israeli athletes at the Munich Olympics. The assignment derails his intended career as a painter.
He subsequently trains in art restoration in Venice, and over the years restoration becomes both his professional cover and a genuine vocation, pursued alongside clandestine operations for Israeli intelligence.
In 1991, a car bombing in Vienna killed his young son and left his first wife, Leah, badly wounded. Allon retreats to Cornwall to restore paintings but is repeatedly drawn back into intelligence work.
Followers of Allon will be delighted with the 26th adventure
Lovers of page-turner novelist Silva, and followers of Allon, will be delighted with the 26th adventure, Ransom. The plot, replete with thrills, surprises, red herrings, and unexpected twists and turns, is set firmly in the contemporary world.
References are made to US President Donald Trump’s bid to annex Greenland, and even to King Charles III’s brother Andrew, formerly the Duke of York, who was stripped of his royal titles over his association with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The war in Ukraine is dragging on and, to counter European support for the Ukrainians, Russia is engaged in covert operations against the West. Hi-tech remote-controlled drones feature strongly – even a drone as tiny as a mosquito, used to spray nerve agent in a target’s face.
Silva’s plot is as ingenious as ever. Beautiful socialite Alice, married to multi-millionaire Edward Knight, is kidnapped, and Allon is cajoled into rescuing her. He negotiates with the kidnappers and has brought their original vast ransom demand down to an acceptable figure when Knight intervenes, Allon is hijacked and, as they say, the plot thickens.
From then on, surprises abound, and the reader is kept glued to the page. The action moves effortlessly across Europe. England, Spain, Italy, Switzerland, Austria, Finland, Denmark, and the Netherlands all feature – even the Luxembourg embassy in London. International corruption is unmasked.
The highlight is an ingenious Russian drone attack on major locations in London, including the prime minister’s residence at 10 Downing Street, as he hosts a European summit.
Who is author Daniel Silva?
SILVA WAS born in Kalamazoo, Michigan. Both his parents were school teachers. When he was about seven, the family moved to California. He studied journalism at California State University and international relations at San Francisco.
This combination of journalism and international relations provided a foundation for the two principal strengths of his subsequent fiction: an interest in the practical realities of political events, and an ability to turn complicated international affairs into accessible narratives.
Silva generally keeps his private life separate from his public literary identity, but he has disclosed that he is married to Jamie Gangel, an American television journalist who has worked for CNN and NBC News, and that they have twins – a girl and a boy.
By a strange coincidence, his Israeli hero, Allon, and his new wife Chiara also have a girl and a boy. Allon joins his family in Venice following a nail-biting climax played out on the cliff-tops in the farthest reaches of Cornwall, very close to Land’s End.
Silva provides an Author’s Note to round off the novel. In it, he lets his readers into the secret of what is true and what is invented in the book.
The political circumstances in which the novel is placed are real, and Silva concludes with his own thoughts about this world and suggests one way, perhaps, of redeeming it.
In chapter 37 of Ransom, he writes, “I describe the French president, the German chancellor, and the prime ministers of Denmark and the United Kingdom as the leaders ‘of what was once fondly known as the free world.’
“It is fair to ask, though, whether ‘the free world,’ or even ‘the West,’ still exists. The collapse of the postwar liberal order was brought about by too many factors to list in this small space, but one element cannot be denied.
“For more than two decades a vengeful and revanchist Vladimir Putin, with the help of his intelligence services, has worked tirelessly to destroy the old order and replace it with one led by Moscow.
“Perhaps it is time, as my fictitious British spymaster Graham Seymour suggests, to take the gloves off and launch a hybrid war against Russia – with stealth and low cunning and, yes, a touch of wickedness. Turnabout, as the old saying goes, is fair play.”
A clue, perhaps, as to Allon’s 27th exploit?■

www.a-mid-east-journal.blogspot.com

(GABRIEL ALLON BOOK #26)
By Daniel Silva

By excluding Arab citizens, Netanyahu's rivals may hand him another term - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:50:49 UTC
23:50:49 KST

As Likud once again emerged as the largest party, someone who had hoped for change told me that he felt as though he were living through the aftermath of Yitzhak Rabin’s assassination in 1995.
For others, the results brought back memories of the 1996 election, when Israelis went to bed with exit polls predicting that Shimon Peres would become prime minister, only to wake to the news that Benjamin Netanyahu had won.
The disappointment and despair are understandable, but those making the comparisons are mistaken. Unlike in those two cases, this time there is a way out.
Rabin’s assassination can be viewed as a specific, if catastrophic, event: the result of a determined gunman and a security failure, both of which reflect mostly on themselves.
There was, of course, a broader political climate, but had the security failure not occurred, the outcome would have been different.
This time, the results tell us something else. October 7, the rising cost of living, Israel’s growing international isolation, the threat of crippling sanctions – none of these appears to have changed the minds of Likud loyalists who continue to support Netanyahu. Unlike Rabin’s assassination, this is not a one-off occurrence. It is a phenomenon.
The second precedent is also different. Netanyahu’s victory in 1996 was narrow but clear. In a direct election for prime minister, there can be only one winner.
This time, however, all it takes is one look at the results to see that we are dealing neither with the finality of death nor with the winner-takes-all logic of a two-candidate contest. Any reasonable person should understand that Netanyahu’s bloc has not won a victory.
What have we witnessed, then? Proof that the man who has presided over failures in virtually every sphere has excelled at one thing: defining the terms of public debate.
That debate presents us with a Netanyahu bloc, an opposing bloc, and a third group that supposedly belongs to neither. Arab Israelis are treated as a separate, detached entity, disconnected from everyone else and from everything happening in this country.
It is bad enough that, even while people who personally suffered at the hands of racists in the Diaspora are still living among us, supposedly liberal leaders in a supposedly democratic country categorically exclude one-fifth of the population because of its group identity, just as we experienced elsewhere.
It is bad enough that these leaders seem unable to imagine how they would react to declarations such as “The Jews are flocking to the polls," as Netanyahu wrongfully declared on Election Day in 2015 regarding Arab citizens of the country he leads, and what they would expect the civilized world to do in response to such demonization.
It is bad enough to discover that Jews can be every bit as racist as anyone else.
But where is common sense? Where is political logic?
Take the opportunity
Every leader of the so-called change bloc has warned that Netanyahu is leading Israel toward disaster. They understand how Netanyahu’s leadership is perceived abroad, and how it will affect Israel’s educated young people, and hence the country’s very future.
Are they really prepared to let this happen?
They have a choice. They can cling to a position that excludes a substantial part of the population, thereby giving Netanyahu a license to continue dismantling everything built here through blood, sweat and tears, through ingenuity, creativity, and determination.
Alternatively, they can acknowledge that all citizens are equal in a democracy, and that they – the political leaders, with the support of the very public they have excluded – have it within their power to save Israel from the fate its current prime minister is steering it toward.
They must understand that there is no victory for the Netanyahu bloc. Nor is there a tie. There is an opportunity – not only to reject the disgraceful racism that is eating away at every decent part of Israeli society, but also to rid the country of this government.
Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid, Avigdor Liberman: the country’s fate is in your hands.
The writer was Israel’s first ambassador to the Baltic states after the disintegration of the Soviet Union, ambassador to South Africa, and congressional liaison officer at the embassy in Washington. She is a graduate of Israel’s National Defense College.

High Court approves demolition of Palestinian rocket suspect's home, rejects family's appeal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:50:44 UTC
23:50:44 KST

The High Court of Justice on Thursday upheld an order to demolish the West Bank apartment of a Palestinian man accused of organizing an attempted rocket attack on Modi’in Illit, ruling that the exceptional severity of the acts justified demolition – even though no one was killed or wounded.
Justices Yael Willner, Yechiel Kasher, and Ruth Ronnen unanimously rejected a petition by the man’s wife and two children. The order covers only the apartment where the family lived in the village of Kafr Nima near Ramallah, rather than the entire building, which belongs to the wife’s father and houses other relatives.
The ruling concerns Abdullah Mahmoud Saud al-Khatib, who faces charges including attempted intentional killing, weapons offenses, and membership in an unlawful association.
According to the indictment as described in the judgment, Khatib formed a cell to carry out repeated rocket attacks on Israeli targets; built rockets and launch systems; and conducted tests. On September 17, 2025, two cell members acting under his direction positioned two rockets near Modi’in Illit and took the steps needed to launch them toward the city.
One rocket fell, damaging the other’s launch mechanism. Neither was launched toward the city.
Failed rocket attack posed exceptional danger, Willner rules
Writing the main opinion, Willner rejected the family’s argument that the operation had remained at the planning stage. She pointed to the cell’s systematic preparations, stock of rockets and explosives, and intention to carry out launches every few days. The failure to cause casualties did not erase the exceptional danger posed by those acts, she found.
The order was issued under Regulation 119 of the British Mandate-era emergency regulations, which permits the confiscation and demolition of homes in specified circumstances.
Willner acknowledged that demolition orders generally follow attacks causing death or serious wounds. However, she cited an earlier ruling upholding demolition over an attempted mass-casualty bus bombing in which no one was hurt, explaining that exceptionally grave acts can justify the measure, even without casualties.
The family argued that destroying their home would amount to collective punishment, challenged the measure’s legality and deterrent value, and stressed that the wife and children had neither participated in nor known about Khatib’s actions. They alternatively sought to limit the measure to sealing one room.
Willner rejected the broader legal challenges on the basis of existing case law. She acknowledged the severe consequences for the children but concluded that the circumstances justified demolition of the apartment.
Ronnen joined the result “not without hesitation,” emphasizing that a family’s lack of knowledge or involvement matters when assessing whether demolition is proportionate.
Justice questions deterrent value of demolishing uninvolved family's home
People cannot be deterred from failing to prevent an attack they neither knew nor could have known about, she wrote.
Destroying an uninvolved family’s home could also weaken the incentive for relatives to discourage attacks by suggesting that their conduct makes no difference.
Nevertheless, Ronnen found that Khatib’s clear residential connection to the apartment, the extreme seriousness of the alleged acts and the decision to limit demolition to that apartment justified leaving the order in place.
The military had initially sought to demolish the entire ground floor but excluded a neighboring empty apartment after the family objected. The judgment also cites engineering measures intended to minimize damage to the rest of the building and nearby properties.
The court rejected a separate challenge to the roughly 11-month delay between the attempted attack and the demolition notice.
The state attributed the delay to wartime demands and the need for individual approval from the prime minister and defense minister because the attack had caused no casualties.
According to the state’s submissions, the National Security Council was still working on a general policy for demolitions following attacks without casualties. The court accepted the explanation for the delay and left the apartment’s demolition order intact.

Rabbi Dov Lando must explain his opposition to haredi IDF service - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:50:33 UTC
23:50:33 KST

Someone should take Rabbi Dov Lando to a Din Torah – a court of Jewish Law for violating one of the most important of all the laws in Judaism. According to Halacha, the compilation of Jewish law, almost every law can be broken to save or prolong a life. It is permitted to drive a woman in labor to hospital on Shabbat, and even on Yom Kippur. The same goes for someone who is seriously ill, or who has been critically injured. Similarly there are certain conditions under which it is permitted to eat non kosher food, or to break a fast on Yom Kippur. In Hebrew, it’s called pikuach nefesh.
Israel is a country which constantly faces an existential threat, This means that there are approximately 10 million lives in danger yet Lando keeps issuing rulings against conscription into the IDF.
According to media reports, some haredi young men who want to serve the country and their fellow beings, have to contend with both their parents and with Lando. In their attempts to dissuade their sons from exchanging their black suits and kapotes for army uniforms, many parents insist that their sons visit Lando. For the sake of family harmony, many acquiesce, and get an earful from Lando as to why they should stick to studying Torah.
Soldiers who identify as religious Zionist have no problem in combining Torah study with military service, nor do those haredi young men who follow their conscience rather than the dictates of a nonagenarian rabbi with a fire and brimstone temperament.
Dov Lando is the co-chair of the Slobodke Yeshiva in Bnei Brak.
The original Slobodka Yeshiva was founded in Lithuania almost 145 years ago, and functioned until the Second World War. A Land of Israel branch was established in Hebron in the early part of the 20th century, but lasted only five years. The Slobodka Yeshiva in Bnei Brak, has been operating since 1947. Its central focus in addition to Torah study is ethics.
That being the case, is Lando going against the doctrines of the institution of which he is the co-chair?
Ignoring call-up notices
Is it ethical to tell religious young men to ignore their call-up notices? Surely people should obey the laws of the countries in which they live. To do otherwise is unethical, and to promote evasion of army service in a country which sits beneath a cloud of pikuach nefesh is not only unethical, but in violation of Halacha.
In ultra-Orthodox circles, the head rabbi of a movement or synagogue or a school is treated like old-world royalty. His wisdom is unquestioned; his orders are executed.
But what would happen if Lando suddenly told the whole ultra-Orthodox community that they can no longer use mobile phones or personal computers because these are no longer morally safe given all the technological advances that enable unbidden and unwelcome data to enter mobile phones and personal computers? Would he be obeyed? Perhaps a few hundred people would comply, but on the whole they would rebel. In fact they have already rebelled. Not everyone has what is known as a kosher phone. Many people have television sets hidden in bedroom closets with sliding doors. Some people watch movies through a laptop or a tablet.
Which is worse – watching blue movies in secret or serving in the IDF in the open?
Perhaps Rabbi Lando has an answer.

France opens attempted murder probe after protest attack
November 1, 2026
Paris prosecutors opened an attempted murder investigation Sunday after a Molotov cocktail was thrown at security forces during a demonstration in the French capital.
Prosecutors said explosive projectiles targeted about 15 gendarmes as well as police officers. No suspects have been arrested over the attack, and investigators were still establishing the number and severity of injuries.
What happened in Paris?
The attack took place at Porte de Charenton, where Saturday's march ended. Photographs and video from the AFP news agency showed an incendiary device exploding at a gendarme's feet and setting his protective equipment alight.
Prosecutors said reported injuries included second-degree burns and tinnitus, although those details remained provisional. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez described the attack as an attempted murder.
How many people were arrested?
The Interior Ministry reported 779 arrests nationwide during the demonstrations and Halloween night. The figure includes both events, updating Saturday evening's provisional total of 565. Authorities said the later part of the night passed without major incidents.
Paris prosecutors separately reported 105 arrests in the capital: 88 linked to the demonstrations and 17 to Halloween night. They said 89 people remained in custody, including at least 22 minors.
The protests focused on high living costs and government policies. The ministry put nationwide turnout at 320,000, while unions estimated nearly 500,000 participants.
The nationwide arrest total was below the 1,314 recorded during the previous Saturday's mobilization and the 2,628 on October 17, when widespread rioting and looting broke out. Authorities had increased security ahead of Halloween amid online calls for violence.

Over 80 meters long, a dry cargo hold, and an owner investigated over Russian drone operations: the ship Sweden boarded off Gotland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:48:47 UTC
23:48:47 KST

Swedish police boarded a Russia-linked cargo ship off the island of Gotland overnight, Swedish broadcaster TV4 reported, without naming the ship. The ship’s owner has faced investigations over suspected Russian hybrid and reconnaissance operations. Police later described the check as routine.
Russia’s war on Ukraine runs partly on ships: tankers carrying oil money and freighters slipping cargo past sanctions. European states have stepped up boardings, yet detained ships are often released within days. Washington, meanwhile, is weighing relief for sanctioned tankers. Some of these vessels are also suspected of serving Russia’s covert war on Europe itself. That ranges from cable cuts to drone flights over airports and military sites.
A night boarding off Gotland’s northwest coast
Police went aboard the ship off Gotland’s northwest coast in the night into Saturday, 31 October, TV4 said. “We are on board during the night, checking the crew and their travel documents,” Carina Skagerlind, spokesperson for the Stockholm police region, told the broadcaster.
The vessel is a dry cargo ship more than 80 meters long. Sweden’s National Task Force, the police’s elite tactical unit, took part, according to TV4’s sources. Skagerlind would not confirm that. “We have used the resources we needed,” she said.
Police later called it a routine border check
Later on Saturday, Skagerlind called it a border check on a ship that had been lying in a port on Gotland, Swedish news agency TT reported. “This is a routine assignment,” Skagerlind said. The travel documents raised no remarks, she added. Asked about the task force, she said the border police are responsible for the area and did the work.
An owner whose ships appear near drone alarms
The company that owns the ship has had its vessels turn up near drone alarms in several European countries, TV4 reported. Investigators suspect the ships acted as depots for Russian intelligence drones. European intelligence sources told TV4 the ships “most likely act in the Russian state’s interest.” The company has offices in Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave and says it recruits its crews there. The crew of this ship are Russian citizens, according to TV4’s sources.
Ships as drone platforms are not a new suspicion in Europe. In September 2025, Germany seized the freighter Scanlark over an alleged drone flight over a frigate at the Kiel naval base. France then held the tanker Boracay, linked to drones over Denmark, and it resumed its voyage about a week later.
Sweden’s earlier boardings
Sweden has boarded several Russia-linked ships over the past year. In December 2025, Swedish authorities boarded the sanctioned Russian vessel Adler, tied to North Korean ammunition shipments.
In March, the Swedish Coast Guard and police seized the Caffa, a cargo ship linked to grain stolen from occupied Ukraine, and a Swedish court later ruled that Kyiv can have it. A week after the Caffa, Swedish forces boarded the tanker Sea Owl I under a suspected false flag. In April, Sweden boarded the sanctioned tanker Flora 1 after a 12 km oil slick appeared east of Gotland.
Ukraine strikes Russia’s ships, with one exception
Ukraine treats Russia’s shadow fleet as a military target. Its drone forces have disabled 300 such ships in 11 weeks, Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert Brovdi said in September.
Tankers carrying Russian diesel to the United States are off-limits, though. “Nobody is touching these ships for sure,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists, Ukrinform reported on 28 October. The ships are connected to the United States, he explained.
Washington cleared Russian diesel blocked by sanctions in October. Three tankers are now carrying Russian diesel to the US. The first, Agioi Fanendes, loaded 40,000 tons at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk. Another of the three, the Leruo, is under EU, UK, and Canadian sanctions, the Financial Times reported, according to United24 Media.

Eisenkot's bloc races to secure mandate as Netanyahu rivals seek to block judicial reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:48:14 UTC
23:48:14 KST

Senior figures in Yashar! party leader Gadi Eisenkot's political bloc are pushing to ensure that he receives the first opportunity to form the next government, warning that failure to unite behind his candidacy could allow controversial judicial reform legislation passed under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.
The effort comes after last week's inconclusive parliamentary election, which left neither Netanyahu's right-wing bloc nor his opponents with a straightforward path to a governing coalition.
Eisenkot, a former IDF chief of staff whose centrist party has won the second-most seats in the election after Netanyahu's ruling Likud party, is seeking the backing of parties opposed to the premier ahead of consultations with President Isaac Herzog, who is expected to begin meeting party leaders Wednesday to determine which lawmaker should receive the mandate to form a government.
Senior officials in Eisenkot's bloc say the order in which the president assigns that mandate could have far-reaching consequences beyond the immediate coalition negotiations.
"If the entire bloc does not recommend Eisenkot, all the judicial overhaul laws passed by the current coalition will take effect on Jan. 1, 2027, as stipulated by law," a senior official from another party in the bloc warned.
The legislation includes laws concerning the attorney general, the Justice Ministry's Police Internal Investigations Department and the composition of the committee responsible for selecting judges.
The measures are part of Netanyahu's government's contentious effort to reshape Israel's judicial system, a campaign that has fueled deep political divisions over the balance of power between elected officials and the courts.
Eisenkot's allies believe that securing the first mandate would give their bloc an opportunity to take control of the Knesset's Arrangements Committee, a temporary parliamentary body that plays a central role in organizing the legislature's work before permanent committees are established.
Under the bloc's plan, control of the committee would allow lawmakers to advance two major objectives: replacing Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana of Netanyahu's Likud party and repealing the judicial reform legislation before it takes effect.
Although the parties opposing Netanyahu do not necessarily agree on who should lead the next government, they could command a parliamentary majority of 67 lawmakers for those specific measures.
The 120-member Knesset requires a majority of 61 seats to pass ordinary legislation and approve a government, making the potential 67-member alignment significant even without an agreement on a governing coalition.
"This is a dramatic event," a senior official in one of the bloc's parties said. "If we don't have a larger majority of recommendations than Netanyahu, the judicial overhaul laws will take effect and we won't be able to repeal them."
Liberman's silence complicates Eisenkot's plans
Eisenkot's allies are working to consolidate recommendations from the parties in the anti-Netanyahu bloc, with an initial effort focused on securing the support of all its members.
They currently believe Eisenkot can count on recommendations from Yashar!, Beyachad and the Democrats.
The major unresolved question is Avigdor Liberman, leader of the nationalist Yisrael Beytenu party, who has not publicly committed to recommending Eisenkot.
According to figures involved in the discussions, Liberman has also avoided revealing his intentions during closed-door conversations among leaders of the bloc.
His silence has puzzled other opposition figures, particularly because he has made few public statements since the election results were announced, apart from posts on social media.
Liberman is expected to convene his party's first parliamentary faction meeting Monday and issue a statement to the media afterward.
He has denied reports that he sought the position of Knesset speaker for himself following claims that opposition figures had offered the post either to him or to fellow Yisrael Beytenu lawmaker Oded Forer.
Liberman's decision could affect the number of lawmakers recommending Eisenkot, though the former military chief is currently expected to receive more endorsements than Netanyahu even without Yisrael Beytenu's support.
According to the bloc's calculations, Eisenkot could secure as many as 67 recommendations if Liberman joins the effort.
Without Yisrael Beytenu, he is expected to receive 60, compared with 46 for Netanyahu.
The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party is expected to remain uncommitted, at least initially.
Those figures would make Eisenkot the leading candidate to receive the first mandate, although the president is not legally required to choose the lawmaker with the most recommendations.
The central question remains whether Eisenkot can translate parliamentary support for replacing Netanyahu into a coalition capable of winning a confidence vote.
Herzog to begin consultations Wednesday
Herzog is expected to begin consultations with representatives of the parties elected to the Knesset on Wednesday, asking each faction whom it recommends to form the next government.
The process is expected to continue Thursday and could extend into Friday.
Under Israeli law, the president has seven days to conduct the consultations, make a decision and assign the mandate to a member of the Knesset.
That places the deadline at Nov. 11, although Herzog could announce his decision earlier.
Unlike political systems in which the leader of the largest party automatically becomes prime minister, Israel's president is tasked with selecting the lawmaker judged most likely to assemble a governing majority.
In practice, the president generally gives considerable weight to the number of recommendations each candidate receives from parliamentary factions.
But recommendations are not binding commitments to join a coalition, and a candidate can receive more endorsements than a rival without having a viable governing majority.
That distinction is especially important after an election in which the balance between the rival political blocs has left government formation uncertain.
For Eisenkot, receiving the mandate first would provide both a political advantage and an opportunity to advance his bloc's legislative agenda while negotiations continue.
For Netanyahu, being passed over would not necessarily end his chances of remaining prime minister.
Israeli law provides several additional stages for forming a government if the first candidate fails.
What happens if Eisenkot cannot form a government?
The lawmaker who receives the first mandate has 28 days to form a coalition and present a government to the Knesset.
The president may grant an extension of up to 14 additional days, giving the candidate a maximum of 42 days.
If that effort fails, Herzog can choose between two options.
The first is to assign the mandate to another member of the Knesset, potentially the leader of the rival bloc.
That candidate would have 28 days to form a government, without the possibility of an extension.
Alternatively, the president can inform the Knesset that he sees no viable prospect of forming a government.
That decision would trigger a 21-day period during which at least 61 lawmakers could submit a written request asking the president to assign the mandate to a particular member of the Knesset.
If such a request is submitted, the designated lawmaker would receive 14 days to assemble a coalition.
If none of those attempts produces a government that wins the Knesset's confidence, parliament would automatically dissolve and Israel would head to another election.

Social Democrats council endorses Jonatan Vseviov's prime minister bid
The Social Democratic Party (SDE) council has formally endorsed Jonatan Vseviov as their party's candidate for prime minister in the 2027 Riigikogu elections.
Vseviov, who stepped down as secretary general at the Foreign Ministry to run in next spring's elections, will head the party's list in Electoral District 4, which covers Harju and Rapla counties.
On the proposal of party leader Lauri Läänemets, the council approved his nomination as the Social Democrats' candidate for prime minister on Sunday.
Läänemets said the party will campaign as a united team.
"Our goal is to win these elections because the Social Democrats are offering the people of Estonia the best possible candidate for prime minister and a strong team to bring Estonia back to the heart of Europe," he said.
The party chair noted that the SDE's support has tripled since the last Riigikogu elections in 2023, crediting the work of both longtime party members and new recruits.
"Now it's up to us to grow that support even further," he added.
'We alone are responsible for us'
In his address to the council, Vseviov called for Estonia to pursue a more ambitious foreign policy and play a greater role in shaping Europe's future. He said Estonia must have a strong and influential voice in decisions affecting the continent.
"We alone are responsible for both telling our own story and ensuring there is room for our freedom in the Europe of the future," Vseviov said. "We cannot assume that questions affecting Estonia's future will stay off the international agenda just because we meekly keep our mouths shut."
Such matters will come up regardless, he stressed, adding that "the less weight our voice carries in those discussions, the more likely others are to decide our future without us."
The next Riigikogu elections will take place on March 7, 2027.

Russia lost more troops in October than in any other month of its full-scale war, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 1 November. Ukrainian forces also took back more land than Russian troops captured over the month, he added.
Russia keeps sending infantry against Ukraine's lines in Donbas and along the northern border. By summer, it was already losing more soldiers than it could recruit, Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi said in June. October's count shows the price climbing again, while the ground Russia gains for it shrinks.
A record month and a record day
Over October, Russia lost 54,400 troops killed and seriously wounded, Zelenskyy said, the most of any month since the full-scale invasion began. The previous monthly high, 48,670, dated from December 2024, according to the General Staff's figures.
Ukraine suffered 10 times fewer casualties than Russia in Vivaldi counteroffensive, veteran says. Ukraine’s innovations in drone and ground robot tactics are changing frontline warfare
Russia's costliest single day came on 21 October, with 2,250 troops lost, Zelenskyy added. Over the month, Russia averaged 1,755 losses a day. The figures are Ukraine's estimates and cannot be independently verified.
A Russian region's worth of soldiers
In infographics published with the figures, the General Staff compared the toll to things Russians know. It is roughly the entire population of Chukotka, a remote Russian region in the Far East home to fewer than 50,000 people. It is also about as many soldiers as march in nine military parades on Red Square, or enough to fill about 200 Moscow subway cars. "This is the price Russia pays for its aggression," one of them reads.
More ground back than lost
Ukraine's Defense Forces liberated 96.2 km² in October, 10.4 km² more than Russian troops captured, Zelenskyy said. That puts Russia's gains for the month at 85.8 km². In mid-October, he said Ukraine had liberated more land than Russia captured since the start of fall.
Zelenskyy thanked every brigade and unit for the result. "To stop these insane losses, Russia only needs to choose a ceasefire and diplomacy," he wrote.
Russia's reported losses have climbed through 2026, and Moscow keeps looking for more men. In September, Brigadier General Denys Prokopenko warned that Russia may mobilize up to 600,000 troops for its next offensive.

US midterm campaign enters last weekend as ballot fights heat up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:42:26 UTC
