Breadcrumb
US midterm campaign enters final weekend as Alaska, California ballot fights heat up
President Donald Trump's administration pressed a criminal investigation into Alaska's pivotal US Senate race and said on Saturday it would likely take its fight over thousands of California mail-in ballots to the Supreme Court, as the midterm campaign for control of Congress entered its final weekend.
In Alaska, federal prosecutors are investigating whether aides to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola helped to recruit a retired schoolteacher, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to run because his name is similar to the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan. The closely contested race is seen as crucial to Democrats' hopes of taking the Senate in Tuesday's vote.
It is one of 35 Senate races, along with all 435 House seats, that will decide whether Trump's Republicans keep control of Congress for his final two years in office.
Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority and a narrow edge in the House.
Early voting has set a record. More than 51 million Americans have already cast ballots in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day at the last midterms in 2022.
In California, a federal appeals court this week ruled 2-1 that the Justice Department had failed to justify its emergency bid to force the state to set aside mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters it alleges are likely noncitizens.
"I hesitate to give a final answer, but I think probably the Supreme Court's next on this one," acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told Fox News on Saturday, adding that any request for Supreme Court consideration would come before Tuesday's election.
Trump has been on a campaign blitz in multiple states over the past month but is spending Saturday at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. He returns to the campaign trail on Sunday in Kansas and Iowa.
Alaska probe intensifies
The Justice Department's top prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a Friday press conference that a recent New York Times article claiming there had been an effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. had driven a "surge" of FBI resources onto the case.
Heyman said he had assigned several prosecutors to it and that investigative steps were taking place "intensely and swiftly."
Peltola and the campaign committee have denied involvement in any effort to recruit the second Sullivan. The retired teacher has denied coordinating with Peltola's campaign.
Voters in Alaska have largely dismissed the fight over the ballot.
"I knew which Dan Sullivan was which Dan Sullivan, you know? It's very clear on the ballot," Anchorage resident Mickey Buster, 36, said as he stood outside a polling place on Saturday.
But another Anchorage voter, Carol Riggs, 52, said she was disappointed by the entire situation and the possibility it "muddies the water for some voters, potentially."
Michigan rift
In Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers in another closely watched Senate race, El-Sayed's feud with the rival he beat in the primary, US Representative Haley Stevens, flared again.
El-Sayed's campaign asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as "not to distract from the central issues of the campaign," a person familiar with the matter said. Stevens has backed El-Sayed but demanded he condemn an outside group's ad blaming Israel for high grocery prices and apologise for past rhetoric about Israel.
"It's certainly unhelpful to the El-Sayed campaign to have continued visible division within the party just before Election Day," said Matt Grossmann, a political scientist at Michigan State University. Polls show El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support.
Trump's pressure campaign on states
Beyond its bid to block the counting of ballots from more than 20,000 California voters it alleges could be noncitizens, the administration has sued roughly 30 states and the District of Columbia seeking unredacted voter rolls.
The legal manoeuvres have alarmed state election officials. Under the Constitution, states have primary authority over how they run elections.
On Friday, a federal judge ordered the Justice Department to stop threatening to prosecute California election officials who defy its directives.
California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, warned the state's top federal judges on Saturday that the Justice Department may seek warrants to seize ballots before results are certified, though he said he did not know of any pending request. Newsom said in a letter to the judges that the only reason to seize ballots "would be to interfere" in the count.
Sean Morales-Doyle of the Brennan Centre for Justice said the efforts, while unlikely to win in court, aim at "creating uncertainty, sowing fear, distrust, chaos," in hopes of pressuring officials such as Alaska's lieutenant governor "to do something that they're not supposed to do."
Even so, 76 percent of US voters are confident their ballots will be counted accurately, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted from 30 September to 5 October, with confidence about equally high among Republicans and Democrats.

Serbians mark railway disaster that led to rise of victorious student movement
NOVI SAD, Serbia – Tens of thousands of people gathered at a Serbian railway station on Nov 1 to mark the anniversary of a deadly roof collapse that gave rise to the protest movement that toppled long-time Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic in an election a week ago.
Crowds converged from across the city of Novi Sad on the main train station, where the concrete awning crashed down shortly before noon on Nov 1, 2024, killing 16 people.
Mourners observed 16 minutes of silence before laying wreaths, flowers and candles near the site.
“On a personal, emotional and social level, I hope for a collective healing,” said Zorana Sijan Oborina, a student supporter.
The disaster, which struck at a station renovated under a China-backed high-speed rail project, ignited Serbia’s massive nationwide anti-corruption protest movement, culminating in last week’s election victory by a student-led bloc.
Protesters saw the collapse as symptomatic of corruption under Vucic. The protests forced resignations, including that of the construction minister, a government reshuffle, and eventually snap elections.
Prosecutors indicted 13 people over the collapse, but pre-trial proceedings have stalled. The defendants denied any wrongdoing.
“I hope we have finally realised that we shouldn’t wait... years to change what is bad, especially when it costs human lives,” said Jelena Trajkovic, 32, an academic from Novi Sad.
On Oct 25, the Student List – a group that includes academics, professionals, farmers, actors and activists chosen by student assemblies – secured 141 seats in the 250-member Parliament, according to a preliminary tally. Final results are due in the coming days and are not expected to change the outcome.
Vucic, who stood as the candidate for prime minister for his SNS party at the end of his presidential term, acknowledged defeat and left office. A presidential election is expected before the end of the year. REUTERS

The former Green party leader Adrian Ramsay has said the party must fix its internal democracy to avoid a takeover by the hard left, saying that some new members “might be more at home” in Your Party or the Socialist Workers party.
Ramsay, who has been critical of the handling of the row over a “Zionism is racism” motion passed at the Green party conference, said there were a “small number” of individuals who used “divisive” tactics to influence the party’s agenda.
“I think there’s a real crossroads point for the party at the moment,” he told the BBC. “And one option is to dig in … but I think that there’s a risk it brings with it a quite divisive approach to politics, which you’ve seen from small groups of people on the hard left of politics who go around different parties to try to influence how those parties are run.”
He said there were some new members who had joined the Greens after the failure of other leftwing movements, such as George Galloway’s party or Jeremy Corbyn’s Your Party, who had their roots in hard left organising.
“There is also a small number of people who have joined, perhaps from the very hard left of politics, who might be more at home in the SWP or with George Galloway or with Your Party. [They] not only want to adopt some very hardline positions on certain issues, but have a very different culture to how they go about it,” he said.
He said those members were “seeking to change the direction of the party” and he said that needed the leadership to reassert the core values and ways of working of the Green party, which was “much more about consensus building, much less about highly fractional, highly tribal politics, and of course about the environment”.
Flaws in the party’s internal democracy meant small groups could have an outsized influence he said. “It was 0.4% of members who voted for this [the Zionism is racism motion] and I don’t think that’s reflective of party members as a whole, it’s certainly not reflective of those I speak to,” he said, adding there should be a ballot or survey of the wider membership.
Ramsay, the MP for Waveney Valley, welcomed the growth in membership of the Green party and said he was not calling for Zack Polanski to stand down as leader over the handling of the row.
He also said he was not intending to quit the party himself. “I’ve got no intention of going anywhere. What I want to see happen is this issue be clearly addressed,” he said.
But it was critical the party disavowed the Zionism motion sooner than the two-year cycle which party rules allow for, he said, and that the party changed its internal rules to give the wider membership more control over policy, rather than the small numbers who attend the party’s annual conference.
A spokesperson for Greens Organise – the grassroots group that backed Polanski’s leadership – said: “Adrian Ramsay put forward his case for the future of the Green party a year ago, and lost – by a landslide 84%. Over 150,000 members have joined the party under Zack’s leadership, and helped bring the party unprecedented electoral success.
“They deserve representatives who focus their energy on fighting for the radical solutions to the crises our country face.”
Ramsay said it was also clear the party needed to refocus on its core missions around climate and nature, as well as the cost of living crisis. “I think that will unite our members. I think it will ensure we still have a wide appeal as a party,” Ramsay told the BBC Newscast podcast.
Asked if he viewed Zionism as racist, he said: “No … I’ve made clear my position on the motion, as lots of other Greens have done.” He said the situation in Gaza was “appalling” but that the motion was contradictory to the Green party manifesto from 2024.
“We support equal rights for both Palestinians and Israelis, and Greens have always supported self-determination for all people.”
He said he had told Polanski directly he should have been present for the debate and vote, despite fighting a byelection in Holborn and St Pancras. “I do think he should have been there and he should have expressed his view clearly,” he said.
Ramsay said the party “need to find a way for this motion to be changed or rescinded sooner than the two years that Zack is talking about … changing the fact that a policy can’t be reviewed until two years is up.”

Judge rebukes police over election bribery probe, orders suspect freed without restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:31:20 UTC
23:31:20 KST

A judge on Sunday sharply criticized police investigating suspected vote-buying linked to the Arab Ra'am party, ordering the unconditional release of a 38-year-old doctor after finding that investigators had failed to strengthen the evidence against him and could not justify restrictions on his freedom.
The ruling by Be'er Sheva Magistrate's Court Judge Eran Tzabari came amid a politically charged investigation into allegations that cash was distributed to voters in Bedouin communities in southern Israel ahead of last Tuesday's parliamentary election.
The investigation has become a focal point of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's allegations of electoral misconduct, with his Likud party seeking to challenge results at polling stations where it claims voting irregularities occurred.
But election authorities have emphasized that the allegations under investigation do not establish that votes were falsified or that voters were actually bribed.
The suspect, Saif Abu Riash, a physician from the Al-Sana tribe, was brought before the court Sunday after being detained by investigators from Lahav 433, the Israel Police's national investigations unit, on suspicion of election-related offenses.
Police asked the court to release Abu Riash to seven days of house arrest and impose additional restrictions, including a prohibition on internet use.
Tzabari rejected the request, ruling that Abu Riash should be released without conditions.
The judge described Abu Riash as a person leading a law-abiding life and said investigators had offered no convincing explanation for restricting his internet access, particularly because his professional work depends on it.
Police also failed to explain why house arrest was necessary, the judge said.
"The state of the investigation is exactly where it was," Tzabari said.
The judge noted that Abu Riash had cooperated with investigators and provided an account of his activities, but police had failed to carry out the checks needed to verify or challenge his explanation.
"The reasonable suspicion has not strengthened, and it can even be said that the strength of the reasonable suspicion has diminished," he said.
Tzabari nevertheless stressed that the court regarded suspected offenses involving the integrity of elections as serious matters.
Police acknowledge searches without warrants
The hearing also exposed questions about how investigators conducted searches of suspects' homes.
Abu Riash's attorney accused police of carrying out an unlawful search of his client's residence.
An investigator acknowledged that officers had entered and searched the home without obtaining a warrant but maintained that the operation was justified by intelligence received shortly beforehand.
"A search was conducted without a warrant. Call it illegal. There was recent intelligence. No search warrant was needed," the investigator told the court.
Police had previously acknowledged during a court hearing on Election Day that officers searched the homes of detained activists without warrants.
Sunday's proceedings also revealed that investigators had attempted to compare money found during the searches with Abu Riash's personal cash withdrawals.
An investigator conceded that police had been unable to complete the examination.
"We tried to carry out an elementary, basic investigative action, and we did not succeed," the investigator said.
Tzabari cited the failure as part of his criticism of the investigation, noting that Abu Riash had provided his version of events but police had not managed to verify it.
Police also sought to extend the detention of two other suspects in the case.
One, Ibrahim al-Gharibi, was released to house arrest under restrictive conditions.
The third, Hussein Masoudin, had his detention extended until Tuesday.
Police had initially planned Saturday night to release the suspects but subsequently changed course and sought additional restrictions or detention extensions.
The intelligence that led to their arrests was provided to police by Ido Norden, acting chief of staff to Netanyahu.
Cash-filled envelopes and allegations of vote-buying
The investigation began in the days leading up to the Oct. 27 election, when police arrested three suspects from the Segev Shalom area and Ar'ara in the Negev.
Officers said searches of their homes uncovered envelopes containing tens of thousands of shekels in cash, along with ballot slips and other materials suspected of being connected to election offenses.
Some envelopes reportedly bore the logo of Ra'am, an Arab political party.
Police alleged that the money was intended to be distributed to voters in exchange for supporting Ra'am at the ballot box.
The initial police announcement did not accuse the party's leadership of involvement in the suspected scheme.
Investigators said the operation was part of broader nationwide efforts to prevent election offenses and ensure that citizens could exercise their voting rights freely.
The case subsequently expanded.
On Thursday, police arrested four additional suspects, including three school principals from Bedouin communities in southern Israel, in connection with the alleged vote-buying operation.
Three of those four suspects were subsequently released to house arrest.
The arrests came as Likud prepared a legal challenge seeking new votes at Arab polling stations where the party alleges bribery and other irregularities compromised the election.
Netanyahu and Likud seized on the discovery of cash and ballot slips on Election Day to allege an attempt to steal the election.
Their rhetoric intensified after the results emerged and escalated further following reports of a separate affair involving allegations that Qatar and Turkey had spent money attempting to influence Israeli public opinion.
The allegations involving foreign influence are distinct from the investigation into suspected vote-buying in Bedouin communities, and no connection between the two cases has been established.
Election authorities, meanwhile, have sought to distinguish suspected criminal conduct from claims that the election results themselves were manipulated.
The Central Elections Committee has emphasized that there is no indication votes were falsified or that voters were bribed, despite the suspicions being examined by police.

Ask LLOG: Convenant?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:28:05 UTC
23:28:05 KST

Ask LLOG: Convenant?
« previous post |
From L.J.:
Could you explain the real pronunciation of "covenant"? In American English, the first vowel is not like that in British English as shown in the Oxford English Dictionary. Please see the attachment. However, theoretically, a word cannot have three schwas because the stress cannot be assigned. Could the first vowel be actually a longer one?
I'll answer the question, while indulging in a short rant about the faults of the International Phonetic Alphabet (and the worse faults of its use, in dictionaries and elsewhere).
To start with, here's the OED's audio for its two top-row pronunciations
"British English" /ˈkʌvənənt/ and "U.S. English" /ˈkəvənənt/
Curiously, the two non-IPA spelled pronunciations are identical, both
KUV-uh-nuhnt
…which is actually fine, since I perceive no difference in perceptual vowel quality between the first syllables of the two (audio) versions.
(If there's a standard term for non-IPA spelled pronunciations of that general kind, I don't know what it is — so I'll call them "lah-lah-lah".)
Even more curiously, the alternative "British English" pronunciation (given in IPA as /ˈkʌvənənt/ vs. /ˈkʌvn̩ənt/, and in lah-lah-lah as "KUV-uhn-uhnt") is actually bit-wise identical in waveform samples to the first British pronunciation — that is, it's the exact same file, decorated with a (therefore empty) claim about a difference in syllabification.
OK, now we get to the question, about how stress can be assigned to one of the three schwas in /ˈkəvənənt/.
The background problem is a fundamental equivocation about what "schwa" means.
Many (not all) unstressed vowels in English are "reduced", which means that they have a unrounded central quality if pronounced in a hyper-articulated syllable-by-syllable style, plausibly represented by IPA [ə] ("schwa"). However, in actual speech these vowels can be deleted (= reduced to non-existence), raised or lowered, fronted or backed, rounded or unrounded, nasalized or not, etc., depending on the sounds around them, and the phonetic realization principles of the speaker's idiolect.
IPA offers no symbol to represent this situation, so most people (phoneticians, dictionary editors, dialect coaches, whoever) use [ə] ("schwa") to fill the gap. This then creates an ambiguity. Does [ə] mean an unstressed-and-reduced vowel, whose actual quality might be [ɪ] or [ɛ] or [ʌ] or etc., depending on circumstances? Or does it mean an unreduced (and perhaps stressed) vowel , in the phonological category that J.C. Wells assigns to the STRUT lexical class, and whose phonetic quality in a particular case might be perceived to correspond best to IPA [ə]?
For most people — though apparently not (some of) the OED's editors — the solution is to reserve the use of [ə] for the meaning "unstressed reduced vowel", and to used [ʌ] to represent the pronunciation of stressed STRUT vowels. This is obviously not what the OED editors have done, though their choice is undermined by their own lah-lah-lah transcriptions and by the phonetic quality of the audio clips they provide.
For comparison, see the entries for covenant from Merriam-Webster, Wiktionary, Cambridge, and so on.
As etymological background, see the Wikipedia entry for Hebrew "shva".
And in place of a longer IPA rant, you can take a look at
"Why I don't love the International Phonetic Alphabet", 1/2/2008
"How truck starts", 8/9/2011
"On beyond the (International Phonetic) Alphabet", 5/19/2018
"Farther on beyond the IPA", 1/18/2020
"First novels", 2/13/2022
"Pronunciation evolution", 3/15/2022
"More post-IPA astronauts", 3/16/2022
"What 'IPA' means now…", 9/28/2022
"Steele v. Monboddo", 7/12/2025

Hundreds Return to Ukraine From Russian-Occupied Oleshky After Rare US-Brokered Ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:27:15 UTC
23:27:15 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Hundreds Return to Ukraine From Russian-Occupied Oleshky After Rare US-Brokered Ceasefire
Hundreds of civilians evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region arrived in Ukrainian-controlled territory on October 31 following a humanitarian operation facilitated by US First Lady Melania Trump and a temporary ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia.
According to RBC-Ukraine on October 31, evacuees crossed the Ukrainian-Belarusian border in the Chernihiv region, where medical teams, emergency services, and relatives were waiting for their arrival.
According to Newsmax journalist Alex Salvi, 11 buses carrying evacuated residents headed to Ukrainian-controlled territory, while another four buses traveled to Russia. Approximately 750 people had registered for evacuation, although Ukrainian authorities have not confirmed the final number of evacuees.
The humanitarian mission involved a convoy of 25 buses, 50 medical workers, and ambulances. The evacuation route took residents from Oleshky through Russian-occupied Crimea to Anapa in Russia’s Krasnodar region. From there, they traveled by aircraft to Gomel, Belarus, before continuing by bus to the Ukrainian border.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the operation, stating that the temporary ceasefire had allowed humanitarian supplies to reach Oleshky, roads to be cleared of mines, and civilians to leave the city and surrounding communities.
Ukraine’s Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets, who accompanied the evacuees, said Ukrainian citizens had not been subjected to Russian filtration procedures, document inspections, or phone searches during the journey.
According to hromadske on October 31, Ukrainian authorities established reception facilities at the border, providing hot meals, medical examinations, wheelchairs, and assistance for children and pets. Among the evacuated animals were dogs, cats, a parrot, and a raccoon.
The oldest evacuated resident was 94 years old, while the youngest was just over one year old. Some residents described severe conditions under Russian occupation. One family had reportedly been trapped in a heavily damaged apartment building after its stairwell was destroyed, leaving a father with limited mobility unable to descend from the eighth floor.
Another resident reportedly survived 16 Russian drone attacks and four missile strikes on his home before being evacuated.
The humanitarian operation was facilitated by US First Lady Melania Trump, who announced arrangements for a localized ceasefire to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
According to hromadske, the mission involved Ukrainian, American, and Russian representatives, with journalists from all three countries present during the operation. The International Committee of the Red Cross and the United Nations were not directly involved.
The temporary ceasefire, established in late October, is scheduled to remain in effect until November 1. Ukrainian officials reported no violations during the evacuation.
Oleshky lies approximately nine kilometers (5.6 miles) from Kherson, across the Dnipro River, and has remained under Russian occupation since the beginning of Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Before the invasion, the city had approximately 24,000 residents. By 2026, fewer than 2,000 people were believed to remain, many of them elderly or with limited mobility, according to local Ukrainian authorities cited by hromadske.

Why is Morocco celebrating the defeat of a UN resolution on Western Sahara?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:26:43 UTC
23:26:43 KST

Why is Morocco celebrating the defeat of a UN resolution on Western Sahara?
The mandate for UN mission that was tasked to monitor 1991 truce and hold referendum in disputed territory expires.
Morocco has welcomed the defeat of a US-drafted resolution which sought to extend the mandate of the UN mission in the disputed Western Sahara.
The mandate of the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) expired on Saturday after a veto by Russia, leaving the future of the peacekeeping mission in limbo. In 1991, the UN established MINURSO to monitor a ceasefire and prepare a referendum on the territory’s future.
Morocco has considered Western Sahara its own territory since 1975, when Spain withdrew from the desert region in northwest Africa which is roughly the size of Britain. The Algeria-backed Polisario Front seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.
So, why is Morocco celebrating the failed UN resolution? What does it mean for the future of the disputed region?
Here is what we know:
What happened at the UN Security Council?
On Friday, the US, which is a permanent member of the UN Security Council, proposed a resolution to support the principle of self-determination in the disputed Western Sahara.
Russia vetoed the resolution, despite support from 11 of the 15 council members, including fellow permanent members France and the United Kingdom.
The US draft would have extended the mission for a year, removed “referendum” from its name and made Morocco’s autonomy proposal the only basis for further talks.
Last October, the UN Security Council adopted a resolution that offered genuine autonomy to Western Sahara. Under that plan, the territory would manage its internal affairs, but remain under Moroccan sovereignty.
The Security Council had already made the proposal a basis for negotiations last year and asked UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to submit a review of the peacekeeping mission.
Speaking after the vote, US ambassador Mike Waltz said it was truly unfortunate that in 2026 the veto was used to “preserve the letter R (in the Mission’s name) for referendum”.
He added that Washington’s proposal “would have moved the 50-year conflict forward” and added that the status quo is not acceptable.
Russia’s UN ambassador, Vassily Nebenzia, said at the same meeting that Moscow opposed the draft because it favoured one side.
“We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically predetermine matters relating to sovereignty,” he said.
Instead, Russia proposed renewing the existing mission without those changes. But that draft also failed to secure the nine votes needed for adoption, receiving two votes in favour, one against and 11 abstentions.
MINURSO’s mission has 155 military personnel and is set to cost $62m in the fiscal year that began in June, according to a UN report. But its mandate expired on Saturday.
How did Morocco and Algeria react to the failure of the UN mission?
Morocco’s royal palace welcomed the failure to renew MINURSO, saying on Friday that UN personnel and equipment should leave the territory in the coming days and that the Western Sahara issue should now be withdrawn from the Security Council’s consideration. Morocco said it remained committed to the ceasefire.
According to a UN media statement, Morocco’s UN representative also questioned why Algeria’s delegate was giving the Security Council “lectures” on the Western Sahara.
“Let these people [in the Western Sahara] go back to Morocco,” he said, “let them go home”.
Algeria expressed regret on Saturday over the failure to renew MINURSO’s mandate. Its foreign ministry criticised what it described as the US draft’s excessive bias towards Morocco.
According to a UN media statement, Algeria’s delegate to the UN thanked Russia for its draft resolution and all other member nations “who have chosen not to associate themselves” with an egregious injustice and a flagrant attack on “the very foundation of our organisation”.
Algeria’s UN representative noted that the country has been a refuge for hundreds of thousands of Sahrawi people who have been denied their right to self-determination.
The “tragedy being endured by the Sahrawi people has oddly been diluted to the concept of refugee populations”, he added.
Sidi Omar, the Polisario Front’s representative at the UN, told reporters on Friday that he welcomed Russia’s veto because the US proposal would undermine Sahrawi self-determination.
What is the Western Sahara dispute all about?
The Polisario Front, the political and military representative, does not recognise Morocco’s annexation of the territory following Spain’s withdrawal in 1975. It has been seeking a UN-supervised referendum for self-determination.
In 1976, it declared the independent Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic.
Decades of fighting drove at least 170,000 Indigenous people into refugee camps in Tindouf in neighbouring Algeria, which backs the Polisario Front.
The Polisario Front signed a UN-brokered ceasefire with Morocco in 1991. It called for a referendum within six months, but it was never held.
Morocco, which retains control of its lucrative phosphate and fishing resources in Western Sahara, claims historic and pre-colonial ties to the land and views the region as an integral part of its territory [“Greater Morocco”].
For decades, the US has provided military and diplomatic support to Morocco. But in 2020, Donald Trump recognised Moroccan sovereignty over the territory during his first term in office. Morocco soon established diplomatic ties with Israel as part of the so-called Abraham Accords.
The region is now the last United Nations-designated “non-self-governing territory” in Africa, where between 100,000 and 140,000 Moroccan military personnel are based.
Low-level fighting has also continued since the Polisario Front said it was resuming armed struggle in 2020.
Why is Morocco celebrating the failed UN resolution?
MINURSO was set up to monitor the 1991 ceasefire and hold a referendum in Western Sahara. The expiry of its mandate will likely boost Morocco’s stance on the referendum question, though its autonomy proposal has already been adopted by the UN.
On Saturday, according to a video report by the Reuters news agency, a festive atmosphere prevailed in the streets of El Aaiun, the capital of Western Sahara.
In the central Mechoua Square, dozens of people were wearing melfas, the traditional Sahrawi women’s garments, and long robes known as darra, as they waved Moroccan flags and displayed portraits of Morocco’s King Mohammed VI.
Selim Balouati Lakhloufi, a historian and researcher based in Morocco, said that Morocco is pleased because “diplomatic developments at the United Nations are supporting its strategy regarding the [disputed Western] Sahara”.
“The support of powers such as the United States, France and the United Kingdom for Morocco’s autonomy proposal strengthens its international position and is gradually shifting the debate away from the right to self-determination and the possibility of independence toward a solution based on autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty,” he told Al Jazeera.
What does this mean for the future of the Western Sahara?
The collapse of MINURSO’s mandate could escalate the dispute in the Western Sahara, according to aid organisations.
Oxfam has warned that losing MINURSO’s “monitoring and de-escalation functions risks undermining security and stability”.
Lakhloufi said that the UN mission’s expiry is also unfavourable for Sahrawi independence aspirations.
Regarding the future of the Western Sahara, he said that Morocco will likely continue to consolidate its territorial, economic and administrative control, while the Polisario Front will face greater difficulties in securing international support.
“The proposal for autonomy could end up becoming the main framework for negotiations, pushing independence further and further out of reach,” he added.

Australia Sells ANZAC Frigate-Building Shipyard to Chinese Company
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:23:32 UTC
23:23:32 KST

Victoria’s last shipyard capable of building and maintaining large warships for the Royal Australian Navy is being sold to a company partly owned by Hong Kong-based EMKC Group.
According to Australian Defence Magazine, the Williamstown shipyard is located near the entrance to the Port of Melbourne, Australia’s largest container port.
The sale of a strategic shipbuilding facility to a company with Hong Kong-based investors has raised concerns about potential risks to Australia’s national security.
China’s national security and intelligence laws, which also apply to organizations operating in Hong Kong, pose potential risks to companies headquartered there. As a result, Chinese intelligence agencies could take an interest in the deal.
The buyer is Australian company EMKC³, which specializes in real estate fund management and is partly owned by Hong Kong-based EMKC Group.
However, it remains unclear whether the Hong Kong company is its majority shareholder.
EMKC³ representative Felicity Richardson confirmed that the company has signed a contract to acquire the shipyard and is discussing potential future uses for the facility with key stakeholders.
The value of the deal has not been officially disclosed. The shipyard was put up for sale in 2024, with an estimated value of AUD 200 million.
The Williamstown shipyard dates back to 1858. It built all ten ANZAC-class frigates for the Royal Australian Navy and the Royal New Zealand Navy.
The shipyard also manufactured the superstructures and carried out the internal fit-out of two Canberra-class amphibious assault ships for the Royal Australian Navy: HMAS Canberra and HMAS Adelaide.
The facility completed its last shipbuilding projects in 2016, after which it laid off a significant portion of its workforce.
The sale of the Williamstown shipyard comes amid a major restructuring of Australia’s shipbuilding industry. The country is gradually phasing out its aging ANZAC-class frigates and moving toward acquiring new Japanese-designed New FFM multi-purpose frigates. Australia plans to acquire a total of 11 of these frigates, eight of which are expected to be built domestically.
Meanwhile, the Australian government is investing in new shipbuilding facilities to construct nuclear-powered submarines under the SSN-AUKUS program.

EU issues new threat to Serbia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:20:55 UTC
23:20:55 KST

EU issues new threat to Serbia
Serbia will need to sanction Russia in order to eventually join the EU, European Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos has said.
The Brussels official spelled out that condition just days after Serbia’s opposition Student List movement secured 52.5% of the vote in the snap parliamentary election, defeating former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic. While conceding defeat, Vucic warned of renewed EU pressure on Belgrade to impose economic restrictions on Moscow, which he had consistently refused to do citing key trading and cultural ties.
In an interview with Polish broadcaster TVP World on Tuesday, Kos was asked if it was possible for Serbia to become an EU member if it also refrained from slapping curbs on Moscow. Brussels has introduced 22 sanctions packages against Russia since February 2022.
She replied by saying the EU demands “strategic alignment” from possible new EU members as part of its pre-accession review.
“Probably, it will not be possible” for a country to join the bloc if it “isn’t aligning uh with us on… foreign policy and security policy, meaning being together in fighting Russia,” especially when it comes to the Ukraine conflict, the commissioner said.
However, Kos stressed that “we haven’t started yet to talk to the new [Serbian] government. So, first, they will have to have a new government and then we’ll see how we’ll be able to move in this field or not.”
There is currently no certainty on Student List’s agenda regarding Russia sanctions. One of its representatives, university professor Jovo Bakic, told RT Balkan earlier this week that the movement’s members “respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector.” Any restrictions imposed by “small Serbia” would have little effect on Moscow, but would be “symbolically very bad” for Belgrade, Bakic argued.
However, the Student List lead candidate, Ilija Srdanovic, did not explicitly rule out reconsidering Belgrade’s longstanding refusal to sanction Russia in an interview with RFE/RL. When pressed on the issue, he said that foreign policy should be “decided by the citizens of Serbia” rather than a single leader of a “very small group of people” in government.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday that Moscow hoped to maintain mutually beneficial relations with Serbia under the Student List leadership. “As you know, it takes two to tango,” he added.
Previously, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova slammed the “heavy-handed, unscrupulous manner,” in which the EU has tried to drive a wedge between Moscow and Belgrade.
Making Serbia join the sanctions against Russia “is not merely a political gesture… It means that Serbia would effectively be shooting itself in the foot by ceasing to receive supplies of our energy and by being unable to sell its own goods to us,” she insisted.

"They're alive, but weak": UAnimals reports on the fate of animals evacuated from Oleshky – videos
Pets and stray animals were evacuated to Ukrainian-controlled territory alongside residents of occupied Oleshky, which has been gripped by a humanitarian crisis.
Source: UAnimals, a Ukrainian animal rescue and welfare organisation, in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life).
Details: UAnimals reported that specialists are examining the cats and dogs to assess their condition. Although no owners have yet collected their pets, some have already contacted the organisation to ask about them.
The organisation said it began making arrangements to help the animals a day before they were evacuated from Oleshky. The organisation did not know exactly how many animals to expect, what species they were or what condition they were in, so it was "preparing for various scenarios".
Quote: "We made arrangements for wild animals to be transferred to a rehabilitation centre and for pets to undergo veterinary examinations before being placed in shelters if necessary.
We coordinated with veterinary clinics and shelters and prepared food, water, cages, pet carriers and other essentials."
Details: Two UAnimals teams, comprising four staff members and a vet, set off to meet the buses carrying the evacuees and their animals.
After the convoys crossed the border from Belarus, the dogs and cats were collected and taken to a veterinary clinic.
The latest figures show that more dogs than cats were evacuated. All the animals are now receiving the care and food they need.
Quote: "All the animals have been settled in and given food and water. Vets began examining them today. All are alive, although some are weak. We'll be able to provide more details about their health and the care they need once the examinations are complete.
We've already counted the animals and drawn up a list. The next step is to digitise the records for each animal so that we can work with the human rights commissioner's office to reunite those who have families with their owners."
Details: The organisation does not yet know exactly how many animals have been evacuated, as more are still arriving after their owners took them along to hospital.
Quote: "This is a complex humanitarian operation: new information continues to arrive and we're taking it into account in our further work. We will share details about the condition of the animals and assistance provided to them on our social media pages."
Background:
- On 31 October, the mission to evacuate the residents of Oleshky concluded. Evacuees were transported by bus from the occupied city, then flown to Belarus before reaching Ukrainian-controlled territory.
- Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights, reported that residents took their animals with them during the evacuation, including dogs, cats, a parrot and even a raccoon. A specially equipped vehicle with cages was brought in to transport them.
- The oldest person evacuated from Oleshky is 94 and the youngest is just over a year old. The evacuees came not only from Oleshky but also from neighbouring settlements. They sang Ukraine's national anthem on the buses.

Iran’s 40-Day War Changed How People Travel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:18:53 UTC
23:18:53 KST

Iran’s 40-Day War Changed How People Travel
Travel disruption can change more than the number of journeys people make. It can affect how far ahead they book, which transport options they consider and whether they travel at all.
MrBilit’s report on travel behaviour during the 40-day war examines these changes through activity on its platform. Its findings offer a picture of passengers responding to uncertainty, with different patterns .emerging across booking times, transport modes and destinations
The report provides insight into MrBilit as a platform influencing users’ travel decisions. Its figures should be understood as platform-level evidence, rather than a comprehensive measure of tourism across Iran
The Initial Shock: Cancellations and Falling Travel Demand
MrBilit recorded a 40% year-on-year decline in trips during the reporting month spanning February 20 to March 20, 2026. The report also shows that 75% of tickets purchased before the war were cancelled.
These figures illustrate two different aspects of disruption: a contraction in travel activity and the reversal of plans already made. For travel businesses, that distinction matters. Supporting passengers with existing bookings becomes an immediate operational priority, even as demand for new journeys falls.
Cancellations also require careful interpretation. A cancelled ticket confirms that a particular booking did not proceed; it does not necessarily establish whether the passenger later travelled by another route or means of transport.
Last-Minute Bookings Became More Common
The share of purchases made less than 24 hours before departure increased from 40% to 60%, a rise of 20 percentage points.
This shift suggests a shorter planning horizon among passengers using the platform. More purchasing decisions were concentrated close to departure, leaving less time between choosing a journey and taking it.
For travel providers, the practical implication is that booking lead time deserves attention alongside sales volume. The same number of bookings can present different operational challenges depending on whether they arrive weeks before departure or within the final day.
The figures do not, on their own, explain every passenger’s motivation. They do, however, show a measurable change in when users committed to their journeys.
When Flights Were Disrupted, Travellers Reconsidered Their Options
Among passengers whose flights were cancelled, MrBilit reports that 84% cancelled their journeys and 16% switched to overland travel. Bus ticket sales increased 200% on the first day of the war.
Alternative transport therefore helped some passengers continue travelling, while many others did not proceed with their journeys. Increased demand for buses should consequently be read alongside lost air journeys, rather than treated as evidence of growth across the entire travel market.
For travellers planning a new journey, checking available flight tickets on MrBilit can be a starting point for assessing air travel options. Before purchasing, passengers should review their itinerary and the ticket’s cancellation and refund conditions.
Where another transport option is available, comparing total journey time, departure and arrival points, and any required connections can help travellers assess whether it meets their needs.
Travel Demand Returned Unevenly Across Destinations
Tehran–Qom and Tehran–Mashhad were among the fastest-recovering domestic routes identified in the report. Southern destinations, including Kish, Qeshm, Bushehr and Chabahar, had not fully recovered demand when the report was prepared.
The contrast highlights the importance of examining individual routes. A rebound in one part of a booking platform does not establish that demand has returned equally across destinations.
It is also important to distinguish travel from leisure tourism. Tickets may be purchased for work, family visits, pilgrimage or other purposes. Without a breakdown of passengers’ motivations, recovering ticket demand cannot automatically be described as a recovery in holiday travel.
For destination businesses, transport bookings provide one useful signal. Accommodation demand, visitor spending and the purpose of travel would add further context when assessing the local tourism economy.
What the Findings Mean for Travel Planning
MrBilit’s findings demonstrate why travel disruption needs to be examined through several measures. Cancellations reveal what happened to existing plans. Booking lead times show when passengers committed to new journeys. Transport choices and route-level demand indicate how travel activity changed.
For passengers, the practical response is to assess the whole journey before making a purchase: the available service, its timing, any connections and the conditions attached to the ticket. This is particularly relevant when plans may need to change.
For the industry, the report offers a basis for asking more precise questions about recovery. Which journeys are returning? How close to departure are passengers booking? Are alternative transport options meeting their needs?
Answering those questions requires keeping the scope of the evidence clear. MrBilit’s report documents behaviour observed on its platform during a period of disruption. Its contribution is a detailed view of changing travel decisions, with lessons for how services can respond to passengers’ needs.

China's logistics sees improved performance as industrial upgrades support growth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
22:17:04 CST
23:17:04 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- China's logistics demand maintained steady growth in the first three quarters of the year, supported by industrial upgrading and resilient high-end manufacturing, official data showed Sunday.
The total value of national social logistics reached 280 trillion yuan (about 41.7 trillion U.S. dollars) in the January-September period, up 4.9 percent year on year, according to data from the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing.
In the first three quarters, the value of industrial goods logistics rose 5.3 percent year on year, contributing 78 percent to the growth of the total.
Within this growth, equipment manufacturing and high-tech manufacturing played a prominent leading role, with their shares rising to 37.6 percent and 18.3 percent, respectively, according to the federation.
Logistics volumes for new products such as smart wristbands, 3D printing equipment and sensors surged 77.1 percent, 62.5 percent and 16.4 percent year on year, respectively, highlighting an accelerated shift toward new and upgraded industrial logistics demand, the data showed.
From January to September, the total cost of social logistics reached 14.8 trillion yuan, up 4.2 percent year on year. The ratio of total social logistics costs to GDP stood at 13.8 percent, down 0.2 percentage points from the same period last year.
"The dividends of logistics cost reduction continue to be released to the real economy," said Liu Yuhang, chief engineer of the federation.
Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, Liu said that with the arrival of the e-commerce peak season and the year-end production rush, logistics demand is expected to be released in a concentrated manner.
High-quality logistics development will provide strong support for the recovery of the real economy and the achievement of the full-year economic and social development goals, he said. ■

Interview: China offers South African fruit growers opportunities to diversify exports, says industry representative
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
22:17:00 CST
23:17:00 KST

by Ntandoyenkosi Ncube
JOHANNESBURG, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- China offers South African fruit growers an opportunity to diversify their export markets and reduce reliance on traditional destinations, while its vast consumer market holds significant long-term growth potential, an industry representative has said.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, Pieter-Steyn de Wet, information manager at Hortgro-Cherries, which represents commercial cherry growers in South Africa, highlighted China's potential as a major export destination, noting that the country imported approximately 586,900 tonnes of cherries in 2025.
South Africa and China have signed a protocol on phytosanitary requirements for fresh cherries, paving the way for South African cherries to enter the Chinese market. The fruit could also benefit from China's zero-tariff treatment for qualifying products from African countries with which it has diplomatic relations.
"Zero-tariff access enhances the competitiveness of South African cherries by reducing landed costs for Chinese importers," de Wet said.
"While zero-tariff access is an important advantage, it will not be sufficient on its own," de Wet said, warning that exporters must compete through "efficient logistics, consistent quality, reliable supply, and competitive pricing."
Beyond the immediate trade prospects, access to China could support the continued expansion of South Africa's burgeoning cherry sector. "Access to China provides a critical outlet for our scaling production and will encourage continued investment in orchards, packhouse capacity, and cold-chain infrastructure," de Wet said.
However, he cautioned that "investment and export growth will ultimately depend on market demand, sustained profitability, and our international competitiveness."
Beyond cherries, China could also serve as an alternative destination for South Africa's broader range of stone fruits, buffering growers against logistics bottlenecks and geopolitical disruptions affecting shipping routes through the Middle East.
"South African stone fruit offers promising avenues in China," de Wet said, noting that protocols governing the export of peaches, apricots, plums and nectarines had already been signed, with commercial shipments expanding.
"Continued investment in market development, consumer insights, product quality, and reliable supply chains will be essential to unlocking this potential," de Wet said.
To capitalize on these opportunities, establishing a lasting presence in China will require South African exporters to navigate stiff competition from established suppliers, high transport costs, logistical bottlenecks and stringent phytosanitary requirements, he said.
Describing the Chinese market as "highly discerning," de Wet emphasized that long-term success also hinges on strict adherence to local consumer preferences and quality expectations.
Closer cooperation between South Africa and China in agricultural research, post-harvest technology and trade promotion could further deepen bilateral agricultural ties, he said.
"Our long-term objective is to build a diversified, competitive, and sustainable agricultural export sector that delivers fair returns for producers, creates jobs, and contributes meaningfully to economic growth," de Wet said. ■

Feature: Dragon boat races return to Cambodia's Takeo, reviving vibrant, centuries-old regatta tradition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
22:16:30 CST
23:16:30 KST

TAKEO, Cambodia, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Under the blazing sun in southern Cambodia's Takeo province, a sprawling lake came alive this weekend as hundreds of locals raced dragon boats, reviving a vibrant, age-old regatta tradition for the Water Festival.
Framed by cheering crowds that lined the shores of Daun Keo city's Takeo Lake, 36 dragon boats and their crews turned the two-day weekend spectacle into a theater of pure speed. The banks erupted in roaring excitement each time a favored boat surged across the finish line, leaving its rivals in the wake.
For 22-year-old spectator Huch Sreynea, the spectacle was an electric bridge across the centuries. She told Xinhua on Sunday that she felt thrilled to see the vibrant boat races, adding that this regatta was held to honor Cambodia's naval forces of ancient times.
That living history dates back to the late 11th century during the ancient Khmer Empire, when naval forces honed their skills on the water.
Celebrated in the Southeast Asian nation, the Water Festival also marks the end of the annual rainy season and the unique seasonal reversal of the Tonle Sap River's flow, which connects the Tonle Sap Lake with the Mekong River.
For 20-year-old university student Chhin Lida, the festival does more than just keep ancient legacies alive -- it acts as a powerful magnet for tourism.
"This event also helps boost the provincial economy by attracting more tourists," she told Xinhua.
Walking through the bustling fairgrounds, Lida noted that the festival offered a rich tapestry of local flavors and sights -- from lively food stalls and "One Village, One Product" showcases to traditional arts and night-time fireworks.
At its heart, Lida reflected, the festival is a deep breath of gratitude: a salute to resilient ancestors who defended the realm, and a quiet "thank you" to the rivers and rains that sustain the land.
The excitement on the water was shared by the athletes themselves.
Ly Sophal, a 37-year-old dragon boat racer competing in Takeo province for the first time, proudly led a crew of 12 members.
"The regatta is an age-old tradition deep within the heart of the Cambodian people and a prime occasion to attract both national and international tourists to Takeo," he told Xinhua. "I am absolutely thrilled to see such massive crowds of spectators cheering us on."
Leang Chanthon, another 37-year-old competitor, echoed the fierce pride of the day. To him, every stroke of the paddle is a tribute to the past.
He explained that the regatta stands as a living monument to the Khmer naval forces who fought and triumphed over their enemies on these very waters centuries ago.
"It is vital for us to preserve this uniquely beautiful tradition for our younger generations," Chanthon told Xinhua. ■

Sri Lanka's fuel import bill in first 9 months of 2026 jumps 51.5 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
22:16:24 CST
23:16:24 KST

COLOMBO, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka's fuel imports expenditure from January to September 2026 increased by 51.5 percent from the same period last year, according to data released by the Central Bank of Sri Lanka.
The bank's latest External Sector Performance report, dated Oct. 30, showed that the country spent 4.49 billion U.S. dollars on fuel imports during the first nine months of 2026, compared to 2.96 billion dollars on fuel imports during the same period in 2025.
Fuel import spending, however, declined slightly in September. Sri Lanka spent 415.1 million dollars on fuel imports during the month, down 5.8 percent from 440.7 million dollars in September 2025. September 2026 also marked the country's fifth consecutive month of fuel imports expenditure decline.
Despite the downward trajectory, the overall fuel import bill remained significantly higher than during the same period last year, said the bank.
The increase came amid higher domestic fuel prices following an escalation of conflict in the Middle East.
Disruptions to global energy supply chains, including restrictions affecting petroleum shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, also pushed up crude oil and petroleum product prices, as well as freight and insurance costs. ■

Israel election: When will government be formed, who will lead it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:16:14 UTC
23:16:14 KST

Israel election: When will government be formed, who will lead it?
President Isaac Herzog must tap a candidate to form a new government after results are certified by November 10, with fraught negotiations likely to follow.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his coalition’s parliamentary majority following legislative elections on October 27.
But a bloc of Jewish parties opposing Netanyahu also failed to win a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, leaving Israel without a clear path to a new government.
What’s ahead is likely weeks of political wrangling as Israel’s disparate factions weigh possible governing arrangements, including a unity government bringing rival factions together or a minority government reliant on outside support. If they fail to reach an agreement, Israel could head back to the polls.
Here’s what you should know:
What are the final results of Israel’s elections?
The pro-Netanyahu coalition won 53 seats:
- Likud – 27
- United Torah Judaism – 7
- Otzma Yehudit – 7
- Shas – 6
- Religious Zionism – 6
A bloc of Jewish parties opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats:
- Yashar – 21
- B’Yachad – 12
- The Democrats – 8
- Yisrael Beytenu – 7
Arab-led parties won 19 seats:
- Joint List – 11
- Ra’am – 8
That leaves all existing blocs short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, meaning some parties would have to realign or join forces across bloc lines to form a new government.
What happens next?
Israel’s election results must be officially certified and presented to President Isaac Herzog by November 4.
The new Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on November 10.
Herzog must task one incoming Knesset member with forming a new government by November 11. He is expected to make his decision with input from party leaders, selecting the candidate he believes has the best chance of building a coalition.
The candidate commissioned by Herzog has 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible extension of 14 days.
Who will Herzog nominate first to form a government?
He has not said yet, but the most likely candidates are Netanyahu or former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar party received the most votes in the opposition bloc.
According to Israel’s Yedioth Ahronoth media, Eisenkot may have an edge over Netanyahu as some Arab-led parties consider endorsing him in a bid to oust Netanyahu.
Herzog, for his part, has urged Israeli politicians to move away from rigid partisan stances and look for “creative solutions” that will lead to a new government and avoid a second round of elections.
Before the election, Herzog said he would do everything he could to spare the country another election cycle, even if that means pressing for a national unity government that brings together rivals Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
Could the opposition bloc join forces with Arab-led parties?
It is unclear.
Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have previously ruled out partnering with the Arab-led parties.
Former Prime Minister Ehud Barak, however, has said he believes they “can change their mind”, arguing that Netanyahu would do in their position.
“If Netanyahu had a similar problem, he would immediately invite Mansour Abbas”, the leader of Ra’am and “give him the role of a minister of interior”, Barak told France 24 on Friday.
Abbas himself has signalled a willingness to work the opposition camp, saying Eisenkot’s conditions would not pose an obstacle for his party, according to Israel’s Channel 12.
Yousef Jabareen from the Arab-led Joint List has also said that his party is ready for the “ousting of the Netanyahu government”.
“The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership,” he wrote on X.
Even if Arab-led parties do not formally join the opposition’s coalition, they could prop it up from outside by helping it pass a confidence vote in the Knesset.
Raluca Ganea, co-founder of Israeli civil society group Zazim, told Al Jazeera that a coalition between the opposition bloc and the Arab-led parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel “is the only path forward for Israeli democracy as a whole”.
What happens if no one can form a government?
If Herzog’s first candidate fails to form a government within the 42 days, the Israeli president has the option of asking another Knesset member to try to do so within 28 days. If that candidate also fails, a majority of Knesset members could put forward a third candidate, who would have a final 14 days to try to assemble one.
Even without a coalition commanding at least 61 seats, a candidate could still try to form a minority government by relying on outside support from smaller parties, including Arab-led parties, or negotiate a power-sharing arrangement with alternating prime ministers.
If none of these options succeed and deadlock persists, the Knesset would be formally dissolved, and Israelis would return to the polls for another round of elections.
Those elections would have to be called within 90 days.
Who is in charge in the meantime?
Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed.
If the process drags out, that could leave Israel’s longest-serving prime minister in power for months more, even if he ultimately fails to become part of the next governing coalition.

Insecurity displaces 1,150 people in Sudan’s North Darfur in 3 days: UN migration agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:15:43 UTC
23:15:43 KST

Adel Abdelrheem and Rania Abushamala
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
Some 1,150 people fled four villages in Sudan’s western North Darfur state over three days due to worsening insecurity, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Sunday.
In a statement, the UN agency said its field teams estimated that an additional 1,150 people were displaced from the villages of Muzbat, Oreri, Tari and Umm Haraz in Um Baru locality between Oct. 29 and 31.
Some affected families moved to other locations within the locality, while others crossed the border into Chad, it said.
The security situation remains highly tense and volatile, the agency added.
On Monday, the IOM reported that 895 people had been displaced from three villages in Um Baru on Oct. 24.
The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese army have been fighting since April 2023 following a dispute over integrating the paramilitary group into the military. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced 13 million.
The RSF controls Sudan’s five Darfur states, apart from parts of North and West Darfur that remain under army control. The army holds most of the country’s remaining states, including the capital, Khartoum.
Darfur accounts for roughly one-fifth of Sudan’s territory, which spans more than 1.8 million square kilometers. Most of the country’s 53 million people live in army-controlled areas.

Ukraine: Russian attacks leave tens of thousands without power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:13:00 UTC
23:13:00 KST

Ukraine: Russian attacks leave tens of thousands without power
Published October 31, 2026last updated November 1, 2026
What you need to know
- Russian strikes leave tens of thousands across Ukraine without power, including in the capital Kyiv
- Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire limited to Kherson region set to expire
- Oleshky civilians arrive in Ukrainian territory from Belarus
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says preparations for talks with US and Russia underway after meeting with Turkey's Recep Tayyip Erdogan
Here is a roundup of events from Russia's war in Ukraine on Saturday and Sunday, October 31 and November 1:
WATCH: Oleshky evacuees recount survival under occupation
Residents evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky have arrived in Ukrainian-held territory after a rare localized ceasefire enabled civilians to leave.
Speaking to DW, evacuees described years of isolation, food shortages, and regular shelling, with some saying they survived by eating grass and dogs as supplies ran out.
The rescue operation brought families back together at a reception point in northern Ukraine, where relatives, volunteers, and local residents welcomed the arrivals after their journey through Russia and Belarus.
Preparations for trilateral talks underway, Zelenskyy says after Erdogan meeting
Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with his Turkish counterpart Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Istanbul on Saturday evening for talks that the Ukrainian president said included preparations for a three-way summit between Ukraine, Russia and the United States.
He said the meeting would be held in the first half of November.
"President Erdogan and I discussed the prospects for this format and other possibilities, including ways to involve Turkey and all of Europe, as well as the possibility of holding meetings here in Turkey," Zelenskyy said.
"At every level, Russia must be sent signals that there is no alternative to peace and that support for Ukraine will not diminish."
Previous rounds of talks between Ukraine and Russia brokered by Turkey failed to yield a lasting peace agreement.
Describing the meetings as "important and substantive," Zelenskyy said he and Erdogan had also discussed security issues concerning shipping through the Black Sea.
"This includes food security, and today President Erdogan and I agreed to work on a Black Sea grain corridor to ensure that the corridor exists and operates effectively," the Ukrainian leader told a press conference.
Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire for Kherson set to expire
A ceasefire limited to the Kherson region in eastern Ukraine that was brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump was set to expire on Sunday evening, after neither Russia nor Ukraine announced an extension.
The rare truce, which began on Tuesday, is the longest since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The ceasefire allowed for a humanitarian mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
While neither side reported violations of the ceasefire, Russian strikes continued overnight, with fresh power outages reported across Ukraine on Sunday, its energy ministry and president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainian strikes on the Russian-occupied region of Luhansk killed at least four people since Sunday evening, Russian-backed local authorities said.
Russian strikes leave vast numbers of Ukrainian homes without power
Hundreds of thousands of households lost electricity after overnight Russian strikes hit energy infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said.
In a post on X, the Ukrainian president said energy infrastructure in four regions — Dnipro, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, and Khmelnytskyi — had been struck.
"Substations, transformers, and power lines that supply electricity to our people's homes were targeted. Repair crews are working everywhere. As of now, hundreds of thousands of families remain without power," Zelenskyy said Sunday.
He added that "massive Russian attacks on Ukraine's other critical infrastructure are also continuing unabated."
"The intensity of the strikes is very high," he said, accusing Russia of seeking to exploit Ukraine's shortage of interceptors used to shoot down ballistic missiles.
Zelenskyy repeated his call to the US, Europe and Ukraine's other partners to do more to deliver missiles and other weaponry to better defend against the Russian attacks.
"These deliveries cannot take years. Russia is destroying infrastructure and killing our people right now, and it is betting on ballistic missiles this winter. Accordingly, decisions on air defense must also be implemented now," the Ukrainian president said.
Kremlin wants initial Ukraine talks without Europe
Russia wants the opening rounds of renewed peace negotiations to involve only Moscow, Kyiv and Washington, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said.
Asked whether European countries should participate, Ushakov pointed to Russia's existing contacts with the United States.
"We have working contacts with the Americans," Interfax quoted him as saying. It was therefore "logical" for at least the first rounds to take place in a trilateral format, he added.
Russia reports major damage after drone attack near refinery
A drone attack caused "significant damage" to an industrial facility east of Moscow, a Russian governor said, following Ukrainian reports of a strike on a major oil refinery.
Nizhny Novgorod Governor Gleb Nikitin reported a "massive drone attack" overnight, saying more than 100 drones were destroyed. Preliminary information indicated no casualties, he added.
Nikitin did not identify the damaged facility. Ukrainian media reported that the target was the Kstovo oil refinery, describing it as one of Russia's largest.
The reports could not be independently verified.
Authorities said they were taking steps to keep fuel available at gas stations.
Russia said Ukraine had resumed attacks on its refineries after a pause. US President Donald Trump had pressured Kyiv to stop such strikes, blaming them for rising diesel prices.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian oil and gas facilities in response to Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.

The Ukrainian president also plans to meet Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew, the Istanbul-based Orthodox Christian leader.
US warns Russia of a 'mass casualty' plot to attack Moscow
The US embassy in Russia warned there was "a credible threat of a mass casualty event" at a historical site in southern Moscow.
"The US government is coordinating with appropriate Russian authorities on a response," the US embassy in Moscow said in a post on X.
The alleged plot would target the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve, a sprawling complex of palaces and gardens built under the orders of Empress Catherine the Great in the late 18th century.
Russia's federal law enforcement agency, the FSB, said it received the warning and was doing "appropriate work" in response to it, according to Russian news agencies.
Ukraine says it hit Russian rocket fuel factory
Ukraine's military said it struck a factory producing solid rocket fuel in Russia's Rostov region, setting a warehouse ablaze and damaging four production workshops.
The attack on the Kamensky plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky involved drones and Neptune missiles, according to the Ukrainian account.
The military said the plant supplies fuel for ammunition used by Russia's Uragan, Smerch and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, as well as other missiles and air-launched weapons.
Ukraine also reported strikes on four Russian military supply depots in occupied parts of the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Luhansk regions.
The claims have not been independently verified.
Ukraine welcomes civilians from Oleshky after complex evacuation effort
The first evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky have reached Ukrainian-controlled territory amid a localized ceasefire.
Oleshky, near the front line in the southern Kherson region, has been occupied by Russia since 2022. In recent weeks, the town has faced a severe humanitarian crisis.
Both sides have recently agreed to a localized ceasefire to extract the estimated 2,000 civilians still in Oleshky, down from its pre-invasion population of 24,000.
Moscow and Kyiv credited the US first lady, Melania Trump, with brokering the truce.
Residents were given a choice to go to Russia or travel via Belarus to the part of Ukraine controlled by Kyiv.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the initiative required "an enormous amount of work."
He said evacuees included a 1-year-old baby and a 94-year-old resident of Oleshky. The evacuees brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon, according to Lubinets.
He expressed hope that the Oleshky arrangement can be replicated elsewhere.
The truce started on Tuesday and is due to end on Sunday night.

International Digi Yatra trials to begin at 7 airports for Indian nationals this year for wider rollout in 2027: Government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:12:03 UTC
23:12:03 KST

File photo: India will trial Digi Yatra for international passengers at seven airports over the next three months
NEW DELHI: Travelling abroad from India could soon be a seamless experience just like taking domestic flights with Digi Yatra (DY). India will hold trials for international passengers at seven airports in the three months of this year, allowing eligible Indian nationals holding e-passports to use DY at designated airport touchpoints while travelling on select flights operated by Air India and IndiGo.The aviation ministry said trials are being conducted at Delhi, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Cochin, Mumbai, Chennai and Amritsar airports. “Eligible passengers will be able to use the facility at terminal entry points, security hold areas (SHA) and boarding gates, wherever the required infrastructure is available. Feedback received during the trial period will inform the planning of a wider rollout in 2027,” it said in a statement.To access this facility, eligible Indian nationals will need to create an e-passport-based “verifiable credential” (VC) through DY mobile application. “The process involves scanning the machine readable zone (MRZ) of e-passport, reading the embedded chip using the near field communication (NFC) feature of a compatible smartphone, capturing a selfie and verifying the details. The credential is stored in the passenger’s Digi Yatra wallet on the device and can be used at airport touchpoints enabled for the trials,” the statement said.
The facility will complement, and not replace, existing travel processes. “Passengers must continue to carry their travel documents and complete all mandatory airline document checks, immigration procedures and other applicable travel formalities,” it added.IndiGo said eligible passengers can upload their boarding pass to the Digi Yatra app. After completing mandatory document verification at airline check-in counter, they can proceed through the security hold area and boarding gates using DY biometric face authentication.IndiGo chief digital and information officer Neetan Chopra said: “At IndiGo, we are committed to redefining air travel by making it more seamless, efficient, and customer centric, and we believe that technology can be a key catalyst in this evolution. Having been a key part of the technical proof of concept earlier this year, we are pleased to partner with Digi Yatra for the launch of these international passenger trials. Expanding secure digital identity and biometric technologies to international departures is a significant step forward for Indian aviation. We are committed to delivering a seamless travel experience for our customers at every touchpoint. The successful deployment of this technology marks an important step in reimagining the airport experience, combining enhanced security, convenience and operational efficiency. As the aviation industry continues to evolve, such innovations will play a key role in shaping the future of passenger travel.”Digi Yatra Foundation CEO Suresh Khadakbhavi said: “Digi Yatra has demonstrated how digital identity can simplify domestic air travel. With the start of international passenger trials, we are taking an important step towards extending this experience to eligible Indian nationals travelling internationally.
Interoperability with global frameworks such as IATA’s One ID and ICAO’s Public Key Directory (PKD) will be an important part of this journey, helping explore how e-passport-based digital credentials can enable more seamless and secure passenger journeys across borders, while keeping passenger consent, privacy and security central to the experience.”Digi Yatra platform has over 2.6 crore users at present and has enabled more than 11 crore journeys across 39 domestic airports, serving domestic airlines. A further 25 domestic airports are planned to be covered by 2027. “The aviation ministry remains committed to leveraging technology to improve airport operations and facilitate seamless air travel, in line with govt's vision of Digital India and ease of flying.”

Andriy Gyurov and Georgi Kandev, as well as Iliana Iotova and Kiril Vilchev, are competing in the second round. The Bulgarian Telegraph Agency reports this, according to UNN.
Details
Nearly 6.6 million people will have the opportunity to vote. Election Day begins at 7:00 a.m. and ends at 8:00 p.m., but no later than 9:00 p.m. if there are voters who have not voted before the polling station closes, according to the schedule of the Central Election Commission (CEC). At polling stations outside the country, voting also begins at 7:00 a.m. and ends at 8:00 p.m., or at 9:00 p.m., local time, respectively
According to available information, 9,373 polling stations in the country are operating with machine voting. Two machines have been installed at 2,249 of them. A total of 11,622 machines have been provided for voting. On July 30, 2026, Parliament decided to introduce fully machine-based voting at polling stations where more than 300 voters are registered.
On July 30, 2026, Parliament lifted the restriction limiting the number of polling stations outside diplomatic and consular missions in countries that are not members of the European Union to 20. Voters with visual impairments or limited mobility will be able to vote at specially designated locations – predominantly on the first floor of buildings housing precinct election commissions (PECs). Immediately after the end of Election Day is announced, but not earlier than 8:00 p.m., the PEC establishes the voting results, draws up the protocol, and submits it to the district election commission (DEC). The work of PECs outside the country is similar
According to available information, the CEC is to announce the final results of the presidential and vice-presidential elections within three days after voting.
Previously
In Bulgaria, they failed to elect a president in the first round. Incumbent President Iliana Iotova received 34.6% of the vote, while Andriy Gyurov received 32%.
