Messages from the Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow hacking groups appeared on the agency’s main website and regional portals, Rosstat told the RBC news website. Among them was a message in Belarusian reading: “No one will escape accountability.”
Both groups are designated as extremist and banned in Russia.
Rosstat said the attacks took place between Oct. 29 and Nov. 1 and were carefully planned, targeting several areas simultaneously and involving specialists with different expertise operating from a wide range of locations.

The same hacking groups claimed responsibility for a July 2025 attack on Aeroflot’s IT systems that caused widespread disruption. Russian prosecutors confirmed that a cyberattack had taken place and opened a criminal investigation into unauthorized access to computer systems.
In January 2025, Silent Crow claimed to have stolen a database containing 2 billion records on property owners from state real estate registry Rosreestr. The agency denied a leak, although journalists were able to verify some of the information the hackers published.

The Myth of ‘Stable Russia’: Why Washington Must Stop Fearing Russia’s Collapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:06:00 UTC
23:06:00 KST

Daily reality for millions of Ukrainians is facing strikes by Russian kamikaze drones and ballistic missiles. Yet, amid the destruction, we are forced to confront a deeply painful paradox: the weapons raining down on our cities are heavily powered by American microelectronics.
For years, Western – and particularly Washington – policymakers have been paralyzed by a phantom fear: “What happens if Russia collapses?”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This anxiety over a fragmented, nuclear-armed state has led to a slow, drip-feed approach to arming Ukraine. But while the West worries about preserving a stable Russia, it is blind to the fact that the so-called “Russian Bear” has devolved into a “hollow imperial machine,” propped up entirely by Western corporate negligence.
The 2026 paradox
Russia is incapable of manufacturing even basic circuit boards for its jet-powered drones and missiles. All these “Shaheds,” “Lancets,” and “Iskanders” fly using microchips smuggled through Central Asia. This is not a matter of old, pre-war stockpiles.
According to official data from Ukraine’s Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy, recent examinations of downed “Shahed-238” drones and “Iskander-M” missiles revealed hundreds of foreign components, prominently including parts from US giants like Texas Instruments, Amphenol, and ON Semiconductor.
Kallas Rebukes Lavrov Over ‘Lies’ and Falsehoods at G20
Shockingly, some of these microchips were manufactured as recently as 2026.
This proves that the smuggling networks are active right now. While these Western corporations may not sell directly to Russia, their products are systematically bypassing export controls, flooding through front companies in intermediary countries. How can the West fear Russian military might when that very might is entirely dependent on bypassed US export controls?
The collapse is already happening
Russian President Vladimir Putin’s regime is a house of cards. The West must stop fearing its collapse and look at the reality on the ground.
Logistics are burning: The unwritten pact between people and regime of stability in Russia is dead. Massive fires at critical logistics hubs and data-centers, like the giant Wildberries, Ozon and Yandex warehouses, are no coincidence. The regime hides military dual-use goods inside civilian supply chains, and as a result, the civilian network is crumbling.
Economic and infrastructural suicide: Top Russian economists openly predict severe shortages. To sustain the military meat grinder—which consumes over 1,000 Russian lives daily – the regime is draining its economy of labor.
Furthermore, domestic infrastructure is rotting away: as federal budgets are aggressively funneled into the military-industrial complex, regional utility systems and public housing infrastructure (JKH) are facing unprecedented systemic failures and physical decay, leaving ordinary citizens to freeze or suffer chronic grid collapses.
The North Korea state is impossible: Some believe Putin will turn Russia into an isolated, manageable totalitarian camp. But you cannot lock down the largest landmass on Earth with people who have already tasted freedom and global integration. As Moscow tightens the screws to feed its war machine, regional elites will inevitably push back to save their populations from the Kremlin’s grinder.
Ultimately, the regions will choose development and democracy over imperial ruin – things the federal center, controlled by Moscow’s mafia-like “Ozero” cooperative and security-criminal structures of the Federal Security Service (FSB), has always denied them.
Military collapse: Beneath the Kremlin’s aggressive rhetoric and nuclear threats lies a hollowed-out system. Russia is no longer the military superpower it claims to be. Its defense-industrial complex, built on the legacy of the USSR (including Ukrainian factories and engineers) and now entirely dependent on stolen Western technology and components smuggled through gray markets, is facing a systemic collapse.
When a regime that claims to rival NATO is reduced to begging for artillery shells from North Korea and kamikaze drones from Iran, it is a clear signal: the sanctions are working, and the Ukrainian resistance is bleeding the empire dry. The recent catastrophic failures of Russia’s prized strategic weapons, such as the Sarmat missile program, only highlight this irreversible degradation.
The call to Washington
As lawmakers in the US Senate and officials in the FBI and Department of Commerce debate “escalation,” American technology continues to flow into Russian weapons. The hesitation in Washington does not prevent Russia’s collapse; it merely prolongs the agony and costs countless Ukrainian lives.
It is time for the West to abandon the illusion of a stable Russia. The FBI and the Department of Commerce must aggressively dismantle these gray-market supply chains.
You cannot defeat an enemy if your own technology is unknowingly – or indifferently – supplying its arsenal. Stop holding back long-range capabilities, cut off the smuggled lifelines, and help Ukraine finish the job. The hollow imperial machine is already burning; it is time to let it fall:first to the side of the road of history, and then into a deep ditch.
The resulting bottom line
It would seem that the only real thing Russia is currently capable of is acts of terror and the genocide of Ukrainians – as well as of its own multi-ethnic population.
It is time to drop the fear of Russia’s transformation and give Ukraine the full means to dismantle this aggressive machine once and for all. Stop holding back and playing it safe. Arm Ukraine decisively, so we can finally end the war that Putin is too terrified to stop.

Swiss foreign minister makes first North Korea visit since 2003 as diplomatic office reopens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:03:21 UTC
23:03:21 KST

Switzerland is renewing direct talks with North Korea as tensions rise on the peninsula. Seoul hopes the Swiss office will help it engage with Pyongyang.
Switzerland has formally reopened its diplomatic office in North Korea as Ignazio Cassis became the first Swiss foreign minister to visit the country since 2003.
Cassis visited Pyongyang on 29 and 30 October before travelling to Seoul. In a statement issued on Saturday, the Swiss foreign ministry said the trip aimed to restore direct political dialogue with North Korea as it looks to maintain contact with both sides of the divided peninsula.
The office restarted operations on 19 October. It falls under the Swiss embassy in Beijing, which remains responsible for diplomatic and consular relations with North Korea. Switzerland’s previous office in Pyongyang handled humanitarian cooperation and closed in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The two countries have maintained diplomatic relations since 1974, but regular political consultations stopped after 2019.
Bern said the office would allow Switzerland to deal directly with North Korean authorities and follow developments in the region.
Talks in Pyongyang
During his visit, Cassis met with North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui and Jo Yong Won, secretary of the ruling Workers’ Party’s Central Committee.
His discussions with Choe covered restoring political dialogue, security on the Korean Peninsula and wider security challenges in Europe and Asia.
Speaking to Swiss news agency Keystone-ATS on Saturday, Cassis said he had offered Switzerland’s help in facilitating dialogue to ease tensions on the peninsula. He said the proposal appeared to have been well received.
North Korea’s state news agency KCNA said on Saturday that the two ministers discussed diplomatic cooperation and international issues in a "friendly atmosphere." It did not provide a detailed account of the discussions.
Asked by Euronews whether the office could support wider European dialogue with Pyongyang, a Swiss foreign ministry spokesperson said the department had nothing to add to Saturday’s statement.
Seoul hopes for renewed engagement
Cassis also made a trip to Seoul on 30 and 31 October, meeting National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac and senior foreign ministry official Jeong Yeon-du.
He briefed Jeong on his Pyongyang talks. Jeong expressed hope that the Swiss office would help South Korea engage with the North, according to Seoul’s foreign ministry.
The visit came amid renewed military tensions. North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles towards the sea on Thursday, according to South Korea’s military, a day after Seoul renewed its call for military talks to prevent accidental border clashes.
In a separate statement on Sunday, South Korea’s foreign ministry said Foreign Minister Cho Hyun had urged support for dialogue between the two Koreas at a G20 meeting in Atlanta.
Switzerland has helped monitor the armistice that halted fighting in the Korean War since 1953 through the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission, based at Panmunjom. Cassis also met the head of the Swiss delegation to discuss the security situation.

====================================================================================================

Estrogen therapy linked to fewer signs of Alzheimer’s disease in brain tissue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:00:55 UTC
23:00:55 KST

Women who use estrogen-only hormone therapy during menopause may have a lower risk of developing the brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease. A large analysis of patient data found that those who used the therapy had less physical evidence of the disease in their brains and better memory test scores. The research was published in the journal Neurology.
Alzheimer’s disease disproportionately affects women, who make up more than two thirds of all patients worldwide. Researchers have investigated whether the natural decline of estrogen during menopause contributes to this disparity. Estrogen helps regulate physiological processes that keep the brain healthy, including inflammation and the integrity of the blood brain barrier. This barrier is a cellular filter that shields the brain from harmful substances in the bloodstream.
Past research on whether menopausal hormone therapy helps protect against dementia has yielded mixed results. Some trials suggested a protective effect, while others found either no benefit or an increased risk of cognitive decline. Variations in the timing of the treatment, the specific chemical formulation used, and the genetic backgrounds of the patients have made it difficult to draw a definitive conclusion.
To understand the relationship better, Stanford University psychiatry and behavioral sciences researcher Jennifer L. Bruno and colleagues examined records from thousands of older women. The research team wanted to see if they could link the use of estrogen-only hormone therapy to physical indicators of Alzheimer’s disease in the brain. They also looked at clinical diagnoses and memory test results.
The researchers analyzed information from two independent, large databases. The first was the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center, which collects data from dozens of research centers across the United States.
The team focused on a specific group of female participants aged fifty and older. They separated these women into two categories: those who reported using estrogen-only menopausal hormone therapy and those who had never used it. Women who used a combination of estrogen and progestin were excluded from the main analysis.
Using this first database, Bruno and her team looked at autopsy records for 2,959 deceased women. Of these participants, 258 had used estrogen-only hormone therapy. The researchers compared the two groups based on a standardized scoring system that measures three distinct signs of Alzheimer’s disease in brain tissue. These signs include the buildup of amyloid proteins and the presence of tangled nerve fibers, both of which disrupt normal brain function.
The team found that women who had used estrogen-only hormone therapy had a measurably lower chance of exhibiting advanced Alzheimer’s disease pathology at the time of their death. The autopsies also revealed that these women had fewer signs of cerebrovascular disease, such as small strokes or damaged blood vessels in the brain. A secondary analysis of the autopsy data showed that the lower odds of brain pathology were specifically linked to a formulation called conjugated estrogens, rather than a different formulation known as estradiol.
Next, the researchers evaluated the clinical records of a large group of living patients from the same national database. This group included 1,841 hormone therapy users and 17,561 non-users. The researchers found that women in the hormone therapy group had lower odds of receiving a clinical dementia diagnosis. These women also showed fewer symptoms of general memory and functional decline compared to those who had not used the therapy.
To understand how hormone therapy might influence brain health while patients are still living, the researchers turned to a second database. The Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative contains detailed biological measurements from living participants. From this dataset, the team identified 110 women who used estrogen-only hormone therapy and 1,948 who did not.
The researchers examined biological markers in the participants’ blood plasma and cerebrospinal fluid, which is the liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord. They measured the levels of amyloid proteins, which can clump together and form the plaques characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease.
Women who used the hormone therapy had higher levels of a specific amyloid protein, amyloid-beta 42, in their blood and spinal fluid. In these fluids, higher levels indicate that less amyloid is being deposited as plaques in the brain, so this pattern points to less Alzheimer’s-related amyloid buildup. Brain scans using a technology called positron emission tomography did not show a difference in amyloid accumulation between the two groups. The blood and fluid tests are generally more sensitive to early protein changes than the brain scans, suggesting that hormone therapy might be associated with lower levels of early stage amyloid buildup.
The team also reviewed cognitive test scores from the imaging database participants. They found that hormone therapy users scored higher on tests measuring immediate verbal memory and learning ability.
The researchers conducted exploratory analyses to see if genetics played a role. They separated the participants based on whether they carried the APOE e4 gene variant, which is a known risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease. The autopsy data showed that the hormone therapy was associated with less brain pathology only in women who did not carry this high-risk gene. The clinical benefits, such as a lower chance of a dementia diagnosis, were visible in both genetic groups.
Because this was an observational study, it cannot prove that the hormone therapy caused the improved brain health. It is possible that women who choose to take hormone therapy are generally healthier or have better access to healthcare to begin with. Unmeasured lifestyle factors could also contribute to the observed differences between the two groups.
The type of therapy examined in the study also limits how broadly the results apply. Estrogen-only hormone therapy is typically prescribed only to women who have had their uterus removed, because taking estrogen without progesterone can increase the risk of uterine cancer. Most women who undergo menopausal hormone therapy take a combined estrogen and progestogen regimen. The protective associations seen with estrogen alone might not extend to the combined treatments that are far more common in everyday medical practice.
The average age at which women in the study reported using hormone therapy was around seventy. Current medical guidelines usually recommend starting hormone therapy during the onset of menopause, typically in a woman’s late forties or early fifties, and stopping by age sixty. The researchers noted that a small subset of women in their data who started the therapy before age sixty also showed a lower chance of developing Alzheimer’s pathology, though the result was not statistically significant due to the small sample size.
Future research will need to follow patients over time in controlled trials to better evaluate how menopausal hormone therapy impacts physical markers of Alzheimer’s disease. Such studies could help medical professionals weigh the risks and benefits of prescribing the treatment to older women.
The study, “Association between menopausal hormone therapy and Alzheimer’s disease neuropathology,” was authored by Jennifer L. Bruno, Jacob S Shaw, and S.M. Hadi Hosseini.

Life is full of suffering – but leaning into moments of pleasure can allow the nervous system to rest | Nadine Levy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:00:19 UTC
23:00:19 KST

There is a particular Buddhist story that reassured me I had found the right path.
The story goes that Prince Siddhartha Gautama was deep in spiritual practice – arduous, unforgiving practice. He had tried everything from breath-holding to extreme fasting. But none of it brought the freedom from suffering he sought.
As is sometimes the case in those moments, he was graced with a memory. He remembered being a child, sitting under the shade of a rose apple tree while his father worked nearby. As he sat there, free from preoccupation, his mind settled and his experience became infused with a deep sense of pleasure and ease.
This memory gestured at what later became a fundamental Buddhist idea: put simply, extreme self-denial is not the path to freedom. More radically, could it be that a certain kind of pleasure – a more refined pleasure – might help point the way?
I’ve always been intrigued by pleasure, its limits but also its invitation. The pleasure Siddhartha remembered was not wily or sneaky, waiting to trick him into attachment, but rather carried him towards freedom of heart.
Admittedly, the Buddha distinguished this kind of pleasure from sensual pleasures, which can become tangled with craving, acquisition and a mistaken belief that happiness lies in getting more.
But the point is not to become sceptical or suspicious of pleasure, but to lean into it when it naturally arises.
As humans, we are strangely adept at trying to elicit and extract pleasure, to plan for it and prolong it, but not so good at receiving it when it is right in front of us.
Stress can diminish our sensitivity to pleasure. Psychologists use the term “anhedonia” to describe the diminished capacity to anticipate or experience pleasure, a phenomenon associated with a range of mental health conditions.
As a teenager, I had a free-spirited friend who wholeheartedly called out, “I love bed!” before she went to sleep. We could hear her down the corridor.
I loved bed too; we all did. But would we admit it?
She noticed the sheets, the relief of placing a tired body down, the privilege of a pillow. Boy, she knew how to receive pleasure when it was being offered.
The Buddha observed that all experience is associated with a tonal quality – pleasant, painful or neutral. In Buddhism, we call this vedanā, or feeling tone. And then there is all the manhandling we do with feeling: judging it, willing it to stay, tweaking it.
When working with mindfulness students who are having a hard time, I often do a pleasure check.
I ask, sometimes provocatively, “What are you doing in your free time?” Then: “Are you able to read a good novel? Could you go for a massage or a meandering walk in the sun?” What I am really asking is: can you be with pleasure intentionally, even in the midst of suffering?
These conversations also make it plain that access to pleasure is not enjoyed equally. The time, safety and space necessary to notice and receive pleasure are impacted by our social and material circumstances. But when pleasure does arise amid turbulence, allowing it to register can offer the nervous system a chance to rest, even for a moment.
We feel this viscerally: a slower breath, a softening, a release. And if we are quiet, we might notice our minds relishing it – “How terrific, I love this.” Or as American novelist Kurt Vonnegut put it, “If this isn’t nice, I don’t know what is.”
Can we let pleasure simply hold our attention without trying to prolong it?
Pleasure arrives with different inflections. Some forms leave us aching for more. Others are more sublime, spiritual even – the kind the Buddha spoke of: the mind that gathers and settles. The simplicity of the breathing body. The sweetness of simply existing.
I once had a teacher who started meditation sessions with, “It feels good to be in the body.” It was a low bar for pleasure, but somehow I felt it.
Then there is the pleasure of living a life of non-harm, of treating ourselves and others with dignity, love and respect. Subtler still is the pleasure of laying down the burden, even for a moment, of having to be and do.
I remember marvelling that in my mother’s final weeks, days in the hospital could still brim with pleasure. Among the many unpleasant experiences, there was the sweetness of laughter, a leg massage, a feeling of togetherness, and a daughter’s recognition of the comfort and familiarity of being with her mum.
Each evening, I would think how strange it was that there was so much pleasure in despair.
And here receptivity was key. I suspect without it, I might have seen only what was painful and missed the pleasure braided through.
Every time I sit to meditate, I consciously luxuriate in the pleasure of breathing.
Of course, pleasure dissipates, and unpleasant and neutral sensations arrive too. Yet in Buddhist practice, these too are met with the same receptive attention: “Oh, this is unpleasant, and it will change.” Sometimes there is even a kind of pleasure in this honesty.
And, for the record, I still love bed.
- Dr Nadine Levy is a senior lecturer at the Nan Tien Institute. She coordinates its health and social wellbeing program and the graduate certificate in applied mindfulness

The truth about testicles: are we facing spermageddon?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:00:16 UTC
23:00:16 KST

“I think you can tell it’s for a lay audience,” says Michael Carroll, holding up his book, Your Nuts, its cover illustrated with two walnuts in a string bag. The book has arrived in tandem with worldwide concerns about falling birth rates. “Spermaggedon” is a chunky piece of this puzzle, part of a wider debate about whether and why we’re heading for species-icide. Are people deciding not to have kids because of climate anxiety and economic precarity? Or is this an unchosen fertility cliff edge, created by forever chemicals and our lifestyles? This is not a drill, says Carroll, a biologist and reproductive scientist at Manchester Metropolitan University. “There’s compelling evidence to support a historical decline in sperm count and sperm concentration over the last number of decades.” However, it’s just not that simple.
First, it’s not a uniform picture and in some populations sperm counts are going up. The Danish Young Men Study, for instance, showed no drop between 1996 and 2022. In Ireland, a study of 15,000 men between 2008 and 2023 showed a 23% increase in sperm concentration.
Second, it’s not a direct read-across from sperm count or concentration to fertility – those statistics don’t tell you anything about functionality. “If you deposit 300m sperm at the cervix, only a couple of dozen might actually reach the egg,” Carroll explains, and we still don’t know really basic things, like “how the sperm find an egg in the female reproductive tract. We can extrapolate from animal experiments and conduct in vitro experiments, but biologically, we don’t really know.”
Third, “reproductive biology is a very complicated, multi-stepped, timed process requiring two individuals,” and even while we all understand that, any focus on a single issue, whether it’s sperm count or maternal age or generational anxiety, drives us away from an appreciation of that complexity and towards narratives so simplistic as to be basically superstitious. Back in the day, that woo-hoo was all “selfish women are leaving it too late”; now, thanks in part to an overheated manosphere, testicles are centre stage, freighted with notions of masculine destiny being threatened by an effeminate modernity. These aren’t ideal conditions for understanding what is going on.
Carroll grew up in Ireland, the youngest of 12; his unimaginably large family seems salient to his career choices. He brushes off any attempt to psychotherapise him, though, saying this is just how Ireland was in the 60s and 70s (he was born in 1974). “It was very much a theocracy then, and the Catholic church wasn’t in favour of contraception.”
He did his PhD in Newcastle, looking at how sperm fertilise eggs in marine animals. Then, after a postdoc at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute in Dallas, Texas, looking at stem cells, he trained as a clinical embryologist, working in IVF, before returning to academia to teach reproductive science and reproductive biology, while researching the impact of lifestyle and environmental exposure.
Although Carroll, who is married, has three children from a previous relationship and a stepdaughter, he is familiar with the pain of infertility, from his experience working in IVF.
“It’s a great job, being an embryologist. You’re working at the very beginnings of life, patients really put their trust into you to handle their gametes, the sperm and eggs, and to culture their embryos and get them to a stage where you can give them a family. It comes with great joy. But you also have to be prepared sometimes to break devastating news.”
Some types of azoospermia – where no sperm is produced in the ejaculate – have no cure or treatment. It can be caused by anabolic steroid use, which is sometimes reparable when you stop taking them, but sometimes not. “Don’t take health advice from social media!” Carroll says, and writes, often.
The global fertility picture, though, can’t just be blamed on TikTok. The total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children a woman will have in her lifetime. In 1963, it was 5.3; by 2024, it was 2.2. Most European nations are well below replacement rate (UK, 1.6; Spain, 1.1) and the only reason the world population isn’t falling is that people are living longer and infant mortality rates have dropped. Carroll keeps the economics front of mind: “some estimates put the total cost of raising a child at $280,000 [£209,000]. I don’t know anybody now who could afford to have 12 children.” Plus there are other social factors, including climate change anxiety. Older maternal age is plainly a factor, though paternal age should be considered more than it is. From 40 to 45 is considered advanced paternal age, and “older men tend to have higher levels of DNA damage or mutations, so there’s a higher prevalence of neuropsychiatric disorders in their offspring – bipolar will be one, schizophrenia will be another”.
But what researchers are starting to call the “disappointment gap” – between the size of family people want and the one they have – is often driven by brute biological realities for both men and women, and where sperm is concerned, individual choices don’t cover it. In 2005, the epidemiologist Christopher Wild coined the expression “exposome”: the combination of environmental and lifestyle factors an individual would be exposed to throughout their life. Pollution, endocrine-disrupting chemicals, plastics, sunshine, processed foods, “everything matters,” says Carroll. “The best way to examine a drop in any biological marker would be prospective surveillance studies, where you follow populations over time.” The Danish data came from military recruits; the Irish sperm research, which was a retrospective study, took place in a fertility clinic.
If longitudinal research yields a frustratingly mixed picture, the understanding of sperm itself is maddeningly partial. We can measure numbers, but that doesn’t tell us anything about function.
For sheer talismanic potency, though, sperm and testosterone are in a class of their own, drawing in social constructs of masculinity and meaning, which collide with these unexplained or only partially understood declines to produce narratives that are unscientific and often work directly against the science. In tandem with that, unwanted childlessness is rising sharply; infertility in broad terms is about 30% down to the woman, 30% down to the man and 30% unexplained. And for men, conventionally the silent partner in this discourse, a diagnosis of low fertility or infertility engenders “feelings of shame, demasculinisation, questioning their own identity and self-worth,” says Carroll. Whether as an embryologist or academic, he just wants people, with or without testicles, to understand what’s going on.
Seeing sperm as magic, and its absence a curse, isn’t a new thing. In 1889, Charles-Édouard Brown-Séquard, a professor of experimental medicine, mashed up the testicles of dogs and guinea pigs, extracted the juice, injected himself with it and reported “a radical change … I had regained at least all the strength I possessed a good many years ago” (he was 72 at the time). This unleashed an industry of quacks, flogging “Brown-Séquard Elixir” or, more commonly in the US, the “Elixir of life”. To be fair to Brown-Séquard, the literature at the time on what testicles may or may not be capable of was very undeveloped, and he was like the Withnail of medical research, gamely experimenting on himself throughout his life, once covering himself in varnish to discover the properties of skin (he was found unconscious and had to be cleaned with alcohol), another time giving himself cholera by eating the vomit of a patient, to see if he could cure it with opium (he was found unconscious again and had to be resuscitated).
What concerns Carroll is the revival of that quackery, this time attached to testosterone. “What’s being promoted, especially by podcasters and social media influencers, is that testosterone is a quick hack to make you feel better and more invigorated, it’s a new elixir.” There is an ambient association of testosterone with “masculinity, aggression and competition, but behaviour is complex and it is too simple to put it down to the level of a hormone released from an endocrine gland”. A lack of vigour is more likely to be down to poor sleep or diet, and testosterone replacement therapy won’t put a dent in that, but it will along the way do the exact opposite of what you took it for. “It’s a very sensitive pathway of signals, the brain telling the testicles to produce testosterone. It’s called the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Some testosterone will be released to do its thing around the body; more is produced in the testicles. And that’s important for spermatogenesis” – or sperm production and development. If you take supplementary testosterone, he says, “it’s telling the brain to shut down your factory downstairs because we have enough testosterone now, thank you. It’s a negative feedback loop, spermatogenesis is affected, and then there’s poor sperm or no sperm output because of that”.
It’s so pronounced with bodybuilders, who use testosterone replacement therapy to build muscle, that they get testicular atrophy, where their testicles shrink from underuse. It even has a name: “The Mossman-Pacey paradox,” Carroll writes, “whereby men enhance their visual cues of reproductive fitness while reducing their actual ability to reproduce.” Finasteride, a medicine that arrests and sometimes reverses male-pattern baldness by blocking the hormone DHT, has the top-line impact of boosting testosterone (because testosterone converts into DHT so, unconverted, it stays in the bloodstream). But libido, erectile function and mood track the androgen environment in general – so blocking DHT, like taking synthetic testosterone, is another signal to the brain to shut down the factory.
Almost more from a geopolitical than a spermatozoic point of view, it’s sobering to see testosterone make it into US defence policy, with Pete Hegseth announcing over the summer the “High-T Department of War”, mandating that all servicemen over 30 have their testosterone tested, to maximise mental and physical readiness, strength and warrior ethos. It’s not even the stupidest thing to come out of the Department of War recently, but it’s a stark illustration of manosphere misinformation working its way up to policy, flooding the knowledge environment.
And the problem with that is, it causes a lot of heartache. “A lot of men think that if they’re producing semen and they can get an erection, their bits are working,” Carroll says. “They don’t realise what’s going on within the testes, what can affect the quality of the sperm, what can reduce their capacity to reproduce. They don’t even start to look for the information until they’re trying to start a family and there’s a problem.”
Smoking is strongly associated with lower semen volume, lower sperm count, and increased DNA damage. Obesity has been linked to reduced testosterone levels and lower sperm count, but not all studies concur on this, and most obese men are fertile (Carroll is careful to stress this in his book, possibly to ward off anyone thinking they can rely on BMI as a contraceptive). The most solid correlation is between obesity and infertility rather than low sperm count, which also has the most obvious mechanical causation – fat cells produce an enzyme, aromatase, which can convert testosterone to oestrogen. This can directly impair the function of testicular cells. Human bodies are amazing, though sometimes in annoying ways.
More broadly, it’d be good for everyone to “know how it works”, Carroll says. “Plenty of lads go to the gym and they’ll know a lot about muscle physiology and contraction and nutrition, and they’ll be able to use that knowledge to make informed decisions to get the physique or fitness level they want. It should be the same with reproductive health. If you know your testicles need to be two to four degrees lower than body temperature, and prolonged high temperatures can damage sperm production; if you know the risks of STIs, which can cause infertility not just in males but in females as well; if you know that taking Finasteride or TRT can have an impact; this will all help you make informed decisions and ask the right questions.”
Fundamentally, Carroll wrote Your Nuts to broach the isolation of infertility. World Health Organization estimates that around 17.5% of the global adult population will experience infertility at some stage. People (like me) rail against the asymmetry of the discourse, that women’s health and choices are endlessly analysed and policed while men and their nuts slip under the radar, but it’s a painful and alienating experience, being the one that nobody talks about. “We’re in an infodemic era,” says Carroll, “and a lot of that information is not correct. I just want to tell people what we know, and more importantly, what we don’t know.”
- Your Nuts: The Science of How They Work and What it Means for Your Fertility by Michael Carroll is published by FiachPress (£22.99)

Book Review: A guide to how the media sanitized Israel’s genocide in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

DON’T SAY PALESTINE
How the Media Manufactured Consent for Genocide
by Assal Rad
242 pp.; Vintage; $20
Anyone who has followed Israel’s war on Gaza over the past few years on Twitter/X has come across Assal Rad’s compelling efforts to rewrite the misleading and dishonest headlines in articles from the mainstream media. She started back in May 2021, and this first example set the tone.
She continued after October 7, 2023, and her work became one of the most effective ways to get the truth to a wider audience. Over the years, she has accumulated 192,000 followers.
But there is much more to Assal Rad’s work than her correction of headlines, vital as that is. She is an accomplished scholar and historian with a deep understanding of Israel, Palestine, and the Middle East. And now, she has written a masterpiece, a combination of brilliant analysis and searing moral outrage that will become a classic and be read for decades, or even longer. Her work on language distortion and dishonesty can actually be placed right up in the same category as George Orwell’s famous essay, “Politics and the English Language.”
This review cannot fully do justice to Rad’s achievement in Don’t Say Palestine: How the Media Manufactured Consent for Genocide. Let’s start with the corrected headlines. She reminds us that “headlines matter because people often do not read beyond them.” She also points out that many articles are behind paywalls, which gives the headlines added power. And she explains:
“My goal was not to nitpick or play semantic games. It is to show how language is used as a weapon to obscure and sanitize. When indiscriminate bombing is called ‘targeted strikes,’ a policy of starvation is described as a ‘humanitarian challenge,’ and genocide as reframed as ‘self-defense,” these linguistic choices are not accidental. They are political decisions that determine whose lives count and whose deaths are permissible.”
Rad reminds us that the mainstream distortions and downplaying kept the larger public surprisingly ignorant. Those of us who followed Israel’s genocide on alternative media may be surprised to learn that
1) Even by March 24, 2024, only half of the U.S. public knew that more Palestinians than Israelis had been killed in the war on Gaza, and
2) Even more astonishing — more Americans could identify “Hamas” than knew who “Benjamin Netanyahu” was.
She points out an awful paradox; alternative media did cover Israel’s mass killing, but most people missed it. She writes: “. . . social media accounts were flooded with images and videos recorded by Palestinians in Gaza themselves. For more than two years, anyone with a social media account could wander into a constant stream of unedited glimpses of apocalyptic destruction, mass slaughter and helpless civilians being carpet-bombed with nowhere safe to go.” She reminds us that some 250 Palestinian journalists paid with their lives to report these terrible truths.
Not all mainstream reporters and editors played along with the whitewash. Leaks from people inside CNN, the New York Times, and others did reveal aspects of the self-censorship; other media people resigned in public protest, or were, in some cases, purged.
Throughout, Assal Rad maintains her focus on the mainstream’s distortions, euphemisms and outright lies. Even those of us who followed the bias closely will find plenty to learn in this remarkable new book. Here’s one strong example: “[Israeli air assaults] often came with the phrase ‘targeting Hamas’ to justify the attack, whether it was on a school, hospital or refugee camp with Palestinians in makeshift tents, and no matter how many civilians were killed. The use of ‘targeting Hamas’ became a means to normalize the mass slaughter of civilians by reframing indiscriminate bombing as a precise military campaign.”
Her carefully documented indictment also confirms the Biden administration’s deep complicity in the mass killing, contributing to the growing revisionist analysis that confirms it was even worse than critics charged at the time.
There is even more. Rad points out that some parts of the Israeli media sometimes told truths that the American mainstream ignored (a point also made regularly at this site). She writes: “In September 2024, Haaretz [Israel’s newspaper of record] published a piece on reports from Israel’s Channel 12 News that outlined ‘Netanyahu’s relentless efforts to block hostage deal.’ A report of this magnitude from Israeli sources should certainly be considered newsworthy at a time when the United States was supposedly leading cease-fire talks. But the story did not attract much attention from the mainstream media.”
Assal Rad is not stopping. Here, from just a few days ago, are her rewritten headlines contrasting the New York Times coverage of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine with Israel’s crackdown in occupied West Bank/Palestine.
Finally, Vintage is publishing Don’t Say Palestine, a major mainstream imprint. Will the bigger publications have the moral courage to at least assign the book for review? Allow Assal Rad space to write opinion pieces? Or will the mainstream remain true to form, and hide?

Lithuanian alternative lender Finpro has secured €5 million in financing from Luxembourg-based Quantic Receivables Fund. The funding will support small and medium-sized businesses in Lithuania across all sectors.
Finpro co-founder and CEO Kęstutis Grinaveckas says the agreement strengthens the company’s international partnerships and broadens its funding base.
“This is the first time we have secured funding of this kind from an international investor, and it is an important vote of confidence in Finpro. It shows that our strategy of making alternative financing more widely available to businesses has growth potential and is attracting interest from international partners. Our goal is to continue diversifying our funding sources. The agreement also allows for additional funding in the future,” says Grinaveckas.
Finpro’s business loan portfolio currently stands at €38 million, up 35% compared with the third quarter of last year.
About Quantic Receivables Fund
Quantic Receivables Fund is a Luxembourg-registered investment fund that invests in a variety of trade finance transactions.
About Finpro
Finpro is a Lithuanian alternative lender that began operating in early 2021. Its team has more than 20 years of financial sector experience gained at Lithuania’s largest banks. The company provides business financing ranging from €10,000 to €500,000.

Qatar on Sunday strongly condemned an attack on the liquefied natural gas (LNG) tanker Al Mayeda while it was sailing in the Gulf, warning that the incident threatened maritime navigation and global energy supplies, Anadolu reports.
In a statement, the Foreign Ministry said the vessel belonged to Qatar Gas Transport Company, known as Nakilat.
The ministry described the attack as “a dangerous act that threatens the safety of maritime navigation and the security of global energy supplies.”
Qatar “reserves the right to take all necessary measures under international law and the UN Charter to protect its property, safeguard its interests and ensure the safety of its vessels and crews,” it said.
The ministry added that the relevant authorities had begun investigations to establish the circumstances of the incident and identify those responsible.
It warned that such “reckless and irresponsible practices” could have serious repercussions for regional security and stability and the global economy.
The ministry also highlighted potential environmental risks arising from attacks on energy tankers, warning of serious consequences for the marine environment and the water security of countries in the region.
Earlier Sunday, Nakilat announced that one of its vessels carrying LNG had been struck by “unidentified objects” while sailing in Gulf waters Friday evening.
READ: Why Qatar is buying American LNG while expanding its own exports
The Qatar News Agency quoted the company as saying that Al Mayeda was struck on Oct. 30, with no injuries among crew members or environmental damage.
The company did not disclose the nature of the objects involved in the attack, identify those responsible or specify the incident’s exact location.
Nakilat is a Qatari public shareholding company with public and private sector ownership and plays a key role in transporting LNG as part of Qatar’s energy supply chain.
The incident comes amid persistent security risks to commercial navigation in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, with commercial vessels and oil and gas tankers facing repeated attacks and security incidents in recent months.
October saw a series of attacks on commercial tankers in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, some of which caused fires and damage to vessels, according to maritime security reports.
Concerns over shipping security have intensified amid continuing tensions between the US and Iran, particularly over the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage for global oil and gas exports.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28 before a ceasefire was reached in April. Fighting between Washington and Tehran resumed in July amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the war.

A hobby computer, a cheap airframe, and a Russian jet drone: how Zirka’s upgrade scored its kill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:52:28 UTC
22:52:28 KST

An upgraded Ukrainian Zirka interceptor caught and destroyed a Russian jet-powered Geran-5 drone, its developer, the ZRK tech project, said. A crew from Ukraine’s drone forces flew the self-guiding drone, ZRK added. At its summer debut, the cheap interceptor looked too slow for Russia’s jet models.
Russia sends waves of attack drones at Ukrainian cities almost every night. It has spent the year moving more of them onto jet engines. The faster models slip past many of the cheap interceptors Ukraine built for propeller Shaheds. That leaves gaps Ukraine often plugs with expensive missiles, and Washington is holding back the ones Ukraine needs most.
Caught at 3,500 meters
ZRK said the upgraded Zirka chased down the Geran-5 at about 400 km/h, at an altitude of 3,500 meters. The developer published the interception video on 31 October.
The crew “Retro” of the Darknode battalion flew the mission, ZRK said. The battalion belongs to the 412th Nemesis brigade of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces. ZRK has not disclosed the upgraded drone’s specifications.
From too slow to catching a jet
When Zirka debuted in late June, its makers listed a top speed above 340 km/h. They also gave a 6 km ceiling and a 30 km radius. At up to $2,000 a unit, they called it the cheapest interceptor in its class with automatic guidance. That speed fell short of the bursts Russia’s jet-powered Shahed variants can reach.
Zirka still found a way against jets. In late July, it downed a jet-powered Geran-4, its maker said in a press release, Militarnyi reported. Instead of chasing the faster drone from behind, Zirka met it head-on or from the side, Ukrainian tech outlet ITC explained.
Oleksii Babenko, director of investor Vyriy Industries, later said Zirka could down jet Shaheds on its own. He also said it once hit a target about 3,000 km from its operator, controlled via Starlink.
A hobby computer does the aiming
Zirka carries a Raspberry Pi 5, a credit-card-sized single-board computer, Militarnyi said. It runs a machine-vision model trained to pick out the features of Shahed-type drones. The system detects a target up to 1 km away. Once the operator confirms it, the system tracks it and steers the interceptor in.
The pilot only has to adjust the closing speed, Militarnyi added. Machine vision makes Zirka up to 60% more effective against maneuvering targets than manual piloting, NOCTIS claims, according to ITC. ZRK’s new video shows the software flagging the Geran-5, then switching to automatic terminal guidance, so the upgraded version likely keeps the same system.
Ukraine’s answer to Russia’s jet Shaheds: a jet drone named Bars, built to strike Russia and now turned around to hunt them
That is the capability Ukraine’s presidential adviser on defense technology Serhii Beskrestnov has pressed for. Speed alone will not catch jet drones, he argued. Interceptors need machine vision to lock on and guide themselves in.
The battalion behind the brief
Ukrainian company NOCTIS built Zirka to a technical brief drawn up with the Darknode battalion, ITC said. The battalion, one of Ukraine’s top anti-Shahed units, has downed more than 1,500 Russian drones, according to ITC. Vyriy Industries holds a 30% stake in NOCTIS, Babenko said.
Cheap answers to cheap drones
Ukraine’s government wants exactly this kind of trade. “We need asymmetric effect,” Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said, as Kyiv funds its own missiles and radars. The goal is to stop spending costly interceptors on Russia’s cheap drones.
Until cheap tools catch up, Ukraine improvises with what it has. One regiment has paired a Soviet Kub launcher with a Buk radar to hunt jet drones. It has also rewired launchers to fire American RIM-7 missiles.
Russia keeps speeding up
Ukraine shoots down 50–60% of Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds, against 85–92% of propeller ones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in October. Russia builds about 3,000 jet drones a month, Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) estimated.
HUR puts the Geran-5’s cruise speed at 450–600 km/h, and Beskrestnov said it has hit 1,000 km/h in maneuvers. He added that Ukraine’s jet interceptors still struggle with guidance, automatic target lock, and mass production.
Zirka is not alone. The 1020th anti-aircraft regiment caught a Geran-5 at 425 km/h in September. Wild Hornets says its new STING-family interceptor has destroyed about ten Geran-4s.

AI reality check triggers $2 trillion tech stock rout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:52:11 UTC
22:52:11 KST

AI reality check triggers $2 trillion tech stock rout
An estimated $2 trillion in market value was wiped from the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 during October as investors grow increasingly skeptical that enormous spending on artificial intelligence will ever pay off.
On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.9% in its biggest one-day fall since June. Over the whole month, the Nasdaq shed about 5.2%, its worst showing since March 2025, while the S&P 500 slipped 1.2%, and the Dow – which includes many traditional businesses – still finished October up 1.5%.
Among the hardest-hit companies was Google owner Alphabet, whose shares plunged 12.6% on Thursday in its worst day on record. The slump was triggered by its earnings showing slower growth in search advertising, its core business.
While search advertising revenue still grew 12%, Google executive Philipp Schindler acknowledged that its AI Mode brings in less ad revenue per search than traditional results. At the same time, Alphabet is spending heavily on AI infrastructure, putting further pressure on its cash flow. The company’s net profit also slid 25% year-on-year, largely due to investment-related losses, while Thursday’s share plunge erased nearly $500 billion from its market value.
Amazon reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the preceding 12 months, largely due to AI investments, with its shares falling 1.4% on Friday. Chipmaker Intel came out worse, plunging 28.6%, its worst day since 1974, after forecasting weaker profits amid trouble in its PC and manufacturing businesses. 
Nvidia – which produces powerful chips used to train and run AI systems – slipped 4.2%, becoming the biggest drag on the S&P 500, while rival AMD dropped 10.9%.
Commenting on the slump, Globalt Investments senior portfolio manager Keith Buchanan, described the current state of the market as “scrutinizing” and “discerning”. “Last year was hope. This year is: At the end of day, how does this all work in real-world terms, like how to finance [it] and who gets the economics. Those questions are much more difficult to answer,” he told CNBC.
Enormous spending on AI and data centers has become a staple of US tech giants in recent years. Together, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Alphabet are projected to spend more than $700 billion on data centers, computing equipment and other long-term investments in 2026 alone, and much of it is AI-related.
According to various estimates, global AI-related investment is valued at between $900 billion and $2.7 trillion dollars this year, depending on the methodology. Companies are also borrowing more to finance expansion, fueling concerns among investors.
Market analysts meanwhile warn of further near-term losses. Bank of America strategist Michael Hartnett expects weakness until mid-November, while Morgan Stanley’s Mike Wilson says the S&P 500 could fall even further within weeks before recovering by year-end.
Other major tests for the US market are the midterm elections on Tuesday, which could reshape AI regulation, as well as quarterly results from Apple, Nvidia, AMD and Palantir, and Friday’s jobs report.

Deep Strikes in October: Missile Production, Oil Refineries and Russian Aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:51:51 UTC
22:51:51 KST

In October, Ukraine’s Defense Forces focused their deep strikes not only on Russian oil refineries, as they traditionally do, but also on military airfields and facilities involved in ballistic missile production.
Russia’s tactical aviation losses were particularly significant: 3 attacks on airfields resulted in the destruction of at least 8 combat aircraft and damage to 2 more.
This overview is based on October data from Militarnyi Strike, a deep-strike map maintained by Militarnyi’s GEOINT team. It records verified, geolocated attacks on Russian territory and deep inside Ukraine’s temporarily occupied territories.
Oil and gas industry facilities accounted for the largest category in the October dataset, with 20 recorded strikes, or about one-third of the total. Defense industry facilities were hit 9 times, while the chemical industry was targeted 6 times.
A further 10 attacks targeted military facilities, 9 hit infrastructure, 4 targeted logistics facilities, and 2 struck electricity infrastructure.
The Samara region and St. Petersburg recorded the most strikes, with 6 each. The Rostov and Voronezh regions were hit 4 times each. The strikes also covered Bashkortostan, Perm Krai, the Komi Republic, and industrial areas of Western Siberia.
The median distance from the front line to targets attacked in Russia in October was 551.5 km. The most distant targets were 2,508 km from the line of contact. The closest was an oil depot in the Belgorod region, which was struck on October 9, just 45 km from the front line.
The most distant targets included the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant and the Omsk Rubber Plant (Omsky Kauchuk). The map estimates that both are approximately 2,500 km from the front line. On the same day, an Ozon logistics center in Omsk was also hit.
The oil and gas category includes refineries, pumping stations, storage facilities, and transshipment sites. October targets included the Ryazan, Novokuibyshevsk, and Ukhta refineries, as well as Bashneft-Novoil.
The Samara oil pumping station, which has Europe’s largest tank farm, was struck at least four times. Four trunk pipelines converge at the facility: Almetyevsk-Kuibyshev, Kaltasy-Kuibyshev, Nizhnevartovsk-Kurgan-Kuibyshev, and Guryev-Kuibyshev.
The blending station combines oil flows to achieve specified quality characteristics. Crude oil with different sulfur content is mixed in the required proportions to maintain the properties of Urals crude for refining and export.
Another category included data centers belonging to Yandex, Sberbank, VKontakte, and Russia’s Federal Tax Service.
These facilities are located in the Vladimir, Kaluga, Ryazan, Saratov, Nizhny Novgorod, and Leningrad regions.
According to industrial media outlets, Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian data centers likely knocked out all three of Yandex’s supercomputers.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces paid considerable attention to facilities manufacturing propellant charges, power sources, and microelectronics for ballistic missiles.
Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara has described the threat of ballistic missile strikes as critical, saying that existing and potential supplies of interceptor missiles are insufficient to fully counter it. Therefore, alongside efforts to secure new interceptor missiles, Ukraine is pursuing an asymmetric response by striking Russian launchers and facilities involved in the missile production supply chain.
On October 3, the Defense Forces attacked the Voskhod enterprise (Voskhod-KLRZ), also known as the Kaluga Radio Tube Plant, in Kaluga. It manufactures RUD20 microchips for 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles, as well as electronic components for the onboard computer and inertial navigation system of 9M727 Iskander-K cruise missiles. The plant also supplies electronics for Kh-101 missiles.
On October 23, the Defense Forces struck the Proton plant in Oryol with cruise missiles, likely Storm Shadow missiles. The plant manufactures 249LP5 switching inverters for 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles, diode modules for S-71 Kover air-launched cruise missiles, and electronic components for the Pantsir-S1 system.
On October 25, Storm Shadow cruise missiles struck the Energia plant in Yelets, Lipetsk region. The facility manufactures 9B283 thermal batteries for 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles and HIT 59I6 power sources for RM-48U strike missiles launched from S-400 systems.
Energia also produces 9B280-1 power cells for 9M727 Iskander-K cruise missiles, batteries for glide bombs equipped with UMPK kits, and UMPB D-30SN munitions. The plant supplies certain types of power sources to manufacturers of Zircon and Kinzhal missiles and the Pantsir air defense system.
On the same day, Ukrainian drones attacked the AVISMA plant in Berezniki, Perm Krai. It produces 96% of Russia’s titanium sponge, which other companies within the parent corporation, VSMPO-AVISMA, process into titanium products. Russian manufacturers of military aircraft and various types of missiles widely use the corporation’s titanium products.
On October 31, the Defense Forces struck the Kamensky Chemical Plant in the Rostov region with Neptune missiles and drones. The facility manufactures propellant charges for 9Kh820 rocket motors used in 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles, as well as charges and igniters for 9Kh837 booster motors used in 9M727 Iskander-K cruise missiles. The plant also supplies propellant to manufacturers of Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket system munitions.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian units attacked a broader network of suppliers of special fuels for cruise missiles, polymers, acids, and other materials used to produce munitions and military equipment.
On October 9, strike drones attacked the Redkino Experimental Plant in the Tver region. The chemical facility manufactures components for the Decilin-M special fuel used in Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, as well as additives for diesel fuel and aviation kerosene.
On October 23, Ukrainian drones attacked the Azot plant in Berezniki, Perm Krai. The facility supplies concentrated nitric acid and melange, a mixture of acids used for nitration, to explosives and chemical plants. These facilities use the raw materials to manufacture explosives and propellant charges.
On October 24, the Defense Forces attacked Tolyattikauchuk in the Samara region. The plant manufactures synthetic rubber, monomers, and high-octane gasoline additives. Manufacturers of solid rocket propellant and rubber products use its polymer output as a raw material.
Special grades of synthetic rubber perform two functions in composite solid propellants: they bind the components into a single charge and serve as fuel that burns during the chemical reaction.
On the same day, Ukrainian drones struck the Omsky Kauchuk plant in Omsk. The facility, part of the Titan Group, manufactures synthetic rubber, phenol, acetone, and the MTBE fuel additive. A major fire broke out at the site following the strikes.
On October 26, Ukrainian drones attacked Voronezhsintezkauchuk. The plant manufactures synthetic rubber and thermoplastic elastomers. Manufacturers of tires and rubber products use these materials, among other things, to make components for military equipment.
On October 28, deep-strike drones attacked the Azot plant in Novomoskovsk, Tula region. Between 2022 and 2024, the facility supplied nearly 5,000 metric tons of nitric acid to the Sverdlov Plant in Dzerzhinsk. That plant manufactures RDX and HMX for military munitions.
On October 29, Ukrainian drones attacked the Bashkir Soda Company facility in Sterlitamak. The facility manufactures terephthaloyl chloride, a raw material for high-strength aramid fibers. Manufacturers of protective equipment use these fibers to make body armor, helmets, and other military gear.
October saw a significant increase in publicly reported successful uses of Neptune cruise missiles, continuing a trend that began in early 2026.
In April, May, and June, one successful use was reported in each month. Two cases were reported in August and September, while October saw three successful attacks: on the Borisoglebsk and Marinovka airfields and on the Kamensky Chemical Plant, which manufactures rocket propellant.
On October 15, the Ukrainian Navy struck the Borisoglebsk airfield in the Voronezh region. The military initially reported hits on 6 Su-34 aircraft. Satellite imagery confirmed the destruction of at least 4 bombers, while two more aircraft were damaged.
On October 29, the Ukrainian Navy attacked Marinovka airfield in the Volgograd region with Neptune missiles. Satellite imagery confirmed the destruction of 2 Su-34 aircraft. The blast and subsequent fire also damaged a nearby aircraft hangar. In total, the 2 missile strikes destroyed 6 bombers and damaged 2 more.
During the night of October 31, the Defense Forces struck the Kamensky Chemical Plant in the Rostov region with Neptune missiles and strike drones. The attack damaged at least 4 production workshops and caused a fire at a warehouse storing finished products at the facility, which manufactures solid rocket propellant.
On October 4, SSU drones destroyed a Su-35 and a Su-34 at Khanskaya airbase in Adygea. Satellite imagery confirmed the loss of both aircraft. Ukrainian drones also struck an ammunition depot at the airfield.
At Borisoglebsk, Marinovka, and Khanskaya airbases, the Defense Forces destroyed at least 7 Su-34s and 1 Su-35, and damaged 2 Su-34s.
In addition, Russian military aviation suffered significant non-combat losses. On October 21, a Su-30SM fighter crashed in the Kaliningrad region during a training flight. The aircraft went down in Chernyakhovsky District, between the settlements of Timofeyevka and Zeleny Bor. Both pilots ejected but sustained injuries.
On the same day, Russia lost another Su-30SM during a training flight. Colonel Oleg Yerofeyev and Lieutenant Colonel Vladimir Kochetov, members of the Russian Knights aerobatic team, were killed. On October 29, the team confirmed their deaths. The circumstances of the crash remain unknown.
On October 29, a Su-57 fighter caught fire at Akhtubinsk airbase in the Astrakhan region. The aircraft is believed to have caught fire following an abnormal incident during engine startup. Satellite imagery showed the aftermath of the fire at the aircraft parking area.
On October 1, Russia lost a Mi-8 military transport helicopter in the Voronezh region. The helicopter was likely shot down by a Russian Su-35 during an attempt to repel a drone attack: the fighter’s crew mistakenly identified it as a Ukrainian drone. All three Mi-8 crew members were killed.
On October 30, the 3rd Assault Brigade released footage showing the destruction of another Mi-8 near Tarasivka in the occupied Luhansk region. Members of the brigade’s SKYFOM platoon, part of its unmanned systems battalion, struck the helicopter twice with HORNET drones after it had landed. The aircraft burned down.
Overall, Russia was confirmed to have irretrievably lost 11 aircraft and 2 Mi-8 helicopters in October alone. Another two Su-34s sustained damage of unknown severity.

'Life simply returned' – Oleshky ceasefire gives Kherson short respite amid years of Russian terror
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:50:56 UTC
22:50:56 KST

'Life simply returned' – Oleshky ceasefire gives Kherson short respite amid years of Russian terror
A woman poses for photographs next to Kherson Gateway Stela, next to a road covered by anti-drone nets, during a temporary ceasefire in the southern Kherson region, at the entrance to the city of Kherson, southern Ukraine, on Oct. 31, 2026. (Roman Pilipey / AFP via Getty Images)
Editor's note: Ukrainian journalist Daria Litovchenko contributed to reporting on the ground in Kherson, while Francis Farrell compiled the material from Kyiv.
In all of Ukraine, perhaps no city has suffered as much, for as long, during Russia's full-scale war as Kherson.
From the initial eight months of brutal Russian occupation in 2022 — with all of the associated torture, looting and deportation — to Russia's man-made flood caused by the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam, to the systematic "human safari" attacks targeting civilians by Russian drones that have gone on since 2024, Kherson has lived from horror to horror without a break until now.
Over the last few days, this city at the delta of Ukraine's Dnipro River enjoyed something that has become an almost unknown sensation: quiet.
On Oct. 27, along the section of front line following the river through Kherson Oblast, Russian and Ukrainian forces began observing a ceasefire of a scale and length unprecedented in four and a half years of the full-scale war.
Every morning that the ceasefire continued, the daily updates of Kherson Oblast Governor Oleksandr Prokudin — normally filled with reports of attacks and casualties in Kherson and other riverbank communities — read "attacks and casualties were not recorded."
The ceasefire, agreed upon as part of a U.S.-mediated humanitarian mission to the beleaguered Russian-occupied city of Oleshky across the river, also gave the residents of Kherson the opportunity to walk the streets of their city without the fear of death from Russian glide bombs, artillery and, especially, drones.
read also
Despite the gloomy autumn weather, the temporary peace brought locals out onto the streets in numbers unseen since Kherson was liberated from Russian occupation in November 2022.
"People can just feel calm and walk around, ride a bike, not run from one place to another," said Iryna Leonova to the Kyiv Independent outside a supermarket.
"It's not that life has changed in the last few days, it simply returned."
Normally, the danger all around Kherson is particularly felt in the so-called "red zone," the neighborhoods and settlements closest to the river, where civilization has almost completely disappeared due to the round-the-clock threat of Russian drones.
Now, these areas are once again accessible, although not completely safe, as landmines dropped over years by Russian forces across the river continue to present a threat, as the tragic death of Marines press officer Volodymyr Obertas showed on Oct. 28.
Usually a resident of the city's Ostriv neighborhood, Inna Sapai has long moved to a safer part of Kherson, further away from the river.
In the last days, she has not only been able to run errands that would have otherwise carried with them too much danger, but she also checked on her home in Ostriv.
"It's strange to feel this sense of movement in the city. Not just the people or the cars, but this intangible feeling in the air," Sapai said to the Kyiv Independent.
"Before, any fleeting moment of quiet just weighed down on you, but now, the silence really lifts your mood."
Since the ceasefire, thousands of Kherson locals have returned to their hometown from outside the city.
Some have come to inspect their homes and collect personal belongings, others just for the short-lived feeling of returning to a hometown that has long become unfit for life.
Markets once almost abandoned have come back to life, while city workers have used the opportunity to repair critical infrastructure that was inaccessible until now due to the drone threat.
But everywhere, local resident Natalia said, who declined to give her last name, the bittersweet feeling of how temporary the quiet will be hangs.
"I feel very mixed emotions, there is not really any joy per se, because even though you see how many people have come to the city — yesterday I was stuck in traffic for the first time in years — but there is an understanding that in just a few days everyone will leave again," she said.
"There have been a lot of tears, as people come home to see how their homes have been damaged or ruined completely. But home is home, and Kherson is a place of power for all of us."
According to Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, the ceasefire will continue until 11 p.m. on Nov. 1, upon which the daily strikes across the river are expected to begin again.
Despite the major international effort to make it happen, the Oleshky ceasefire also displayed to the world how quickly the fighting can end in Ukraine if Russia makes the decision to stop.
But with the resumption of hostilities, residents now anticipate that the worst of Russia's campaign to rid the city of life could still be ahead of them.
"I feel sad knowing that soon this will all end, and a great fear of the unknown, that we don't know what will come next," said Natalia.
"People are worried, and I am too, at the fact that it can only get worse."

On Kramatorsk’s Peace Square, a Russian airstrike takes down the building that outlasted Russia’s 2014 occupation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:48:22 UTC
22:48:22 KST

A Russian airstrike destroyed the city executive committee building on Peace Square in central Kramatorsk late on 31 October, the head of the city's military administration, Oleksandr Honcharenko, said. The building outlasted Russia's occupation of the city in 2014, the fighting, and its liberation. Overnight, Russia sent hundreds of drones across Ukraine, wounding people from Volyn to Sumy.
Russia's offensive in Donetsk Oblast grinds toward the last large cities Ukraine holds there. Kramatorsk serves as the oblast's provisional administrative center and sits about 15 km from Russian-held ground. Moscow already counts the city as its own: it included Kramatorsk in a district for Russia's parliamentary elections. Strikes on its center hit the institutions that keep the city Ukrainian.
"The foundation of Ukrainian Kramatorsk"
Honcharenko called it "the central building of Ukrainian statehood in Kramatorsk." He wrote that it held the city's history and its plans.
"One can destroy a building, burn out our land, and steal memories. But they will not destroy our right to a future," Honcharenko wrote.
Russian forces struck Kramatorsk 10 times over 31 October, four times with guided aerial bombs and four times with FPV drones, Donetsk Oblast head Vadym Filashkin said. Six people were wounded, and 11 apartment blocks, an administrative building, and three cars were damaged. In neighboring Sloviansk, Russian strikes killed one person and wounded two.
Hundreds of drones overnight
From 18:00 on 31 October, Russia launched 433 attack drones, 64 of them jet-powered, Ukraine's Air Force said. Air defenses downed or jammed 371 by 07:30, while more than 40 were still in the air. Drones hit 16 locations.
In Volyn Oblast, drones hit Kamin-Kashyrskyi district and wounded one person, the regional administration said. A house caught fire in Rivne Oblast's Ostroh district, and four people were hurt, Ukraine's emergency service reported. In Kyiv Oblast, a morning attack wounded a man in Bila Tserkva district and left another in acute stress, the oblast administration said. A drone hit the Reshetylivka community in Poltava Oblast, and a child was hurt, according to preliminary information.
According to preliminary information, Russian strikes injured six people in Sumy Oblast, and in the Hlukhiv community a drone struck again where rescuers were fighting a fire, the emergency service said, though none of the rescuers were hurt. Strikes on energy sites left more than 650 settlements in Zhytomyr Oblast without power, its administration said. The attack carried on into Sunday, when Russian forces hit an industrial plant in Dnipro and started a fire, the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast administration said.
Over the past day
Russian attacks wounded 17 people in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast on 31 October, including three children, the oblast administration reported. Ten of them were hurt in Pavlohrad. Seven people were wounded in Kharkiv Oblast, including a 16-year-old girl in Zolochiv, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Russian forces hit 55 settlements 699 times, wounding six people, regional head Ivan Fedorov said.
Kramatorsk has come under rising Russian fire this fall. On 8 October, a Russian bomb hit two passenger buses there, and Russia later cloned Euromaidan Press's website to blame Ukraine for it. Days earlier, Russian FPV drones hit three ambulances in the city and killed a woman in her apartment block.

At least 8 Palestinians killed in new Israeli violations of Gaza ceasefire

13:47:47 UTC

Eight Palestinians, including a child, were killed and others wounded in Israeli attacks across the Gaza Strip on Sunday amid Israel’s daily violations of last year’s ceasefire, a medical source said, Anadolu reports.
The source at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, southern Gaza, told Anadolu that five Palestinians were killed in an airstrike in al-Mawasi, west of the city.
Local sources said that the strike hit near schools for children, causing panic among them.
In a separate attack, a medical source at al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City said three Palestinians, including a child, were killed in an Israeli airstrike on al-Thawra Street.
The source added that six other Palestinians sustained injuries of varying severity.
Local sources said that an Israeli drone targeted a gathering of civilians on al-Thawra Street.
The ongoing ceasefire violations have killed 1,580 Palestinians and wounded 5,711 others since Oct. 10, 2025, according to figures from Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, Israel’s war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000 others, figures from the ministry showed. The war has also destroyed around 90% of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure.

Chinese President Xi Jinping has mounted a direct defence of the campaign for strong Communist Party governance and internal discipline, describing them as a “fundamental guarantee” for China’s rise and warning against any easing of scrutiny, according to state media.
Xi took the floor as the party’s 20th Central Committee closed its fifth plenum on Thursday, to directly address the scepticism over the sweeping campaign, state news agency Xinhua reported on Sunday.
According to “side notes” released by Xinhua on a document formally approved at the end of the four-day plenary session, Xi emphasised the need to “further raise awareness of the importance and urgency of relentlessly advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”.

Pope Leo XIV welcomes successful completion of humanitarian mission in Oleshky
The pontiff made the statement on Sunday, November 1, after the Angelus prayer in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican, Ukrinform reports, citing Vatican News.
"In recent days, a humanitarian operation has been carried out to assist the civilian population in the city of Oleshky. I hope that the cooperation between the parties, which made this necessary gesture of humanity possible, will foster a greater willingness to engage in dialogue and lead to new concrete initiatives for peace," the Pope said.
He also called on the faithful to pray to the Virgin Mary for all those suffering from wars in different parts of the world.
On October 23, 2026, an agreement to carry out a humanitarian mission in Oleshky was officially confirmed. International humanitarian mediation was provided by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump and her team. The agreement was confirmed on the Ukrainian side by Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets and on the Russian side by Russia's Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova. Lubinets headed the Ukrainian negotiating team for the mission, while his Russian counterpart, Lantratova, led the Russian side.
On October 31, the Ukrainian delegation that had carried out the humanitarian mission in the temporarily occupied city of Oleshky, Kherson region, returned to territory controlled by Ukraine.
