UK flies Protector drone on first home operation against Russian frigate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:46:01 UTC
22:46:01 KST

- An RAF Protector RG1 flew its first operational sorties in UK airspace, providing more than 10 hours of surveillance over the English Channel.
- The aircraft supported HMS Dauntless and HMS Tyne as they tracked the Russian frigate Neustrashimy between Oct. 1 and Oct. 14.
An RAF Protector RG1 remotely piloted aircraft has flown its first operational missions in UK airspace, giving the Royal Navy more than 10 hours of surveillance over the English Channel while warships tracked the Russian frigate Neustrashimy, the UK Ministry of Defence said.
The unarmed Protector flew alongside military and civilian air traffic while the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless (D33) and offshore patrol vessel HMS Tyne (P281) monitored Neustrashimy and accompanying merchant ships through the Channel between Oct. 1 and Oct. 14. The ministry did not say how many sorties the aircraft flew, which sensors it used or how much of the frigate’s transit it covered.
“Protector’s first operational sorties in UK airspace demonstrate the significant value this capability brings to UK Defence. Working alongside Royal Navy vessels, it provided persistent intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance coverage, highlighting its ability to operate seamlessly across military and civilian airspace in support of maritime security, NATO commitments and wider UK tasking,” said Wing Commander Sam Haley, officer commanding XIII Squadron.
Protector is the RAF’s version of General Atomics’ MQ-9B SkyGuardian, flown from RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire by 31 and XIII squadrons. The UK Military Aviation Authority issued it a military type certificate on April 29, 2025, clearing it to fly without geographic restrictions in UK airspace, and it entered service in June 2025 as the first remotely piloted aircraft authorized to do so. The MQ-9A Reaper it replaced never flew in UK airspace during its RAF career. The first of 16 Protectors arrived at RAF Waddington in 2023.
The RAF lists the aircraft’s endurance at more than 30 hours and its ceiling at up to 40,000 feet (12,200 m), with full-motion video, infrared imagery, synthetic aperture radar and ground target tracking among its sensors. In June 2026, a Protector flew from Waddington to RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus through European civil airspace, covering more than 2,000 nautical miles in about 13.5 hours.
The Channel mission was one of several Royal Navy operations against Russian ships between late September and mid-October. Merlin helicopters from Royal Naval Air Station Culdrose deployed to Glasgow Prestwick Airport under Operation Iceblast, a test of how quickly the Merlin force can operate away from its home base. From Sept. 29 to Oct. 8, they tracked the Vishnya-class intelligence-gathering ship Viktor Leonov near the Outer Hebrides, where NATO’s Exercise Strike Warrior was underway with more than 2,000 personnel from six nations.
From Oct. 11 to Oct. 14, HMS Tyne and a Wildcat helicopter from 815 Naval Air Squadron followed the Ropucha-class landing ship Aleksandr Shabalin, the cargo ship MV Energy-2 and the tug Proton through the Channel as they headed for the Baltic.
“HMS Dauntless monitored the movements of RFN Neustrashimy during her transit through the English Channel, contributing to the wider maritime picture and supporting UK maritime security,” said Commander Neil Skinner, commanding officer of HMS Dauntless.
Royal Navy activity monitoring Russian movements rose 25% in the first seven months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, the ministry said. Most of that work falls to patrol ships, frigates and helicopters; in January, HMS Mersey, HMS Severn and a Wildcat shadowed a Russian corvette and tanker through the same waters in a two-day operation coordinated with NATO allies.
“For the first time, Protector has joined Royal Navy warships and helicopters monitoring activity around our shores, demonstrating how we are constantly innovating to monitor and deter threats and irresponsible provocation,” said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting.
The ministry tied the operations to £298 billion (about $399 billion) in planned defense spending over the next four years and a commitment to reach 3% of GDP on defense in 2030. It also pointed to £330 million (about $442 million) over four years to protect undersea infrastructure and to Atlantic Bastion, a Royal Navy effort combining warships, patrol aircraft and autonomous systems against Russian submarines in the North Atlantic.

Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:45:14 UTC
22:45:14 KST

The EU has called on Polish authorities to ensure that the country's Constitutional Tribunal functions in accordance with the constitution and European legal standards amid an escalating political crisis.
"The Commission is following the recent developments closely," a European Commission spokesperson told Anadolu on Sunday.
"It is for the Polish authorities to ensure that the Constitutional Tribunal can function in accordance with the Polish constitution and in respect of the relevant case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union," she said.
The spokesperson noted that appointing eight new members of the Constitutional Tribunal falls within the constitutional powers of the Sejm, the lower house of Poland's parliament.
She cited an October 13, 2026, opinion by the Venice Commission confirming the Sejm's authority to make the appointments.
"Also, on May 5, 2026, the European Court of Human Rights issued interim measures obliging the competent Polish authorities to refrain from hindering the taking up and exercise of judicial duties by judges appointed by the Sejm in March 2026," she added.
Political crisis escalates over tribunal control
The European Commission's remarks followed a sharp escalation Friday, when the Constitutional Tribunal announced the immediate suspension of its president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and vice president, Bartlomiej Sochanski.
Control of the tribunal was transferred temporarily to Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, an appointee of the current parliamentary majority.
Police were deployed around the building after Korwin-Piotrowska warned of threats to judges and staff and possible public disorder.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki cut short an official trip to Senegal on Friday night and returned to Warsaw, heading directly to the tribunal's headquarters.
Media footage showed tense confrontations inside the building between presidential aides and newly appointed judges.
After leaving the tribunal, Nawrocki declared the situation a violation of Poland's constitutional order and called for urgent consultations among parliamentary leaders.
Tusk accuses opposition of undermining rule of law
Prime Minister Donald Tusk defended the government's actions, saying restoring the rule of law remained his responsibility.
In a televised address Saturday evening, Tusk accused Nawrocki and the conservative opposition of undermining the rule of law.
He also said police had protected the Constitutional Tribunal from attackers.
The dispute has intensified tensions between the president and the government over the legitimacy and control of one of Poland's highest judicial institutions.

Qatar condemns attack on LNG tanker in Gulf, warns of threat to global energy supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01

Amer Solyman and Rania Abushamala
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
Qatar on Sunday strongly condemned an attack on the liquefied natural gas (LNG) tanker Al Mayeda while it was sailing in the Gulf, warning that the incident threatened maritime navigation and global energy supplies.
In a statement, the Foreign Ministry said the vessel belonged to Qatar Gas Transport Company, known as Nakilat.
The ministry described the attack as “a dangerous act that threatens the safety of maritime navigation and the security of global energy supplies.”
Qatar “reserves the right to take all necessary measures under international law and the UN Charter to protect its property, safeguard its interests and ensure the safety of its vessels and crews,” it said.
The ministry added that the relevant authorities had begun investigations to establish the circumstances of the incident and identify those responsible.
It warned that such “reckless and irresponsible practices” could have serious repercussions for regional security and stability and the global economy.
The ministry also highlighted potential environmental risks arising from attacks on energy tankers, warning of serious consequences for the marine environment and the water security of countries in the region.
Earlier Sunday, Nakilat announced that one of its vessels carrying LNG had been struck by “unidentified objects” while sailing in Gulf waters Friday evening.
The Qatar News Agency quoted the company as saying that Al Mayeda was struck on Oct. 30, with no injuries among crew members or environmental damage.
The company did not disclose the nature of the objects involved in the attack, identify those responsible or specify the incident’s exact location.
Nakilat is a Qatari public shareholding company with public and private sector ownership and plays a key role in transporting LNG as part of Qatar’s energy supply chain.
The incident comes amid persistent security risks to commercial navigation in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, with commercial vessels and oil and gas tankers facing repeated attacks and security incidents in recent months.
October saw a series of attacks on commercial tankers in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, some of which caused fires and damage to vessels, according to maritime security reports.
Concerns over shipping security have intensified amid continuing tensions between the US and Iran, particularly over the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage for global oil and gas exports.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28 before a ceasefire was reached in April. Fighting between Washington and Tehran resumed in July amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the war.

Estonia's Selevko wins bronze, Petrõkina third ahead of free skate in Canada
Estonia's Mihhail Selevko struck bronze at Skate Canada International in Kelowna, where Niina Petrõkina heads into Sunday's free skate in third after setting a personal best.
Fifth after the men's short program, Selevko climbed to third overall by winning the free skate with 169.08 points, just shy of his personal-best 169.78, set a month and a half ago. The Estonian skater finished with 248.66 points across the two programs.
Selevko also became the third Estonian figure skater to reach the podium at an International Skating Union (ISU) Grand Prix event, joining his older brother Aleksandr and training partner Niina Petrõkina.
"I fought through the entire program and was more nervous before the competition than I had been for the short program, because yesterday's event was difficult," he said. "Today I needed and wanted to do better, so I focused on every jump. I'm very happy it worked."
While placing second in both programs, France's Kevin Aymoz won his second career Grand Prix event with a combined 258.43 points, earning 168.17 for his free skate to Estonian composer Arvo Pärt's "Spiegel im Spiegel."
Japan's Rio Nakata, a two-time world junior champion, slipped to fourth in the free skate with 156.61 points but held onto second overall with 249.25 in his senior Grand Prix debut.
Personal-best short program
In the women's event, two-time European champion Niina Petrõkina sits third heading into Sunday's free skate after setting a personal-best 77.24 in the short program, edging out her previous best of 77.20 set in Italy six weeks ago.
Petrõkina delivered a clean program, executing all her jumps without error and earning the highest rating, Level 4, on all her other elements.
Japan's Mao Shimada, a four-time world junior champion who turned 18 on Friday, won the short program with a personal-best 82.11 points, including 49.23 points for her technical elements, the third-highest score ever.
American Isabeau Levito, another former world junior champion who won gold in Tallinn in 2022, was second with 78.50 points in her first competition of the season.
The 2026 Skate Canada International is the second of seven events in the 2026 ISU Figure Skating Grand Prix series, which concludes with the final in Chongqing, China, in December.
The women's free skate in Kelowna begins Sunday at 10 p.m. Estonian time.

Russia’s Warplanes Are Burning, Crashing, and Disappearing—13 Lost in Five Weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:40:40 UTC
22:40:40 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Warplanes Are Burning, Crashing, and Disappearing—13 Lost in Five Weeks
Russia has reportedly lost approximately 13 military aircraft in just five weeks, including Su-34 fighter-bombers, Su-30SM fighters, a Tu-95MS strategic bomber, and a Su-57 stealth fighter, following Ukrainian strikes on Russian airbases and a series of aviation accidents.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on October 31, Ukrainian open-source monitoring project Oko Gora recorded 11 Russian combat aircraft and one helicopter lost in October, with two additional Su-34 bombers damaged. Including a Tu-95MS that crashed on September 29, the reported losses reached approximately 13 aircraft since late September.
The Su-34 fighter-bomber accounted for the largest share of reported losses. Russian forces regularly use these aircraft to launch guided glide bombs against Ukrainian military positions and cities.
On October 4, Ukrainian Security Service (SBU) drones reportedly struck a Su-34 and a Su-35 fighter at Khanskaya airbase in Russia’s Republic of Adygea, approximately 500 kilometers (310 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Another attack followed on October 14–15, when Ukrainian Neptune cruise missiles targeted Borisoglebsk airbase in Russia’s Voronezh region. Satellite imagery reportedly confirmed four Su-34 bombers destroyed and two others severely damaged.
On October 29, Ukrainian forces reportedly struck Marinovka airbase in the Volgograd region with Neptune missiles, destroying another two Su-34 aircraft. In total, seven Su-34 bombers were reportedly destroyed during October, while two more sustained damage.
According to Ukrainian military intelligence, Russia had approximately 140 Su-34 aircraft in service as of October 22. Russian manufacturers delivered 22 new aircraft of this type between October 2025 and October 2026, meaning the seven reported losses in October alone amounted to nearly one-third of the previous year’s deliveries.
However, Ukrainian strikes were not the only cause of Russia’s aviation losses. As Defence Blog reported, a Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed during takeoff near Ukrainka airbase in Russia’s Amur region on September 29, killing six of its seven crew members. The aircraft, which Russia uses to launch Kh-101 cruise missiles against Ukraine, is no longer in production.
On October 21, a Su-30SM fighter crashed during a training flight in Russia’s Kaliningrad region. Russian authorities said both crew members ejected. A second Su-30SM was reportedly lost the same day, although Moscow has not officially confirmed that incident.
One of the most significant reported losses involved Russia’s fifth-generation Su-57 stealth fighter. On October 29, a Su-57 reportedly caught fire during engine startup at Akhtubinsk airbase in the Astrakhan region, one of Russia’s principal military aviation testing facilities.
Satellite imagery published by Ukrainian open-source researchers showed a burn mark at the airfield, although Russian authorities have not confirmed the aircraft’s destruction.
The reported losses occurred across a wide geographical area, from Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave on the Baltic Sea to its Far Eastern regions.
For context, the open-source intelligence project Oryx has visually documented 205 Russian military aircraft destroyed or damaged since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, according to figures cited by Defence Blog. The Su-34 accounted for 48 of those documented cases.
The losses also extended to Russian helicopters. On October 30, Ukraine’s Third Assault Brigade reported destroying a Russian Mi-8 transport helicopter in the Luhansk region using two Hornet attack drones after the aircraft landed.

Norwegian frigate deal shaped new offset policy

The Chancellor has cited Norway’s own requirements as an example of the thinking behind Britain’s new offset policy, telling reporters that Norwegian industry is part procuring the frigates being built on the Clyde and that Britain will now ask the same of foreign suppliers in return, according to remarks made at a press huddle in Glasgow.
John Healey was asked what role Scotland will play in the Defence Investment Plan, in manufacturing and jobs, and what impact the plan will have in Scotland specifically.
He said: “Defence is our number one priority. We also announced today the defence secretary and policy, where people have seen this is a government that will direct our defence investment first and foremost in British jobs and British businesses. But there will be things that we need to buy from abroad and from allies.

We will buy some of the things the Norwegians produce that we can’t here.
“Now, in future, when Britain places contracts abroad, we’ll make sure that those we place those contracts with invest in Britain as well, jobs, business support, innovation, so that we can make sure that every pound of British taxpayers’ money works twice. It works for the national security of this nation, and it works also to reinforce jobs and businesses in the future of this country, including across the UK here in Scotland.”
Norway ordered five Type 26 frigates from Britain in a £10 billion deal that supports 2,000 jobs on the Clyde, the largest warship export in a generation, and Norwegian industry expects work in return under arrangements of exactly the kind Britain is now adopting. Oslo has run an industrial cooperation requirement for decades, obliging foreign suppliers of significant defence equipment to place work with Norwegian firms.
Under the British policy published today, contracts above £50 million placed with overseas companies will be considered for offsets, and suppliers can be required to deliver benefits worth up to the full contract value through jobs, apprenticeships, factories, investment in British suppliers or transfers of technology. A central Offset Authority will agree, value and monitor each arrangement, and the policy applies to a select number of procurements from April 2027.

More than 50 million votes cast in US midterm elections: What does it mean?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:32:59 UTC
22:32:59 KST

More than 50 million votes cast in US midterm elections: What does it mean?
A record number of early votes is cast as both parties campaign before Tuesday’s polls.
Early voting has surged in the 2026 United States midterm elections with more than 50 million Americans casting their ballots as of Sunday, according to an analysis by the University of Florida.
Most of the 50 states allow early in-person voting while all of them allow mail-in voting. About 23 million people voted through mail-in ballots, which President Donald Trump unsuccessfully tried to curb before the elections.
With two days left to go before Election Day on Tuesday, support for Democrats was 51.5 percent and for Republicans 43.1 percent, the latest national polls suggested.
The president’s tariff policy and his decision to launch a war with Israel on Iran are hurting his Republican Party. Both have been blamed for contributing to a cost-of-living crisis.
Why are so many Americans voting early? How does it work?
Here’s what we know:
How many Americans have voted early?
Early voting gives US citizens a chance to cast their ballots before Election Day.
According to the US government, people may vote early in person in most states by visiting designated polling stations. All states offer vote-by-mail options, in which registered voters may receive and return ballots by Election Day by mail.
The number of states offering options to vote in person before November expanded from 24 in 2000 to 47 in 2026, plus Washington, DC. But early-voting periods, eligibility requirements and procedures vary widely by state.
This year, out of about 210 million registered voters, 53.14 million had voted early as of 6:56am East Coast time (11:56 GMT) on Sunday , according to the University of Florida analysis. This includes 29 million in-person votes and 23 million mail-in ballots.
In the 2022 midterm elections, 46 million people had voted early.
Early voting enthusiasm has been higher among Democrats this year with more than 11 million registered Democrats having voted early, compared with about 8 million registered Republicans, according to the university’s analysis.
Which states have seen a surge in early votes?
Early voting has particularly surged in the state of Texas, a key battleground, where more than 7 million people have already voted early. This is over 1.5 million more than voted early in the 2022 midterms, according to the University of Florida analysis.
According to an Associated Press polling analysis, in South Carolina, where Trump won by nearly 18 percentage points in 2024, early voting has surged 83 percent compared with the same point in 2022. The state has open races for governor and US Senate this year.
In Kansas, where Republican Senator Roger Marshall faces Democratic Methodist minister Adam Hamilton, early voting has increased 34 percent with roughly 83,000 more ballots cast than at the same point four years ago, AP reported.
In Maine, where Republican Senator Susan Collins faces Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson, early voting is up 44 percent. Michigan has also recorded roughly 409,000 more early votes than at the same point in 2022, a 32 percent increase.
Why are people voting early?
According to the University of Maryland’s Center for Democracy and Civic Engagement (CDCE), there are many reasons why Americans are voting early.
This could be because “some voters find early voting to be more logistically convenient than Election Day voting” or have been “mobilised” to vote early, it said.
“Many voters report voting early because of anxiety about the election or a feeling of wanting to ‘get it over with’ or ‘cross it off their list’ as soon as possible,” the CDCE said.
The centre added that some voters choose to vote early for social or cultural reasons. It noted how efforts like “Parties at the Polls” and community celebrations of voting “try to create a more celebratory environment at certain voting locations, especially during early in-person voting”.
While early turnout figures don’t show which candidates voters have chosen or what the final results will be, Democratic political strategist Celinda Lake told Al Jazeera this past week that many voters were looking for change.
“You got a lot of voters who say, ‘I’m going to do a Hail Mary for change, but I hope you do something,’” she said.
“We all just really want a better future for everyone, especially like the next generation,” one young voter told Al Jazeera.
Another young voter pointed to social media as a reason for the increased interest in the election. “Definitely social media. Social media and the media have put voting in the limelight,” the voter told Al Jazeera.
What has Trump said about mail-in voting?
Trump has repeatedly cast doubt on the security of mail-in voting, which enables people to vote early by mail. Trump, who himself has repeatedly voted by mail, cited debunked claims of widespread election fraud associated with it.
Mail-in ballots, which have been in place for decades, have been found to increase voter turnout and currently account for a third of all votes cast in the US.
State and county officials in eight states send ballots to the homes of all registered voters, who then mail them back before a deadline. The rest of the states send ballots only to the registered voters who request them. Voters may return the ballots through official election drop boxes. In some states, the ballots have to reach the voting centre by Election Day while in others, ballots postmarked by Election Day but received after it may still be counted.
Eight states, several of them Democratic-leaning – California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington – as well as the District of Columbia allow all elections to be conducted entirely by mail.
Others allow smaller elections to be conducted by mail.
Trump has falsely blamed his 2020 presidential election loss on mail-in voting fraud. He and his supporters also opposed changes made during the COVID-19 pandemic to expand mail-in voting.
In March, Trump signed an executive order directing the US Postal Service to take control of mail-in voting by designing new envelopes with special barcodes that would allow the federal government to ensure ballots are only from eligible voters.
For the midterms, that move would have forced all states to adopt a uniform envelope style in a short time.
Democrats and activists challenged the order in several courts, resulting in a series of back-and-forth rulings from May to August.
Last month, however, the Supreme Court rejected Trump’s bid to require the mail-in voting restrictions before this month’s elections.

NEW DELHI: In a major breakthrough against transnational organized crime, CBI in coordination with other Central agencies, has extradited Sourabh Chandrakar, the promoter and alleged kingpin of the Mahadev App illegal online betting syndicate, from the Sultanate of Oman.A special CBI team travelled to Muscat, took custody of Chandrakar, and escorted him back to India. Following a mandatory medical examination and the acquisition of a transit remand, he will be taken to Raipur and produced before the CBI Special Judge Monday.Chandrakar is wanted in two CBI cases, in which chargesheets have already been filed, as well as an Enforcement Directorate (ED) case where a prosecution complaint has been submitted and several properties in India and abroad have been attached.The investigation into the Mahadev Online Book cases was taken up by the CBI at the request of the Chhattisgarh government.The probe revealed that the syndicate operated as one of the country's largest illegal online betting networks run from outside India, facilitating unlawful betting on cricket, football, card games, and other events through a widespread system of franchised "panels" and "branches."Proceeds from the illegal betting network were funneled through numerous mule bank accounts, layered via multiple transactions, and moved overseas through hawala channels.
CBI investigations also established that a portion of the illicit funds was used to pay protection money to public servants to ensure the unhindered operation of the syndicate.Chargesheets in the matter have been filed under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, provisions of the Indian Penal Code relating to criminal conspiracy, cheating, and forgery, as well as the Chhattisgarh Gambling (Prohibition) Act, with Chandrakar named as a key accused.
Chandrakar was initially located and detained by the Royal Oman Police following a Red Corner Notice issued against him. Subsequent extradition proposals, accompanied by gathered evidence, were submitted by the CBI and ED, and pursued in close coordination with Indian government agencies, the Interpol National Central Bureau, and Omani authorities.The CBI expressed gratitude to the Government of the Sultanate of Oman and the Royal Oman Police for their cooperation, highlighting the strong bilateral relations and mutual commitment to combating international crime. The extradition represents a key milestone in India's ongoing efforts to hold foreign-based fugitives accountable under Indian law, CBI said.

Column: Small producers, big markets -- the CIIE story
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
21:29:13 CST
22:29:13 KST

by Maya Majueran
At a time when global trade is increasingly disturbed by tariffs, protectionism and geopolitical competition, a different story is emerging from Shanghai's exhibition halls.
It is not about multinational giants or the strategic interests of major economies. It is about Peruvian artisans, Kenyan avocado farmers and Malagasy herders -- ordinary producers seeking access to international markets and opportunities to improve their livelihoods.
The China International Import Expo (CIIE) is helping turn "inclusive globalization" from a diplomatic slogan into economic reality by creating market opportunities, generating employment, and improving livelihoods.
For many developing countries, the greatest obstacle to international trade is not a lack of products or entrepreneurial ambition, but limited access to markets, financing, logistics and commercial networks. Through targeted support, dedicated exhibition areas for least-developed countries, and direct connections with Chinese buyers, the CIIE seeks to reduce these barriers.
The objective is not charity, but meaningful participation in global trade.
The CIIE's significance also lies in its continuity. Through its "6 days + 365 days" model, the expo connects temporary exhibitions with year-round trading platforms. Bonded warehousing, cross-border e-commerce, and buyer matchmaking help businesses turn initial orders into sustained commercial relationships.
In July 2025, Burundi shipped 38.4 tonnes of Arabica coffee directly to China for the first time, followed by contracts exceeding 900 tonnes worth over 5 million U.S. dollars.
At the seventh CIIE in 2024, 13 of 16 participating Nigerian companies reportedly secured agreements, including a cocoa contract worth over 1.2 million dollars.
The eighth CIIE last year recorded 83.49 billion dollars in one-year intended deals, up 4.4 percent from the previous edition and hitting a new high.
Smaller economies face structural disadvantages in international trade. Regulatory compliance, logistics, marketing, and distribution impose disproportionately high costs on low-volume exporters. By connecting buyers and sellers and facilitating market entry, the CIIE helps reduce these barriers.
The CIIE offers one practical model for smaller economies to access international markets. For artisans in Peru, farmers in Kenya, and herding communities in Madagascar, the benefits can extend beyond export contracts to employment, household incomes and local development.
Inclusive globalization should be measured not simply by how much trade expands, but by how widely its opportunities are shared.
It is an approach worth drawing on.
Editor's note: Maya Majueran serves as the director of the Belt and Road Initiative Sri Lanka, an independent and pioneering organization with strong expertise in Belt and Road Initiative advice and support.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of Xinhua News Agency.

Palestinians in Lebanon suffering worsened by high energy prices, inflation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:25:27 UTC
22:25:27 KST

Palestinians in Lebanon suffering worsened by high energy prices, inflation
As one of Lebanon’s most vulnerable communities, Palestinians are struggling to make ends meet.
Beirut, Lebanon — Osama Najjar is a Palestinian refugee living in the Beddawi refugee camp in Tripoli, Lebanon’s second-largest city, where he used to have a shop selling aluminium.
Palestinians are barred from working in specific professions in Lebanon, including medicine, law, engineering and pharmacy, meaning that owning a shop is a crucial economic lifeline for many, regardless of their education levels.
But Najjar, like other Palestinians in Lebanon, says the situation has grown increasingly difficult, as rising inflation and energy costs hit one of Lebanon’s most vulnerable communities particularly hard. With business stuttering and unable to keep up with his bills, he was forced to close his shop in early 2024. Since then, he has found work hard to come by.
“The whole Palestinian situation in the camps is tragic,” he said, citing high prices and rising electricity bills as two of his most recent concerns.
Palestinian discrimination
Palestinians first became refugees in Lebanon during the 1948 Nakba, when Zionist forces established the state of Israel. In the process, they destroyed more than 500 Palestinian towns, killed about 13,000 Palestinians, and turned 750,000 more into refugees who fled to camps in the occupied West Bank and neighbouring countries.
Of those, about 100,000 people went north to Lebanon, many of them promising themselves that they would return home one day. Many slept in informal settlements and tents at first, but as the years passed and hopes of an immediate return to their hometowns and villages faded, tents gave way to informal and often unregulated concrete structures.
In 1964, Lebanon passed a decree on foreign workers that required non-Lebanese nationals to obtain work permits. During the country’s civil war, which lasted from 1975 to 1990, a wide range of Palestinian political groups took part in the fighting. This legacy left behind ill will towards Palestinians from some segments of the Lebanese population.
In 2010, amendments were made to the Lebanese labour law that reduced certain permit fees and eased other restrictions for Palestinian labourers, but experts say implementation was limited. In 2021, the Ministry of Labour issued a decree that was supposed to ease restrictions on some professions, which led to political backlash.
In February 2026, the Lebanese government introduced an administrative mechanism that allows Palestinian nursing students to apply for employment sponsorship. However, experts say many of these legal changes do not alter the structural exclusion of Palestinians from the Lebanese labour force.
Today, UNRWA, the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, recognises 12 Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon. According to its Lebanon office, about 222,000 Palestinians resided in the country as of February 2025.
“Palestinians in Lebanon have been treated very differently in a very discriminatory way,” Elia Ayoub, a United Kingdom-based Palestinian-Lebanese researcher and podcaster, told Al Jazeera.
He pointed to the fact that Palestinians can study for but cannot work in many top professions in Lebanon. They are not allowed to own land, and are not politically represented in the country’s parliament.
“Lebanon has an ethno-sectarian system, but Palestinians are not [recognised] one of them,” he said.
Funding cuts
Despite long-running institutional and social discrimination, the situation for Palestinians in Lebanon has become particularly acute in recent months.
The country is yet to recover from 2019’s economic and banking crisis. But rising energy costs and domestic inflation have hit Palestinians particularly hard.
The Lebanese state provides only a few hours of electricity per day, leading most residents to rely on private generators or alternative energy providers. Meanwhile, the World Bank predicts Lebanon’s inflation could reach as high as 17.5 percent in 2026.
In such difficult times, many Palestinians turn to UNRWA for aid. But many countries cut funding to the agency in 2024 after Israel alleged, without providing evidence, that its employees took part in the October 7, 2023 attacks.
UNRWA fervently denied the accusations, and in recent years many states have reinstated funding to the group. Still, in July, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of a funding shortfall of about $100m.
In September, the group reported that it will likely face a minimum $200m financial deficit between the end of 2026 and the start of 2027.
Taking to boats
With no options for a dignified life at home, many Palestinians are risking their lives by trying to reach Europe by sea. In 2022, at least 86 people died on a boat that left Lebanon and sank off the coast of Syria. Many of the dead were Palestinians from the camps.
The number of vessels leaving Lebanese shores increased in the years following 2019, with Palestinians on board many of them. The number of boats attempting to cross the Mediterranean to Europe doubled between 2020 and 2021 and increased by 121 percent the following year, according to the Friedrich Naumann Foundation.
As the cost of living becomes increasingly unsustainable on Lebanese shores, there are fears that more Palestinians and other vulnerable communities in Lebanon could start taking to the seas with increased regularity.
In late October, the European Union approved a support mission to Lebanon that would help strengthen security forces, including “support [for] maritime security governance”.
Najjar said today, the camps are filled with talk of people boarding boats to travel to Turkiye and then on to Greece. Without any kind of economic relief on the horizon, Palestinians may continue to look for reprieve, no matter the risk.
“All of this is still because the situation for Palestinians in Lebanon is poor,” he said.

With just two days remaining before the US midterm elections, President Donald Trump is facing growing accusations of attempting to interfere with the electoral process, as federal authorities pressure election officials, pursue disputed voter fraud allegations and seek greater control over voting procedures. Meanwhile, opinion polls indicate a substantial Democratic lead, raising the possibility that Republicans could lose control of Congress.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
A federal judge in California has ordered the Trump administration to stop threatening state and local election officials with criminal prosecution for refusing to segregate ballots belonging to voters the government suspects of being noncitizens.
The Justice Department demanded that California election authorities set aside ballots from about 20,000 registered voters the government suspects are ineligible. Armed Department of Homeland Security officers subsequently delivered letters warning election workers of possible criminal charges if they failed to comply.
US District Judge Trina Thompson ruled that the administration's actions threatened to disrupt election administration and prevent eligible citizens from voting.
"Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters," Thompson wrote.
Trump criticised the ruling on Saturday, questioning why judges would oppose what he described as efforts to combat election fraud.
The confrontation comes amid broader concerns about possible federal interference in Tuesday's elections, which will determine control of the House of Representatives and Senate.
An extensive Reuters investigation, based on interviews with more than 50 election officials, lawyers and voting specialists, identified nine potential scenarios through which the administration could disrupt the electoral process.
These include federal seizures of ballots and voting equipment, pressure on officials to reject results, immigration enforcement operations near polling stations, military deployments, emergency declarations and attempts to delay certification or prevent elected lawmakers from taking office.
The Justice Department also plans to deploy approximately 1,000 federal election monitors, nearly twice the number sent during the 2024 presidential election. Officials in several states have expressed concerns that federal personnel could exceed their traditional observational responsibilities.
The White House maintains that its measures are intended to protect election integrity and prevent unlawful voting. However, election experts interviewed by Reuters warned that even unsuccessful interventions could delay vote counting, create confusion and undermine public confidence.
Questions have also emerged over the reliability of federal efforts to identify noncitizens on voter registration lists.
According to research published by the Center for American Progress, the Department of Homeland Security has relied on potentially inaccurate database comparisons that risk incorrectly identifying American citizens as ineligible voters.
In Nevada, federal authorities initially flagged nearly 16,000 registrations as potentially belonging to noncitizens. After the government provided 185 names for examination, state officials determined that all 185 individuals were US citizens.
The political stakes are particularly high as Democrats maintain a significant advantage in national polling.
The RealClearPolling average placed Democrats at 51.5 per cent compared with 43.1 per cent for Republicans on Sunday afternoon.
More than 51 million Americans have already voted, while closely contested Senate races in Michigan, Kansas, Iowa and other states could determine whether Republicans retain control of the chamber.
Economic dissatisfaction, rising living costs and the consequences of the US-Israel war on Iran have become central campaign issues. Democrats need a net gain of three House seats and four Senate seats to secure majorities in both chambers.
Trump is scheduled to campaign in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday as Republicans make their final effort to mobilise supporters.
Meanwhile, the president suffered another embarrassing development on Saturday when a federal judge permanently dismissed his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal over its reporting on an alleged birthday letter to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Judge Darrin Gayles ruled that Trump's complaint failed to establish actual malice, the legal standard required in defamation cases involving public figures. Trump denies writing the letter.
The ruling prevents Trump from refiling the lawsuit in the same court, although his legal team has indicated that it intends to continue pursuing the matter.

Practical conservation workshop held at ruined Sassanid palaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:19:20 UTC
22:19:20 KST

Practical conservation workshop held at ruined Sassanid palaces
TEHRAN - A practical training workshop on emergency conservation and restoration at the Palace of Ardashir and Qal'eh Dokhtar (“Maiden Castle”) near Firuzabad, southern Iran, has brought together heritage conservation specialists and university students to provide hands-on experience in protecting historic structures.
Afshin Ebrahimi, director of the Sassanid Archaeological Landscape of Fars World Heritage Site, said the workshop was held on Friday, October 30, with the participation of the World Heritage site management team, facilitators from Isfahan University of Art and 12 students.
He said the program aimed to familiarize students with practical procedures for heritage conservation, monitoring, documentation and emergency restoration, while bridging the gap between academic knowledge and field experience at historic sites.
During the workshop, participants learned about the site's specialist conservation activities and periodic monitoring procedures. They also took part in practical exercises, including surveying, preparing detailed sketches, mapping and assessing damage to selected wall surfaces at Qal'eh Dokhtar, and completing conservation monitoring records.
Ebrahimi said training in the proper identification and documentation of structural damage was essential to the effective conservation of historic monuments. Participants were also introduced to monitoring forms and the technical information required to assess and record the conservation conditions of historic buildings.
Another part of the program focused on emergency conservation work at the Palace of Ardashir. Students, working under the supervision of specialists, participated in repointing sections of the palace's walls and preparing a gypsum witness to help monitor changes in the structure.
Ebrahimi said continuing such workshops could strengthen the technical capabilities of the next generation of conservation professionals, facilitate the transfer of practical experience and promote scientifically grounded approaches to safeguarding Sassanid heritage.
The Palace of Ardashir, also known as Ardashir Papakan Palace, dates to the early third century and was built by Ardashir I, founder of the Sassanid Empire. Located near Firuzabad, the monument is distinguished by its domed chambers, monumental iwan and stone-and-mortar construction.
Qal'eh Dokhtar, another major Sassanid-era monument in the Firuzabad area, is a fortified structure traditionally attributed to Ardashir I. Its architectural features include vaulted halls, arches, domes and stairways.
Both monuments form part of the Sassanid Archaeological Landscape of Fars Region, which was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2018. The property encompasses archaeological remains in Firuzabad, Bishapur and Sarvestan, illustrating the development of Sassanid architecture and the early history of the empire.

Qeshm launches multimedia documentation project to preserve island’s intangible heritage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:19:06 UTC
22:19:06 KST

Qeshm launches multimedia documentation project to preserve island’s intangible heritage
TEHRAN - Qeshm Island has launched a multimedia documentation project to record and preserve its indigenous knowledge, oral history and intangible cultural heritage, with the aim of passing the island’s traditional knowledge and cultural practices on to future generations.
Seyyed Mehdi Mousavi-Ojagh, deputy for cultural, social and tourism affairs of the Qeshm Free Zone Organization, said the initiative involves conducting multimedia interviews with local cultural figures and tradition bearers to document their knowledge, experiences and accounts of the island’s cultural heritage.
According to the official, the project focuses on several aspects of Qeshm’s traditional culture, including indigenous maritime knowledge, local stories and narratives, traditional knowledge related to water heritage, and other elements of the island’s oral history.
He stressed that much of a community’s intangible heritage is preserved in the memories, skills and personal experiences of local people, warning that valuable knowledge could disappear permanently if it is not documented before its bearers pass away.
The initiative seeks to prevent the loss of indigenous knowledge and facilitate the transmission of previous generations’ experiences and cultural practices to younger people, ensuring their continued recognition as part of Qeshm’s historical and cultural identity.
Mousavi-Ojagh also identified community-based cultural tourism as one of the expected benefits of the project, saying that documenting local narratives, skills and traditional knowledge could help introduce the island’s cultural attractions more comprehensively and encourage tourism rooted in local identity and authenticity.
Located in the Persian Gulf, Qeshm is Iran’s largest island and is known for its distinctive combination of natural, geological and cultural heritage. Its cultural traditions include traditional wooden boatbuilding, known as Lenj construction, Bandari embroidery and mat weaving, as well as distinctive local customs and oral traditions.
The island is also home to the Hara mangrove forests and the Qeshm Island UNESCO Global Geopark, which encompasses 26 geological sites and was the first geopark of its kind in West Asia.
The documentation project is intended to turn the knowledge and experiences of older generations into a lasting cultural resource, supporting heritage preservation, education and the development of cultural tourism, the official underlined.

Germany’s youth protests followed by night of unrest, more than 200 detained
More than 200 people were detained as overnight violence followed largely peaceful youth protests across Germany, with shops looted and dozens of police officers injured, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Tens of thousands of young people joined demonstrations organized by the Gen Z Regelt initiative in more than 30 cities Saturday. They demanded greater investment in education, relief from rising living costs and opposed plans to revive compulsory military service.
According to Anadolu’s report citing police, clashes broke out in several cities after the main gatherings ended, with groups erecting barricades and throwing stones, bottles and pyrotechnics at officers.
In Frankfurt, masked groups separate from the main demonstrations smashed shop windows and looted businesses, including a gun store. At least two firearms were stolen before police arrested a suspect and recovered the weapons. Authorities reported more than 30 provisional arrests and extensive property damage.
In Hamburg, police took 120 people into custody after groups erected burning barricades near the central bus station. Eleven officers were injured.
Berlin police temporarily detained up to 56 people during an evening demonstration separate from the earlier peaceful gathering at the Brandenburg Gate. Twenty-seven officers sustained minor injuries. Police halted the march after demonstrators threw objects at officers and blocked a tram.
Cologne police said in an official statement that officers used water cannons after coming under attack following the end of a rally. One officer suffered a hand injury and could not continue working.
Meanwhile, Stuttgart police reported that around 6,000 people attended a demonstration in the city. Five officers sustained minor injuries, and several suspects were temporarily detained. Police said some people threw bottles, stones and pyrotechnics at officers after the rally ended, prompting the use of pepper spray.
By early Sunday, the situation had largely calmed across the affected cities, while investigations and damage assessments continued.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that around 15,000 people took part in protests across France on Saturday, with 27 arrests recorded by 2 p.m. local time. France’s Interior Ministry described the situation nationwide as generally calm during the third consecutive weekend of demonstrations.

Welsh health board considers closing urgent primary care centres at three hospitals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:13:25 UTC
22:13:25 KST

A struggling Welsh health board could close urgent primary care centres at three hospitals, citing funding and recruitment issues, prompting widespread criticism.
Betsi Cadwaladr University health board, which serves about a quarter of Wales’s population, said it was consulting on ending urgent primary care centres (UPCCs) at Ysbyty Penrhos Stanley in Holyhead, Ysbyty Alltwen in Tremadog and Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor by April 2027.
UPCCs staffed by GPs, advanced nurse practitioners and physiotherapists – similar to urgent treatment centres in England – have been set up across Wales since 2020 to ease pressure on GP practices and emergency departments.
Local MPs and MSs from across the political spectrum have written to the board to warn of “dire consequences” – including additional strain on the services they were originally intended to help.
The Conservative MS Janet Finch-Saunders, who represents Bangor Conwy Môn, said: “These centres help to relieve pressure on our accident and emergency departments when people are unable to get an appointment with their GP but require immediate care.
“It is vital that [the health board] supports these centres to remain open. Without them, existing waiting times could increase, potentially leading to delays in treatment.”
Betsi Cadwaladr has been in special measures since 2015 due to concerns over care quality, patient safety and leadership. In June, it was given a “final chance” to improve.
The board’s chief executive, Carol Shillabeer, said in a statement that access to urgent and emergency care remained “a priority”.
The Welsh NHS has fallen behind the other UK nations in several key metrics despite significant funding increases. NHS spending takes up nearly half the Welsh government’s £27.5bn budget. Six of the country’s seven health boards were recently found to have failed in their statutory duty to break even over a three-year period as they struggle to control day-to-day costs.
In September, Powys health board, which spans a quarter of the country, announced it was considering cutting 100 community hospital beds and consolidating minor injury services such as X-rays. Critics say the plans will make accessing care even more difficult for an ageing population in a rural region which is poorly served by public transport.
Opinion polls show that the NHS is overwhelmingly Welsh voters’ top concern. Turning the service around is widely seen as the most important of several fiscal challenges facing the new Plaid Cymru government elected in May.

Ayhan Simsek
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
The EU called on Polish authorities Sunday to ensure that the country's Constitutional Tribunal functions in accordance with the constitution and European legal standards amid an escalating political crisis.
"The Commission is following closely the recent developments," a European Commission spokeswoman told Anadolu.
"It is for the Polish authorities to ensure that the Constitutional Tribunal can function in accordance with the Polish constitution and in respect of the relevant case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union," she said.
The spokeswoman noted that appointing eight new members of the Constitutional Tribunal falls within the constitutional powers of the Sejm, the lower house of Poland's parliament.
She cited an Oct. 13, 2026, opinion by the Venice Commission confirming the Sejm's authority to make the appointments.
"Also, on May 5, 2026, the European Court of Human Rights issued interim measures obliging the competent Polish authorities to refrain from hindering the taking up and exercise of judicial duties by judges appointed by the Sejm in March 2026," she added.
Political crisis escalates over tribunal control
The European Commission's remarks followed a sharp escalation Friday, when the Constitutional Tribunal announced the immediate suspension of its president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and vice president, Bartlomiej Sochanski.
Control of the tribunal was transferred temporarily to Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, an appointee of the current parliamentary majority.
Police were deployed around the building after Korwin-Piotrowska warned of threats to judges and staff and possible public disorder.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki cut short an official trip to Senegal on Friday night and returned to Warsaw, heading directly to the tribunal's headquarters.
Media footage showed tense confrontations inside the building between presidential aides and newly appointed judges.
After leaving the tribunal, Nawrocki declared the situation a violation of Poland's constitutional order and called for urgent consultations among parliamentary leaders.
Tusk accuses opposition of undermining rule of law
Prime Minister Donald Tusk defended the government's actions, saying restoring the rule of law remained his responsibility.
In a televised address Saturday evening, Tusk accused Nawrocki and the conservative opposition of undermining the rule of law.
He also said police had protected the Constitutional Tribunal from attackers.
The dispute has intensified tensions between the president and the government over the legitimacy and control of one of Poland's highest judicial institutions.

Nov 1 (Reuters) - Iranian negotiators were in Doha on Sunday for a third consecutive day of talks with Qatari mediators aimed at pushing for a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran, an official briefed on the discussions told Reuters.
The talks come amid concerns that the conflict could escalate again after the November 3 US midterm elections. Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera quoted Araqchi as saying in an interview on Saturday that Iranian and Qatari negotiators had developed a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days of a potential agreement with Washington.
Iran has repeatedly said it would respond to any new attacks by striking US and Israeli targets in neighbouring countries, as the eight-month-old war continues to disrupt global oil supplies and spill over across the Middle East.
“We are doing our best in this process, and we hope that there is rationality on the other side so that they prioritise diplomacy over other paths,” Araqchi said of the talks with Qatari officials.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday ordered the armed forces to be prepared for any attack, while the military later announced steps to strengthen its readiness.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that Trump has not decided whether to launch new strikes against Iran, but would prefer to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Friday for discussions with Iranian officials before moving the talks to Doha on Saturday, an official had told Reuters. The talks were being coordinated in regular contacts with Washington, the official added.

Ukrzaliznytsia confirmed that the Dnipro station was hit several times during the Friday evening assault. Station personnel had initiated precautionary evacuation protocols ahead of the strikes, moving passengers and rail employees into subterranean bomb shelters, which prevented mass casualties.

Press Release
Muhammad Hazem Salah Abou Ismail was born on 16 June 1961 and has been registered with the Egyptian Bar Association under registration number 54053 since 1990. He is a practising human rights lawyer known for representing individuals and groups subjected to repression and persecution, including opposition figures and activists. He has pursued public interest cases and engaged in legal action against alleged human rights violations. He also stood as an independent presidential candidate in the 2012 presidential elections held in Egypt.
Mr. Abou Ismail was arrested on 5 July 2013, two days after the military coup of 3 July 2013. He was arrested following a raid on his home by heavily armed security forces. Since then, he has been subjected to severe ill-treatment, torture and prolonged solitary confinement. His family has not been permitted to visit him. Since 2016, his family has been unable to obtain verifiable information about his health. Reports that he has lost approximately half of his body weight have further heightened concerns about his physical condition.
Video footage reportedly recorded in a courtroom approximately five months after his arrest appears to show Mr. Abou Ismail telling the judge that, shortly before the hearing, police officers had raided his cell and confiscated his law books, legal reference materials, case notes, pens and papers. These were materials he had accumulated in order to prepare his own defence. The account available indicates that this prevented him from preparing his defence and also deprived him of effective legal assistance.
Mr Abou Ismail was subsequently subjected to multiple trials and sentenced to various terms of imprisonment, all of which, according to the information obtained by us, had ended by July 2026. It has been reported that the fair trial safeguards were not observed in these proceedings. One of the sentences was imposed following a charge of contempt of court arising from his objection to the manner in which the proceedings were conducted.
In 2020, Egyptian police forces again visited the home of Abou Ismail’s family and arrested Baraa Abou Ismail, his eldest son, who was in his final year at university. To date, Baraa Abou Ismail has also been arbitrarily detained. This pressure on the family has likewise been regarded as an action directed against Mohamed Hazem Salah Abou Ismail, with the sole aim of completely breaking his will.
Despite the expiry of his sentences, he has not been released. We have received no information indicating that any new detention, prosecution or other judicial proceedings exist that could explain the continuation of his deprivation of liberty. It is therefore imperative that the legal basis for his continued detention after July 2026 be urgently clarified.
In recent months, the family has been unable to obtain any reliable information about Mr Abou Ismail and, more generally, has been unable to access information that would enable them to verify his condition for years. The family fears that his life may be in danger. He was previously held in Scorpion Prison and is reportedly currently being held in Badr Prisons.
These correctional facilities have been the subject of human rights concerns in reports issued by official institutions and civil society organisations. The absence of independent information about his current condition, considered alongside the reported torture and ill-treatment to which he was previously subjected, prolonged isolation, severe weight loss and inability to communicate with his family, makes this case one requiring urgent intervention.
The information set out above raises serious concerns regarding the rights to liberty and security of person; freedom from torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment; access to a lawyer; a fair trial and adequate facilities for the preparation of a defence; communication with family members; and access to appropriate medical care.
Despite the expiry of all the sentences reportedly imposed on Mr Abou Ismail, his detention continues. According to the latest information, it has also been reported that his voice was interfered with through an unusual throat operation in order to silence his powerful oratory.

Sasanian-era rock carvings of human hands discovered in Marvdasht
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:09:59 UTC
22:09:59 KST

Sasanian-era rock carvings of human hands discovered in Marvdasht
TEHRAN - Archaeologists have identified previously undocumented Sasanian-era rock carvings depicting human hands without accompanying figures in the historic Marvdasht Plain in Fars province, southern Iran.
The unusual engravings, found alongside a Sasanian-era prayer inscription in Middle Persian (Pahlavi), may shed light on ancient practices of prayer, oath-taking and religious rituals.
Archaeologist and historian Abolhassan Atabaki announced the discovery during ongoing archaeological surveys and documentation in the Marvdasht Plain, Ana news agency reported on Sunday.
He said the newly identified carvings depict human hands together with parts of the forearms, engraved directly onto rock surfaces without any accompanying human figures. Their artistic style and visual characteristics suggest that they date to the Sasanian period (224–651 CE).
Atabaki noted that although hands frequently appear in Sasanian rock reliefs as symbols of respect and homage, their independent depiction also has precedents in seals and seal impressions from the period.
Examples held in collections at the British Museum, Bandar Abbas, Takht-e Soleyman, Tell Abu Shaaf in Iraq and the University of California, Berkeley, demonstrate that Sasanian artists sometimes depicted hands independently of other parts of the human body.
Studies of Sasanian art suggest that the hand motif was associated with concepts such as greeting, goodwill and benevolence. In some instances, researchers have also proposed connections with covenants, the deity Mithra and religious ceremonies.
One notable example is a seal impression discovered at Takht-e Soleyman, which depicts a hand accompanied by a Pahlavi inscription reading abestan o yazdan, meaning “seeking the assistance of the deities.”
In that regard, Najmeh Ebrahimi, a historian, said the available evidence suggests that the independent depiction of hands may have served as a symbolic means of expressing prayer, oaths, covenants and wishes for good fortune.
She explained that because the hand plays a central role in carrying out such acts, depicting it independently could have conveyed the intended meaning without the need to portray the entire human figure.
Ebrahimi said the Marvdasht carvings may likewise have had a devotional purpose, possibly representing prayers or appeals for divine assistance.
She added that this interpretation is reinforced by the discovery of a Sasanian-era prayer inscription beside one of the hand carvings.
The depiction of part of the forearm, ending in a straight edge, together with the distinctive positioning of the fingers, gives the newly documented carvings particular archaeological and artistic significance.
Researchers say further examination and documentation will be needed to establish more precisely the meaning and function of the unusual motifs.

How to properly prune currants in autumn: five steps for a healthy bush and a good harvest
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:07:17 EET
22:07:17 KST

How to properly prune currants in autumn: five steps for a healthy bush and a good harvest
Kyiv • UNN
After the leaves have fallen, currants are cleared of dry and diseased branches and thinned out. Black currants are rejuvenated gradually, while red and white currants are pruned more carefully.
Autumn pruning of currants helps remove damaged branches, rejuvenate the bush, and make it easier to care for in the next season. A sharp pair of pruning shears and gloves are all that is needed for the job, but it is important to consider the plant’s age and which type of currant is being grown on the plot.
A bush can produce berries for years, but without care it gradually becomes overcrowded: old branches take up space, young shoots lack light, and harvesting becomes inconvenient. Regular pruning helps remedy the situation. UNN explains how to do it correctly.
When to start the work
A convenient time for inspection and sanitary pruning is after the leaves have fallen, when currants enter dormancy. Dry, broken, and unnecessary shoots are clearly visible on bare branches. Choose a dry day for pruning bushes, and do not work when the wood is frozen: it may break under the tool. If severe frosts have already arrived or there is uncertainty about which branches to leave, major shaping is best postponed until late winter or early spring, before the buds begin to grow. This is especially true of red and white currants.
What is needed for pruning currants
For an ordinary bush, pruning shears with sharp blades are sufficient. Thick old shoots are easier to cut with loppers or a small garden saw.
Before starting work, check the blades. Dull pruning shears crush and split the wood, leaving uneven wounds. The tool should cut cleanly, without excessive effort. If signs of disease are visible on the bushes, the pruning shears should be cleaned and disinfected after working with affected shoots to avoid transferring pathogens to other plants.
Step one: remove dry, diseased, and broken branches
First, the gardener carefully inspects the bush from all sides. Dry branches are often easy to recognize by their brittleness, lack of live buds, and wrinkled bark. They should be cut back to healthy tissue or removed completely at the base, depending on the extent of the damage. If a shoot has suspicious growths, unusual spots, or signs of dieback, it is better to remove it from the plot and not put it in ordinary compost. This cleanup is beneficial for both young and old bushes.
Step two: remove the oldest shoots
In black currants, relatively young branches produce the best fruit. Therefore, a mature bush should be rejuvenated gradually: each year, remove some of the oldest shoots, making room for new ones. Old branches are usually thicker, darker, and more heavily branched in appearance. Young growth, by contrast, more often has lighter bark and grows straighter.
On an established blackcurrant bush, up to one-third of the oldest main shoots are usually removed in a single season. Make the cut as close to the ground as possible, without leaving a long stub. Trying to remove all the old growth at once can sharply reduce the future harvest.
Step three: leave strong branches of different ages
After sanitary pruning and the removal of old shoots, inspect what remains on the bush. For a mature blackcurrant bush, a good guideline is approximately 6–10 strong main stems that do not shade one another. Sometimes 8–12 branches are left, but the exact number depends on the variety, age, and vigor of the plant. Young branches are needed for future harvests, while healthy, established branches already have fruit buds. Do not remove all young growth simply because it is thinner than the old branches.
Newly planted bushes are pruned according to different rules. Their initial task is to develop a strong framework, so the same scheme used for perennial currants should not be applied to a young plant.
Step four: thin out the center of the bush
If branches grow inward, cross, or rub against one another, keep the stronger and better-positioned one. In addition, remove weak shoots that thicken the center, as well as those lying on the ground or leaning heavily toward it.
After pruning, the bush should be open enough for sunlight to reach the inside and for air to circulate more freely between the branches. This makes berry picking easier and helps prevent excessive moisture in dense growth.
Step five: make clean cuts and remove the branches
Thin shoots are cut with one clean, decisive motion. If a branch is removed completely, cut it close to where it emerges from the base of the bush. Do not leave long dry stubs, but do not damage neighboring healthy stems either.
After pruning is complete, branches and fallen leaves are collected, especially if they showed signs of disease. The secateurs' blades are cleaned of sap and dirt and, if necessary, treated with 70-percent alcohol, dried, and stored in a dry place.
Pruning diagrams sometimes recommend covering all cuts with garden-var. In reality, small, clean cuts generally do not require such a coating. Garden sealants do not necessarily protect the plant and may retain moisture. It is much more important to prune the branch correctly and use clean tools.
How pruning red and white currants differs
The rule about removing a significant portion of old branches every year applies primarily to black currants. Red and white currants also form berries on short fruiting spurs of older wood. Therefore, hastily cutting out all the dark branches can deprive the gardener of part of the harvest. For these bushes, formative pruning is usually carried out at the end of winter or in early spring, before the buds open. Well-positioned main branches are retained, while overly dense, damaged, and poorly productive ones are gradually removed. The aim is to preserve an open center and fruiting spurs.
What mistakes should be avoided when pruning currants
The most common mistake is trying to rejuvenate a very old bush drastically in a single day. If the currant bush has grown without care for several years, restore it gradually over the course of several seasons.
The second mistake is cutting all the tops at the same height: this can trigger unwanted thickening instead of rejuvenation. A properly pruned bush does not necessarily have to look small. It should have strong, healthy, conveniently positioned shoots. This approach will help the currant bush overwinter well, renew itself, and provide a stable harvest in the following years.
A reminder
Earlier, we wrote about exactly when to carry out autumn pruning, at what temperature it is safe, and how care differs for various trees in the garden.
