What happened when Isaac Herzog asked 150 Jews to solve their people’s problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:06:02 UTC
22:06:02 KST

After a gala dinner attended by Israeli President Isaac Herzog, most of the guests at the closing conference of his Voice of the People (VOP) initiative in Budapest were in no hurry to call it a night, staying on to dance to Israeli pop music.
That so many stayed for the obligatory let-your-hair-down activity, so often a cringe-inducing, sparsely attended affair at gatherings like these, was an encouraging sign. There was plenty to unwind from: 18 months grappling with some of the Jewish world’s most divisive problems, with war disrupting their work along the way.
Herzog conceived the initiative amid Israel’s bitter divisions over judicial reform, but its launch was delayed by Oct. 7. Run in partnership with the Jewish Agency and the World Zionist Organization, the VOP receives funding from the Azrieli Foundation, the Wilf Family Foundations and the Patrick and Lina Drahi Foundation. Part global networking venture, part Jewish version of “Shark Tank,” VOP divided 150 council members, drawn equally from Israel, North America and the rest of the world, into 10 working groups tasked with coming up with solutions for five major challenges: antisemitism, polarization, Jewish identity and heritage, Israel-Diaspora relations, and relations between Jews and non-Jews.
Over the 18 months, the groups developed 38 initiatives, with more than 20 reaching the proof-of-concept stage and 21 receiving seed grants of up to $20,000.
At the three-day finale in Budapest last month, council members presented projects ranging from artificial intelligence tools designed to bridge communal divisions to programs exploring Jewish identity through meditation and movement.
Yet only 89 of the original 150 council members attended the conference in Budapest. The conference had been postponed because of the war with Iran, leaving some unable to attend, while others had dropped out or disengaged along the way. Organizers had established an ethics committee and barred those who had failed to meet their participation commitments.
One council member from North America, who requested anonymity to speak candidly, said their 15-person working group had dwindled to nine after the inaugural gathering in Haifa in March 2025. It raised questions about whether Herzog had set himself an impossibly ambitious task: bringing together a diverse array of Jews and expecting them to produce lasting results. Or, as the council member quipped, if two Jews have three opinions, what happens when you bring together 150?
One condition for admission: Recognizing Israel as the state of the Jewish people
An algorithm helped select council members according to age, gender, religious affiliation, professional background and other characteristics, organizers said, with the aim of assembling a group that reflected a far wider cross-section of Jewish life than conventional communal leadership forums.
One of the few conditions for admission was recognizing Israel as the state of the Jewish people. But that hardly eliminated ideological tensions, with some left-leaning participants feeling silenced in disputes over Israel’s actions in Gaza, while Haredi participants objected to pluralistic values being treated as axiomatic.
Shirel Dagan Levy, Voice of the People’s CEO, said the aim was to cultivate “generous leadership,” in part through what she called “radical listening” to people with opposing views.
“It’s tough. You have to sit there and feel uncomfortable with listening, but you realize, what can I learn from this?” she said.
During one session at the Budapest conference, Rachel Goldberg-Polin, whose son Hersh was murdered in Hamas captivity, spoke about the difficulty of engaging with people whose views are deeply upsetting.
“This is what really being human is about: grappling, struggling and wrestling with how we do this. How do we see the godliness in the person across from us who’s saying things that we digest as hateful? How does that work?” she said.
Aleeza Ben Shalom, the star of Netflix’s “Jewish Matchmaking,” said the relationships forged among council members were the initiative’s greatest achievement.
“The most powerful thing about this is the network that we created,” she said.
It was a sentiment shared by Ranit Budaie-Hyman, CEO of Meitarim, an Israeli network of integrated religious-secular schools, who collaborated with fellow council members on Mitzion Tetze Torah, a project promoting social cohesion among Israeli schoolchildren. Its educational materials, sent to 50 schools, include games introducing children to Jewish and democratic values. One of the others in her group, Jeremy Leibler, president of the Zionist Federation of Australia, invited Budaie-Hyman to speak at a Jewish educators’ conference in Melbourne, an opportunity she said would never have arisen without the council.
The project’s name, Hebrew for “From Zion shall go forth the Torah,” reflected the group’s belief that divisions affecting Jewish communities worldwide needed to be addressed first in Israel.
“Polarization starts in Israel and affects the world,” Budaie-Hyman said.
Not everyone agreed. Other members of her wider working group argued that each Jewish community faced its own particular divisions and went on to develop a separate initiative.
Herzog, who combined the conference with a state visit to Hungary, said Israel needed to listen more closely to Diaspora Jews, telling reporters on the conference sidelines that “whatever we do or say in Israel affects Jews around the world.”
Yuval David, a filmmaker and LGBTQ activist, was part of a working group focused on relations between Jews and non-Jews.
“Being here means being with doers,” he said. “They don’t just talk about what needs to be done, they take action. They’re motivated and they motivate others.”
The group developed the Jewish & Indian Alliance, seeking to strengthen ties between Jewish communities and the vast Indian diaspora. The alliance has already organized gatherings in Los Angeles and Tel Aviv, bringing together diplomats, entrepreneurs and community leaders to explore cooperation in business, technology and education.
'Everyone is extremely busy...but it's totally worth it'
But coordinating the working groups across continents was no small undertaking. Interviews with council members and facilitators revealed the difficulties of scheduling lengthy, sometimes weekly Zoom meetings across time zones, particularly as members were participating on a voluntary basis alongside demanding professional commitments.
“Everyone is extremely busy,” Budaie-Hyman said. “But it’s very important so I feel like there’s no choice. It’s totally worth it.”
For at least one participant, pursuing the project meant giving up his day job. Joshua Buchalter left his position at an Israeli software company to concentrate on OneBayit, a nonprofit platform connecting Israelis traveling abroad with Jewish families willing to host them for Shabbat and holiday meals.
Some council members complained that the inaugural gathering in Haifa had been dominated by lectures and presentations, leaving insufficient time for networking and practical collaboration. Ben Shalom said organizers had taken that feedback seriously, significantly increasing opportunities for members to interact at the Budapest conference.
Other complaints were more fundamental. Several council members questioned whether they had been recruited to exercise leadership or to participate in a tightly managed process in which organizers ultimately determined which ideas could proceed. Frustrations included the rejection of proposals that members had hoped to pursue. One member, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the expectations had never been adequately explained.
“We weren’t told the rules of the game,” the council member said. “We asked from the beginning what the goal was and were told: Go figure it out.”
Dagan Levy pushed back, saying that some proposals had failed to pass the evaluation process, while other groups produced no projects. But she argued that projects were not the only measure of success.
“You don’t have to come up with an initiative to be a great council member,” she said.
A former technology executive, Dagan Levy compared the experience to launching a startup, where trial and error are expected. “We had failures, but I’m proud of them,” she said. “You test, you pivot, you grow.”
Nate Looney, a transgender US Army veteran and director of community safety and belonging at the Jewish Federations of North America, was among those not working on an initiative, but the uncertainty that frustrated other participants was precisely what appealed to him.
“Honestly, that was a part of what drew me to it,” he said. “They made it clear from the beginning that they’re figuring it out and the fact that they were approaching it that way versus saying, ‘we know exactly what we’re doing so jump on board,’ made me more interested.”
Organizers have promised clearer guidance for Voice of the People’s second cohort, which attracted 2,500 completed applications. The program has been shortened to 16 months, with its first four months devoted to building relationships before members vote on which challenges to address. Working groups will have three possible outcomes: launching a new initiative, organizing a campaign or developing a proposal for an existing organization to implement. Organizers also said they were working to improve how contentious discussions and ideological disagreements are handled.
Looney said he remained invested because he believed in where the initiative was headed, despite some bumps along the way.
“If you’re in innovation, your first idea is not always going to be what gets you to your moonshot,” he said. “But it gets you started on the path.”

13:06:00 UTC
22:06:00 KST

As Israeli society participates in its democratic process, I find myself reflecting on a question that remains painfully distant for the people of Gaza: what does it mean to have the freedom to choose one’s leaders and influence one’s future?
From Gaza, Israel’s internal democracy presents a striking contrast with the political reality Palestinians have experienced for years.
This observation does not mean that Israel is beyond criticism. Rather, it raises an essential question about political accountability, public participation, and the right of every society to determine its own destiny.
Gaza’s missing political choice
Hamas has controlled Gaza since 2007, and no general elections have been held there since then. Generations of Palestinians have grown up without a meaningful opportunity to renew their political leadership through the ballot box.
Political restrictions, division, and years of devastating conflict have further weakened the possibility of building accountable civilian institutions.
Gaza’s future cannot be determined solely by external actors or by political movements that claim to speak for its people. Its residents must have the freedom to choose their representatives, express disagreement, and hold their leaders accountable.
Elections alone will not solve every problem. Democracy also requires independent institutions, political pluralism, freedom of expression, and respect for the individual.
After years of repression and war, Gaza will need time and genuine opportunities to rebuild these foundations.
Gaza does not need others to choose its future on behalf of its people. It needs the freedom to choose that future for itself.
Learning without idealizing
Israel’s parliamentary system offers a perspective worth examining. Political parties compete, governments face opposition, and public disagreements are expressed through institutions. These mechanisms do not eliminate injustice or guarantee wise decisions, but they create channels through which citizens can influence political life.
My conversations with friends have helped me reflect on this contrast. One of them, Sami, traveled from Switzerland to visit a kibbutz near Gaza. We discussed Israeli democracy and the importance of political participation, even amid deep divisions and security concerns.
Such conversations do not require me to overlook the suffering of Palestinians or abandon criticism of Israeli policies. They remind me that recognizing the strengths of a political system is not the same as endorsing every decision made by its government.
I believe societies can learn from one another without surrendering their identities or ignoring their disagreements. The important question is whether political systems allow citizens to question their leaders and pursue change without fear.
A future beyond today’s imagination?
When I think about Gaza’s future, I sometimes consider an idea that may sound unrealistic today: could Palestinians from Gaza, Arab citizens of Israel, Jewish citizens, and other Israelis one day participate in a shared political framework in which everyone enjoys equal rights and meaningful representation?
Could a future generation imagine new arrangements, potentially including representation within the Knesset, if the people concerned freely chose such a path?
I present this not as a ready-made political program, but as a question about what future generations might decide is possible.
Any such arrangement would require genuine consent, equality before the law, protection of collective and individual rights, and serious answers to questions of citizenship, national identity, and political self-determination.
Palestinians must remain free to choose their own national and political future. No shared framework can be legitimate if it is imposed on them or used to dismiss their aspirations.
Yet history repeatedly reminds us that ideas once considered impossible can become subjects of serious discussion. How many things that once seemed unimaginable have eventually become possible?
The right to choose
For me, the central lesson is not that Gaza should copy Israel or that one society should be judged superior to another. It is that people deserve the ability to shape their own political future.
Israelis can debate their leadership and participate in elections. Palestinians in Gaza deserve that same fundamental opportunity: to choose, to disagree, to organize, and to hold those in power accountable.
Before discussing distant political arrangements, Gaza needs security, dignity, functioning civilian institutions, and the freedom for its people to determine what comes next.
The future may take a form that neither Israelis nor Palestinians can fully imagine today. But any lasting future must begin with a simple principle: every people deserves a genuine voice in deciding its own destiny.
The writer is a Palestinian peace activist from Gaza who advocates for Israeli-Palestinian coexistence and amplifies the voices of Palestinians who reject violence.

US midterm elections 2026: Four key House races that could determine control of Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:05:32 UTC
22:05:32 KST

Americans will head to the polls on Tuesday for midterm elections that will determine control of Congress during the final two years of President Donald Trump's second term.
With Democrats hoping to regain control of both chambers, redistricting could prove decisive in determining the balance of power in Washington.
Cook Political Report found that the Democrats would only need to take one or two seats out of 435 in the House of Representatives to regain a majority. Cook labeled 21 seats in races across the US as “toss-ups”; 16 of them are held by Republicans, and five are held by Democrats.
While the data collected shows potential for a series of wins for the Democrats, CNN noted that the House and the Senate rarely change control in the same year. The last time the Democrats took control of both chambers was in 2006 as part of the Blue Wave against the war in Iraq.
Historically, the US president's party has tended to lose seats in Congress during midterm elections, a pattern that has held across both Democratic and Republican administrations.
While affordability and inflation remain central campaign issues, US foreign policy, particularly Washington's relationship with Israel and the war with Iran, has become increasingly intertwined with domestic debates.
Ahead of the elections, here are The Jerusalem Post’s key House of Representatives races to watch.
Florida's 25th Congressional District: Jared Moskowitz (D) v Scott Singer (R)
Democratic incumbent Jared Moskowitz faces Republican Scott Singer, former mayor of Boca Raton, in a competitive race following Florida's 2026 redistricting.
The newly drawn district stretches along South Florida's Atlantic coast from Palm Beach County to Miami Beach. Redistricting has increased Republican competitiveness in an area where approximately 25% of residents are Jewish, according to demographic data analyzed by The Miami Herald and Sun Sentinel.
Singer has secured the Republican Jewish Coalition's (RJC) endorsement, while Moskowitz is backed by AIPAC.
Economically, Moskowitz emphasizes protecting the Affordable Care Act, Medicare, and SNAP benefits. Singer advocates lower taxes and reduced government spending to address inflation.
"Obviously we'd like to see prices come down; some items have come down. Government can do two things: lower taxes, and cut spending," Singer said during an October 27 candidate forum.
Both candidates strongly support Israel, reject accusations of genocide in Gaza, and oppose conditioning US military assistance to the Jewish state.
Both supported Israel's 2025 strikes on Iranian facilities, although Moskowitz has since called for an end to America's war with Iran.
New York's 17th Congressional District: Mike Lawler (R) v Cait Conley (D)
Republican incumbent Mike Lawler is seeking a third term against Democrat Cait Conley in the Lower Hudson Valley, where affordability, Israel, and antisemitism have emerged as major campaign issues.
The district includes Rockland and Putnam counties, northern Westchester County, and portions of southern Dutchess County. Despite its Democratic voting history, Lawler has won two consecutive elections.
Conley, a West Point graduate and retired Army officer who served in Special Forces and completed multiple combat tours in the Middle East, hopes to flip the seat for Democrats.
Lawler's economic platform emphasizes expanding domestic energy production, restricting insurance companies' ownership of healthcare providers, and stabilizing Social Security.
Conley advocates restoring the full state and local tax (SALT) deduction, limiting utility company profits, and reforming corporate lobbying practices.
"Ratepayers shouldn't be paying for monopoly utility companies or Big Pharma to hire lobbyists to try to buy their way to political outcomes," Conley said.
Israel became a prominent issue during a September debate.
“Israel is our greatest ally in the Middle East,” Lawler said. “They are a beacon of hope and opportunity and freedom and democracy.”
“They have not committed a genocide,” he continued, criticizing Democratic colleagues who have “wavered in their support” for Israel.
Conley condemned rising antisemitism in both parties, describing it as “fundamentally un-American.”
She emphasized Israel's right to exist and the importance of ensuring “the safety and security of the people of Israel.”
However, she has also distinguished supporting Israel from supporting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
“I also criticize Netanyahu when I believe he’s doing the wrong thing for Israel and for America,” she said.
Both candidates opposed a proposed House amendment that would have cut $3.3 billion in annual US assistance to Israel.
Ohio's 7th Congressional District: Max Miller (R) V Brian Poindexter (D)
Republican incumbent Max Miller, a former Trump White House aide, faces Democrat Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker and former Brook Park City Council member, in a race highlighting the divide between white-collar and blue-collar backgrounds, amid economic concerns and allegations of personal misconduct involving both candidates.
Miller, seeking a third term, has highlighted tax cuts, eliminating taxes on tips and overtime, and expanding workforce development programs.
Poindexter has focused on affordability, manufacturing jobs, workers' rights, and collective bargaining.
The district encompasses Cleveland's southern and western suburbs, Medina and Ashland counties, and much of Wayne County.
"I got into this race because too many people who are working as hard as I am are falling further and further behind," Poindexter told 3News on October 29.
He has linked rising prices to the war with Iran and the administration's tariffs.
"The war in Iran has driven up the cost of gas. The blanket tariffs have driven up the cost for our farmers, leading to increased prices at the grocery store and everyday goods," Poindexter said.
The contest has also attracted attention over allegations involving both candidates.
Miller faces domestic abuse accusations from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, daughter of Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno. The allegations prompted calls for his resignation and a House Ethics Committee investigation. Miller denies the accusations.
Poindexter has faced Republican attack advertisements highlighting previous arrests involving suspected drug possession and an altercation at a baseball game. He was not charged in either incident.
“I've been open and honest about my record," Poindexter told 3News. "I got in some fights, got caught with marijuana, had a little too much to drink at Browns games, things like that. But some of the ads are complete nonsense, you know? I was never charged with hard drugs."
Texas 15th Congressional district: Monica De La Cruz (R) v Bobby Pulido
Republican incumbent Monica De La Cruz faces Democrat Bobby Pulido, a longtime Tejano music star, in a Southern Texas race shaped by immigration, affordability, and shifting Latino voting patterns.
The district extends from the Rio Grande Valley north through the Coastal Bend and rural South Texas. Redistricting in 2025 altered its boundaries while preserving its Republican lean.
De La Cruz, who has Trump's endorsement, has represented the district since 2023.
Pulido, a Latin Grammy Award-winning singer, is part of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee's Red to Blue program, targeting Republican-held seats.
Despite supporting Trump, De La Cruz has diverged from some administration positions on immigration and trade. She supports stronger border security alongside bipartisan proposals providing legal status for certain longtime undocumented immigrants.
Her economic agenda emphasizes lower taxes, reduced spending, and support for farmers and small businesses.
Pulido has criticized aggressive immigration enforcement, arguing that deportations harm families and businesses. He supports comprehensive immigration reform, affordable healthcare, and legal pathways for immigrant workers.
He has also opposed tariffs, arguing that they increase consumer costs and hurt farmers and ranchers.
The race comes as Republicans seek to consolidate recent gains among historically Democratic communities in the Rio Grande Valley, while Democrats attempt to rebuild support through economic and immigration policy.

Michigan race: All you need to know about Abdul El-Sayed v Mike Rogers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:03:38 UTC
22:03:38 KST

Michigan race: All you need to know about Abdul El-Sayed v Mike Rogers
Al Jazeera examines the crucial US Senate race in Michigan, including the candidates’ positions and largest spenders.
Dearborn, Michigan – Chadi Abdulrazek, an Arab American political activist who has been volunteering to help elect Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, says he’s spoken in recent days to journalists from Denmark, Sweden, the Netherlands, France and the United Kingdom.
The United States Senate race between El-Sayed and his Republican rival Mike Rogers is attracting national and international attention, reflecting the potent political symbolism that belies its outcome, which extends far beyond one seat in the upper chamber of Congress.
Supporters in each camp paint the contest as a crucial fight that could shape the political direction of the state and the nation for years.
Abdulrazek, a small business owner, said the election is a chance to hold Trump accountable for breaking his promises to pursue peace in the world and focus on the needs of Americans.
For Arab and Muslim communities that have been facing Islamophobic attacks as part of the Senate race, the vote is pivotal, he added.
“What’s on the line is they have to stand up for themselves and say, ‘We are part of this country, and we’re going to be voting, and we will actually make a change’,” Abdulrazek told Al Jazeera.
Here, Al Jazeera looks at the US Senate race in Michigan and why it has gained so much attention.
Who are the candidates?
El-Sayed is a public health advocate who previously led the health department in Detroit and Wayne County in southeast Michigan. He is 42.
If elected, the Democrat of Egyptian descent would become the first-ever Muslim US senator.
El-Sayed ran for governor in 2018 but fell short in the Democratic primary against eventual winner Gretchen Whitmer. The Democratic nominee has embraced progressive policies, especially Medicare for All – a plan to expand government-funded healthcare to everyone in the US.
Rogers is a 63-year-old former US Congress member and state legislator. The Republican nominee ran for the Senate in 2024 and narrowly lost to centrist Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin.
He is a close ally of Donald Trump, but has sought to create some distance between his campaign and the unpopular president.
For example, Rogers has supported Trump’s decision to join Israel in launching the war against Iran, while also calling for an end to the conflict.
The Republican candidate also backs tax cuts, increasing domestic energy production and deregulation.
Why is the race so important?
It will be difficult for Democrats to gain control of the Senate if they lose Michigan. The seat is currently held by retiring Democrat Gary Peters.
A Rogers win would hand the swing state Senate seat to Republicans for at least six years.
The race, however, is not just about the partisan math in the Senate. It is a test of the electoral viability of progressive ideas, including sharp criticism of Israel, in a swing state.
While the Senate has many progressive members, most come from coastal states considered Democratic strongholds.
A victory for El-Sayed in Michigan would show that his message can attract a winning coalition, which could influence how Democratic presidential candidates may go about their campaigning in 2028.
There is also the factor of El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, which had become the subject of near daily attacks by Rogers and Trump.
The race has raised questions about whether Michigan and the US are ready for a Muslim senator.
Why has Israel become a major issue in the race?
El-Sayed has accused Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza, echoing the findings of major human rights organisations and United Nations investigators.
The Democrat has also linked wars, including the conflict in Iran and US aid to Israel, to domestic issues. He says that US taxpayer money is better spent on addressing issues at home, such as healthcare and crumbling infrastructure. Pro-Israel groups, namely the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), have spent tens of millions of dollars to help defeat El-Sayed.
AIPAC backed El-Sayed’s opponent Haley Stevens with more than $30m, making Israel policy one of the most discussed subjects in the election.
El-Sayed overcame the spending onslaught in the primaries, but Rogers – a staunch Israel supporter – has seized on the criticism of El-Sayed from pro-Israel advocates, including some Democrats.
Rogers – who has pledged unconditional support for Israel – has accused El-Sayed of caring more for Palestine than Michigan.
After a lull in spending in Michigan, AIPAC has returned to the race to back Rogers.
The pro-Israel lobby group’s election arm, United Democracy Project, has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on mailers against El-Sayed. According to The New York Times, it has funnelled $9m to a Republican group supporting Rogers.
Why is Haley Stevens back in the headlines?
It is uncommon for the candidate who lost a primary to be part of a major storyline in the general election, but Stevens has been making headlines days ahead of the vote after her fiance endorsed Rogers, citing El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Stevens, a Democrat in the US House of Representatives, has also criticised El-Sayed for his positions on Israel while saying she would still vote for the Democratic candidate.
The congresswoman’s repeated media appearances bashing El-Sayed have earned the scorn of some Democrats.
On Friday, El-Sayed and several Democratic-aligned groups and politicians responded to Stevens, saying that the party must focus on winning the Senate seat.
El-Sayed said in a statement that while “defeating Trump’s hand-picked candidate” should be the priority, “Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.”
What are the voters saying?
Both Rogers and El-Sayed supporters interviewed by Al Jazeera have stressed the race’s importance.
Former Democratic state legislator Cynthia Johnson said the negative campaigning around El-Sayed’s religion and ethnicity makes the election especially crucial.
“What’s really at stake is life or death. Our children are being exposed to some very negative, nasty things,” Johnson told Al Jazeera.
“We have to vote like our lives depended on it because we have a person who’s in the White House right now who’s a maniac and we need as many people who are going to speak up as possible – people like Abdul.”
Outside a Trump rally on Sunday, Rogers supporter Rob Cortis expressed similar urgency.
“This election is so important. Our country is at stake. Our border is at stake. The future of our children in America is at stake,” Cortis told Al Jazeera.
“If it flips to communism, socialism or if it goes to Muslim rule America was never intended for that. America is intended to be a nation of Christians, showing the goodness of God.”
What are the polls saying?
Most recent polls have shown El-Sayed with a narrow lead over Rogers – ranging from four to seven percentage points.
However, polling in Michigan – a diverse state of more than 10 million people – has been unreliable over the past decades, often getting the results wrong by several percentage points.
The Cook Political Report has classified the race as a toss-up and both campaigns have warned their supporters that the result may come down to a few thousand votes.
Who is spending in the race?
With nearly $300m spent, Michigan’s Senate race is quickly becoming one of the most expensive in the country.
Political action committees (PACs) aligned with both major parties have been buying ads in support of their respective candidates.
On the Republican side, one of the largest spenders has been Senate Leadership Fund, whose largest donors include pro-Israel billionaire Miriam Adelson.
MAGA Inc and its subsidiary No Going Back, a pro-Trump group funded by the US president’s allies, including Adelson and Elon Musk, have also spent millions of dollars on the race.
Great Lakes Conservatives Fund (GLCF), a Michigan Republican PAC that AIPAC has backed in general elections, has also been a big spender, according to media reports.
The Senate Majority PAC (SMP) and an affiliated group called WINSENATE have been the largest spenders. SMP’s top funders include businessmen Eychaner Fred and Amos Hostetter Jr.
When is the election?
Early voting is underway across Michigan and hundreds of thousands of people have already cast their ballots.
Election day, Tuesday, November 3, will be the last day to vote. Polls in Michigan close at 8pm (01:00 GMT on Wednesday).
When will the result come out?
That depends on how close the race is. If it’s a tight contest, Michigan likely will not find out who won until Wednesday. In the primaries in August, when El-Sayed narrowly defeated Stevens, the Associated Press did not call the race until about 10am (15GMT) on the Wednesday after election day.
Likewise, Michigan was called for Trump in 2024 around 1pm (18:00 GMT) on the day after the election.
However, if one of the candidates acquires a commanding lead across the state, he could be projected as the winner hours after the polls close.

U.S. Marine Corps attack helicopters set for major upgrade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:02:58 UTC
22:02:58 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps is refining the SPINE upgrade for AH-1Z and UH-1Y helicopters using data from two test aircraft at Patuxent River.
- PMA-276 and Bell are preparing the Amarillo plant to begin modifying operational fleet helicopters in fiscal 2027.
The U.S. Marine Corps’ H-1 program office is using flight test data from the first two upgraded AH-1Z Viper and UH-1Y Venom helicopters to lock down the SPINE configuration, with modification of the first fleet aircraft set to begin in fiscal 2027. Naval Air Systems Command’s Light/Attack Helicopter Program Office, PMA-276, said test points flown so far are feeding into the final aircraft configuration and the technical drawing package for Phase 3.0, the stage that moves the upgrade from test aircraft to operational helicopters.
SPINE, short for Structural and Power Improvements for NextGen Effects, strengthens the airframes to carry heavier loads and adds electrical generating capacity so the helicopters can take on new weapons and mission systems. The Marine Corps lists SPINE among its H-1 lethality priorities in its 2026 Aviation Plan. The program office did not say how many test points remain, when the configuration will be frozen or how much additional power the upgrade provides.
Developmental testing continues at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland, with Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 21, Bell Textron and PMA-276 working as an integrated test team. Bell finished the two test aircraft, one AH-1Z and one UH-1Y, in March 2026 after 19 months of structural and electrical work at its Amarillo Assembly Center in Texas. The effort was known as the Structural Improvement and Electrical Power Upgrade, or SIEPU, until early 2026.
PMA-276 and Bell are now preparing the Amarillo plant to take in operational helicopters. The work includes buying parts, setting up manufacturing and production lines, readying support equipment and specialized tooling, planning how aircraft will be moved to and from Texas, and aligning SPINE with other H-1 modifications so the work can be done in the same visits. The two organizations are also choosing which aircraft go first and scheduling inductions to keep squadrons supplied with helicopters and to keep the fleet’s configuration consistent.
“H-1 modernization is critical to maintaining a capable and ready force for aviation-delivered fires in support of Marine Air-Ground Task Force crisis response,” said Lt. Col. Benjamin Carlton, capabilities and combat relevance pillar lead for PMA-276. “SPINE will provide greater flexibility for utility mission kits and a digital weapons bus capable of integrating advanced lethality systems, including AIM-9X and other digital weapons.”
The contracts for that first batch are already in place. In July, the U.S. Navy awarded Bell $33.6 million for SPINE Phase III hardware, including A-kits, D-kits, power generation components and drivetrain assemblies. Bell described the award as a base contract with three option years covering up to 49 aircraft, 28 AH-1Zs and 21 UH-1Ys, with work in Amarillo starting in mid-2027 and first deliveries in 2028. In October, the U.S. Navy exercised a $114.7 million option for 15 A-kits, four mission kits and nine aircraft installations, all due by June 2028.
Fiscal 2027 began on Oct. 1, 2026, and runs through September 2027, so the first inductions would fall inside the window Bell gave for the start of work in Amarillo.
A digital weapons bus is a data connection between the aircraft’s mission computers and its stores stations. It lets the helicopter exchange data with smart weapons before launch, which analog connections cannot do, and new weapons can be added largely through software. That matters for a fleet that is no longer being built: U.S. production of the UH-1Y ended in 2020 and of the AH-1Z in 2022, and the Marine Corps operates about 189 Vipers and 160 Venoms. The two types share about 85% of their components, so one set of SPINE changes covers both.
The Marine Corps is already testing missions that will draw on that capacity. On May 13, during an exercise at Twentynine Palms, California, Marine Light Attack Helicopter Squadron 169 used UH-1Ys as airborne control nodes for Neros Archer first-person-view drones, launching one from a helicopter in flight and taking over another launched from the ground.
“Government and Bell SPINE teams are continuing developmental testing while preparing for Phase 3.0 modifications in FY27,” Carlton added. “The team has prioritized critical test points before the first installations and maintained close coordination throughout engineering reviews. By addressing critical test requirements early and incorporating refinements as the program progresses, the team is delivering enhanced capability to the fleet sooner.”
Bell and PMA-276 are also working to keep a common technical baseline for the upgraded aircraft, combining Bell’s role as original equipment manufacturer with PMA-276’s program management, so the modified airframes and mission systems can be supported for the rest of their service lives.

Iran’s Foreign Minister speaks to Al Jazeera about US proposals
Tehran, Iran – Ongoing contacts through mediators have provided a potential diplomatic opening between Iran and the United States, even as both sides express readiness for renewed military escalation.
After two days of Qatari-mediated talks, Iranian authorities have signalled that a deal remains possible provided that their demands are tangibly implemented. At the same time, they have doubled down on a willingness to expand attacks or even launch preemptive strikes if they deem war is inevitable.
“We are prepared for all scenarios,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday. “We have upgraded our weaponry, addressed our vulnerabilities, and tested new arms. Our forces are at the highest level of readiness.”
His comments came as US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the talks were going “fine” but added that Iranian authorities were not “reliable”.
The Republican leader, who ordered attacks alongside Israel against Iran on February 28, has repeatedly raised prospects of once more hitting the country’s civilian infrastructure. In recent weeks, he has suggested that an attack could potentially take place after the November 3 midterm elections in the US.
“We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” Trump told reporters at a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago Club in Florida about further bombing Iran’s nuclear facilities.
Sequencing and timeline
The mediated talks in Tehran on Friday, and then in Qatar on Saturday, appear to have produced a new tangible result by shortening the period after which Iran’s proposal to partly reopen the Strait of Hormuz can be enforced.
Tehran had previously offered seven days, but that has now come down to two, Araghchi said in his interview with Al Jazeera.
Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow with the Center for International Policy, said there are “indications” of US interest in a negotiated settlement, citing the continuing Qatar-mediated talks and US Vice President JD Vance’s recent outreach.
“However, Iran is seeking a series of concessions while the United States insists on progress on Iran’s nuclear programme before concessions are made,” she told Al Jazeera.
“Therefore the central difficulty is sequencing and leverage. Each side wants the other to act first.”
Araghchi’s two-day offer indicates some flexibility over sequencing that could also allow both sides to claim an initial diplomatic achievement without immediately resolving their fundamental disagreements, according to Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group.
“However, the military statements show the limits of this opening. Iran appears increasingly determined to prevent a repetition of previous scenarios in which negotiations or temporary ceasefires were followed by renewed military conflict,” he wrote on social media. “From Tehran’s perspective, the objective is to make another attack so costly and unpredictable that Washington would have to reconsider the option altogether.”
As the talks were ongoing on Saturday, the office of Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said he had a meeting earlier with top military commanders to demand “maximum deterrence” through preparedness for an immediate response “without geographical restriction” to any threat.
Targets would include “tangible and intangible” US and Israeli assets, Khamenei said. Iranian authorities have previously said if Iran’s civilian infrastructure is attacked again, seabed cables and infrastructure across the region could also become targets.
After Khamenei’s statement, commanders of the general staff of the armed forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the traditional army separately expressed readiness to launch missile, drone and other attacks in case of an escalation of conflict.
State media on Sunday also aired footage of missiles and drones being taken out of massive underground storage sites and deployed during the eight months of war so far.
The authorities also signalled that they expect more potential attacks from the US and Israel, including against Iran’s power grid.
Gholamreza Jalali, commander of the National Organization for Passive Defense, said during a speech on Sunday that they have identified 14 sectors most dependent on electricity that would need support if the war restarts, without naming any.
“Adopting preventive measures in the area of passive defence for the electricity grid is a fundamental principle that all authorities must follow up in their capacities,” he said, adding that officials were considering “network islanding” practices to create different segments that would not all be simultaneously affected by potential bombing.
‘Positive change in tone’
In and around the Strait of Hormuz, vessels continue to be attacked if they refuse to coordinate with the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, the entity set up by Iranian authorities to enforce control and sovereignty in the critical waterway.
At least four tankers were identified as being hit on Friday and Saturday, although not all attacks are reported by vessels and monitors. According to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, a vessel carrying liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) was struck by three Iranian projectiles on Saturday about 40 nautical miles (74km) south of Iran’s Lavan Island, deep into the Gulf.
Transit in the strait and surrounding waterways will not return to normal unless the US takes steps towards Iran’s conditions, security chief Mohsen Rezaei told state television during an interview on Saturday night.
For the sequencing to work, he said Tehran wants the US to lift its naval blockade that has halted oil exports and the majority of Iran’s trade, which used to be facilitated through its southern ports. The US must also issue waivers for oil sanctions, unfreeze Iran’s assets abroad, stop fighting on all regional fronts, including Lebanon, and recognise a bilateral Iran-Oman arrangement for Hormuz.
Rezaei said he has yet to respond to a letter addressed to him by Vance, although he said the missive indicated a “change in tone” that he described as “positive”.
Mostafa Najafi, a Tehran-based political analyst said to be linked with Rezaei, said if the conditions are not met, the letter is likely to go unanswered and negotiations – including on Iran’s nuclear programme – will not enter a higher level.
“It is unclear how willing Washington is to accept these demands. It is clear that not recognising rights emphasised by Iran will lead to the failure of the negotiations,” he wrote on X.
The US has also doubled down on the effectiveness of its Operation Economic Outcast involving the blockade, sanctions and pressure on overland trade and aviation.
A report by the US Treasury to inform Trump’s decision-making, which was publicised by news outlet Axios, said no new oil had been loaded onto tankers at Iran’s terminals since August 25. It also showed overseas crude deliveries were down, while Iran’s year-on-year inflation neared 90 percent in September and the national currency continued to dwindle.
The report said Iran’s economy was “crippled” by the combined measures, but did not argue that it was close to collapsing.

Australia nears 'largest property downturn in 40 years' as prices plunge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:01:00 UTC
22:01:00 KST

'Largest property downturn in 40 years' in sight as house prices fall for seventh time
In short:
The median value of Australian homes has dropped $63,400 since March.
The decline is tracking faster than any past downturn over the past 40 years.
What's next?
Experts predict it will be some time until interest rates start to fall and the market turns.
National house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, with the speed of the decline in home values tracking at the fastest pace seen over the past 40 years, according to property research group Cotality.
Its latest national Home Value Index (HVI) was down 1.2 per cent in October and is now 6.7 per cent below its March peak, equivalent to a decline of about $63,400 in the value of the median Australian dwelling.
The index shows the median national house price now stands at $884,855.
Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said the speed of decline was tracking faster than any previous downturn over the past 40 years, with capital city values down 8.1 per cent in seven months.
Virtually every suburb across Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide has recorded a drop in values over the past three months as buyers struggle to get loans because of higher interest rates.
It sits alongside investor demand also waning because of the federal government's budget changes to property tax breaks.
"This is really a demand-led downturn," Mr Burg said.
"That's reduced the borrowing capacity of households, but also increased the repayments for people to make on a mortgage, and it's pushed a lot of buyers to the side."
Mr Burg is among many economists anticipating higher rates for longer and further house price falls.
"We are already on track to see the largest downturn across the last 40 years,"
he said.
"The previous record was 2017 through 2019, which stood at 8.2 per cent [falls] across the combined capital cities. Now, at the moment, as of October, the downturn that we've seen over the past seven months is 8.1 per cent [falls], so it looks like we're easily going to push past that mark."
How much further will house prices fall?
The number of home sales has dropped sharply as demand weakens.
Cotality puts the number of home sales over the past three months 23 per cent lower than a year ago and 18 per cent below the previous five-year average.
With fewer buyers, it has become harder to sell homes. Auction clearance rates across the combined capitals are consistently tracking below 50 per cent, while private treaty metrics have also weakened.
The median time on market, at 39 days, is the highest since August 2020, while vendor discounting, at 4.7 per cent, is the largest since May 2019.
Mr Burg said buyers would hold back until the Reserve Bank of Australia indicated a different direction on rates, and that likely would not happen until the latter half of 2027.
"The eventual recovery that we do see in the housing market is likely to be more subdued than we've seen in previous episodes,"
Mr Burg said.
"It [the RBA] doesn't necessarily require rates to come down, but [give] the clear signal that that is the direction that they are going to take."
Domain's chief economist Nicola Powell says it could be well into next year before rate cuts are on the agenda.
"We've already seen about a 6 per cent shave from the median house price, so the reality is a 10 per cent drop in price is quite possible,"
Ms Powell said.
"We need something to change to improve buyer confidence. And that isn't going to come at least until we have the discussion of a potential rate cut. And that's unlikely to happen until the latter part of 2027."
Inquiries at some open homes down 300 pc
Harcourts real estate agent and auctioneer Sam Devlin, who sells homes in Brisbane, said over the past six months enquiries at open homes had been down in some instances by 300 per cent.
"That's been brought on since the May budget," he said.
"The government's taxation policies around negative gearing and capital gains tax have certainly affected what is happening there."
Mr Devlin said even buyers looking to upsize were heading to auctions unsure whether they could stump up the cash.
"Right now, we're seeing a real lack of confidence from people who have to sell homes, being able to transact without subject to sale clauses,"
he said.
"There would be more interest if there was more confidence in the market that buyers could actually sell the house that they're already in."
Jin Ling at real estate agent Vic Prop sells homes in Melbourne's eastern suburbs. He said enquiries were down and buyers were far more cautious.
"Right now, they don't have the confidence that, if rates go up two or three more times over the next 12 months, whether that's a comfortable position for them," he said.
"They're thinking, 'Do we wait 12 months? Do we wait to see what the market does? Do we wait for prices to maybe potentially pull back a bit more before kind of pulling the trigger?"
Mr Ling said it could take years for property values to rise strongly again.
"I think it'll be a three-to-four-year period, where hopefully we can see a level of recovery," Mr Ling said.
Property bargains for some?
In the meantime, some buyers could get better value.
Recent data from Domain showed Melbourne was just $14,000 away from the median house price falling below $1 million.
Cotality's data is modelled differently and already had Melbourne well below that. Its October figures show Melbourne's median dwelling price is $773,027.
"We've seen the upper end of our markets, particularly in Sydney and Melbourne, see price falls for a much longer period of time. Those price falls were happening at the end of 2025," Domain chief economist Nicola Powell said.
"It can create opportunities for some types of buyers, particularly those looking to upsize, because you tend to find the upper end, so the more expensive the property is, the deeper the price falls."
Mr Ling said he had already seen greater buyer interest from people living interstate for homes in Melbourne.
"Previously, it was Melbourne investors going, 'Hey, you know [we are looking at] buying in Perth, buying in Brisbane, buying in Adelaide. And I think now [that's] reversed,"
Mr Ling said.
He said for all the dire predictions, there was going to be greater value for those looking to buy their first home or wishing to upsize.
"I think that there are incredible buying opportunities out there," he said.

Genes may explain about a third of earnings differences, according to a study of 44,500 U.S. twin pairs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:00:52 UTC
22:00:52 KST

A massive analysis of census and tax records indicates that inherited genetic factors account for nearly one-third of the variation in earnings among steadily employed Americans in their late 20s and 30s. At the same time, the research suggests that standard twin studies may overstate the genetic component of career success, partly because same-sex twins are unusually likely to end up working at the same company. The findings were published in PNAS.
Why do children from certain families consistently earn higher paychecks in adulthood than children from other families? Social scientists examine this question using a statistical concept called heritability, which measures the proportion of differences in a trait across a population that can be traced to inherited genetic variation rather than environmental conditions.
To estimate heritability without directly sequencing DNA, researchers have traditionally relied on the classical twin design. This method compares identical twins, who develop from a single fertilized egg and share 100 percent of their genes, with fraternal twins, who develop from two separate eggs and share about 50 percent of their genes, just like ordinary brothers and sisters.
Because both types of twins grow up in the same household, researchers attribute any extra similarity between identical twins to their shared DNA. This rests on what is known as the equal-environments assumption, which holds that identical and fraternal twins share their home environment to the same degree.
Sorting out genetic inheritance from family upbringing has proven challenging in economics. For instance, a 2008 study of American brothers and sisters found that siblings’ adult earnings are moderately correlated, indicating that family background accounts for a sizable share of economic inequality. But ordinary sibling comparisons cannot separate shared DNA from parental wealth and parenting styles.
Twins offer a way to separate those channels. A 2012 review of genetics and economics indicated that long-term income appears roughly as heritable as personality traits or many medical conditions. The review’s authors also warned that separating true genetic effects from social influences remains difficult.
Complicating matters further, a person’s paycheck is not determined solely by the individual skills, education, or personality they bring to the labor market. Labor economists separate wages into two main parts. The first is a portable worker component, which reflects an individual’s earning capacity across different jobs. The second is an employer pay premium, the extra pay or discount a specific company gives to all of its staff.
In a 2013 study of West German workers, study co-author David Card and colleagues found that growing differences between workers and in company pay premiums, along with the increasing sorting of high-earning workers into high-paying companies, accounted for much of the rise in wage inequality. Whether access to these high-paying companies reflects inherited traits, personal connections, or simple luck has remained an open question.
Because population registries rarely record whether twins are identical or fraternal, previous twin studies of income have typically relied on small survey samples. To investigate how genetics and social interactions shape both individual earning power and workplace pay premiums on a national scale, Card and Jesse Rothstein of the University of California, Berkeley, along with Moises Yi of the US Census Bureau, analyzed administrative records covering the full population of young adult twins in the United States.
Unlike physical traits such as height, career outcomes depend heavily on social choices, including where a person wants to work and who else works there. The authors reasoned that if twins influence each other’s job choices or prefer working together at the same workplace, standard twin comparisons could mistake that social coordination for genetic inheritance.
The researchers linked household records from the 2000 United States Census to quarterly wage records from state unemployment insurance tax filings. These records cover formal wage and salary jobs, and the team used data from 2018 through the first quarter of 2023. They omitted the last three quarters of 2020 to avoid labor market disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.
The sample tracked biological children of household heads who were between 9 and 17 years old in 2000 (born between 1983 and 1990). Twins were defined as children in the same household born within two days of each other, and non-twin siblings as children born at least nine months apart. The employment analysis encompassed 87,000 twin pairs (60,000 same-sex and 27,000 opposite-sex) and 2,168,000 non-twin sibling pairs (1,072,000 same-sex and 1,096,000 opposite-sex).
For the detailed wage analysis, the authors focused on pairs in which both siblings maintained stable full-time work. This meant having at least eight quarters in which they earned more than $3,800 from one employer (roughly full-time minimum-wage pay), excluding the first and last quarters of each job spell. That restriction yielded 44,500 twin pairs (31,500 same-sex and 13,000 opposite-sex) and 1,007,000 non-twin sibling pairs (507,000 same-sex and 500,000 opposite-sex).
Because census files do not record whether twins are identical or fraternal, the researchers relied on biological sex. All opposite-sex twins are fraternal, whereas same-sex twins are a mix of fraternal and identical twins. Identical twins made up an estimated 58.7 percent of same-sex pairs in the sample.
Families may also treat sons and daughters differently. To filter out that possibility, the team used a statistical technique called difference-in-differences. They subtracted the similarity gap between same-sex and opposite-sex regular siblings from the similarity gap between same-sex and opposite-sex twins.
The team analyzed average quarterly earnings using a logarithmic scale, a standard economic measure that captures proportional differences in pay. They also used a statistical wage decomposition model to split each worker’s pay into two parts: their portable individual earning capacity and the average pay premium of the companies they worked for. The model controlled for work experience and calendar time.
That employer pay premium was further broken down into three pieces. These were a geographic location premium (the average employer pay premium among companies in the local commuting zone), an industry premium (the average employer pay premium among companies in that industry), and a remaining workplace-specific pay premium.
Across the full wage sample, same-sex twins showed a correlation in average earnings of 0.543 (on a scale where 0 indicates no relationship and 1 indicates that one twin’s earnings perfectly predict the other’s). By comparison, the correlation was 0.317 for opposite-sex twins, 0.386 for same-sex non-twin siblings, and 0.265 for opposite-sex non-twin siblings.
The researchers also examined non-twin siblings separated by age gaps of one to three years, excluding pairs born less than a year apart to avoid adoption or recording errors. Earnings similarity barely faded as the age difference grew, and the gap between same-sex and opposite-sex siblings remained steady. This pattern supported the assumption that shared family and gender influences do not change drastically for siblings born close together.
Based on their extended twin model, the researchers initially estimated that inherited genetic factors accounted for 36 percent of the variance in overall earnings. Genetic factors also accounted for an estimated 23 percent of the variance in having any employment and 32 percent of the variance in the number of quarters employed.
When the researchers separated earnings into individual and workplace components, portable individual earning power had an estimated heritability of 40 percent. The employer pay premium had an estimated heritability of 21 percent.
Within the workplace component, the industry pay premium had a heritability estimate of 26 percent and the remaining workplace-specific premium had an estimate of 20 percent. The geographic location premium (18 percent) was not statistically significant, because most siblings remained in the region where they grew up.
Finding heritability in employer pay premiums even within regions and industries made it look on the surface as though genetic factors affected not just workers’ skills, but also their access to high-paying companies. Because the 21 percent estimate was roughly twice as large as what skill-based hiring alone would produce, the authors examined whether twins were ending up at the same establishments.
The employment records showed that 11.4 percent of same-sex twin pairs worked at the exact same establishment at some point between 2018 and 2023 (not necessarily at the same time). That was double the rate for same-sex non-twin siblings (5.7 percent), triple the rate for opposite-sex twins (3.8 percent), and more than five times the rate for opposite-sex non-twin siblings (2.2 percent).
The researchers then re-estimated their model after removing all twin and sibling pairs who ever worked at the same establishment. The estimated heritability of the employer pay premium dropped by two-thirds, from 21 percent to 7 percent, and was no longer statistically significant. The heritability of the industry premium fell from 26 percent to 12 percent, and that of the workplace-specific premium fell from 20 percent to essentially zero.
The remaining link between genetics and employer pay premiums fit what would be expected from high-paying companies hiring high-skilled workers alone. Excluding coworkers also lowered the estimated heritability of portable individual earning power from 40 percent to 35 percent. The estimated heritability of overall earnings fell from 36 percent to 31 percent (a relative decline of about 15 percent), and the authors regard these lower figures as their best estimates.
Even with that downward adjustment, the finding that genetics account for roughly a third of individual earning differences aligns with a recent German study, which found that higher cognitive ability at age 23 predicted higher socioeconomic status at age 27 largely due to shared genetic factors. That study looked at educational attainment and occupational prestige in young adulthood rather than wages, but both point to a substantial genetic influence on socioeconomic outcomes.
“The results show that estimated heritability is clearly present, as one would totally expect, but the effect depends a lot on whether the twins work at the same firms,” said Felix Bittmann, a postdoctoral researcher at the Leibniz Institute for Educational Trajectories and the University of Bamberg who was not involved in the research. “It’s an interesting aspect that deserves more attention. Clearly, the paper shows that even well-done genetically informed studies cannot partial out ‘pure’ genetic effects as social interactions will always be present and can influence the findings strongly.”
“While this study is done with twins, its implications extend a lot further: in the social sciences, it is an important question to understand how success is determined (nature vs. nurture),” Bittmann noted. “Twin designs are usually an elegant way to attempt to account for both factors, which classical research designs (surveys) cannot capture at all, as genetic transmission pathways are usually not measured; often, even proxies are lacking (like IQ tests for both children and parents).”
Sociologists often try to separate what they call primary and secondary effects: how family background shapes a child’s academic performance, and how families make choices about continuing education. Those two pathways are harder to separate when genetic inheritance goes unmeasured.
“Especially in sociology, when primary and secondary effects are to be separated, genetic pathways are usually ignored, which is a biasing factor,” Bittmann said. “This research can help to estimate how large such a bias could probably be.”
“The research design is clever, as they exploit a huge US database with official statistics,” Bittmann told PsyPost. “These databases do not contain information about twins, so this information is lacking, but they can reconstruct it from birth dates, which is a good idea. While they need to make some assumptions and correct for the aspect that same-sex twins can be identical or not …, they can account for this statistically; I think this part is fine.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. A heritability estimate of 31 percent describes variation across a population. It does not mean that 31 percent of any one person’s paycheck comes from their genes, or that an individual’s earnings are biologically fixed at birth.
Even when genetic differences influence earnings, they can operate through indirect or social pathways, such as how parents’ genetic traits shape the home environment they create for their children. In addition, the wage analysis only included sibling pairs in which both people held stable, full-time wage and salary jobs. That leaves out self-employed workers, federal employees, and adults with minimal attachment to the labor market.
Model assumptions can also pull the heritability estimates in opposite directions. The baseline model assumes parents pair up randomly with respect to genes related to earnings. If spouses instead tend to share genetic traits tied to education and earning potential (known as assortative mating), regular siblings and fraternal twins would share more than half of those relevant genes. The authors calculate this could make the estimates about 16 percent higher than reported (for example, roughly 36 percent rather than 31 percent).
On the other hand, even after removing siblings who worked at the same company, the remaining estimates for portable earning power may still be inflated by unmeasured social interactions. Twins might, for instance, influence each other’s education choices or decide to attend the same college.
The authors suggest this kind of sibling influence could be one contributor to the “missing heritability” problem in genetics. Studies that directly analyze DNA using polygenic scores (scores that add up the small effects of many genetic variants) estimate lower heritability for social outcomes like education and income than twin studies do.
“I’d say the paper confirms known aspects with a larger and better sample size and is generally trustworthy,” Bittmann said. “When it comes to disentangling nature vs. nurture, the paper contributes but can, of course, not give a definite answer. Maybe other researchers can use the same research plan on other databases from other countries to add more insight and external validity.”
The study, “Heritability and social interaction in labor market outcomes: Evidence from the population of twins in the United States,” was authored by David Card, Jesse Rothstein, and Moises Yi.

How to make the perfect venison casserole – recipe | Felicity Cloake's How to make the perfect …
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:00:14 UTC
22:00:14 KST

Because I don’t eat it very often, I always forget how much I like venison. Or, rather, how much I like it in certain contexts: the natural leanness of a wild animal doesn’t naturally lend itself to soloing in juicy burgers or sausages, but, when slow-cooked, it’s fabulous – rich in flavour, and soft enough to eat with a spoon, should you so desire. It also tends to be good value both in season and frozen for the rest of the year, and, as red meat goes, a pretty climate-friendly option (though not straightforwardly so, as this piece explains) that pairs beautifully with seasonal spuds and kales, and is even better when made ahead of time and reheated. In fact, it’s the perfect autumn and winter entertaining option, even if the only people you’re entertaining are yourselves, the dog and the cast of Celebrity Traitors.
The meat
Few recipes specify the cut, perhaps because venison is so often sold in chunks, so the assumption is that it’s going to be used for just this purpose, and rarely do the vendors elucidate further than saying the meat is for “stewing” or simply “diced”. Caroline Conran, whose recipe in her 1978 British Cooking is attributed to nameless “ghillies” (Scottish hunting guides), suggests using leg or haunch, while Gary Rhodes is firm in his belief that “venison for stewing should come from the haunch, or you can use neck”. Meanwhile, David Eyre calls for a whole shoulder in The Eagle Cookbook, which, like the haunch, feels like a great extravagance, even though, in truth, it is my favourite – the shoulder is better marbled than either the haunch or the diced venison I buy, which, once slow-cooked, makes for a richer, stickier result. That said, you can counteract the meat’s leanness by adding other fats, of which more later, so the only cut you should steer clear of, simply because it’s too tender for such treatment, is the saddle.
John William, “the deer man” of Raasay, whose recipe is included in Sue Lawrence’s A Taste of the Scottish Islands, soaks the meat overnight in “gutsy red wine”. I cannot speak for Raasay venison, and I imagine William knows what he’s talking about, but my testers and I don’t detect much difference with the wild Devon meat I use. Indeed, chemist Hervé This concluded that one would have to marinade meat for several days for the alcohol to have a noticeably tenderising effect, while the flavour penetration of any marinade is mere millimetres. By all means, marinate if you like, then, but I think you’re better off trusting in the mingling of flavours that takes place in the pot.
Rhodes tells readers of his book More Rhodes Around Britain that, “I like to cut the meat into large pieces rather than dice. It takes a little longer to cook, but the texture and taste are better.” Sceptical though I am that it will cook through, after trialling it I find myself inclined to agree; two-bite chunks remain juicier in the middle.
The vegetables
Everyone starts their stew with onions (though you could use shallots instead, not least because their sweetness would be welcome here), but after that is where the recipes start to diverge. Rhodes and Eyre go for a classic triumvirate with carrot and celery, and the latter, like William, also includes leek. Clarissa Dickson Wright champions beetroot, writing in the Game Cookbook she co-authored with Johnny Scott that “the brilliant food writer Claire Macdonald discovered there is an enzyme in [it] that breaks down the fibres in venison. When I was staying at Kinloch Lodge, the blissful hotel on Skye, she told me it would tenderise even the toughest old stag.” Again, wild animals are particularly hard to generalise about, especially one that might be anything from a 9kg muntjac to an 190kg red deer, but, on this evidence, I wouldn’t be rushing to add chunks of beetroot for anything other than flavour – its sweet earthiness is delicious with the meat.
Indeed, I’m going to focus on sweetness: even more than beetroot, we love the fruitiness of both the prunes in the Claire Macdonald Game Cookbook, and Clarissa Dickson Wright’s redcurrant jelly (in truth, most fruity jellies would work, should you have something similar hanging out in the cupboard). And if you’re a fan of sweet-and-sour combinations, may I encourage you to consider popping in some of Macdonald’s pickled walnuts as well – as one of my testers put it, along with the prunes, they “completely blended into the gravy and gave it a lovely richness and depth of flavour – neither too sweet nor too salty”.
I like to include as many vegetables in a casserole as possible, hence the onions, carrots and leek here, all of which will echo the sweetness of the prunes and preserve. If rich, sweet and savoury doesn’t appeal, bear William’s recipe in mind; with its chopped red pepper and tomatoes, it has a lighter, more southern feel, though if you do go down that road, maybe add some of Eyre’s garlic, too (I’d be tempted to include a glug of red wine to beef it out a bit as well, but then I don’t know the meaning of the world light).
The seasoning
Though bacon might seem to belong in the “meat” paragraph above, it’s purely here for its delicious, savoury fat, fat that the free-roaming deer hasn’t had the chance to build up on its wild perambulations. If you don’t care for pork, an extra slug of oil, plus a dash of William’s Worcestershire sauce, should prove a satisfactory replacement.
Rhodes adds bay, Dickson Wright and Eyre thyme, Eyre parsley stalks and Conran juniper berries, a classic seasoning for venison and one that I love. But seeing as we already have the jelly, I’ve stuck with thyme here, because I think its austere, savoury aromatic quality works with fruit and meat.
The liquid
Dickson Wright, who probably couldn’t move for deer carcasses and pheasant skeletons while writing her Game Cookbook, instructs me to make a game stock, which drives the dog wild for the hour it takes in the pressure cooker (expert guidance via Catherine Phipps’ excellent Modern Pressure Cooking). Should you also have bones going to waste, it’s worth your while doing the same, though both the beef stock in Conran’s recipe and the vegetable version in Macdonald’s won’t do any harm, and we don’t find we miss anything in Eyre’s version, which tops up red wine with water.
Wine, in fact, features in almost every recipe, and with good reason: its fruit, acidity and tannins combine with the browned meat and bacon to produce a richly savoury sauce. If you’d prefer to leave it out, use the same amount of beef stock and add either a glass of port, as Conran does, or an extra spoonful of redcurrant jelly and a squeeze of lemon. You’ll notice I’ve been generous with the quantity, because a couple of the recipes I try don’t have enough gravy for my testers’ liking – and what’s the point of a casserole without gravy, as one tartly (and ungratefully) observes.
The cooking
Everyone except Conran bakes their casseroles – you can, of course, use the hob for the recipe below, but I find it much easier to keep things at a constant low simmer in the oven. To my surprise, the venison doesn’t need as long as I’d imagined either: two hours at 160C proves quite sufficient for both Eyre and Dickson Wright’s offerings, and though you can stick it in a very low oven overnight, as William recommends (no doubt particularly useful if you have an AGA or similar), there’s really no need. In the interests of making the most of the fuel, I’d strongly urge you to consider baking some potatoes at the same time.
A final piece of advice: should you have the luxury of time, Macdonald’s tip that “twice cooking is almost obligatory for casseroles; the flavours are vastly better than if the casserole is made and eaten straight away”, is a good one. Take it out of the oven after 90 minutes, then, when you’re ready to eat it the next day or the day afterwards, put it back in there at the same temperature for half an hour. It also freezes well.
Prep 20 min
 
Cook 2½ hr
 
Serves 4
100g streaky bacon
  
800g venison, preferably boned shoulder, if available
 
2 tbsp neutral oil, or lard or dripping
 
2 tbsp plain flour
  
Salt and black pepper
  
1 large onion, peeled and chopped
 
1 leek, trimmed, washed and chunkily sliced
 
1 carrot, coarsely diced
  
2 sprigs fresh thyme, or ½ tsp dried thyme
 
fr300ml red wine
  
8 stoned soft prunes, halved
 
1 tbsp redcurrant jelly, or other fruit jelly
Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Chop the bacon into wide pieces. Drain any liquid from the venison and, if it isn’t already diced, cut it into large, two-bite chunks.
Heat the oil in an ovenproof casserole dish for which you have a lid on a medium-high flame.
Fry the bacon in the hot fat until it releases its fat and begins to turn golden.
Meanwhile, toss the venison with the flour and a good pinch of salt and pepper.
Scoop out the bacon with a slotted spoon and put in a large bowl, then add a few pieces of the venison and brown on all sides – don’t overcrowd the pan or you won’t achieve that deep, brown colour that brings with it such flavour. Scoop each batch out as soon as it’s done and add to the bacon bowl.
When all the venison is browned, turn down the heat to medium-low and add the onion, leek, carrot and a pinch of salt. Fry, stirring regularly, until the veg have softened and are starting to colour; stir in the thyme towards the end.
Scoop the vegetables into the meat bowl, then add a splash of wine to the pan, and stir to dislodge and dissolve any bits from the base.
Stir in the prunes and fruit jelly, then return the meat and vegetables to the pan, and add the rest of the wine and just enough water mostly to cover the meat – a few bits will stick out of the top like icebergs, but, without knowing the diameter of your pan, it’s impossible to give a precise amount of water.
Bring to a simmer, then cover and put in the oven for 90 minutes if making ahead of time, or two hours if serving immediately. If reheating later, return the stew to the oven and cook at the same temperature for 30 minutes. Check the seasoning, stir in a little extra water if it’s too dry for your liking, then serve with mashed potato and greens.
- Venison – love it, hate it, or somewhere in between? Is it the ethical red meat, or is this pure greenwashing and speciesism, as Peta claims? Why don’t we eat more of it in this country (Bambi?) and, if you love it, what’s your favourite way to prepare it?
