‘Dark money made darker’: funding labyrinth conceals donors to Republican campaigns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:00:13 UTC
22:00:13 KST

In the summer of 2024, a non-profit called the Green Dragon Coalition wired the last $20,000 of a $445,000 grant to a Super Pac. Its tax return for that year would describe the purpose of the transfer as “educational”.
The same day, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) records, the Super Pac spent $8,000 attacking Celeste Maloy, the Republican congresswoman for Utah’s second district, four days before the primary that would decide whether she kept her seat. It had already spent more than $400,000 promoting her challenger, Colby Jenkins, who was running to her right with the endorsement of the rightwing Utah senator Mike Lee.
One man was involved at every stage, and his name is on the paperwork for the charity that raised the money, the non-profit that passed it on, the Super Pac that the non-profit donated to and the campaign this money eventually supported.
His name is Thomas Datwyler, and his businesses are mostly headquartered in a rented address in Hudson, Wisconsin, a town of 15,000 near the border with Minnesota. Datwyler operates at an industrial scale, acting as treasurer of more than 350 federal political committees in the current election cycle, including 115 congressional campaigns and 100 Super Pacs, and as an officer of more than two dozen non-profits.
The extent of Datwyler’s activities over several political cycles raises questions about the attitude of Republican campaigns and candidates to campaign finance in the run-up to the November midterm elections, and the evolution of so-called “dark money” electoral funding.
Across the 2024 and 2026 cycles, Super Pacs whose books Datwyler also keeps have spent more than $2m supporting 14 candidates that are also his clients, or attacking their opponents, according to FEC filings. In several of those races the money reached the Super Pac through charities and social welfare groups for which he is a treasurer.
Datwyler-tied groups have been funded by donors connected to the rightwing megadonor Leonard Leo, along with the Conservative Partnership Institute and the personal foundation of the Claremont Institute’s board chair, the Thomas Klingenstein Fund, among others.
Money raised from these conservative donors has gone into organisations that Datwyler runs the books for, and those organisations have passed money on to Super Pacs that spent in Republican primaries. Non-profit tax filings do not show which donors’ funds made up any particular onward transfer.
Along the way, the same firms are paid by both the campaigns and the groups that are legally required to be independent of campaigns in order to maintain their tax-exempt status. In Florida’s 19th district, a campaign and the supposedly independent Super Pac backing it share 14 vendors, according to FEC filings.
Federal law prohibits coordination between Pacs and campaign committees, but proving it is challenging. The FEC is a reluctant cop, and while Datwyler has attracted significant controversy and state-level investigations, what he does may not be illegal.
“Somebody in Datwyler’s position is well aware of where all the cracks and crevices in the system are, how to sort of exploit the rules in a way that maximises his clients’ ability to secretly influence elections,” says Saurav Ghosh, director of federal campaign finance reform at the non-profit Campaign Legal Center.
“There’s a reason why the same handful of people – and Datwyler’s probably the chief among them – tend to come up in connection with these dark money operations. It’s because they have the knowhow of how to do it. And they’re willing to be the public face on each of these entities.
“The actual donors providing the money don’t want to be publicly outed as the source of the outside money pouring into the race.”
Datwyler wrote to the Guardian that “AxCapital [where he is CEO] is grateful that so many clients entrust our team to facilitate their participation in the democratic process. As an industry leader, we have strict internal firewalls, strong safeguards, and robust policies to ensure full compliance with all laws, regulations, and requirements.”
The Green Dragon pipeline
The Green Dragon entities exemplify a pattern that recurs across Datwyler’s network.
The Green Dragon Coalition is a 501(c)4 social welfare non-profit, and one of three entities registered in Delaware in 2023 with sequential IRS employer numbers, all listing the same address in Hudson, Wisconsin. The other two were the Green Dragon Society, a 501(c)3 charity, and the Constitutional Conservatives Fund, a Super Pac.
Datwyler is treasurer of all three, and is the only officer that any of the organizations pay: the Green Dragon Coalition paid him $25,012 during the 2024 cycle and the Green Dragon Society paid him $29,066.
This is just a fraction of the compensation Datwyler has received across various arms of the political operation he works on. Tax filings indicate that he received at least $487,545 in the 2023-2024 cycle from non-profits. FEC filings indicate that during the last two election cycles at least $793,470 flowed to Datwyler directly, or to two Delaware-registered consultancies, 10Six Consulting and Same Day Processing, that share a Wisconsin address with the vast majority of his political and charity organizations.
Meanwhile, AxCapital, where Datwyler is CEO, brought in $4.9m across both cycles. AxCapital was created in a 2022 merger of HenryAlan and Datwyler’s 9Seven Consulting.
The Green Dragon Coalition’s $445,000 “educational” grant to the Constitutional Conservatives Fund in 2024 is recorded in the Pac’s FEC receipts in five payments between 15 March and 21 June 2024. In turn, the Pac spent $447,347 supporting Jenkins. Datwyler was also treasurer of Colby Jenkins for Congress, a role he had held since October 2023, and of the candidate’s joint fundraising committee. Datwyler is therefore keeping the books for the charity, the social welfare group, the Super Pac attacking the incumbent and the campaign it was attacking her on behalf of.
The Green Dragon Coalition’s 2024 revenue was $917,002, of which $750,000 – or about 82% – came from the Concord Fund, the Leonard Leo-network group formerly called the Judicial Crisis Network. The Green Dragon Society, a 501(c)3, also took $250,000 from Purple Action, a 501(c)4 whose officers include tech mogul and former Trump administration “crypto czar” David Sacks, and $200,000 from the Conservative Partnership Institute, and $90,000 each from “dark money” vectors DonorsTrust and Fidelity’s donor-advised fund. The Thomas D Klingenstein Fund gave the 501(c)3 $75,000 in 2023, before the 2024 payments to the Super Pac.
Lawson Bader, the president and CEO of DonorsTrust, said the organisation was “unfamiliar with the Constitutional Conservatives Fund, and the fact that the Green Dragon Coalition has an affiliated 501(c)4”. Grants from donor-advised funds to a 501(c)3 “cannot be used for political purposes”, he said, adding that DonorsTrust “would reconsider future grant recommendations made to organizations that violate the rules governing charitable activities”.
A Fidelity Charitable spokesperson said: “Use of Fidelity Charitable grants for political contributions or campaign activities is prohibited. The terms all non-profits receive when grant funds are issued to them include explicit language to that effect.”
These are not the only money flows from major conservative funders through Datwyler-connected entities.
In 2024 American Majority Action, a 501(c)4 founded by conservative activist Ned Ryun, gave Integrity Minnesota, for which Datwyler served as treasurer, $250,000 for “voter registration and activation plans”. (A 2020 Campaign for Accountability complaint asked the IRS and two state agencies to investigate whether Ryun’s groups spent more than half their money on politics, which would violate IRS laws governing 501(c)4 groups. Campaign for Accountability communications director Michael Clauw told the Guardian that the IRS did not respond to the complaint or take any action.)
American Majority Action did not respond to a request for comment.
Integrity Minnesota also received $50,000 that year from Restoration of America, which the Chicago Sun-Times reported in October 2024 was part of “a sprawling empire of organizations pushing far-right agendas and election denialism”, funded by at least $150m from shipping-supplies billionaire Richard Uihlein.
The Guardian contacted Restoration of America for comment.
And a separate Datwyler vehicle, Aurora Venture, received $300,000 from Ardleigh Impact Corp, a Delaware 501(c)4 with one director, no employees and no website, registered to the Springfield, Virginia, home of Staci Goede, a former Republican State Leadership Committee finance chief who is the treasurer of 26 federal political committees this cycle.
The Daily Beast reported on 16 May 2024 that Ardleigh had moved more than $2.5m to Republican Super Pacs within months of being formed, raising the suspicion that it may be a straw donor.
The Guardian contacted Goede for comment.
The money pipeline functions such that none of these organizations are named as donors in the FEC filings of the Super Pacs.
The Guardian contacted the Concord Fund, Thomas Klingenstein and the Conservative Partnership Institute for comment, and emailed Purple Action at an address that returned the message undelivered. None responded.
This cycle, the Green Dragon Coalition has put a further $177,500 into the same Super Pac in seven payments since 5 December 2025, the most recent on 21 April 2026. The Pac’s independent expenditures so far this cycle total $15,000 in support of Barry Moore, the Alabama congressman currently running to replace Tommy Tuberville, who is departing the US Senate to run for the Alabama governor’s seat.
The Guardian contacted Barry Moore for comment.
Elsewhere, the Pac’s expenditures have gone to organizations connected to Datwyler’s associates.
Its payments to L4 Consulting LLC total $164,809 across 13 installments between 2 January and 5 June 2026, with the disbursements booked as “PAC strategy consulting” and “fundraising consulting”. L4 is run by Dan Hauser, who is president of both Green Dragon entities and takes no salary from either.
Hauser was reported in October 2025 to have been a paid senior adviser to the Utah senator Mike Lee, another Datwyler client, during the same period. In the 2024 cycle, L4 took $207,560 from the same Super Pac. Green Dragon’s charity separately paid L4 $128,033 for “event production”.
The Guardian contacted Hauser for comment.
Ghosh, the campaign finance reformer, pointed out that while non-profits have to disclose donors to the IRS, with the exception of private foundations and some political non-profits, they do not have to disclose them to the public.
“So if the entire object is to conceal the sources of the money, the [501](c)4 on its own can accomplish that objective. The only thing the [501](c)3 layer adds is that [501](c)3 donations are tax deductible for the donor,” he said.
Ghosh added: “But that’s a little riskier because if they are using the [501](c)3 to first obtain a tax deduction and then that money is being used to influence elections, that’s one of the few things that federal tax law does prohibit.”
Either way, he said that “that’s a transparency nightmare. It becomes this problematic daisy chain where the [501](c)3 is sending money to the [501](c)4, theoretically not to support its political advocacy. But again, who can say exactly whether that’s happening or not? These are opaque entities. They are black boxes.”
Alyssa Bowen, executive director of True North Research, put the same structure more bluntly. “It’s like dark money made darker,” she said. “It’s almost like he’s running science experiments to find out all the ways you can conceal who’s donating.”
She said the charity layer carried a second advantage for the giver. “The Pacs are legally required to disclose your donors, but you’re not [required to do so] for a 501(c)3 or [501(c)]4. And then there’s also the tax benefits – donors receive tax benefits for donating to a 501(c)3,” she said. “So it’s twofold for these donors that are trying to make sure that they’re not held accountable for some of the more political spending that they do.”
Parallel pipelines
A similar pattern is visible across four other 2026 races. In each, Datwyler is treasurer of the campaign and of the Super Pac spending in that race, and in each he held both roles before the spending began.
The Love America Uphold Freedom Pac spent $248,091 for Catalina Lauf in Florida’s 19th district between 13 and 24 July 2026, which is all the independent spending it has ever made. It is registered at Datwyler’s own address, and amended its registration on 11 July to add the domain LAUFPAC.com, two days before the advertising started.
It shares 14 vendors with Lauf’s campaign, seven of them substantive digital firms, over overlapping periods – which engages the FEC’s common-vendor conduct standard independently of who the treasurer is.
The Guardian contacted the Lauf campaign for comment.
On shared vendors, Ghosh said this is “more pressing than just having a treasurer in common. The use of vendors in common for things like media production, placement – that’s exactly the kind of spending that would be the subject of prohibited coordination. If the vendors they’re using are actually taking what they learn from their work for the campaign clients and then utilising that information or passing that information to their Super Pac clients, that’s exactly what the law prohibits.”
The Defending Conservative Values Pac was registered on 9 May 2026 and spent $485,213 against Blake Moore, the incumbent Karianne Lisonbee is challenging, between 29 May and 20 June – again, 100% of its spending, and again in Utah’s second district. The Show Me Valor Pac was registered six weeks after Taylor Burks’ campaign, with Datwyler as treasurer, and spent $166,051 supporting him. The American Honor Pac spent $162,800 for David Flippo in Nevada’s second district; Datwyler is its treasurer, custodian of records and only named officer, and its entire 2026 income – $155,000 – came from Stephen Flippo.
The American Liberty Foundation is simultaneously the name of a 501(c)3, a 501(c)4 and a Super Pac, all with Datwyler as treasurer, the first two presided over by Raymond Yonkura, Jim Jordan’s chief of staff for nearly a decade. The Super Pac spent $294,021 for Jenny Costa Honeycutt in South Carolina’s first district in June 2026, funded by $355,000 from the social welfare arm, $250,000 from the Geo Group’s Pac and $250,000 from a group called Voice of the Children of Israel.
What those campaigns knew is the open question for True North’s Bowen. “It’s concerning that all of these organisations and entities are using him, because what do they know about his past?” Bowen said, referring to Datwyler. “Is that why they’re using him – or are they totally unaware?”
She was skeptical that one person could service so many committees properly. “It feels far-fetched that he could be doing a good job,” she said.
‘Stunning … inexplicable’
In the current electoral cycle, Datwyler has already attracted controversy.
The Delaware Republican party reportedly claims he went unresponsive and then left in January 2026 amid five straight months of negative federal cash balances, missing a filing deadline and drawing an FEC warning of “civil money penalties, an audit or legal enforcement action”; he says he resigned because the party had not paid him.
In Alabama he is the sole officer of a Pac registered to a rented mailbox that has reportedly drawn legal threats over its attack mailers. A former state senator, Dell Hill, reportedly said in April that he had launched the Pac, whose registration names only Datwyler. Datwyler reportedly said he was “strictly the accountant doing the books” and had “nothing to do with producing the ads”.
One of the Republican incumbents it targeted, the state representative Matt Simpson, lost his primary in May.
In a telephone conversation, Simpson said of Datwyler: “If he found loopholes to try to exploit for his purposes, then that’s the nature of the business that we’re in. You can’t lie, though. That’s the problem that I have with it.”
He gave the Guardian a copy of a later mailer in which the Pac said a false claim about Simpson’s positions “was a printing error”.
The Guardian contacted Phillip Pettus, another incumbent the Pac targeted, for comment.
A Texas campaign Datwyler keeps books for drew a watchdog complaint in May 2026, and Andy Ogles, whose campaign he still runs the books for, confirmed in 2024 that, at that time, the FBI was investigating his campaign finances.
The complaint has not moved because the FEC needs four votes to open an investigation and has had only two commissioners since October 2025. Donald Trump’s two nominees have sat with the Senate rules committee since 11 February with no further action.
In May this year, the Campaign Legal Center asked the commission to investigate Datwyler again, over a $250,000 payment to one of his Super Pacs from the private prison company Geo Group, ICE’s largest contractor.
Datwyler has not been charged with any offence, and several of the investigations closed without findings. His firm’s general counsel has called the allegations against him “baseless attacks”.
The incidents are part of a longer pattern of scandal and regulatory scrutiny.
To date, Datwyler has been named as a respondent in 24 complaints before the FEC. Two ended in penalties, both for conduct that predated his appointment as treasurer. The other 22 were dismissed or closed without a penalty, at least three of them after commissioners deadlocked 3-3.
In January 2023 the FEC fined Josh Mandel’s Senate campaign $15,080 for failing to promptly report contributions totalling $147,601 received between 14 and 30 April 2022, before the 3 May Ohio primary.
Datwyler’s successor as Mandel’s campaign treasurer, Elizabeth Curtis, wrote to the FEC about “the stunning number of inexplicable reporting errors made by Mr Datwyler … ignoring the FEC and potentially incurring significant fines without notifying the Committee”.
The Guardian contacted Curtis for comment via a consultancy website contact form.
In 2023, the FEC fined four campaigns for failing to file required notices of late contributions in the 2022 elections while Datwyler was their treasurer: Mandel’s Senate campaign ($15,080) and the House campaigns of Rodney Davis ($5,820), Ann Wagner ($3,560) and Joe Kent ($3,304), for a total of $27,764. Fines against the campaigns of Rich McCormick and Kyle Sinclair also named Datwyler as treasurer, for failures that predated his appointment.
Those were not the only cases. A Guardian review of FEC enforcement records found 13 cases in which a committee was penalised for failures that occurred, at least in part, while Datwyler was its treasurer, with penalties totalling $110,791. The largest came in April 2024, when Rodney Davis’s campaign agreed to pay $43,475, in a settlement Datwyler signed, after it failed to refund $479,783.82 in general-election contributions within the permitted time once Davis had lost his 2022 primary.
The largest penalties to name Datwyler concerned reporting from before he took over.
In March 2024, Mike Braun’s Senate campaign agreed to pay a $159,000 civil penalty over improperly reported loans from the 2018 race. The FEC’s file on the matter records that Datwyler became the campaign’s treasurer on 29 January 2019, after the period in question, and that the campaign blamed its former treasurer for the errors. Commissioners deadlocked 3-3 on a separate allegation, that the campaign had misreported receipts and disbursements.
A representative for Datwyler reportedly said he “served as treasurer at the time the issue was corrected, reviewed, and resolved, not at the time of the underlying activity”.
In July 2022 Jim Jordan’s campaign agreed to pay $60,000 for failing to accurately disclose $1.2m in receipts and disbursements in five reports covering late 2018 to mid-2020. The FEC’s referral lists Datwyler as its treasurer from 15 July 2020, and the campaign told the commission he had “identified hundreds of errors” in its earlier accounting and filed corrected reports.
He was the shared treasurer of Joe Kent’s 2022 congressional campaign and of a Super Pac backing it – an arrangement the Guardian examined in February 2025, when campaign finance experts questioned the campaign’s routing of more than $1m through a company they described as a possible shell.
Liberty Ohio
In December 2021 Mike Dowling, a former FirstEnergy executive defending himself in a shareholder lawsuit over the $60m scheme that secured passage of Ohio’s HB6 energy bailout, subpoenaed two dark-money groups at the centre of that scandal: Partners for Progress and Generation Now, the latter of which had pleaded guilty to racketeering that February.
He asked for their communications with a list of people and organisations that included Liberty Ohio Inc, a non-profit for which Datwyler was treasurer, as well as Datwyler himself and the group’s secretary, Scott Guthrie. The same list named Ohio’s governor and lieutenant governor and every current and former member of the state legislature. Neither Datwyler nor Liberty Ohio was served with a subpoena or was a party to the lawsuit.
The lawsuit settled in August 2022, with $180m paid to FirstEnergy by insurers to resolve the derivative claims, less $36m in court-awarded legal fees. The defendants admitted no liability or wrongdoing.
Both Datwyler and Guthrie were working at the time on Josh Mandel’s Senate campaign, with Datwyler as its treasurer and Guthrie as its manager. Mandel subsequently lost the 2022 Republican primary to JD Vance, who was subsequently elected Senator for Ohio, and then vice-president as Donald Trump’s running mate.
Committees for which Datwyler served as treasurer spent more than $7m across the race – more than $5.4m of it from the USA Freedom Fund, a Super Pac registered to his own post office box, which put $831,281 behind Mandel and a further $4.6m into attacking his three main rivals: $3m against Mike Gibbons, $1.5m against JD Vance and $36,530 against Jane Timken.
The Guardian can reveal other striking transactions involving Datwyler during that campaign. Between September 2021 and June 2022, Team Josh – the joint fundraising committee for Mandel’s campaign and his leadership Pac – transferred $1.1m in seven installments to the federal account of the Shelby county Republican party, a committee registered not in Ohio but at Datwyler’s post office box in Hudson, Wisconsin. The federal account of a second Ohio county party, Delaware, sent a further $362,458.
Those two transfers were the entire declared income of the Shelby county account, amounting to $1,471,200. It then spent $1,398,811 on independent expenditures supporting Mandel, amounting to 95 cents of every dollar it took in, and wound itself up that December. Datwyler was treasurer of all three committees, and of Mandel’s campaign.
The Guardian contacted Scott Guthrie for comment. An email to Josh Mandel was returned undelivered.
State-level enforcement
Twice, state authorities have probed Datwyler as opposed to his clients.
The most developed coordination allegation against him is in Tennessee. In 2024, the state’s registry of election finance referred a complaint to the attorney general over the Republican primary in the fourth senate district, where a dark-money Pac spent more than $600,000 to defeat the incumbent, Jon Lundberg. Datwyler was treasurer and officer of that Pac, East Tennessee Conservatives; he was also treasurer of the congressional campaign of Diana Harshbarger, whose son Bobby was the challenger.
The attorney general’s report found that Datwyler had helped Bobby Harshbarger set up his campaign in April, after being introduced by the congresswoman’s chief of staff. According to the report, Datwyler sent him guidance on appointing a treasurer, obtained a tax number for a bank account and opened a fundraising account with Republican donation processor WinRed, and that the Pac he ran then spent heavily against Lundberg.
Investigators could not reach a conclusion, mainly because Datwyler declined, through counsel, to be interviewed or to produce documents. Two registry members said he should be subpoenaed. “The system’s not working the way it needs to on the dark money side,” the registry’s chair, Tom Lawless, said, “and I don’t know if we’ve got the tools to do anything for it.” Datwyler’s lawyer, Eric Brown, reportedly said that “news reports confirm that the AG report found no factual or legal basis to support the allegations of improper coordination”.
The registry dismissed the complaint in May 2025 at the request of Ken Yager, the Republican state senator who had filed it. “It’s just one of those where nobody was here to prosecute it,” Lawless said at the time.
The Guardian contacted Bobby Harshbarger for comment.
A second Tennessee complaint went further. Lawyers for the Civic Engagement Forum and Datwyler conceded to the registry that the group had operated as a political campaign committee and should have registered and disclosed its spending, and offered $2,500 to settle. The registry’s chair, Tom Lawless, said the offer was not high enough. In July 2025, the registry deferred a decision and ordered the group to register and file its disclosure reports, and in September it accepted a revised offer of a $6,000 penalty and closed the case.
Datwyler reportedly told the attorney general’s investigators that he had no personal knowledge of the Citizen Engagement Forum, a second group named in the complaint.
In April 2024 Emily’s List asked the FEC to investigate an Arizona group with a Democratic-sounding name, the Turn AZ Blue Pac, which had disclosed neither its spending nor its donors and which was listed with Datwyler as its treasurer. Through a lawyer, Datwyler told the commission he “is not, nor has he ever been, the treasurer” of the group, and the FEC’s dismissal report records that he swore he had never heard of it before the complaint. The commission dismissed the case in April 2025.
That July, a Nevada leadership Pac formed to back the Republican Senate candidate Jim Marchant asked the justice department to investigate Datwyler for alleged wire fraud over a $500 cheque written from its account to his compliance firm, AxCapital, after he had stepped down as its treasurer. The complaint, written by the Republican election lawyer Dan Backer, alleged “a long history of running roughshod over federal campaign finance law”. It said Datwyler first described the payment as a bank error made through an online bill-pay system, then said he would refund it; the Pac’s own FEC filings record a $500 “compliance refund” from AxCapital on 22 April 2024. Eric Brown, general counsel of Axiom Strategies, which owns AxCapital, reportedly said the firm faced “baseless attacks” and that the letter was “nothing more than a stunt”. No charges have followed.
Backer told the Guardian this week that he believed the $500 was refunded “only after filing the [justice department] letter”; his letter is dated 26 July 2024. Asked whether the justice department had responded, he said: “Law enforcement agencies generally do not comment on pending investigations.” He said Datwyler had “cost the GOP vast sums of money” and was “just not cut out for this line of work at this level”, and that aggrieved former clients rarely act because “no one ever wants to spend the money or put their reputation out there, to sue or to file an FEC complaint”.
The Guardian also contacted the Tennessee complainant, the state representative Michele Reneau, and Emily’s List for comment. They did not respond.
In Maryland, Datwyler was listed as the treasurer of “Dan Cox for US Congress”, a committee registered in the name of a candidate who had not filed to run. In Ohio’s Mahoning valley, county party chairs of both parties could learn nothing about a group attacking local officials beyond his name on the treasurer designation.
In Texas, a Super Pac Datwyler kept books for reportedly spent almost everything it raised on credit card fees and nothing on campaigning, according to its own FEC filings.
Perhaps most notoriously, George Santos’s campaign named him treasurer in January 2023 and his lawyer told the FEC the appointment was unauthorised – a position the same lawyer later retracted, writing that he had lost confidence in his client’s account.
Santos, the New York Republican who fabricated most of his biography, was expelled from the House in December 2023 and sentenced to more than seven years in April 2025 for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. He served 84 days before Donald Trump commuted the sentence in October.
Secrecy
Datwyler is steadfast in maintaining secrecy on behalf of funders.
Asked in October 2024 about $200,000 that arrived at a Super Pac opposing Sheldon Whitehouse from his Wisconsin address, Datwyler said a Florida couple were the primary funders and declined to name them.
Occasionally, Datwyler’s denials have been undone by his own filings.
Asked in October 2025 about attack mailers in a Utah school board race, he said the address on them “is not associated with us at all”; hours later, the Pac filed state paperwork listing him as its primary officer.
Time after time, however, investigations that reached committees he kept have ended without action against him. Three executives of Navatek, a Hawaii defence contractor, pleaded guilty over schemes that included routing $150,000 of company money through a sham entity, the Society of Young Women Scientists and Engineers, to 1820 Pac, a Super Pac backing Susan Collins for which Datwyler was treasurer. The Pac told the FEC the contribution was lawful. Commission lawyers later recommended finding that it had failed to refund the money once its source came to light, but the commissioners never voted on that, and in January 2025, with the statute of limitations running out, they dismissed the allegation against the Pac and Datwyler in his official capacity. The Pac’s FEC reports show no refund.
On Datwyler’s overall operation, Saurav Ghosh said: “What you’re describing is both incredibly common and incredibly problematic for our elections.”

‘We spend our days in silence’: fear and repression in Ohio as ICE terrorizes Haitian immigrants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:00:13 UTC
22:00:13 KST

Michaelle Louis’s feet and legs are aching. She can barely walk.
Surrounded by corn fields and the distant hum of a busy highway, the native of Haiti and dozens of other activists are 23 miles into a 45-mile march from Springfield to Ohio’s statehouse in Columbus to demand better rights for Haitian immigrants.
But the pain she’s feeling now is nothing compared to the mental anguish and fear she was subjected to last summer.
In August, she spent five days huddling with her daughter and brother in the basement of her Springfield home. The family went without electricity during daylight hours out of fear that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers might come knocking on her door to deport them.
“I closed the curtains. I didn’t want anyone to know there was people living in our house,” she recalls.
“We spent our days in silence.”
For months, ICE has terrorized members of Springfield’s immigrant community, speeding after vehicles down normally placid streets and causing crashes. Chief among those being targeted are the city’s Haitian community, who began immigrating to the struggling town of 60,000 residents eight years ago to fill hundreds of open blue-collar jobs.
But a supreme court ruling allowing the Trump administration to end temporary protected status (TPS) for more than 350,000 Haitian nationals in July meant they could no longer work legally, and within days, dozens of ICE agents descended on Springfield. In September, Markwayne Mullin, the US homeland security secretary, said 380 people had been detained by ICE agents in Springfield.
Louis grew up in Haiti’s capital city Port-au-Prince, and says she came to Springfield in 2021 having entered the country legally through the southern US border. Her 31-year-old brother was murdered by a gang in Haiti in December 2018.
“I had so many threats from the gangs. I left three months after he was killed,” she recalls.
“It was very hard for my mom and dad to lose their son.”
It’s not only Haitians who feel harassed by federal immigration agents in Springfield. When ICE began patrolling city streets in August, resident Sean Moorman set about monitoring their activities and following their vehicles around town.
But that soon drew unwanted attention from arguably the most powerful federal law enforcement agency in the country today.
In a lawsuit filed on his behalf by the American Civil Liberties Union of Ohio against seven ICE officers last month, Moorman claimed agents swerved one of their vehicles towards his, “as if to ram him”, took photos of his car and used several of their vehicles to corner Moorman in his car, “making him fear for his life”.
Agents also allegedly drove by and photographed his home while his wife was inside.
Last month, a federal judge ordered ICE to stop “retaliatory action” against Moorman and granted a temporary restraining order against seven of its agents, all of whom remained unnamed.
But many of the ICE officers operating in Springfield at the time were moved out of state and the judicial order ran out on 18 September.
“It is disappointing, but unfortunately not surprising, that ICE chose to play a shell game by shuffling their officers around rather than allowing them to face accountability in court for their lawless actions,” says David Carey, managing legal director at the ACLU of Ohio and Moorman’s legal representative in the case against the ICE agents.
“We certainly disagree with the court’s decision to entertain that shell game, but the fact that the court had already entered and extended a temporary restraining order against these officers also sent the most important message: ICE does not have a blank check to violate first amendment rights.”
Moorman declined an interview with the Guardian, fearing further retaliation from ICE. His lawsuit was thrown out by a federal judge on 2 October.
ICE says it “is aware of the lawsuit filed by the ACLU in Ohio and is reviewing appropriate next steps in coordination with the Department of Justice”.
“Every day, [the Department of Homeland Security] is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe,” an ICE spokesperson said.
“Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences. Illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”
Around the country, ICE “watchers” such as Moorman have become essential in bringing to light the agency’s dangerous and often homicidal actions in their attempts to detain immigrants.
More than two dozen people have been shot by ICE officers, many in front of their children, since the beginning of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in February 2025. Among them are three US citizens who were shot dead in Minneapolis and Texas. Two of those people, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were, like Moorman, monitoring the actions of Ice agents.
For Louis, the false statement Trump made during his presidential election campaign in September 2024 about immigrants in Springfield eating people’s pets hurt her the most.
“That opened my eyes. Until then, all I did was go to work and come home. I wasn’t that interested in community issues. I was helping people – Americans facing domestic violence. I served the nation; I served citizens,” she says.
Millions of immigrants from dozens of countries around the world have lost their ability to work legally in the US under the Trump administration. According to the Migration Policy Institute, ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) have deported 980,000 people since the beginning of Trump’s second stint in office.
“And when you say I’m eating dogs and cats and I’m coming illegally, that’s something that’s shaken me. I was sleeping and now I woke up for my community.”
Louis says the three-day march across Ohio is to raise awareness for activists’ demands to end ICE’s detention of and use of ankle monitors on immigrants, for its agents to leave Springfield and for authorities to establish a permanent residency pathway for Haitians who have contributed to life in the US.
On day two of the march, as a large Amazon warehouse where dozens of Haitians were employed before the Trump crackdown comes into view, Louis talks about a Haitian woman she knows whose husband was recently deported to Haiti, where violence and political unrest has reigned for more than a decade.
“They had bought a house here [but] now they are moving back to Haiti,” she says.
“I think this is a method by ICE – take the man and the family will follow.”

Ethnic Germans in Kazakhstan face legacy of the Soviet Union
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Ethnic Germans in Kazakhstan face legacy of the Soviet Union
November 1, 2026
She wants to keep history alive. Yunna Kinereish, 22, is studying public relations in Kazakhstan's modern capital, Astana. She describes herself as a Kazakh German.
"I am German by ethnicity. But I also feel that I'm Kazakh, because I keep the traditions with my family, and I have this mentality," she told DW.
Kinereish, who belongs to the Wiedergeburt (Revival) Association of Germans in Kazakhstan, is one of 223,000 Kazakh Germans living in the Central Asian republic of Kazakhstan today.
Kinereish recently acted in a play at the association's youth theater that told the fate of her Russian German forebears.
From the 18th century onward, Germans were incentivized to leave Germany and settle in the Russian empire, including in Ukraine's Black Sea region.
But after the armies of Hitler's Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941, Soviet dictator Josef Stalinstarted deporting hundreds of thousands of Germans living in Russia and Ukraine to Siberia and Kazakhstan.
Collective punishment
Innocent people who had nothing to do with Nazi Germany's invasion and atrocities were collectively held responsible by the Soviet power and denounced as spies and collaborators.
There were more than a million deportees, of whom at least 200,000 died as a result of expulsion, hunger, and forced labor.
"My family is part of this history, these terrible times. They were driven out of the Ukrainian village Kleinwärter, a settlement of ethnic Germans in Ukraine."
Yunna Kinereish says she was very moved by the personal stories she and her friends had brought to the stage at the House of Friendship, where the association has its office. "It's not easy for me, because it all touches my heart very deeply. I actually feel like crying. But when I'm on stage ..., I have to be strong."
Culture and remembrance under one roof
The modern-looking House of Friendship in the capital Astana is the center for German culture in the city. Financed primarily by the German government, it offers language courses, engages in social work and fosters a culture of remembrance, focusing on the themes of deportation and repression under the Soviet regime.
Yunna Kinereish doesn't only present the history of her people on stage: She is also documenting it on film. In 2025, she made a film about German women incarcerated in ALZhIR (Akmolinsk Camp for Wives of Traitors to the Motherland), among the most infamous in the Soviet Gulag system.
During Stalin's brutal campaign of political repression and state-sponsored terror in the 1930s, a period known as the Great Terror, the Soviet Union established its biggest camp system in Kazakhstan. 18,000 women passed through the ALZhIR camp alone. These women were imprisoned there only because their husbands had been convicted of being traitors or enemies of the people. Among them were 167 ethnic German women, whose stories are told in the film.
The memorial for the ALZhIR women's camp is located just outside the gates of Astana, which only became the capital in 1997.
Astana's roads are permanently clogged with traffic. There are almost no pedestrians, and no cyclists at all. The city is growing, with new buildings shooting up all along the outskirts of the city. Beyond them is the barren steppe; the village of Akmol is about an hour's drive away.
Before entering the actual ALZhIR museum, the visitor passes through the Arch of Grief, a huge steel construction that commemorates the suffering and forced labor the women endured. The museum itself contains personal items that belonged to the female prisoners, models of their primitive quarters, original documents and photographs.
Representative stories
One of the photos is of Gertrud Platais, a woman with German roots who spent years incarcerated in ALZhIR. Platais was a print worker from Lower Silesia, part of modern-day Poland. She married Karl Eduard Platais and became a Soviet citizen. In 1938, during the Great Terror, her husband was arrested. Gertrud was convicted, too as a "relative of a traitor to the homeland."
She was transferred to ALZhIR, in a region where temperatures hit 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) in summer and minus 40 degreees Celsius in winter. Here, she was forced to work as an embroiderer until 1946. After this, she was banished for life to the huge Karaganda Corrective Labor Camp, known as Karlag. Gertrud Platais wasn't rehabilitated until 1956. Hers is just one story documenting the terror of the Soviet system on Kazakh soil.
Karlag was by far the biggest camp system and its complex covered an area about 22 times the size of New York City. Karlag was not just a prison camp, but a huge economic and agricultural complex. Almost one million people passed through it between 1931 and 1959.
Around 10,000 prisoners are believed to have died here between 1940 and 1950 alone: of starvation, cold, sickness, and the effects of forced labor.
Staged remembrance
The museum sits in the middle of the Kazakh steppe, near the city of Karaganda, about 250 kilometers south of Astana. It is located in the building that used to house the camp system administration. Visiting German historians and specialists are slightly puzzled: People were not tortured or tormented in this building, it was simply where the administration was done.
Here, interrogation and torture cells have been reconstructed, and everything is underscored by melodramatic music pouring from ubiquitous loudspeakers. It comes across as staged rather than authentic. As at the ALZhIR memorial, the Karlag museum has few visitors. Even well-educated young Kazakhs probably don't know about it."
Many people in Kazakhstan, and certain areas of politics, have almost no interest in coming to terms with the country's often brutal history," says Katherine M. Erdman. An American anthropologist and archaeologist at the Nazarbayev University in Astana, she has been researching the Gulag system for about a decade now.
"The landscape has been shaped by forced labor"
"We wanted to find out where exactly the camps were, and how they can still be recognized today." Erdman and her students relied on modern technology such as drone flights, but conducting interviews and research on the ground was also a part of it.
"In many regions, the landscape has been shaped by forced labor," Erdman says. Factories were often constructed alongside the primitive living quarters. Houses were built using bricks made by forced laborers.
The researchers share their findings directly with neighbors and with local administrations. "Often we're just met with apathy, or flat-out rejection," says Erdman. At a time of economic and social advancement, many don't want to be reminded of the inglorious aspects of the past.
Erdman says there is a desire to demonstrate to the international community that the country is dealing with the dark side of its history, but that she often experiences lack of interest and even rejection. The academic has been conducting research in Kazakhstan for a decade, but there is no state funding for a further lectureship.
The Kazakh German Yunna Kinereish is one of the young people in Kazakhstan who want to ensure that the past is not forgotten. "My ancestors survived the Gulag system in Kazakhstan," she tells DW. "So it's important to me that we don't forget our roots, and that what our forefathers experienced and suffered is passed on."
This article, originally published in German, was written in the context of a study trip organized by the Federal Foundation for the Study of the Communist Dictatorship in Germany. Since 1998, the foundation, funded by the German taxpayer, has dedicated itself to studying and reappraising the former communist dictatorships in Germany, the GDR, and other countries.

One in four young men now say violence for a cause can be justified
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Rise in young men open to 'extreme measures' for a cause, survey finds
In short:
A new survey has revealed a rise in young men who say "extreme measures" could sometimes be justified to advance a cause.
The McKinnon Index data also shows trust in politicians and governments has fallen among Australians in the past year.
Australia's democracy has been in the spotlight since the alleged attack on Helen Haines.
One in four young men say "extreme measures", such as violence, can sometimes be justified to advance a cause, according to new research tracking Australians' views on democracy.
The second McKinnon Index, released today, also shows trust in politicians and government has fallen compared to last year, while almost three-quarters of Australians believe the country is more divided than 12 months ago.
More than 4,000 Australians were surveyed on their attitudes towards democracy, led by the not-for-profit organisation McKinnon and conducted with Roy Morgan in June and July this year.
The results have been released amid a broader conversation about political safety and the state of Australian democracy after an alleged attack on Independent MP Helen Haines near her parliamentary office in regional Victoria last month. An alleged motive in that incident remains unknown.
The survey finds that Australians largely support democracy, with more than three quarters still saying it is preferable to any other system of government.
Support for democracy slides for young men
Some of the largest movements in the data occurred for men aged 18 to 24.
There was an increase in the proportion of young men who said extreme measures could sometimes be justified, rising to more than 27 per cent.
That compares to one in 10 across the whole population, while more than three-quarters of Australians disagreed.
Support for democracy also declined among young men to 54 per cent, while there was a sharp 23-point drop in the proportion who believed people could freely express political opinions, to about 50 per cent.
McKinnon interim executive chairman and former Victorian deputy premier John Thwaites said it was important to acknowledge that while those who said violence could be justified in some circumstances were in the minority, it was an increasing proportion.
"We need to do more to ensure that all of our community, but young men here in particular, understand our democracy, understand the importance of it, and understand that their voice is important and can be heard," he said.
Confidence in politics drops in regional areas
The survey more broadly showed Australians were less satisfied with democracy, with fewer than half believing the political system gave people like them a say.
Those who said they had low trust in the federal government cited broken promises, dishonesty and politicians being out of touch as the most common reasons.
The trend was more pronounced for people with lower education levels and those who lived in the regions.
In inner regional areas, dissatisfaction in democracy rose to nearly 39 per cent, higher than the national proportion of about 30 per cent.
Cathy McGowan, who was the Independent MP for Indi before Ms Haines, said people in rural and regional Australia were bearing the brunt of inequality.
But she said since the alleged attack on Ms Haines, she has heard calls all over Australia "for us to be better and do better".
"There's also a role for community to be much more active in holding each other to account and creating the environment that they want to protect the democracy that they value."
Trust in the public service is steady
While trust in politicians and governments has declined, faith in public servants and democratic institutions has largely remained steady or increased.
Nearly half of Australians said they trusted the federal public service, while satisfaction in the education system and public infrastructure also rose.
The Australian Electoral Commission had the highest trust level, with more than 70 per cent, followed by government regulators and advisory bodies at 57 per cent and the courts at 55 per cent.
University of Melbourne political science associate professor Aaron Martin said he had observed similar trends in his own research, including that support for institutions like the electoral commission remained high for the most part.
While he said it was difficult to read a trend from the two years of data provided by the McKinnon Index, other studies like the Australian Election Study showed satisfaction with democracy had risen between the 2019 and 2025 federal elections.
"I think over the longer term, the picture is a little more optimistic than the sort of snapshots that we're getting at the moment," he said.
Dr Martin said globally Australia sat between countries doing "really badly", such as the US, the UK, France and Spain, and countries doing "really well", like Denmark.
"Australia is in a pretty reasonable position, but that's not to say that we're in a sort of unassailable position either," he said.
Mr Thwaites said leaders needed to take note of the loss of trust.
"People need to know their voice matters. They also need to see leaders acting with integrity, keeping their promises and delivering outcomes that make a difference to their lives."

No paneer, no honey, no milky chai? The real challenge of going vegan in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:56:26 UTC
21:56:26 KST

World Vegan Day is observed annually on November 1.
For many Indians, the day begins with a cup of milky chai, followed by breakfast cooked in ghee. Lunch may come with a bowl of curd and paneer on the menu, while a Sunday meal is often incomplete without chicken curry.These familiar food habits are so deeply woven into everyday life that giving up all animal-derived products can seem like a difficult choice.But for people who turn vegan, the change goes beyond replacing meat with vegetables. It means rethinking everyday ingredients, from milk and butter to honey, as well as choices involving clothing, cosmetics and other products.“There are alternatives for practically everything. You can make curd at home using plant milk, use tofu instead of paneer, and use different nut and soy milks,” says Sarahana, who has been vegan since 2018.On World Vegan Day, observed on November 1, the question is not just why people choose veganism, but what it takes to follow the lifestyle.
Dal, rice, roti, rajma, chole, idli, dosa, poha, upma and vegetable dishes can all be part of a vegan diet.
What is veganism?
According to The Vegan Society, veganism is a way of living that seeks to exclude, as far as possible and practicable, all forms of animal exploitation and cruelty.
While a vegan diet avoids meat, fish, eggs, dairy and honey, the lifestyle also extends to products made from animals, those tested on animals and activities that use animals for entertainment.
For some, the decision is rooted in animal welfare; for others, environmental concerns or health considerations play a role.But the experiences of vegans show that the transition is as much about changing everyday habits as it is about changing one's perspective.India has a long tradition of vegetarian food, but veganism goes a step further by excluding all animal-derived products, including milk, curd, ghee, paneer and honey.According to estimates compiled by World Population Review, around 9% of India's population followed a vegan diet in 2021, amounting to an estimated 121.5 million people. The country also has a substantial vegetarian population, reflecting its diverse food traditions.However, the figure should be treated as an estimate rather than a definitive count, as veganism surveys often rely on self-reported responses and vary in methodologies.
Rice with tofu and cucumber. (Photo credit: Utkarsh)
What does a vegan Indian kitchen look like?
A vegan diet does not necessarily mean giving up familiar Indian food or relying on expensive, imported alternatives. Dal, rice, roti, rajma, chole, idli, dosa, poha, upma and vegetable dishes can all be part of a vegan diet, provided they are prepared without animal-derived ingredients.Utkarsh Garg, a representative of People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA), says their meals are a mix of familiar Indian dishes and plant-based alternatives.“Breakfast is usually a protein smoothie bowl or soaked oats, although I’m definitely not above a plate of poha, chhole-kulche or one enormous aloo paratha when the mood strikes!”“Lunch and dinner usually include things like tofu, soybeans, dals, rajma and plenty of vegetables. My current obsession is tempeh. I seem to be finding increasingly creative excuses to put it into everything I eat.”“As for living without milk, paneer, curd or ghee, I genuinely don’t find it difficult anymore. There are so many vegan alternatives available now, and many things are surprisingly easy and inexpensive to make at home as well.” Utkarsh said.Sarahana says she relies largely on everyday Indian food rather than packaged substitutes.“As for food, my everyday diet is actually quite simple and Indian. Dal, rice, roti, vegetables, chickpeas, rajma, seasonal produce and different legumes. There are so many naturally plant-based foods available in India. You don’t need expensive imported alternatives or packaged vegan products to survive without dairy.“There are alternatives for practically everything. You can make curd at home using plant milk, use tofu instead of paneer, and use different nut and soy milks. Ghee is essentially clarified butter, and personally, I don’t feel the need to replace it.”The distinction is important. A vegan diet does not require a direct substitute for every non-vegan food. It can instead be built around naturally plant-based ingredients that are already widely used in Indian kitchens.
Breakfast is usually a protein smoothie bowl or soaked oats. (Photo credit: Utkarsh)
Why are people choosing veganism?
For Utkarsh, the decision began in childhood. Watching a chicken being slaughtered made them connect the food on their plate with the animal it came from. He turned vegetarian that day and later went vegan.“For me, veganism has always been about animals. I’ve loved animals for as long as I can remember. While most kids my age were watching Cartoon Network or Pogo, I was glued to National Geographic, completely fascinated by dogs, cats, cows, snakes, and pretty much every animal I came across,” Utkarsh said.As he learnt more about animal exploitation, vegetarianism no longer felt enough. “My love for animals naturally led me to veganism. I’ve been vegan for four years now, and honestly, it is one of the best decisions I have ever made. More than changing what I eat or wear, it has changed the way I look at the world and my place in it.”
Yellow Thai Curry. (Photo credit: Sarahana)
For Sarahana, the turning point came in 2018, when she watched a video of a pregnant cow being slaughtered after she was no longer productive for the dairy industry.“My decision came from questioning something very basic: why do we, as human beings, consider ourselves superior to other animals? Why do we love some animals, consider some family, see some as entertainment, and others as food?” she said.While studying gender, Sarahana began drawing parallels between the exploitation of women's bodies and that of female animals in the dairy industry.“How can I study feminism, gender and the exploitation of female bodies and not extend that understanding beyond human beings? How can I talk about patriarchy and exploitation while continuing to pay an industry that repeatedly impregnates female animals, takes away their babies and exploits their reproductive systems?” she said.Coming from a Dalit community, Sarahana also views veganism through the lens of social justice, questioning how societies decide whose lives are valued.“We love cats and dogs, welcome them into our homes and call them family, but we look at chickens, goats and buffaloes and see food. We have created categories of animals that deserve affection and animals that can be exploited,” she added.
The figure should be treated as an estimate rather than a definitive count, as veganism surveys often rely on self-reported responses.
The price of going vegan
One common perception is that veganism is an expensive lifestyle, largely because plant-based milk, meat substitutes and other packaged alternatives can cost more than conventional products. However, both Utkarsh and Sarahana say that a vegan diet need not depend on these products.Utkarsh points out that many Indian staples are naturally plant-based. “India is one of the easiest places in which to eat vegan, because so much of the food we already know and love either naturally contains no animal-derived ingredients or can be veganised with ridiculously small changes.“Think about dal, rajma, chole, idli, dosa, poha, upma, roti, sabzis, rice dishes and countless regional foods. Veganism doesn’t have to mean buying an expensive imported mock meat or drinking a fancy packaged plant milk every morning. Those products are great if you enjoy them, but they aren’t what veganism depends on.”
Vegan food item. (Photo credit: Utkarsh)
Sarahana agrees that the bigger challenge is often social rather than financial.“I don’t think being vegan in India is inherently expensive. Our traditional food already has so many affordable plant-based options. What can become expensive is the packaged vegan alternatives, not the basic diet itself. The bigger challenge is social conditioning. At family gatherings, weddings or even casual conversations, you constantly have to explain why you don’t consume something that everyone else considers normal.”Both say their families initially had questions and reservations. Utkarsh says their family is now supportive and has started incorporating more vegan foods and products into their lives. Sarahana, meanwhile, says she continues to face comments that she has been “brainwashed”.
Is a vegan diet actually healthier?
Veganism is often associated with better health, but a plant-based diet is not automatically a balanced one. Its nutritional value depends on the foods included and whether essential nutrients are adequately supplied.Dt Gausiya Aziz, consultant and head of nutrition and dietetics at SPARSH Hospital, Yelahanka, says a well-planned vegan diet can support cardiovascular and metabolic health.“Research suggests that plant-based dietary patterns rich in fibre, antioxidants and unsaturated fats can help lower LDL cholesterol, improve blood pressure and support healthy weight management. They may also reduce the risk of developing type 2 diabetes,” she says.However, claims that veganism automatically prevents cancer, reverses chronic diseases or guarantees a longer life are exaggerated, she cautions. Health outcomes depend on overall diet quality, lifestyle and individual medical conditions.
White sauce (made with soy milk) pasta with nutritional yeast (Photo credit: Sarahana)
A key concern is meeting nutritional requirements. Vitamin B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D, iodine, zinc, omega-3 fatty acids and protein need particular attention.Vitamin B12 is especially important because reliable natural plant-based sources are limited. Fortified foods or supplements may therefore be necessary.Aziz recommends a varied diet containing whole grains, legumes, vegetables, fruits, nuts and seeds, along with appropriate supplementation and regular nutritional assessment.Utkarsh says he pay close attention to their nutritional needs and take vitamin B12 supplements.“I am also quite particular about my nutrition. I take my B12 regularly and pay attention to vitamin D and other essential nutrients. B12 supplementation is important for vegans, and these supplements are accessible at pharmacies,” he said.The PETA representative added that he has noticed less bloating since turning vegan and feel healthier, but stresses that dietary planning matters.“Of course, I think any diet needs to be properly planned rather than treated as automatically healthy simply because it carries a particular label. For me, veganism has actually made me more conscious of what I eat and what my body needs.”Aziz also warns that highly processed vegan foods are not necessarily healthy. Packaged snacks, meat substitutes and desserts can contain high amounts of sodium, refined carbohydrates, added sugars and saturated fats. She advises prioritising minimally processed foods and checking nutritional labels.“Children, pregnant women and older adults have specific nutritional requirements that demand careful consideration before adopting a vegan diet. During childhood, adequate energy, protein, calcium, iron, vitamin B12 and vitamin D are essential for growth and development. Pregnant women must additionally ensure sufficient folate, iodine, choline and omega-3 fatty acids to support maternal health and fetal development. Older adults should prioritise protein intake, calcium and vitamin D to preserve muscle strength and bone health. Vitamin B12 supplementation is particularly important across these groups,” Aziz added.Nutritionist Aziz also recommends consulting a qualified dietitian or healthcare professional before making significant dietary changes.
Vegan Pizza with Oat Milk Coffee
Is veganism about health, animals or the planet?
Animal welfare is not the only reason people choose veganism. Environmental concerns are also part of the conversation.Aziz says vegan diets generally have a lower environmental footprint than diets containing substantial amounts of animal products, particularly red meat and dairy.Plant-based food production typically requires less agricultural land and generates fewer greenhouse gas emissions than livestock farming. It can also reduce pressure on biodiversity and freshwater resources.However, the environmental impact varies with farming methods, transportation, processing and food waste. Choosing locally available, seasonal and minimally processed plant foods can help reduce the footprint further.For Utkarsh, the values behind veganism are also connected to ideas of compassion and non-violence.“We grow up hearing about ahimsa and vasudhaiva kutumbakam, the idea that the world is one family. To me, animals shouldn’t be excluded from that circle of compassion simply because they belong to another species,” he said.
Utkarsh says lunch and dinner usually include things like tofu, soybeans, and plenty of vegetables.
What should you know before going vegan?
Going vegan involves more than changing what is on the plate. It can mean checking product labels, asking about ingredients when eating out and finding alternatives to everyday items.Some medications and personal-care products may also contain animal-derived ingredients, making it important to check rather than assume that a product is vegan.For someone considering the transition, Utkarsh suggests starting by understanding where everyday products come from.“For anyone considering going vegan because they care about animals, I would say: start by looking. Look honestly at where our milk, meat, eggs, leather, wool, silk, cosmetics and entertainment come from.”“Once I did that, veganism stopped feeling like something I was ‘giving up’. It started feeling like the most natural extension of something I had believed all along.”Sarahana says the idea is to extend compassion beyond the animals people traditionally consider companions or pets.She also points to the growing number of Indian businesses offering vegan alternatives. For her, such businesses are helping make animal-free choices more accessible.
For those thinking of making the switch, the practical starting point may be simple: understand what a vegan diet excludes, plan for essential nutrients and explore the plant-based foods already available in the kitchen.World Vegan Day was established in 1994 by Louise Wallis, then president of The Vegan Society, to mark the 50th anniversary of the organisation's founding in November 1944.The day is now observed annually on November 1 to raise awareness about veganism and its ethical, environmental and health-related aspects.
Kanchan Yadav is a writer at The Times of India, where she covers business, politics, international affairs and social issues. Her reporting also focuses on policy, governance and economic developments, with a close lens on how decisions in corridors of power affect everyday lives and community well-being.

- The U.S. Army’s HADES Prototype 1, a modified Bombardier Global 6500 jet, made its first flight on Sept. 11, the service announced Oct. 30.
- The aircraft now enters developmental flight testing of its multi-domain sensing and signals intelligence systems ahead of operational demonstrations.
The U.S. Army’s first HADES prototype, a Bombardier Global 6500 business jet modified by Sierra Nevada Corporation for long-range signals intelligence and deep sensing, made its first flight on Sept. 11, the service announced on Oct. 30, seven weeks after the event.
The flight followed a flight readiness review and moves the High Accuracy Detection and Exploitation System into mission system integration and a developmental flight test program. The Army said those tests will check the aircraft’s multi-domain sensing and signals intelligence equipment ahead of operational demonstrations. It did not say where the aircraft flew, how long the flight lasted or what mission equipment was installed.
“The first flight of HADES Prototype 1 transitions our vision for deep sensing from concept to reality,” said Lt. Col. (P) James Hickey, project manager for the Fixed Wing Project Office. “This achievement reflects the dedication, technical precision, and shared mission focus of our military, civilian, and industry partners working to deliver transformational capabilities to the Army and joint force.”
The Fixed Wing Project Office ran the flight with SNC, the program’s lead systems integrator, and with the Project Director Sensors–Aerial Intelligence, part of the Army’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Command and Control/Counter-Command and Control. Before the flight, engineers, test pilots and mission system architects completed the structural modifications, installed mission system hardware and finished preliminary airworthiness checks. HADES is government-owned and contractor-operated, and SNC told Defense Daily in January that its own pilots and technicians would fly the tests alongside the Army.
Bombardier delivered the first Global 6500 for the program to the Army in Wichita, Kansas, in November 2024, and the Army passed it to SNC’s facility in Hagerstown, Maryland, for conversion. The Army had picked SNC as lead systems integrator in August 2024 under a 12-year contract worth $93.5 million at award, with a ceiling of $991.3 million, beating a team of L3Harris, Leidos and MAG Aerospace. L3Harris protested the decision, which stopped work until the Government Accountability Office denied the protest on Dec. 23, 2024. SNC received the second Army-owned jet in September 2025, and at the end of 2025 it bought a fourth Global 6500 with its own money to become the first non-prototype aircraft in the fleet.
The Army plans to field HADES in stages. In April 2026, Army officials said the program would deliver three prototypes, with the second adding an advanced radar and the third described as “combat credible”, and that the first aircraft would reach units later this year. The service also wants to pair HADES with launched effects, small unmanned systems released from the aircraft. In 2025, the Army said it would buy about half as many of the jets as it had previously planned, and it has not published a final fleet size.
When it announced the 2024 award, the Army said SNC would integrate communications intelligence, electronic intelligence, synthetic aperture radar and moving target indicator sensors on the Global 6500. A Pentagon budget reprogramming document approved in early 2025 confirmed that Raytheon’s Advanced Synthetic Aperture Radar System-2B, developed for the U.S. Air Force’s U-2, is part of the HADES sensor suite. The Oct. 30 release mentions only multi-domain sensing and signals intelligence for the current test phase.
HADES grows out of a string of contractor-owned bridging aircraft the Army has flown since 2020. Leidos built ARTEMIS on a Bombardier Challenger 650 and ARES on a Global 6500, and ARES deployed to the Indo-Pacific in 2022. Under the follow-on ATHENA effort, a MAG Aerospace and L3Harris team modified Global 6500s for radar collection, while SNC converted two jets to its RAPCON-X signals intelligence configuration, which became the basis for HADES. SNC says the HADES aircraft will be the first Army-owned large-cabin business jets used for aerial intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.
The jets are meant to replace the Army’s legacy turboprop intelligence aircraft. The Army says the Global 6500 airframe offers greater speed, range, payload and operating altitude than those platforms, which lets HADES collect from farther away and spend more time on station in large-scale operations.
“Deep sensing is critical to maintaining decision advantage in the future fight,” Hickey said. “HADES will help commanders see farther, understand faster, and act with greater precision across the multi-domain battlefield.”

Polling stations in Australia report higher voter turnout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:51:03 UTC
21:51:03 KST

Author
Vesela Krasteva
News
Presidential Election 2026-Runoff
Polling stations in Australia report higher voter turnout
Vladimira Hristov invites Bulgarians to visit Sydney and connect with the Bulgarian Cultural and Social Association ‘Rodina’
Sunday 1 November 2026 13:55
Sunday, 1 November 2026, 13:55
The first ballot was cast at the polling station in Brisbane at 7:26 a.m. local time
PHOTO personal archive
Font size
Voting for Bulgarians in Australia is drawing to a close. On the Day of the National Awakeners, they were able to cast their ballots at six polling stations across the continent, in Brisbane, Canberra, Melbourne, Sydney, Perth and Adelaide. The first ballot was cast at 7:26 a.m. local time at the polling station in Brisbane. Our compatriots there marked the occasion with a social media post carrying the message: “Take responsibility for the future of our homeland. Be like Kolyo...!”
In Melbourne, the Bulgarian community was eagerly awaiting the arrival of 98-year-old Ivan, who just a week ago became the oldest person to cast a ballot at the polling station and an inspiration to dozens of Bulgarians. Election day passed peacefully and without any reported violations in Melbourne. The local election commission reported turnout nearly 25% higher than in the first round, with 90 people having cast their ballots two hours before polls closed.
PHOTO courtesy of Mancho Manev
''Several factors may explain this. First and foremost, perhaps, is the lovely weather, whereas last Sunday we had torrential rain. There is greater interest in the runoff. The first-round result was very close, so more people may have decided that their vote could make a difference. We should also bear in mind that there is greater polarization between the candidates here. The choice has come down to two candidates with clearly differing positions, which has motivated more people to take part in the election”.
Mancho Manev notes that the trend of more and more young people heading to the polls is becoming increasingly evident, with many voting willingly and enthusiastically
“Some young people come because their parents encourage them to, while others turn up on their own, which is wonderful. We are also looking forward to seeing the elderly gentleman, Ivan, again. He is 98 years old, and we hope he will come and exercise his right to vote. We have also noticed that quite a few older Bulgarians do not hesitate to come out and vote. They take their civic duty much more seriously than other age groups”, our compatriot says.
PHOTO courtesy of Mancho Manev
And on this November 1, which is not only election day but also a holiday for Bulgarians, we also ask Manev who the modern-day enlighteners are for the Bulgarian community in Melbourne.
“Today’s enlighteners are local figures who preserve Bulgarian identity and keep our traditions alive here. We have an organisation dedicated to supporting the Bulgarian church in the city and its congregation. There are also various groups, including folk dance ensembles, that come together and take part in events across Australia. They have taken on the important task of keeping our Bulgarian heritage, traditions and language alive.”
One of these modern-day Bulgarian enlighteners is Vladimira Hristov, President of the Bulgarian Cultural and Social Association ‘Rodina’ Sydney. After spending eight years in the UK, Vladimira moved to Australia in 2013. Today, she says with a smile: “I truly adore Bulgaria, but I adore Australia, too.”
Vladimira Hristov
PHOTO personal archive
“I’ve often heard Bulgarians ask: ‘If you love Bulgaria so much, why do you live so far away from it?’ It’s difficult to explain, but Australia has many well-developed sectors, healthcare being one of them. And when you walk down the street, people smile at you and say hello. I’ve even said that if I smiled at a stranger or greeted someone so enthusiastically in Bulgaria, they might think there was something wrong with me. Yes, Australia is a wonderful place, and I would encourage everyone to come and visit the Bulgarian Cultural and Social Association ‘Rodina’ Sydney. We have a Bulgarian Sunday school named after Dr Petar Beron, organise weekly folk dance classes and put on performances. It’s truly wonderful. When you live so far away from home, you become even more connected to your roots, however hard that may be for some people to believe. We miss Bulgaria so much that we do everything we can to bring it closer to us – we make traditional Bulgarian costumes, organise celebrations, and all this brings our community closer together”, Vladimira Hristov tells Radio Bulgaria.
PHOTO personal archive
On this sunny Sunday in Sydney and rainy one in Sofia, the Bulgarian woman is chairing the election commission in Australia’s largest city. She says the voting process is proceeding smoothly, with no reported irregularities.
PHOTO personal archive
She attributes the high voter turnout to the fact that many Bulgarians living there had anticipated a runoff. “Distances here are enormous, and today we had someone who travelled 130 kilometres to vote, with the round trip taking five hours. So it is understandable that those who expected a second round may have found it more convenient to wait and cast their ballots in the runoff''.
Both on October 25 and today, Bulgarians in Sydney are voting for one thing:
PHOTO personal archive
“I believe we are all voting for a better Bulgaria for our families. Many of us dream of returning one day, even though, for one reason or another, we live 15,000 kilometres away in Australia. As for my own family, we visit Bulgaria every year, and we hope that one day our children might go and live there, and that we too will return''.
A cleaner Sofia, a richer summer cultural programme, better job opportunities and higher wages are among the positive changes Vladimira Hristov sees in Bulgaria. Following today’s election, she hopes to see Bulgarians become even more united, convinced that this is the only way for the nation to build a better future.
The election day ended in Sydney with 162 ballots cast, while 99 Bulgarians turned out to vote in Melbourne to elect Bulgaria’s seventh president and vice president.

Binance restarts withdrawals after $6.3bn heist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:50:55 UTC
21:50:55 KST

Binance restarts withdrawals after $6.3bn heist
The FBI says hackers from North Korea are responsible for the theft.
Binance has begun restoring customer withdrawals after hackers stole about $6.3bn in cryptocurrency in a record theft that United States authorities have blamed on North Korea.
The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange resumed some of its services on Sunday, following a suspension imposed after Thursday’s attack as the company investigated the breach and carried out security checks.
Binance said it had replaced approximately 95 percent of the affected assets. “Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X on Sunday.
Withdrawals are being restored in stages, with major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ether, along with some stablecoin services, being reopened.
The exchange warned that high demand could cause delays as services return, advising customers whose transactions fail to try again after a short wait.
It said further services would reopen as security checks were completed, while teams continued working with law enforcement and industry partners to trace and recover the stolen assets.
FBI blames North Korea
The FBI said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the theft, identifying the operation as cyber-activity it tracks under the name TraderTraitor.
Investigators had observed the attackers converting stolen assets primarily into ether, the cryptocurrency used on the Ethereum network, the agency said. It warned that further laundering was expected through decentralised finance platforms and instant cryptocurrency exchange services.
The FBI previously attributed the theft of approximately $1.5bn from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit in February 2025 to the same actors.
Binance initially said a compromised employee laptop might have enabled the intrusion, but later reported that investigators had also uncovered additional points of breach.
The company said its investigation remained ongoing and that it would publish a detailed report once the inquiry was complete.
