U.S. Marine Corps wants new cargo drones that fly 100 pounds 40 miles out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:50:44 UTC
21:50:44 KST

- The U.S. Navy will host a cargo drone demonstration in Huntsville from Jan. 25 to Feb. 5, 2027, for the U.S. Marine Corps’ TRUAS Increment II.
- Entrants must carry 100 pounds 40 nautical miles and back without refueling, using heavy fuel or hybrid power.
The U.S. Navy is inviting companies to bring cargo drones to Huntsville, Alabama, from Jan. 25 to Feb. 5, 2027, to compete for the U.S. Marine Corps’ second-generation Tactical Resupply Unmanned Aircraft System, or TRUAS Increment II, which must carry 100 pounds (45 kg) to a point 40 nautical miles (74 km) away and fly back without refueling. Applications to take part in the demonstration are due Nov. 30, 2026.
The Navy’s new Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Robotic and Autonomous Systems posted the notice on Oct. 30 through its Air Warfare program office at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland. Companies that perform well in Huntsville may receive an other transaction prototype agreement under 10 U.S.C. § 4022, and a successfully completed prototype can lead to a follow-on production agreement without further competition. The government may award no agreements, one or several, and the notice gives no dollar value or planned quantity.
Each selected company must show ground setup, flight preparation and refueling, then fly up to five autonomous sorties. On the first required flight, the drone carries a 100-pound load 40 nautical miles, releases it, flies 40 nautical miles back empty and lands at its launch point. On the second, it carries at least 150 pounds (68 kg) out 10 nautical miles (18.5 km) and returns empty, again without refueling. The aircraft must cruise at no less than 50 knots (93 km/h), stay below 1,000 feet (305 m) above ground, launch and recover without a catapult, net or arresting cable, and carry a transponder with at least Mode 3/C capability. Up to three more flights may be allowed to show other features.
Applicants must meet two threshold requirements just to be considered: the payload-and-range performance above and a powerplant that runs on heavy fuel such as JP-5, JP-8 or diesel, or on a hybrid fuel-battery system. The Navy also states a preference for aircraft with a maximum gross takeoff weight of up to 350 pounds (159 kg).
The Marine Corps’ current TRUAS is the TRV-150C, a battery-electric aircraft with eight rotors on four arms, designed by Malloy Aeronautics and sold in the United States by Survice Engineering. The Navy bought the first 21 in April 2023 for $8.4 million and declared initial operational capability on Oct. 27, 2023, with the 3rd Littoral Logistics Battalion at Marine Corps Base Hawaii. The Marine Corps later ordered 31 more TRV-150Cs in a $9.8 million contract modification. The Marine Corps rates the TRV-150C at about 9 miles (14 km) with a full 150-pound load. Increment II asks for the same load carried 18.5 km out and back, plus a 100-pound load over a round trip of 80 nautical miles (148 km).
Heavy-fuel engines would let the new aircraft draw from the same JP-8 or diesel supply that Marine vehicles and generators already use, instead of depending on charged battery packs in the field. The notice does not explain why the program chose that requirement.
Marine units have been using the TRV-150C for two years to work out how drone resupply fits into logistics formations. In October 2025, Marines pushed the TRUAS through field tests aimed at giving company and platoon commanders their own way to resupply small units in hard-to-reach places. In 2024, Marine officials said they planned to issue three to six TRUAS drones to every logistics battalion by 2028. The U.S. Army has also evaluated the TRV-150 at Fort Stewart, Georgia, in February 2026. The notice describes Increment II as an organic aerial distribution capability for small-unit logistics across the last tactical mile, in Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations and Distributed Operations.
The requirements tables attached to the notice go well beyond the demonstration flights. A single operator must be able to control up to four aircraft at once, and the system must accept natural-language voice commands such as changing heading or altitude. The complete system has to fit in one ruggedized container no larger than 4 by 3 by 2 feet and weighing no more than 150 pounds, be ready to launch within 20 minutes, and reach a mean time between failures of at least 30 flight hours, with 90 as the objective. By default, the aircraft must not launch without mission approval from the Marine Corps’ Multifunction Air Operations Center, though a designated supervisor can override that rule when no airspace control authority is available. It must also navigate without GPS, use encrypted radios that meet FIPS 140-3 Level 2, and keep its electrical components sealed to an IP-56 rating.
“Operating the TRUAS UCC shall be comparable in terms of ease and intuitiveness to common smartphone tasks, such as ordering food delivery or ride-sharing services,” the requirements table states.
Participation is limited to U.S.-based, U.S.-owned companies using U.S. manufacturing and repair facilities, or to firms that can show strict compliance with 10 U.S.C. § 4881 and the American Security Drone Act, which restrict the government’s purchase and use of foreign-made drones. Companies pay their own costs, must sign a cooperative research and development agreement before flying and must join the Naval Aviation Systems Consortium to be eligible for an award. There is no fee to apply.
The program has changed owners since Increment I, which was run by the Navy and Marine Corps Small Tactical Unmanned Aircraft Systems program office, PMA-263. Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao established the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Robotic and Autonomous Systems on Aug. 5, 2026, to bring requirements and acquisition of unmanned systems for the Navy and Marine Corps under a single office.
On request, the Navy may also share flight performance data with the Army-run Drones.mil Marketplace, an online storefront where U.S. units and allies can buy vetted drones. The Army said in October that the marketplace had generated more than $800 million in sales in its first four months.

Yemeni government appoints governors for 2 provinces partly controlled by Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:47:10 UTC
21:47:10 KST

Mohammed Sami and Serdar Dincel
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council issued two decrees on Sunday appointing new governors for al-Bayda in central Yemen and al-Jawf in the north, two provinces partially controlled by the Houthis.
The government-run version of Saba news agency said that Major General Hussein al-Ajji Ali al-Awadhi was appointed as governor of al-Bayda. Major General Amin Ali al-Akimi was also named as governor of al-Jawf and commander of its military axis, the agency added.
Al-Awadhi replaces former al-Bayda governor Nasser al-Sawadi, while al-Akimi takes over al-Jawf from al-Awadhi, who had served as the province’s governor.
The appointments come as both provinces face a complex military situation, with clashes continuing between government forces and the Houthi group over control of strategic positions.
The Houthis control most areas of al-Bayda, while control of al-Jawf is divided between the group and government forces.
Al-Bayda holds strategic importance because of its central location in Yemen and its borders with eight other provinces, four in the north and four in the south.
Al-Jawf is also of military and geographic significance because it shares a land border with Saudi Arabia and lies near the Houthi-controlled provinces of Saada, Amran and Sanaa. It also borders Marib and Hadhramaut, which are under government control.
Since Oct. 5, Yemeni government forces have launched Operation “Dawn of Yemen” to restore state institutions from Houthi control and retake the capital, Sanaa.
Military escalation between government forces and the Houthis resumed in July, killing and wounding thousands and displacing more than a quarter of a million people, according to UN reports.
The escalation ended a period of relative calm that had prevailed in Yemen since April 2022, while the humanitarian crisis has worsened amid continued fighting and displacement.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Russia Turns to African and Asian Recruits for Frontline Assaults After Heavy Losses in Ukraine
Russian forces are deploying foreign recruits from African and Asian countries in infantry assaults near Huliaipole in Ukraine’s southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, as mounting battlefield losses force Russian commanders to rotate and replace frontline units.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s 7th Air Assault Corps on October 31, Russian troops have suffered approximately 900 killed and wounded over the past week in the Huliaipole sector, nearly 150 more than during the previous reporting period.
The Ukrainian military said the figure represents the highest weekly Russian casualty count recorded in the area over the past two months.
The losses have reportedly prompted Russian commanders to reorganize their forces and replace depleted formations. Within Russia’s 5th Combined Arms Army, personnel from the 60th Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade are reportedly replacing elements of the 57th Separate Guards Motorized Rifle Brigade.
Ukrainian commanders expect Russian forces to attempt to increase the intensity of their assaults once additional personnel arrive. Despite these changes, Russian troops continue to rely primarily on small infantry groups of one to five soldiers attempting to infiltrate Ukrainian defensive positions.
The 7th Air Assault Corps also reported identifying foreign nationals among Russian assault troops, including recruits from countries across Africa and Asia.
According to the Ukrainian military, recruitment schemes frequently involve promises of civilian employment or relatively safe military contracts. Upon arrival in Russia, foreign recruits allegedly have their passports and mobile phones confiscated, leaving them without outside communication before being forcibly deployed to frontline positions.
Earlier, on October 29, it was reported that nearly 80% of foreign nationals captured while fighting for Russia want to return to the country, although Moscow is largely unwilling to take them back. Ukrainian officials also revealed that nearly half of the captured foreigners surveyed admitted they had known they were joining Russia’s military to fight against Ukraine.

Germany 'Gen Z' protests turn violent as shops looted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:46:01 UTC
21:46:01 KST

The violence followed largely peaceful protests earlier on Saturday and came amid a wave of similar demonstrations across Europe. The unrest was reminiscent of scenes across France last month.
"Gen Z" protests in Germany on Saturday descended into violence in parts of the country as rioters clashed with police and looters targeted shops.
After largely peaceful protests against issues including rising living costs took place in the afternoon, rioting broke out in several cities as darkness fell.
The situation became particularly tense in Frankfurt, Cologne, Hamburg and Berlin. Shop windows were smashed and flaming barricades blocked streets as police deployed water cannons against crowds.
In Berlin, a youth demonstration involving what police said was around 3,500 people started at Rosenthaler Platz and moved towards Prenzlauer Berg on Saturday.
Pro-Palestinian and anti-fascist protesters also joined the march, some chanting anti-capitalist, anti-Israeli and anti-German slogans as flares and firecrackers were set off.
According to Berlin police, 27 officers sustained minor injuries during the unrest and almost 60 people were arrested.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt blamed "left-wing groups and troublemakers from a migrant background" for the riots and called for harsh penalties for those found to have taken part.
Hamburg
Hamburg in northern Germany also saw violent scenes on Saturday evening, as rioters built burning blockades and attacked officers with stones, bottles and fireworks.
“Unfortunately, troublemakers have today mingled with the peaceful demonstrators in order to deliberately provoke and commit criminal offences," a spokesperson for the Hamburg Police said. "The police will rigorously pursue the offences identified and exhaust all necessary investigative measures.”
The force has yet to release final figures on the number of arrests and injuries to officers, although it said around 120 people had been temporarily taken into custody during the evening.
Around 1,300 police officers were deployed during the violence.
Frankfurt
Frankfurt am Main also saw serious rioting and looting. The Zeil shopping street was particularly affected, where rioters smashed shop windows as they sought to gain access to stores.
A gun shop was also attacked in the city. Police seized two weapons at the site and arrested several suspects.
More than 1,000 police officers, including special units, were deployed in the city, as well as water cannon, armoured vehicles and a helicopter.
According to police, Molotov cocktails and other objects were hurled at officers during the unrest.
In total, more than 30 temporary arrests were reported.
The situation grew calmer in the early hours of Sunday morning, although police said there had been considerable damage to property.
Around 8,000 people are thought to have demonstrated in Frankfurt, largely peacefully, before the violence broke out. Organisers have distanced themselves from the violence.
Cologne
In Cologne, a rally was ended at around 4 pm after some participants covered their faces and set off fireworks before officers were attacked.
"Following the gathering, attacks were carried out on the emergency services; the police deployed water cannons against the groups causing disruption," Cologne police said in an update on Saturday evening.
"One police officer sustained a hand injury and was subsequently unable to continue on duty," the force continued, adding that "several criminal proceedings" cases had been opened.

The UK’s legal cannabis market is booming – so why can’t this talented artist get any to treat his epilepsy? | Kojo Koram
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:33:55 UTC
21:33:55 KST

In 2022, a prodigiously talented young artist named Louis Petit was preparing to return to the UK, having been effectively exiled in the Netherlands as a teenager so he could access the medical cannabis he needed to control his epilepsy. Six years earlier, Louis, then 12, had been diagnosed with a rare form of the neurological disease when medical cannabis was still illegal in the UK.
But in Rotterdam, where it was legal, doctors helped him discover that a medical cannabis oil called Bedrolite, in combination with the right mix of anti-epileptic treatment, could slow and eventually stop his seizures. This was something his neurologists in the UK had previously considered impossible.
By the time Louis won a place at City and Guilds of London Art School in 2022, the UK government had legalised medicinal cannabis, pressed by parents needing the drug to treat their epileptic children – most notably Charlotte Caldwell and Hannah Deacon.
Louis assumed his troubles were behind him. “It seems naive now, but I think both me and my mum thought Britain would welcome me back, saying, ‘Thank God you’re better’,” Louis told me. But Louis has never been able to get a prescription for medical cannabis through the NHS. Instead, like almost everyone who needs the drug in this country, his only access has come through the expensive private sector. And now the producer of Bedrolite, a Dutch company, Bedrocan, has declared bankruptcy.
This means there is a high chance that, in the near future, the drug that keeps Louis well will stop being available privately, in a huge blow to all patients who rely on it. If this was people with diabetes facing a shortage of insulin, or people with high blood pressure running out of beta blockers, politicians would be falling over themselves to be seen trying to secure the long-term supply. But because this is epilepsy and cannabis – a medicine that has been stigmatised by a 50-year “war on drugs” – successive governments have avoided the issue, allowing this current crisis to develop, despite patients warning for years that they can’t be just abandoned to the private market.
When the then home secretary, Sajid Javid, legalised medicinal cannabis in 2018, he stood up in parliament and promised patients who needed cannabis medication that their arduous fight was finally coming to an end. “Having been moved by heartbreaking cases involving sick children,” Javid said, “it was important to me that we took swift action to help those who can benefit from medicinal cannabis.”
But these benefits reached a fraction of those who needed help. Since the first few patients received their prescriptions on the NHS, the vast majority of others – including Louis – have been met with a wall of refusal from the healthcare system, with doctors’ requests for public funding to prescribe cannabis medication rarely granted in practice.
Until 2025, there were fewer than five prescriptions for unlicensed cannabis-based products such as Bedrolite given out across the entire NHS. In the absence of an accessible NHS route, the private market has become the only route to treatment for most patients, costing them anything up to £4,000 a month for their medicine.
The result of medicinal cannabis being handed over wholesale to the private sector is that cannabis has quietly become one of the new growth sectors in Britain, with many cannabis companies getting rich from the boom. Remote online prescriptions, 48-hour door-to-door delivery and targeted advertisements on social media have all helped grow the private customer base.
But while private suppliers offer customer-friendly products such as cannabis vape pens and gummies on prescription, Bedrolite is a cannabis oil that was modified specially for children with drug-resistant epilepsy, and can’t be replaced with general cannabis. There is a much larger market for presenting cannabis as the new must-have wellness treatment for the on-the-go millennial suffering from anxiety, sleep issues or chronic pain medicine than there is for trying to treat acute but rare ailments such as complex epilepsy or multiple sclerosis.
And there is little commercial incentive for private companies to spend huge amounts of money on the expensive, large-scale, clinical, randomised control trials that are needed to get more cannabis medication licensed and mainstreamed on the NHS. Successive governments washed their hands of this issue once legalisation eased the immediate pressure from families with sick loved ones who were campaigning against an outright ban.
This dynamic leaves us in the paradoxical position whereby medical cannabis has become one of Britain’s new growth industries at exactly the same time that the most vulnerable patients, who desperately need the medication, cannot access it.
“It’s been one shock after another since we came home,” said Louis’s mother, Emma. “If his neurologists’ funding request to NHS England had been approved last year, his Bedrolite supply would be guaranteed. There is enough stock in the Netherlands to last into 2028. But it’s not available to those without NHS prescriptions.”
Initially, it was feared that the drug would stop being on sale in the UK before Christmas, but last week one UK drug manufacturer, Target Healthcare, told families it will secure a six-month stockpile of Bedrolite, offering temporary relief. However, what happens in six months’ time is anyone’s guess.
The possible consequences of epileptic patients such as Louis suffering a forced withdrawal from the medication they use to control their seizures could be severe. The UK government needs to intervene and negotiate with Bedrolite’s manufacturer to secure the supply for all patients who need it in Britain.
But beyond this emergency, the UK government needs to stop ignoring the medical cannabis industry and put in place the necessary investment and regulatory frameworks for it to become an accepted prescription on the NHS.
Even before the recent bankruptcy of Bedrocan, families and campaigners have been insisting that patients shouldn’t be forced to live at the mercy of the volatile private market, all because politicians are too scared of the negative headlines that might come from mainstreaming a still-stigmatised drug such as cannabis on the NHS.
“Health shouldn’t be an issue of whether you are wealthy enough to afford it or even be able to access it,” Louis said to me as we parted. We will see over the next couple of months if the politicians in charge of this country agree.
- Dr Kojo Koram is professor of law and political economy at Loughborough University and the author of The Next Fix: The Winners and Losers in the Future of Drugs

====================================================================================================

Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:33:13 UTC
21:33:13 KST

Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Los Angeles Health Sciences
- Summary:
- A UCLA study found that long-term exposure to a common pesticide was linked to more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease. Scientists also uncovered how the chemical damages brain cells and identified a promising way to protect them.
- Share:
A pesticide used for decades in agriculture may be linked to a much greater risk of Parkinson's disease, and scientists have uncovered a possible explanation for how it damages the brain.
Researchers at UCLA Health found that people with long-term residential exposure to chlorpyrifos, a widely used pesticide, had more than 2.5 times the risk of developing Parkinson's disease compared with those who were not exposed. Laboratory experiments also revealed how the chemical can interfere with the brain's ability to remove damaged proteins, leading to the loss of nerve cells essential for controlling movement.
The study, published in Molecular Neurodegeneration, goes beyond identifying a connection between pesticide exposure and Parkinson's. By examining what happens inside affected brain cells, the researchers uncovered a biological mechanism that could eventually provide new ways to protect the brain from damage.
A Common Pesticide With a Troubling Link to Parkinson's
Parkinson's disease affects nearly one million Americans. The progressive neurological condition gradually damages brain cells involved in movement, often causing tremors, muscle stiffness, slowed movement, and difficulties with coordination.
One of the defining features of Parkinson's is the loss of neurons that produce dopamine. This chemical messenger allows nerve cells to communicate and helps the brain coordinate smooth, controlled movements. As dopamine levels decline, the brain becomes less capable of regulating those movements.
Although inherited genetic factors can influence who develops Parkinson's, researchers have increasingly focused on environmental exposures that may also contribute to the disease. Pesticides are of particular interest because some chemicals used to kill insects or other agricultural pests can also interfere with biological processes in the nervous system.
Chlorpyrifos has been used extensively in agriculture for decades. Its residential use was banned in the United States in 2001, and agricultural applications faced additional restrictions in 2021. However, the pesticide remains in use on many crops in the United States and continues to be widely applied in other countries.
Because exposure may have occurred years before symptoms appeared, understanding the potential long-term effects of chlorpyrifos is particularly important. Identifying specific chemicals associated with Parkinson's could help researchers develop prevention strategies and determine whether previously exposed individuals might benefit from additional neurological monitoring.
Researchers Find More Than Double the Parkinson's Risk
To investigate the connection, UCLA scientists examined information from 829 people diagnosed with Parkinson's disease and 824 people without the condition. All participants were enrolled in the university's long-running Parkinson's Environment and Genes study, which investigates how environmental exposures and inherited factors influence Parkinson's risk.
The researchers combined California's detailed pesticide application records with participants' residential and workplace address histories. This allowed them to estimate how much chlorpyrifos individuals may have encountered over time based on where they lived and worked.
The results revealed a striking association. People with prolonged residential exposure to chlorpyrifos had more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease compared with those who had no such exposure.
Although this population analysis could not establish that the pesticide directly caused Parkinson's, the researchers took an additional step to investigate whether chlorpyrifos could produce the kinds of brain damage seen in people with the disease.
How the Pesticide Damages Brain Cells
The team exposed mice to chlorpyrifos in aerosol form for 11 weeks. The inhalation approach was designed to resemble a common way people may encounter pesticides in the environment.
The exposed mice developed movement difficulties and lost neurons responsible for producing dopamine. This was particularly significant because the degeneration of these same nerve cells is a central feature of Parkinson's disease.
The researchers also detected inflammation in the animals' brains, along with abnormal accumulations of a protein called alpha-synuclein.
Under normal conditions, alpha-synuclein is found in nerve cells and plays a role in their functioning. However, the protein can accumulate in abnormal clumps that are closely associated with Parkinson's disease. These deposits are a major focus of research into why certain brain cells gradually deteriorate.
Together, the findings showed that chlorpyrifos exposure could reproduce several important characteristics of Parkinson's in laboratory animals, strengthening the biological evidence behind the human population findings.
Scientists Uncover a Breakdown in the Brain's Cleanup System
The researchers then turned to zebrafish to investigate exactly how chlorpyrifos harms neurons. These small fish are frequently used in neuroscience research because they allow scientists to study biological processes involved in nerve cell development and survival.
Their experiments pointed to a disruption in autophagy, a natural cellular maintenance process that helps remove damaged proteins and other unwanted material.
Autophagy functions much like an internal recycling system. Cells use it to break down worn-out or defective components so that potentially harmful material does not accumulate. This process is especially important for neurons, many of which must remain functional throughout a person's lifetime.
When chlorpyrifos interfered with this cleanup system, damaged material accumulated inside neurons, contributing to their deterioration.
The researchers also made an encouraging discovery. When they restored the cellular cleanup process or removed synuclein protein in their experiments, the neurons were protected from damage.
This finding suggests that the pesticide's harmful effects may depend partly on a biological pathway that researchers could potentially target with future treatments.
A Potential New Strategy for Protecting Against Parkinson's
The discovery raises the possibility of developing therapies that strengthen the brain's cellular cleanup mechanisms and help protect vulnerable neurons. Such treatments might eventually prove useful for people exposed to chlorpyrifos or other pesticides that disrupt similar processes.
However, the protective effects have so far been demonstrated in laboratory models. Additional research will be needed to determine whether enhancing autophagy can prevent or reduce pesticide-related brain damage in humans.
Scientists also want to investigate whether other commonly used pesticides interfere with the same cellular mechanisms. Although chlorpyrifos use has declined in the United States, many people were exposed before restrictions were introduced, and related agricultural chemicals remain widely used.
The findings could also help identify people with a history of substantial pesticide exposure who may benefit from closer neurological monitoring. Earlier recognition of possible changes in brain function could become increasingly important as researchers work toward treatments that slow or prevent Parkinson's progression.
Dr. Jeff Bronstein, professor of Neurology at UCLA Health and the study's senior author, emphasized the importance of identifying a particular chemical rather than treating all pesticides as a single category.
"This study establishes chlorpyrifos as a specific environmental risk factor for Parkinson's disease, not just pesticides as a general class," said Dr. Jeff Bronstein.
"By showing the biological mechanism in animal models, we've demonstrated that this association is likely causal. The discovery that autophagy dysfunction drives the neurotoxicity also points us toward potential therapeutic strategies to protect vulnerable brain cells."

Deliveryman chases his poetic dream
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:32:32 CST
21:32:32 KST

Wang Jibing and his wife arrange goods at their family-run small store in Kunshan City, east China's Jiangsu Province, Oct. 8, 2026. Born in 1969 in east China's Jiangsu Province, Wang Jibing dropped out of school during junior high. To make a living, he worked as a construction worker, a sand dredger, a street vendor and a scrap collector. Yet, he never lost his appetite for reading, often lingering at secondhand book stalls and sifting through discarded newspapers. Life was hard, yet his love for literature never faded. "Literature is a candy in my life." He said. "I've never found that writing is mentally challenging. Passion is all that drives me."
In 2019, hearing that delivering food could pay well, Wang decided to give it a shot. At 50, he became the oldest courier at his station. On his way to deliver takeout food, while waiting for red lights and for the food to be served, he composed verses. When inspiration struck, he used his mobile phone to jot down moments of his experience on streets and the sentiment.
This year, Wang's poetry collection "Low Flight" won him the Lu Xun Literature Prize, making him the first takeout rider-turned-laureate. In plainspoken language, Wang captured the rhythms, challenges and moments of warmth that mark the lives of delivery riders: slippery roads during storms, brief exchanges between couriers and customers, and solitary journeys beneath streetlights late at night.
Since receiving the honor, he has received many work invitations. Even so, whenever he has free time, he still puts on his delivery uniform and rides through the streets of Kunshan.
"Delivering food keeps me grounded. It is where my power lies. To find fresh emotion and creative inspiration, I must stay immersed with real life." He said. (Xinhua/Ji Chunpeng)

Australia expands subsidized access to medicines for cystic fibrosis, cancer, thyroid disease
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:32:26 CST
21:32:26 KST

CANBERRA, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- The Australian government has expanded access to subsidized medicines for patients with cystic fibrosis, blood cancer and thyroid eye disease under the country's Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS), Health Minister Mark Butler said on Sunday.
Under the changes taking effect on Nov. 1, children aged six to 11 with cystic fibrosis who weigh less than 30 kg will be eligible for a granule form of Trikafta, a medicine targeting the underlying cause of the genetic condition.
The new formulation is designed to help children who have difficulty swallowing tablets. About 3,300 Australians are expected to benefit from the expanded listing each year, according to a government statement.
Without PBS subsidies, the treatment could cost patients more than 20,300 Australian dollars (about 14,200 U.S. dollars) per prescription.
The government has also added Tepezza to the PBS as a treatment for active, moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease, with around 310 Australians expected to benefit annually.
Meanwhile, subsidized access to Adcetris has been expanded to provide a new first-line treatment option for patients with advanced CD30-positive classical Hodgkin lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, benefiting an estimated 370 Australians each year.
The PBS listing for Repatha, a medicine used to treat high cholesterol, has also been amended to allow eligible patients to obtain larger quantities under the government's 60-day prescription initiative.
Under the PBS, eligible patients will pay a maximum of 25 Australian dollars per prescription, or 7.70 Australian dollars for concession card holders.
The government said it has approved additional funding for 511 new and amended PBS listings since July 2022. ■

Australia introduces upfront fees for protection visa reviews
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:32:26 CST
21:32:26 KST

CANBERRA, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- People seeking reviews of most protection visa decisions in Australia are now required to pay an upfront application fee of 1,863.50 Australian dollars (about 1,300 U.S. dollars), the country's Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) announced on Sunday.
The new requirement, which took effect on Nov. 1 following amendments to Australia's Migration Regulations 1994, applies to applications for reviews of decisions to refuse or cancel protection visas, as well as certain decisions to withdraw protection findings.
Under the new rules, applicants must pay the fee when lodging a review application, rather than after the review process.
The tribunal said non-citizens held in immigration detention and applicants whose cases can be combined with another application for which a fee has already been paid are exempt from the requirement.
Applicants who successfully challenge a protection decision, or whose applications are found to be invalid, will receive a full refund.
However, those who withdraw their applications after Nov. 1 will be eligible for refunds only in very limited circumstances.
The tribunal said people who started online applications before Nov. 1 but failed to submit them before the new rules took effect must restart the application process and pay the upfront fee.
Applications lodged before Nov. 1 will generally remain subject to the previous payment arrangements, under which unsuccessful applicants are required to pay a fee after their reviews are completed. ■

China

2026-11-01

Gold medalist Shang Chunsong (C) of China, silver medalist Nagai Nene (L) of Japan and bronze medalist Isa Smits of the Netherlands pose on the podium during the awarding ceremony of the women's freestyle competition at the Parkour World Cup Beijing 2026 at Shougang Park in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Chenlin)
BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- China's Shang Chunsong won the women's freestyle gold medal at the 2026 Beijing Parkour World Cup on Sunday, securing the overall World Cup title in the season's final event.
The 30-year-old former artistic gymnast, who claimed bronze at the 2016 Rio Olympics, added to a successful season that included freestyle gold medals at the World Games in Chengdu, the World Championships in Kitakyushu and the World Cup in Montpellier.
Shang entered the Beijing event ranked second in the overall World Cup standings, level on points with Japan's Nene Nagai and the Netherlands' Noa Man, who had won the women's speed title.
The overall World Cup title is awarded to the athlete with the highest points total after the season's events, with rankings determined by each competitor's two best results.
Man failed to qualify for the freestyle final after competing in three speed runs on Saturday, while Shang topped the women's freestyle qualification standings by more than six points.
In Sunday's final, Shang impressed the home crowd with a series of difficult tricks across bars and walls, earning 26.8 points to claim both the event gold and the overall title.
Her teammates rushed onto the course to celebrate, lifting her into the air after her victory was confirmed.
"I'm very proud to win this gold at home. It has a special meaning for me and my team," Shang said. "I could have done better on my landing, but I'll work on that later. Right now, I just want to celebrate with my friends."
Nagai finished second with 22.3 points, while the Netherlands' Isa Smits edged China's Zhou Jie by 0.1 points to take bronze.
In the men's speed competition, Montpellier World Cup winner Siebe Van de Spijker claimed gold in 22.46 seconds, also securing the overall World Cup speed title.
Ukraine's Bohdan Kolmakov took silver, while Italy's Luca Demarchi finished third.
The Beijing competition, held from October 30 to November 1, was the third and final stop of the 2026 Parkour World Cup series. ■

DAR ES SALAAM, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Tanzania is sending 36 enterprises and government institutions to the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), scheduled for Nov. 5 to 10 in Shanghai, as the country seeks to boost exports and expand access to the Chinese market.
The delegation was introduced at a farewell ceremony organized by the Chinese Embassy in Tanzania in Dar es Salaam on Saturday, where some participating exhibitors displayed their products, including coffee, tea and honey.
Deputy Minister for Industry and Trade Dennis Londo said the expo offered Tanzanian businesses an important opportunity to showcase their products, establish partnerships and attract investors from China and other international markets.
He urged exhibitors to actively engage with potential buyers, understand Chinese market requirements and explore opportunities to increase exports of agricultural and value-added products.
Director of Trade Promotion at the Tanzania Trade Development Authority (TanTrade) Jonathan Nkwabi said that 36 enterprises from the public and private sectors had been mobilized for the country's participation, demonstrating a coordinated effort to promote Tanzanian products internationally.
Chinese Ambassador to Tanzania Chen Mingjian said China's zero-tariff policy for African countries maintaining diplomatic relations with China was creating new opportunities for Tanzanian exporters.
She said China's imports from Tanzania reached 290 million U.S. dollars in the first half of 2026, up 12 percent year on year, adding that the first consignment of Tanzanian honey had entered the Chinese market through a dedicated green channel for African agricultural products.
Chen said 15 categories of Tanzanian agricultural products had been granted access to the Chinese market, while 469 Tanzanian enterprises had registered to export agricultural and food products to China.
She encouraged Tanzanian businesses attending the expo to use the platform to establish commercial partnerships and bring more high-quality local products to Chinese consumers.
Cathy Wang, managing director of the East Africa Commercial and Logistics Center, said Tanzania's participation grew from six enterprises in 2021 to 36 enterprises and institutions this year, reflecting growing interest among local businesses in the Chinese market.
She said her organization was working with TanTrade to help exhibitors meet Chinese import standards and navigate export procedures, customs clearance and logistics. ■

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelensky, have agreed to work toward reviving the Black Sea grain initiative during talks in Istanbul, with both leaders stressing the importance of ensuring maritime security.
Speaking at a joint news conference after their meeting on Oct. 31, Zelensky confirmed the agreement and said ensuring security in the Black Sea would be critical to reviving the initiative.
For his part, Erdoğan said it is “clear that attacks on civilian ships and steps that would escalate tensions in the Black Sea will benefit no one,” calling on all parties to act responsibly.
He said Türkiye would continue talks with the parties concerned to ensure safe navigation in the Black Sea and expressed hope that the agreement would also give fresh impetus to efforts to achieve lasting peace in Ukraine.
The president added that Ankara aimed to advance the process by discussing the issue with Russia as well.
Erdoğan condemned the recent increase in attacks on civilian vessels in the Black Sea, saying such incidents were unacceptable regardless of who was responsible or what justification was offered.
“We cannot accept this under any circumstances, regardless of who carries them out or what the justification may be,” he said.
The meeting took place at the Dolmabahçe Office in Istanbul. Turkish Defense Minister Yaşar Güler, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, Türkiye’s intelligence chief İbrahim Kalın and former Ukrainian Defense Minister Rustem Umerov also attended.
Commercial shipping in the Black Sea has faced growing risks in recent months, with drones and missiles increasingly targeting vessels. Some ships owned by Turkish companies or carrying Turkish crew members have also been affected.
At least 12 people were killed in attacks on vessels off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria in early October, including Turkish nationals, according to the information provided.
The previous grain initiative was brokered by Türkiye and the United Nations in July 2022, several months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The agreement established a mechanism for the safe export of Ukrainian grain and other agricultural products through designated Black Sea corridors, helping ease disruptions to global food supplies and curb pressure on food prices.
Russia withdrew from the agreement in July 2023, arguing that its demands concerning the export of Russian food and fertilizer had not been met. Ukraine subsequently pursued alternative export routes, including a maritime corridor along the western Black Sea coast.
Meanwhile, Erdoğan departed Türkiye on Nov. 1 for a visit to South Korea at the invitation of his counterpart Lee Jae Myung.
Official talks scheduled for Nov. 3 would cover all aspects of the strategic partnership between the two countries, Türkiye’s Communications Director Burhanettin Duran said in a statement.
The leaders are also expected to exchange views on current regional and global issues and sign several agreements aimed at strengthening the legal framework for bilateral relations, Duran said. Erdoğan’s visit is scheduled to conclude on Nov. 4.

Ukrainian Defense Forces have struck the “Kamensky” missile-production chemical enterprise in Russia’s Rostov region alongside high-value Russian air defense assets, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Nov. 1.
He added that the attack destroyed a Pantsir-S2 surface-to-air missile, an anti-aircraft artillery complex, and an S-400 Triumf command-and-staff vehicle with an aggregate value of approximately $70 million.

“We are justly defending ourselves against Russian aggression and doing everything to reduce Russia’s capabilities to continue it,” the president emphasized.
Strategic missile propellant manufacturing at Kamensky
The targeting of the Kamensky plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, located roughly 20 kilometers east of the Ukrainian border in Rostov region, constitutes a direct blow to the Russian Federation’s production of solid rocket motors and guided munitions.
The enterprise operates as a primary supplier for the Russian defense industry, specializing in the chemical synthesis of solid rocket propellants, propulsive charges, and specialized nitrocellulose compounds.
The output of the Kamensky facility supplies propellant motors for multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), including 220mm Uragan, 300mm Smerch, and modernized 300mm Tornado-S systems, as well as specialized rocket propellants integrated into tactical guided missiles and aircraft-delivered strike weapons.
The presidential confirmation follows earlier operational assessments released by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, which reported that overnight into Saturday, Oct. 31, a coordinated strike involving strike drones and Ukrainian Navy Neptune coastal cruise missiles in a land-attack role ignited a warehouse storing finished solid rocket propellant and inflicted structural damage on four production workshops across the facility.
Broadened campaign against defense supply chains
Concurrent with the Rostov operation, Ukrainian precision units executed synchronized strikes against four Russian military logistics depots across occupied Ukrainian territories, hitting supply bases near Khartsyzk and Dokuchaievsk in Donetsk region, Novovasylivka in Zaporizhzhia region, and Novoaidar in Luhansk region.
The operation also coincides with resumed long-range interdictions against Russian downstream oil refining and chemical processing centers.
Overnight into Sunday, Nov. 1, Ukrainian strike drones penetrated Nizhny Novgorod region, striking the 17-million-ton Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez refinery and the adjacent Novogorkovskaya combined heat and power plant in Kstovo, triggering large-scale blazes across Russia’s second-largest automotive gasoline production center.

Biological weapons: The weaponization of disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:25:00 UTC
21:25:00 KST

Biological weapons: The weaponization of disease
November 1, 2026
Artificial intelligence could potentially be misused to develop biological weapons. This may sound like science fiction, but scientists, security services, and international organizations are all looking at how to deal with this scenario.
Pathogens can be analyzed and altered with ever greater precision thanks to ongoing developments in biotechnology. Meanwhile, AI is able to evaluate vast quantities of data at astonishing speeds. As a result, experts are warning that, in the long term, modern technologies could also be misused to develop biological weapons.
Security services are concerned. In October 2026, Ken McCallum, head of the British domestic intelligence service MI5, warned that artificial intelligence could increase the risk from existing, or new, biological weapons – including from non-state actors.
Fine line between valid research and misuse
A report by the American AI company Anthropic in September 2026 highlights the topicality of the debate. Anthropic said it had identified and blocked numerous attempts to use its AI assistant Claude in connection with possible biological weapon research. The report said these attempts included grant applications for so-called "gain-of-function" research, as well as projects to research avian influenza variants that were potentially the most transmissible to mammals.
At the same time, Anthropic stressed that, although it could have a military application, such research could also relate to medical prevention. The difficulty in distinguishing between legitimate science and its possible misuse is one of the biggest problems in terms of the control of modern biotechnologies.
What are biological weapons?
Concerns about biological weapons are by no means new. Many pathogens — bacteria, viruses, fungi, and certain biological toxins — have the potential for weaponization. Familiar diseases include plague, smallpox, and botulinum toxin, but anthrax is one of the most notorious biological agents. Its resistant spores can survive a long time in the environment, and it has also been the focus of research by state biological weapons programs.
The World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs define a biological weapon as the targeted release of such biological substances for the purpose of injuring people, animals, or plants.
A biological weapon usually has two components: The biological substance itself, and a system for disseminating it. Experts refer to these as the "agent," such as a virus or bacterium, and the "delivery mechanism." Examples of the latter include missiles, spraying systems, and contaminated food.
Biological weapons belong to the so-called ABC weapons, alongside atomic (nuclear) and chemical weapons. They are often also counted as weapons of mass destruction.
How do they differ from chemical weapons?
Biological and chemical weapons differ in their mode of operation. Chemical weapons injure people through the toxic effects of chemical substances such as sarin or mustard gas. They will often take effect within minutes, or even seconds. Examples of the use of chemical weapons are the gas attacks in World War I, which involved chlorine gas, and later mustard gas; and the deployment of the nerve gas sarin in the Syrian civil war and by Saddam Hussein in Iraq.
Biological weapons, on the other hand, cause infectious disease. The effects become apparent only hours, days, or even weeks after they have been deployed. Some pathogens are also capable of spreading from person to person, meaning that the outcome is difficult to predict.
To summarize: Chemical weapons kill or injure through immediate toxicity, whereas biological weapons cause diseases. The possibility of human-to-human transmission makes the effect of a biological weapon particularly hard to calculate.
Are biological weapons subject to a worldwide ban?
Biological weapons are prohibited under international law. The first Biological Weapons Convention (BWC) came into force in 1975. This prohibits the development, stockpiling, acquisition, retention, production, and transfer of biological and toxin-based weapons.
The Convention, which has been ratified by 189 countries, can be seen as a development of the Geneva Protocol of 1925, which banned the use of biological weapons as a method of warfare. Only a few countries have not signed the agreement, or have signed but not ratified it, including Israel, Egypt, and Syria. All those who have acceded to the Convention have also committed themselves to destroying all stocks, production sites, and means of conveyance.
Chemical weapons are also internationally banned, but their control is seen as much more highly developed. The Chemical Weapons Convention is implemented by the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), which can carry out inspections and oversee the destruction of chemical weapons stocks.
There is still no comparable system for controlling biological weapons. States fear that inspection could expose sensitive research data pertaining to medicine, biotechnology, or the pharmaceutical industry. This is why the control of biological weapons relies to a great extent on transparency, voluntary reporting, and good faith.
One of the best-known examples of why the ban on biological weapons is insufficient on its own to prevent their use occurred in the United States in 2001. A few weeks after the attacks of September 11, several people received letters containing anthrax spores. 22 were infected, and five died.
Why are biological weapons so hard to expose and control?
Finding biological weapons programs is much harder than controlling the production of nuclear or chemical weapons. Many technologies that could be used to develop biological weapons also have civilian applications. The same laboratory equipment used to develop vaccines and medicines could, in theory, also be used for military research.
Experts refer to this as the problem of dual use. Research can be done for peaceful medical purposes and, at the same time, have a military application.
Furthermore, a biological attack can initially look like a natural outbreak of disease. It is often only possible after extensive investigation to establish whether a pathogen was deliberately released or occurred naturally.
Perhaps that is also why biological weapons have been deployed at various times throughout history. Historical reports range from the poisoning of wells to catapulting the corpses of plague victims over the walls of a besieged town. The effectiveness of these methods is, however, disputed.

India trying to bring Russia, Ukraine &amp; Europe to the table on 3 fronts: Jaishankar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:24:51 UTC
21:24:51 KST

India's External affairs minister S Jaishankar has discussed the protection of civilian shipping with Russia, Ukraine, and European nations
External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Sunday said India has held discussions with Russia, Ukraine and European countries on protecting civilian shipping, restoring grain exports through the Black Sea and preventing attacks on energy infrastructure amid the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war.According to news agency ANI, Speaking on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Jaishankar said India was engaging with the parties on three key aspects of the conflict, including the safety of civilian vessels and seafarers, the restoration of grain shipments from Russia and Ukraine, and preventing attacks on energy infrastructure. He said India was trying to bring the concerned parties together to address these issues."One, not to attack civilian shipping and seafarers," he said, outlining the first of the three areas discussed with Russia, Ukraine and Europe.
On the second issue, Jaishankar stressed the need to restore grain shipments from both Russia and Ukraine, warning that exports through the Black Sea had declined sharply amid the conflict."The second, to find a way by which the grain exports from both Russia and Ukraine, these are two major exporters of grain for the global markets, can be restored, because that flow has cut down very sharply in the Black Sea," he said.
Jaishankar further highlighted the complexities involved in ensuring the safety of energy infrastructure, saying different parties had different interpretations of what should be covered under such an understanding."And the third is with regard to energy. Non-attack on energy is probably the most complicated piece because it means different things to the different players. There is energy infrastructure itself. To some, it would mean a refinery; to some, it would mean grids. There would be issues relating to ships carrying fuel," he said.He added that India is attempting to bring the concerned parties together to find common ground on these issues, particularly on the protection of energy infrastructure and fuel shipments.
The concerns raised by Jaishankar extend beyond the immediate conflict, given the Black Sea's importance to global trade. Any disruption to commercial shipping can affect the movement of essential commodities, raise freight and insurance costs and put pressure on international supply chains.Similarly, attacks on refineries, electricity grids and fuel-carrying vessels can disrupt energy supplies and push up global prices. Together, the safety of maritime routes, grain exports and energy infrastructure remains critical to maintaining stability in global food and energy markets.

Iran among 30 countries with rare blood preservation technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:24:26 UTC
21:24:26 KST

Iran among 30 countries with rare blood preservation technology
TEHRAN - Iran is among only 30 countries worldwide with the technology to preserve rare blood types for 10 to 30 years through glycerol-based cryopreservation, and is the only country in the region with this capability, according to the head of the Iran Blood Transfusion Organization (IBTO).
Rare blood types refer to blood groups that have a very low prevalence in society and are classified into three categories: rare, very rare, and extremely rare. A rare blood type is defined as one occurring in only 1 out of every 1,000 or one million people, Ahmad Qarah-Baghian, IBTO’s chief executive, told Mehr News Agency.
Once a rare blood type is identified, the IBTO collects required samples and freezes them for long-term storage. According to published scientific articles, rare blood type storage spans from 10 to 30 years. Based on some documentation, blood frozen for 20 years still remains usable.
People with rare blood types are identified in different ways, and they are invited to donate blood. Like others, these individuals can donate blood four times a year if they meet the requirements, he added.
According to Mehdi Karbadizadeh, an official with the IBTO, a total of 350 rare blood units are frozen and stored in the rare blood bank. Some 1,500 individuals with rare blood types are identified in the country. However, not all of them are eligible to donate blood.
‘Iran the only Islamic country in Eastern Mediterranean with rare blood program’
Iran is the only Islamic nation in the Eastern Mediterranean region that has a rare blood program, an official with the Iranian Blood Transfusion Organization (IBTO) has said.
In the Iranian year 1389 (2010-2011), the country joined the International Rare Blood Association, which currently has 30 member states, IRNA quoted Mehdi Karbasizadeh as saying.
The official went on to say that Iran, China, and Japan are the only member states of the association in Asia that have rare blood management programs.
One out of 5,000 to 10,000 individuals in Iran has a rare blood type. The frequency of rare blood types in each country depends on its population and the blood type. Bombay blood type is among the rarest blood groups known in the country, the official added.
There are currently fewer than 10 of the rarest blood types and 30 rare blood types in the country. About 150 out of 376 solidified units of blood stored at a rare blood bank are the rarest, Karbasizadeh said.
Presently, 262 individuals with a really rare blood type are identified in the country, but not all of them can donate blood.
The official urged those with (really) rare blood types to donate blood at least once a year, saying that blood units solidified at minus 65 to 85 degrees centigrade can be stored for 10 years.
In 2025, Jaffar Hussain, the former World Health Organization (WHO) Representative to Iran, highlighted Iran’s capacity to serve as a model for other nations in the realm of blood transfusion and rare blood management.
Addressing National Rare Blood Day on January 22, the official praised the country’s steadfast commitment to equitable health care access, ensuring that no one is left behind, regardless of their blood type.
National Rare Blood Day is a day dedicated to celebrating the lives saved, challenges overcome, and unwavering commitment to ensuring every individual, regardless of their blood type, has a fighting chance at life.
The official commended the country’s unwavering dedication to tackling the unique challenges surrounding rare blood, emphasizing the critical importance of collaboration, innovation, and unwavering determination in this global endeavour, the WHO website announced in a press release on January 27.
Hussain painted a vivid picture of the struggles faced by those with rare blood types, individuals who often find themselves in desperate need, their lives hanging in the balance as they search for that elusive, compatible match.
He paid tribute to these unsung heroes, recognizing their generosity and unwavering commitment to the well-being of others. “Blood donors,” he declared, “represent the epitome of human solidarity, offering a lifeline to those in need without expecting anything in return.”
WHO, Hussain emphasized, believes that universal health coverage must encompass access to safe blood and blood products. He lauded IBTO’s leadership in blood safety and transfusion services, highlighting their remarkable achievement of a 100 percent voluntary, non-remunerated blood donation system, a testament to the principles of universal health coverage in action.
In closing, the official extended his deepest gratitude to the IBTO for their unwavering dedication to advancing blood transfusion services and ensuring equitable access to rare blood. He thanked the blood donors, whose selflessness serves as an inspiration to all.
The event concluded with a renewed commitment to innovation, partnership and universal health coverage, leaving attendees with a sense of determination to continue the fight for rare blood access, ensuring that every drop counts, every donation matters and every life is valued.
In July 1979, the IBTO was established to organize blood transfusion activities, promote blood donation, and supply safe blood and its products free of charge for patients suffering from diseases like hemophilia, thalassemia, and leukemia.
Iran is the only Islamic country that is a member of the International Society of Blood Transfusion’s rare blood donor working party (ISBT WP).
Thanks to a rich culture of selflessness, the country maintains a six-month blood reserve ensuring preparedness for crises.
Blood reserves and their products are considered strategic and vital resources for the country, and voluntary donations help to meet the needs of the country, particularly during crisis.

Russia is fighting for a border village near Kharkiv that leads it nowhere. What it is after is fewer Ukrainian troops in Donbas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:22:44 UTC
21:22:44 KST

Russian forces have widened their foothold at Hraniv on the border north of Kharkiv, a Ukrainian military spokesman said. Viktor Trehubov of the Joint Forces Grouping said they spread sideways rather than deeper toward the nearby town of Kozacha Lopan.
Russia's main offensive grinds on in Donetsk Oblast, but it keeps pressing along the northern border too. Brigadier General Denys Prokopenko warned in September that Russia wants buffer zones in Sumy and Chernihiv oblasts, a push meant to keep Ukrainian reserves there instead of in the east. Such pushes gain little: in Sumy Oblast, the Russian advance reached about 3–4 km deep, more than 35 km short of the city.
The wedge grew at its flanks
Trehubov described the Hraniv gain as a separate wedge toward Kozacha Lopan, right by the border. "But they managed to widen it," he said on Suspilne Studio on 31 October. He said Russian troops did not deepen the wedge or move further into Kozacha Lopan, and called the widening "a certain problem."
The Ukrainian volunteer monitoring project DeepState marked a Russian advance near Hraniv on 30 October. On its map, the Russian-held area around the village grew from about 2 to 11 square kilometers, according to EP's calculation based on DeepState's data. The gray zone around it, where control is unclear, more than doubled to some 19 square kilometers. The new ground runs southeast of Hraniv along the border, in line with Trehubov's account of a wider, not deeper, wedge.
The wedge dates back to late June, when a spokesman for Ukraine's 14th Army Corps, Colonel Vitalii Sarantsev, said Russian troops had crossed the border near Hraniv and were trying to storm Kozacha Lopan. He said Russia was trying to open new wedges along the Sumy and Kharkiv borders to tie down Ukrainian forces and widen a so-called controlled zone. On 1 July, the 425th Skelia Assault Regiment said it had pushed Russian troops out of Kozacha Lopan, 2 km from the border, and cleared Hraniv. Ukraine's General Staff reported 13 Russian attacks northeast of Kharkiv over the past day, none of them listed near Hraniv.
The northern pushes have been on Ukraine's radar for months. Buffer zones in Kharkiv, Sumy, and Chernihiv oblasts remain on Russia's list, Pavlo Palisa, deputy head of the Presidential Office, said in April, though he saw no Russian forces to carry them out. Military analyst Yevhen Dykyi described the aim as a zone of constant tension along the border, like the one in parts of Chernihiv and Sumy oblasts, which forces Ukraine to spread its forces more thinly.
Other movements along the front
In Donetsk Oblast, DeepState mapped a Russian advance near Mykolaivka, just west of Chasiv Yar, on 31 October, turning a patch of its gray zone there red. Just after midnight on 29 October, it marked Russian gains near Maiske, northwest of Chasiv Yar.
Ukrainian forces advanced northeast of Borova in Kharkiv Oblast, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported on 31 October, citing geolocated footage. DeepState has not mapped that change. Russian milbloggers claimed gains in and around Kupiansk, but ISW could not confirm them.
Russia tries to drag a village north of Kupiansk into no-man’s-land after its losses in Ukraine’s underground operation
Near Kupiansk, Trehubov said Ukrainian troops cleared a gas pipeline under the Oskil River that Russian infiltration groups had used to reach the city.
Losses force a Russian rotation near Huliaipole
Near Huliaipole, Ukrainian forces killed and wounded about 900 Russian troops last week, the 7th Corps of Ukraine's Air Assault Forces said. That is almost 150 more than the week before and the highest count in two months, the corps added. It said that, according to available information, Russia's 5th Combined Arms Army is replacing its 57th Motorized Rifle Brigade with the 60th while the 57th refills its ranks.
The corps also said Russia sends recruited mercenaries from Africa and Asia into assaults there. Ukrainian troops captured a citizen of Indonesia fighting in Russia's 39th Motorized Rifle Brigade, it added.
Since 21 October, DeepState's updates have added about 40 square kilometers to the Russian-held area on its map, by EP's count. Besides Hraniv and Chasiv Yar, it mapped Russian advances near Dobropillia, east of Sloviansk, near Kostiantynivka, and near Huliaipole and Orikhiv in Zaporizhzhia Oblast. Still, Ukraine has liberated more land than Russia captured since the start of fall, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in October.

By Max Hunder and Alessandra Prentice
Nov 1 (Reuters) - Russian strikes left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, while Russian authorities reported major damage to an industrial site following Ukrainian drone attacks on Nizhny Novgorod region.
Even as a six-day local ceasefire held on its final day around the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky, there was no letup in fighting elsewhere along the front line and both sides kept up long-range air attacks.
Zelenskiy said Russia had hit power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, cutting electricity to hundreds of thousands of households.
“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” he said on Telegram.
He said Ukraine, meanwhile, had hit the Kamensky plant in Russia’s Rostov region, which he said was involved in the manufacture of Russian missiles.
Moscow did not comment on the reported attack in Rostov. In Nizhny Novgorod region, however, Governor Gleb Nikitin said a large-scale overnight Ukrainian drone attack caused “significant damage” to an industrial facility.
He did not identify the site that was hit. The region is home to the NORSI oil refinery, one of Russia’s largest.
Overall, Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces had downed 235 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight. Ukraine’s air force said it had shot down 371 of 433 long-range drones launched by Russia since Saturday evening.
In its morning update, the air force said dozens of Russian drones were still in the air as of Sunday morning. Six separate drone alerts had been issued in Kyiv since midnight.
FUEL SUPPLIES
Nizhny Novgorod’s regional government also did not identify the facility that was struck, but it said it was taking steps to ensure gas stations were supplied with fuel, urging motorists to “buy fuel only as needed and avoid panic buying,” Interfax reported.
The warning suggests the damaged facility was linked to the region’s oil-refining or fuel-supply infrastructure. Kyiv did not immediately claim responsibility for the Nizhny Novgorod attack.
On Friday, Russia said Ukraine had resumed strikes on its oil refineries and accused Kyiv of ignoring a request from US President Donald Trump to stop such attacks, which Trump has blamed for raising the cost of diesel before US midterm elections next week.
Ukraine says it supports a full ceasefire on energy targets, including its own battered power grid, but that Moscow is unwilling to agree to this.
In an interview with state TV channel Vesti on Sunday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees the energy sector, did not mention the Nizhny Novgorod strike, but said Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries were adding to global fuel market imbalances and affecting prices.

FRANKFURT, Nov 1 (Reuters) - German ministers threatened tough penalties for looters and rioters who damaged stores and injured more than 100 police officers in Frankfurt overnight, still praising public forces for preventing larger-scale violence.
Frankfurt late on Saturday became the hot spot for violent protests after tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets of dozens of German cities during the day to demand better education and lower living costs in protests led by the campaign group “Gen Z regelt” — “Gen Z takes charge”.
In the financial hub Frankfurt, hooded rioters damaged 17 shops and stores, of which five were looted, Roman Poseck, interior minister of the state of Hesse, told a press conference on Sunday.

Poseck said most of those arrested were German nationals, adding that many of those involved in the disturbances were of a migrant background, citing information from the police.
“Police currently estimate that they are dealing with between 1,000 and 1,500 violent troublemakers, predominantly from a migrant background,” he added.
Frankfurt police reported violent disturbances including windows being smashed and petrol bombs being thrown at the emergency services.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt was quoted as telling the Bild tabloid on Sunday, “The rioters and looters will be identified and held accountable.”
“This breach of the peace must be followed by tough penalties.”
He accused “violent left-wing groups and troublemakers from the migrant community” of hijacking the otherwise peaceful protests, without elaborating.
Dobrindt said the police strategy of maintaining a large presence while deploying officers across multiple locations had worked.
“Excesses of violence like those in Paris were prevented thanks to our highly committed police forces,” Dobrindt, a member of the conservative Christian Social Union, said.
In France, protests continued largely peacefully for a third weekend after extensive riots and looting on October 17 damaged shops, public buildings and businesses.

Among the provinces of the country, Khorasan Razavi experienced the highest number of earthquakes with 14, followed by Yazd with 9, Semnan with 9, and Khuzestan with 7 earthquakes.
During the same period, four earthquakes hit Tehran. No earthquakes were recorded in Alborz, Ilam, Zanjan, Sistan-Baluchestan, Qom, Qazvin, Kordestan, Markazi, and Hamedan provinces.
A total of 2,380 earthquakes with a magnitude of more than 2.5 on the Richter scale were recorded across the country over the past calendar year (March 2025–March 2026), according to the Seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran, Mehr news agency reported.
Out of recorded earthquakes, 910 had a magnitude greater than 3, 130 had a magnitude greater than 4, and 15 had a magnitude greater than 5 on the Richter scale.
The Iranian plateau is located in a very seismically active region of the world and is known not only for its major catastrophic earthquakes but also for the disasters relating to natural hazards, especially earthquakes.
About 2 percent of the earthquakes in the world occur in Iran, but more than 6 percent of the victims of the world’s earthquakes during the 20th century are reported from Iranian earthquakes.

Tel Aviv University Honors US Envoy Steve Witkoff and Hostage Advocate Einav Zangauker at Ceremony
Unknown

2026-11-01
12:15:22 UTC

Tel Aviv University Honors U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Hostage Advocate Einav Zangauker
Einav Zangauker, Jon and Mindy Gray, Prof. Michal Lipson, Prof. Joanna Aizenberg, Enrico Macias, Rachel Shapira and Nina Avidar Weiner receive honorary doctorates; Witkoff awarded the George S. Wise Medal
When Hamas abducted Matan Zangauker from Kibbutz Nir Oz and took him to Gaza on October 7, 2023, his mother Einav was a private citizen. She went on to become a grassroots leader and a prominent voice for the hostage families, mobilizing tens of thousands to action. Tel Aviv University has now awarded her an honorary doctorate for her extraordinary determination and her tireless campaign for the return of the hostages.
Zangauker was among the honorees at the university's annual Honorary Degrees Ceremony at the Smolarz Auditorium, where Tel Aviv University honored leading figures from Israel and around the world for exceptional contributions to society, science, culture, philanthropy and the State of Israel. After Matan's return in October 2025, Zangauker continued advocating on behalf of those who remained in captivity and their families.
The George S. Wise Medal
U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff received Tel Aviv University's George S. Wise Medal in recognition of his advocacy on behalf of the hostages held by Hamas following the October 7 attacks and his contribution to diplomatic efforts aimed at securing their return. The university also recognized his commitment to diplomacy, dialogue and conflict resolution, as well as his solidarity with the people of Israel and the families of the hostages. Witkoff was appointed U.S. Special Envoy to the Middle East and U.S. Special Envoy for Peace Missions in 2025.
Philanthropy
American philanthropists Jon and Mindy Gray, co-founders of the Gray Foundation, received honorary doctorates for their philanthropic leadership in cancer research, education, healthcare and social welfare, and for their commitment to Israel and the Jewish people following October 7. In 2025, the Grays endowed Tel Aviv University's Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences through the largest gift in the university's history.
Science
Two Israeli scientists at leading U.S. universities were honored for work that has reshaped their fields.
Israeli physicist and engineer Prof. Michal Lipson, Eugene Higgins Professor of Electrical Engineering and Professor of Applied Physics at Columbia University, was honored for her groundbreaking contributions to silicon photonics. Her work has transformed the fields of optics and communications technology and helped lay the foundations for faster and more efficient computing. Lipson is a member of both the U.S. National Academy of Sciences and the U.S. National Academy of Engineering, holds more than 45 patents and has authored over 300 scientific publications.
Israeli American materials scientist and engineer Prof. Joanna Aizenberg of Harvard University received an honorary doctorate for her pioneering achievements in science, engineering and innovation, particularly her groundbreaking work in biomimicry and advanced materials. Her research, inspired by nature's ingenuity, has transformed the understanding and design of advanced materials and led to technological innovations with wide-ranging applications. Also a member of both national academies, Aizenberg was recognized for her longstanding ties with the Israeli scientific community and her collaborations with Tel Aviv University.
Culture
Internationally renowned French singer-songwriter Enrico Macias received an honorary doctorate recognizing his career spanning more than six decades, his contribution to world culture and his role in building bridges between cultures and faiths through his distinctive fusion of Andalusian, North African and French musical traditions. The university also recognized his longstanding and outspoken support for Israel.
Israeli poet and lyricist Rachel Shapira received an honorary doctorate in recognition of a body of work spanning more than half a century. Hundreds of her songs have become part of the fabric of Israeli cultural life.
Education
Israeli American educator and philanthropist Nina Avidar Weiner, co-founder of the Israel Scholarship Education Foundation (ISEF), received an honorary doctorate for five decades of work advancing equal opportunity and social mobility in Israel through education. Through ISEF, which she established in 1977 together with Edmond and Lily Safra, Weiner helped expand access to higher education for thousands of talented young Israelis from underserved communities and nurture generations of academic and civic leaders.
