Drone technologies and countermeasures to develop in parallel in coming years – defense company CEO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:12:00 UTC
21:12:00 KST

Drone technologies and countermeasures to develop in parallel in coming years – defense company CEO
Taras Bublyk, CEO of Ukrainian defense-tech company UNWAVE, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Drones are becoming increasingly sophisticated. At the same time, electronic warfare systems will become smarter. Therefore, in the coming years, drone technologies and countermeasures will develop in parallel, constantly adapting to each other,” Bublyk said.
He sees technological progress in both the improvement of existing technologies and the potential use of emerging technologies to counter drones, including laser systems, electromagnetic pulses and other solutions. The main challenge will be the economic viability of such solutions, since even the most expensive equipment can be destroyed quickly in wartime. Therefore, effective and scalable means of both destruction and protection will remain a priority in the near future.
Bublyk also noted that the integration of artificial intelligence would make it possible to work more effectively with various communication protocols and counter increasingly autonomous drones. With the volume of battlefield information growing rapidly, AI will help compare data more quickly, filter out irrelevant information and build a more comprehensive picture of the situation.
The defense sector representative said that the biggest challenge in countering drones at present is the lack of a universal solution, making comprehensive approaches essential. Drones are adapting and improving rapidly and becoming more autonomous, meaning that countermeasures increasingly require an integrated approach.
“This involves combining electronic intelligence with radar, optical, thermal imaging, acoustic and other detection systems. It also requires rapid processing and fusion of data from these sources,” Bublyk said.
Equally important, he said, is choosing the right means of direct counteraction based on the type of threat: not only detecting and classifying a drone as early as possible, but also quickly determining the most effective and cost-efficient way to neutralize it.
Another challenge, according to Bublyk, is scale: the modern battlefield generates such a volume of sensor data that a human cannot physically analyze it in real time. This is why automation, artificial intelligence and data fusion are becoming increasingly important.
As Ukrinform reported, Commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces Robert “Madyar” Brovdi said that Ukrainian engineers had already developed the first countermeasures against jet-powered Shahed drones and carried out their first successful launches, shooting down the targets.

Number commercial trucks going into Gaza falls by over 50%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:11:19 UTC
21:11:19 KST

Breadcrumb
Number of commercial trucks into Gaza falls by over 50% in October amid Israeli restrictions
The number of commercial trucks entering the Gaza Strip fell by 53.5% in October compared to September, marking a sharp decline that reduced the flow of goods into local markets.
This coincided with a drop in food supplies and consumer goods, continued shortages, and rising prices following the closure of the crossing to commercial traffic for more than a week.
Statistics released by the Crossings and Borders Authority showed that 1,758 commercial trucks entered the Gaza Strip in October, compared with 3,781 in September—a decrease of 2,023 trucks. The total number of incoming trucks, including commercial shipments, aid and fuel, also fell from 5,265 to 3,836, a decline of 27.1%, or 1,429 trucks.
By contrast, the number of aid trucks increased from 1,244 in September to 1,815 in October, a rise of 45.9%. Fuel trucks also increased from 240 to 263, representing a 9.6% increase. However, these increases did not offset the sharp decline in commercial traffic, which is a key source of goods and product variety in local markets.
Decline in food supplies
By category of goods, the number of trucks carrying food supplies and groceries fell from 3,450 in September to 2,337 in October, a decrease of 1,113 trucks, or 32.3%.
The number of trucks carrying consumer goods and household items also declined from 1,273 to 799, a drop of 37.2%. Meanwhile, trucks carrying medical and healthcare equipment and supplies fell from 104 to 76, a decrease of 26.9%.
Trucks carrying shelter and relief supplies increased from 139 to 330.
Trucks carrying animal feed and seeds fell from 45 to 27, a decline of 40%. Those carrying corrugated zinc sheets decreased from five to four, while October's statistics recorded no trucks specifically designated for transporting water, compared with nine in September.
These figures reflect a widening gap in the flow of commercial goods into the Gaza Strip, despite the increase in aid trucks. The impact of this decline is not limited to the volume of incoming goods; it also affects the variety of products available and traders' ability to meet consumer needs.
Rising prices
These developments come as local markets continue to experience shortages of a number of essential and consumer goods, alongside rising prices and declining purchasing power among residents as a result of the war, damage to economic activity, and the loss of income sources.
Reduced commercial imports mean smaller quantities of goods are available to consumers and limit traders' ability to replenish depleted stocks. This adds to pressure on markets, particularly given the heavy reliance on imported goods and the decline in local production.
The effects of the closure of the Kerem Shalom crossing—the only crossing connecting Gaza to the outside world for commercial traffic—continue to weigh on the market. Shortages of supplies are continuing to affect the availability and prices of goods, as residents face increasingly difficult living conditions.
The comparison between September and October highlights the scale of the decline in commercial activity: commercial trucks fell by more than half, while the total number of incoming trucks decreased by more than a quarter. This underscores the challenges facing local markets and the need to resume a regular flow of commercial goods to address shortages and ease price pressures and the growing cost-of-living burden.

Iran’s supreme leader warns of 'geographically unrestricted response' if US attacks again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:10:19 UTC
21:10:19 KST

Iran ramps up its threats and does not exclude pre-emptive military action, but its officials have nevertheless noted positive steps in mediated negotiations with the US ahead of the decisive midterm elections. The Gulf countries remain "braced for the worst."
Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has issued a warning to the world that “any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Khamenei's threat comes as urgent diplomatic efforts continue to avoid a new all-out Iran war, which would have devastating consequences for the Middle East and beyond, as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that Tehran hopes "that there is rationality on the other side to prefer diplomacy to other paths," as "drawing on the experiences of the past two wars, we are much stronger than before."
The supreme leader met with Iran’s top military commanders on Saturday, presenting them with directives to prepare for potential new US-Israeli military action, according to the official IRNA news agency.
It follows warnings from the US that its forces could conduct a short but intensive military campaign against Iran after the US midterm elections next week.
The threat of a "geographically unrestricted response" means Iran could look to target Europe as well as Turkey and the South Caucasus in response to a renewed attack.
The description of “any level or type of threat” could indicate that Iran may act pre-eemptively, before a US-Israeli military strike.
State media said that Khamenei - who hasn’t been seen publicly since the Iran war began with US and Israeli strikes in late February - also called for an updated list of potential US and Israeli targets, to include “all kinds of physical and non-physical assets."
Khamenei also said that Iran would decide the duration of any new war.
"Should Iran’s enemies resume military or terrorist attacks, it will be the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine when and under what conditions those attacks will end," he said.
Iranian state media reported that in a meeting on Saturday, the commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Major General Ahmad Vahidi, together with the Iranian army commander and his chief of staff, briefed the supreme leader on Iran’s military readiness and told him that Iran’s weapons production has increased “seven-fold”.
The commanders report directly to Khamenei and have previously overruled the civilian Iranian leadership fuelling constant speculations as to who makes the decisions in Tehran.
Tehran's threats were reiterated on Sunday by Iranian army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia who told Iranian state media that “should a new war erupt, the geography of the conflict will not be confined to the West Asia region,” that "any potential future war could prove significantly longer than past conflicts.”
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a Washington-based think tank, estimated that Khamenei’s threats were “likely part of an Iranian effort to deter the United States and Israel from striking Iran.”
Gulf countries remain "braced for the worst"
While multiple speculations are swirling in the Gulf about the imminence of the war breaking out again versus the state of negotiations, with purported lists of demands from both sides being circulated by medias or whether US negotiators will meet the Iranian ones directly or not, the Gulf nations are bearing the brunt of the months-long state of war, with severe consequences on their economies.
While both the US and Iran have repeatedly pushed previous standoffs to the limit in their attempt to pressure each other into concessions, the Gulf countries continue hoping that a last-minute diplomatic breakthrough of some kind can lead to a peaceful resolution and avert another round of war, especially after the US warned the Gulf that it could launch a new attack on Iran.
UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash told a conference in Bahrain on Sunday that the Gulf states remain "braced for the worst," while hoping that mediation efforts, also led by Qatar, will prevail.
He warned that the Gulf has been blocked in a prolonged state of “no war, no peace,” and that if Washington and Tehran’s “positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst.”
The UAE diplomat also decried the Gulf countries’ lack of unity in action as a bloc, stating that “we have not collectively risen to the challenge” and that rebuilding trust with Iran would take an "extremely long time."
Iran recognizes "positive steps" from Washington
While Tehran continues its threats and defiant rhetoric, its foreign minister and its security chief have signalled positive steps in their mediated negotiations with the US via Qatar.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi announced on Saturday evening that Tehran could agree to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in just two days, instead of the previous timeline of seven days.
He said that Iranian diplomats were in Qatar for talks after a Qatari delegation mediated discussions in Tehran over the last few days.
Araghchi last month proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz within a week if the US agreed to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions. That was rejected.
In an interview with Qatar-based broadcaster Al Jazeera, Araghchi said that Iran was not planning to meet with US officials but called recent US efforts toward “broader dialogue” a positive step.
Araghchi said a decision on whether negotiations would be direct or indirect would be made “once Washington agrees to Iran’s conditions.”
It comes as the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, said he had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance’s proposing negotiations.
Commenting on the letter, Rezaei said “the tone has completely changed” and called it a “very good sign.” Araghchi also called Washington’s attempt to open dialogue a “positive step.”
Rezaei singled out an important change to one of Iran’s conditions: Ships in a reopened Strait of Hormuz would travel on a route agreed upon by Iran and Oman. And “everyone passing through this waterway will do so under Iranian management.”
He said that Iran was now awaiting the latest US response. Separately, Rezaei warned on X that any attack would bring “devastating blows on the aggressor using new weapons.”
Rezaei, who state media this past week said had met with Iran’s supreme leader, also said that there has been no decision to change Iran’s nuclear doctrine, but he noted that some Iranians have questioned whether that should be rethought if Iran is attacked again.
Meanwhile on Sunday, Qatar condemned Friday's attack on one of its LNG tankers in the Gulf, which was hit by "unidentified objects," calling it “a dangerous act that threatens the safety of maritime navigation and the security of global energy supplies”.
Qatar's foreign ministry denounced in a statement “these reckless and irresponsible practices," warning of "serious repercussions that may ensue for the security and stability of the region and the global economy”.

Russia’s Independent Journalism Will Survive in Exile, Gershkovich Says at Inaugural Derk Sauer Lecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:04:57 UTC
21:04:57 KST

AMSTERDAM — Exiled Russian journalists are preserving the foundations of a future free press despite the Kremlin’s destruction of independent media at home, Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich said Saturday at the inaugural lecture honoring The Moscow Times’ founder Derk Sauer.
Speaking at the De Balie cultural center, Gershkovich paid tribute to the publisher who helped launch his reporting career in Russia and supported him during his 16 months in Russian detention.
“Putin’s regime has wiped away the institutions that Derk helped build in a free Russia in the ’90s, but the seeds of the principles of independent journalism that he imparted remain,” Gershkovich said. Those principles, he added, are carried by journalists scattered around the world and “will flourish again when the right time comes.”
The lecture, organized by De Balie, Het Parool and The Moscow Times, took place on what would have been Sauer’s 74th birthday. The Dutch journalist and media entrepreneur died last year following a sailing accident.
The event was at once a tribute to Sauer’s role in building Russia’s independent media and a discussion of Gershkovich’s arrest, imprisonment and recovery after his release.
Gershkovich, who worked for The Moscow Times from 2017 to 2020, was arrested while reporting in the Urals city of Yekaterinburg in March 2023. He was sentenced to 16 years in prison on espionage charges that he, his employer and the U.S. government rejected as fabricated.
His account of his imprisonment and release in an August 2024 prisoner swap form the bulk of his memoir, “This Cursed Beautiful Land,” which was released in September.
When asked about his choice to stay in Russia after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Gershkovich said foreign correspondents had underestimated the risks of being imprisoned themselves, as foreign journalists had generally operated under a different set of rules than their Russian colleagues.
“My reasoning then was, if you’re a foreign journalist, you should try to be there if you can, because this country is becoming a black box,” he said.
Soon after his arrest, he came to understand that Russia intended to use him as a bargaining chip for a prisoner exchange with Washington. Despite accusing him of espionage, investigators did not put him through the intensive questioning he would have expected for such charges.
Nor did he face the harsh conditions, including torture, experienced by Russian political prisoners and Ukrainian civilians in Russian prisons.
He recounted how he tried to tried to maintain an emotional balance during his imprisonment, reading a steady diet of Russian literature, history and prison memoirs and practicing meditation. He would cook his own food using products delivered to him by his friends, improvising a way to make fresh pasta sauce using an electric kettle.
The psychological consequences of his ordeal would emerge after he returned home.
“In the beginning, I wasn’t sleeping. I had panic attacks, real anger that I took out on the people closest to me,” he said, but going to therapy and writing his memoir helped him process his trauma.
Gershkovich also credited the people who supported him in prison, including his Russian lawyers, whom he described as fighting for legal principles even as Russia’s conviction rate hovers around 100%.
He compared these lawyers’ work to Sauer’s legacy. Both preserve the knowledge and principles needed to rebuild institutions after a country emerges from authoritarianism.
Sauer founded The Moscow Times in 1992 and later helped establish the business newspaper Vedomosti. After the 2022 full-scale invasion, he facilitated the relocation of The Moscow Times, TV Rain and Meduza to the Netherlands so their journalists could continue to report from exile.
For Gershkovich, Sauer had been both a mentor who urged him to pursue more ambitious stories and a friend.
Sauer’s son Pjotr, a Guardian correspondent and former colleague of Gershkovich’s at The Moscow Times, read from one of the letters his father had written to Gershkovich while introducing the lecture.
“It’s all about the mind, Evan,” Sauer wrote. “So my friend, we have to deal with what life throws at us.”
Gershkovich recalled writing to Sauer before his death, joking that he might have taken his advice to be “a bit more rock and roll” in his reporting too far.
Even then, Sauer had kept his sense of humor, he said.
But his lasting contribution was the generations of journalists he had encouraged and trained, Gershkovich said.
“I believe that this is ultimately Derk’s legacy in Russia, too, and one all of us still involved in journalism have a duty to carry on.”

BRUSSELS, Belgium — The European Commission reaffirmed the Polish parliament's right to appoint judges to the country's top court on Nov. 1, a clear alignment with the center-right government of Donald Tusk.
Tusk's government is fighting to bring the country's legal system back to EU standards, after the previous Law and Justice Party (PiS) government put the judiciary under its political control, causing the EU to initiate a legal procedure against Warsaw in 2017.
"The appointment of eight new members of the Constitutional Tribunal lies within the constitutional power of the Sejm (Poland's parliament)," a Commission spokesperson told the Kyiv Independent.
The spokesperson also mentioned that the Strasbourg-based European Court of Human Rights "issued interim measures obliging the competent Polish authorities to refrain from hindering the taking up and exercise of judicial duties by judges appointed by the Sejm."
Democratic backsliding by Poland under PiS and Hungary under its previous Prime Minister Viktor Orban led the EU to introducing annual rule-of-law reviews across the bloc, and to it demanding far more safeguards from countries wishing to join the EU, such as Ukraine.

Poland's President Karol Nawrocki, who also hails from PiS, refused to hear the newly appointed judges swear their oaths, in an attempt to turn what is usually a procedural step into a permanent block on the appointees being able to begin work.
The stand-off came to a head on Oct. 30 when the most senior of the new appointees took charge of the Constitutional Tribunal.
That move was immediately followed by a stand-off between PiS politicians and supporters, parties further to their right, and the police.

Drones set fire to Lukoil’s refinery in Kstovo, one of Russia’s largest, overnight on 1 November, Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported. The raid came days after a US newspaper reported a pause in Ukraine’s refinery strikes, though Zelenskyy said units never had an order to stop. Over the same weekend, Ukraine’s military reported striking a rocket-fuel plant in southern Russia, and drones also hit a refinery in Ufa.
Russia’s war runs on fuel and oil money, and refineries have been Ukraine’s main long-range target. Ukraine says its drones hit 12 Russian refineries in September alone. Strikes then went quiet after Washington declared an energy ceasefire in mid-October. US President Donald Trump later called Ukraine’s renewed refinery strikes “a disgrace.” Every new refinery fire revives a campaign Washington has pressed Kyiv to drop.
Fire burned past dawn at Lukoil’s Kstovo plant
Exilenova+ began posting footage of explosions over Kstovo shortly after 04:00 Kyiv time. The fire kept growing past dawn, sending up a huge plume of smoke. The channel suggested the blaze centered on the AVT-6 and AVT-5 crude units and a tar visbreaker, or on unit 35/11-600. Satellite images would give a clearer picture, it added.
Nizhny Novgorod Governor Gleb Nikitin claimed drone strikes caused “significant damage” to an “industrial enterprise” in Kstovo district, Russian Telegram channel Astra reported. He did not name the facility. The regional government later urged drivers to fill up “as needed, without creating a rush,” Astra added. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed it downed 235 drones over 17 Russian regions overnight, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast among them. Ukraine’s General Staff had not commented on Kstovo by midday.
Kstovo was the third Russian refinery attacked in three days, after Novokuibyshevsk and Ufa, Russian Telegram channel Agentstvo calculated. Together, the three plants process about 24 million tons of crude a year, roughly 10% of Russia’s refining, and make more than 10% of its diesel. Nikitin also claimed air defenses destroyed more than 100 drones over the region overnight and in the morning. Regional authorities said they were taking measures to keep gas stations supplied, Agentstvo Novosti noted.
The Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez plant can process 15 million to 17 million tons of crude a year, depending on the estimate. It supplies about 30% of Moscow Oblast’s gasoline. The plant sits about 780 km from Ukraine’s border. Ukraine has hit it repeatedly: in November 2025, in April, and in May, when a strike halted its main crude unit.
Explosions rock Russia’s Kstovo as drone strikes target the oil industry hub overnight (MAP)
Days after a reported pause
On 29 October, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that Ukraine had paused refinery strikes under US pressure until after the 3 November midterms. Hours later, drones hit the Novokuibyshevsk refinery in Samara Oblast. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on 30 October that “every Russian strike on our cities and communities always gets our fully justified response.” Ukraine’s deep-strike units will also be expanded, he added. On 27 October, he told reporters that units had been “a little more careful” but “do not have an order” to stop, WSJ reported.
Neptune missiles and drones hit a rocket-fuel plant
Ukrainian forces struck the Kamensky Combine in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Rostov Oblast, overnight on 31 October, Ukraine’s General Staff reported. Strike drones and the Navy’s Neptune coastal missiles hit the plant together. The strike set a finished-goods warehouse on fire and damaged four workshops. The combine makes solid rocket fuel for Russia’s Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple rocket launchers, Ukraine’s General Staff said.
Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed it intercepted four of Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles and two Neptunes that night. Ukraine’s General Staff also reported hitting four Russian supply depots in occupied Ukraine. They sit near Khartsyzk and Dokuchaievsk in Donetsk Oblast, Novovasylivka in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, and Novoaidar in Luhansk Oblast.
A refinery fire in Ufa
On the morning of 31 October, drones hit the Bashneft-Novoil refinery in Ufa, Bashkortostan, Astra’s OSINT analyst found from eyewitness photos. Local residents said two plants came under attack. By the afternoon, the fires had been contained, Ukrainian Telegram channel Supernova+ said. Ukraine’s drones struck Bashneft’s Ufa refineries in June, and a fire in the city’s refinery zone was last reported on 21 September, Astra noted.

Local sources also reported drone attacks on Pochep in Bryansk Oblast. Two Belgorod Oblast villages came under attack on the evening of 31 October. The results remain unknown.

Anatoly Tsurkin, head of the Russian-installed freight carriers’ association in Crimea, claimed daily truck traffic from Rostov Oblast fell from 2,000–3,000 to 600–800. He claimed the M-14 highway, which occupation officials call the R-280, is the only road trucks can use. Drone strikes have also scared off drivers, he claimed.

Your teenage mental health may say something about your vote at 40, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:51 UTC
21:00:51 KST

A person’s mental health trajectory starting in adolescence predicts their political preferences nearly three decades later. Researchers found that early experiences with anxiety or behavioral issues are associated with distinct voting patterns and lower political trust in midlife. The research was published in the journal Political Psychology.
Political scientists and psychologists often study how adverse life events shape civic participation. Many studies evaluate how factors like poverty, discrimination, or dropping out of high school change adult voting habits. The specific role of mental health development over a person’s life has received less attention in political science.
Researchers wanted to understand if persistent psychological challenges correspond with specific political profiles. Sam Fluit, a psychology researcher at the University of Oslo, led a team to investigate this relationship. They focused on two broad categories of mental health conditions that often begin in youth.
The first category is internalizing problems, which refer to inward-facing symptoms. These typically include feelings of depression, general anxiety, and a sense of hopelessness about the future.
The second category involves externalizing problems, which describe outward-facing maladaptive actions. In adolescence, this might look like vandalism, skipping school, or getting into physical fights. In adulthood, externalizing behaviors often transition into issues like substance abuse, driving under the influence, or aggression in the workplace.
The researchers analyzed data from a large study of 2,215 individuals in Norway. The participants were tracked across five different time points over 28 years. The study began in the early 1990s when the subjects were around 15 years old and concluded in 2020 when they were in their early forties. At each stage, the participants reported the frequency and severity of their mental health symptoms.
During the final survey in midlife, the participants answered questions about twelve different political preferences. These included their voting history, their level of trust in government, their trust in other people, and their general interest in politics.
The survey also measured specific ideological attitudes. Participants placed themselves on the left-to-right political spectrum and answered questions about their views on social equality. They also reported their perceptions of immigrants and their support for conservative policies, such as stricter punishments for criminals.
To understand the data, the team grouped participants based on how their mental health symptoms changed over time. For internalizing problems, they identified three distinct life paths. Most people maintained a low, stable level of symptoms. A second group started with elevated symptoms in adolescence that decreased over time, while a third, smaller group experienced elevated symptoms that actually increased as they grew older.
For externalizing problems, the researchers categorized the participants into two paths. The vast majority of the sample had elevated outward-facing behavioral issues in their youth that eventually declined. A smaller group exhibited elevated externalizing problems that remained steady from adolescence into adulthood.
The researchers then examined how these distinct mental health paths corresponded to adult political outcomes. They discovered that elevated levels of either internalizing or externalizing problems were associated with lower voter turnout. Among the internalizing groups, those whose elevated adolescent symptoms later decreased were less likely to have voted in the last national election than those with low, stable symptoms. Among the externalizing groups, those with persistently elevated problems were less likely to have voted than those whose problems declined.
Both categories of mental health challenges were also linked to lower political and social trust in midlife. Participants in the elevated internalizing groups and the stable externalizing group reported less faith in political institutions. They were also less likely to agree that other people could be trusted in general.
When looking at specific political leanings, the two types of mental health problems diverged. Participants who had elevated internalizing problems in adolescence tended to develop a more left-wing political profile by midlife, regardless of whether their symptoms later increased or decreased. They were less likely to vote for mainstream center-right parties. Those whose internalizing symptoms decreased over time were especially likely to vote for far-left political parties.
The researchers proposed that people dealing with depression and anxiety might be drawn to egalitarian political platforms. Left-leaning ideologies often focus on systemic inequalities, which might resonate with individuals seeking political environments that prioritize social inclusion and community support.
On the other hand, individuals with persistently high externalizing problems demonstrated a more right-wing political profile. This group was more likely to oppose social equality and express support for conservative policies. They also reported higher levels of perceived threat from immigrants.
When casting their ballots, people in this stable externalizing group were twice as likely to vote for populist-right parties. They were half as likely to vote for center-left parties compared to their peers. Externalizing problems are often characterized by antagonism and a general opposition to others. The authors suggested this adversarial worldview might translate into support for populist politicians who use exclusionary rhetoric or position themselves against the established political system.
Because the study relies on observational survey data, the results do not prove that mental health conditions directly alter a person’s political ideology. The relationship might work in multiple directions, with political beliefs and emotional well-being influencing each other over time in a reinforcing loop.
The researchers could only measure political attitudes at the final survey in midlife. This limitation meant they could not track how those specific views shifted simultaneously with mental health changes during adolescence. The externalizing behavior assessments also had to change as the participants aged, since teenagers and adults break rules in different ways.
The data also comes from a single country with a strong social welfare system and a multi-party political landscape. The extensive social safety net in Norway might buffer some of the political disillusionment that can accompany chronic health problems. Different associations might emerge in nations with fewer social protections or in countries dominated by a two-party electoral system.
Future research could explore these dynamics in other populations and track political attitudes from an earlier age. Measuring specific mechanisms, such as how educational attainment or economic hardship link mental health to political choices, might help explain how early psychological experiences translate into adult voting behavior.
The study, “The mental health–politics nexus: How mental health trajectories from adolescence to midlife shape political attitudes and voting patterns,” was authored by Sam Fluit, Kinga Bierwiaczonek, Jonas R. Kunst, and Tilmann von Soest.

The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:12 UTC
21:00:12 KST

Donald Trump’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.
The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.
The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.
But neither China nor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.
The new arms race is different from those in the past. Rather than building weapons to blow each other up, China and the US are focusing on ensuring the resilience of the international supply chains on which they rely and figuring out how to constrain – and if push comes to shove, throttle – the supply chains essential to the economic and technological progress of their rival.
The paired strategies go back at least to the Covid pandemic, when China’s Xi Jinping called on the nation to “tighten international production chains’ dependence on China, forming a powerful countermeasure and deterrent capability against foreigners who would artificially cut off supply [to China]”.
Early in the Biden administration, national security adviser Jake Sullivan articulated the American goals: to limit China’s access to a narrow set of advanced technologies with military applications without upending the global economic order. He described the strategy as building a “small yard” of forbidden tech surrounded by a “high fence” of trade and investment controls.
By now, the conflict has breached the bounds of these initial rationales. Restrictions on American tech exports, investments and technology transfers to China have proliferated over the last half decade. And they are hitting not only China’s military capabilities but slowing its technological progress writ large. And Trump’s wanton deployment of tariffs is not helping.
China, on the other hand, is becoming increasingly assertive, leveraging its overwhelming dominance over the supply of critical minerals that are essential to high-tech industries for civilian and military uses. Last year, it stunned the Trump administration by throttling exports of rare earths and magnets made from them to retaliate against US tariffs and efforts to restrict China’s access to high-end semiconductors and the lithography machines needed to make them.
It has relaxed some of these controls, but it maintains many other restrictions. While they have largely been imposed to retaliate against American actions, they have also been used to hit other countries for a variety of policies it dislikes. The stakes are high. The International Energy Agency has estimated that if China were to block the US’s and Europe’s access to rare earth magnets, it could cost their economies about $1.5tn per year.
Where does the supply chain war go from here? The Trump administration is pouring hundreds of millions into projects to mine and process rare earths and other critical minerals, hoping to close China’s lead. It is also doubling down on efforts to limit China’s access to frontier semiconductors and to bar it from buying the machinery needed to make them.
China, on the other hand, has announced a range of high-tech export restrictions, covering things such as artificial intelligence chips and solar power technology. Moreover, it has threatened to punish countries that work to reduce their dependence on its mineral inputs.
One hopes there is a path to a peaceful entente. This would probably require some shared understanding of what constitutes a legitimate national security risk that may warrant actions to block supply chains. Defining the “yard” is essential. Frustrations of standard commerce should not be dealt with on a wartime footing.
China will probably dominate renewable energy technologies, especially the solar power industry, into the foreseeable future. It may also dominate the electric vehicle industry. This might hurt in Brussels and Washington, but it’s not worth a war. China, on the other hand, will have to accept that its mercantilistic economic strategy is not tenable for the rest of the world. Its combination of massive export growth with zero import growth is not sustainable.
This might seem doable. And yet the odds that the world economy will remain at peace seem slim. One might recall the Axis powers’ efforts to seize territories as the League of Nations curtailed their access to raw materials in the early stages of the second world war. Or FDR’s blocking of sales of American scrap steel and oil to Japan, which likely contributed to Tokyo’s decision to attack Pearl Harbor. Today, American fighter jets, submarines and missiles use rare earth magnets. What would happen if China blocked access to these materials?
The moment is strange. It’s not that long ago that trade was proposed as perhaps the most powerful tool to deliver world peace, building positive-sum interdependence among nations. That’s over. Interdependence has become a vulnerability. As China and the United States fight over who will control the next generation of technology, trade has become a theater of war.

A curmudgeon’s guide to the 2026 US elections | Dave Schilling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:10 UTC
21:00:10 KST

Chances are, as you’re reading this, your bunker is fully stocked, your doors are locked, and you’re peeking at your computer screen through gaps between your fingers.
After all, it’s election day on Tuesday. Once again, democracy will be tested – like Beavis & Butthead taking the SATs. I’m not looking forward to it, and I’m sure you aren’t either.
I’m old enough to remember when American elections, and especially the once-sleepy midterms, were a placid affair that anyone with a calculator and a friend at the Associated Press could predict.
Now, it feels like anything can and will happen this week – from delayed results and slow counts to Donald Trump sending in the DC Comics Suicide Squad to your local polling place. That’s all we need, John Cena checking your ID before you vote.
It’s enough to make you crawl up into a ball and beg for mommy. But fear is a passive emotion, one that leaves a person paralyzed and incapable of action.
My preference is for the fully formed anger of the middle-aged curmudgeon. A shaken fist and a choice expletive is healthier than babbling for hours in your panic room. So, in lieu of a voter guide telling you how to fill out your ballot, here’s a list of all the most irritating, confounding and downright stupid things to scream about on Tuesday.
The Cheesecake Factory discourse
During a recent campaign stop, the former president Barack Obama compared the aesthetics of the recent Trump-led White House renovations with a Cheesecake Factory. Not only am I annoyed that this is even a talking point during a crucial campaign, I also resent the comparison being made. I’d rather eat at a Cheesecake Factory than the White House, any day of the week. I have to assume Bill Maher agrees with me.
The continued importance of Spencer Pratt
Here in California, the race everyone is talking about is a contest for Los Angeles mayor, a famous stepping stone to jobs as prestigious as “Ambassador to Country Chosen by Random Lottery Draw” or “Special Adviser to Herbalife”. It’s neck-and-neck between incumbent Karen Bass and the city councilperson Nithya Raman. The unfortunate twist in this daytime soap opera is that the reality show star they combined to defeat in the first round of voting this summer, Spencer Pratt, is still popular enough that his supporters could tip the scales toward one candidate or the other. The only thing I can think of that’s worse than Spencer Pratt as mayor of LA is Spencer Pratt deciding the next mayor of LA.
The curious case of the two Dan Sullivans
According to the New York Times, some Democrats figured out that the best way to unseat the senator Dan Sullivan was to force him to run against himself. Retired teacher Dan Sullivan was allegedly recruited to run for US Senate by the campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola, in the hopes of unseating … Dan Sullivan. (The Peltola campaign has denied any involvement in his candidacy.)
The Sullivan v Sullivan smackdown has the Republican party so worried that the justice department is suing to invalidate the results of the election if Sullivan (the senator) narrowly loses to Sullivan (the not-senator) or Peltola (the not-Sullivan).
I’m no fan of Dan Sullivan, but I’m not sure how I feel about Dan Sullivan either! This is the kind of goofy dirty trick that makes people hate politics. Who are you really fooling here? Old people? People who are too busy to read the fine print about which Dan Sullivan is the incumbent Alaskan senator? People with an acute case of Sullivantitis (a crippling disease that causes blindness to the name “Dan Sullivan”)? Can’t this country ever be normal?
Please don’t message me. I realize the answer is no. I just hope this election is more entertaining than The Undertaker v The Undertaker at WWF SummerSlam 1994. Unlike that match, this face-off of doppelgangers won’t involve Leslie Nielsen.
The continued push to close polling places
In an attempt to depress turnout amongst Democratic-leaning voters, red state election boards in states such as North Carolina are shutting polling places in blue areas. In North Carolina in particular, voting sites were shut on numerous college campuses, but that didn’t stop a group of predominantly students from organizing marches in excess of two hours so that they could maintain the franchise.
When I was a young man, the main tool crooked politicians had to keep people from voting was good, old-fashioned apathy. We should have changed the motto on the quarter from “E pluribus unum” to “They’re all bums, anyway.” In 2026, politicians have infuriated people to such a degree that they’ll walk miles just to vote.
It’s inspiring to see young people exercising their rights in the face of an actively hostile state government, but I find the notion of our nation’s leaders blatantly making it more onerous for citizens to vote absolutely abhorrent. I mean, the peer pressure is bad enough.
‘I voted’ stickers and selfies
I get why the stickers exist. An elaborate campaign of shame and embarrassment for those that didn’t bother to vote. I can’t think of two more powerful forces in my life than shame and embarrassment. They’re really the only two reasons I get out of bed these days, but I don’t have to like it.
Like a lollipop at the end of a haircut, the “I voted” sticker is the little treat at the end of a long period of interminable waiting. The only difference is, I don’t need to take a picture with my root beer-flavored Dum Dum. And I hate to be cynical here, but anyone who hasn’t planned on or even considered voting will not be swayed by a sticker.
As much as I despise people shirking their responsibility to democracy, I hate internet trends even more. Instead of wearing an “I voted” sticker on Tuesday, just slap it on your laptop. That way, anyone in your general vicinity will have to stop and double-check that there isn’t an election that day.
Donald Trump’s Mr America beauty pageant
This is Donald Trump’s last campaign of his risible political career. He has been a cancerous influence on our discourse since 2011, breaking traditions, norms, rules, and some priceless artifacts along the way.
I’m sure he’s getting nostalgic for the rush of election fervor – the ups and downs, the thrill of victory and the agony of not admitting defeat. These are some of the last campaign rallies he’ll ever lead, some of the final moments of political combat he’ll engage in in his lifetime.
Most of us would get wistful, maybe a tad somber. These days will never come again. Instead, the president is pondering the strength and power that emanates from various Republican buttocks.
Nothing, and I mean nothing, makes me bang my head against a wall this election cycle than my social media feed being littered with clips of Donald Trump sexualizing his colleagues.
- Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

Top Trump Officials Are Hitting the Campaign Trail Ahead of the Midterms. Are They Allowed To?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

Top Trump Administration officials have taken to the campaign trail to boost Republican candidates ahead of the pivotal midterm elections as the party battles to retain control of Congress.
Last month alone, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr, and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum appeared alongside President Donald Trump to support Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in his tight reelection fight against Democrat Mary Peltola at a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on Oct. 13. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth appeared in Wisconsin alongside GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden on Oct. 20 to speak to manufacturing workers during a Pentagon tour highlighting U.S. defense production. Last Monday, Vice President JD Vance and Burgum spoke at a rally in Topeka, Kansas. And on Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefly joined Trump on stage, at the President’s urging, during a rally in Corpus Christi, Texas.
Cabinet members and other leading Trump officials have been wading into the midterms in these and other ways for months. In August, for instance, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan.
Legal experts and advocacy groups contend that in making such moves, members of the Administration have violated a decades-old law: the Hatch Act, passed by Congress in 1939, which places restrictions on certain political activities for federal executive branch employees.
The Administration has argued that the officials have participated in political events in a strictly personal capacity, which is permitted under the Hatch Act, and that their actions have been cleared by lawyers and ethics officials.
But several top Trump aides—including at least nine of his 15 Cabinet secretaries—have been hit with formal complaints that their actions have violated the law.
“The number of Hatch Act violation complaints is extreme and abnormal for election time, especially for complaints against senior officials,” Kedric Payne, the head of ethics at the Campaign Legal Center, a legal non-profit that has filed a complaint against the Trump Administration for using taxpayer money to fund political ads, tells TIME.
“We are seeing with the Trump Administration why the Hatch Act is so important,” Payne says, “because when it is not enforced quickly, it can be abused.”
Here’s what to know about the Hatch Act, and the accusations that Trump officials have violated it.
What is the Hatch Act?
The Hatch Act is an 87-year-old federal law that prohibits certain government employees from using their “official authority or influence for the purpose of interfering with or affecting the result of an election,” among other limits it imposes on officials’ political activity. It states that such interference applies to “an activity directed toward the success or failure of a political party” or candidate.
The law was established to ensure that “federal programs are administered in a nonpartisan fashion, to protect federal employees from political coercion in the workplace, and to ensure that federal employees are advanced based on merit and not based on political affiliation,” according to the Office of Special Counsel (OSC), which enforces it.
Many of the Hatch Act complaints against Trump officials on the campaign trail have centered around one specific aspect of the law that says federal employees cannot use or identify with their official title while engaging in political activity. In a handful of such complaints against members of the Administration, legal and press advocacy groups have pointed out that they were introduced at rallies by their Cabinet positions.
“Political activity must be conducted purely in your personal capacity, without using your official title, without implying endorsement of the United States government. In your personal time at your own personal expense,” Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer under George W. Bush and a professor at the University of Minnesota law school, tells TIME.
The Trump Administration has pushed back on the accusations, saying that its members were acting in a personal capacity at the times in question.
How Trump Administration officials have been accused of violating the Hatch Act on the campaign trail
A number of complaints have been filed against the Trump Administration for violating the Hatch Act in recent months.
Two advocacy non-profits, The Democracy Defenders Fund and Reporters Without Borders, filed a complaint in October over the rally in Alaska that featured Trump, Lutnick, Burgum, and Carr. The groups claimed that Carr “impermissibly mixed his official work into his personal remarks” and requested that the OSC open an investigation into each Trump official’s conduct at the rally.
In September, the two advocacy groups also filed a complaint against Duffy for his appearance in Michigan and his endorsement of Rogers.
Chief Counsel at the Democracy Defenders Fund said in a statement that Duffy’s conduct “crossed the legal and ethical line” and more broadly stated that it was “part of a broader pattern of this administration playing fast and loose with the law.”
Spokespeople for the Interior and Transportation departments have denied wrongdoing on the part of their respective leaders to media outlets. The FCC and Commerce Department did not immediately respond to TIME’s request for comment.
These complaints are among many more that have been filed over Administration officials’ participation in campaign activities.
“We haven't seen since the first Trump Administration this number of complaints against officials, and I've lost track, but I do think it's well over 20 complaints just in recent weeks,” Payne says.
In addition to complaints over officials’ appearances at campaign rallies, others have similarly alleged that Trump officials used their official titles in efforts to influence the midterms through social media and television network appearances.
CREW, a nonprofit government watchdog organization, has made several such claims. In one complaint from earlier this month, it argued that White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller violated the Hatch Act during an interview on Fox News in which he spoke against specific Democratic candidates running for office and urged voters to support a “pro-American Trump agenda.” The group has also filed complaints against Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Federal Bureau of Investigation Director Kash Patel for comments made while speaking to Fox.
“These accusations are baseless and amount to a manufactured political attack," the Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement. "Secretary Kennedy takes his ethical obligations seriously, follows federal ethics laws, and consults HHS career ethics officials to ensure his activities comply with the standards governing public service.”
The Department of Department of Justice, which houses the FBI, did not immediately respond to TIME’s request for comment regarding the accusations against Patel.
When asked about the various Hatch Act complaints against Administration officials, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis tells TIME that “it has long been established that senior administration officials are allowed to discuss current events, policies, and the candidates involved with those policies in order to advance the agenda of the administration.”
Complaints allege further Hatch Act violations
Top Trump officials have additionally been accused of violating the Hatch Act through other means than direct statements and appearances in support of—or opposition to—midterm candidates that complaints allege may also affect the outcome of upcoming elections.
Payne and his colleagues filed a complaint accusing several Administration officials of using taxpayer money for political ads which the complaint describes as “touting partisan and political rhetoric” to influence the outcome of the midterms. The complaint cites three ads: one that promotes Trump’s actions in Iran, another that decries socialism, and a third that features Trump speaking at Mount Rushmore. The Campaign Legal Center in its complaint quotes parameters set by the OSC that say the Hatch Act is designed “to prevent the use of federal power and taxpayer resources to shape electoral outcomes and to preserve public confidence in the nonpartisan administration of the law.”
“Voters deserve to know that elected officials are campaigning using their own money and not taxpayer dollars,” Payne says. “Clearly these advertisements that were paid for by U.S. taxpayer dollars were intended to promote the Republican Party and influence the upcoming election.”
The complaint specifically requests an investigation into Trump officials including Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, and White House Appointments Secretary Natalie Harp for their involvement in putting together the ads.
“There’s a statute that prohibits use of government funds for publicity or propaganda, unless expressly permitted by Congress,” Painter says. “Those ads that Trump was paying for with taxpayer dollars that said ‘paid for by the White House,’ that was propaganda. That violated that statute.”
Trump has defended the ads by saying he was “only promoting the country,” rather than specific candidates. “That’s an ad for the spirit of our country,” he said when asked about the ads in the Oval Office in September.
A Hatch Act complaint was also filed against the Administration by the Democracy Defenders Fund over the raid federal agents conducted at Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home in Minnesota in October. The raid was reportedly part of an ongoing Department of Justice investigation into potential immigration fraud. Omar has denied all wrongdoing.
“The timing of this outrageous action against a long-time target of Trump’s evinces illegal political intent,” Norm Eisen, the co-founder of Democracy Defenders Fund, said in a statement. “Staging a public raid on the home of a sitting member of Congress weeks before a consequential election is an abuse of power.”
Trump has maintained that he has “nothing to do” with the investigation, but has continued to levy public attacks against Omar, including calling her “crooked.”
The flurry of recent complaints against the Trump Administration are far from the first instances in which the President and his aides have come under fire for alleged Hatch Act violations.
An OSC report from 2021, for instance, found that in 2020, at least 13 senior Trump Administration officials violated the Hatch Act.
What is the penalty for a Hatch Act violation?
Following an investigation by the OSC, disciplinary measures for Hatch Act violations are determined by the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), an independent judicial agency within the Executive branch. For Cabinet or senior officials, OSC refers its findings to the President, who determines disciplinary action.
“The potential of those consequences happening under this President are small because it is up to the President usually to hold members of the administration accountable when they violate the Hatch Act,” Payne says, noting that in some cases, officials may be required to only issue a public apology for their violation, or face no consequence at all.
Federal officials who have previously been found to have violated the Hatch Act under Trump largely have not faced repercussions because the President either declined to punish them or because the OSC reported the violations after Trump and the officials in question left office.
After one OSC report from 2018 found Kellyanne Conway, a former counselor to Trump, had violated the Hatch Act, for example, Trump declined to fire her, telling Fox & Friends at the time that “it looks to me like they’re trying to take away her right of free speech and that’s just not fair.”
The OSC itself has meanwhile acknowledged that it was reporting other violations at a point when disciplinary action could not be taken. “Though discipline is no longer possible once subjects leave government service, OSC is issuing this report to fully document the violations, highlight the enforcement challenges that OSC confronted in investigating the violations, and to deter similar violations in the future,” one OSC report from 2021 reads.
Federal employees can face several civil penalties if they are found to have violated the Hatch Act, however, including a fine, a suspension, or a letter of reprimand. For a criminal violation, up to three years in prison may be imposed as a penalty if an official is found to have “intimidate[ed], threaten[ed], command[ed], or coerce[ed] … any employee of the Federal Government … to engage in, or not to engage in, any political activity.”
“If President Trump or anyone overreaches the point of trying to coerce someone in the government to engage in partisan conduct, that's a violation of the criminal provision of the act, but all the rest of it's civil,” Painter explains.

The Hollywood Color Nerd Who Shot ‘Knives Out’ Explains His Viral iPhone Camera App
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Steve Yedlin is a certified color nerd. He almost immediately starts explaining “the math” behind his passion for color science.
But I didn’t call to chat about psychophysics or color theory. I called to talk to Yedlin about his Chromagraph Camera app, newly released, virally popular, and available only on the iPhone.
Yedlin is a longtime collaborator with director Rian Johnson, shooting his films like Knives Out and Star Wars: The Last Jedi. The duo teamed up again for this launch. “I write all of my own image processing that we use on the movies,” he says. The Chromagraph Camera app brings a taste of Yedlin’s special sauce to your smartphone camera.
Instead of the iPhone’s built-in image processing, this app shoots RAW image data and processes it with a similar formula to what he uses in film production. After Johnson promoted Chromagraph Camera on social media in late October, it quickly became the top paid download in the iOS store. The app costs a one-time fee of $13 and only shoots still photos. (There’s no video support yet.)
I am far from the resident photography nerd on WIRED’s gear team. (That award goes, in part, to my wonderful editor, Julian.) I’m often just whipping out my iPhone and snapping a picture with the default settings. Even so, I really enjoyed capturing some of San Francisco’s fall vibes using the Chromagraph Camera. Although Apple gives iPhone owners plenty of built-in tools for adjusting the color on your own images, I loved this app’s ability to capture highly stylized shots without me needing to fiddle with anything at all.
When you open the app, what you see in the viewfinder before snapping the shot is not what the Chromagraph Camera will spit out. The photo is essentially “developed” in the app after you capture the image. This is because the app needs a moment to run its unique processing for the specific tone, color, and grain effects. You can also alter how an image looks in the app after it’s processed, if you want to tweak the overall exposure or texture of an image.
Yedlin is adamant that he’s not attempting to replace your iPhone camera app or release a professional tool for editing everything. It’s all about that color, man. “It's just this curated app that takes the pictures the way we like,” he says. Yedlin and Johnson teamed up with programmer Eric Cameron to build the app centered around their color tastes, experimenting with it for a couple of months before launch.
Even after all of this custom image processing, Yedlin still sees the iPhone as a fundamentally limited device. “This idea that you can actually have the control that a professional camera would have is not really true anyhow,” he says. Software can only do so much to change how hardware works, especially when developing an app within Apple’s parameters that limit how far the software can push the phone’s hardware.
As advances in computational photography and generative AI have renewed discussions about what a smartphone photo even is anymore, Yedlin’s approach isn't an attempt to find a sense of neutrality. He doesn’t see any image as a literal rendering of what exists. It’s always an interpretation, whether that's a stylized, artful depiction or a more stagnant shot. He says that the look of the Chromagraph Camera app is consciously “opinionated” and specific.
“You can describe how the different rendering looks in words, but you just have to look at it,” he says. The color speaks for itself.

London Bridge gets early review to test structural condition
LONDON – London Bridge is undergoing an earlier-than-planned engineering review as concerns grow over the state of the British capital’s ageing river crossings.
The assessment will deepen “understanding of the condition” of the cables within the bridge, the City Bridge Foundation, a charity that manages five crossings over the River Thames, said in its 2025-26 report.
Initial investigations found no defects, it said in an emailed statement.
The bridge charity brought forward the review after a railway bridge in the German city of Dresden collapsed into the Elbe River in September 2024.
The dramatic failure left engineers searching for answers and led the foundation to accelerate its assessment of London Bridge.
Like Dresden’s Carola Bridge, the building of London Bridge was completed in the early 1970s and shares some design features.
London’s river crossings are facing growing attention after Westminster City Council warned that Waterloo Bridge could be forced to close unless it secures funding for needed repairs.
Structural reviews are also planned for Blackfriars Bridge, Southwark Bridge and Tower Bridge, according to the bridge charity.
London Bridge, which commuters walk every day on the way to work in the City of London financial district, is already closed to general traffic on weekdays from 7am until 7pm to reduce congestion.
The latest evaluation follows essential maintenance completed in 2020 that helped waterproof the structure, the City of London Corporation said at the time.
The foundation, which has about £1.5 billion (S$2.5 billion) in funds, will continue to manage only crossings under its existing mandate despite pressure to take on more, Chair Paul Martinelli said in a recent statement.
The five bridges the foundation manages “cost the taxpayer nothing. Today they are open, safe and in good condition,” Martinelli said.
“London’s other bridges belong to other organisations. We can’t take on the whole river.” BLOOMBERG

There’s a Free Video Editor Inside Google Drive That Anyone Can Use

Mention the online apps available as part of Google Workspace, and most people will immediately think of Google Drive, Gmail, Google Docs, Google Sheets, and Google Slides—those speedy, lightweight office apps that let you get work done from any browser tab.
There's more to the suite of Google Workspace tools than you might have realized though, including an online video editing package called Google Vids. Originally launched in 2024 for business and enterprise users, the app was made available to individuals in 2026 and continues to get regular updates from Google.
Since it's both free to use and designed to run in a web browser, it's not capable of pro-level, high-resolution, multitrack video editing. But for personal and hobbyist use, it works well, and it won't take you long to learn the basics.
The Google Vids Interface
Finding Google Vids isn't difficult: You can either open Google Drive on the web, then click New and Google Vids, or head straight to the Google Vids app page and click the + (plus) button under Start a new video. (Any videos you've previously made are shown here, too.)
Besides beginning with a clean state (the Blank vid option), there are plenty of other ways to get started: You can generate AI videos with the Veo 3.1 model, turn a slideshow into a video, work from a template, upload an existing video as a starting point, create an AI music track, record a video using your camera, produce a video with an AI avatar, or create a storyboard outline. Note you can also pick the video orientation at the top.
Most of these options use a similar layout, and we're going to focus on the traditional video-making approach here—though the AI options are well worth exploring, too, if you don't have source material to work with. If you're new to Google Vids, then picking Templates from the opening splash screen will ease you in gently.
When it comes to picking a template, the topic isn't as important as the layout. Look for something that matches what you want to create as closely as possible (hover over any of the thumbnails to see an animated preview). The next dialog lets you choose whether you want to use the entire template or just selected scenes. After that, you're into the video editing interface proper.
Most of the elements should be relatively familiar if you've ever used a timeline-based video editor in the past. At the bottom you've got your video and audio tracks, while the main window shows the currently selected segment of your video. The panel on the right lets you edit whatever's currently selected.
Down the right side of the interface you've got all the options for loading in new content. You can record webcam clips, create AI videos, import footage from Google Drive and Google Photos, add voiceovers, and drop in text, images, music, and shapes. If you've started with a template, some of these elements will be styled to match.
Along the top of the Google Vids interface are more editing and formatting tools. These menus are where you should head to change transitions between scenes, to manage how elements are arranged in a particular scene, to drop in new scenes, and to manage your video project as a whole.
Building Video Projects With Google Vids
To begin building your projects, you'll probably want to load in audio, video, and images via the buttons on the right. On the most basic level, you can click the + (plus) button on the timeline to create a new scene, then drag in a photo or video from the right-hand panel to fill the scene you've just created.
A whole host of options present themselves when you right-click on the timeline. You can, for example, mute the audio track imported with a video, then add a voiceover or some different music. You're also able to split scenes (if you only want to keep half a scene maybe) and duplicate scenes (for quickly expanding the running time of your project) with a right-click.
Keep your eye on the panel on the right, which changes depending on the context. With audio tracks, you can apply fades, and with video clips you can choose from different transitions. If your scene has several elements (like shapes that scroll over a video), you're able to adjust how they look and behave.
Let's say you have a video scene and want to put some text over it. Select the scene in the timeline, click the Text button on the right, then click Add a title to do just that. If you then select the title in the scene itself, you can change the text and its styling.
Using the handles around the text box you can change its position, size, and rotation. There are also three buttons underneath on a floating toolbar: Animation lets you animate the text, Resize will resize the text box to fit the text you've entered, and Format options brings up a panel where you can change text size, padding, rotation, and so on.
Click and drag on elements inside a scene to reposition them, and right-click for more options—including Cut, Copy, Paste, and Delete. If you need more material to work with, choose the Stock option on the right, which gives you a library of material you can make use of in addition to your own content and anything created with AI.
There's a lot more to Google Vids, but that should be enough to get you started—try experimenting with a few of the templates to see what else is possible. As with the other Google Drive apps, all your edits are saved instantly, and up in the top right corner you've got a Play button for viewing your work in progress, and a Share button for when it’s ready for the world to see.

Eisenkot explores minority government backed by Ra’am, UTJ abstentions - report
The proposal could give Eisenkot enough votes to take office, but faces opposition from Lieberman and disputes over military conscription
Gadi Eisenkot has authorized an examination of a possible minority government that would take office with Ra’am and United Torah Judaism abstaining, Ynet reported Sunday, outlining a potential route to replacing Prime Minister Netanyahu after Israel’s inconclusive election.
Under the scenario, Eisenkot’s 48-seat bloc would gain the active support of Ra’am lawmaker Yoav Segalovitz, bringing it to 49 votes. If United Torah Judaism withheld its seven votes from Netanyahu, the incumbent’s opposing bloc would fall from 53 seats to 46.
The proposal also assumes that the Joint List would refrain from voting against the government.
According to Ynet, Eisenkot’s bloc does not intend to negotiate with the faction, but is relying on its previously stated willingness to allow Netanyahu’s replacement. Joint List lawmaker Ahmad Tibi has said his party wants to bring down Netanyahu’s government.
The arrangement remains exploratory and would require significant compromises across parties with conflicting priorities.
Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman has publicly rejected joining a government dependent on Arab or ultra-Orthodox parties, whether “directly or indirectly.” His position presents a major obstacle to the proposed arrangement.
Eisenkot’s team is reportedly examining whether United Torah Judaism would provide support from outside the coalition until legislation addressing exemptions from military service is passed, then formally join the government.
Reaching such an agreement would be difficult. Conscription exemptions are a central priority for the ultra-Orthodox party, while the scope of any concessions Eisenkot would accept remains uncertain.
Ra’am’s demands would also need to be addressed. Party leader Mansour Abbas wants his faction to be part of the coalition, even if Segalovitz is its only representative serving in the government, according to the report.
Ynet reported that the minority-government option could also serve as leverage in negotiations with Netanyahu over a unity government. Such an arrangement currently faces resistance from many within Eisenkot’s bloc.
The parties seeking to replace Netanyahu have yet to agree on a candidate to succeed Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana. Eisenkot wants the position allocated to his faction, while Lieberman is seeking it for Yisrael Beytenu lawmaker Oded Forer.
Responding to the report, Eisenkot’s Yashar party said it remained committed to replacing the current government but declined to discuss private deliberations.
“The various reports are not issued on our behalf and do not necessarily describe reality as it is,” the party said.
