Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:55:46 UTC
20:55:46 KST

Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of Augsburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have built a groundbreaking molecular motor that spins in either direction using electricity, inspired by a machine invented more than 2,000 years ago. Even more remarkably, its rotation can boost electrical conductivity by up to 100 times, potentially transforming the future of molecular electronics.
- Share:
Scientists have developed a remarkable new molecular motor that spins when electricity passes through it. Inspired by an ancient invention, the tiny machine can even reverse its direction when the electrical voltage is switched. The achievement marks an important step toward creating working machines at the smallest possible scale.
Molecular machines are widely seen as a promising next frontier in miniaturization. Nature already provides examples inside living cells, where molecular motors use energy to produce movement. Researchers have spent decades trying to recreate these remarkable biological systems artificially, and progress in this field was recognized with the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
An Ancient Invention Inspires a Molecular Motor
Scientists first developed molecular motors powered directly by electricity in 2011. However, those earlier designs operated on surfaces and relied on the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope to drive their movement.
The new motor takes a different approach, borrowing its basic design from the Archimedes screw, one of the oldest machines in recorded history. Traditionally used to move water uphill, this simple device relies on a rotating spiral to transport material.
Researchers adapted that principle to the molecular scale. Instead of moving water, their design allows electrons to travel through a spiral-shaped molecule, causing it to rotate as electrical current passes through.
A Tiny Molecular Screw Suspended Between Gold Tips
The motor's central component is a specially designed spiral molecule created by the research group of Prof. Michael Pittelkow at the University of Copenhagen. Measuring only a few millionths of a millimeter, the molecule can attach to gold surfaces through sulfur atoms.
At the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, researchers led by Prof. Oren Tal and Dr. Anil Kumar Singh positioned individual molecules between two gold tips sharpened to atomic dimensions. By carefully changing the separation between these electrodes, the team could stretch or compress the molecular screw.
When the scientists applied an electrical voltage, measurements revealed that the molecule began rotating. Even more importantly, they could reverse its direction simply by changing the voltage's polarity.
This represents the first demonstration of a molecular motor that is driven by electrical current, firmly connected to two metal electrodes, and capable of rotating in a controllable direction.
How Electricity Makes a Single Molecule Spin
The driving force comes directly from electrons traveling through the spiral molecule. As they move, they transfer angular momentum to the molecular structure, producing rotation in much the same way that moving air turns a wind turbine.
The spiral's shape determines how it responds to this flow, similar to the difference between screws with right- or left-handed threads. Once the applied voltage exceeds a certain threshold, the movement becomes continuous rotation.
But the experiments revealed another intriguing effect. The rotating molecule conducted electricity much more efficiently than it did when stationary, raising an important question about what was happening inside the tiny machine.
Scientists Discover a Surprising 100-Fold Electrical Effect
To investigate this unexpected behavior, Prof. Dr. Fabian Pauly and his PhD students Léon Martin and Yuta Ito, working at the Chair of Theoretical Physics I at the University of Augsburg, used quantum mechanical simulations on the LiCCA supercomputer.
Their calculations revealed a close relationship between the molecule's rotation and its ability to carry electrical current. Conductivity changes dramatically depending on the angle of the molecule, increasing by as much as two orders of magnitude, or 100 times, during rotation.
The reason turned out to be particularly surprising. Some of the molecular positions that allow electricity to pass most easily are also positions that the molecule naturally avoids when it is not moving. Rotation makes those highly conductive arrangements accessible.
"The surprising thing is that it is precisely the positions that the molecule avoids when at rest that conduct electricity best. It is only the rotation that makes these positions accessible," explains Léon Martin.
The finding demonstrates that molecular motion does more than simply consume electrical energy. The movement itself can strongly influence how electricity flows through the machine.
International Collaboration Solves the Mystery
The researchers then worked with theoretical physicists Per Hedegård of the Niels Bohr Institute in Copenhagen and Jing-Tao Lü of Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan.
Using the simulation results, the scientists developed a simplified theoretical model that successfully recreated both the rotation observed in the experiments and the accompanying increase in electrical current.
This combination of experimental measurements and theoretical calculations was essential to understanding the mechanism. Although researchers could measure the current passing through the molecule, they needed simulations to determine what was happening at such an extraordinarily small scale.
"In the experiment, you only see the current. Our calculations allow us to glimpse what is happening inside the nanocontact. It was only through close collaboration between experiment and theory across several countries that the mystery of the current increase could be solved," says Yuta Ito, a PhD student originally from Japan.
A New Frontier for Molecular Electronics
The achievement could eventually contribute to the development of molecular electronic components and technologies involving spintronics, which uses properties of electrons beyond their electrical charge. It may also offer possibilities for microfluidic systems, which manipulate extremely small quantities of fluids.
Beyond these potential applications, the motor provides scientists with a new way to investigate physical processes at the atomic scale. Its ability to convert electricity into controlled rotation, while allowing that rotation to influence electrical current, introduces a new principle for designing extraordinarily small machines.
"We have shown that an electric current can be used to generate a directed rotation and that this rotation, in turn, controls the current. This is a new operating principle for machines at the very limits of miniaturization," explains Pauly.
The work at the University of Augsburg received funding from the German Research Foundation (DFG) through Collaborative Research Center (SFB) 1585 (project number 492723217). The computational research was conducted using the University of Augsburg's LiCCA supercomputer (DFG project number 499211671).
Additional support for the collaborating institutions came from the European Research Council (ERC, Horizon 2020, Grant 864008), the Israel Science Foundation (2129/23), the Minerva Foundation, the Villum Foundation, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the Independent Research Fund Denmark (DFF), the National Key Research and Development Program of China, and the National Natural Science Foundation of China.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Augsburg. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Anil Kumar Singh, León Martin, Matea Sršen, Freja Schou Guttesen, Bing-Zhong Hu, Yuta Ito, Stephan Korsgaard Pedersen, Fadhil Suleiman Kamounah, Fabian Pauly, Michael Pittelkow, Jing-Tao Lü, Per Hedegård, Oren Tal. Current-Driven Molecular Machine with Rotation-Enhanced Conductance. Nature, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11312-x

Habiba was due for her two-month vaccinations on Saturday. Instead, her family mourned her death alongside that of seven-month-old Aseel after a fire tore through the tent where their relatives had gathered in the southern Gaza Strip, Anadolu reports.
The family’s visit in al-Mawasi, west of Khan Younis, ended in a desperate attempt to save the two infants when flames broke out Friday afternoon.
Both suffered severe burns and were admitted to intensive care. They died Saturday morning.
Nasser Medical Complex identified them as Habiba Mohammed Zanoun, two months old, and Aseel Abu Suhayban, seven months old.
Sources told Anadolu that the fire started while food was being cooked inside the tent. Severe shortages of cooking gas and basic supplies under Israel’s blockade have forced displaced families to prepare meals over open flames, they said.
– ‘Why is all this happening to us?’
The girls’ grandmother, who did not give her name, told Anadolu that her daughter had come to visit the family at their tent when the fire suddenly broke out.
Habiba was her daughter’s baby, she said. The infant died on the day she was supposed to receive her two-month vaccinations.
Aseel’s mother rushed to rescue her daughter and suffered burns. She, too, was taken to hospital.
The grandmother said neither infant could withstand the severity of her injuries.
“Why is all this happening to us?” she asked. “Every day there are accidents, bombings and fires, and people are dying in so many ways.”
“For three years, we have been living like this, amid displacement, anguish and pain.”
– Cooking without safe alternatives
The blaze was one of three fires reported Friday in displacement tents in central and southern Gaza, according to sources.
With cooking gas scarce, families have resorted to makeshift fires to prepare food. Inside crowded shelters built from flammable materials, an everyday necessity can put lives at risk.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned in June that cooking inside displacement tents was a leading cause of fires.
Blankets, old fabric, cardboard and plastic sheeting used to reinforce shelters allow flames to spread rapidly and make fires harder to control, it said.
Fire is one of several dangers facing families in deteriorating tents that offer little protection from the weather.
OCHA also reported that Israeli authorities denied entry on Aug. 26 and Sept. 2 to a previously approved shipment through the Egyptian corridor containing 36,960 pieces of timber and 660 emergency shelter kits.
The Gaza Government Media Office previously reported that more than 800,000 displaced Palestinians were living in tents unfit for human habitation. It estimated that 162,000 of Gaza’s 270,000 displacement tents needed immediate replacement.
The grandmother, mourning the loss of two grandchildren, appealed to the world to pay attention to Gaza’s displaced families and help end their suffering.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:52:55 UTC
20:52:55 KST

Labour looks less likely to meet its manifesto pledge to equalise the minimum wage for younger workers before the next election, after the chancellor failed to guarantee the rise would happen within that timeframe.
John Healey said on Sunday the government was still committed to the increase but failed to spell out when it would be achieved. In the budget, a rise in the minimum wage was handed to adults – to £13.21– and under-20s – to £11.27 – but a larger rise for younger workers would have been needed to move towards equalisation.
Speaking on the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Healey said he would “take it one step at a time” amid fears a rise could exacerbate youth unemployment.
Labour’s 2024 manifesto committed to closing the gap on pay for 18- to 20-year-olds, but last week’s budget brought in a blanket increase of 3.9%.
Some senior MPs – including the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, while she was out of government – have previously expressed concern at the slow pace of the equalisation. In June, Rayner warned the government it must deliver on the promise.
Healey said on Sunday the government was still committed to the eventual equalisation. “I legislated as a new MP for the national minimum wage when we first brought it in [in 1998], and so we’re going to have to continue to make those trade-offs between jobs and wages,” Healey said. But he denied Labour would break its manifesto commitment.
“There’s no question about whether or if. It’s a question of when. It’s a question of how fast. And I want to make sure that we can look hard at those trade-offs that inevitably are there between jobs and wages.
“I want to take business, I want to take trade unions with me, and with the government, because together we have to get into what at the moment is a moral shame on this nation, a million youngsters written off, without any prospect of being helped into work and making a contribution to this country for the future.”
Healey also told the BBC he was prepared to keep the spending cuts – some more than 2% year-on-year – planned for before the next election in the last spending review.
Some thinktanks including the Institute for Fiscal Studies have criticised how the government’s deficit reduction plans seem predicated on making unpopular cuts that are unlikely to be enacted at a crucial electoral moment.
“We will carry that through to the 10-year plan and the spending review next year,” Healey said. “But in the budget I also set out the ways that we’re preparing and the work we’ve got under way to prepare for those spending review decisions.”
Speaking on GB News on Sunday, the chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said the government would not make “crude cuts” to welfare to balance the books, because of the costs that would incur elsewhere.
“We will set out proposals in the new year, and then we will legislate to bring the welfare bill down in a fair and sustainable way, and according to our values as a Labour government. I know that other parties, such as the Conservatives and Reform, claim that they can do crude cuts to welfare,” she said.
“The Conservative government didn’t manage to do crude cuts because they know full well that if you push people into crisis, then you end up pushing costs into a different part of the public sector. So that’s not the right way to do it because, frankly, this isn’t realistic.
“The prime minister and the chancellor and the whole government is very clear that we do need to bring the welfare bill down, and we’re also not running away from difficult decisions.”

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s General Staff on October 31, the coordinated attack targeted the Kamensky Combine in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, a facility involved in producing solid rocket propellant for several Russian weapons systems.
The operation involved Ukrainian attack drones and Neptune coastal missile systems operated by the Ukrainian Navy.
The General Staff confirmed that a warehouse containing finished products caught fire, while four production workshops sustained damage. The extent of the damage and its potential impact on production capacity have not yet been independently established.
The Kamensky Combine manufactures solid rocket propellant used in ammunition for Russia’s Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems. Its products are also used in other missile systems and air-launched weapons.
Solid rocket propellant is a critical component of these weapons, providing the thrust needed to launch and propel rockets toward their targets.
Disruptions to its production could affect Russia’s ability to manufacture ammunition for systems used against Ukrainian military positions and populated areas. Satellite imagery showing the reported aftermath of the attack was also published by the OSINT project Absolutely Reliable Source.
Just two days before the missile and drone strike, the ATESH partisan movement reported sabotaging electrical infrastructure at the same facility on October 29. According to the group, damage to a power distribution node caused localized disruptions to the plant’s operations, requiring repairs before normal production could resume.

Commission backs Tusk as he vows no compromise in court showdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:52:15 UTC
20:52:15 KST

The European Commission has reiterated that Poland’s parliament must have the right to appoint new judges, lending support to Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in an escalating confrontation over the country’s Constitutional Tribunal.
The dispute pits Tusk’s government against President Karol Nawrocki over efforts to reverse judicial changes introduced by the nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) government between 2015 and 2023, which drew condemnation from European courts over concerns about judicial independence.
Nawrocki, elected with PiS backing in 2025, has refused to swear in some Tribunal judges elected by the current parliamentary majority, while the court’s PiS-linked leadership has prevented them from working.
Advertisement
The Commission said it was closely monitoring developments and, in a carefully worded statement to POLITICO, appeared to show support for Tusk’s position.
“The Polish Constitutional Tribunal needs to be able to function in accordance with the Polish constitution and the case law of the Court of Justice of the EU,” Commissioner for Democracy, Justice and the Rule of Law Michael McGrath said.
“This matters for every Polish citizen, and it is for the Polish authorities to ensure that,” McGrath added, stating that “the Venice Commission has been clear that appointing the new judges lies within the power of the Sejm [Poland’s lower house of parliament].”
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk vowed Saturday night not to back down on the dispute. “In some matters there can be no compromise,” Tusk said in an address to the nation, comparing calls for reconciliation to a thief demanding to keep half the contents of a stolen handbag.
“We have waited too long for the treasure of an independent, democratic Poland to be frightened into retreat,” Tusk said.
The prime minister also targeted Nawrocki, who turned his plane around mid-flight en route to Senegal and returned to Warsaw, where he pushed his way into the Tribunal shortly after midnight Saturday, confronting judges challenging its leadership.
Advertisement
“In a state governed by the rule of law, a politician cannot enter a court or tribunal and give orders or intimidate judges, even if he is the president,” Tusk said.
He pledged to ensure the Tribunal could operate independently and safely.
Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, taking charge of the Tribunal, suspended Święczkowski and Sochański after they blocked judges elected by the Tusk-led parliamentary majority from work for months.
Nawrocki denounced the move as an unlawful takeover and held talks with parliamentary leaders Saturday, boycotted by Tusk’s Civic Coalition and its government ally, the New Left.
Korwin-Piotrowska has convened an assembly of Tribunal judges for Tuesday, potentially setting up another confrontation over who controls the court.

The Avenger systems were deployed amid heightened security measures surrounding the U.S. President.
Two systems were positioned on a floating platform in Lake Worth Lagoon, near the coast of the President’s residence, while another was deployed directly on the beach. At least two additional systems were also stationed at the airport.
U.S. Northern Command (USNORTHCOM) and the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) have confirmed the deployment of ground-based air defense systems and counter-drone systems. The deployment was carried out at the U.S. Secret Service’s request as part of enhanced security measures around President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago residence.
In addition to the Avenger systems, the military deployed mobile Counter-UAS Fly-Away Kits designed to detect and track drones. These kits include passive and active detection and tracking equipment, including electro-optical and infrared cameras.
The kits may also include electronic warfare systems designed to jam drones.
The deployment comes amid heightened security concerns over threats against Donald Trump, including previous assassination attempts against the U.S. President and threats from Iran.
Meanwhile, the U.S. military and the Secret Service have not disclosed the specific reason for deploying additional air defense systems.
According to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), more than 160 incidents involving aircraft and drones violating flight restrictions have been recorded since the airspace restrictions over Palm Beach were introduced in October 2025.

Feature: Myanmar star elephant's 73rd birthday brings back generations of memories
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
19:39:02 CST
20:39:02 KST

Children wear elephant headbands during the celebrations of the 73rd birthday of Momo, a female Asian elephant, at the Yangon Zoological Gardens in Yangon, Myanmar, Nov. 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Myo Kyaw Soe)
YANGON, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- At 73, Momo, a renowned female Asian elephant at Yangon Zoological Gardens, was once again the center of attention as children, parents and elderly visitors gathered on Sunday to celebrate her birthday.
As children and other spectators sang the song "Happy Birthday," Momo gently swayed her trunk and moved her legs, seemingly joining in the celebration. Later, she chomped on an assortment of fruits and vegetables arranged in the shape of a cake.
For some visitors, it was their first time seeing the gentle giant. For others, the occasion brought back fond childhood memories of visiting Momo at the zoo, memories they are now passing on to their own children and grandchildren.
For 11-year-old Thuta Nyan Kywal, visiting the zoo with her mother and sister was an exciting opportunity to see elephants in real life rather than simply reading about them in textbooks.
"In the past, I only saw elephants in textbooks. Now I can see them in real life and learn how they behave and what they eat. I did not know about Momo before coming here, but today I learned about her and am very happy to join her birthday celebration," she said.
"I wish Momo a long and healthy life. Happy birthday, Momo!" she added.
For 60-year-old Thida Soe, seeing Momo again was like taking a journey back to her childhood.
"I have known Momo since I was young and used to visit her at the zoo. Seeing her brings back so many childhood memories," she said.
"Although Momo is an animal, people treat her like a human being and celebrate her birthday. She is very gentle. She has changed as she has grown older and cannot be as active as she once was, but she has lived to 73. Not everyone, even among humans, gets to live that long," she said.
According to Than Myint Tun, warden of Yangon Zoological Gardens, Momo was donated to Yangon Zoo in 1961. Over the decades, she has grown from a young performing elephant into a much-loved grandmother figure and one of the zoo's most recognizable residents.
During her younger years, Momo entertained visitors with performances and dances. She also took part in significant national events, including the opening ceremony of the Shwedagon Pagoda stairway, he said.
"Momo stopped performing when she turned 60 in 2013. Since then, we have celebrated her birthday every year. Now she has turned 73," he said.
"Momo is loved by the public and is one of Yangon Zoo's trademarks. By celebrating her birthday, we can also raise public awareness about elephants and their nature," he added.
For more than four years, Momo has been under the care of her keeper, Thant Sin Tun, who inherited the responsibility from his senior colleagues.
"Momo is polite and gentle. As she has grown older, she has become less patient. She does not like being scolded, so we have to speak to her softly," he said.
"When we call her name, she responds. When we ask her to dance, she dances," he added.
Momo loves cleanliness. If her food falls on the ground and gets mixed with sand, she refuses to eat it. She also likes drinking tap water and enjoys scrubbing herself when taking a bath, he said.
Age, however, has brought some physical challenges. Her eyesight has become blurry, and she can no longer chew hard food as easily as before. Apart from these age-related changes, her keeper said she has no major health problems.
At the zoo, Momo receives regular medical attention and care. Unlike elephants in the wild, she does not have to search for food herself or face some of the dangers associated with life in the forest, he said.
"If she could speak, I think she would say that she wants to live longer here because so many people love her and we take care of her health," he said. ■

Momo, a renowned female Asian elephant at the Yangon Zoological Gardens, celebrates her 73rd birthday in Yangon, Myanmar, Nov. 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Myo Kyaw Soe)

Over 4,000 Australian GP clinics now offer free consultations to all patients: gov't
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
19:38:26 CST
20:38:26 KST

CANBERRA, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- More than 4,000 general practitioner (GP) clinics across Australia now provide free consultations to all patients under the country's Medicare system, up from 2,300 a year ago, the government said on Sunday.
Australian Minister for Health and Ageing Mark Butler said in a statement that 50 percent of all general practices nationwide now exclusively offer bulk billing, compared with 30 percent a year earlier.
Under the bulk-billing system, doctors bill Medicare directly for medical services, allowing patients to receive treatment without out-of-pocket costs.
The increase follows the introduction of the government's Bulk Billing Practice Incentive Program, which provides higher Medicare rebates to clinics where all doctors bulk bill all patients.
According to the statement, more than 97 percent of Australians now live within a 20-minute drive of a general practice that bulk bills all patients.
The proportion of fully bulk-billing practices has more than doubled in South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania and the Australian Capital Territory (ACT) over the past 12 months.
The Northern Territory recorded the highest proportion among states and territories at 80 percent, followed by New South Wales at 58 percent and Victoria at 55 percent, while the ACT had the lowest at 21 percent.
Rural areas saw the largest increase, with the proportion of fully bulk-billing practices rising to 59 percent, while remote areas remained at 77 percent.
Butler said the expansion was helping Australians save hundreds of dollars a year in out-of-pocket medical expenses. ■

KYIV – Russian strikes left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power on Nov 1, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, while the Russian authorities reported major damage to an industrial site following Ukrainian drone attacks on Nizhny Novgorod region.
Even as a six-day local ceasefire held on its final day around the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky, there was no let-up in fighting elsewhere along the front line and both sides kept up long-range air attacks.
Zelensky said Russia had hit power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, cutting electricity to hundreds of thousands of households.
“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” he said on Telegram.
He said Ukraine, meanwhile, had hit the Kamensky plant in Russia’s Rostov region, which he said was involved in the manufacture of Russian missiles.
Moscow did not comment on the reported attack in Rostov. In Nizhny Novgorod region, however, Governor Gleb Nikitin said a large-scale overnight Ukrainian drone attack caused “significant damage” to an industrial facility.
He did not identify the site that was hit. The region is home to the NORSI oil refinery, one of Russia’s largest.
Overall, Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces had downed 235 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight. Ukraine’s air force said it had shot down 371 of 433 long-range drones launched by Russia since the evening of Oct 31.
In its morning update, the air force said dozens of Russian drones were still in the air as at the morning of Nov 1. Six separate drone alerts had been issued in Kyiv since midnight.
Fuel supplies
Nizhny Novgorod’s regional government also did not identify the facility that was struck, but it said it was taking steps to ensure gas stations were supplied with fuel, urging motorists to “buy fuel only as needed and avoid panic buying”, Interfax reported.
The warning suggests the damaged facility was linked to the region’s oil-refining or fuel-supply infrastructure. Kyiv did not immediately claim responsibility for the Nizhny Novgorod attack.
On Oct 30, Russia said Ukraine had resumed strikes on its oil refineries and accused Kyiv of ignoring a request from US President Donald Trump to stop such attacks, which Trump has blamed for raising the cost of diesel before US midterm elections next week.
Ukraine says it supports a full ceasefire on energy targets, including its own battered power grid, but that Moscow is unwilling to agree to this.

New Party gears up for first convention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:35:29 UTC
20:35:29 KST

İHA Photo
The emerging main opposition New Party is continuing preparations for its first ordinary convention, scheduled to take place on Nov. 14-15.
Citing the party sources, the Turkish state-run Anadolu Agency on Nov. 1 reported that the countdown has begun for the congress of the New Party, which began operating this year as Türkiye’s 189th political party and assumed the title of the main opposition party by virtue of its parliamentary seat count.
Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu was reinstated as the party leader of the Republican People’s Party (CHP) following a court ruling over alleged irregularities at the party’s 2023 convention. He had lost the leadership race at the convention to Özgür Özel.
Özel resigned from the CHP on July 24, taking 90 lawmakers with him to establish the New Party.
As part of the New Party’s congress calendar, which began on Aug. 26, delegates to the congress have been determined through primaries and provincial and district-level conventions held across the country.
Under the congress schedule, New Party leader Özel will stand in primaries across all 81 provinces on Nov. 8, seeking to secure his leadership through a vote by party members.
Those who join the party by Nov. 5 will be eligible to cast ballots in the primaries.
The congress, the party’s highest decision-making body, will subsequently convene on Nov. 14-15, following a decision taken at a meeting of the Party Assembly (PM) on Oct. 28.
The two-day congress will begin with the election of the congress presidium, followed by an address by party leader Özel.
More than 1,000 delegates will then cast their votes to elect the party chairman, the 80-member Party Assembly and the 15-member High Disciplinary Board.
Under the party’s rules, anyone seeking to run for party chairman must submit a written application to the congress presidium backed by the signatures of at least 5 percent of the total number of delegates.
The party chairman is elected by secret ballot and must secure an absolute majority of the total membership. If no candidate obtains the required votes in the first two rounds, the candidate receiving the highest number of votes in the third round is declared elected.

Healey also rules out reparations for Britain's slave trade
At the end of his interview with Kuennsberg, Healey was also asked to comment on a potential apology for Britain’s near-250 years of perpetrating the slave trade and why the government should or shouldn’t pay reparations to enslaved people and their countries.
Sitting in the grand settings of Number 11 Downing St, Kuenssberg pointed out the lavish interiors:
“So many Commonwealth countries think that this country’s wealth, maybe the wealth in this building, this gilt chandelier, came off the back of slavery. So why is a government not willing to contemplate reparations?”
Healey replied saying the PM was open to “a discussion about an apology”, but “he doesn’t believe that reparations are the right approach”. He makes the same argument as Burnham that the current British people shouldn’t have to pay for past wrongdoings.
Considering a formal apology doesn’t mean accepting that British people now should accept the financial liability for any party and things that happened hundreds of years ago, in which they had no role.
For almost 250 years (1560s-1807), British ships trafficked more than three million enslaved African men, women and children in a state policy backed by the monarchy and parliament.
Many were taken to British-owned plantations in the Caribbean, which enslaved generations. Children were born into slavery, uprisings were put down with extreme brutality
There were still 800,000 enslaved people on British plantations when enslavement was finally abolished by parliament in 1833
Abolishment was only achieved because the government agreed to “compensate” the enslavers. The government paid an enormous sum, the equivalent of billions of dollars these days, to the “owners” of enslaved people; this came from a huge loan that was only paid off in 2015.
Britain has never paid any compensation or reparations to the people who were enslaved, or their countries.
U.K. politicians have traditionally focused on the country’s role in banning the slave trade in 1807 and outlawing slavery throughout the British Empire in 1833.
It’s Independence Day in Antigua & Barbuda and special guests like King Charles III are participating in local activities.
His visit has mainly sparked discussions on reparations with at least two civil society groups planning protests during the international summit.
But for residents, discussions on reparations are not on their priority list especially as something as simple as an apology from the King and his UK government seems to be so controversial.
Many brush it off as us “never getting money” while academics are calling for reparations in the form of investment in health, education and industries that will improve the standard of living of people living in Antigua and Barbuda.
For many locals, their top concerns continue to be the growing cost of living and increased gas prices. Others have taken to social media to make jokes about what infrastructural changes the King’s arrival has caused. Potholes, roads and buildings that have been neglected for years have overnight garnered the attention of the government’s Public Works Department.
320 people arrested for supporting Palestine Action at US embassy protest
The Met Police has disclosed the total number of arrests they made on Saturday at the anti-genocide demonstration outside the US embassy in London.
In total, 325 people were arrested. Police said the vast majority – 320- were arrested for expressing support for Palestine Action, which has been listed as a banned organisation under the UK’s terrorism laws for the past 15 months.
Below are pictures from the rally. People were arrested for holding placards reading: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action”. Many were forcibly removed from the protest site by police.
Register of British Slave Traders includes kings, queens, Handel and Locke
In case you missed it earlier, just wanted to highlight again the database put together by specialist historians which identifies the investors in Britain’s slave trade.
This was a project three years in the making. It provides biographical detail for as many of 10,500 investors from historical records, building the most comprehensive single picture so far of those who perpetrated the enslavement of African people.
They include the composer George Frideric Handel, and the philospher John Locke, who both were shareholders in the Royal African Company.
It is a legacy of the dehumanisation inflicted on so many African men, women and children that much less was documented about them than about their enslavers.
The weight of historical evidence is adding to the growing global movement calling on European governments to be accountable; to issue a full, formal apology and engage in reparatory justice discussions.
Successive British governments have refused to do so, arguing there is no duty to make reparations because enslavement and the slave trade were not against the law at the time. The Burnham government is arguing that British people today shouldn’t be saddled with the wrongdoings of the past.
Jamaica has sought a legal challenge on this government petition; it has petitioned King Charles for a ruling from the Privy Council, the final court of apppeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.
The former chancellor Rachel Reeves has argued Britain’s future should be back in the European Union, saying Brexit has made the UK “poorer, weaker and less secure”.
In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury when Andy Burnham took office, she said those forging a path back towards EU membership had to make compelling arguments to the public.
Reeves, who was sacked as chancellor by Burnham, said in an article for the Sunday Times that no one who worked with her in the Treasury could be in doubt about her pro-European instincts. “I am proud of the progress we have already made in strengthening our relationship with the European Union. Brexit has made us poorer, weaker and less secure,” she said.
“There is a debate to be had about our future relationship with Europe, and I welcome Andy Burnham’s leadership in facing up to this. No one in the Treasury ever doubted where my instincts were.”
The current focus for British negotiations is the EU summit later this month to seal an agreement to ease some trading restrictions and a youth mobility deal. But the prime minister has made it clear he wants to see a long-term and stable relationship with the bloc.
Burnham has said he believes there should be “honest discussion” about freedom of movement and that rejoining the single market could be done without the need for another referendum, if Labour put it in its manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll.
“The royal family enslaved us! Apologise now! Reparatory justice now!”
King Charles has faced some protests for reparations in Georgetown, Guyana in recent days.
He and PM Andy Burnham, will be greeted with such messages again as they travel through Antigua’s capital, St John’s to the Commonwealth leaders’ summit next week.
On billboards, placards and T-shirts, in letters and at a candlelight vigil for the thousands of Africans trafficked to Antigua and Barbuda during the transatlantic slave trade, the message from the Caribbean will be pervasive: slavery reparations is not an issue they “are going to be able to dodge”.
James Knight of Citizens for Reparatory Justice, which is organising some of the demonstrations, said the king and UK government had made protest necessary.
“It is definitely necessary that we make known our deep sense of indignation in response to what has been announced ahead of the meeting by the British government and King Charles that there will be no apology, no reparations,” he said.
“And to make that announcement when you’re coming to a meeting where people have been asking to have the matter discussed, to us, is extremely insulting [and] insensitive”.
The Commonwealth meeting is the culmination of more than a decade of calls from Caribbean leaders for Britain to acknowledge its role in the enslavement of millions of Africans and the colonisation of African and Caribbean countries, and to address the enduring consequences.
Professor Verene Shepherd, vice-chair of the Caribbean Reparations Commission, described Burnham’s announcement as “good news”, but rejected the suggestion that Britain today cannot be held liable for reparations.
“Only a full and formal apology can allow for the healing of wounds and the destruction of cultures caused by colonialism,” she said, adding that “a full apology accepts responsibility, commits to non-repetition, and pledges to repair the harm caused”.
The Caricom body was established in 2013 by Caribbean community heads of government to build the argument for reparations from former colonial powers.
Shephered said descendants of enslaved people wanted “a conversation on actual reparations, not debt restructuring but debt cancellation rooted in the reality of the lingering legacies of colonialism”.
Confronting that ‘complicated history’ of which the PM speaks includes paying for the wrongs of chattel slavery. In fact, it is not complicated at all. It is very straightforward.
Shepherd, a professor emerita of social history at the University of the West Indies in Mona, Jamaica, also challenged Britain’s traditional narrative around abolition, saying:
Enslaved people, including in Ayiti, not Britain, led the fight for abolition. British development benefited from the blood, sweat and tears of millions of enslaved Africans.
We reject the notion that a nation that profited from chattel slavery should not now be held responsible for its actions. Britain is liable! As that late reparations warrior, Jamaican Dudley Thompson, said: ‘The Debt Has Not Been Paid, the Accounts Have Not Been Settled.’ Settle it now! We want equal rights and justice in Peter Tosh’s formulation.
In Guyana, President Irfaan Ali welcomed Burnham’s statement and called for a Commonwealth subcommittee to work out the details of the dialogue.
I want to acknowledge the statement by the British government, and I’m happy that finally the discourse has moved to a position where it should have been, where the British government is involved, because that’s the state we are dealing with.
But Ali questioned what such dialogue should ultimately achieve.
“I’ve always made the case that we need to sit down in a mature conversation. The indignity cannot be paid for.
“But how do we identify a formula? How do we identify a system of support where the UK government, with its financial institutions, can sit with countries, can sit in a deliberate way and work on a development pathway, identify development gaps, whether in health, education, social services, infrastructure; development gaps that affect countries’ ability to invest in adaptation and mitigation for climate disasters, especially in this region.”
Ali said he wanted Commonwealth leaders to establish a subcommittee within the next six to 12 months to work with the British government on identifying and costing development gaps resulting from slavery.
For some, the next meeting of Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm)is crucial for King Charles. Already campaigners have warned that his position as head of state is at risk in several countries unless he does more to confront the monarchy’s historic links to slavery.
As my colleagues write:

Charles is expected to deliver three significant speeches during the trip, but will follow government advice not to issue a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade. The British government has also ruled out paying reparations.
The visit is expected to be met with protests over the monarchy’s colonial legacy and demands for a formal apology and reparations. It comes four years after the Prince and Princess of Wales’s controversial 2022 Caribbean tour, where images of the couple greeting Jamaican children through a wire fence sparked widespread criticism across the region.
Truth telling and transparency is key to acknowledging Britain’s history of enslavement and the transatlantic slavery.
Some descendants of British people who profited from the slave trade have already apologised and offered compensation.
That includes The Guardian newspaper. In 2023, we apologised for the role our newspaper’s founders had in transatlantic enslavement, and launched a 10-year programme of restorative justice involving community engagement with descendant communities linked to the Guardian’s founders in Jamaica and the US.
For example, this is the case that has been made about the logic of slavery reparations – and how it’s not just about payment but addressing inequalities and engaging in good faith with descendants of enslaved people.

Britain trafficked enslaved African people for centuries; kings and queens were investors
David Conn
The Guardian has done extensive reporting on Britain’s centuries-long trafficking of enslaved African people, a policy that was supported by parliament and the monarchy from the 1560s-1807.
Britain’s trafficking operations – which included royal companies led by kings and, later, entrepreneurs in Bristol, Liverpool and other port cities, violently transported more than 3 million enslaved African men, women and children to colonial plantations in the Americas and Caribbean.
The Register of British Slave Traders, the product of a three-year project by a team of specialist historians, documents the investors in Britain’s near 250-year transatlantic slave trade.
It shows the relentless involvement of the British monarchy, parliament and financial and business elites; the role of the church in legitimising it; and how the investors’ wealth was woven deep into the country’s fabric and used to fund hospitals, schools, welfare organisations, the arts, science and culture.
Key elements include:
A series of British kings and queens were leaders and investors in the trafficking of enslaved African people;
More than 100 MPs were investors in slave-trading companies, including scores in the Tory and Whig parties – the forerunners of today’s Conservatives and Liberal Democrats;
Dozens of directors and original financiers of the Bank of England were investors in the slave trade;
More than 1,000 women invested in slave-trading companies;
Forty-five Church of England clergymen were investors in the slave-trading Royal African Company.
The publication of the register last month will provide further evidence for the growing global movement calling on European governments to acknowledge their perpetration of enslavement, issue a full, formal apology and engage positively with discussions for reparatory justice.
Successive British governments have refused to do so, arguing there is no duty to make reparations because enslavement and the slave trade were not against the law at the time.

Some historical context here – the historical Tory party were directly involved in and supported enslavement for nearly 200 years.

Caribbean leaders welcome 'significant development' of apology move

Burnham open to issuing apology over Britain's role in slave trade
Andy Burnham says the UK will listen to calls to issue a formal apology, but doesn’t believe that reparations is the “right answer”.
He argued yesterday in The Guardian that Britain needs to acknowledge its “complicated history” in order to protect the Commonwealth, the 56 nations that grew out of the British Empire.
He’s headed to Antigua and Babuda in coming days. King Charles has been in the Caribbean this week where he’s faced calls for Britain to apologise and pay reparations.
The King, whose forebears directly benefited from trafficking of enslaved people, admitted the “great suffering and injustices of the past” but did not issue an apology. It is UK government policy currently, to not apologise for the country’s role in the slave trade.

The Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.

By Andrew Goudsward, David Morgan and Nathan Frandino
WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE, Alaska, Nov 1 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump returns to the campaign trail on Sunday with rallies in Iowa and Kansas, Republican-leaning Farm Belt states where his party is fighting to hold US Senate seats, two days before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.
Trump, who spent Saturday at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida after weeks of campaigning across multiple states, won Iowa by double digits in 2024. But polls show Democrats tied with or leading Republicans in many of the state’s races, and Trump’s approval among rural Americans fell to a new low of 45% in October, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling. Kansas, which last elected a Democratic senator in 1932, is also facing an unexpectedly close race.
Thirty-five Senate seats and all 435 House seats are on the ballot on Tuesday. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority and a narrow edge in the House. Losing either chamber would let Democrats block Trump’s agenda for his final two years in office and launch investigations of an administration that has so far faced largely compliant Republican majorities.
More than 52 million Americans have already voted in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, a record for a midterm and up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day in 2022.
LEGAL FIGHTS
Senate control could come down to a handful of states, including Alaska, where polls show incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican, in a tight race with Democrat Mary Peltola.
Sullivan on Sunday said he would accept the results of Tuesday’s election even as the Trump administration presses a criminal investigation into the presence of another challenger named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot.
The US Justice Department has asked a federal court to prevent the certification of Alaska’s vote if the incumbent senator loses narrowly. Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, has suggested he may not certify a victory by Peltola after the New York Times reported her campaign was involved in recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. into the race.
Although the senator said he would accept the election result, he declined to say whether he would support efforts to refuse certifying it if he lost. But he joined his party colleagues in accusing the other Sullivan of trying to confuse voters with his similar name.
“They got the decoy guy on the ballot,” Senator Dan S. Sullivan told CNN’s “State of the Union” program. “I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery. So what I say to Alaskans is, don’t let them get away with the tricks.”
Peltola and the campaign committee have denied involvement, and Sullivan Jr. has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.
Voters who spoke to Reuters on Saturday in Anchorage, Alaska, had mixed views on the investigation and legal fights.
“I am concerned that the longer it takes for those votes to be counted, the more shenanigans will happen, especially with our current president making comments about wanting to invalidate the current election and the current votes that are coming in,” said Ames Tonneson, 24.
Art Paul, 52, took the potential upheaval in stride.
“In this case, if there’s a close race or investigation, I understand. … It’s part of the process,” Paul said. “And you gotta be patient. So I’d like it to be faster, but I understand why it’s not.”
Separately, the Trump administration signaled it would likely ask the US Supreme Court to take up its legal battle with California over alleged noncitizen voting.
A federal judge earlier this week rejected the Justice Department’s request to block California from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters it alleges are likely noncitizens. A federal appeals court has twice rejected the DOJ’s arguments. California has said the state’s safeguards against noncitizen voting, which is illegal, are robust.
MICHIGAN RIFT
In Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers in another closely watched Senate race, it was unclear whether US Representative Haley Stevens, a Michigan Democrat and the rival El-Sayed beat in the primary, would attend a Detroit event with him on Sunday that had been billed as a show of party unity.

“I understand that some folks are upset about that,” El-Sayed told reporters at a rally in Sterling Heights, Michigan, that took place on his 42nd birthday. “But I’m here trying to beat Mike Rogers.”
El-Sayed’s campaign asked Stevens to skip his events through election day so as “not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” a person familiar with the matter said. Stevens has demanded he condemn an outside group’s ad that she says blames Israel for high grocery prices.
“It’s certainly unhelpful to the El-Sayed campaign to have continued visible division within the party just before election day,” said Matt Grossmann, a political scientist at Michigan State University. Polls show El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support.

Democratic wins would shift Congress’ trade debate but fall short of US tariff rollbacks
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:31:26 CET
20:31:26 KST

By David Lawder
WASHINGTON, Nov 1 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s trade agenda will face a new source of friction if Democrats win control of Congress on Tuesday, with a cascade of oversight hearings and symbolic tariff rollback votes likely next year, but Trump will remain undeterred in his zeal for more tariff actions, trade experts and congressional aides say.
Democrats are eager to pass legislation to negate many of Trump’s tariffs and the more archaic statutes backing them, but any gains by the party will run into the reality of Trump’s veto power.
“One of the most obvious priorities would be repealing Trump’s tariffs on Canada, which are raising prices and harming communities on both sides of the border,” said Senator Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the tax- and trade-focused Senate Finance Committee.
Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the US House of Representatives and the US Senate to overturn Republicans’ narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities. Opinion polls favor Democrats to win the House, while the Senate remains too close to call, leaving Democrats far short of a veto-proof two-thirds majority.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration is developing plans to rely more heavily on executive actions, including on trade, without the need for congressional approval.
If they win at least one chamber, Democrats could stage symbolic votes on long-sidelined trade bills such as Senator Chuck Schumer’s “End Trump’s Tariff Tax Act,” which would scrap the statute backing the punitive tariffs on Canadian goods, Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, along with the statute used for Trump’s temporary 10% global tariffs, Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974.
The bill, with 28 co-sponsors including Wyden, also calls for refunding all duties collected under the archaic trade laws.
“Democrats are going to try a lot of things. I just don’t think anything’s going to get across the finish line because neither party will have a veto-proof majority in any scenario,” said William Reinsch, non-resident adviser to the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.
OVERSIGHT HEARINGS
But gaining control of trade committee gavels would give Democrats a platform to launch a steady stream of oversight hearings and investigations into Trump’s trade policies, Reinsch and other trade experts said.
Key oversight targets would include shedding light on the opaque process for determining tariff exemptions that benefit specific companies, how tariffs are impacting small businesses, and how the Trump administration is doling out hundreds of billions of dollars in investment funds pledged by Japan, South Korea and other trading partners in recent trade deals.
A confrontational oversight agenda from Democrats would mark a shift from Republicans’ largely hands-off approach to Trump’s tariffs, which has persisted for two years despite recent pushback from some struggling Republican incumbents, including Senator Susan Collins of Maine.
Coupled with some symbolic tariff rollback votes staged by Democrats, this will start to shift the trade debate to influence the 2028 election cycle, said Greta Peisch, a former general counsel at the US Trade Representative’s office and a former trade counsel to Senate Finance Committee Democrats.
Even if Democrats can’t muster the votes to pass a bill to reform trade authorities right out of the gate, the effort could “form the basis of a proposal for the presidential elections,” said Peisch, now a trade partner at Wiley Rein in Washington.
“I think it’s really the beginning of how Democrats, and Congress as a whole, think about whether and how to enact trade legislation and reforms in the next two to four years, really,” Peisch added.
NO WAVERING
The increased noise from Capitol Hill is unlikely to deter Trump from pursuing more tariffs over his final two years in office, including from a forthcoming investigation into excess industrial capacity in 16 major trading partners, even as he grants exemptions or delays some duties.
Trump will continue to pursue his tariff-driven trade agenda aimed at protecting American workers, farmers and businesses from being “ripped off” by past trade deals, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said.
“President Trump will never waver from putting America First, whether in trade negotiations or through an economic agenda of tax cuts and deregulation,” Middleton said in an emailed statement. “That agenda has already secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments, with even more progress, jobs, and opportunities ahead for everyday Americans.”
Trading partners also understand Trump’s commitment to keeping tariffs in place, and realize that Congress will not be in a position to remove them, said Milos Ivkovic, an international arbitration law expert and adjunct professor at Washington University in St. Louis.
A wait-and-see approach to the vote will not benefit trade deal holdouts such as India, Vietnam or Canada, he said.
“For all of those countries who think that midterms will have such an effect that the United States government and President Trump will change foreign policy, they’re mistaken,” Ivkovic said. Countries that are holding off on trade discussions with the Trump administration “are actually jeopardizing their negotiations,” he added.
(Reporting by David Lawder; Editing by Andrea Ricci )

Explainer-How US news organizations will make midterm race calls
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:31:14 CET
20:31:14 KST

By Jaspreet Singh
Nov 1 (Reuters) - On Tuesday night, newsrooms across the US will call winners in one of the country’s most closely contested midterm election cycles in recent years, long before all the votes are counted.
Most television networks and digital outlets rely on two providers for vote counts: the Associated Press or election-data firm Decision Desk HQ.
Some news outlets such as the Wall Street Journal and MS NOW will rely solely on the AP for race calls, while others like Fox News and CBS News will make their own projections based on the AP vote count, exit polls, early-vote totals and their own statistical modeling.
The first calls will start soon after polls begin to close in the United States, first with Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. ET (2300 GMT), and shortly after in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia at 7 p.m. (0000 GMT on November 4). In certain races there may be an instant call if much of the voting has already taken place.
Low public trust complicates race calls for news outlets. While more than 60% of Americans have some confidence in news organizations to report accurate election results, only 32% have high confidence, with Democrats more trusting than Republicans, an October poll for the Medill Local News Initiative and the Alliance for Trust in Media found.
While most of the major TV networks all use the same AP vote count tabulation to make their calls, the ones who decide to call winners use a proprietary mix of their own data analysis, historical models, exit poll interviews and expert judgment to call races when they determine that they’ve become a statistical certainty.
Here’s how it works:
AP COUNTS AND RACE CALLS
The AP, a nonprofit newsroom supported by member newspapers, has counted votes in every US election since 1848, working with a national network of reporters and election officials to verify results.
For the 2026 midterms, the AP said it would deploy more than 4,000 reporters at county election offices and local polling locations, gathering and providing data to the decision desks at ABC News, CBS News, Fox, CNN and NBC News. ABC, CBS, CNN and NBC also rely on research firm SSRS, which acquired exit-polling company Edison Research in 2025.
When making calls, the AP uses vote totals and estimates how many votes remain uncounted based on past voting patterns and early-vote data. It calls a race only when the trailing candidate cannot catch up.
DDHQ COUNTS AND RACE CALLS
DDHQ collects vote counts from official state sources, usually secretaries of state or state election departments.
The firm uses statistical analysis, modeling and expert review to project election winners. Its clients include NewsNation, the Hill and Newsmax, and it recently signed up X, the social network owned by Elon Musk.
It uses automated software to repeatedly check official election websites and collect newly posted vote totals in addition to using reporters on the ground. DDHQ says roughly 80% of all votes are processed by pulling data directly from official election sites, or by manually monitoring election sites. The remaining counts are collected by reporters.
It calculates the percentage of ballots counted by dividing the votes reported by election officials by its estimated total turnout for a race. It determines remaining votes by subtracting reported votes from this overall turnout estimate, which is refined on election night using actual data.
Final projections require unanimous team agreement and a sign-off from the head of data science, Scott Tranter. “We’re preparing to have several thousand people working on election night to gather data,” Tranter told Reuters.
RACE PROJECTIONS CAN BE WRONG
Retractions are rare, but both the AP and DDHQ have withdrawn calls in the past.
In 2025, DDHQ withdrew a projection in the Seattle mayor’s race. Earlier this year, DDHQ withdrew its call in the Democratic primary for a special election in New Jersey’s 11th Congressional District after Election Day vote counts shifted the race away from its initial projection.
In 2018, after a projected winner fell behind in California’s 21st Congressional District, AP posted on its race-call account that it was retracting the call because Democrat T.J. Cox had taken the lead in the vote count.
THE NEWS OUTLETS MAKING RACE CALLS
Fox’s decision desk will be making its own calls in all statewide races as well as the calls for control of the House and control of the Senate. It uses the AP vote count and applies its own analysis.
MS NOW, covering its first midterms since separating from NBCUniversal’s cable portfolio, will rely on the AP’s race calls.
The New York Times relies on AP calls for most contests but independently reviews competitive races using precinct-level data and its Needle model. It may make a call before or after the AP.
Bloomberg does not make its own race calls. For election results, it uses established third-party sources. Reuters will also be citing the race calls from other news organizations.
The Washington Post did not respond to requests for comment on how it will call races.
(Reporting by Jaspreet Singh in Bengaluru. Editing by Edmund Lee, Michael Learmonth and Deepa Babington)

Trump White House maps path to govern without Congress if Democrats win
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:31:06 CET
20:31:06 KST

By Nandita Bose and Tim Reid
WASHINGTON, Nov 1 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s White House has spent months preparing for a possible Democratic takeover of Congress, developing plans to keep advancing major parts of his agenda through executive power while bracing for investigations of his administration, according to a White House official and two people familiar with the plans.
Senior officials, including deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and budget director Russell Vought, have been working with the White House Counsel’s Office since April to identify executive actions on immigration, tariffs, housing costs and federal spending that Trump could pursue without congressional approval, said the three people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
White House counsel Will Scharf and his team also are looking at “what Trump can legally do on his own, where he could push the limits of his authority and how to defend those decisions in court,” the White House official said.
The planning underscores a paradox of Tuesday’s midterm elections: Capturing control of Congress would give Democrats the power to investigate Trump, block legislation and constrain his spending priorities. But Trump would retain broad executive authority over trade, foreign policy and the federal bureaucracy that he has already used aggressively during his second term.
Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the US House of Representatives as well as the US Senate to overturn Republicans’ narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities. Opinion polls favor Democrats to win the House, while the Senate remains too close to call.
For the past month, Trump has held rallies across the country trying to preserve Republican control of Congress, even as his aides privately prepare for a very different political landscape in 2027.
The White House pushed back on the prospect of Republican losses and accused the media of promoting a false narrative.
“This administration and commonsense Republicans will continue to secure our borders, restore law and order, putting more money back into the pockets of hard-working Americans, and deliver wins for the American people,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.
Among the executive actions under consideration are new tariffs on imports of critical minerals and wind turbines, tighter rules on visas for international students and temporary foreign workers, and measures aimed at lowering housing and construction costs, the White House official said.
Federal agencies have submitted proposals and legal reviews of actions the administration could take unilaterally, one of the people with knowledge of the plans said.
Vought, whose US Office of Management and Budget oversees federal spending, is examining which priorities can move forward using money already appropriated by Congress, two of the people said.
He also wants to change federal grant rules to give political appointees more say in which government programs receive taxpayer money, they said, potentially giving the White House more influence over federal spending without seeking congressional approval.
Trump has been briefed on the preparations and has taken part in discussions about them, the White House official said.
When asked how comfortable Trump would be governing through executive authority under a Democratic Congress, one of the people said, “very comfortable.”
GOVERNING WITHOUT CONGRESS
Trump has already tested the reach of presidential power since returning to office in January 2025, using executive authority to impose sweeping tariffs, intensify immigration enforcement, shrink the federal workforce, and pursue foreign-policy goals including the war against Iran without Congress’ approval or new laws.
A major exception was Trump’s massive package of tax and spending cuts that was passed by the Republican-controlled Congress and signed into law by the president in July 2025.
“President Trump in the last two years has basically ignored Congress and tried to do as much as possible through executive orders and executive power,” said Nathan Gonzales, editor at Inside Elections, which provides nonpartisan political analysis. “I think he will only continue if there are Democratic majorities.”
Trump has repeatedly invoked national emergencies to expand his ability to act without new legislation. Congress can vote to end those emergencies, but Trump could veto such a move, requiring two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override him.
A Democratic Congress could still create significant obstacles.
Control of the Senate would allow Democrats to block Trump’s judicial and executive-branch nominees, including any Supreme Court pick.
“I would anticipate they will be very reluctant to approve any of the president’s appointments,” said Andrew Busch, a public policy professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and author of a history of midterm elections.
Democrats could also refuse to pass Trump-backed legislation. But Trump could veto Democratic legislation he doesn’t like, and Democrats are unlikely to have enough votes in the House to override him.
Courts could block executive actions that exceed Trump’s legal authority. The White House plans to seek legal opinions from the Justice Department to determine what Trump can do without Congress and how to defend those actions if they are challenged in court, one of the people said.
DEMOCRATIC INVESTIGATIONS
One challenge, however, cannot be sidestepped through executive action: congressional investigations.
Reuters previously reported that senior House Democrats and committee aides have discussed using hearings, subpoenas and document requests to examine whether Trump has used his presidential power to benefit himself, allies or donors.
Trump aides have been preparing for that prospect for months, all three people said.
White House lawyers have been briefing political appointees and agency leaders on how to handle congressional inquiries, document requests and subpoenas, one person said. They have advised officials to be careful about what they put in writing.
They also sought a Justice Department opinion that could allow Trump to invoke executive privilege to shield communications with private advisers from congressional scrutiny, the person said.
(Reporting by Nandita Bose and Tim Reid in Washington; Editing by Colleen Jenkins and Alistair Bell)

Lenovo LOQ 15: The Only Gaming Laptop Worth Buying Below $1,500
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Prices on gaming laptops are out of control. The ongoing memory shortage has made laptops more expensive across the board, but it's hit gaming laptops especially hard. Some manufacturers have even resorted to launching “new" gaming laptops in 2026 with the RTX 4050 as the starting configuration—and that graphics card is more than three years old.
Given this landscape, there's really only one gaming laptop under $1,500 that I feel comfortable recommending. That's the Lenovo LOQ 15. It's not the thinnest or most powerful gaming laptop in the world, but for this price, there's nothing else like it.
It's not that the price of the LOQ 15 hasn't gone up over the past year alongside its gaming-laptop brethren. (It certainly has.) For the first few months of 2026—the good old days—it was selling for less than $1,000. But even then, it was technologically ahead of its rivals in a number of ways, offering strong performance paired with a high-quality IPS display. So many cheap gaming laptops come with pitifully desaturated screens that put a damper on the gaming experience. That's really what sets the LOQ 15 apart from the competition.
Also significant is the fact that, right now, you can buy the LOQ 15 with an RTX 5060 for just $1,300. That's not any cheaper than it normally has been (at least not for the past few months). However, the RTX 5060 is a big upgrade over the RTX 5050, especially with the 100 watts of power that the system can throw at it. Every game I tested could play at well over 60 frames per second at the medium preset, including heavier games like Black Myth: Wukong and Monster Hunter Wilds. You can always push frame rates higher by adjusting settings further or by adding a dash of upscaling.
Amazon has the RTX 5060 configuration, which also comes with 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage, for $1,300, but Lenovo also has a killer deal on the RTX 5050 configuration that's about as cheap as it gets: $999 for an RTX 5050 (and otherwise identical specs). I've tested a number of other gaming laptops that sell for around this price, such as the MSI Cyborg A16 and the Acer Nitro V 16, and none can compete with the LOQ 15. I've also tested the Alienware 15 and Lenovo LOQ Essential 15 recently, and both suffer from the same problem.
As much as I wish I could recommend a budget gaming laptop that's newer, none I've tried have successfully dethroned the Lenovo LOQ 15. While you could wait until Black Friday to see if prices dip further, note that I haven't seen much fluctuation over the past few months. For example, it wasn't on a deeper sale during the October Amazon Prime Day—and yet, it was still the best gaming laptop deal you could get.

Binance covers 90% of $6.3 billion hack losses, but what about the rest?
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance says it has replenished 90% of the assets stolen in a $6.3 billion cyberattack, but replacing the remaining funds could take longer because some cryptocurrencies are harder to obtain, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the company's latest recovery update, the proportion of replenished assets has increased from 80% to 90%, with Binance continuing to purchase replacement tokens through public markets and over-the-counter transactions.
The exchange confirmed that 10 major cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Tether (USDT), BNB, Solana (SOL), USD Coin (USDC), XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and Zcash (ZEC), are now fully backed by reserves.
Why is the remaining 10% taking longer?
Binance explained that the outstanding assets consist of less liquid cryptocurrencies, meaning they are not as readily available for purchase in large quantities.
Unlike widely traded cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, these tokens may require additional time to acquire without disrupting market conditions.
The company said it is working with industry partners to secure the remaining assets and intends to continue purchasing replacement tokens until all affected cryptocurrencies are fully backed.
Importantly, replenishing stolen assets does not mean the stolen funds themselves have been recovered from the attackers. Binance is using its own financial resources to replace missing assets while separate efforts to trace and recover the stolen cryptocurrency continue.
Where is the replacement money coming from?
Binance identified three sources of funding: its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a portion of its Futures Insurance Fund, and corporate funds.
SAFU, established in 2018, serves as an emergency reserve designed to protect customers during exceptional incidents, including security breaches.
The company also pledged to replenish SAFU to approximately $1 billion after using part of the fund to cover losses.
Binance announced that it had taken a new Proof of Reserves snapshot on October 31, providing updated information about assets held by the exchange.
The company said preparing the complete cryptographic proof would take approximately 40 to 50 hours because of the computational resources required.
Once published, the results are expected to allow customers holding the 10 fully backed cryptocurrencies to independently verify that their assets are supported by reserves at a ratio of at least 1:1.
The complete verification results are expected by November 3.
Binance also identified restoring withdrawals as a priority, with services scheduled to resume in phases from November 1, subject to security checks.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that investigators had linked the $6.3 billion Binance hack to a North Korean state-backed hacking group, with stolen assets transferred across multiple blockchain networks.
