Are the Houthis attacking Mecca and Medina? Saudi claims ignite battle over Islam's holiest cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:26:49 UTC
20:26:49 KST

Houthi forces have been attacking Saudi Arabia relentlessly in recent months, launching missiles and drones toward targets including the capital Riyadh and the areas of Al-Kharj, Jeddah, Yanbu, Khamis Mushait and Najran. But when it comes to alleged attacks on Mecca and Medina, Islam's two holiest cities, the facts are far less clear. In recent weeks, Saudi authorities have repeatedly reported air raid alerts in both cities, while the Houthis have vehemently denied targeting either of them. For Muslims, Sunni and Shiite alike, the religious significance of the two cities is profound, as are the implications of attacking them.
Within the broader war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, another battle is now unfolding over which side is violating the sanctity of Islam's holiest sites and behaving like an "enemy of Islam."
On Friday morning, the Saudi-led coalition reported intercepting a drone that it said had been launched by the Houthis toward Mecca. Hours later, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree dismissed the allegation as fabricated. "Our operations target their oil facilities and military bases, and no one in the world believes these lies and fabrications," he said. Later that day, the coalition announced that it had intercepted another drone in the Medina area, prompting another Houthi denial.
Mecca is Islam's holiest city, regarded as the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad and home to the Grand Mosque, or Masjid al-Haram, the most sacred mosque in Islam. Within it stands the Kaaba, the ancient structure toward which Muslims around the world face during their daily prayers and the focal point of the annual Hajj pilgrimage. Medina, Islam's second-holiest city, is where Muhammad migrated from Mecca in an event known as the Hijra. It is also home to the Prophet's Mosque, where he is buried.
The Houthis regularly emphasize their connection to Islam and the Prophet Muhammad. In August, they held celebrations marking the Prophet's birthday in areas under their control. From the group's perspective, Saudi accusations that it is attacking Mecca and Medina amount to allegations that it is threatening Islam's most sacred places. The Houthis insist that Riyadh is exploiting the cities' religious significance for political purposes, while accusing the Saudi authorities themselves of violating their sanctity.
Claims and denials
The war of competing narratives has continued for weeks. The current round of escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began in July, while Saudi allegations of launches toward Mecca first emerged on September 15, when authorities reported alerts in several areas of the kingdom, including the holy city. The Houthi-affiliated Saba news agency quoted a military source categorically rejecting the accusation. "We strongly deny the existence of any threat from Yemen against the holy city of Mecca or any other sacred sites," the source said. "Promoting these reports is intended to tarnish our image and win sympathy from the Islamic world, a familiar tactic of the Saudi enemy."
Mohammed al-Farah, a member of the Houthi political bureau, also rejected the accusations. "The talk of an attack on Mecca from Yemen is a lie," he said. "Saudi Arabia is facing a real crisis. It is begging the international community and trying to mobilize Muslims using a false pretext to divert attention from its failure. The solution is clear: Stop the aggression, lift the blockade, leave Yemen alone and compensate Yemenis for the years of war and destruction."
The Saudi-led coalition subsequently issued a statement indicating that the alert in Mecca had been triggered by a Houthi drone launched toward the city and intercepted outside its boundaries. "This hostile attempt marks the second time Mecca has been attacked, following an initial attempt to launch a ballistic missile on July 27, 2017," the coalition said. It described the alleged attack as "a black stain on the history of the Houthis" and an attempt to provoke the religious feelings of millions of Muslims, stressing that "the security of the Two Holy Mosques is a red line."
On September 17, Houthi leader Abdul-Malik Badr al-Din al-Houthi rejected the Saudi accusation, saying the alleged attack was an invention that itself violated the sanctity of Mecca, a city sacred to all Muslims, particularly Yemenis. The following day, Houthi supporters demonstrated in areas under the group's control against Saudi Arabia and what they called "the lie about attacking Mecca." The denials continued into October. In a statement on October 16, Saree said: "The lies spread by the Saudi regime about targeting holy Mecca are fooling no one. They are the ones desecrating the holy city through immorality and debauchery. Yemen poses no threat to the holy sites. Our operations are directed against the regime's oil facilities and military bases, which are far from the holy places."
The Houthi political bureau also denied targeting Mecca, describing the accusation as "the biggest lie of our time." It said Mecca and all Islamic holy sites hold a sacred place in the hearts of Muslim peoples, particularly Yemenis, while accusing the Saudi authorities of exploiting the cities' religious significance for warfare. The statement also alleged that Saudi Arabia was desecrating Mecca by "hosting Zionist Jews," as the Houthis put it, and organizing parties characterized by debauchery and moral corruption. "The Saudi regime remembers the sanctity of Mecca only when it needs to exploit the holy sites to serve its positions," it said. Yemeni cartoonist and Houthi supporter Kamal Sharaf joined the campaign with a cartoon and video intended to demonstrate that the Houthis were attacking Aramco, the Saudi oil company, rather than the Kaaba.
‘An unforgivable act’: Turkey and Pakistan back Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia's partners in the "Mecca Defense Alliance," Turkey and Pakistan, backed Riyadh in the dispute. Pakistan's Foreign Ministry issued an official statement condemning the alleged Houthi attack on Mecca, while Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed outrage in a post on X on October 16. "The people of Pakistan feel deep sorrow and concern over this act," he wrote. "Words cannot describe the depth of the pain and grief we feel over this unforgivable act. We salute the vigilance, courage and professionalism of the Saudi forces for their swift action."
"Pakistan stands with Saudi Arabia in defending its sovereignty and territorial integrity, and in ensuring the security and sanctity of the Two Holy Mosques, a duty that every Pakistani carries deep in their heart," Sharif added. Turkey also issued official condemnations following the reports of an attempted attack on Mecca.
The allegations continued over the following weeks. On October 21, the Houthi military spokesman responded to a Saudi-led coalition announcement that drones had been intercepted, including in the Medina area. "The armed forces carried out no military operations deep inside Saudi Arabia today," Saree said. "The Saudi enemy's claim that drones were intercepted over Medina is a lie and a smear against our honorable and courageous people and armed forces."
On October 24, Saudi Civil Defense reported debris falling in several locations following the interception of two ballistic missiles allegedly launched by the Houthis toward the Mecca and Medina regions. According to the Saudi account, fragments fell in Wadi al-Marmas in Mecca, the Al-Nuzha neighborhood in the Jeddah area, Wadi Jalil in the Taif area and the Rabigh district. The Houthis again denied targeting the holy cities, maintaining that their military operations were directed against oil facilities and military bases. In recent weeks, Houthi officials have also repeatedly warned that Saudi airspace is "unsafe," while explicitly excluding the skies over Mecca and Medina from those threats.
On Friday, Houthi government spokesman Omar al-Buhaiti brought Israel into the dispute, alleging that Saudi Arabia and its "Zionist partner" were plotting to attack Islamic holy sites and blame Yemen. "The Saudi enemy's repeated claim that Yemen has attempted to target holy sites reveals malicious intentions already harbored by the Saudi enemy and its Zionist partner," he said. "We hold the Saudi regime fully responsible for any harm, attack or plot targeting the holy sites in Mecca and Medina." He warned that any attack on the Two Holy Mosques by what he called the Saudi enemy would have "devastating consequences" for Riyadh. The accusations against Israel were made without supporting evidence.
Where does the truth lie? ‘The Saudis have an interest’
For now, Saudi Arabia continues to accuse the Houthis, and the Houthis continue to issue categorical denials. But conclusive evidence that Mecca and Medina themselves have been targeted remains lacking. That raises a fundamental question: Are the Houthis really aiming at the two cities, and would they have any reason to attack places that hold such profound religious significance for them as well?
Dr. Yoel Guzansky, a former Israeli National Security Council official and senior researcher who heads the Gulf program at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told ynet that the issue is exceptionally sensitive. He questioned whether the Houthis had actually fired toward the two cities. "It is completely contrary to the Houthis' interests, because doing so could unite the entire Islamic world in opposition to them," he said.
"The Saudis have an interest in showing that the Houthis are attacking Islam's holy sites, Mecca and Medina," Guzansky explained. "That could help them mobilize legitimacy and international support, especially from Pakistan, Turkey and other countries whose assistance Saudi Arabia wants. It could be presented as, 'Here we are, coming to defend Islam's holy sites because Saudi Arabia is in trouble.'"
But he warned that repeatedly invoking the holy cities could also backfire on Riyadh. "The more the Saudis use this, the more dangerous it could become for them. It could create an image of weakness: 'Are they incapable of protecting Mecca and Medina?'"
According to Guzansky, there have been no confirmed strikes on either city. "There were warnings issued to the population, but there were no impacts in those areas, which raises further questions because there have been impacts elsewhere," he said. "The Saudis are taking their struggle with the Houthis into the religious arena as well. That's why I think they may be cautiously bringing Mecca and Medina into the picture. They want to portray the Houthis as infidels and present their actions as being directed against religion."

These tattoos can magically disappear—here’s how they work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:25:41 UTC
20:25:41 KST

How handy would it be if you could make your tattoos invisible for a job interview in the morning, and reveal them again for a party in the evening? This sounds like science fiction, but it may soon be reality.
Researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder have developed invisible tattoo ink than can be revealed with a UV torch and stays visible until switched off with white light. They have published their research in the journal Matter & Light.
They created different motifs with this ink ranging from a lantern that reveals its light when activated, to multicolored scales like those in the much-loved children’s book The Rainbow Fish.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The pigments used in these inks are so-called photochromic dyes(from the Greek “photos”, which means “light” and “chroma”, which means “color”). In other words, they are compounds that change colour when exposed to light. These dyes have been used for years in color-changing sunglasses.
Light carries energy, and photochromic compounds are designed in such a way that this energy is enough to cause a chemical change that alters the shape and therefore the properties of the molecule.
In the case of the “invisible” tattoo ink, two or three seconds of bright ultraviolet (UV) light is enough to form a new ring in the dye molecule, which switches a colorless pigment to a colored one. A variety of colors are available depending on the exact structure of the molecule.
A blast of bright white light reverses the reaction, breaking the ring and turning the colour off again. For a long time, the challenge with this chemistry was that the colored form of the dye was relatively unstable and quickly reverted to the more stable, colorless form—especially at higher temperatures.
Another issue was fatigue: after a certain number of on-off cycles, the dyes degraded and took on a permanent coloured hue. Have you ever bought transition lens sunglasses and noticed that they became less effective over time? This is due to the same deterioration of photochromic compounds in the lenses. But thanks to recent research efforts, remarkably stable dyes have been designed that reliably hold their colour for months and can undergo over 10,000 activation and deactivation cycles without degrading.
Carson Bruns’ team at the University of Colorado Boulder showed that these pigments could be formulated into tattoo inks by encapsulating them in poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA), a polymer approved for medical use in bone cement, dentures and intraocular lenses. This family of inks is known as PhotoTat.
Time to market
So, when will you be able to get one of these switchable tattoos? A red pigment was already launched in 2024 under the name Magic Ink by Colorado-based biotech company Hyprskn. A 2 millilitre (ml) vial will set you back £77, which is about 100 times more expensive than regular tattoo ink due to the specialised dyes and formulation process required. The ink is fully compliant with the EU’s Reach (Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals) safety regulations.
Now, Bruns’ research team has developed three more PhotoTat inks – blue, magenta and yellow – that can combine into 16 other colours. “So far,” Bruns says, “the only person who’s tested this ink is me. I actually have hundreds of these tattoos on my legs now and they’ve all gone really well.”
Some challenges remain though: direct sunlight contains enough UV radiation to activate the tattoos unless they are protected by sunscreen. Indoor light will slowly switch them off over a period of several days.
In addition, the blue ink currently degrades after only 10–100 activations, leaving a permanent, purple-coloured mark. Most importantly, the inks need to undergo thorough toxicity and safety testing before they can be rolled out to tattoo shops for general use, which will likely take several years. Don’t get your hopes up just yet about your new “business during the day, party at night” look.
When Hyprskn launched Magic Ink, the reception in the tattoo community was mixed. While some tattoo enthusiasts viewed it as a revolutionary creative tool, others thought it was an overpriced gimmick. Bruns does not only see his photochromic tattoo inks as fashion accessories, however.
He also envisages medical applications, for example for patients who need permanent skin markings to guide radiation therapy or identify sites for biopsies. Bruns argues that these markings “become a permanent reminder of a traumatic experience” which can be mitigated by making the tattoo invisible once it is no longer needed in a clinical setting.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

====================================================================================================

New public spending category PDEL is a welcome and could have big impact | Heather Stewart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:22:07 UTC
20:22:07 KST

John Healey’s debut budget was far from a blockbuster, but it may come to be remembered for the birth of a plucky new character in the tax and spend universe – little PDEL.
It may not have the charm of Disney’s Wall-E, but PDEL (pronounced P-Del), or preventative departmental expenditure limit, to give it its full name, marks a welcome, and potentially very consequential, addition.
The chancellor made clear that ahead of what the Institute for Fiscal Studies has said will be a “brutal” spending review next year, the Treasury is prepared to ringfence the budget for preventive policies.
The impetus for the move came partly from No 10. Andy Burnham knows that to achieve some of the missions closest to his heart, such as tackling rough sleeping, he will have to make the argument that it’s worth spending more upfront to save the state in the longer term.
It’s an intuitive idea, yet it’s not how the government tends to think about spending – and it’s certainly not how the Treasury makes decisions.
In the cut and thrust of a spending review, a process in which the Treasury’s power over the public purse is at its most muscular, individual departments are under pressure to show how they will save money from their own budgets.
Yet many of society’s greatest challenges have impacts across several departments. The future savings made by spending on, say, family hubs, may show up years in the future, and across several other departments – in the welfare bill, the health budget, even the criminal justice system.
In a 2023 paper that introduced the idea of PDEL, the thinktank Demos identified £22bn of costs to government that it claimed could have been averted by preventive programmes.
“For decades, governments have talked about the importance of prevention, but the system has consistently rewarded spending on dealing with crises rather than stopping them from happening in the first place,” said Demos’s chief executive, Polly Curtis.
In the Treasury documents that accompany the spending review, and more importantly in the months of wrangling beforehand, PDEL will have its own storyline, alongside RDEL – day-to-day, or “resource” spending for each department, and CDEL – investment.
It sounds technical, and it is – but we have plenty of evidence that the way public spending is categorised changes the way it is debated and understood.
Before Labour came to power in 1997, day-to-day spending and investment were not formally separated in the public finances, but Gordon Brown was rightly keen for long-term investment and day-to-day spending to be considered separately.
Disaggregating RDEL and CDEL allowed him to set the “golden rule” – that it was fine for the government to borrow to invest, but current spending should be covered by taxation.
Separating out capital spending didn’t prevent the Tories raiding it repeatedly during the austerity years – and indeed, Whitehall departments have just been asked to cut back future capital budgets to fund the defence investment plan.
But it does allow additional scrutiny, and a new kind of conversation about which areas of public spending are most important.
Demos’s argument is that some kinds of day-to-day spending, while not “investment”, in strict accounting terms, are worth protecting, because scrapping them could bring short-term cash benefits but carry net costs to the government over time.
Gavin Kelly, the chief executive of the Nuffield Foundation, which funds social research, says the shift to thinking about preventive spending makes sense now, because we have better data to inform policymakers.
He points to a series of IFS studies, funded by Nuffield, which showed Labour’s Sure Start centres boosted children’s education performance, increased their future wages, and even reduced hospital admissions, for example.
“Over the last decade, we’ve become more able to forensically link datasets across different aspects of services, illuminating how decisions in one public service can go on to impact other services and outcomes. That wasn’t possible in the same way in the past. The agility of decision-making about how and where we spend has not kept up with some of these data advances.”
Healey offered precious few details in the budget as to how PDEL will be defined but the Treasury says departments will have to make the argument for individual projects to be considered as preventive.
Rough sleeping is one area it highlights. Alan Milburn appears poised to make a similar argument in his soon-to-be-published review into young people not in education, employment or training, saying that money spent now on employment support potentially saves future costs on welfare, health and housing. Demos also highlights early mental health support and obesity prevention.
It does not seem beyond the bounds of possibility that, if defined tightly enough, preventive spending could even come to be considered “investment,” for the purposes of the fiscal rules, though the Treasury says that is not the plan.
That would mean the government being prepared to borrow today to fund projects it strongly believes would save money over time – a similar logic to the argument for investment in bridges or roads, but with a more social slant.
However, no amount of accounting tweaks can disguise the fact that, based on the figures Healey set out in the budget, next year’s spending review – which could take place as late as the autumn – looks impossibly tough.
He clearly hopes better news will come along, to ease the squeeze. But you can’t ringfence your way out of what the IFS reckons is £27bn-worth of spending pressures.
Against that bleak narrative arc, it remains to be seen if PDEL can play a starring role, or turns out to be just a side character. But perhaps it can at least help to bring some longer-term thinking to bear.

US midterms 2026: 52 million vote early, including the Pope, as Israel ad divides Democrats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:22:00 UTC
20:22:00 KST

With just 48 hours remaining before Americans head to the polls in the November 3 midterm elections, the United States is making final preparations for a vote widely seen as a referendum on President Donald Trump's performance. Republicans face the possibility of losing control of both houses of Congress, potentially complicating Trump's ability to advance his agenda during the final two years of his presidency. Trump is expected to participate in at least two Republican campaign rallies Sunday, hoping to mobilize conservative voters and prevent a "blue wave" that would hand Democrats majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives.
The urgency was evident at campaign rallies over the weekend. Trump appeared at an event in Daytona, Florida, where he told supporters that "these are the most important midterm elections ever." Meanwhile, Democrats enlisted former President Bill Clinton for a rally in Tupelo, Mississippi. Clinton delivered a similar message, invoking another former president, Republican George W. Bush. "My friend George Bush once said, 'Democracy corrects itself,'" Clinton told the crowd. "We're about to find out in Mississippi whether that's true."
More than 52 million Americans have already cast ballots through early voting, over 10 million more than at the equivalent point in the 2022 midterm elections. Particularly sharp increases have been recorded in states with closely contested Senate races, including Iowa and Kansas, where early voting has surged by approximately 30%. Trump plans to visit both states Sunday. In Kansas, he is seeking to help Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who trails Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton by 2.6 percentage points in the RealClearPolling average. In Iowa, Trump is campaigning for Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, currently a member of the House of Representatives, who holds a narrow polling lead of about 0.5 percentage points over Democrat Josh Turek.
Among those who voted early was Pope Leo XIV, who made history over the weekend as the first sitting pope known to cast a ballot in a U.S. general election. Leo, the first American-born leader of the Catholic Church, submitted a mail-in ballot from the Vatican. The Vatican said the pontiff, born Robert Prevost in Chicago, believes in civic participation and has "exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen whenever he was eligible to do so," including during the more than 20 years he spent in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop.
As an American citizen living abroad, Leo was able to vote by absentee ballot, despite also serving as the sovereign of Vatican City. His choices remain private, but his participation attracted attention following a series of disagreements with Trump over the past year. The president has criticized the pope for repeatedly condemning the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran and calling for humane treatment of migrants amid the administration's aggressive immigration enforcement operations through Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Earlier this year, Trump called Leo "weak" and described him as captive to the radical left. The pope responded: "I am not afraid of the Trump administration, and I am not afraid to speak loudly about the message of the Gospel."
Trump's fight to hold the Senate: keeping at least 50 seats
Midterm elections are held halfway through a president's four-year term. Americans elect representatives to Congress as well as governors, state legislators, attorneys general and other officials. They are often regarded as a national judgment on the incumbent president, whose party has historically tended to lose ground in these contests. The focus is on Congress because a president whose party controls both chambers enjoys greater freedom to advance legislation. When the opposition controls Congress, the president can become a political "lame duck," facing substantial obstacles to implementing his agenda.
The Senate, Congress' upper chamber, has 100 seats, two for each of the 50 states. Senators serve six-year terms, with roughly one-third of the chamber up for election every two years. The Senate confirms presidential appointments, including Cabinet secretaries, ambassadors and federal judges, and has the power to convict and remove a president following impeachment. The House of Representatives has 435 members, all elected every two years. Seats are allocated according to population: California, for example, has 52 representatives, while Alaska has just one. Legislation approved by the House generally also requires Senate approval and the president's signature to become law.
Republicans currently hold narrow control of both chambers. In the House, they have 218 seats compared with 214 Democrats, alongside one independent who generally leans Republican and two vacant seats. In the Senate, Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, meaning they can afford to lose three seats and still retain control through Vice President JD Vance's tie-breaking vote in a 50-50 chamber.
The party enters the elections under considerable pressure. Polling has indicated for months that Democrats could take control of the House, while the surge in gasoline prices following the war with Iran has intensified the contest for the Senate. Races have become unexpectedly competitive in traditionally conservative states, including Texas, Kansas and Alaska.
Michigan Democrats clash over Israel: ‘Take Israel out of the explanation’
One of the most closely watched Senate contests is in Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is facing Republican Mike Rogers. The race has become increasingly contentious following renewed divisions within the Democratic Party over Israel, particularly between El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens, whom he narrowly defeated in the Democratic primary.
El-Sayed, a Muslim candidate from the party's progressive wing and an outspoken critic of Israel, defeated Stevens, a moderate Democrat with pro-Israel positions who received backing from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), by less than one percentage point. Democratic leaders had hoped the two would put the bitter primary behind them and unite ahead of the general election. Instead, the dispute has intensified in the final days of the campaign.
Although Stevens declared after her primary defeat that she would vote for El-Sayed and encouraged her supporters to do the same, tensions resurfaced when her fiancé, Jason Turkish, announced that he intended to vote for Rogers. Hours later, Stevens appeared on CNN and reiterated that she would personally support El-Sayed, but urged his campaign to "stop the hate and condemn it" and rebuild its relationship with Jewish and Black voters.
For a brief period Thursday, it appeared that the two Democrats might reconcile. They even coordinated a joint appearance at a campaign event scheduled for Sunday at a Detroit church. But on Friday, Stevens published a lengthy social media statement criticizing El-Sayed and demanding that he condemn a controversial advertisement linking U.S. support for Israel to rising grocery prices. The ad, produced by an outside political action committee supporting El-Sayed, had already provoked considerable backlash.
The advertisement depicts an American couple shopping at a supermarket and struggling to decide which groceries they can afford. The woman asks her husband to put back a carton of eggs intended for their children. When he asks, "They don't like eggs anymore?" she replies: "No, they like eggs. But we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians."
She goes on to claim that the United States provides Israel with billions of dollars to finance the war in Gaza, leaving American taxpayers to foot the bill. When her husband notes that Israelis also have universal health care, she replies: "Yeah, we're probably paying for that too." He then puts the bananas back on the shelf as well.
Stevens represents a district in suburban Detroit with a substantial Jewish community. In her statement, she criticized El-Sayed for repeatedly bringing Israel into discussions about domestic economic hardship. "Abdul promises to get money out of politics. He can start by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michiganders cannot afford," she wrote.
Following her remarks, El-Sayed's campaign asked Stevens not to attend Sunday's church event. When reporters asked whether he wanted her to appear alongside him, El-Sayed avoided a direct answer, saying she "wants to talk about other things." Asked explicitly whether Stevens was "deliberately trying to sabotage" his campaign, he laughed and replied: "That's not a question for me."
El-Sayed has recently apologized for some of his past statements in an effort to unite Democratic voters. But in a statement Friday, he highlighted his primary victory over Stevens and suggested that she appeared "determined to relitigate the primary." He urged supporters to focus on defeating Rogers.
Rogers, who trails El-Sayed by approximately 3.5 percentage points in polling and has been courting Jewish Democratic voters, praised Stevens as "a courageous leader deserving the respect of every Michigan voter." He said she was "absolutely right" to demand that El-Sayed condemn the anti-Israel advertisement. "It is shameful and disappointing that his response to her comments makes clear he doesn't care about these concerns," Rogers wrote on X. He also said Stevens would be welcome at his campaign events.
Trump has meanwhile launched sharp personal attacks on El-Sayed. In statements criticizing the Democratic candidate, the president highlighted his Muslim identity, called him a "jihadist," accused him of siding with terrorists and even compared him with the terrorists responsible for the September 11 attacks.
Dan Sullivan versus Dan Sullivan: Alaska's unusual Senate controversy
Another controversy is intensifying in Alaska, where the Senate race has been overshadowed by the candidacy of Dan J. Sullivan, a former teacher and U.S. Forest Service employee with little name recognition or political experience. His entry into the race this summer immediately raised suspicions among Republicans because he shares a first and last name with the incumbent Republican senator, Dan S. Sullivan.
Republicans have accused the newcomer of running as a spoiler candidate intended to confuse voters and draw votes away from the incumbent, potentially helping Democratic candidate Mary Peltola win the seat. With recent polls showing Peltola ahead by approximately 1.2 percentage points, even a small shift in voting could become politically significant.
The controversy escalated over the weekend after Michael Heyman, the U.S. attorney for Alaska, confirmed that a federal criminal investigation into the candidacy of Dan J. Sullivan had been underway for several months. Heyman said additional law enforcement resources had been sent to Alaska following a New York Times report alleging that people associated with Peltola's campaign had been involved in recruiting the namesake candidate.
The Justice Department has issued subpoenas requiring witnesses to appear before a grand jury, as well as requests for documents and the preservation of records that could assist investigators. No criminal charges have been announced against those involved in the race.
Trump last week called for Peltola and her campaign officials to face criminal prosecution. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche also accused Democrats of "cheating," saying: "They're trying to take votes away from the incumbent senator, not by running a campaign and not by competing on the issues, but by putting up a person with the same name."
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, ordered a separate state investigation. He said the New York Times report revealed "troubling new evidence" of an organized effort to deliberately confuse voters and divert their ballots. The state investigation is distinct from the federal criminal probe.
Peltola denied Thursday that she had any knowledge of an effort to recruit Dan J. Sullivan to confuse supporters of the Republican incumbent. She insisted that she had "no interest in misleading voters" and accused Republicans of using the controversy to distract from their own record.
"They can't win on their record, so they're trying to intimidate me into backing down," Peltola said. "This is just another distraction while they dodge accountability for the skyrocketing cost of living we're facing because of their tariffs and endless wars. It won't work."
Dan J. Sullivan has also denied for months that he entered the race at the request of Democrats and insists he has had no contact with Peltola's campaign.
With Americans preparing to vote Tuesday, the fight for control of Congress has become intertwined with disputes over Israel, accusations of electoral manipulation and unusually personal political confrontations. For Trump, the immediate objective is to hold enough Republican seats to preserve the Senate majority and avoid facing an opposition-controlled Congress for the remainder of his term.

Tehran, New Delhi hold talks to deepen ties in technology sector

Tehran, New Delhi hold talks to deepen ties in technology sector
TEHRAN – Iran and India have discussed ways to expand cooperation in information and communication technology (ICT), promote specialized exchanges, and strengthen coordination in international forums.
ICT Minister Sattar Hashemi and India’s Ambassador to Iran, Vishwesh Negi, held a meeting on Saturday to explore the two countries’ capacities for joint initiatives in the sector, Mehr News Agency reported.
 
The discussions focused on identifying opportunities for cooperation between government bodies and private-sector ICT stakeholders, enhancing professional interactions, and making greater use of the two countries’ scientific, technical, and technological capabilities.
Given the respective capacities and the regional and international standing of Iran and India, both parties underlined the need for the promotion of cooperation and coordination within specialized international forums and organizations, particularly those related to the ICT sector.
The officials also highlighted the importance of harmonizing views, participating in ongoing consultations, and strengthening joint initiatives to ensure a more effective presence on the international stage.
The two sides agreed to continue discussions, follow up on the discussed issues, and enhance ties in areas of mutual interest.
Tech ties with India in key sectors
In February, Hashemi, in a meeting with Indian Minister of Electronics and Information Technology, Jitin Prasada, voiced the country’s readiness for the expansion of scientific and technological ties with India in key sectors, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity, and the digital economy.
The officials met on the sidelines of the India AI Impact Summit 2026, being conducted in person at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, from February 16 to 20, IRIB reported.
During the meeting, Hashemi highlighted the capabilities of the two sides in emerging technologies. Referring to Iran’s strong scientific and human infrastructure, he said the country has taken great strides in advancing modern technologies.
The official went on to say that India is one of the global hubs for software development, a powerful country with high capacity in developing and exporting IT, cybersecurity, and AI. So, promoting technological ties between the two countries will lead to the formation of a digital powerhouse.
According to Hashemi, enhancing interactions between the private sectors is among the top priorities. “We are interested in developing operational cooperation in large language models (LLMs), the development of an AI joint platform in the agriculture sector, and the establishment of innovative centers to utilize AI in different fields,” he said.
Highlighting the importance of securing critical infrastructure in the years ahead and India’s capacity in training specialized human resources, Hashemi announced Iran’s readiness to share experiences in cyber threats, combating emerging malware, and strengthening the security of financial infrastructure.
The ICT minister also proposed developing a joint fund to support Iranian and Indian startups, holding joint technological events, and talent exchange programs, allocating special zones in the technology parks of the two countries, and facilitating the issuance of ‘tech visas’ for IT professionals as practical ways to foster cooperation.
For his part, Prasada underscored expanding collaboration between the two sides, saying that India is willing to expand ties with Iran via sharing expertise in AI and cybersecurity, holding workshops on training specialized human resources, and kicking off operational cooperation in collaborative technological projects.
“Establishing joint innovation centers and exchanging experts would help accelerate technological development in both countries, strengthen digital infrastructure, and improve data security,” Prasada noted.

Portugal police storm housing protest camps in Lisbon, Porto

Portugal police storm housing protest camps in Lisbon, Porto
November 1, 2026
Police on Sunday cleared out protest camps in Portugal's capital, Lisbon, and Porto after thousands of housing protesters marched against a rental bill.
Around 4:30 a.m. local time (0430 GMT), dozens of officers moved in to dismantle camps in Lisbon's Rossio Square and Porto's Dom Joao I Square, where participants had set up tents following peaceful marches against soaring housing costs on Saturday.
Police used shields and batons to disperse protesters, and said some of the demonstrators threw bottles and paint at officers as they stormed the camps.
Police arrest 13 in Lisbon, Porto
Six people were arrested in Lisbon and seven in Porto for refusing orders to disperse, according to a police statement. It said 13 police were injured as they tried to take down the camps, with eight taken to hospital.
The statement also said an unspecified number of civilians were also injured.
Meanwhile, one of the lawyers representing those detained in Porto said the police response was disproportionate, arguing that both the size of the operation and the actions were excessive.
Activist group Acampada Lisboa said more than 30 protesters were injured, including 10 who required hospital treatment.
It called a fresh rally against the police operation in the capital on Sunday afternoon. "We will not be silenced," the group said in a statement posted on social media.
Portugal's housing crisis
Hours before the eviction, more than 1,000 people marched through central Lisbon to protest against Portugal's deepening housing crisis.
Demonstrators are calling for the country's minority center-right government to scrap plans that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases.
Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro has ruled out withdrawing the bill, though he has acknowledged that modifications could be made before the final vote.
Portugal is facing one of Europe's most severe housing crises, with house prices more than doubling since 2017.

Moscow Reports Drone Attack On Nizhny Novgorod As Russian Strikes Cut Power In Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:20:00 UTC
20:20:00 KST

Moscow and Kyiv traded strikes on November 1, with dozens of drones reportedly destroyed over Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region and energy infrastructure hit in four Ukrainian regions, leaving hundreds of thousands without power.
The governor of Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, Gleb Nikitin, said that an "industrial enterprise" in the Kstovo district had been struck by a "massive drone attack" overnight, causing "significant damage."
He added that more than 100 drones were destroyed in the attack, with no casualties reported so far.
Ukrainian media reports suggested the strike had hit the LukOil refinery in Kstovo as well as the combined heat and power plant in Novogorkovskaya. RFE/RL could not independently verify the information.
The development came less than 24 hours after the Ukrainian military said it targeted the Russian state-owned Kombinat Kamensky chemical and defense enterprise in Russia's Rostov region with drones and Neptune coastal missile systems.
Bordering Ukraine, the region is a strategically important industrial and logistics hub in southwestern Russia. Last month, Reuters reported that Russia had nearly finished building a major new base for launching jet-powered drones there in just six weeks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that the October 31 attack on the Rostov region had caused tens of millions of dollars' worth of damage, as Kyiv seeks to curb Moscow's war efforts with what it calls "long-range sanctions," referring to its strikes inside Russia.
With the Kremlin showing no interest in compromising to end the war while continuing to pound Ukraine with devastating strikes, the country's military has increasingly responded by targeting energy and military sites deep inside Russia.
On November 1, Zelenskyy said Russia attacked energy infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, leaving hundreds of thousands without power as cold weather sets in accross the Eastern Europe.
"Just this night, our energy sector in four regions was under Russian attacks: Dnipro, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytsky. These are substations, transformers, and power lines that provide electricity to our people's homes," he wrote on Telegram.
"Repair crews are working everywhere. As of now, hundreds of thousands of families remain without electricity," Zelenskyy said, adding that this week along Russia has launched 1,940 strike drones, over 1,580 glide bombs, and 44 missiles of various types over Ukraine, 36 of which are ballistic.
"The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic interceptors," he added.
The Ukrainian military said Russian forces attacked the country with 433 drones just on November 1 and that the drones were fired from Oryol and Shatalovo in Russia, as well as the Russian-occupied region of Donetsk.
Last Day Of Oleshky Cease-Fire
The evacuation of residents from the Russian-occupied southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been completed as Moscow and Kyiv continued a localized cease-fire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump on November 1.
Trapped in the largely ruined city, which was surrounded by land mines and cut off from the outside world, Oleshky residents had endured extreme conditions for months, with little to no access to food, drinking water, medicine, or electricity.
On October 30, dozens of buses carrying civilians left the war-torn area for the first time in more than four years without incident, with people choosing whether to travel to Ukrainian- or Russian-controlled territory.
Melania Trump said on November 1 that "the ceasefire across Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack."
"Let Oleshky become the starting point for lasting peace," she wrote on X. 
Zelenskyy, thanking the United States and Melania Trump for their mediation, said residents who wished to travel to Ukraine had crossed into the country on October 31.
"Until we got on the buses, we were still afraid," Oleshky evacuee Liubov told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service. "We were so worried and nervous. Before that, we couldn't sleep at night, wondering how this would go."
While the humanitarian efforts in Oleshky have set a rare precedent for cooperation between Ukrainian and Russian civilian representatives, the Kremlin said the temporary cease-fire there should not be extrapolated to the broader peace settlement process in Ukraine.
Moscow has repeatedly said it was not seeking a partial easing of the conflict, urging a complete resolution that would include its hard-line demands, including full control over Ukrainian territories that Russian forces have been unable to seize on the battlefield.
Zelenskyy, in turn, has been for years calling for a leaders' meeting in response, saying that issues surrounding control of Ukrainian territories have to be discussed at the highest level.
As Russian and Ukrainian officials are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi in mid-November amid US-mediated negotiations to end the war, a senior Russian official said that Russian President Vladimir Putin would respond if Zelenskyy wished to speak to him by phone.
"I think he will, of course. Putin has never refused to talk," Putin aide Yuri Ushakov was quoted as telling Russian media on November 1.
Putin has previously sought to cast doubt on Zelenskyy's legitimacy and has repeatedly said the presidents could only meet when a comprehensive peace deal has been agreed, though he has also suggested he and Zelenskyy could meet in Moscow.
The Kremlin knows that the prospect of a meeting in the capital of the country that is attacking Ukraine is unacceptable to Kyiv. Zelenskyy has expressed readiness to meet with Putin in a third country.

New academic plan expands support for reservist students, career soldiers for 2026-27 school year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:19:25 UTC
20:19:25 KST

Israel’s universities and colleges have significantly expanded accommodations for military reservists and career soldiers across all fields of study under a new plan for the 2026-27 academic year, giving students whose extended service has disrupted their studies critical tools to keep up, the IDF announced on Sunday.
The plan builds on those introduced in the 2024-25 and 2025-26 academic years, strengthening support for students in uniform so they can maintain a regular academic routine despite long stretches of reserve duty.
At its core, the 2026-27 plan expands alternative assessment to all programs and fields of study. Options include submitting a paper instead of taking an exam, taking a modified exam, or counting the higher of two exam grades.
Students are grouped into tiers based on how much reserve duty they have served. Those in the top tier, along with career soldiers in frontline roles, will be eligible for alternative assessment in three courses, meaning they may submit papers instead of attending class. Students in the top tier who are not in frontline roles will be eligible for two courses. Students in the second tier, who served 21 days or more in a semester, will be eligible for one or two courses, depending on the nature of their service.
Students forced to extend their studies by a semester or a year to receive further aid
Students whose service forced them to extend their degree by a semester or a year will receive further help. They will remain entitled to the accommodations matching their reserve-duty tier or type of career service, to ensure they can graduate.
Reservists and career soldiers will also benefit from eased eligibility for merit scholarships, so their service does not cost them dean’s and rector’s awards. The minimum number of credits they need to qualify for these scholarships will be 10% lower than for other students, giving them a fair chance in the competition.
In graduate programs, universities will offer individual accommodations to students whose research has been set back by their service. These include extended deadlines, consideration regarding research grant payments, and a personalized accommodations plan, all aimed at helping them complete their research within a reasonable time.
Students applying for a master’s degree whose transcripts show a “binary pass” grade (a pass/fail grade adjusted for reserve duty), and where that grade affects admission, can reveal their actual grade to the admissions committee without affecting their undergraduate GPA.
The plan also extends eligibility to spouses: partners of career soldiers and frontline reservists who are parents of children up to age 13 will be included alongside career soldiers.
Lecture recordings will be kept for three months after the end of the semester
To help students catch up, lecture recordings will be kept for three months after the end of the semester in which the course was taught. The plan also provides one-on-one tutoring on missed material, rescheduled exam dates, and maximum credit exemptions.
“Following another long year in which career and reserve soldiers have proudly carried the country’s security on their shoulders, we face an unequivocal duty and demand: to see them and their needs when they go out to study as well. To prove that we care for them not only when they are in uniform, but also during their studies. The plan we created together with the Council for Higher Education provides a safety net that addresses needs arising authentically from the field. Those who serve are not asking for discounts; they are demanding fairness. It is our duty to make sure they receive as equal an opportunity as possible, and encounter fairness from all parties in actual deeds,” said Maj.-Gen. Dado Bar Kalifa, head of the IDF Personnel Directorate.

Iran to receive Russian Su-35 fighter jets after US-Iran war ends, IRGC spokesman says - report

2026-11-01
11:19:20 UTC
20:19:20 KST

Iran will reportedly receive Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets after the US-Iran war ends, Revolutionary Guards spokesman General Mohammad Akraminia told Iranian media on Sunday.
Akraminia claimed that before the war began at the end of February, the IRGC was in the final stages of procuring the fighter jets. He told the Persian-language outlet Tabnak that the Su-35s were meant to arrive before the war.
Akramina did not elaborate as to why they were not delivered before the fighting began.
“We had already completed the necessary preliminary work, including the procurement process and the signing of contracts. The necessary work concerning pilot training and instruction had also been completed, and there were no longer any problems in that regard,” he said.
“In fact, these aircraft were supposed to arrive before the war. God willing, we will certainly receive them after the war and upgrade our air fleet.”
Iran claims it plans to strengthen air defenses after war with US
Akraminia added that the IRGC plans to roll out more advanced aircraft, including the Su-35.
“We have also made progress domestically. Of course, purchasing equipment from abroad will bring us closer to advanced technologies, which we can then use as a foundation for further development,” he added.
While he did not specifically name Russia in the interview, it is the only established manufacturer of Su-35s. The fighter jet is Russian-designed and produced by Sukhoi, part of Russia's United Aircraft Corporation.
However, Russia allows other countries, including Iran, to operate the fighter jets.
Akraminia added that Iran is working to develop ground-based and airborne radar systems, as well as satellites to strengthen the country’s air defenses.
“When you operate an advanced aircraft such as the Su-35, you must also have ground-based systems, airborne systems, and satellite capabilities supporting it. Only then can the aircraft reach its full operational potential,” he added.
Akraminia noted that the US sanctions against Iran have made it difficult to rebuild the country’s military.
“Sometimes sanctions affect trade, goods, oil, and similar areas. But they also affect defense and military technologies,” he said.
“The Americans have absolutely refused to allow these new technologies to enter our country. They have imposed very severe sanctions.
“Everything we have achieved, all the capabilities you mentioned, has been developed domestically through the efforts of our own specialists and young people working in the country's defense industries, universities, and knowledge-based companies.”
He then claimed that during both wars with the US, Iran “did not use a single foreign-produced weapon.”

Lebanon charges 13 Hezbollah members over explosive shipment amid push to curb Iran's influence

2026-11-01
11:19:09 UTC

Lebanon’s Military Court has charged 13 members of Hezbollah in connection with the half-ton shipment of explosives seized from a vehicle traveling toward Beirut earlier this month, Lebanese officials announced over the weekend.
Judge Claude Ghanem issued charges against the 13 members of the terror group, including the two Hezbollah operatives arrested in the vehicle transporting the explosives, identified by Lebanese media as Ali Al Kurdi and Haitham Amhaz. However, only the two men named remain in Lebanese custody.
The defendants were charged with endangering state security, defying government decisions, membership in a banned organization, and possessing firearms and explosives.
While the National News Agency reported that the defendants could face up to 10 years in prison, Lebanese military courts have previously handed down lenient sentences to Hezbollah operatives accused of violating the country’s arms laws. In March, four Hezbollah members were released by the Military Court, presided over by Wassim Fayad, on symbolic bail of $21 after spending just six days in detention for possessing illegal weapons.
Explosives discovered at a checkpoint in Dahr al-Baidar in the Bekaa Valley earlier this month
The explosives were discovered at a checkpoint in Dahr al-Baidar in the Bekaa Valley earlier this month, prompting concerns that they could have been intended for a political assassination. Although Hezbollah claimed the explosives were destined for Israel, several Lebanese commentators noted that the materials seized were of the same types used in the truck bombing that killed former Lebanese prime minister Rafic Hariri. The Special Tribunal for Lebanon found that Hezbollah members were responsible for the attack, which killed 22 people and wounded hundreds.
Hezbollah has demanded the release of its operatives and the return of the 250 kilograms of TNT-type explosives and 250 kilograms of C4 seized in the operation. Both demands have so far been rejected.
The incident comes as Jerusalem awaits evidence that Beirut can contain the threat posed by Hezbollah as part of efforts to secure a lasting ceasefire.
According to the National News Agency, Hezbollah parliamentary bloc MP Hussein Hajj Hassan criticized the charges as “unfair and unjust,” alleging that the indictment violated the principles of the National Pact, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the United Nations Charter, and numerous Lebanese laws.
“The detainees and the other defendants were performing a national duty in defense of their country and the sovereignty of the state, and to protect the Lebanese people,” he claimed, despite recent polling indicating that most Lebanese want Hezbollah disarmed and the elected government to have sole authority over military decisions.
“They have no connection to the baseless accusations leveled against them by parties within and outside the government.
“These resistance fighters were not in a position to harm the security or safety of the state, but were confronting the Israeli enemy, which threatens Lebanon’s existence through its continued occupation and the assassinations, bombings, and destruction.”
Lebanese FM pushes back against Iran’s influence in the country
The charges come as Lebanon’s Foreign Minister Joe Rajji publicly pushes back against Iran’s influence in the country. Speaking on Saturday, Rajji said Lebanon would no longer allow its territory to be used to threaten the security of Arab countries, stressing that foreign policy decisions must be made in Beirut, according to the National News Agency.
“Lebanon will no longer accept its territory being used as a platform to threaten the security of its Arab brothers or as an advanced defense line serving the interests of other countries,” Rajji said during the Manama Dialogue in Bahrain.
“Foreign policy is decided in Beirut, and national security is exclusively the responsibility of the state.”
“Lebanon has long suffered the devastating consequences of the instrumentalization of these armed organizations for the benefit of foreign interests, as well as the hijacking of its national decision-making power to serve regional agendas foreign to the interests of the Lebanese people,” he said.

Rahul's Ramlila 'jalsa' to 'rub salt in wounds' of 1984 Sikh riot victims: Amit Shah

Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01

"Rahul Gandhi's November 1 'jalsa' in Delhi will only rub salt in wounds of anti-Sikh riot victims," Amit Shah said.
NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Sunday staunchly criticised Congress leader Rahul Gandhi for holding an INDIA bloc rally in Delhi's Ramlila Gound on the anniversary of the 1984 anti-Sikh riots.He said the "jalsa" would reopen painful memories for the victims and their families, accusing the Congress of showing little sensitivity towards the tragedy.Shah made the remarks in Chandigarh while addressing a gathering after inaugurating and laying the foundation stones for development projects worth Rs 258 crore.
"Rahul Gandhi's November 1 'jalsa' in Delhi will only rub salt in wounds of anti-Sikh riot victims," Shah was quoted as saying by the news agency PTI.The INDIA bloc held its 'Chalo Dilli' protest at Ramlila Maidan as part of its campaign against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.
Shah invokes memories of 1984 riots
Targeting the Congress over the violence, Shah said thousands of Sikhs were killed in Delhi on November 1, 1984. He recalled how families were torn apart, with people burnt alive, children orphaned, women widowed and homes destroyed.“The day the Sikh genocide happened, on that very day, they had to hold a rally,” Shah said, criticising the INDIA bloc for choosing the date for its protest.He also referred to a statement made by then Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi after the killings, saying he had watched it on television and could never forget it.
"And the then Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi gave a statement and I saw that on TV and I cannot forget that for rest of my life. He had said when a big tree falls, the earth shakes," he said.Shah added that only Congress leaders could make such a remark after thousands of Sikhs had been killed. He also said the Modi government reopened cases linked to the 1984 riots after coming to power in 2014, provided compensation of Rs 5 lakh to the next of kin of each victim and jailed prominent Congress leaders.“India has never witnessed, nor will it ever witness, riots of this kind, incited by a political party,” Shah said.
'Stay in mock Parliament if you want to be PM'
Shah also targeted Rahul Gandhi over the INDIA bloc's symbolic proceedings against CEC Gyanesh Kumar. On Saturday, opposition parties had held a mock 'public impeachment' of the poll panel chief, accusing him of facilitating electoral irregularities and demanding action against him.
Taking a swipe at Gandhi's political ambitions, Shah said the Congress leader should continue holding mock Parliament sessions if he wanted to become Prime Minister."If you want to become PM, stay in mock parliament your entire life. Your turn won't come," Shah said.He also referred to Gandhi's electoral defeats and took a dig at Sonia Gandhi's reported ambition to see her son become Prime Minister.Shah accused the opposition of disrupting Parliament, spreading falsehoods and creating disorder. He said such conduct would keep the INDIA bloc out of power.“Telling lies, spreading anarchy, not letting Parliament function, this is your 'fitrat' (true nature),” Shah said of the opposition.He also described Rahul Gandhi's 'mohabbat ki dukaan' slogan as a message of hatred, arguing that holding the rally on the anniversary of the 1984 riots showed a lack of sensitivity towards the victims.

Mediators continue US-Iran negotiations amid war rhetoric: What we know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:14:27 UTC
20:14:27 KST

Mediators continue US-Iran negotiations amid war rhetoric: What we know
Trump says latest talks ‘going fine’; while Iranian leaders say they favour diplomacy but are ready for maximum response if the US resumes war.
Iranian officials have been speaking with Qatari mediators about a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, in the latest effort to find a diplomatic path out of the US-Israel war on Iran that has caused a serious global energy crisis.
But even amid signs of diplomatic progress, officials from both sides say they are ready for renewed military escalation.
President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly suggested the United States could attack Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, said the latest negotiations were “going fine”, but added that the US still had several Iranian targets to “take care of”.
Meanwhile, Araghchi has also said Iran’s military was more prepared than ever for renewed war, while the country’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, threatened Iran would use “new weaponry” in response to any future attack.
Here’s what we know about the latest diplomatic efforts and the sharp rhetoric from both sides, and what it could mean for what lies ahead:
What is the status of talks?
Araghchi said on Saturday that an Iranian delegation, including one of his aides, travelled to Doha to meet Qatari mediators. Earlier, Qatari officials also travelled to Tehran for consultations.
The latest discussions in Doha centred on a plan that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a global energy chokepoint, within two days and restart peace talks with the US, provided Washington meets a set of demands from Tehran, Araghchi told Al Jazeera.
Those demands include the lifting of recently imposed US sanctions, the reinstatement of oil waivers granted in June, a reduction in the US military presence in the region, recognition of new shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz designated by Iran and Oman, and an end to the conflict on all fronts, including Israel’s attacks on Lebanon, said Araghchi.
Qatari and Pakistani mediators were “continuing consultations regarding our conditions”, said the top Iranian diplomat.
Pakistan has been mediating between the US and Iran, with its army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, visiting Tehran several times as part of the diplomatic efforts to end the war. Doha and Islamabad played key roles in the signing of the June memorandum of understanding (MoU) that collapsed in August.
Iran’s Rezaei said the US had “indicated its readiness” to accept its conditions, although Washington has not confirmed this.
On the US side, Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed Qatar-led talks were ongoing, but said he was not aware of a timeframe for them.
“There are multiple talks. Talks have actually never stopped,” said Rubio. “If there is a diplomatic solution, we would be open to it.”
Why has Iran noted a change in the US’s ‘tone’?
The renewed diplomatic activity comes after US Vice President JD Vance sent a letter earlier this week to Rezaei, reportedly seeking to gauge the prospects of restarting negotiations and averting another round of military escalation.
Rezaei confirmed on Saturday that he had read the letter, whose tone he said had “completely changed” compared with earlier correspondence from Trump.
Araghchi also said he had studied Vance’s letter, which he described positively.
“The American side’s attempt to open the door to dialogue and understanding more broadly is a positive step,” Araghchi told Al Jazeera.
However, he warned, “If Washington’s goal in sending this letter is to stir up discord, it would be yet another mistake to add to its previous ones.”
What has Iran said about prospects for peace and war?
Iranian officials have said they are open to new peace talks if the US meets their conditions, but also ready to act more aggressively in any new military confrontation.
“I know that our armed forces are more prepared for war than any time before, and we are ready for any scenario,” Araghchi told Al Jazeera.
In the event of any new military threat from the US or Israel, Iran’s response would be “immediate” and “without geographical limitations”, according to a statement by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.
Khamenei ordered commanders to update Iran’s target list to include “all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy”.
Rezaei told Al Jazeera that Iran would use “new weaponry” in its response to any future attacks. He also said Iran’s government was weighing a change to its “nuclear doctrine”, which currently includes a ban on nuclear weapons.
Iran’s nuclear programme has been a major point of contention in the conflict with the US, and Trump has repeatedly said Iran must never be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon. Tehran insists its nuclear programme is for civilian purposes.
What is the latest from Trump?
The US president has sent mixed signals about the status of peace talks. On Saturday, he said negotiations were “going fine” but added that they were “not very reliable”.
He also said the US military still needed to “take care of” several Iranian sites, singling out a suspected underground nuclear complex known as Pickaxe Mountain.
Trump added that the US could achieve its military objectives “very quickly” and was not in a hurry.
Previously, he threatened to renew attacks that would “finish off” Iran, while the US has reportedly warned its Gulf allies to prepare for a short, high-intensity round of conflict after the midterm elections.
Rubio said Trump had not yet decided on whether to carry out new strikes, but warned the US “can achieve military objectives if we seek to”.
How could Israel play into the calculation?
Israel, which joined the US in initiating the war against Iran in February, is preparing for another round of potential conflict right after the US midterm elections, according to a senior Israeli official cited by Israel’s Ynet News site.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said Israel has a “historic, one-time opportunity … to remove the Iranian threat once and for all”. While Netanyahu’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority in recent legislative elections, the 77-year-old leader remains in office as caretaker until a new government is formed.
Andreas Krieg, an associate professor of security studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that Netanyahu’s threats complicate Iran’s calculus because Tehran fears “even a nuclear agreement with Washington may not end the threat of another Israeli attack”.
Brigadier-General Yadollah Javani, the deputy for political affairs of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said Iranian forces are operating on the assumption that the US or Israel could strike at any moment.
What explains the parallel diplomatic efforts and war rhetoric?
Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst with the Crisis Group, said Tehran is pursuing diplomacy while also “attempting to redefine” the military implications of another potential conflict.
“For now, diplomacy and military preparations are proceeding simultaneously,” he wrote in a post on X. “The emerging Iranian position seems to be that an agreement remains possible, but another war would be fought under different rules and on a much wider battlefield.”
He added, “Whether Washington takes these warnings as credible deterrence or further escalatory threats could significantly influence what happens next.”
Krieg said the November 3 elections give Iran an incentive to delay concessions to deny Trump a diplomatic victory. But that calculus could change afterwards when he has fewer domestic political restraints on military action.
“We could therefore reach a situation where Iran becomes more willing to compromise precisely when Washington becomes more willing to strike,” said Krieg.

Lebanon's team of tradies win in all-time great finish at World Cup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:14:13 UTC
20:14:13 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
analysis
Wild finish to Rugby League World Cup classic between Lebanon and France
Rugby league fans had been salivating over what might transpire at Western Sydney Stadium on November 1 for months.
It was the first fixture of the World Cup to sell out weeks ago.
Everyone was hyping it up as the moment we would see this tournament catch fire and the international men's game ascend to higher levels than ever seen before.
And that all transpired, except it came a game early.
There was a triple header here, the Jillaroos against Wales, followed by Lebanon and France, to whet the appetite before the main event of Tonga and Samoa.
What no-one anticipated was that Lebanon and France, two minnows who were already well out of contention for the semifinals, would dish up what is roundly being called one of the greatest finishes in the international game.
One that has proven that just because this sport does a World Cup a little differently from the rest, it doesn't diminish its meaning.
Tradies' time to shine
The vast majority of players spread through the teams in this tournament were born in Australia or New Zealand, choosing to represent the country of their heritage.
The French are a rare exception, and after humbling defeats in their first two pool games, they were the underdogs against a Lebanese squad almost entirely consisting of Australian-born players.
But this was no mismatch.
Trailing by two late, France was denied a match-winning try when Lebanon just grounded the ball in the in-goal.
France's Arthur Mourgue then kicked a two-point field goal to send it to golden point shortly after, and in the first period of extra time, Cesar Rouge slotted a one-pointer.
The scenes were beautiful, joyous, crushing, devastating, a chaotic melting pot of emotions savoured by the growing crowd of largely Tongan and Samoan fans.
But it was disallowed for an escort. And so it went on.
The Cedars' Alex Conti missed a long-range penalty goal, which was collected by Mourgue.
He should've held onto it. A more experienced player under this sort of pressure would've taken the tackle, and the quick breather.
But he went for glory, a chip and chase that could've been his crowning glory.
Instead it became his never-ending nightmare.
Abbas Miski gleefully grabbed the goodies, and strolled the short distance to unleash mayhem unlike anything else we've seen at this tournament so far.
Most of the 30,000 tickets for this game were snapped up by Tongan and Samoan fans.
But a healthy contingent of Sydney's huge Lebanese diaspora turned up, and they were in a heady delirium, as the players danced dazed but delighted, alongside Lebanese drummers on the sidelines.
"It was the saddest I've been this whole tournament and then the happiest I've been this whole tournament. I don't even know what to feel," Lebanon captain Alex Twal told Channel 7.
"We've got plumbers, electricians, foreman, builders … these blokes came here just to have a crack and they're playing against some of the best in the world.
"Abbas, he's a winger, he's never played back row. For him to come up with a play like that, it's true Lebanese spirit.
"I've got goosebumps. I love being Lebanese."
Twal was born a stone's throw from this stadium at Westmead. He played his junior footy for the Parramatta City Titans and his entire NRL career has been with Wests Tigers.
Born and raised in Australia, he has a Jordanian father and Lebanese mother.
It is a story similar for so many children of migrants in Australia. An identity that is multidimensional, not having to remain in one neat box, but able to feel connection to many places, roots spread near and far.
And so often sport is the powerful vehicle that helps drive that message home.
That is why even though this game was a dead rubber, a result that ostensibly wouldn't change the world, it still meant something more than footy.
Because for people who have sometimes felt like they're between worlds, between cultures, there is somewhere they belong.
The hundreds of Lebanese fans who sang and marched to the beat of their traditional drums to the stadium today felt it, and no doubt many more in Australia's sizeable Lebanese community.
This may be the end of the line for the Cedars, in the short term at least.
They are ineligible for future tournaments having been downgraded to an affiliate member by the International Rugby League.
Meaning, for now, their greatest World Cup moment may very well be their last.
And the French must take heart from showing fight till the very end.
They were a team always up against it when facing players who have had league in their blood from birth.
And there will be hope they can try to inspire some sort of renaissance in the sport in the Northern Hemisphere, where it is currently on life support.
But rising from the ashes is what rugby league does best.
