Explainer-How US news organizations will make midterm race calls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:12:01 UTC
20:12:01 KST

Explainer-How US news organizations will make midterm race calls
Nov 1 - On Tuesday night, newsrooms across the US will call winners in one of the country's most closely contested midterm election cycles in recent years, long before all the votes are counted.
Most television networks and digital outlets rely on two providers for vote counts: the Associated Press or election-data firm Decision Desk HQ.
Some news outlets such as the Wall Street Journal and MS NOW will rely solely on the AP for race calls, while others like Fox News and CBS News will make their own projections based on the AP vote count, exit polls, early-vote totals and their own statistical modeling.
The first calls will start soon after polls begin to close in the United States, first with Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. ET (2300 GMT), and shortly after in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia at 7 p.m. (0000 GMT on November 4). In certain races there may be an instant call if much of the voting has already taken place.
Low public trust complicates race calls for news outlets. While more than 60% of Americans have some confidence in news organizations to report accurate election results, only 32% have high confidence, with Democrats more trusting than Republicans, an October poll for the Medill Local News Initiative and the Alliance for Trust in Media found.
While most of the major TV networks all use the same AP vote count tabulation to make their calls, the ones who decide to call winners use a proprietary mix of their own data analysis, historical models, exit poll interviews and expert judgment to call races when they determine that they've become a statistical certainty.
Here's how it works:
AP COUNTS AND RACE CALLS
The AP, a nonprofit newsroom supported by member newspapers, has counted votes in every US election since 1848, working with a national network of reporters and election officials to verify results.
For the 2026 midterms, the AP said it would deploy more than 4,000 reporters at county election offices and local polling locations, gathering and providing data to the decision desks at ABC News, CBS News, Fox, CNN and NBC News. ABC, CBS, CNN and NBC also rely on research firm SSRS, which acquired exit-polling company Edison Research in 2025.
When making calls, the AP uses vote totals and estimates how many votes remain uncounted based on past voting patterns and early-vote data. It calls a race only when the trailing candidate cannot catch up.
DDHQ COUNTS AND RACE CALLS
DDHQ collects vote counts from official state sources, usually secretaries of state or state election departments.
The firm uses statistical analysis, modeling and expert review to project election winners. Its clients include NewsNation, the Hill and Newsmax, and it recently signed up X, the social network owned by Elon Musk.
It uses automated software to repeatedly check official election websites and collect newly posted vote totals in addition to using reporters on the ground. DDHQ says roughly 80% of all votes are processed by pulling data directly from official election sites, or by manually monitoring election sites. The remaining counts are collected by reporters.
It calculates the percentage of ballots counted by dividing the votes reported by election officials by its estimated total turnout for a race. It determines remaining votes by subtracting reported votes from this overall turnout estimate, which is refined on election night using actual data.
Final projections require unanimous team agreement and a sign-off from the head of data science, Scott Tranter. "We’re preparing to have several thousand people working on election night to gather data," Tranter told Reuters.
RACE PROJECTIONS CAN BE WRONG
Retractions are rare, but both the AP and DDHQ have withdrawn calls in the past.
In 2025, DDHQ withdrew a projection in the Seattle mayor's race. Earlier this year, DDHQ withdrew its call in the Democratic primary for a special election in New Jersey's 11th Congressional District after Election Day vote counts shifted the race away from its initial projection.
In 2018, after a projected winner fell behind in California's 21st Congressional District, AP posted on its race-call account that it was retracting the call because Democrat T.J. Cox had taken the lead in the vote count.
THE NEWS OUTLETS MAKING RACE CALLS
Fox's decision desk will be making its own calls in all statewide races as well as the calls for control of the House and control of the Senate. It uses the AP vote count and applies its own analysis.
MS NOW, covering its first midterms since separating from NBCUniversal's cable portfolio, will rely on the AP's race calls.
The New York Times relies on AP calls for most contests but independently reviews competitive races using precinct-level data and its Needle model. It may make a call before or after the AP.
Bloomberg does not make its own race calls. For election results, it uses established third-party sources. Reuters will also be citing the race calls from other news organizations.
The Washington Post did not respond to requests for comment on how it will call races. REUTERS

Bulgarians head to the polls in tense presidential runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:11:49 UTC
20:11:49 KST

The vote puts together two candidates with sharply contrasting views on how Bulgaria should engage with Russia and the war in Ukraine moving forward.
Bulgarians are voting on Sunday in a tense presidential runoff between incumbent President Iliana Iotova and pro-Western rival Andrey Gyurov.
Iotova won the most votes, around 35%, in the first round of voting, giving her a lead of 43,000 over Gyurov - a surprise result as earlier opinion polls had suggested a more comfortable victory.
Polling stations opened at 7 am local time on Sunday and will close at 8 pm.
The vote puts together two candidates with sharply contrasting views on how Bulgaria should engage with Russia and the war in Ukraine.
Iotova, who is backed by the ruling Progressive Bulgaria party, the Bulgarian Socialist Party and the nationalist VMRO, has pushed for dialogue with Moscow and opposes continuing military aid to Ukraine.
Gyurov is supported by the opposition, Democratic Bulgaria and We Continue the Change, and argues that the Kremlin must end its war before coming to the negotiating table.
In a televised debate on Thursday evening, Iotova said "peace can only be achieved through negotiations."
"If we pour even more money into Ukraine and deliver new, more sophisticated weapons, this will only lead to further destruction and many deaths on both sides," she added.
In contrast, Gyurov argued that "Russia must put an end to its aggression so that the next steps can be taken."
"Let us name the country from which the threats originate," he said.
Bulgaria, an EU and NATO member, has historically had close ties with Russia, and the country is deeply divided over how it should move forward with this relationship.
The vote comes amid a series of attacks on vessels in the Black Sea off Bulgaria, which has further intensified conversations around the topic of relations with Russia.
Prime Minister Rumen Radev maintains that a ceasefire in Ukraine and peace talks are the only guarantees that the Black Sea will once again be a safe route for commercial ships.
While Radev has said the attacks appeared to serve Russian interests and has summoned the Russian ambassador over the incidents, the government says there is so far no evidence directly linking them to Moscow.
Political analyst Teodor Slavev told the AFP news agency that the presidential election would see voters give their verdict on "Iotova's unconvincing response regarding Russian threats in the Black Sea."

Cash received by Joint List lawmaker examined in election interference probe
Investigators have found no evidence linking the hundreds of thousands of shekels to Qatar, Election Day activities or payments to voters, while senior officials differ over the affair’s seriousness
An investigation into suspected foreign interference in Israel’s elections is examining hundreds of thousands of shekels in cash received by a member of the Joint List faction in the Knesset.
The cash transfer is among the details under scrutiny, but key questions about the money’s origin and purpose remain unresolved. At this stage, investigators have found no evidence that the funds were used to finance Election Day activities or that any of the money reached voters.
Despite claims suggesting a connection to Qatar, no evidence currently establishes that the funds originated there. The information available so far does not demonstrate that the payment formed part of a foreign effort to influence the vote.
The affair has also prompted differing assessments within Israel’s security leadership. Shin Bet chief David Zini and other senior officials disagree over its severity.
Official election results are expected to be announced this week. The investigation will continue alongside that process, with the understanding that the inquiry itself will not affect the election results.

Veteran diplomat warns Estonia's 'predictable' Russia message losing impact
Unknown

Veteran diplomat warns Estonia's 'predictable' Russia message losing impact
Former longtime diplomat Jaap Ora says Estonia should carefully calibrate its public statements on Russia to avoid being sidelined internationally by predictable rhetoric.
Ora, who recently joined Isamaa, criticized Prime Minister Kristen Michal's (Reform) response to recent reports that the U.S. had asked the Baltic states to tone down their rhetoric about the threat posed by Russia.
He also warned that Estonia's foreign policy messaging has become predictable, risking fatigue among international partners.
"Foreign policy is not the place to speak your mind," Ora wrote on social media, adding that diplomats have to think carefully about what they say and calibrate their message each time accordingly.
"Words are an important tool in diplomacy, but they have to serve a purpose," he said. "Your heart may be burning, but your public message should be measured."
Ora said treating foreign policy as simply "expressing positions" is an oversimplification.
"Our message has gotten predictable, and there's a risk that people will grow tired of hearing it," the ex-diplomat said, warning that Estonia could lose its seat at the table for important discussions.
"Those invited are expected to bring fresh ideas and something valuable [to the discussion]," he explained. "If our message is already predictable, there may be less interest in having us there."
Estonian leaders stand firm
Citing several anonymous sources, Reuters reported Friday that the United States had asked the Baltic states to tone down their public statements about Russia and put less emphasis on the threat it poses.
Michal responded that he had no intention of holding back, saying pressure on Russia should be maintained instead.
Other Estonian officials echoed the prime minister's sentiments, including outgoing Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov, who snoted he was not aware of any official requests from U.S. officials for Estonia to change its Russia rhetoric.
"Perhaps also because a proposal like that would always and in any case get rejected," Vseviov said.
"Estonia's voice is our most important trump card, the most important weapon for taking part in international politics," he emphasized. "And while that voice must be used wisely and never belligerently, surrendering that voice is something we should never even consider."

Trump heads to Iowa, Kansas for rallies before midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Trump heads to Iowa, Kansas for rallies before midterms
WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE, Alaska, Nov 1 - President Donald Trump returns to the campaign trail on Sunday with rallies in Iowa and Kansas, Republican-leaning Farm Belt states where his party is fighting to hold US Senate seats, two days before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.
Trump, who spent Saturday at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida after weeks of campaigning across multiple states, won Iowa by double digits in 2024. But polls show Democrats tied with or leading Republicans in many of the state’s races, and Trump’s approval among rural Americans fell to a new low of 45% in October, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling. Kansas, which last elected a Democratic senator in 1932, is also facing an unexpectedly close race.
Thirty-five Senate seats and all 435 House seats are on the ballot on Tuesday. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority and a narrow edge in the House. Losing either chamber would let Democrats block Trump’s agenda for his final two years in office and launch investigations of an administration that has so far faced largely compliant Republican majorities.
More than 52 million Americans have already voted in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, a record for a midterm and up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day in 2022.
LEGAL FIGHTS
As Trump campaigns, his administration is pressing a criminal investigation in Alaska’s pivotal Senate race and said on Saturday it would likely take its fight over thousands of California mail ballots to the Supreme Court.
“I hesitate to give a final answer, but I think probably the Supreme Court’s next on this one,” acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told Fox News, adding that any request would come before Tuesday’s election.
A federal judge earlier this week rejected the Justice Department’s request to block California from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters it alleges are likely noncitizens, after a federal appeals court denied an earlier emergency request. California has said the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting, which is illegal, are robust.
In Alaska, federal prosecutors are investigating whether aides to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola helped recruit a retired schoolteacher, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to run because he shares a name with the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Peltola aides worked with staff at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee on the effort.
Peltola and the campaign committee have denied involvement, and Sullivan Jr. has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.
The US Justice Department has asked a federal court to prevent the certification of Alaska's vote if the incumbent senator loses narrowly.
Voters who spoke to Reuters on Saturday in Anchorage, Alaska, had mixed views on the investigation and legal fights.
“I am concerned that the longer it takes for those votes to be counted, the more shenanigans will happen, especially with our current president making comments about wanting to invalidate the current election and the current votes that are coming in," said Ames Tonneson, 24.
Art Paul, 52, took the potential upheaval in stride.
"In this case, if there’s a close race or investigation, I understand. … It’s part of the process," Paul said. "And you gotta be patient. So I’d like it to be faster, but I understand why it’s not."
MICHIGAN RIFT
In Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers in another closely watched Senate race, it was unclear whether US Representative Haley Stevens, a Michigan Democrat and the rival El-Sayed beat in the primary, would attend a Detroit event with him on Sunday that had been billed as a show of party unity.
El-Sayed has previously accused Stevens of "relitigating" the Democratic primary. On Saturday, he again alluded to the outcome of the primary.
“I understand that some folks are upset about that,” El-Sayed told reporters at a rally in Sterling Heights, Michigan, that took place on his 42nd birthday. “But I'm here trying to beat Mike Rogers.”
El-Sayed’s campaign asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as “not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” a person familiar with the matter said. Stevens has demanded he condemn an outside group’s ad that she says blames Israel for high grocery prices.
“It’s certainly unhelpful to the El-Sayed campaign to have continued visible division within the party just before Election Day,” said Matt Grossmann, a political scientist at Michigan State University. Polls show El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support. REUTERS

Zhanna Kadyrova: Making Art When They’re Trying to Kill You
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:07:00 UTC
20:07:00 KST

PinchukArtCentre presented the first monograph by Zhanna Kadyrova, one of Ukraine’s most internationally recognized contemporary artists. Published in English by German art publisher Distanz, the book traces more than two decades of her work, from early projects to those developed after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
                                                                                                                                                                         The first monograph dedicated to internationally renowned Ukrainian artist Zhanna Kadyrova published by Distanz                             
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The publication is the result of a collaboration between the artist, PinchukArtCentre, and Germany’s Kunstverein Hannover. It brings together critical essays by international contributors, Kadyrova’s own reflections, and different perspectives on the evolution of her artistic language, with particular attention to works shaped by the experience of war.
One of the book’s recurring themes is “Russian Rocket,” a project that places the threat of Russian aggression within familiar, peaceful urban landscapes. Its message extends beyond Ukraine, prompting international audiences to question how secure the peace they have long taken for granted really is.
Kadyrova’s multidisciplinary practice spans sculpture, installation, photography, video, drawing, public art, and performance. Her work explores memory and social transformation. Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, she has increasingly focused on the experience of living in a country resisting Russian aggression.
Russian Forces Intensify Shelling of Epicentr K Chain Across Ukraine in 48-Hour Wave of Strikes
In 2026, Kadyrova represented Ukraine at the 61st Venice Biennale with her solo project “Security Guarantees.” She previously participated in the Biennale’s main curated exhibition, “May You Live in Interesting Times,” in 2019.
Her works are held in major museum collections worldwide, including the Centre Pompidou in Paris, Museum Ludwig in Cologne, Castello di Rivoli in Turin, the Museum of Modern Art in Warsaw, and Helsinki Art Museum.
Kyiv Post: What became impossible in your artistic practice after 2022, and what, conversely, acquired new meaning?
Zhanna Kadyrova: I used to love going on residencies, discovering local stories, and creating works from scratch using materials that inspired me in a particular place. I would explore the people, history, and character of a city or location.
That has become impossible for me now because I turn down all the residencies I am offered. I decided to stay in Ukraine, live here, and observe the reality of war. The war itself inspires me.
Through my own experience and artistic perspective, I want to communicate what is happening here to European and global audiences, tell them more about Ukraine, and share my personal experience of the war.
You have chosen to remain in Ukraine despite your international career and opportunities to work abroad. What keeps you here?
I travel to present my projects, and there is no way around that because I consider it part of my mission. In a sense, it is also a privilege to receive invitations and have the opportunity to share my work.
But I find it difficult to spend long periods in other countries. Only here am I surrounded by people who understand me. Five years is a considerable amount of time, and there are experiences that feel comfortable to share only with people who have been through something similar.
I am happy to see my friends and talented artists who have left Ukraine, but sometimes our interests and perspectives diverge. Here, I am among people with whom I do not even need to speak. We can simply look into each other’s eyes, and I feel understood.
It is hardly surprising that art becomes particularly active under such difficult circumstances. Artists seem to live on the edge of reality, perceive events more acutely, and work as though they are doing it for the last time – with responsibility, intensity, and emotion. That resonates with me.
In “Russian Rocket,” the threat of Russian aggression is presented as more than just Ukraine’s problem. Have you been able to convey to international audiences that this war concerns the entire world?
I call it an export project. It was created in 2022. In my view, there is little point in putting rocket stickers on things in Ukraine, where actual missiles are already flying. Instead, abroad, I place them on the windows of public transport, trains, and buses, so that a rocket appears to fly over landscapes familiar to local residents.
The contrast is meant to provoke an emotional response. I hope it encourages people to think about Ukrainians living under real missile attacks and to consider how long their own cities will remain peaceful. Could missiles one day fly over them, too?
The project is deliberately simple, with an approach close to street art. A single sticker can disrupt someone’s perception of reality.
We also have an Instagram page, Russian Rocket 2022, where people post their own interventions and photographs of rockets placed in their cities. The project was conceived as a kind of flash mob. I continue to travel and document it.
Which of your projects created during the full-scale war has become particularly significant to you?
Usually, the work I love most is the one I am working on right now. One of the major and most significant projects is “Instrument,” an installation made from a church organ and fragments of exploded missiles.
Of course, there is also “Security Guarantees,” as well as “Palyanytsia,” a project that raises money to support Ukrainian service members, including artists serving in the military. So far, this humanitarian initiative has raised half a million euros. We recently launched a foundation that will provide assistance officially.
                                                                                                                                                                         Zhanna Kadyrova’s “Palyanytsia” project. (Images from the monograph dedicated to Zhanna Kadyrova published by Distanz)                             
Another important project is “Refugees.” It consists of plants I evacuated from various front-line and formerly occupied territories. I found houseplants there – traces of life amid destroyed buildings. I documented burned-out, ruined interiors on camera, while taking the plants home and bringing them back to life.
These are probably among the most important projects for me.
In 2026, you represented Ukraine at the Venice Biennale with “Security Guarantees.” What did the experience reveal about the relationship between art and politics at one of the world’s most influential international cultural events?
I am pleased with how we organized the Ukrainian pavilion. We managed to accomplish everything we had planned. We even secured a better location for presenting the deer sculpture from Pokrovsk than we had expected.
                                                                                                                                                                         The central work in the Ukrainian national pavilion, titled “Security Guarantees,” was “Origami Deer,” a concrete sculpture created by Zhanna Kadyrova and Denys Ruban in Pokrovsk in 2019. It stood on the pedestal of a dismantled Soviet jet aircraft associated with nuclear weapons. In 2024, as the front line approached, the sculpture was evacuated. (Photo courtesy Ministry of Culture of Ukraine)                             
But many political developments unfolded around the Biennale. I doubt we would have received such a central location had it not been for the controversy over the Russian pavilion. Criticism of Russia’s participation began, and the Biennale’s management tried to offer us certain accommodations. I call it the instrumentalization of the Russian pavilion’s presence. (Laughs.)
Every project has its own behind-the-scenes story. But it is important to acknowledge that the Biennale management’s claim that art exists outside politics – that it is free and stands above everything – does not reflect reality. Many decisions, even seemingly technical ones, were made for political reasons.
What message would you like to convey to international audiences on behalf of Ukraine’s artistic community during Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, a war of aggression taking place in Europe?
First and foremost, I want to emphasize that a great deal is being created and happening in Ukraine.
The fact that the war is now in its fifth year does not mean our culture has died. It is alive and powerful. Even under extraordinarily difficult circumstances, artists find ways to realize ambitious projects.
I would ask international audiences to believe in us and support us. Ukraine is a country with a distinctive cultural identity and a great deal to offer the world.

Trump White House maps path to govern without Congress if Democrats win
- Trump’s White House is planning to use executive power to keep pushing his agenda if Democrats win Congress, especially on immigration, tariffs, housing and spending.
- Senior aides are checking what Trump can do alone, how far he can go, and how to defend those moves in court, while agencies prepare legal reviews.
- Democratic control could bring investigations, blocked nominees and legal fights, but Trump would still have strong power over trade, foreign policy and the federal bureaucracy.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump’s White House has spent months preparing for a possible Democratic takeover of Congress, developing plans to keep advancing major parts of his agenda through executive power while bracing itself for investigations of his administration, according to a White House official and two sources familiar with the plans.
Senior officials, including deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and budget director Russell Vought, have been working with the White House Counsel’s Office since April to identify executive actions on immigration, tariffs, housing costs and federal spending that Trump could pursue without congressional approval, said the three sources, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
White House counsel Will Scharf and his team also are looking at “what Trump can legally do on his own, where he could push the limits of his authority and how to defend those decisions in court”, the White House official said.
The planning underscores a paradox of the Nov 3 midterm elections: capturing control of Congress would give Democrats the power to investigate Trump, block legislation and constrain his spending priorities. But Trump would retain broad executive authority over trade, foreign policy and the federal bureaucracy that he has already used aggressively during his second term.
Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the US House of Representatives as well as the US Senate to overturn Republicans’ narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities. Opinion polls favour Democrats to win the House, while the Senate remains too close to call.
For the past month, Trump has held rallies across the country trying to preserve Republican control of Congress, even as his aides privately prepare for a very different political landscape in 2027.
The White House pushed back on the prospect of Republican losses and accused the media of promoting a false narrative.
“This administration and commonsense Republicans will continue to secure our borders, restore law and order, putting more money back into the pockets of hard-working Americans, and deliver wins for the American people,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.
Among the executive actions under consideration are new tariffs on imports of critical minerals and wind turbines, tighter rules on visas for international students and temporary foreign workers, and measures aimed at lowering housing and construction costs, the White House official said.
Federal agencies have submitted proposals and legal reviews of actions the administration could take unilaterally, one of the sources with knowledge of the plans said.
Vought, whose US Office of Management and Budget oversees federal spending, is examining which priorities can move forward using money already appropriated by Congress, two of the sources said.
He also wants to change federal grant rules to give political appointees more say in which government programmes receive taxpayer money, they said, potentially giving the White House more influence over federal spending without seeking congressional approval.
Trump has been briefed on the preparations and has taken part in discussions about them, the White House official said.
When asked how comfortable Trump would be governing through executive authority under a Democratic Congress, one of the sources said: “very comfortable”.
Governing without Congress
Trump has already tested the reach of presidential power since returning to office in January 2025, using executive authority to impose sweeping tariffs, intensify immigration enforcement, shrink the federal workforce, and pursue foreign-policy goals including the war against Iran without Congress’ approval or new laws.
A major exception was Trump’s massive package of tax and spending cuts that was passed by the Republican-controlled Congress and signed into law by the President in July 2025.
“President Trump in the last two years has basically ignored Congress and tried to do as much as possible through executive orders and executive power,” said Nathan Gonzales, editor at Inside Elections, which provides non-partisan political analysis. “I think he will continue only if there are Democratic majorities.”
Trump has repeatedly invoked national emergencies to expand his ability to act without new legislation. Congress can vote to end those emergencies, but Trump could veto such a move, requiring two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override him.
A Democratic Congress could still create significant obstacles.
Control of the Senate would allow Democrats to block Trump’s judicial and executive-branch nominees, including any Supreme Court pick.
“I would anticipate they will be very reluctant to approve any of the president’s appointments,” said Andrew Busch, a public policy professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and author of a history of midterm elections.
Democrats could also refuse to pass Trump-backed legislation. But Trump could veto Democratic legislation he does not like, and Democrats are unlikely to have enough votes in the House to override him.
Courts could block executive actions that exceed Trump’s legal authority. The White House plans to seek legal opinions from the Justice Department to determine what Trump can do without Congress and how to defend those actions if they are challenged in court, one of the sources said.
Democratic investigations
One challenge, however, cannot be sidestepped through executive action: congressional investigations.
Reuters previously reported that senior House Democrats and committee aides have discussed using hearings, subpoenas and document requests to examine whether Trump has used his presidential power to benefit himself, allies or donors.
Trump aides have been preparing for that prospect for months, all three sources said.
White House lawyers have been briefing political appointees and agency leaders on how to handle congressional inquiries, document requests and subpoenas, one source said. They have advised officials to be careful about what they put in writing.
They also sought a Justice Department opinion that could allow Trump to invoke executive privilege to shield communications with private advisers from congressional scrutiny, the source said. REUTERS

Hellenic Navy Receives Second French-Built FDI Frigate

The Hellenic Navy has received the second of four FDI HN-class frigates ordered by Greece – HS Nearchos (F602) – built by French shipbuilder Naval Group.
Naval News reported on this, citing Greece’s Ministry of National Defense.
The handover ceremony took place on October 30, 2026, at Naval Group’s shipyard in Lorient, France. Nikos Dendias, Greek Minister of National Defense, and Catherine Vautrin, French Minister of the Armed Forces, attended the ceremony.
HS Nearchos is the second frigate of this class to be delivered to the Hellenic Navy, following the lead ship, HS Kimon, which was handed over in December 2025. Nearchos is also the first Greek FDI frigate delivered in the Standard 2 configuration, which provides enhanced combat capabilities.
In particular, this configuration includes two additional SYLVER A50 vertical launching system modules, four SYLENA Mk1 decoy-launching systems, and a 21-cell RAM launcher for short-range surface-to-air missiles, providing the ship with additional air-defense capabilities.
Today, Naval Group delivered HS Nearchos, the second FDI frigate for the Hellenic Navy, in presence of @NikosDendias , Minister of National Defence of the Hellenic Republic, and @CaVautrin, Minister of the Armed Forces. https://t.co/ZdfQ1E4rlD
— Naval Group (@navalgroup) October 30, 2026
The Greek frigates are scheduled to receive further upgrades to the Standard 2+ and Standard 2++ configurations. In particular, the third ship of the class, HS Formion, is expected to be the first delivered in the Standard 2+ configuration, in April 2027. HS Nearchos is scheduled to be upgraded to the Standard 2++ configuration by April 2029.
Greece ordered four FDI frigates under a procurement program launched in 2022. More than 75 Greek companies are involved in the project, supplying equipment, producing mechanical and electronic systems, and manufacturing individual structural sections of the ships.
In addition to Greece, Sweden has also ordered frigates of this class, with construction of the first vessel beginning on October 4, 2026.
Greek FDI HN frigates differ from their French counterparts through their enhanced armament and additional defensive systems.
A key feature of the Standard 2 configuration is the increased number of Sylver A50 vertical launch system cells, bringing the total to 32. These cells are designed to accommodate Aster 15 and Aster 30 surface-to-air missiles.
The ship is equipped with a 21-cell RAM surface-to-air missile launcher for close-range air defense, as well as four SYLENA Mk1 launchers for deploying decoys and countermeasures.
The Greek version also features Leonardo LIONFISH 20 remotely operated weapon stations, the Saab NLWS electronic warfare support system, and integration with the Camcopter S-100 unmanned helicopter.

Reading for pleasure is linked to better brain health across the lifespan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:00:49 UTC
20:00:49 KST

Picking up a book for fun might do far more than simply pass the time. A new editorial synthesis published in Psychological Medicine indicates that reading for pleasure is tied to better cognitive performance, differences in brain structure, lower stress, and a reduced risk of dementia in later life. Based on the evidence, the authors argue that recreational reading and participating in book clubs could serve as accessible, low-cost tools to support mental well-being and protect the aging brain, including among people from lower-income or less-educated backgrounds.
Reading for pleasure, often called voluntary or recreational reading, is the act of reading materials of one’s own free will in anticipation of the satisfaction the activity brings. This encompasses not only printed novels and nonfiction books, but also digital formats, magazines, comic books, and graphic novels. In their editorial, the authors examine this everyday pastime through the lens of preventive psychiatry, an approach aimed at lowering the risk of mental health disorders before they take hold.
World Health Organization data indicates that more than one billion people globally live with a mental health condition, and roughly one in seven adolescents aged 10 to 19 experiences a mental disorder. In this age group, anxiety, depression, and behavioral disorders are among the leading causes of illness and disability.
In response to these numbers, researchers are looking closely at modifiable lifestyle habits that build psychological resilience, which helps people weather stress, and cognitive reserve. Cognitive reserve is the brain’s capacity to keep functioning well despite aging or damage, which is thought to build up through mentally stimulating experiences and act as a buffer against cognitive decline and dementia.
Because reading is mentally stimulating and can be shared with others, the authors suggest it may simultaneously strengthen cognitive reserve and ease social isolation. The authors of a 2020 review on socioeconomic inequality noted that growing up in lower-income households is linked to measurable differences in how brain circuits supporting language, memory, and emotion regulation develop. In light of these disparities, the editorial’s authors emphasize the need to identify low-cost habits that can help offset environmental disadvantages.
To evaluate how recreational reading might serve this protective role from childhood through old age, Barbara J. Sahakian of the University of Cambridge and her colleagues brought together findings from literacy charity surveys, long-term cohort studies, and brain imaging research.
The authors first examined survey data from the United Kingdom’s National Literacy Trust tracking reading habits among young people. Data from the 2024 and 2025 Annual Literacy Surveys indicated that recreational reading among children and teenagers has continued to fall and may have reached its lowest levels since tracking began, particularly among boys aged 11 to 16. In 2025, the gap between girls and boys who read daily widened to 6.2 percentage points, and children who did not receive free school meals, a standard UK indicator of low household income, were more likely to read daily (19.4 percent) than peers who did receive them (15.8 percent).
Despite this downward trend, the 2024 survey data pointed to a link between reading enjoyment and scores on the STAR Reading assessment. Children and adolescents who reported enjoying reading (1,211 participants) achieved an average score of 109.13, compared to an average of 102.65 among the 2,593 students who did not enjoy reading. Similarly, the 789 students who read daily scored an average of 109.49, compared to 103.35 among the 3,026 non-daily readers.
The 2025 survey also suggested ways to reengage reluctant young readers. In that survey, 38.1 percent of youth felt motivated by material tied to a favorite film or television series, 37.1 percent were motivated by material matching their interests or hobbies, and 26.6 percent valued choosing their own reading material.
The synthesis also examined longitudinal research on how reading ability relates to mathematical development. Reading and math share several underlying mental processes, including phonological awareness, which is the ability to recognize and manipulate the spoken parts of words, and executive functions, the mental skills used to plan, focus attention, and juggle multiple tasks. In a study following 554 elementary school children from an average starting age of 6.5 years, average and high reading performance predicted faster growth in math skills over time, especially among students who initially performed below average in math.
To examine how recreational reading relates to adult emotional well-being, the authors cited several self-report surveys conducted by literacy organizations. In a 2015 survey of 4,164 adults, 64 percent of those who read for at least 30 minutes a week reported a better understanding of other people’s feelings, compared to 48 percent of non-readers. Among readers, 17 percent said they remained calm during disagreements, compared to 5 percent of non-readers, and 38 percent identified books as their preferred method for stress relief.
In a 2022 survey of roughly 2,000 people conducted by the reading charity The Reader, 74 percent of respondents reported that reading benefited their mental health, and 41 percent said it helped them feel more connected to other people. Among young adults aged 18 to 34 in that poll, 59 percent felt reading increased their connection to others and 56 percent said it helped them feel less alone during pandemic lockdowns.
Shared reading in book clubs also appeared to offer social benefits across different age groups. A qualitative study of 168 tenth-grade students in book clubs found that 61.2 percent reported a greater understanding of other people’s perspectives, 42.9 percent felt an increased sense of connection, and 14.3 percent reported feeling less lonely. Similarly, a 2025 systematic review of 11 studies indicated that group reading activities among older adults reduced depressive symptoms and eased social isolation, though the review’s authors noted that study methods varied widely.
These findings are consistent with a recent study of older adults, which found that maintaining a daily reading routine was associated with lower loneliness scores among people with small social networks, offering a stronger protective effect than monthly social activities.
The editorial also draws on an earlier analysis co-authored by Sahakian and Langley of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) cohort, a large U.S. study that tracked 10,243 adolescents from ages 9 to 11 through ages 11 to 13. Roughly half of the sample (51.8 percent) had started reading for pleasure early in childhood, logging between 3 and 10 years of recreational reading, while the remaining 48.2 percent had little or no early reading experience, ranging from 0 to 2.5 years.
Adolescents in the early-reading group showed better performance on tests of working memory, attention, and verbal learning, alongside fewer symptoms of depression, stress, and behavioral problems. They also logged less daily screen time and slept longer than peers who did not read early.
Brain scans of these early readers showed larger tissue volumes and surface areas across several regions involved in language processing, attention, and emotion regulation. These associations held even after the researchers statistically controlled for age, biological sex, body mass index, puberty status, race and ethnicity, family structure, parental education, and household income. That analysis, first published in 2023, also found that cognitive benefits peaked at around 12 hours of reading per week.
In older adulthood, long-term cohort studies reviewed by the authors linked reading to a lower risk of cognitive decline. One study tracking 5,437 cognitively healthy adults aged 55 and older over five years found that frequent engagement in mental activities like reading and playing chess was tied to a lower likelihood of developing cognitive impairment.
Another study following 801 adults aged 65 and older for an average of 4.5 years reported that each one-point increase on a measure of cognitively stimulating activities, which included reading books, magazines, and newspapers, was associated with a 33 percent lower risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease. A separate study of 469 adults aged 75 and older over 5.1 years linked reading itself to a 35 percent lower risk of overall dementia.
Reading also appeared to offset the cognitive disadvantages often seen in older adults with fewer years of formal schooling. In a cross-sectional study of 459 older adults who reported no thinking or memory problems, where 36.82 percent read regularly, readers outperformed non-readers across all cognitive assessments, even among those with less formal education. Brain MRI scans in that study, however, showed no structural differences between the two groups.
Similarly, in a 14-year study that followed 1,962 adults over age 64 across four assessment waves, reading at least once a week was linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline at the 6-, 10-, and 14-year marks across all levels of formal education. Together, those studies suggest that regular reading habits in later life may help compensate for limited early schooling.
To explore how reading might physically shape the brain, the authors reviewed neuroimaging studies of both gray matter, which contains neural cell bodies that process information, and white matter, the bundled nerve fibers that connect different brain regions. In children aged 8 to 13, stronger performance on word identification tests correlated with better organization of white matter pathways, particularly in the left hemisphere, which is heavily involved in language. Researchers measured this pathway organization using a specialized MRI technique called diffusion tensor imaging.
In a separate line of research, one small study of 11 children aged 7 to 11 with dyslexia, a learning difference that makes reading difficult, found that after an eight-week training program focusing on mental imagery and word tracing, reading skills improved and gray matter volume increased in brain areas involved in memory and language, including the hippocampus. Some of the reading gains were still present eight weeks later.
Similar structural patterns appeared in adult brain imaging studies. Among young adults aged 18 to 25, greater exposure to print, measured by familiarity with author names and book titles, was linked to a thicker cerebral cortex, the brain’s outer layer, in areas that process language, independent of the person’s reading skill. Intensive literacy training in adults who previously could not read or write well enough to manage everyday tasks was also associated with gray matter growth in language-related brain regions.
In a study using functional MRI, which tracks brain activity by measuring changes in blood flow, 26 young adults aged 19 to 26 read literary passages inside a scanner. The texts activated the default mode network, a connected set of brain regions active when people daydream, recall memories, or imagine another person’s thoughts and feelings, a skill known as theory of mind. Vivid descriptive scenes and socially rich passages engaged distinct parts of this network, and activity in the social-processing portion statistically accounted for part of the link between frequent fiction reading and stronger performance on tests of social understanding.
“The most important takeaway is that reading for pleasure is associated with a range of healthier outcomes, including better mental and social health as well as better cognitive function,” Angelina R. Sutin, a professor in the Department of Behavioral Sciences and Social Medicine at the Florida State University College of Medicine who was not involved in the research, told PsyPost. “This summary of the research on the health benefits of reading largely supports conclusions from existing work. This summary does do a nice job of organizing this literature to demonstrate both the broad reach of the benefits of reading and how reading benefits health across all stages of the lifespan.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting the findings compiled in this paper. The article is an editorial rather than a systematic review, meaning the authors selected which studies to highlight rather than following a formal protocol to gather all available evidence. Much of the survey data on reading habits, stress, and empathy comes from reports published by literacy charities rather than peer-reviewed journals, and self-selected survey respondents may not reflect the general public. In addition, the school test data cannot rule out reverse causation: children who are already strong readers may simply find reading more enjoyable, rather than reading enjoyment driving higher test scores.
More broadly, most of the human studies on lifelong reading are observational, meaning they track people’s existing habits rather than assigning them to read, so they cannot prove that reading directly causes brain changes or prevents dementia. “As much as I appreciate the results and want to support the benefits of reading, most of the studies reviewed in this piece were observational,” Sutin explained. “The longitudinal studies are helpful to test whether reading can predict outcomes in the future. Still, there is the possibility that individuals who are healthier, and maintain their health over time, are also the kinds of people who read.”
“General readers might overinterpret the findings to mean that they will have better health if they start reading for pleasure,” Sutin added. “I think the real value of this summary is laying the foundation for exciting research that should come next. The authors nicely argue and present foundational evidence for the importance of reading for better mental, social, and cognitive health. The next step is to experimentally test whether individuals randomly assigned to read for pleasure improve in these aspects of health more than individuals randomly assigned to an active control.”
An active control is a comparison group that spends the same amount of time on a different activity, such as doing puzzles, rather than doing nothing. The editorial’s authors similarly note that further experimental research is needed to establish causal pathways and map out the exact brain mechanisms behind reading’s benefits. They also hope to investigate whether brain plasticity, the brain’s ability to change in response to experience, can support better brain structure, cognitive function, and well-being among adults who take up reading for pleasure later in life. The University of Cambridge team plans to pursue these questions in a collaboration with the UK literary charity The Queen’s Reading Room, and the paper discloses that co-author Vicki Perrin is the charity’s chief executive officer.
The study, “Reading and associations with brain health, cognition, well-being, and mental health,” was authored by Barbara J. Sahakian, Vicki Perrin, and Christelle Langley.

‘He’s a force’: Obama answers call to boost Democrats – and rattle Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:00:10 UTC
20:00:10 KST

That could have been awkward. Barack Obama, campaigning for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, acknowledged that his fellow Democrat has criticised some aspects of the Obama presidency.
“Yeah, Abdul didn’t agree with some things we wanted to do – that our administration was doing – when I was president,” he told a rally in Detroit. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama.” The crowd erupted in laughter. “I’d say about five times a day, she says, ‘You knucklehead. Why you do that?’”
It was an elegant attempt to bridge the gap between the old Democratic party and the new. The US midterm elections have brought anti-incumbent sentiment to the fore. Some candidates have actively shrugged off their party labels, eager to cast themselves as outsiders running against the Washington establishment.
Against that backdrop, who wants a 65-year-old former president who left office nearly a decade ago with his promise of hope and change still only partly realised? It seems that Democrats do.
“Yes, we can!” chanted the crowd this week inside an arena in suburban Atlanta, Georgia, reviving the cadence of an Obama 2008 campaign that now feels like an artefact from a vanished age.
With days to go before midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in Congress for the remainder of Donald Trump’s second term, Democrats have turned to their most formidable orator for a series of blistering speeches in the campaign’s closing days.
America’s first Black president has mercilessly mocked Trump’s autocratic pretensions and derided his foreign policy misadventures in the Middle East.
“This election is our last, best chance of at least reining him in, reining in some of the foolishness of this administration,” he said in Georgia. “It’s the circuit-breaker in the system, and we need to flip it.”
For party strategists, the decision to deploy Obama in the campaign’s closing stretch was a calculated gamble. Unlike Trump, who has spent weeks staging grievance-filled rallies in traditional Republican strongholds, Obama maintained a selective public profile until the final weeks, allowing a new generation of Democratic candidates to establish their own identities before delivering a late burst of star power.
David Litt, a former Obama White House speechwriter, said: “What you’re seeing is him coming in to support a new generation of Democratic leaders who have emerged organically, rather than trying to be involved from day one. He still has both a credibility and an ability to drive turnout that, if you’re a candidate in a close race, you can absolutely benefit from – especially among young voters and Black voters.”
The former president possesses a rare currency in modern US politics, according to Litt: the ability to command attention, and unnerve his successor.
“Obama is good at getting attention, and attention is hard to get these days,” he continued. “The other thing is he continues to live in Trump’s head rent-free. Donald Trump is out there on the stump, and in theory, he should be talking about his accomplishments. Instead he’s relitigating his decisions involving ballroom renovations, because he can’t help but get triggered by a single sentence from a former president.”
That sentence came at a rally in Cleveland, Ohio, when Obama observed that Trump’s gold-encrusted renovations have left the White House looking as if “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory”.
The comment triggered a mini-culture war in rightwing media – not because Obama had invoked a murderous Iraqi dictator, but because he had dared to suggest that a popular restaurant chain was a symbol of vulgar excess.
Trump waved his arms to mimic a lettuce leaf, accused Obama of snobbery and said: “Every piece of lettuce he eats has to be perfect, and I’m not that choosy.” He defended his gilded White House decor and claimed Obama had left the executive mansion “deteriorated”.
Trump’s treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, a wealthy former hedge fund manager, even staged a photo-op outside a Cheesecake Factory in Washington, ordering a french-dip cheeseburger in an apparent attempt to rebut accusations of elitism and urging “the Martha’s Vineyard set” to sample the chain’s multi-page menu.
To Obama, the outcry merely proved his case. In Atlanta, he said: “They mobilised a whole-of-government response to a joke, not to inflation, but to a joke. They don’t have solutions to actual problems, so they’d rather have the media and you talking about the Cheesecake Factory.”
For Litt, the Republican outrage betrayed a glaring double standard. “This is a party that spent years complaining, ‘Oh, you’re not allowed to say anything offensive any more,’” he said. “It turns out all these people who would die on the hill of allowing someone to use offensive language suddenly think [the] Cheesecake Factory is a line you just can’t cross.”
In rural east Tennessee, Corbin Trent, a media strategist and former communications director for Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, scoffed at Republican attempts to portray Obama’s remarks as elite condescension toward working people.
He said: “They thought they were going to do this liberal elite stuff. I live in rural America. You’ve got this guy, Donald Trump, who presents himself like a mafioso, running our country like a mob – how can he enrich himself? There’s no accountability. You’re reminded of it every time you go to the grocery store, fill up your gas tank, turn on the TV and see that we’re bombing more places.”
Democrats have also mobilised former vice-president Kamala Harris for their midterm effort, while ex-president Bill Clinton campaigned with David Jolly, who is running for governor of Florida. But Obama has been unusually active in presidential, congressional and gubernatorial elections since he left the White House.
In 2024 he backed Harris in the final stretch of the presidential race, which Trump ultimately won. When Obama opened his presidential centre in Chicago in June, all living former presidents were in attendance – but Trump was not.
Yet within the broader Democratic coalition, Obama’s legacy remains complicated. For a younger generation of activists who came of age during Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaigns and the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the former president is remembered as much for his institutional constraints and moderate compromises as for his inspirational rhetoric.
Norman Solomon, a co-founder of the progressive group RootsAction, said: “It’s like a great oil painting. If you walk up to it and look real close, it’s not going to look so great. If you look too close at Obama’s record – the collapse on peacemaking in Palestine, tripling troops in Afghanistan, presiding over the greatest upward transfer of wealth in anybody’s lifetime – it does not look so great.
“Then he leaves the White House and jets off to an island owned by a billionaire [the Obamas spent a post-presidency vacation on private islands owned by the British billionaire Sir Richard Branson in 2017]. That is not solidarity.”
Solomon acknowledged, however, that in the immediate crisis of 2026, Obama’s tactical value is undeniable. “Almost anybody is going to look great compared to Trump. In Michigan, where there’s been resentment between African American and Arab American communities, it’s helpful for Obama to present a wiser outlook on what’s at stake.”
Other progressives welcome Obama back on the campaign trail, seeing his involvement not as a concession to the old order, but as evidence that the former president recognises how far the party has moved to the left.
Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution, a group that grew out of Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign, said: “Obama hitting the campaign trail is a net positive because it’s strategic. He helps pull in key demographics including African American voters.
“But more broadly, I interpret Obama being on the campaign trail as a validation of the progressive movement’s momentum. He is the epitome of the establishment, and he is out there pounding the pavement for progressives, saying our agenda isn’t radical – it’s mainstream. It’s an affirmation of how powerful our movement has become.”
Geevarghese also highlighted Obama’s ability to shield minority candidates from xenophobic attacks. “Obama represents a candidate who overcame the opposition’s ‘othering’ – when they called him un-American and used his middle name, Hussein. In the case of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who is weathering some of those same attacks, having Obama on the trail validates his candidacy and bolsters him within the American mainstream.”
Since 2016, the DSA has grown from 6,000 members to over 130,000 nationwide, scoring high-profile mayoral victories with Zohran Mamdani in New York while looking to expand its congressional caucus.
Ashik Siddique, co-chair of the DSA, said: “Today, Obama appearing alongside progressive candidates shows where the decisive shift is happening. Voters want real results toward an alternative to the factors that produced Donald Trump. Barack Obama coming out and campaigning with candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan shows a recognition of where voters are.”
Yet Obama, like Trump, remains a political unicorn: a figure who defies easy categorisation. That remains a strength. Nina Turner, a former Ohio state senator and prominent progressive voice, said: “President Obama, because of his uniqueness, transcends the anti-establishment movement.”
“He is still an extraordinarily positive figure among the Democratic base,” she added. “Even on the progressive side, for those of us who were disappointed with the ultimate analysis of his presidency – the drone wars, running on hope and change but not making a whole lot of change – he still has ‘that thing.’ He’s a force.”
“The critique of President Obama is he was very much establishment: he ran on hope and change, but didn’t make a whole lot of change,” said Turner. “People were hopeful, though, and it’s the hopeful portion of his candidacy that still looms large – even as people critique his presidency, particularly on the progressive side of the ledger. Overall him being out there will be good for Democrats of all generations.”

Tommy Robinson conviction leaves far right with leadership void
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:00:09 UTC
20:00:09 KST

The verdict was met with a groan from Tommy Robinson’s supporters, who had sat behind the dock throughout his harassment trial.
It took more than 11 hours of jury deliberations to find the far-right activist guilty of harassment causing fear of violence to two journalists, enough time for a band of lieutenants and hangers-on to get their hopes up that he might be acquitted.
Yet as Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, potentially faces up to 10 years in prison, another narrative has now taken hold. A miscarriage of justice has taken place, according to messages pumped out across his own media platforms and the ecosystem of self-styled “citizen journalists”. Some carried wild commentary during the trial, including from Robinson himself, who wondered aloud about a “Muslim” member of the jury.
Other voices have since joined in, including Reform UK members and Rupert Lowe, the leader of the Restore Britain party and Nigel Farage’s main rival for hard-right voters. “Tommy Robinson has been found guilty – it is my view that the system has, again, treated him unfairly. We live in dark times,” tweeted Lowe, the MP for Great Yarmouth.
Evidence at Southwark crown court heard how Robinson used what the prosecution described as “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” against Daily Mail reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber after they reported on his alleged role influencing the 2024 Southport riots.
They were forced to employ security or leave their homes, while a statement from Young’s daughter told of encounters outside the family address with men believed to have been sent by Robinson, a self-styled champion of women’s safety.
Robinson also admitted “paying” for the personal number of the editor of the Daily Mail, Ted Verity, who was left a message in which Robinson threatened to make the paper’s journalists and their families “famous”.
While Robinson will learn his fate on 16 December, there are now wider implications for Britain’s far right. If he goes to jail again, the far right will be deprived of its most effective and – arguably – most charismatic leader, with little or no apparent replacement.
The obvious heir apparent is anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas, AKA Danny Tommo, the leader of the Patriot Platform movement that has brought groups of masked men on to the streets of Dover and other towns this year. He, however, is in custody ahead of a trial over the alleged slashing of a dinghy in the Channel.
“With the Robinson conviction and Thomas being away there is definitely a leadership void in the anti-migrant space, with no obvious significant figure who can step in,” said Joe Mulhall, director of research at Hope Not Hate, which has closely monitored the recent targeting of asylum accommodation and Robinson’s own rallies.
“It’s a really disparate scene made up of lots of little groupuscules, and I think the most likely thing we will see are lots of ad hoc actions being taken by various self-styled ‘patriot groups’. That can be harder to monitor and police, but this conviction is clearly a big blow for the movement nationally.”
The wind has also been taken out of the sails of the anti-migrant movement by other police arrests, including in connection with vandalism attacks targeting houses in multiple occupation (HMOs).
Of continuing concern to observers of the far right is the role of Elon Musk, who Robinson once again thanked for bankrolling his legal expenses after the multibillionaire owner of X was credited with supporting the activist’s terror charges acquittal last year.
One day alone at Southwark court cost £20,000, Robinson told supporters, a drop in the ocean to Musk. Perhaps not surprisingly, others on the far right have been eyeing up that aid.
Question marks now hover over a supposed pivot by Robinson and others around him towards encouraging a voter registration drive by their supporters, though Mulhall points out that Robinson had already appeared to be struggling with this year’s takeoff of protests.
“Patriot Platform suddenly emerged and you could see him [Robinson] scrambling to try to keep up with a support base who had already become quite impatient with what they viewed as his money-making grift,” Mulhall said. Over recent weeks, Robinson’s X feed has been taken up with reposting old footage of him confronting journalists and others in a bid to reinforce his direct action credentials.
One figure who is looking over his shoulder at Robinson, however, is Farage. The Reform UK leader responded with sarcasm when asked about the conviction, and he has clearly changed his party’s policy on permitting members who support Robinson.
Divisions could reignite between figures such as Richard Tice, vocal in the past about not wanting to have anything to do with Robinson and “his lot”, and Reform members embracing the narrative that he has become a martyr.
Meanwhile, Robinson faces up to 10 years in prison, in the worst case, although sentencing guidelines provide a wide range of flexibility to Mr Justice Cavanagh, who will first consider culpability.
A specialist criminal law barrister told the Guardian that at least two “high culpability” factors could be considered. Robinson telling journalists he was coming to get them could amount to “conduct intended to maximise fear or distress”, while hiring an investigator suggested a “high degree of planning and/or sophisticated offence”.
“In terms of harm, I suspect it will be seen in the most serious category, particularly as at least one victim moved house as a result,” the barrister said. “When it comes to the type of sentence, Robinson’s problems are that his track record of previous offences raises questions about the prospect of rehabilitation. There is also a lack of strong personal mitigation and he presents an ongoing risk, namely to journalists who say something he disagrees with.
“The judge might decide that, given the current prison overcrowding crisis, a suspended sentence will suffice. If it’s suspended for the full three years in line with guidelines, it could well have a greater impact on reining in his behaviour.”

Why Doctors Are Last to Know What’s in the Drug Supply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

The illicit drug supply has changed rapidly over the last few months, with nitazenes, medetomidine, cychlorphine, and other novel synthetic substances appearing in rapid succession. Rapid tests for emerging substances are being developed and marketed with impressive speed, and these can return results within minutes. Law enforcement, medical examiners, employers, community organizations and even the general public can use them, if their states have decriminalized them. Physicians treating overdoses cannot.
The contrast is hard to ignore: A test can be used to fire someone or support a criminal case, yet it remains unavailable to the physician in an emergency room trying to save that person’s life, when minutes are essential.
The divide is largely regulatory. Many tests for emerging drugs are labeled for forensic use only, and clinical tests for living patients require approval by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a diagnostic tool. As such, they cannot legally be used by medical clinics that adhere to federal law and funding policies.
Tests used in patient care must meet FDA requirements for clinical diagnostics. Point-of-care testing—testing performed at or near the bedside—also requires an additional determination that the test is simple and low-risk enough to qualify for waived status under the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA). There is a legitimate reason for that regulatory distinction. Tests used to make medical decisions should be accurate, reliable, and interpreted appropriately. A rapid screen is not definitive toxicology, and it should not be treated as such.
Fentanyl shows why speed matters. In early 2023, we pointed out that rapid fentanyl tests already existed outside clinical medicine, yet hospitals relied on expensive spectrometry testing that could take an hour or longer, if the equipment was available onsite at all. By the time FDA-cleared and CLIA-waived rapid fentanyl tests arrived, the illicit market had already changed again.
Starting in 2020, xylazine spread through the fentanyl supply, introducing a new clinical hurdle: naloxone reverses opioids, but not xylazine. Patients can remain dangerously sedated or unstable even after naloxone is given. Further, xylazine is associated with necrotic skin wounds that increase risk of sepsis, and withdrawal syndromes that are more complex to treat than opioids alone.
Not long after, medetomidine overtook xylazine supplies. It, too, does not react to naloxone, causes profound sedation and cardiovascular instability, and its withdrawal syndrome—which can come on just hours after someone stops using it—can trigger extreme hypertension and tachycardia that has been connected to heart attacks in younger people. Knowing these facts could significantly alter a patient’s treatment or discharge plan.
There are no point-of-care tests for either of these drugs or other alarming and novel chemicals like cychlorphine, an opioid that does not show up on fentanyl tests. Because of that, clinicians have to follow information from law-enforcement seizures, public-health alerts, and months-old fatality data rather than from tests at the bedside. These data are in siloes and not easy to access or combine.
The result is a system that can identify emerging drugs in seized samples and autopsies before clinicians can identify them in living patients. There is a better approach.
The FDA should establish an expedited pathway for clinical tests targeting emerging drug threats, triggered when agencies such as the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) or the Office of National Drug Control Policy identify a substance of significant and growing public-health concern. The agency already has a dual pathway through which manufacturers can seek a special clearance and a CLIA waiver together. That framework could be prioritized and adapted for emerging drugs rather than forcing each new threat through the ordinary timeline.
Federal agencies could also help fund independent validation. The economics of emerging drugs are unusual: a substance can appear quickly, spread unevenly, and be replaced by something else before a manufacturer can justify the cost of extensive clinical studies. Federal and state agencies could make up this gap if the threat of the new drug is significant. A small market does not mean a small public health or public safety need.
None of this requires pretending a test strip is mass spectrometry. Point-of-care testing should be explicitly treated as presumptive. Positive results can be confirmed when necessary. Clinical care rarely rests on a single perfect source of information, anyway.
Physicians already make decisions by combining an imperfect history, physical examination, vital signs, laboratory results, and response to treatment. A rapid drug screen would simply be another tool in that toolbox that helps dispel the fog of drug supply changes.
Further, the value extends beyond the individual patient. Better hospital data could become an early-warning system rather than a retrospective record of a crisis already underway. Emergency departments are on the front lines of the overdose crisis; they should have access to the most innovative testing tools at the bedside, when minutes can make a difference.
