What Democrats Can Learn From New York’s Data Center Moratorium
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.
When New York became the first state in the country to enact a moratorium on data center development, Adrienne Yocina was excited. For the past two years, the mom of three has been organizing in western Genesee County to stop a 600-megawatt data center from coming to a site close to the Tonawanda Seneca Nation’s reservation and a federal wildlife refuge.
But almost four months after the one-year moratorium began, Yocina tells me that she’s “getting nervous.” She’s worried that Democratic governor Kathy Hochul won’t sign a stronger bill to impose a stricter moratorium, and is concerned that the state Department of Environmental Conservation is not adequately involved in the process of evaluating data centers in New York.
“I feel like she’s just trying to shut us up,” she says of Hochul.
Data centers are at the center of midterm races across the country, with politicians of both parties making promises to enact regulations or moratoriums on development. After next week comes the tough part: Newly elected officials must either break their word or follow through on those promises as they weigh large infrastructure projects coming to their states and residents who say they’ll reject data centers no matter what.
How will those compromises go—and will they appease voters? New York’s moratorium, and the continued opposition from some groups, may offer clues.
In July, just two months after dismissing the idea of a data center moratorium, Hochul signed the nation’s first executive order to put a pause on development. Her order was a compromise. Just weeks prior, the state legislature had passed an omnibus bill that would have implemented a one-year moratorium throughout New York. The bill contained several provisions that made it more aggressive than Hochul’s moratorium, including stricter limits on the size of data centers and a mandate that the Department of Environmental Conservation conduct a thorough environmental impact review of data center operations. Rather than sign the bill, Hochul issued her own order. (The governor has until the end of the year to sign that bill, and her office says they are still looking at it.)
One of the bill’s State Senate sponsors, Democrat Kristen Gonzalez, has been publicly supportive of Hochul’s moratorium. The governor’s office, Gonzalez says, proactively reached out to her after her bill passed to help design the moratorium for more immediate relief for New Yorkers.
Gonzalez went on a data center tour of New York at the end of the summer, talking to residents around the state about their concerns. She told me that the people she talked to overwhelmingly wanted Hochul to go further and implement more aggressive measures to protect communities from data centers.
“There are local communities statewide that are living near existing data centers, dealing with significant air pollution and noise pollution, who are struggling with rising utility bills and rising water bills,” she told me. “We see the moratorium as a first step, but it can’t be the last.”
Hochul has a comfortable lead over Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman ahead of Tuesday’s election—something that may have been helped by the moratorium’s passing. In a recent Quinnipiac poll of New York voters, 53 percent of respondents said they trusted Hochul to do a better job in handling AI and data centers, compared to just 31 percent trusting Blakeman. Blakeman, who has voiced support for data centers, called Hochul’s moratorium “crazy” when it was passed in July. His campaign didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
Hochul has also touted her tough-on-data-center bona fides on the campaign trail. Early last month, she hosted a roundtable discussion on data centers with agricultural, environmental, and business leaders at a farm in the Hudson Valley. There, she told reporters that she wanted to work with the state legislature to implement more aggressive protections, including banning tax breaks for data centers. At the event, Hochul was flanked by Gonzalez and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, one of Washington’s most prominent data center critics.
I asked Hochul at the event how she anticipates handling continued opposition after her moratorium ends. How does New York balance economic development with community opposition if some people don’t want data centers in their backyards under any circumstances, even with the assurances from the state that Hochul’s office is working to create?
The purpose of her pause, she said, was that communities should be able to choose. “This is democracy in action,” she said. “If you want it, it should come with all kinds of guardrails and restraints, but if you don’t want it, it doesn’t come.”
More New Yorkers may end up choosing the latter option. A Siena poll from September found that 63 percent of New Yorkers would oppose data centers being built in their area even after Hochul’s moratorium expires. (It’s even higher for New York Democrats, with 75 percent saying they’d remain opposed to data center development post-moratorium.)
Many newly elected (or reelected) governors will face a similar dynamic: At least 20 gubernatorial candidates have promised a data center moratorium or pause, according to research compiled by government relations company MultiState. Even more have promised to regulate the industry more tightly. Formerly data-center-friendly incumbents like Texas’s Greg Abbott and Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro have also made pledges to be stricter on their development.
Come January, new governors will face highly engaged constituents who are finding a political home for the first time in the fight against data centers. That includes Yocina, who says she had never voted in a local election before.
She says she understands the need for industries and jobs in upstate New York: Her youngest son decided to join the Army after a fruitless job search and is about to be deployed. Now, her organizing group is moving from focusing on just stopping the data center to brainstorming new ideas for the site.
“We’re trying to figure out what we can say yes to that’s not a data center,” she says.
What We’re Writing
Buried in Anthropic’s IPO documents filed last week was a startling admission. The tech giant’s plan to develop its own data centers exposes it to financial risk, thanks to its projected reliance on natural gas. Of course, Anthropic isn’t alone in its reliance on gas, and the filing acknowledges that’s a real problem. The heavy demand could “drive up the price of natural gas” and make it harder to purchase. I took a look at Anthropic’s plans for data centers and the brewing competition between data centers over natural gas supply in the US.
What We’re Reading
- The Verge’s Gaby Del Valle takes readers out west for a deep dive on data centers’ water woes in Arizona—and why a massive and thirsty chip manufacturing plant seems to have escaped the public’s ire.
- New findings from Pew Research Center show that advertisers spent $12 million on political ads mentioning data centers in a 90-day period leading up to the midterms.
- Two professors who study real estate and urban economics write in The Conversation about their most recent research on data centers and job creation. Their findings: Data centers lead to modest job growth in certain sectors like transportation and warehousing, but not in local services like restaurants and retail.

Tiered immigration hub by Aedas opens at Shenzhen-Hong Kong border

Tiered immigration hub by Aedas opens at Shenzhen-Hong Kong border
Architecture studio Aedas has completed a tiered, round-edged building designed to accommodate an immigration hub between Hong Kong and Shenzhen, China.
Perched on the banks of the Shenzhen River, the New Huanggang Port Development opened earlier this month in replacement of the original Huanggang Port, which first opened between the two cities in 1989.
Conceived by Aedas as a “large-scale integrated hub”, the nine-storey facility combines border control and transport networks with 25,000 square metres of public space.
Its stacked volume is complete with a “flowing facade” formed of horizontal metal fins, while its rounded form was designed to evoke a pebble, in reference to its riverside location.
“The grounded, rounded form responds to the building’s large scale and waterfront setting, evoking a pebble resting on the banks of the Shenzhen River,” the studio told Dezeen.
“Flowing metal fins wrap the elevation like ribbons, reinforcing the building’s fluid appearance and symbolising the close connection between Shenzhen and Hong Kong.”
“[The building’s] integrated transport networks, flowing facade and welcoming civic spaces express the close relationship between the two cities while establishing a distinctive point of arrival,” the studio added.
A modular, prefabrication approach was employed to construct the building’s volume, which opens up at ground level via two sunken plazas and is topped with a solar panel-covered roof terrace.
Across its four elevations, its rhythmic horizontal fins have been lifted to form large glass curtain walls that draw daylight into the interior.
Inside, the hub’s transport, immigration and public programmes are stacked vertically and connected by a network of internal escalators.
To accommodate an expected average of 200,000 passengers per day, two of these floors have been dedicated to immigration halls complete with a “barrier-free” design.
Direct connections to transport networks are provided on the floors below, where the hub links to four of Shenzhen’s rail and metro lines to “support a seamless border-crossing journey”.
“Transport, immigration and public programmes are vertically organised under one roof,” the studio said.
“The nine-storey building uses vertical stacking to organise pedestrian crossing, vehicle crossing, public transport and civic amenities efficiently within a constrained site, separating passenger and vehicular flows while maintaining convenient connections between programmes,” it added.
A series of structural, arched columns informed by Shenzhen’s emblem flower – the Bougainvillea – divide the expansive interiors, which are illuminated by 73 roof skylights, facade openings and an integrated lighting system.
Nearby, RHSP has unveiled designs for a skyscraper with a “striking butterfly layout” and MAD has completed a series of boulder-like galleries across a green-roofed museum.

Barabak: This desert duel is a key test of Trump's effect on the midterm election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani and Democratic challenger JoAnna Mendoza are battling over some of the hardest-fought political turf in America.
- But many voters regard the contest as more of a proxy fight between the president and his antagonists.
MARANA, Ariz. — Michael Falk was heading into the Pima County branch library to drop off his ballot when he stopped to discuss Tuesday’s midterm election.
Pima County, in south-central Arizona, is home to one of the most competitive congressional races in the country. Falk, a 66-year-old retiree and political independent, was casting his vote for the Democrat, JoAnna Mendoza, even though he hardly knows a thing about her.
But Falk knows — and loathes — a good deal about President Trump.
“From the very beginning, when he stepped on the political stage, he made it quite clear to the people who were silenced for a long time, the bigots of the United States, he gave them a voice, and he told those people, ‘It’s OK for you to think the way that you do.’
“And then that just took off like wildfire,” Falk said, sweeping his arm like a moving wall of flame, “and that’s why we have all these laws that are against brown people and illegal people.”
Gregory Corron confessed he’s not too familiar with Mendoza’s opponent, the Republican incumbent Juan Ciscomani.
But Corron, a 67-year-old computer programmer, voted for Trump three times and believes the president is moving the country in the right direction.
“I think, for instance, exposing fraud is a big thing. Technology is taking off. I’m totally excited about that,” said Corron, who was killing time at a strip mall in Oro Valley while the tires on his Lexus were being replaced. “I think the economy is strong. The stock market is doing well. Employment is doing well.”
For that reason, Corron cast his ballot for Ciscomani, fearful of what might happen if Democrats take control of Congress. “The reforms that Trump started,” Corron said, “need to continue.”
Mendoza and Ciscomani have assaulted the voters of southern Arizona for months, overwhelming their senses and curdling the airwaves with a ceaseless barrage of acrid advertising. Together, the two rivals and their allies have spent tens of millions of dollars on the contest, which both parties have made a top priority.
And yet, to a large degree, Mendoza and Ciscomani are mere stand-ins, their candidacies serving as little more than proxies for the president and his opposition.
Barabak: Your Nov. 3 election results right here. (Not really. But at least some perspective)
Democrats appear a cinch to win control of the House, but the Senate remains a toss-up. Save your sanity by ignoring the polls. And don’t put too much weight on Republicans’ big financial advantage.
Laura Lentner, another Oro Valley resident, allowed as how Ciscomani has done some good things. He is not, the Democrat said, a bad man.
“But his continued support of Trump negates it all for me,” said the 73-year-old retired dental hygienist. It’s about time, Lentner suggested, Republican lawmakers stand up and “stop being afraid of [Trump] and his constituents.”
Arizona’s 6th Congressional District is anchored in eastern Tucson and its suburbs, sprawling north toward Phoenix, east to New Mexico and south all the way to the U.S.-Mexico border. The arid landscape is creased with rugged mountain ranges, cleaved by scenic canyons and filled with vast stretches of open space interrupted by midsize cities and small towns that spring like oases from the desert floor.
In recent years, the terrain has been some of the hardest-fought political turf in the nation.
Joe Biden carried the district in 2020 by less than a percentage point. Four years later, Trump flipped it by the same tiny margin.
Ciscomani, bidding for a third term, has won two nail-biters. He’s facing a fresh opponent in Mendoza, a Marine veteran and former congressional staffer.
The district has a significant Latino population — Ciscomani and Mendoza are Mexican American — and a sizable number of seniors, veterans and military personnel. Mendoza has leaned into her Navy and Marine Corps service. “Battle Tested. Ready To Lead,” her billboards declare, including one near the Ft. Huachuca Army base. (His signs tout “Veterans For Ciscomani.”)
Mendoza has attacked the incumbent as a “spineless” tool of Trump, putting the president front and center in her avalanche of advertising. Ciscomani’s incessant ads tout his bipartisanship — he hails from the establishment wing of the Republican Party — and portray Mendoza as a tool of the unhinged left.
Ordinary citizens across the country are participating in grassroots efforts to guard against possible election interference by the Trump administration.
In that way their campaigns distill the push-pull of this midterm election, which, like every one before, amounts to a referendum on the occupant of the Oval Office.
For Trump supporters, that means explaining away vexations like inflation and the war with Iran, twin anchors dragging down the president and fellow Republicans.
Higher costs, Trump voters said, are a hangover from Biden’s time in office, a needed sacrifice or an inconvenience that will pass. Echoing the president, they said the record-breaking cost of gas was a trade-off — and a good one — to keep Iran from building a nuclear weapon.
“I wish gas prices were lower,” said Susan Summers, a Republican who stopped to chat while grocery shopping in Vail. The old railroad town has become a destination for retirees like Summers, 74, a former administrator at Cal State San Bernardino, and for commuters who don’t mind the roughly 25-mile drive to Tucson.
But, Summers went on, she’s willing to accept higher gas prices “because I think it was important to stop a fanatical regime from acquiring nuclear weapons that would actually threaten us in the longer range. Once there is some kind of resolution ... prices will come down somewhat and it will make life easier for a lot of people.”
Merilyn Prentice, 78, is another refugee from the state next door. She moved to Benson (population 5,500) from Southern California after a career in nursing. She praised Trump for demonstrating a resolve that other presidents lacked.
“They’re terrorist supporters, and we have terrorist cells in this country,” Prentice said of Iran. “No one wants to talk about that. None of the other presidents wanted to touch it.”
If backers of the president often seemed defensive — justifying, rationalizing, urging patience — Trump critics were seething.
In Sierra Vista, Ann Nichols, 72 and a Democratic-leaning independent, could scarcely get the words out fast enough as she cataloged her outrage.
“Let’s not forget how the tariffs have wrecked the economy,” she said, “how the war that [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu tricked Trump into declaring on Iran has wrecked the economy, driven up gas prices, and the rampant corruption in the government, and how the Environmental Protection Agency might as well be known as the Environmental Pollution Agency, and the attempt to wreck the Education Department, and we’ve got a twit who knows nothing about medicine in charge of medicine.”
Nichols paused to adjust her N95 mask. She spent decades as a medical librarian at the Ft. Huachuca Army base.
Her vote for Mendoza, Nichols said, was a vote to leash Trump and start undoing some of the damage he’s inflicted over the last two years.
For all that passion, however, it would be wrong to assume a blue wave — should one come Tuesday — means there’s great regard or overflowing affection for Democrats.
The contest in Nevada’s 2nd Congressional District should be a shoo-in for Republicans. But a problematic candidate, inflation and Trump’s unpopularity give Democrats not far-fetched hopes for a massive upset.
Clayton Surratt, 63, a retired actor and screenwriter, was passing out boxes of groceries — veggies, protein, a loaf of bread — at the food bank in Vail when he paused to share his unhappiness with both Trump and the Democratic Party.
“I think our current government thrives and lives on cruelty,” he said as a steady stream of cars pulled up for delivery. “It upsets me to see our world, our leaders, acting in ways that we would punish an 8-year-old at school if they behave that way.”
At the same time, Surratt said, he’s not sure what Democrats stand for, beyond opposition to Trump.
Adam Thompson, a Democratic-leaning independent, was blunter still. “I don’t like either party,” he said. The 39-year-old lives in Tanque Verde and travels throughout south-central Arizona, delivering soda and snack foods to major retailers. He’s particularly upset these days with Trump.
Why, Thompson asked, are so much time and resources being devoted to matters overseas?
“We need to take care of the people here,” Thompson said. “The war in Iran, the war in the Middle East is not helping me put food on my table. I work my ass off. But at the end of the day, I have to pay that price because … we’re so busy fighting wars for other people.”
Barabak: Is this purple state about to go blue? Nevada’s GOP governor faces an anti-Trump backlash
Joe Lombardo is no MAGA warrior, but his Democratic opponent ties him to the president at every opportunity. Lombardo hopes Nevada voters judge him on his performance, not Trump’s.
The big question is how many discouraged Trump voters sit the election out. Their level of apathy and absenteeism will spell the difference between a good and a great night for Democrats.
Alex Lagerberg, a 35-year-old tattoo artist and libertarian, is a three-time Trump voter. He was initially attracted by his seeming authenticity and background as a New York real estate developer. “He was a good option because he was not a politician,” Lagerberg said outside a mercado in Casa Grande. But, he continued, it turns out that Trump’s supposed entrepreneurial prowess wasn’t all Lagerberg thought it was, or that Trump purported it to be.
“Treating the country like a business was a good thing for a little bit, but it really hasn’t helped,” Lagerberg said. “We haven’t seen much change.”
He’s not particularly motivated to vote, Lagerberg said, or decide between Ciscomani and Mendoza, especially with the two heaving so much mud at each other.
Rick, who declined to give his last name because he doesn’t want to be hassled for his opinion, has made up his mind. He’s done voting — forever.
The 67-year-old retired government worker, a right-leaning libertarian, soured on politics and politicians long ago. “Democrat, Republican,” he said, “it’s all the same thing.”
He voted for Trump in 2024, giving the political system one last shot. And now? Trump promised “no new wars. What do we have?” Rick asked. “New wars. Taxes are still too high. And Medicare? Medicare sucks.” So no, he said, he’s not bothering with the election.
As he left Vail’s thrift shop, steamed about Trump, Mendoza, Ciscomani and the whole lot, Rick clutched his purchase, a compilation of Ray Price’s greatest hits. One song by the country singer seemed to sum up Rick’s attitude: “You Done Me Wrong.”
He’s not alone.

A potential Democratic wave looms over Trump. Where does MAGA go after the midterms?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Heading into the vote, Trump faces the lowest job approval ratings of his career.
- Trump’s team is still staking his movement on the same thing that has defined it in the past: Trump himself.
WASHINGTON — The specter of a Democratic wave on Tuesday and retreat of Republican power has quietly sparked conversations within GOP circles about President Trump’s eventual exit from the political stage — and the future of a party that has revolved around him for the past decade.
Heading into the vote, Trump faces the lowest job approval ratings of his career. Factions of the Republican Party long loyal to his brand are beginning to break ranks. Candidates who have aligned themselves most closely to the president are among the most imperiled. From the shores of Lake Ontario to rural Kansas, signs point to a voter coalition under strain, as Republicans grappling with a troubled economy question the party’s direction.
Recent polls show that 67% of Trump’s 2024 voters approve of his job performance, down from 95% early in his second term. The steepest drops are among younger voters and Latino support, according to a Pew Research Center poll.
While a majority of Republicans still want to see the next leader of the party follow Trump on most issues, a third want to see the next GOP presidential nominee take a different approach, according to a New York Times/Siena poll in May.
Marc Short, who served as Trump’s first White House director for legislative affairs, said that Republicans were “essentially in triage mode” entering the midterms, citing “inflation challenges” and an “avalanche of corruption stories.” Bryan Lanza, a former communications director for Trump, expressed concern last week that Republican enthusiasm has reached such lows that races in Mississippi and Texas are genuine toss-ups.
Federal grand jury subpoenas have demanded that county election officials turn over internal communications and testify, raising concerns that investigations could intimidate workers.
The Republican reckoning tests a party infrastructure reshaped around the president since his insurgent rise in 2015 transformed the GOP.
At the top of the party, warning signs of a splintering coalition have not changed the view that Trump still maintains the grip on the GOP’s future — and that any future decisions should take that into account.
“I think he’ll help decide who the next president is going to be,” Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters said. “I think he’ll be super involved with not only the party but the process, and I welcome that as the chairman.”
Gruters called Trump “the single most important person in the Republican Party” and said he doubts the movement will reshape itself into a different kind of coalition based on the outcome of Tuesday’s election.
“I think it will continue to be Trump’s movement for as long as he’s alive,” he said. “It will be Trump’s movement.”
Others in Trump’s inner circle are making the same bet. His team is still staking Trump’s movement on the same thing that has defined it in the past: Trump himself.
“We’ve been with him for 10 years,” the official said. “Do you think he’s going away after the next two? No.”
What comes after that, the official wouldn’t say.
“Everyone wants to jump ahead and ask what 2028 looks like and what does beyond look like,” the official said. “I think the really smart thing about the president, and he’s even admitted it about himself, he’s always focused on the now, and he just works his a— off at the task at hand.”
The question of who inherits the movement is already taking shape, but Trump has avoided saying much when asked who he thinks should be the heir apparent.
Asked in the Oval Office last month whether he would endorse Vice President JD Vance — who had said a day earlier that he expected Trump’s backing if he decides to run for president in 2028 — Trump called Vance a “very talented person” and a “very good person,” but would not commit.
“I don’t think we’ve ever talked about it,” Trump said. “It’s early, very early right now. We have to get through the midterms.”
A New York Times/Siena poll released last week found that Republican primary voters favor Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio to be the party’s next nominee. Underscoring Trump’s grip on the party, the poll found, 8% said they want it to be Trump, who cannot run because of term limits.
The challenge for Republicans in the future will be to figure out a way to capture the MAGA base without isolating themselves from more mainstream Republican voters, said a GOP lobbyist with ties to Trump speaking on condition of anonymity to speak candidly.
“I think it would be foolish to ignore the MAGA base for any future candidate,” the lobbyist said. “The movement can evolve, but you need those voters to come out and vote.”
Mike Madrid, a longtime Republican political strategist and co-founder of the Lincoln Project, which staunchly opposes Trump, argued that the future of the GOP will be influenced more by right-wing media personalities than policy because Trump consciously upended the party’s ideology over the last decade.
“The Republican Party is far, far more likely to balkanize than split along ideological lines because there is no ideological glue holding the GOP together anymore,” he said. “That’s gone.”
Madrid doubts Trump will change course even if Republicans suffer big losses on Tuesday night.
“Donald Trump is not going to adjust. He’s not capable of that. He never has. He never will,” Madrid said. “It doesn’t even occur to him. And even if it did, he wouldn’t know how to do it.”
California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.
If Democrats win a majority in Congress, history shows that it can be an opening for a president to pivot.
“What often happens in the last two years [of a term] is presidents bounce back,” said Christopher Warshaw, a Georgetown University public policy professor.
Presidents who “lose control of Congress and get shellacked in the midterms” often pivot to the political center, and tell voters “we’re going to try a new approach,” Warshaw said.
President Clinton did that after Republicans swept Congress in 1994, Warshaw said. President Biden did not after the 2022 midterms, a choice Warshaw said probably hurt Democrats in 2024, when Trump was elected. If Democrats win on Tuesday, Trump has signaled that he would be open to working with them to get things done.
“I hope that won’t be the case, but if it is, that has happened before with many presidents,” he told reporters. “You have strong veto and you end up working out deals.”
However Trump might deal with a divided Washington, the coalition he built is unlikely to dissipate when he leaves office, said Lynn Vavreck, a political science professor at UCLA.
“They want to build a very specific kind of world,” Vavreck said. “Those desires are not going to go away next Wednesday, or in 2028.”

Bulgarians vote in presidential run-off amid Black Sea tensions
Voters in Bulgaria weigh economic challenges and attacks on ships in a race marked by record low turnout.
Voting is under way in a Bulgarian presidential run-off marked by growing regional security threats and domestic economic concerns.
President Iliana Iotova, 61, led over former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, in the first round but fell short of the 50 percent threshold needed to win. The first round drew record low turnout. Only 23 percent of eligible voters cast a ballot, according to election officials.
Exit polls will be published after voting ends at 8pm (18:00 GMT) on Sunday, with a result expected on Monday.
The presidential vote comes against the backdrop of a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast in the past month, which have sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of Russia’s war on Ukraine.
About two dozen seafarers are feared dead, and the strikes have prompted the government to seek help from Bulgaria’s allies to bolster maritime security. On Wednesday, a Greek container ship sank after being hit by sea drones.
Both leading presidential candidates have condemned the attacks. Prime Minister Rumen Radev, who backs Iotova, said the strikes’ outcome “benefits the Russian Federation”. They have both called for a diplomatic end to the war in Ukraine.
A victory for Iotova would make her Bulgaria’s first elected female president. She became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter and win a parliamentary race on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine.
He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
Gyurov said he wants Bulgaria to be a reliable NATO ally able to stand for up its interests with strong diplomacy and a firm position.
A host of right-leaning political figures, among them ex-Prime Minister Boiko Borisov, have expressed support for Gyurov.

Venezuela’s army attacked Colombian leftist rebels camped on its side of the border, leaving several people dead, an NGO told AFP on Oct. 31.

Campaigning enters homestretch before key US midterm elections

The battle for control of Congress entered its final campaign weekend as President Donald Trump’s administration pursued a criminal investigation into Alaska’s pivotal U.S. Senate race and said Saturday it would likely take a dispute over thousands of California mail-in ballots to the Supreme Court.
In Alaska, federal prosecutors are investigating whether aides to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola helped recruit a retired schoolteacher, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to run because his name is similar to Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan.
The closely contested race is crucial to Democrats' hopes of taking the Senate in Tuesday's election.
It is one of 35 Senate races, along with all 435 House seats, that will decide whether U.S. President Donald Trump's Republicans keep control of Congress for the next two years.
Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority and a narrow edge in the House.
Early voting has set a record. More than 51 million Americans have already cast ballots in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day at the last midterms in 2022.
In California, a federal appeals court this week ruled 2-1 that the Justice Department had failed to justify its emergency bid to force the state to set aside mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters it alleges are likely noncitizens.
"I hesitate to give a final answer, but I think probably the Supreme Court is next on this one," acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told Fox News Saturday, adding that any request for Supreme Court consideration would come before Tuesday's election.
U.S. President Donald Trump has been on a campaign blitz in multiple states over the past month but is spending Saturday at his Mar-a-Lago Club in Palm Beach, Florida. He returns to the campaign trail Sunday in Kansas and Iowa.
The Justice Department's top prosecutor in Alaska, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a Friday news conference that a recent New York Times article, which reported an effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., drove a "surge" of FBI resources to the case.
Heyman said he assigned several prosecutors to it and that investigative steps proceeded "intensely and swiftly."
Peltola and the campaign committee have denied involvement in any effort to recruit the second Sullivan. The retired teacher has denied coordinating with Peltola's campaign.
Voters in Alaska have largely dismissed the fight over the ballot.
"I knew which Dan Sullivan was which Dan Sullivan, you know? It is very clear on the ballot," Anchorage resident Mickey Buster, 36, said as he stood outside a polling place Saturday.
But another Anchorage voter, Carol Riggs, 52, said she was disappointed by the entire situation and the possibility it "muddies the water for some voters, potentially."
In Michigan, where Democrat Abdul el-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers in another closely watched Senate race, el-Sayed's feud with the rival he beat in the primary, U.S. Representative Haley Stevens, flared again.
El-Sayed's campaign asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as "not to distract from the central issues of the campaign," a person familiar with the matter said.
Stevens has backed el-Sayed but demanded he condemn an outside group's ad blaming Israel for high grocery prices and apologize for past rhetoric about Israel.
"It is certainly unhelpful to the el-Sayed campaign to have continued visible division within the party just before Election Day," said Matt Grossmann, a political scientist at Michigan State University. Polls show el-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support.
The administration, beyond its bid to block the counting of ballots from more than 20,000 California voters it alleges are likely noncitizens, has sued roughly 30 states and the District of Columbia seeking unredacted voter rolls.
The legal maneuvers have alarmed state election officials. Under the Constitution, states have primary authority over how states run elections.
On Friday, a federal judge ordered the Justice Department to stop threatening to prosecute California election officials who defy its directives.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, on Saturday warned the state's top federal judges that the Justice Department may seek warrants to seize ballots before results are certified, though he said he did not know of any pending request.
Newsom said in a letter to the judges that the only reason to seize ballots "would be to interfere" in the count.
Sean Morales-Doyle of the Brennan Center for Justice said the efforts, while unlikely to win in court, aim at "creating uncertainty, sowing fear, distrust, chaos," in hopes of pressuring officials such as Alaska's lieutenant governor "to do something that they are not supposed to do."
Even so, 76% of U.S. voters are confident their ballots will be counted accurately, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted from Sept. 30 to Oct. 5, with confidence about equally high among Republicans and Democrats.

That statement set out a package built around Typhoon fighters flying defensive air missions, with the accompanying operational update confirming that the aircraft will not conduct offensive strikes. An A400M transport will move defence materiel within Saudi Arabia, military advisers will support Saudi staff officers, and existing air to air refuelling support for Saudi defensive air operations is being extended, including for operations against Houthi military sites in Yemen.
Ministers were asked earlier this month whether legal advice had been sought on that refuelling support and declined to say, in keeping with the long-standing convention that the fact and content of law officers’ advice are not disclosed. The Houthis have attacked Saudi territory repeatedly since 2015 and resumed strikes on the Kingdom after a period of relative quiet.

Nearly 3,000 Canadian Armored Vehicles Now in Ukrainian Hands—and More Are Coming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:55:57 UTC
19:55:57 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Nearly 3,000 Canadian Armored Vehicles Now in Ukrainian Hands—and More Are Coming
Ukraine has received nearly 3,000 Canadian-made Roshel Senator armored vehicles since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, with deliveries continuing as demand for protected military transport remains high despite the growing dominance of drones on the battlefield.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on October 30, the latest delivery figures were revealed by Canadian manufacturer Roshel in an announcement about a first-generation Senator MRAP joining the permanent exhibition at the Canadian War Museum. The vehicle will serve as a symbol of Canada’s military support for Ukraine.
The milestone highlights the scale of Roshel’s contribution to Ukraine’s defense, with its armored vehicles used for troop transportation, logistics, and evacuation missions.
Roshel’s deliveries have expanded steadily. By early December 2025, Ukraine had received more than 2,000 vehicles. That figure exceeded 2,500 by late May 2026 and has now approached 3,000.
Between May 2025 and May 2026 alone, approximately 700 armored vehicles were delivered to Ukrainian forces, according to company figures cited by Defense Express. The publication suggests that annual deliveries could remain at similar levels or increase further.
The Senator MRAP is built on a Ford F-550 chassis and features a V-shaped hull designed to redirect the force of explosions away from its occupants. Its protection is rated at Level 2 for ballistic threats and Level 3 for mine blasts under NATO's STANAG 4569 standards, including protection against explosions equivalent to eight kilograms of TNT.
The vehicles remain essential for moving soldiers, delivering supplies, and evacuating wounded personnel. Defense Express notes that additional anti-drone protective structures may be fitted to the vehicles as battlefield threats evolve.
Canada has also committed to supplying another 383 Senator armored vehicles under a military assistance package announced in February 2026.
The package includes 100 medical evacuation vehicles, 82 command vehicles, and 201 personnel carriers. Roshel’s CEO said in October that all 383 had already been delivered ahead of schedule, meaning they should not be counted as additional future deliveries.
Meanwhile, Roshel has established armored vehicle assembly operations in Ukraine and is working to localize component production, expanding cooperation beyond direct deliveries from Canada.

Arab parties to back Eisenkot in Israeli coalition talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:55:24 UTC
19:55:24 KST

Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, waves an Israeli flag onstage after the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election. (AP Photo)
Arab parties in Israel are set to recommend opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot for prime minister during consultations with President Isaac Herzog, potentially reshaping the balance of power in the country’s coalition-building process, Israeli media reported on Nov. 1.
The Oct. 27 elections ended without either of the two main political blocs securing a clear majority.
The results showed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats.
The main opposition bloc won 48 seats, while Arab-led parties secured another 19, marking a historic showing.
With neither camp able to command a majority on its own, Arab parties have emerged as potential kingmakers in negotiations to form the next government.
Parties must now negotiate alliances and secure the support of at least 61 lawmakers in the 120-seat Knesset to form a government.
The president is expected to begin consultations with representatives of parties elected to Israel’s Knesset as early as Nov. 4, summoning them to his official residence even before the new parliament is formally sworn in.
During the meetings, Herzog will ask party representatives which candidate they support to lead the efforts to form the next government.
The president typically entrusts the mandate to form a government to the lawmaker he considers most likely to secure a parliamentary majority.
While the candidate who receives the backing of the largest number of fellow lawmakers usually has the strongest claim, the president is not bound solely by the number of endorsements.
The consultations could bring unexpected developments, including a possible endorsement of Eisenkot by Arab parties seeking to bring an end to Netanyahu’s rule, several media reports said.
Under the current projections, Eisenkot appears to be the frontrunner for the mandate.
In a speech on Nov. 1, Herzog urged political factions to approach the consultations with an open mind.
Opposition to Netanyahu’s government was among the factors behind the increased turnout among Arab voters.
According to The Times of Israel, the Joint List is prepared to support anti-Netanyahu parties from outside the government, although it has ruled out joining a coalition itself.
“We want to help anyone who wants to bring down this awful government… and switch it for a different government. We want to be part of the correction, part of the hope,” veteran Arab lawmaker Ahmad Tibi was quoted as saying.
Meanwhile, Jafar Farah, a prominent figure in the Arab political movement, told The Telegraph that both Ra’am and the Joint List are expected to inform Herzog of their readiness to support the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot.
Farah confirmed that the two factions will recommend the former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff for prime minister.
Hundreds of Israelis took to the streets on Oct. 31 to urge the opposition to ally with Arab parties to oust Netanyahu.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (AA Photo)

The recently reelected leftist leader is a leading figure in global warming discussion.
Brazil hosted the previous summit last year in the heart of the Amazon.
Despite the symbolism of holding the talks in the world’s largest tropical rainforest, delegations failed to set binding targets or deadlines for phasing out coal, oil and gas.
Experts say an agreement on that front is unlikely this year, with markets under intense pressure from the war in the Middle East.
Among its 10 “priority issues,” Türkiye proposes reducing emissions by increasing electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035. The current share is around 23 percent.
Türkiye will hold the presidency of this year’s annual climate summit, while Australia will lead the negotiations. The meeting of heads of state is scheduled for Nov. 11-12.
Lula, 81, won the Oct. 25 presidential runoff against conservative Flavio Bolsonaro.
“It was a victory for the fight against climate change” over “climate change denial,” Brazilian Health Minister Alexandre Padilha, who will accompany the president to COP31, told AFP on Oct. 28.

Hundreds of thousands of protesters inspired by frustrated high school students took to the streets across France on Oct. 31 in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.
Youth-led protests were also held elsewhere in Europe, including in Germany and Portugal.
France’s protests were overwhelmingly peaceful, but gatherings in Paris and other cities ended in clouds of tear gas and scattered fires set by small groups on the margins.
About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country after French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a “very high risk” of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Paris marches were rerouted to the capital’s edge to protect stores, government buildings and touristed areas in the city center.
France’s government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide on Oct. 31, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France’s worst rioting in years drew 550,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers’ turnout estimates are higher.
Authorities in France reported more than 560 arrests nationwide by Oct. 31 night. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred marches the previous two Saturdays.
In the main Paris march on Oct. 31, each group carried its own banner: High school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.
The head of a student group said yesterday a campaign of high school blockades would restart from today, adding the government’s proposals did not go far enough.
In Germany, a youth initiative called “Gen Z regelt” — roughly “Gen Z’s got this” — rallied in more than 30 cities “for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life,” and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren’t immediately available.
In Berlin, young protesters gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Oct. 31 afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.
While most people rallied peacefully, some protests turned violent on Oct. 31 night.
In downtown Frankfurt, some rioters smashed several storefronts and stole goods from inside. They also stole weapons from a gun store, which police were able to retrieve later. Some rioters also threw Molotov cocktails at police after pummeling them with stones and bottles earlier in the day, Frankfurt police said on X.
In Cologne, police ended a protest march early after protesters used pyrotechnics, threw stones at them and covered their faces despite a ban. Police also used water cannons to disperse demonstrators.
In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds in Hamburg.
Elsewhere in Europe, people also protested against the housing crisis and for a better future.
Thousands of protesters, including families with small children, converged in downtown Lisbon to peacefully protest Portugal’s housing crisis, holding up placards reading “Houses or Fire” and “We are not Afraid.”
However, riot police with dogs stormed protest camps in Lisbon and Porto early yesterday, charging demonstrators with batons, arresting 13 people and leaving dozens injured.
Clashes quickly broke out as dozens of officers moved in on an encampment in Lisbon’s Rossio Square and a smaller camp in Porto’s Dom Joao I Square at around 4:30 a.m.
In The Hague, Netherlands, there was a strong police presence in and around the downtown shopping area on Oct. 31 afternoon after online appeals for protests and fears of rioting and looting. However, there were no major disturbances by midafternoon. Many stores in the city were boarded up as a precaution.

HANOI, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Vietnam's total import-export turnover reached an estimated 1.01 trillion U.S. dollars in the first 10 months of 2026, up 32.3 percent year on year, the Voice of Vietnam reported Sunday.

Feature: Benin company breathes new life into used cooking oil
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
18:49:51 CST
19:49:51 KST

Handmade soaps produced from used cooking oil are displayed in Ouedo-Kpossidja, a locality about 40 km north of Cotonou, Benin, Oct. 31, 2026. (Photo by Seraphin Zounyekpe/Xinhua)
COTONOU, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Once discarded into the environment or sometimes reused for cooking, used cooking oil is finding a new lease on life in Benin, where a local company is turning the waste into useful products such as soap and biofuel.
At Ouedo-Kpossidja, a locality about 40 km north of Cotonou, the country's economic capital, AMAVI collects and processes used cooking oil from hotels and restaurants, helping reduce environmental pollution while exploring the potential of renewable energy.
"Consuming used cooking oil is harmful to human health and can cause cancer and respiratory problems in the long term," Carmel Djiha, founder of AMAVI, told Xinhua, warning that improper disposal can also contaminate soil and disrupt aquatic ecosystems.
More than 100 restaurant operators are currently working with AMAVI to collect their used cooking oil, Djiha said.
Once collected, the oil undergoes several stages of filtration and settling to remove water and solid residues. It is then processed into soap or converted into biofuel for use in power generators and agricultural machinery, he explained.
Since launching operations in 2023, AMAVI has collected and recycled more than 150,000 liters of used cooking oil, according to Djiha.
Benin has had legislation governing the management of used oil since 2003. The regulations prohibit the disposal or discharge of used oil in places where it could pollute the environment, including soil, surface water, groundwater and sewage systems. Burning used oil in unauthorized facilities is also prohibited.
Against this backdrop, specialized companies such as AMAVI are helping channel used cooking oil into productive uses rather than allowing it to become an environmental and public health hazard.
AMAVI's efforts have also opened the door to international cooperation. It has signed a partnership agreement with Chinese company Henan Hengyong, which supplies oil-processing equipment and provides technical training for AMAVI employees.
Looking ahead, AMAVI plans to industrialize its biodiesel production by 2030, targeting a daily output of more than three tonnes, Djiha said, adding that the initiative is expected to strengthen the company's contribution to environmental protection and public health while helping reduce greenhouse gas emissions. ■
Carmel Djiha, founder of AMAVI, speaks to Xinhua journalist in an interview in Ouedo-Kpossidja, a locality about 40 km north of Cotonou, Benin, Oct. 31, 2026. (Photo by Seraphin Zounyekpe/Xinhua)

====================================================================================================

Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:49:13 UTC
19:49:13 KST

Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of Virginia Health System
- Summary:
- Scientists at the University of Virginia have developed a promising new strategy to fight glioblastoma, one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat forms of brain cancer. Their experimental approach combines focused ultrasound, tiny nanoparticles, and genetic molecules called microRNAs to attack multiple cancer-driving genes simultaneously.
- Share:
Scientists at the University of Virginia Comprehensive Cancer Center have developed a promising experimental strategy for treating glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive malignant brain tumor in adults. The new approach could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles that have limited the effectiveness of existing brain cancer treatments.
The research team, led by UVA's Roger Abounader, MD, PhD, identified tiny genetic molecules known as "microRNAs" that can interfere with several genes responsible for the development and growth of glioblastoma. To deliver these molecules into the brain, the researchers combined specialized nanoparticles, focused ultrasound and microscopic bubbles. Together, these technologies offer a way to temporarily cross the brain's protective barrier, which normally prevents many treatments from reaching brain tumors and other neurological conditions.
"This new approach could help target numerous molecules that promote cancer growth, including those for which no drugs exist, at the same time to achieve better therapies," said Abounader, a professor at UVA's School of Medicine in the Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Cancer Biology, as well as its Comprehensive Cancer Center and Center for RNA Science and Medicine. "We are hoping to translate our findings into future clinical trials for patients with glioblastoma and other brain tumors."
Why Glioblastoma Is So Difficult to Treat
Glioblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults and one of the most aggressive forms of cancer. It claims more than 13,000 lives in the United States each year. One reason it is so difficult to treat is that cancer cells spread into surrounding healthy brain tissue, making it nearly impossible for surgeons to remove the entire tumor.
Another major challenge is the brain's natural "blood-brain barrier." This protective system helps shield the brain from harmful substances, including toxins and infectious agents. Unfortunately, it also blocks many drugs that could otherwise be used to attack brain cancer.
Current treatment generally begins with surgery to remove as much of the tumor as possible. Patients then receive radiation therapy and chemotherapy to help control the remaining cancer and extend survival. Despite these efforts, glioblastoma remains exceptionally difficult to manage.
The UVA researchers are pursuing a different strategy. Instead of relying on drugs that target individual cancer-related processes, their approach uses microRNAs, small pieces of genetic material capable of suppressing the activity of multiple problematic genes at the same time.
By disrupting several genes that help glioblastoma grow and survive, the treatment could potentially slow or even stop tumor growth. This ability to target multiple cancer-driving mechanisms is especially important because combining several conventional cancer drugs can produce harmful side effects. In addition, many of the molecules involved in cancer growth cannot currently be targeted by available medications.
Using Ultrasound to Deliver Cancer-Fighting Molecules
Getting these genetic molecules into the brain presents another major challenge. To overcome it, Abounader's team uses focused ultrasound guided by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), allowing researchers to direct sound waves precisely toward the intended area.
The ultrasound works with tiny "microbubbles" to temporarily open the blood-brain barrier. This creates a brief opportunity for nanoparticles carrying the microRNAs to pass through the barrier and enter the brain, where they can act on genes involved in tumor growth.
The researchers tested this approach in laboratory experiments and animal models of glioblastoma. Their findings showed that the microRNA treatment slowed tumor growth and helped the animals survive longer.
Although these results are encouraging, the strategy remains experimental and will require additional research before it can be evaluated in human patients. Abounader believes the findings provide an important early indication that the technology could eventually benefit people with glioblastoma and potentially those with other types of cancer.
"This approach could have broad applications for several brain and other human diseases," Abounader said. "We and many others are intensively working to lighten the burden of cancer, and hopefully also completely cure it, but this requires a continued investment in cancer and medical research."
UVA Expands Focused Ultrasound Cancer Research
UVA Health has been at the forefront of focused ultrasound research since the technology's early development. Over the years, its scientists have built an extensive research program investigating how precisely directed sound waves might be used to treat a wide range of medical conditions.
Recognizing the technology's potential in cancer care, UVA partnered with the Charlottesville-based Focused Ultrasound Foundation to establish the Focused Ultrasound Immuno-Oncology (FUSION) Center. It is the first center in the world devoted specifically to investigating how focused ultrasound can be combined with cancer immunotherapy. Researchers believe this combination could lead to major advances in cancer treatment during the 21st century.
The effort also supports the broader missions of UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center and UVA's Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology, both of which are working to improve care through new medical discoveries.
UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center is among just 57 cancer centers nationwide to receive the National Cancer Institute's prestigious "comprehensive" designation. The recognition reflects its excellence in cancer research and patient care.
The Manning Institute was established to speed the discovery and development of new medicines and potential cures for some of the most difficult diseases. Its work is supported by a statewide clinical trials network designed to make emerging treatments more accessible to patients as they move through research and testing.
Study Findings and Research Support
Abounader and his colleagues published their experimental approach and initial laboratory findings in JCI, the Journal of Clinical Investigation. The study is open access and can be read free of charge.

Türkiye nominates Sinirlioğlu for next UN chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:48:54 UTC
19:48:54 KST

Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) head Feridun Sinirlioğlu has been nominated for U.N. secretary-general. (AP Photo)
Türkiye has nominated Feridun Sinirlioğlu, head of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), to be the next U.N. secretary-general, a diplomatic source confirmed on Oct. 31.
The move came after a deadlock in the selection process, with the latest straw poll at the U.N. Security Council held on Oct. 30 returning an inconclusive outcome.
The Turkish diplomatic source confirmed that the nomination letter from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan was submitted to the presidents of the U.N. General Assembly and the Security Council.
In the letter, published by Turkish media, Erdoğan said the nomination reflected Ankara’s commitment to “effective multilateralism” at a time when “geopolitical divisions are deepening and trust between nations is diminishing.”
With more than four decades of experience in international relations and diplomacy, Sinirlioğlu has held some of Türkiye’s highest diplomatic positions including foreign minister and permanent representative to the United Nations, Erdoğan said in the letter.
The choice of next U.N. chief would be crucial in steering the international community towards “a more peaceful, just and sustainable future” amid mounting global challenges, he added.
The outgoing secretary-general, Antonio Guterres of Portugal, ends his second five-year term on Dec. 31.
Even if a candidate earns the required nine votes from the 15 available in the Security Council, they must also avoid a veto by the five major powers, which are deeply divided.
Once a candidate clears those bars, their name will go to the General Assembly of all U.N. members for confirmation.
Seven other candidates are vying to replace Guterres. Under an informal regional rotation of the U.N.’s top job, a candidate from the Latin American and Caribbean region could be selected.

India's capital hit by new wave of protests over voters list revision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:48:00 UTC
19:48:00 KST

Thousands rallied in India’s capital Sunday in an opposition-led protest demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief over a voter list overhaul they say unfairly favors the ruling party.
The nationwide revision of electoral rolls has sparked political disputes and street protests in the world's largest democracy over the past month.
The Election Commission says the initiative is necessary to ensure accurate voter rolls, but the opposition claims it is being manipulated to favor Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Both the Election Commission and the BJP deny the accusations.
On Sunday, protesters led by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi of the Congress party chanted "vote thief, leave your seat" and beat drums while marching from central New Delhi to Ramlila Maidan, a large outdoor venue.
"I have been a voter since I was 18 and now I find myself removed from the list," protester Nandita, 46, said, who gave only one name.
"It's important to be here because of the way things are going. The cost of living is going up. The only option is to take to the streets peacefully," she added.
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online youth-led protest movement, has also thrown its weight behind the campaign against the voter roll revision.
The overhaul of India's voter rolls led to the removal of more than 133 million names, according to figures reported by Indian media and cited by opposition parties in court filings.
Critics say the removals have disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.
Members of the Hindu-nationalist BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighboring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India's voter rolls.
Election authorities say the revision was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries and that eligible voters remain entitled to apply for inclusion on the voter rolls.
Human Rights Watch said the removal of voters was "arbitrary and deeply flawed."
"The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India's most marginalized people their right to vote and other government services," it said in a statement this week.
The CJP has been heavily involved in the pushback to the voter roll revision and police temporarily detained several of its leaders during protests last month.
The CJP has gained millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May.
Earlier protests organized by the CJP in July over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climb down by Modi's administration.
