Germany news: Gen Z group calls for new protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:46:00 UTC
19:46:00 KST

Germany news: Gen Z group calls for new protests
Published October 31, 2026last updated November 1, 2026
What you need to know
- Gen Z regelt says it had no influence on violent looting after its protests ended
- German Interior Minister Dobrindt blames left, migrant 'troublemakers' for violence
- Former Chancellor Angela Merkel calls for Germany's first female president
- Berlin's Left Party voted in favor of coalition talks with the Social Democrats and Greens, talks could start Monday
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of October 31 - November 1, 2026:
Over 100 officers injured in Frankfurt, 54 people taken into custody
More than 100 officers were injured, one of them seriously, during violent confrontations in Frankfurt after largely peaceful demonstrations on Saturday, according to Roman Poseck, the interior minister in the state of Hesse, where Frankfurt is located.
He added that up to 1,300 officers were on duty in Frankfurt on Saturday night and into Sunday morning.
The minister said 17 stores were damaged and five were looted. Police took 54 people into custody, all between the ages of 13 and 29.
Of the more than 8,000 people who took part in the protests in Frankfurt, authorities estimated there were 1,000 to 1,500 violent troublemakers, "predominantly from a migrant background."
Poseck said, "An enormous potential for violence on the part of left-wing extremists and violence-prone young people, mostly from migrant backgrounds, has been unleashed."
"This group of offenders was predominantly made up of migrants. And we must address that too," he added. "There must be no false taboos here."
After blaming migrants for the violence, Poseck said German citizens made up the vast majority of those detained.
In Cologne, which also saw violent confrontations between rioters and police, state Interior Minister Herbert Reul said left-wing extremists hijacked the Gen Z protests.
"Anyone who throws rocks and firecrackers at police officers, sets off fireworks, and rampages through the streets has no political agenda," Reul said in a statement. "People who cover their faces don't want to discuss or persuade. They want trouble and violence. There’s no justification for that."
Europe needs to close AI gap with US, China, German president says
Despite considerable attention given to regulating artificial intelligence, European countries need to do more to understand how AI is applied and to keep up with advances made in China and the United States, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier told public broadcaster ARD.
"We can only have a serious say in the regulatory framework — an international regulatory framework — if we actually understand the conditions under which it is applied," Steinmeier said, according to remarks released ahead of the broadcast of ARD's Sunday evening interview program. "In that respect, I believe Europe does not have the option of saying no to AI."
He said how countries decide to use and regulate AI could "be a matter of European security."
"But above all, it is also an ethical question of where the limits of our ability to control this technology actually lie," Steinmeier said.
Steinmeier, who is finishing his second and final term in office, wrapped up a multi-day tour of China on Saturday. Germany is currently debating who could succeed him.
German Gen Z group calls for more demonstrations
The group that organized this weekend's protests, "Gen Z regelt" roughly "Gen Z takes charge," distanced itself from violent riots that occurred after the rallies and called for new demonstrations later this month.
The initiative's organizers issued a positive assessment of protests across Germany.
"Today, 100,000 people showed why they're taking to the streets," a spokesperson for the initiative said Saturday, adding that estimates of participation in six to eight cities would come later.
Gen Z regelt planned protests in 34 cities, including Berlin, Frankfurt, Cologne and Munich, and has called for people to take to the streets again on November 14.
The group has called for more funding for schools, addiction treatment, and psychotherapy as well as measures to combat rising living costs. While it promotes social justice and greater climate protection, it opposes the introduction of mandatory military service, as well as an expansion of government surveillance.
"We are here today to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion," Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said Saturday in Berlin. "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favor of a fairer distribution of the burden."
Gen Z regelt distanced itself from the violent riots and looting that followed the protests in some cities.
"We did not have any influence on what happened after the demonstrations," the group's spokesperson said.
Police also confirmed the demonstrations themselves were largely peaceful and that looting and riots afterward were set off by extremists using the protests for cover.
"The Gen Z protests turned out to be very peaceful," Andreas Rosskopf, chairman of the police union representing the Federal Police, told the Rheinische Post. He added that the groups responsible for the violence consisted of "autonomous and, in some cases, masked individuals."
In Cologne, which also saw looting, a police spokeswoman said the incidents were more likely linked to Halloween celebrations than to the aftermath of the Gen Z protests.
People in Germany buying more organic food
Consumers in Germany bought more organic food products through the summer, with overall sales rising 2.8% to €4.42 billion ($4.95 billion) between July and September.
The German Federation of Organic Food Producers (BÖLW) reported that organic products' share of the German food market reached a record 8.1% in the third quarter.
"The growing organic market is a wake-up call," BÖLW head Tina Andres said, adding that many consumers see the organic sector as producing food locally and protecting water resources, insects and birds.
Supermarkets and discount retailers accounted for the largest share of third-quarter sales for organically produced food, at 31.3% and 27.8%, respectively. Drug store chains followed in third place with a market share of 12.7%. Specialty organic food retailers saw a 2.0% decline in sales, with a 17.3% market share.
Demand for organic products, which generally cost slightly more than traditionally produced products, has continued to grow steadily in Germany, except for a slowdown in 2022 caused by exceptionally high inflation at the time.
Interior minister blames left, migrant 'troublemakers' for post-protest violence
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt condemned the riots that followed demonstrations in several major cities, including Berlin, Cologne and Frankfurt, blaming troublemakers for the violence and calling for severe criminal punishment of looters.
"Violent left-wing groups and troublemakers from migrant communities in the evening hijacked the peaceful demonstrations that took place," he told the mass-market Bild newspaper on Sunday without elaborating on the identities of those taken into custody.
"The rioters and looters will be identified and held accountable," he added. "Serious penalties must follow these breaches of the public peace."
Dobrindt said German police prevented widespread violence, such as that seen during protests in parts of some French cities.
"Excesses of violence like those seen in Paris were prevented thanks to the highly committed efforts of our police officers," said Dobrindt, a member of the conservative Christian Social Union. "The police operation strategy, involving a strong visible presence and the decentralized deployment of forces, proved successful."
Following peaceful demonstrations involving over 100,000 mainly young people, violent incidents and riots broke out after dark, particularly in Frankfurt and Cologne.
In France, protests continued largely peacefully for a third weekend after extensive riots and looting on October 17 left significant damage to shops, public buildings and businesses.
Police sent to protect vandalized shops in Frankfurt
Police were patrolling the streets of downtown Frankfurt on Sunday morning, following looting that saw shop windows smashed and what a police spokesperson said was "considerable" damage to property.
The unrest followed demonstrations by young people demanding better schools, relief from rising living costs and greater social justice. Though the protests were largely peaceful, there were incidents of violence and rioting in Frankfurt and some other big German cities.
In Frankfurt, rioters smashed shop windows, stole goods from shops and attacked police officers. More than 30 people were detained and officers cordoned off parts of the city center. It was not immediately clear how many people were injured in the protests.
The police spokesperson said shops that were looted during the unrest also needed protection.
Hesse's state Premier Boris Rhein said he was shocked "by the violent excesses in Frankfurt," which "will not remain without consequences."
"Anyone who behaves like the attackers in Frankfurt's city center places themselves outside our society," Rhein said. "We will carefully assess the aggressors, perpetrator groups and the course of events, and draw our conclusions."
The group that organized the protests, "Gen Z regelt" roughly "Gen Z takes charge," had explicitly called for peaceful protests. German media in several cities observed extremists mixing into crowds of peaceful protesters.
IG Metall union begins warning strikes after pay talks collapse
Germany's IG Metall union began limited "warning strikes" in the metalworking and electrical sectors at midnight on Sunday.
The strikes began with about 300 night-shift employees at a factory in the western German state of Rhineland-Palatinate holding a rally outside the facility's entrance. A protest also began overnight at the mobile communications supplier RF 360 Europe/Qualcomm in Munich.
The warning strikes are set to spread across Germany next week. IG Metall is Germany's largest union and represents about 3.7 million workers in industrial sectors such as automotive manufacturing, mechanical engineering, electronics, and metal production.
The union has demanded a 5% pay increase over 12 months, as well as job and plant security.
In the second round of negotiations, employers presented an offer that included a one-time payment next year and a 1.3% step increase in July 2028, saying industry faced high cost burdens operating in Germany.
Union Chair Christiane Benner announced "major warning strikes" because the "so-called offer" met only with "incomprehension" in the workplaces, as the pay increases were well below the rate of inflation in Germany.
Berlin's Left Party votes in favor of coalition talks with Greens, SPD
The Left Party in Berlin overwhelmingly voted in favor of formal talks to form a three-party coalition government with the Greens and Social Democrats.
Negotiations could begin on Monday as the Greens and SPD both already agreed to open formal talks for a government led by The Left in the city-state.
"We will not let ourselves be ground down, and I will not give up," Elif Eralp, The Left's parliamentary group leader, told party members during a congress on Saturday. She aims to be Berlin's first governing mayor from her party.
"Not a day passes without someone trying to force us and me to give up," she said, accusing Chancellor Friedrich Merz of trying to "blackmail" the Greens and SPD into abandoning plans for a coalition.
The Left emerged as the strongest party with 25.7% of the vote in the state elections on September 20. Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) followed with 18.8%, the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) with 16.3%, the Greens with 14.3% and the SPD with 12.1%.
"The people of this city voted for us for change, and we will implement it," Eralp said. "They rightly expect us to pull every lever to improve their lives."
The three parties are expected to base their coalition negotiations on a preliminary agreement presented two weeks ago.
Its most controversial proposal would see around 160,000 flats owned by five major property companies transferred into public ownership in exchange for compensation.
Ahead of Saturday's vote, Berlin's Left Party has been dogged by allegations of antisemitism as well as a debate over Eralp's independence and ability to address crime in the capital after Der Spiegel published her interview comments indicating she chose not to mention a pro-Palestinian activist by name due to fears for the safety of her family.
Our coverage of Germany's Gen Z protests
We've been busy covering Gen Z protests in Germany in a separate blog.
The demonstrations were largely peaceful throughout the day, but reports switched to instances of violence and rioting in some cities, especially Frankfurt and Cologne, as night fell.
Follow the latest here.
Young Germans take to the streets
Youth protests have begun in cities across Germany, with demonstrators demanding better-funded schools, action on living costs and stronger climate protection. They also oppose a possible return to military conscription.
Read more about the story here.
Cologne's tiny crossing barrier has a bigger future
A railway crossing barrier just 46 centimeters (18 inches) long has become an unlikely selfie attraction in Cologne — but the city's transport operator says it serves a purpose.
The miniature arm stands beside tracks leading to a tram maintenance depot in the Weidenpesch district. It has even appeared on Google Maps as "Germany's smallest barrier."
Despite online mockery, it is no mistake. "It serves as a placeholder," said Cologne transport operator KVB spokesman Stephan Anemüller.
Installed in 2020, the barrier is to be extended once a planned cycle path is built alongside a nearby housing development. That avoids having to overhaul the crossing equipment later.
KVB is enjoying the attention. Anemüller called it "an amusing attraction" and said the operator would try to secure it a place in Cologne's city museum when it is eventually removed.
Merkel calls for Germany's first female president
Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel has called for a woman to succeed President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, pointing out that no woman has held the office in the country's 77-year history.
Everyone should ask "whether it might finally be time," Merkel told MagentaTV.
She said she knew women capable of doing the job but declined to name anyone.
The Federal Convention elects Germany's next head of state on January 30. Steinmeier cannot seek a third consecutive term. The presidency is mostly a ceremonial role.
Bavarian parliamentary speaker Ilse Aigner has the backing of Markus Söder, leader of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU).
Other names being discussed include Bundestag president Julia Klockner, Education Minister Karin Prien and former Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer, all from Merkel's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
Merkel described the debate as "strange" and criticized its "unpleasant undertone."
She also challenged her party's direction, saying the CDU's identity went beyond economic policy. "The CDU was always about building bridges to all parts of society — and that must be brought back to the forefront."
Berlin's Left Party weighs coalition talks under tight security
Berlin's socialist Left Party is expected to approve coalition negotiations with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and environmentalist Greens, potentially paving the way for the city's first Left Party mayor.
The SPD and Greens have already backed talks, which could begin on Monday. But the Left Party's youth wing opposes the alliance, calling instead for a "strong socialist opposition."
Delegates gathered under tight security in Berlin's Lichtenberg district following calls for protests accusing the party of betraying voters. Its candidate for mayor, Elif Eralp, has been given personal protection.
The Left Party won September's election with 25.7% of the vote. The governing coalition of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and SPD lost its majority.
If the three parties reach a deal, Eralp, currently the Left Party's parliamentary leader in Berlin, could become the city's next governing mayor.

Quad ministers discuss supply chains, denounce export restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:41:00 UTC
19:41:00 KST

ATLANTA, Georgia (Reuters) -- Foreign ministers from the U.S., Australia, India and Japan on Saturday pledged to work on building reliable global supply chains and expressed grave concerns about what they called "economic coercion" through export restrictions and non-market practices, but stopped short of calling out China.
The joint statement by the foreign ministers of the Indo-Pacific "Quad" came at a time when Japan has been extremely critical of Beijing over its restrictions on critical mineral exports, and the U.S. has been assembling a coalition aimed at uniting G20 countries concerned about China's dominance in rare earths and other critical minerals.
The meeting was held shortly before U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio hosted the final session of a meeting in Atlanta of foreign ministers from the broader Group of 20 major economies, which includes China.
The Quad ministers reiterated their support for a free and open Indo-Pacific, underscoring the importance of economic security in maintaining global stability and prosperity, including through reliable and open global supply chains.
"They expressed grave concerns regarding economic coercion, including through arbitrary export restrictions, as well as non-market policies and practices that result in overcapacity to disrupt global supply chains in critical industries," the joint statement said.
The ministers also emphasized the "absolute necessity to protect and preserve navigational rights and freedoms in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait," the statement said.
The group pledged more than $85 million in assistance to support trusted artificial intelligence technologies across the Indo-Pacific region and said it would launch a new effort to identify vulnerabilities in semiconductor and related supply chains before they cause disruptions.
It was the third meeting of the Quad foreign ministers this year, with plans taking shape for U.S. President Donald Trump to attend his first formal meeting of the leaders of the four countries next month in Manila during a conference of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
Rubio told reporters that a Quad leaders meeting in Manila would "hopefully" be announced very soon, but gave no further details.
He said the Quad was not "an anti-China or anti-anybody coalition," adding that the joint statement was raising concerns about behaviors and activities that he said were "coming repetitively from one country."
He said the U.S. had invested a lot of time in the Quad group and wanted to continue to build on its work on specific projects and initiatives, including a $20 million project in Palau aimed at improving its digital infrastructure.
Rubio said the four countries had already made substantial progress in ensuring they could pool resources in the event of a humanitarian crisis or national disaster, and also planned to set up a business forum so that businesses in all four nations could find new opportunities to work together.

Rare short-necked oil beetle rediscovered in Wales after nearly 60 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:40:25 UTC
19:40:25 KST

A rare beetle has been rediscovered in Wales after nearly 60 years, conservationists have said.
The short-necked oil beetle, driven to the brink of extinction in Britain due to habitat loss over the course of the 20th century, has been found at the Castlemartin range in Pembrokeshire, according to Natural Resources Wales (NRW).
The species’ name comes from the adult beetles’ stubby shape and ability to secrete an oily yellow-orange substance from their knee joints when alarmed.
The unusual creature relies on solitary bees and thick vegetation and flower coverage to survive. Its larvae have hook-like feet to snag on to bees, and once in their nest, they feed on pollen until ready to emerge as adults, with a lifespan of about a year.
Only a handful of sites in the UK are suitable for the beetle, according to NRW, and only about one in 10,000 larvae make it to adulthood. It is classed as nationally rare.
The bug was rediscovered in Devon in 2006, and populations have since been found in the Hebrides and on Salisbury Plain.
The nature conservation charity Buglife reported the beetle was found at the Pembrokeshire site in 2020, but surveys carried out in 2022 and 2025 only found dead adults, raising concerns about the species’ viability in the area.
However, the 2026 survey discovered larvae distributed in such a way to suggest hatchlings from a larger batch of immature beetles had thrived.
Anna Hobbs, the project delivery officer for the Bumblebee Conservation Trust, said finding evidence the species was breeding again was very exciting.
“The short-necked oil beetle is an amazing creature and not only depends on a very specific habitat to survive, but the presence of solitary bees as well. So, the work we do needs to consider the needs of several species to be effective,” she said.
“We are very grateful to our partners and volunteers for persevering with us after two years without larval sightings and look forward to the continued management of the site so that this amazing species can survive now and into the future.”
The beetle project, part of Wales’s flagship species recovery programme, Natur am Byth, is working to conserve several endangered animals and plants that share similar habitats to the short-necked oil beetle, including the shrill carder bee, goldilocks aster and pale dog violet.

Ukraine Drone Force Hits Target Every 41 Seconds in Record Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:40:00 UTC
19:40:00 KST

Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) struck an adversary target every 41 seconds on average and neutralized a Russian soldier every 159 seconds throughout October, marking a historic monthly record in casualties inflicted on Russian military personnel by drone detachments, USF Commander Robert “Madyar” Brovdi announced.
Presenting a comprehensive monthly operational assessment on social media, Brovdi reported that USF formations engaged and struck 64,807 adversary targets over the course of October. Russian personnel losses directly attributable to USF strikes reached 16,796 soldiers killed or wounded.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The casualty tally represents the highest monthly toll achieved by the drone service branch since the launch of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022. The October figure marks a 52.6 percent increase compared to August and a 24.7 percent increase over September.
According to operational data compiled by the USF command, drone operators neutralized an average of 542 Russian servicemen per day. The peak single-day casualty figure occurred on Oct. 24, when USF units recorded 701 Russian personnel neutralized within a single 24-hour cycle.
Over the month, USF units executed 255,605 individual combat missions. The operational total encompassed approximately 151,500 direct-strike sorties alongside roughly 104,000 aerial reconnaissance, target-designation, and surveillance flights.
Melania Trump Hails Oleshky Rescue as Hope for Peace
Tactical concentration along eastern and southern sectors
Brovdi emphasized that USF operational activities were heavily concentrated along critical combat vectors in eastern and southern Ukraine, where Russian assault formations attempted to sustain high-tempo offensive pressure.
Approximately 69.5 percent of all Russian personnel losses inflicted by the USF occurred across three focal axes: the Dobropillia-Pokrovsk, Oleksandrivka, and Huliaipole operational sectors.
The Pokrovsk and Dobropillia sectors in Donetsk region have remained focal points of intense ground fighting, with Russian assault groupings attempting to bypass defensive bastions through saturated infantry attacks and mechanized pushes.
Heavy multi-rotor bomber drones and first-person view (FPV) strike drones operated by the USF played a pivotal role in interdicting Russian motorized columns and logistics staging areas before forward infantry reached defensive trenches.
Brovdi stressed that the published metrics reflect solely the combat actions executed by the Unmanned Systems Forces grouping and do not incorporate casualty figures or equipment losses inflicted by other branches of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the National Guard, or specialized security agencies.
Asymmetric battlefield impact
Brovdi, who has commanded the USF since June 2025 after rising to prominence as leader of the “Madyar’s Birds” tactical aerial reconnaissance unit, notedthat the drone force constitutes approximately 2.5 percent of Ukraine’s total armed forces personnel but accounts for roughly one-third of all adversary casualties across the theater.
“A small modern Ukrainian army is winning over the old Soviet system that was in Ukraine,” Brovdi told the publication, describing the branch’s shift toward institutionalizing high-speed digital coordination, autonomous targeting algorithms, and decentralized drone platoons.
In September, Brovdi disclosed that 79 members of his original unit had been killed since 2022, asserting that his forces had achieved an attrition ratio of 656 Russian soldiers killed or wounded for every fallen member of that foundational detachment, while stressing that even higher efficiency is necessary to offset Moscow’s demographic advantages.
Because of the severe attritional damage inflicted by his formations, Russian authorities have aggressively targeted Brovdi personally.
Moscow offered a $20 million bounty for actionable intelligence regarding his whereabouts, seeking to locate him through cross-border criminal syndicates, while a Russian military court sentenced him in absentia to life imprisonment on state-directed terrorism charges in March.
Strategic interdiction of the maritime shadow fleet
Beyond tactical front-line interdiction, the Unmanned Systems Forces have played a central role in strategic operations targeting Russian economic lifelines and logistics nodes across regional maritime waters.
In late September, the USF revealed the operational results of “Operation MoLoChKa” – a Ukrainian backronym translating to “Moscow Will Lie Across Crimea” – an 11-week campaign targeting Russia’s maritime “shadow fleet” in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.
The shadow fleet consists of aging, non-Western flagged commercial crude oil and petroleum tankers used by Moscow to circumvent G7 price caps and export restrictions.
During the multi-week maritime interdiction campaign that began on July 6, USF maritime and aerial drone units struck 300 Russian shadow fleet tankers, including 134 vessels operating in the Sea of Azov and 166 tankers transiting the Black Sea.
The initial surge phase resulted in 159 tankers being struck within the operation’s first 12 days.

Bulgaria’s presidential runoff vote begins
Bulgarians go to the polls on Sunday to vote in the second round of the country's elections for president and vice president, Xinhua reported.
Nearly 6.6 million voters are eligible to choose between incumbent President Iliana Iotova, running with Kiril Valchev as her vice-presidential candidate, and Andrey Gurov, who is seeking the presidency with Georgi Kandev as his running mate.
The Iotova-Valchev ticket, backed by the ruling Progressive Bulgaria party and the Bulgarian Socialist Party, among others, came on top in the first round on Oct. 25 with 34.76 percent of the votes.
The Gurov-Kandev ticket, supported by the parties We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria, came second among the 27 candidate pairs with 31.95 percent.
The first exit polls are expected to be released at 8:00 p.m. (1800 GMT), immediately after the close of the polls. Official results are due no later than Wednesday.
The Bulgarian president and vice president are elected directly by voters for a five-year term. Iotova's term is set to expire at the end of January 2027.
Iotova, 62, was elected vice president twice, in 2016 and 2021, serving alongside President Rumen Radev. In accordance with the country's Constitution, she succeeded Radev as head of state after he resigned in January this year. Before that, she served on the National Council of the Bulgarian Socialist Party from 2000 to 2016, as well as in the Bulgarian National Assembly and the European Parliament.
Valchev is director general of the Bulgarian News Agency.
Gurov, an adjunct professor of finance at the American University in Bulgaria, has less political experience than Iotova. He served as Bulgaria's caretaker prime minister for 78 days in the first half of this year and chaired the parliamentary group of We Continue the Change in two legislatures from December 2021 to February 2023.
Kandev is a former career police officer who served as acting secretary general at the Ministry of Interior for several months this year.

Five killed in fresh ethnic violence in India’s Manipur state
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01

19:37:14 KST

By Tora Agarwala
NEW DELHI, Nov 1 (Reuters) - Five people were killed in two separate incidents in India’s northeastern state of Manipur, police said on Sunday, as fresh ethnic violence erupted in the conflict-hit region.
Three men from the Kuki tribal group were killed in an exchange of gunfire between “unidentified armed miscreants” in the state’s Noney district on Saturday, according to a police statement.
The bodies of two other men from the same community, who had gone missing earlier this week, were recovered in Kangpokpi district on Sunday morning after security personnel launched a search operation, a second police statement said.
A top Kuki tribal body blamed Naga separatist outfits for the killings, describing them as a “direct unprovoked assault … in their homeland.”
The killings came amid mass protests attended by hundreds of thousands of people in the state capital Imphal and other areas, demanding the abrogation of a ceasefire arrangement between Kuki armed groups and the Indian state.
The predominantly Christian Kuki and Naga tribes have a long history of conflict over competing claims to ethnic homelands in the remote northeastern state.
The latest fighting erupted after a Naga man was allegedly assaulted by men from the Kuki community in February this year.
The killing of three Kuki pastors in May, allegedly by Naga armed groups, triggered a series of retaliatory abductions and killings by both sides.
The latest Kuki-Naga clashes have added to tensions in Manipur, where the Kuki community is also embroiled in a bloody ethnic conflict with the mainly Hindu Meitei community that began in May 2023 over economic benefits and job quotas.
More than 60,000 people displaced by the conflict, which has claimed more than 300 lives, continue to live in temporary shelters.

Rioters loot stores in Frankfurt as Gen Z-led protests in Germany turn violent
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:37:02 CET
19:37:02 KST

(Corrects story to drop erroneous reference to Frankfurt as Hesse’s capital in paragraphs 12)
By Kai Pfaffenbach, Tilman Blasshofer and Miranda Murray
FRANKFURT/BERLIN, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Hooded rioters looted stores in Frankfurt late on Saturday after tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across Germany’s biggest cities to demand better education and lower living costs.
The protests followed a wave of Gen Z-led demonstrations across Europe this year. In Serbia, student-led activism helped unseat the country’s longtime leader at the ballot box, while protests in France have descended into rioting and looting.
The German protests organised by the campaign group “Gen Z regelt” — “Gen Z takes charge” in German — took place in 34 cities including Berlin, Frankfurt and Munich. The group says it opposes compulsory military service and wants greater investment in education as many young Germans struggle with rising costs.
In Frankfurt, Germany’s financial hub, at least two stores were looted as protests turned violent, with several more damaged and police trying to get the situation under control, according to a Reuters witness.
“Violent disturbances are continuing,” Frankfurt police said on X. “In the city centre, windows have been smashed at several shops. Molotov cocktails are also being thrown at the emergency services. We urge all bystanders to avoid the city centre or to leave the area.”
Official numbers on Saturday afternoon suggested turnout was below the 182,000 participants that organisers initially expected. Police in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, half the roughly 36,000 on the organisers’ website.
German authorities said Saturday’s demonstrations, which coincide with Halloween festivities, had been largely peaceful, but warned of attempts by extremist groups to exploit the movement.
In Hamburg, some barricades had been set on fire.
“We are here today to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion,” Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said in Berlin on Saturday.
“What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden.”
LUXURY SHOPS BOARD UP WINDOWS
Parts of Germany’s far-left extremist scene and some groups linked to foreign extremist movements have joined efforts to mobilise support, according to the federal interior ministry.
“We all have those images from France in our minds — looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers,” said Roman Poseck, interior minister for the state of Hesse, which includes Germany’s financial hub, Frankfurt.
“France must not be held up as a model in this regard.”
Some businesses across German cities boarded up windows and planned early closures ahead of the demonstrations due to concerns over possible unrest, including along Berlin’s luxury Kurfuerstendamm shopping boulevard.
Organisers have focused on what they see as the growing pressure on younger generations in Europe’s largest economy.
“The government has offered no response to our concerns other than to continue making cuts and piling further burdens upon us,” said Steve, an 18-year-old due to speak at a rally in Munich, addressing Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
“We will continue to exercise our fundamental right to assemble until you stop ignoring us.”
Germany has struggled to revive economic growth. The country also faces growing pressure on pensions and public services as baby boomers retire and the working-age population shrinks.
Questions have been raised about who is driving the campaign and whether it is genuinely youth-led, given the broad mix of political and civil society groups involved.
Germany’s national school student umbrella organisation, BSK, has distanced itself from the initiative and plans to hold a separate day of protest on November 20.
Sean Baker, a student at the Technical University of Berlin, said he would join the protests on Saturday to call attention to the poor state of buildings on campus.
“When you go inside and enter the rooms, it looks like an abandoned building,” he told Reuters. ”Yet this is where we’re expected to study on a regular basis.”
(Reporting by Miranda Murray, Timm Reichert, Tilman Blasshofer, Stephan Schepers and Martin Schlicht; Additional reporting by Christoph Steitz; Editing by Ros Russell, Joe Bavier, Alex Richardson and David Gregorio)

Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:32:46 UTC
19:32:46 KST

Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
A remarkable 18-million-year-old fossil discovered in Egypt suggests that the evolutionary roots of humans and other modern apes may lie in an unexpected part of Africa.
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center (MUVP)
- Summary:
- A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.
- Share:
An ancient ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging a long-standing theory about where the ancestors of modern apes, including humans, first evolved. The remarkable find suggests that a crucial chapter of our evolutionary history may have unfolded much farther north than scientists previously believed.
The newly identified species, named Masripithecus moghraensis, lived approximately 17 to 18 million years ago during the Early Miocene. Its fossilized remains were recovered from Wadi Moghra in northern Egypt, making it the first definitive fossil ape ever discovered in North Africa.
The discovery, described in a study published March 26, 2026, in Science, comes from an international team at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center (Egypt) and the University of Southern California (USA). Their findings suggest that northern Africa and the Middle East may have played a central role in the emergence of the evolutionary lineage that eventually gave rise to all living apes.
A Missing Piece of the Ape Evolutionary Puzzle
For decades, scientists believed that early apes and their close relatives were concentrated primarily in regions farther south in Africa. Fossil sites in North Africa had produced remains of ancient monkeys from the Early Miocene, but researchers had never found definitive evidence of apes from the same period.
That gap helped shape prevailing theories about ape evolution. Although younger ape fossils have been discovered across Africa, Europe, and Asia, their evolutionary relationships and geographic origins remain subjects of scientific debate.
The newly discovered Egyptian fossil may help explain what was missing from this picture.
"We spent five years searching for this kind of fossil because, when we look closely at the early ape family tree, it becomes clear that something is missing -- and North Africa holds that missing piece," said Hesham Sallam, a paleontologist at Mansoura University and senior author of the study.
The discovery is especially important for understanding the origins of crown Hominoidea, the evolutionary group that includes the last common ancestor of all living apes and its descendants. Today, that group encompasses gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, and humans.
Scientists suspect that the incomplete geographic distribution of ancient fossils has obscured important details about when and where this group first emerged.
An 18-Million-Year-Old Ape With Unusual Teeth
The fossils were uncovered during expeditions in 2023 and 2024 by researchers from the Sallam Lab at Wadi Moghra, a well-known fossil site in northern Egypt.
The team named the species Masripithecus moghraensis. Its genus name combines Masr (مصر), the Arabic name for Egypt, with píthēkos, the Greek word for ape. The species name honors Wadi Moghra, where the fossils were found.
Although the remains consist only of lower jaw material, they contain an unusual combination of anatomical features that distinguishes the animal from other apes of similar age.
The jaw is exceptionally sturdy, with remarkably large canine and premolar teeth. Its molars also have rounded chewing surfaces covered in pronounced textures. These characteristics offer valuable clues about the foods the animal could eat and how it survived in its environment.
Researchers believe Masripithecus primarily consumed fruit but had teeth powerful enough to process tougher foods when necessary. This dietary flexibility may have been an important survival advantage.
"Together, they suggest that Masripithecus was adapted for versatility. The study interprets its chewing anatomy as evidence of a flexible, mainly fruit-based diet, with the ability to process harder foods such as nuts or seeds when needed. This flexibility would have helped Masripithecus to thrive at a time when climatic changes were leading to more pronounced seasonality in northern Africa and Arabia," said Shorouq Al-Ashqar, a researcher at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center and a first author of the study.
As seasonal differences became more pronounced, the availability of certain foods likely changed throughout the year. An ape capable of eating a wider range of foods would have been better equipped to cope with those fluctuations.
A Discovery That Challenges the Ape Family Tree
The importance of Masripithecus extends well beyond its unusual anatomy. When researchers examined where the species belonged on the evolutionary family tree, they uncovered a surprising result.
Their analysis suggests that Masripithecus was more closely related to living apes than any known ape species from the Early Miocene of East Africa.
To investigate these relationships, the team used advanced statistical techniques known as Bayesian methods. These approaches allow scientists to compare different evolutionary possibilities and estimate how strongly the available evidence supports each one.
The researchers combined anatomical information from living and extinct apes with genetic evidence from living species. They also incorporated the geological ages of fossil specimens, helping them estimate when different evolutionary branches separated.
By bringing these sources of evidence together, the scientists reconstructed relationships among ancient and modern apes and explored where their shared ancestors may have lived.
The results challenge the long-standing assumption that the evolutionary roots of all living apes were centered in or around East Africa.
Could North Africa Be the Birthplace of Modern Apes?
Additional analyses of ancient animal distributions pointed toward northern Africa and the Middle East as the most likely geographic home of the common ancestor of all living apes.
That ancestor is estimated to have lived during the Early Miocene, an interval spanning roughly 23 million to 16 million years ago. This was an important period in primate evolution, when early ape lineages were diversifying, and environments were undergoing substantial changes.
Geography may help explain why this region was so important.
Millions of years ago, Africa, Arabia, and Asia were moving toward a new geological arrangement. As the African and Arabian tectonic plates traveled northward and approached the final stages of their collision with Asia, the connections between these landmasses began to change.
Sea levels also rose and fell, periodically reducing the stretches of water that separated different regions. At certain times, these changes made it easier for animals to move between Africa and Eurasia.
Northern Africa and the Middle East therefore occupied a potentially crucial position in the movement and evolution of ancient mammals, including apes.
The discovery of Masripithecus helps connect previously separated fossil records from Africa and Eurasia. Its presence suggests that apes were already evolving into distinct forms in this region before new land connections made it possible for them to expand into Europe and Asia.
Rather than being a peripheral location in ape evolution, the region may have been an important center of evolutionary diversification.
Scientists Rethink Where Our Ancient Ape Ancestors Lived
The findings have even prompted some of the researchers to reconsider ideas they held throughout their careers.
Erik Seiffert, a paleontologist at the University of Southern California and co-author of the study, explained how the evidence has changed his understanding of ape origins.
"For my entire career, I considered it probable that the common ancestor of all living apes lived in or around East Africa. But this new discovery, and our new and novel analyses of hominoid phylogeny and biogeography, now strongly challenge that idea. And, importantly, the likelihood of this scenario doesn't depend on Masripithecus -- but it is very much consistent with it."
Importantly, the researchers are not claiming that Masripithecus was a direct ancestor of humans or even necessarily the direct ancestor of living apes. Instead, its position on the evolutionary family tree provides evidence about where the broader ancestral lineage may have originated.
The distinction matters because humans emerged much later in evolutionary history. The Egyptian fossil offers clues to an earlier stage, when the distant ancestors shared by humans and other living apes were evolving.
The team's findings also suggest that the traditional emphasis on East African fossils may have provided an incomplete view of this much older evolutionary story.
More Evolutionary Secrets May Be Hidden in Egypt
Although the discovery offers compelling new evidence, scientists still have much to learn about Masripithecus and the early history of modern apes.
Only part of the animal's jaw has been recovered, leaving important questions about its overall appearance, body size, movement, and behavior unanswered. Additional fossils could provide a more complete picture of how this ancient species lived and how it relates to other early apes.
The researchers believe that further exploration of North Africa and the Middle East could reveal additional species and help clarify when and where the major branches of the modern ape family tree began to emerge.
For now, Masripithecus moghraensis offers a striking reminder that even fundamental ideas about our distant evolutionary past can change when scientists uncover evidence in places that have received relatively little attention.
A fossil jaw preserved for nearly 18 million years may be helping scientists piece together a chapter of evolutionary history that was missing all along.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center (MUVP). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Shorouq F. Al-Ashqar, Erik R. Seiffert, Sanaa El-Sayed, Belal S. Salem, Abdullah S. Gohar, Hossam El-Saka, Mohamed Amin, Hesham M. Sallam. An Early Miocene ape from the biogeographic crossroads of African and Eurasian Hominoidea. Science, 2026; 391 (6792): 1383 DOI: 10.1126/science.adz4102

7 Best Travel Mugs (2026): Insulated, Leakproof, and Self-Heating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:31:00 UTC
19:31:00 KST

If there’s one thing WIRED staffers love almost as much as tech gear, it’s caffeine. We take our coffee so seriously that we don't suffer fools when it comes to travel mugs. Through painstaking testing that's yielded spilled lattes, lukewarm brews, and dented thermoses, WIRED testers have pinpointed the very best travel mugs available. Whether you need a sturdy option that can survive the chaos of an NYC morning commute or a self-heating tumbler for all-day sipping, consider yourself covered.
Want more help leveling up your morning brew? Be sure to check out our guides to the Best Coffee Subscriptions, Best Coffee Grinders, Best Espresso Machines, Best French Presses, Best Portable Coffee Makers, Best AeroPress Coffee Makers, and How to Make Better Coffee at Home.
Updated November 2026: We've added the BrüMate Strova and Ember Tumbler 2, and information on what to look for in a travel mug. We've also updated links and prices throughout.
The Best Travel Coffee Mug
The Hydro Flask Coffee with Flex Sip Lid is my go-to travel mug. It’s low-maintenance and built like a tank, making it a forgiving choice for the clumsiest of sippers. The brand's powder coating can handle clammy hands, and the 16-ounce tumbler fits into most car cup holders.
It's also a multipurpose mug that isn't limited to housing just your steaming morning brew. Because Hydro Flask wide-mouth lids are conveniently interchangeable, you can swap in a straw lid for cold beverages (or anything else you'd like to drink). And if you purchase the travel mug directly from Hydro Flask, you can get it engraved with text or a graphic, in addition to picking from the 10-plus available color options.
A Mug That Can Handle Your Mornings
Imagine sitting by a campfire under the stars, sipping hot cocoa, then waking up at sunrise to a cup of coffee by the lake. A handleless mug just doesn't do that scene justice. Hydro Flask's travel coffee mug brings that camp aesthetic to life. It also just feels great to hold in any setting—including for morning dog walks or while you get yourself ready for your day at home. The slider lid keeps out curious bugs and helps to slow the release of heat, but it’s not leakproof.
I also appreciate the mug's stainless steel rim that's smooth to sip from sans lid. Just note that it’s not TPU powder-coated like most Hydro Flask bottles, so it's a bit less grippy and you’ll have to hand wash it.
Best Value
If you’re a fan of the Owala FreeSip’s spout, then the lightweight SmoothSip Slider will not disappoint. Its triple-layer insulation helps to keep drinks hot for around six hours or cold for 24. The slider lid works fine for everyday use and didn't leak when I flipped it upside down. But I still wouldn’t toss it into a bag because of how easy it is to unlock. Alongside being available in fun colors, Owala also releases limited-edition designs you can shop. Also notable is that Owala bottles are lead-, BPA-, and phthalate-free.
Best Flippable
After an unfortunate entanglement with a coffee mug and my computer, there was a period of time when the only bar where everybody knew my name was the Genius Bar. Now, lid security is my top priority for any liquid I tote around. For that singular concern, BrüMate's cupholder-friendly Strova gets a W from me. The brand claims its patented BevLock lid is fully leakproof, and after putting the mug through its paces—flipping, shaking, and dropping it—before I even considered placing it in my purse to intermingle with my water-sensitive electronics, I came to trust the promise: I couldn't make a single drop of coffee slip through the closed-mouthpiece edges or perimeter of the lid. Further, the mug's ceramic-lined interior both protects the temperature and taste of whatever you're drinking, and it comes in more than a dozen colors and designs any aesthete would be happy to show off.
The compromise you'll have to make is that the Strova is a bit awkward to sip. The mouth opening is quite small, running in a thin, tight line, like an expressionless face, as opposed to larger, easier-to-sip options that might conjure more of an open-mouthed cackle. The construction means you have to tip the mug up past your nose to sip when it's half full or less. This may look a bit aggro while you're drinking, but it’s frankly a small price to pay for confidently avoiding spillage. —Alexis Berger
Best Self-Heating
A long morning commute can be a slog. Add in successive underwhelming sips of tepid coffee, and you're less and less likely to walk into work bright-eyed and bushy-tailed. For owners of the Ember Tumbler 2, that vignette is mere fiction. This travel tumbler, from the brand that normalized spendy warming mugs, holds a generous 16 ounces, fits into a car cupholder, and—most importantly—keeps your beverage hot. It claims to have a battery life of three-plus hours, but I noticed my brew losing its steam after about two. You can control the temperature on the tumbler itself by pressing a button on the bottom that toggles between five heat levels, or you can choose a precise temp via the Bluetooth-connected app. But if you're driving, you'll probably just want to default to the hottest temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit before you depart.
The Tumbler 2's slim profile is easy to pick up with one hand while you keep the other firmly on the steering wheel. Do keep the tumbler upright in that cupholder when you're not sipping, though. It dripped when I flipped it upside down, even with the sipping lid's slider closed, so I certainly wouldn't throw it into a purse or computer bag. (The tumbler also comes with a screw-off, top-handle lid, which is less leaky, but also less useful.) Drips aside, the drinking experience is nice, with the lid's smooth texture and curved lip allowing for easy, natural sips.
If cupholder compatibility isn't your priority, you might consider the new 16-ounce Ember Mug 3 ($160), the first edition of the brand's classic line that's available in this larger capacity. It's not formally a travel mug, but it does come with a sipping lid that helps your drink stay warm longer, making it a nice option for the work-from-home crowd. Both the Mug 3 and Tumbler 2 are conveniently top-rack dishwasher safe. —Alexis Berger
Best for Iced Coffee and Matcha Lattes
Fellow nailed it with the Carter Move. This sleek mug has a ceramic-coated interior that doesn't hold scent or taste, meaning your matcha today won’t taste like yesterday’s coffee. A 270-degree twist locks the lid effectively; I’ve tossed it in my bag without a second thought and have never experienced annoying leaks or regrettable spills. The included splash guard keeps ice cubes from smacking your teeth and protects against drips and splatters while you walk and drive. Fellow also drops limited-edition colors and sometimes releases design collaborations with artists. The mug fits into most car cup holders and is conveniently compatible with the Cold Lid + Straw ($12) and the Carry Lid ($12), allowing flexibility in how you drink and tote it.
The Carter Move fits most standard drippers but isn’t compatible with the AeroPress Coffee Maker or Prismo AeroPress Attachment. If that's a deal-breaker, you might consider the Carter Wide ($30), a great alternative to the Move that works with most manual coffee brewers. In that case, you'll have to compromise on a splash guard, which I really like in the Move.
Best Budget Mug With a Handle
For less than $25, the Ello Campy delivers a nostalgic charm, harking back to the enameled camp cups that ooze 20th-century Americana. The Campy isn’t enameled—just painted to look like it—but it pulls off the effect well. The cork-lined handle stays cool even when piping-hot brew fills the mug, while the vacuum insulation retains your drink’s heat. The screw-on plastic lid is designed to avoid heat conduction, and the mug also features a sliding lever for sipping. It’s not spill-proof, but if you hold it upright, it should keep its contents contained. However, it doesn't fit into cupholders, which may be a deal-breaker for drivers, and the paint is likely to chip off with wear.
Honorable Mentions
Some travel mugs are perfectly good enough—just not as great as the top picks above.
KeepCup 12-ounce Coffee Cup for $31: This double-walled, insulated mug aims to replicate (and replace) paper cups from coffee shops. It's a solid option if you're looking for a glass cup (the rubber grip is plastic, though). That said, it’s not the best at preserving the temperature of your drink, and the lid is a tad wobbly.
Oxo Good Grips Thermal Mug for $29: WIRED reviewed this bottle in 2022, and it earned high marks for its sturdy build and dishwasher-friendliness. But since it's older, it now fluctuates in and out of stock.
REI Co-op Camp Mug for $23+: REI's stainless steel cup is decent enough, but it doesn't particularly stand out in the wider category of travel mugs. Our tester says the exterior coating was tough enough to show no scratches, even after knocking it over a few times outside.
Zojirushi Stainless Steel Mug for $40: In addition to having a lid lock that's effective for avoiding accidental spillage, the mug is also a great option for temperature control: A reviewer once left tea in it for 18 hours (unintentionally) and discovered the drink was still hot when she finally opened the lid. The downside is that the cover has three separate parts—a mouthpiece, a gasket, and a lid—that are deeply ridged and annoying to clean.
Avoid These Mugs
They can't all be winners. These two cups fell short compared to our favorites.
Greens Steel Beast 20-Ounce Insulated Tumbler for $23: The Beast Tumbler has more than 81,000 positive reviews on Amazon, but the rubber seal around the lid easily comes out of place. That meant it leaked like a sieve.
Toaks Titanium Double Wall 450-Milliliter Cup for $40: More often than not, we at WIRED champion Toaks gear as an affordable source of titanium camp cookware. But this mug costs $12 more than the Hydro Flask pick above, and has a rougher finish.
Frequently Asked Questions
What to Know About Lead Soldering
Since WIRED editors began testing reusable water bottles and travel mugs, we've discovered that some brands use lead soldering to seal their insulated bottles. While exposure is unlikely (you'd have to drop or damage the bottle or mug to detach the lead pellet), we still believe it's an unnecessary risk, especially since many of our top choices use safer sealing methods. We've removed mugs from brands that have admitted to using lead in their products.
What to Look for in a Travel Mug
There's no shortage of travel mugs available to buy. Narrowing down the best options for you depends on your priorities and how a given mug can satisfy them. Here are key considerations for selecting a great travel mug:
- Leakproof design: When you're buying a mug with the express purpose of toting it around with you, I'd argue that its most important quality should be holding the beverage without leaks or spills. Some travel mugs feature patented locking technology that promises no drips at all, while other models are less intensely engineered—and sometimes the latter works perfectly well. For example, if you're using your mug to sip a coffee during your morning walk or while taking in the sunrise during a camping trip, you might not need the same promise of leakproofing as someone who tosses their mug into their laptop bag.
- Material: Travel mugs are often made from stainless steel, ceramic, or BPA-free plastic—and often a combination of all three. Glass mugs are also available, though less common.
- Stainless steel is a common material in travel mugs. It's effective for retaining heat, especially options that are double-wall–insulated, which basically means the mug will keep your drink hot from the inside without burning your hand from the outside. Stainless steel mugs are often dishwasher-safe, but not microwave-safe, and can sometimes give off a bit of a metallic taste into beverages.
- Some mugs have a smooth, ceramic lining on the inside, which helps to preserve the taste of the beverage—i.e., your afternoon tea won't have a hint of yesterday's coffee—and protect against that metallic hint of a stainless-steel option.
- Plastic appears often in travel-mug lids. Prioritize options that are free of bisphenol A (BPA), a known endocrine disruptor.
- Glass, like ceramic, provides a neutral taste, but it can be heavy and is typically less durable than other materials, opening you to the messy risk of a shattered mug.
- Shape: If you're commuting in a car with your travel mug, you'll want to ensure it fits into your cupholder, and if you're carrying it with you on walks, you'll likely want it to have a handle.
- Price: Our top-pick travel mugs currently span in price from less than $20 to nearly $200. If having precise temperature control of your coffee at any given moment matters to you, a spendy mug may be worth the investment. Most of the picks, though, hover around $30. —Alexis Berger
How I Tested
I’ve been running on caffeine since I was 12 (sorry, Mom and Dad) because I took middle school way too seriously. Fifteen years later, caffeine is basically part of my personality, and I’ve been unofficially testing travel mugs for most of my life.
To officially test the mugs in this guide, I, along with other editors, drank both coffee and tea at piping-hot and ice-cold extremes, rating heat retention and taste, ensuring no picks have any hint of metallic notes. Shape and design matter, too: How comfortable is it to hold a given mug? Does it fit into a car cup holder? Does it offer additional features worth considering? I aggressively shook the mugs that promised to be leakproof and dropped those that claimed to be durable from about 4 feet high onto both wood and concrete surfaces to evaluate how well they held up. Finally, travel mugs can be a pain to scrub, so I factored in ease of cleaning.
Simply put, I need a travel mug that pulls its weight. If it didn't keep my coffee warm, my bag dry, and make my life a little easier, it didn’t make the list.

Chatbots Are Leading Hikers Astray, With Dangerous Consequences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

This story originally appeared on High Country News and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
By the time the three hikers called for help from a rocky face on Mount Shasta in Northern California, they’d made a series of bad decisions. They didn’t bring enough food, and they’d overestimated their fitness. Instead of turning back in late afternoon when they hadn’t yet reached the top, they summited at 7:30 pm and had to descend in the dark. Their lack of preparation and poor planning, as they admitted later, came partly from relying on Google’s artificial intelligence chatbot Gemini. By morning, they were lost on a gnarly part of the mountain, and one hiker had banged up his knee.
“We get plenty of people who come unprepared or don’t do any research at all. To these guys’ credit, they did try,” said Nick Meyers, US Forest Service program manager of the Mount Shasta Wilderness Climbing and Avalanche Center, which responded to the call. “But I think they kind of turned their brains off.”
The three 20-year-olds aren’t the only ones making missteps in wild spaces with the help of artificial intelligence. Another Mount Shasta visitor pitched her tent near a “No Camping” sign, insisting she had a right to do so because AI told her she could, Meyers said. His team also encountered a man wandering around at a trailhead with an AI-generated map that showed prominent features on the wrong side of a nearby mountain. In British Columbia, a helicopter crew rescued a 16-year-old hiker from a ledge in the Widowmaker Arete on the back of Crown Mountain. The teen had used Anthropic’s chatbot Claude to help him plan his trip. News stories focused on that fact went viral across Canada and the US, though the hiker said later that he also consulted Google Maps and the popular hiking app, AllTrails.
Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming has also seen a marked uptick over the past year in the percentage of visitors who report using AI for travel information, said Park Superintendent Chip Jenkins. “It went from zero to 26 percent. And I’m guessing that curve is not going to flatten.”
It remains to be seen whether increasing AI use will lead to an increase in backcountry accidents and search and rescues, Meyers said. His office, which oversees a massive wilderness area in Northern California, averages a dozen rescues each year, and 2026 is shaping up to be an average year. Calls to search and rescue in Wyoming have actually gone down compared to 2025, with only 312 calls so far in 2026 compared to a total of 466 in 2025 and 377 in 2024.
Some search and rescue veterans say that AI chatbots are just the latest tools giving people new ways to get into trouble. Roughly a decade ago, when hikers, backpackers, climbers and other outdoor enthusiasts began to source their destinations, inspiration, and information from Instagram and other social media sites, they faced sometimes deadly consequences. Before that, hikers and other recreationists were led astray by their reliance on Google Maps or smartphone connectivity.
“Over the last two decades, there’s been a phenomenal push in the media to get more people outdoors, and consequently we have more people outdoors and recreating,” said Jim Moss, a Colorado-based recreation attorney and search and rescue volunteer. It’s still unclear how questionable advice from a robot will influence all those people, he added.
Turning to an AI chatbot for guidance does come with unique risks. Chatbots can “hallucinate” persuasively presenting misinformation as real, and their use can lead to a phenomenon called “cognitive surrender,” said Chris Flathmann, a human-centered computing professor at Clemson University in South Carolina who has studied AI and search and rescue.
“When humans work with AI systems, they can get so deep into it they give up thinking critically for themselves,” he explained. When AI pretends to be an expert on an unfamiliar topic, “you can’t call BS on that because you don’t have the expertise.” And once you stop thinking critically, it can be hard to start again, especially in a stressful backcountry situation.
Chatbots also tend to tell users what they want to hear and to do so with authority regardless of whether the sources they’re consulting are reliable, Flathmann and others said. Claude or ChatGPT might answer a query with extensive directions and advice that sound credible but are actually scraped from Reddit threads and out-of-date YouTube videos—and might even be entirely fabricated.
TikTok and Instagram may offer a viewer inspiration, but AI tends to offer instructions—right or wrong—as well as encouragement, Flathmann said. “AI isn’t trying to trick people into going up mountains, but I think it’s the natural evolution of what happens when you get a tool like this.”
Regardless of the resources recreators use, experts have the same advice: When you’re headed to a new place, make sure you double-check your information against reliable, authoritative sources like up-to-date public-land agency maps and websites, trail association websites, or guidebooks. Even better, talk to a real-live guide, a national forest official, or a park ranger.
“If you’re going to go into places that will kill you,” Meyers said, “you should take your planning seriously.”

‘Did they really have to choose this day?’ BJP targets Congress over INDIA bloc rally on anniversary of 1984 riots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01

19:26:18 KST

BJP targets Rahul Gandhi, Congress over 1984 violence as INDIA bloc holds Delhi rally
NEW DELHI: BJP on Sunday organised a protest march in West Delhi's Hari Nagar, demanding an apology from the Congress and its leader Rahul Gandhi for the 1984 anti-Sikh violence, as the INDIA bloc held its 'Vote Bachao, Desh Bachao' rally at Ramlila Maidan.Leading the march, Union minister Hardeep Singh Puri described the killings of Sikhs in 1984 as a “well-planned” massacre rather than a riot or spontaneous outbreak of violence. He cited official figures showing that 2,733 Sikhs were killed in Delhi during the violence.
“It was a well-planned massacre and a genocide and crime against humanity as pointed by the courts, not any spontaneous riot. Congress leaders should think seriously about it,” Puri said, addressing protesters before the march, according to news agency PTI.Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta, Delhi BJP president and Union minister of state Harsh Malhotra, Delhi Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa and senior advocate H S Phoolka were among those who participated. Several Sikh leaders and members of the community also joined the march from the Sikh-majority areas of Hari Nagar towards Tilak Nagar.Protesters wearing black headbands raised slogans against the Congress and Gandhi, demanding an apology for the killings.
Puri recalls 1984 violence, questions Congress over apology
Puri said he was in Geneva when the violence broke out in 1984 and recalled how his Hindu friends protected his parents, who were living in Delhi.He rejected the description of the killings as spontaneous violence following the assassination of then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi on October 31, 1984.
“When mobs were arriving at the houses of our Sikh brothers in Delhi, they were not carrying ordinary voter lists. Because on a voter list, a name might say Harnam Singh and Harnam Singh could be from Madhya Pradesh, or Haryana, could be a Jat, a Rajput, or wearing a safa [turban]… no! The preparations were made for it,” he said.Puri also referred to the Delhi High Court's observations on the violence and said the killings should not be described as riots.“Even now, a term is often used referring to it as ‘riots’ or ‘a riot.’ These were not riots. Riots are when two groups fight each other. Here, one group… 2,733 people were killed in cold blood in Delhi. Narsanhar [massacre/carnage] is the right word. In English, narsanhar means ‘genocide.’ And as far as I recall, the Delhi High Court specifically used the term: ‘This is a crime against humanity.’ Genocide and a crime against humanity,” he said.He questioned the INDIA bloc's decision to hold its rally on November 1, saying the wounds of the violence had not healed.“Even today, I believe our community and our nation have not fully accepted or forgiven what happened in 1984. Nor did they ever apologise for it properly. Did they really have to choose this very day?” Puri said.He added that it was the responsibility of citizens to remember the violence to ensure that such incidents did not recur.
Rekha Gupta targets Gandhi family over 1984 killings
Gupta, who wore a black headband during the march, accused the Congress and the Gandhi family of failing to acknowledge the suffering of Sikh families affected by the violence.“The Sikh community in India is asking those who carry a copy of the Constitution in their pockets and invoke democracy today: what about what happened in November 1984? Was that not a murder of democracy, a murder committed by the Gandhi family itself?” she said.
She also referred to the Emergency imposed by Indira Gandhi in 1975 and accused the Congress leadership of repeatedly undermining democratic institutions.“Thousands of Sikh families are weeping tears of blood, still grieving the loss of their loved ones in that Congress-sponsored massacre... yet they have never received justice. Has the Gandhi family ever uttered even a few words about them?” Gupta said.Malhotra also criticised the INDIA bloc for holding its rally on November 1, alleging that the timing hurt the sentiments of the Sikh community.“Congress has not apologised to the country or the Sikh community for this incident to date,” he said, adding that the rally was an attempt to disrupt normal life in Delhi.The 1984 anti-Sikh violence followed the assassination of Indira Gandhi on October 31 that year. According to official figures cited by Puri, 2,733 people were killed in Delhi.
BJP's protest march was held alongside the INDIA bloc's demonstration against alleged irregularities in electoral rolls during the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.The opposition alliance has demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.The two political events prompted heightened security arrangements across the capital, with police and paramilitary personnel deployed along the rally routes and at key locations.

According to a report released by Newsweek, a total of 4,574 names appeared on the Federal Register’s US expatriation list over the first three quarters of the year, representing individuals whose loss of US citizenship or long-term permanent resident status was reported to the Treasury Department.
The latest quarterly update, issued on Thursday, shows that 1,331 names appeared on the register between July and September alone, although the number was down from 1,462 between January and March and 1,781 between April and June.
Despite this modest quarterly dip, it is clear when comparing these numbers to previous years that 2026 has seen an unusually high number of Americans renounce US citizenship or give up their permanent residency.
The report said that since Trump’s return to the White House, the number of names on the Treasury’s register has been rising.
In the first quarter of 2025, 1,285 Americans formally expatriated or renounced their US citizenship.
The figure fell to 1,057 in the second quarter, rose to 1,593 in the third, and dropped to 954 in the fourth.
The report quoted Peter Spiro, a professor who holds the Charles Weiner Chair in international law at Temple University, as saying that for some who renounced their citizenship or permanent residency, there’s a "sense that America’s future is increasingly problematic."

Thousands joined a protest led by opposition politicians in India's capital on Sunday, renewing demands for the country's election chief to resign over an overhaul of voter lists they say unfairly benefits the ruling party.
The nationwide revision of electoral rolls has sparked political disputes and street protests in the world's largest democracy over the last month.
The Election Commission says the initiative is necessary to ensure accurate voter lists, but the opposition claims it is being manipulated to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Both the Election Commission and the BJP deny the accusations.
On Sunday, protesters led by opposition Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi chanted "vote thief, leave your seat" and beat drums while marching from central parts of New Delhi to Ramlila Maidan, a large outdoor venue.
"I have been a voter since I was 18 and now I find myself struck off the list," protester Nandita, 46, told AFP, giving only one name.
"It's important to be here because of the way things are going. The cost of living is going up... The only option is to take to the streets peacefully."
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online youth-led protest movement, has also thrown its weight behind the campaign against the voter-roll revision.
The overhaul of India's voter rolls has resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to figures reported by Indian media and cited by opposition parties in court filings.
Critics say the removals have disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.
Members of Hindu-nationalist BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India's electoral rolls.
Election authorities say the revision was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries, and that eligible voters remain entitled to apply for inclusion on the roll.
Human Rights Watch has said the removal of voters was "arbitrary and deeply flawed".
"The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India's most marginalised people their right to vote and other government services," it said in a statement this week.
The Cockroach movement has been heavily involved in the pushback to the voter-roll revision and several of its leaders were temporarily detained by police during protests last month.
The CJP has gained millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May.
Earlier protests organised by the CJP in July over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi's administration.

The tactics of fighting in gas pipelines: why it matters in the Russian-Ukrainian war

The tactics of fighting in gas pipelines: why it matters in the Russian-Ukrainian war
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian and Russian troops move through gas pipelines, avoiding drones and launching surprise attacks on the enemy’s rear.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces have adopted the Russians’ tactic of fighting in underground tunnels. Military personnel from both warring countries are covering considerable distances through gas pipelines, trying to avoid the threat of drone strikes and catch the enemy by surprise. This is reported in an article by The New York Times, UNN reports.
Details
According to Maria Varenikova, a correspondent for The New York Times, while heading toward the entrance to the tunnel network, she narrowly escaped being hit by a Russian drone. She, the publication’s photographer, and the Ukrainian soldiers accompanying them had to jump out of the pickup truck on the move and hide from the Russian UAV along the road.
At the same time, journalist Simon Shuster notes in a publication on The Atlantic’s website that the new tactical methods are important for the course of the war. He discussed the issue with Ihor Obolenskyi, commander of the 2nd “Khartia” Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine.
The brigadier general said that initially, the Defense Forces tried to find the points where the Russians emerged onto the surface and destroy them. But they continued to appear several kilometers behind Ukrainian positions and attack.
The “Khartia” commander then turned to the state energy company with a request to provide maps of the pipeline network. The documents revealed the scale of the danger: it was a labyrinth of at least 57 steel pipes running beneath the combat zone, most of them one to two meters in diameter.
Previously, these pipes were used to pump Russian gas through Ukraine to European countries. But this stopped in 2025.
That same year, the Russians carried out “Operation Pipe”: between one hundred and several hundred soldiers crawled several kilometers along a section of the Urengoy–Pomary–Uzhhorod main gas pipeline and emerged behind Ukrainian troops in the Kursk region.
According to Obolenskyi, in October, after approximately six months of underground fighting, “Khartia” regained control of approximately 14 kilometers of pipelines in northeastern Ukraine as part of an operation codenamed “Veles.”
