Kiril Totev, USA: Voters are disillusioned and don’t believe their voices matter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:22:32 UTC
19:22:32 KST

Author
Vesela Krasteva
News
Presidential Election 2026 – Runoff
Kiril Totev, USA: Voters are disillusioned and don’t believe their voices matter
“There is interest in the election, but voter turnout is very low”, a Bulgarian compatriot in Minneapolis tells Radio Bulgaria
Sunday 1 November 2026 11:20
Sunday, 1 November 2026, 11:20
Kiril Totev
PHOTO personal archive
Font size
Election day for Bulgarians in the United States begins at 1:00 p.m. Bulgarian time. The first to cast their ballots will be Bulgarian citizens on the East Coast, in cities such as New York, Washington, and Naples, Florida. A total of 44 polling stations have opened across the country, 24 more than during the parliamentary elections in April 2026, when a restriction limiting the number of polling stations to 20 in countries outside Bulgaria prevented many Bulgarian citizens from exercising their right to vote. Among those affected was the Bulgarian community in Minnesota’s Twin Cities – Minneapolis and St. Paul.
PHOTO personal archive
Following amendments to the Electoral Code and the submission of 40 preliminary applications to vote, a polling station has been opened in Minneapolis–St. Paul, allowing more than 1,000 Bulgarians to take part in today’s runoff to elect the country’s seventh president. Among them is Kiril Totev, who has lived in Minneapolis for 34 years but has never lost touch with his homeland. Speaking to Radio Bulgaria, he noted that voter turnout in the first round last Sunday was almost one-third lower than at elections held over the past seven years, with just 66 Bulgarian citizens casting their ballots in the city.
PHOTO personal archive
“Interest in these elections has been quite low, perhaps for a number of reasons. There have been many elections in recent years, and people have become disillusioned and no longer believe that these elections can bring about any change, regardless of whether Iotova or Gyurov becomes president. Only a very small, politically active segment of the community is turning out to vote here. The situation is similar in Chicago and in other places with larger Bulgarian communities, where voter apathy is even more pronounced.”
Despite growing voter fatigue and increasingly fragile faith in the power of their vote to bring about change, Bulgarians in the United States continue to follow the political and social developments in their homeland.
“Every Bulgarian who has left the country, whether for the United States, Europe or somewhere else in the world, wants to see change. They want Bulgaria to become a country, where people can lead a decent life without having to constantly struggle with corruption and administrative hurdles. These are the things that Bulgarians who have left their homeland want to see, and our compatriots here in Minnesota share the same expectations. This is nothing new, but Bulgaria still seems unable to deliver on these expectations, and this is one of the main reasons why people have become disillusioned. Bulgarians want a normal life - a decent job, adequate pay, an efficient public administration and healthcare system. For younger people, education is also very important. Many of the people I speak to who are considering returning to Bulgaria are already older or at retirement age. This is why Bulgarians continue to live abroad: it is very difficult for them to find decent jobs and earn a good living in their own country. Many return to Bulgaria not to work, but rather to spend their retirement years there.”
PHOTO personal archive
Kiril Totev expects voter turnout at the Minneapolis-St. Paul polling station to be higher in today’s second round of the presidential election than it was on October 25. But does the publication of preliminary voting results from Bulgaria at 8:00 p.m, as soon as polling stations close in the country, influence the attitudes of Bulgarians in the United States, where voting continues?
“Many people, particularly those who were already reluctant to vote, decide not to go to the polls in the afternoon and evening, once the preliminary results from Bulgaria are out. They say, ‘There’s no point in voting. The outcome is already clear.’ This effect does exist, although I cannot say how significant it is”, Kiril Totev says and adds:
PHOTO personal archive
''We vote in Bulgarian elections for a better Bulgaria. Of course, everyone has their own understanding of what that means, but most people have more or less the same views when asked what a ‘better Bulgaria’ means. We will continue to vote, and we will keep doing so as long as elections are held, as long as we are able to. A better Bulgaria - that is what we are striving for”, says Kiril Totev from Minneapolis.

Eisenkot weighs minority government with outside backing from Arab and Haredi parties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:20:18 UTC
19:20:18 KST

Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar! party, has authorized an examination of a plan to form Israel's next government with outside backing from the Arab Ra'am party and the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party, sources told ynet. Under the proposal, the parties would help Eisenkot replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu by abstaining from a crucial parliamentary vote, allowing his government to take office without formally joining the coalition.
The unusual arrangement would depend on cooperation between parties with sharply different political positions. The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party and Arab lawmakers would effectively allow Eisenkot to establish a government by choosing not to vote against him. One lawmaker from the Arab Ra'am party, Yoav Segalovitz, would vote in favor, while the remaining Ra'am lawmakers and the Joint List would refrain from opposing the government in the initial vote. Unlike Ra'am and United Torah Judaism, however, the Joint List would not be part of the proposed arrangement to keep the government in power afterward.
The plan hinges on a feature of Israel's parliamentary system: a new government does not necessarily need the support of 61 lawmakers, an absolute majority in the 120-seat Knesset, to take office. It needs more votes in favor than against. If enough lawmakers abstain, they can allow a government to be formed without joining it or formally endorsing its policies.
Under the proposed scenario, Eisenkot's bloc of 48 lawmakers would gain Segalovitz's vote, giving it 49 supporters against 46 lawmakers from Netanyahu's bloc. The remaining 25 lawmakers would abstain, including United Torah Judaism's seven representatives, the other seven Ra'am lawmakers and the Joint List's 11. The result would be a minority government dependent on continued outside support from Ra'am and United Torah Judaism, rather than the Joint List.
The Joint List's abstention would be necessary for that initial vote, but its continuing support would not be required under the proposed arrangement. Instead, Eisenkot's associates are examining whether Ra'am and United Torah Judaism could provide an ongoing parliamentary safety net, allowing the government to remain in office without formally joining the coalition.
Joint List lawmaker Ahmad Tibi has already indicated that his party would not oppose the formation of an alternative government, saying its priority is removing Netanyahu from power. That position could help Eisenkot clear the first parliamentary hurdle without having to secure a formal agreement with the Joint List. The plan to sustain the government, however, rests on cooperation with Ra'am and United Torah Judaism.
Liberman and the ultra-Orthodox draft dispute
The plan faces significant obstacles, beginning with Avigdor Liberman, chairman of the secular nationalist Yisrael Beiteinu party and a key member of Eisenkot's political bloc. Following the election, Liberman declared that he would not agree to establish a government dependent on Arab or ultra-Orthodox parties, "either directly or indirectly." His opposition poses a major challenge because the proposal would require precisely the kind of outside parliamentary cooperation he has ruled out.
Another major obstacle involves United Torah Judaism and the issue of compulsory military service for ultra-Orthodox yeshiva students. Eisenkot's associates want to examine whether the party would agree to allow a new government to take office without opposing it, providing temporary outside support until legislation regulating military exemptions is passed. United Torah Judaism could then potentially join the government at a later stage.
However, the possibility of such an agreement remains uncertain. Military conscription is among the ultra-Orthodox party's most pressing demands, and its leaders want legislation providing broad exemptions for religious students. Eisenkot, meanwhile, is unwilling to accept a lenient law that would allow widespread avoidance of military service, making compromise difficult.
The Arab parties would also have demands of their own. Ra'am chairman Mansour Abbas wants his party represented in the coalition, even if Segalovitz is the only Ra'am lawmaker to join the government. Reaching an agreement with Ra'am would therefore involve more than securing abstentions during the initial vote.
The Joint List has also sought concrete achievements for Israel's Arab community, as Tibi has stated. However, the proposed arrangement does not depend on negotiating continuing parliamentary support from the Joint List, a significant distinction given the reluctance among parties in Eisenkot's bloc to enter direct negotiations with its representatives.
The proposal is only one of several options being examined by Eisenkot and his allies as they search for a way to replace Netanyahu following the inconclusive election. It could also serve as leverage in negotiations with the prime minister over a possible national unity government, although that option faces considerable opposition within the bloc seeking to oust him.
Meanwhile, Eisenkot's political allies have yet to agree on a candidate to replace Amir Ohana as Knesset speaker, the official who presides over parliament. Eisenkot insists that the position should go to a member of his Yashar! faction, while Liberman wants the job for Yisrael Beiteinu lawmaker Oded Forer.
In response to the report, Yashar! said: "We are working with tremendous commitment to fulfill the voters' desire to replace the government responsible for the failures. At this stage, we will not comment on what takes place behind closed doors. The various reports were not issued with our approval and do not necessarily reflect the reality as it stands."
For now, the arrangement remains one possibility rather than an agreed coalition plan. While the Joint List's abstention would be needed to get the government sworn in, the longer-term proposal depends on securing cooperation from Ra'am and United Torah Judaism, while overcoming Liberman's opposition and fundamental disagreements over military conscription.

Ukraine flies the first drone rescues of wounded troops
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:13:19 GMT
19:13:19 KST

Ukraine has carried out the world’s first medical evacuations by heavy uncrewed aircraft, lifting wounded soldiers out of positions that could not be reached from the ground, and is developing evacuation drones as a dedicated capability of its own, according to the Ukrainian defence ministry.
Brave1, the defence innovation cluster working with the Ministry of Defence, set the requirement in 2024 after working with the military to define what such an aircraft would have to do. The criteria given to the defence technology market were that the aircraft must reliably carry 130 kilograms over a distance of at least fifteen kilometres and must carry an integrated communication system with at least three alternative types to survive in an electronic warfare environment, with lidar, optical stabilisation and navigation that works without satellites listed as options.
The first of those evacuations took place in October, when an infantryman of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade was lifted out of a position the enemy had blocked. A Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 hexacopter built by a Brave1 participant flew the mission, an aircraft weighing 98 kilograms with a payload capacity of 130 kilograms, and it covered more than fifteen kilometres on the outbound leg.
Preparation ran to months and drew on the experience of the uncrewed ground vehicle company of the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade. Equipment had been dropped to the soldier in advance and he had to secure himself to the aircraft’s winch without help, while adjacent units launched bomber drones to pull enemy interceptors away from the rescue aircraft.
A second system, Stargate, was built specifically for evacuation at the request of assault troops. It deploys in ten minutes, carries 150 kilograms at speeds up to 105 kilometres an hour and holds a medical module with a stretcher, and its software can plot a route and return to a safe area without help if navigation is completely jammed.
Assault troops of the CODE 9.2 regiment used it twice in a single week to bring out severely wounded soldiers from the grey zone five kilometres from the Russian border, where terrain, water obstacles and first person view drones ruled out any ground rescue. The aircraft flew nearly thirty kilometres each way and came back with the casualties aboard while under electronic attack, relying on artificial intelligence alone for navigation, with heavy strike drones suppressing enemy positions to cover the run.
Conventional casualty evacuation has become close to impossible along much of the front because the density of drone coverage turns any vehicle movement into a target, and uncrewed ground vehicles took over much of the work at the cost of speed. Survival after serious trauma depends heavily on reaching surgical care quickly, and a crawling robot moving along a mined route can take many hours to cover ground a helicopter would cross in minutes.
Ukraine’s Defence Procurement Agency has contracted three times as many uncrewed systems of all types this year as it did last year.

Russia Extends Diesel Export Ban to 2027 With Trump Carve-Out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:13:00 UTC
19:13:00 KST

The Russian government has extended its ban on commercial diesel fuel exports through January 2027 while introducing specific exemptions for designated suppliers to fulfill a commercial arrangement struck with US President Donald Trump, Bloomberg reported.
Under regulatory adjustments finalized by Russian energy authorities, Moscow plans to export approximately 2.15 million metric tons of refined diesel in November, up from an estimated 510,000 tons shipped in October.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The sharp increase in planned outbound volumes follows waivers granted by the Russian government in October after Trump announced a bilateral understanding with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel onto global markets to mitigate fuel benchmark inflation.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak stated that while recurring Ukrainian long-range drone interdictions against domestic oil refineries could lead to temporary contractions in export quotas, energy officials do not anticipate substantial reductions in aggregate supply.
Novak confirmed that as of late October, four commercial tankers laden with Russian refined diesel had departed Baltic Sea ports.
Baltic departures to Turkey and Brazil
The regulatory carve-outs align with commercial maritime tracking data revealing that Moscow resumed seaborne diesel loadings bound for major non-Western buyers following the mid-October deal with Washington.
Ship tracking data compiled by analytics firms Kpler and LSEG showed that multiple diesel tankers cleared Russia’s primary Baltic oil terminal at Primorsk. The tanker Dolunay departed Primorsk bound for the Turkish port of Alanya on Oct. 14, followed on Oct. 16 by the tanker Leruo, which set sail for Manaus, Brazil.
Rubio Doubts Ukraine Peace Deal Before Spring 2027
Turkey and Brazil have operated as the principal seaborne buyers of Russian refined diesel since 2023, circumventing Western sanctions through independent payment rails and non-Western maritime fleets.
According to Kpler market data, Turkey has accounted for approximately 34 percent of all Russian seaborne diesel liftings so far this year, absorbing an average of 95,000 barrels per day (bpd). Brazil accounted for 24 percent of loadings, taking roughly 66,000 bpd.
Beyond maritime shipments, Moscow previously exported 427,000 metric tons of diesel to Central Asian republics under intergovernmental supply contracts in September to satisfy regional bilateral trade obligations.
Contradictory volume targets and macroeconomic impact
The prospective export scale has highlighted discrepancies between projections published in Washington and higher delivery estimates formulated in Moscow.
Trump previously asserted that Russia would supply up to 2 million tons of commercial diesel to the US and the broader global market to alleviate retail price pressures exacerbated by armed conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. However, Novak subsequently projected that Russia could supply up to 3.5 million tons by the end of 2026 under the authorized exemptions.
Energy economists and market analysts have questioned the macroeconomic impact of the Russian fuel volumes. Kyiv Post calculated that even an export volume of 3.5 million tons would satisfy US and Chinese domestic fuel consumption for approximately one week, while representing less than a single day of total global diesel consumption.
To facilitate the transactions, the US Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian refined diesel through April 7, 2027.
On Oct. 16, Trump reinforced the arrangement by signing an executive order invoking Section 115 of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, waiving mandatory 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports and 100 percent duties on third-party petroleum buyers just 48 hours before statutory implementation.

Pro-EU Polish PM brings ‘Russian bots’ into court showdown
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has accused his political opponents of receiving support from an “army of Russian bots”amid an escalating constitutional crisis in Warsaw. The pro-EU leader offered no proof for his claim, which came after a government-backed judge moved to oust two key officials supported by his rival, right-wing President Karol Nawrocki, from the Constitutional Tribunal, triggering public outrage.
Unrest erupted on Friday when Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a judge elected by Tusk’s governing majority, ordered the suspension of Constitutional Tribunal President Bogdan Swieczkowski and his deputy Bartlomiej Sochanski, both linked to the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. The tribunal’s existing leadership rejected the suspensions, declaring that all those participating in the attempted takeover “are committing the crime of a coup d’état.”
The development triggered street protests around the court building and a heavy police deployment. Nawrocki, who canceled a planned trip to Senegal, personally pushed his way into the tribunal to confront Korwin-Piotrowska and her allies, telling them that “you are not judges of the Constitutional Tribunal.”
In a televised address on Saturday evening, Tusk scrambled to defend his actions, accusing his rivals of “seeking to destroy democracy and the rule of law.” The Polish PM, a strong supporter of EU integration who served as president of the European Council from 2014 to 2019, has long criticized PiS judicial reforms – which he said undermined judges’ independence – as well as Nawrocki’s refusal to administer the oath to five Constitutional Tribunal judges elected by the current parliamentary majority.
“Is it greed, stupidity or treason?” Tusk asked, claiming that the opposition was receiving support from “pro-Russian forces worldwide.”
“In this conflict, they’re using an army of Russian bots online. In fact, they’ve even received public compliments from the Kremlin’s chief ideologue,” the prime minister claimed, without providing further proof or elaborating.
Moscow has repeatedly said it does not interfere in other countries’ domestic affairs. While Russian officials have yet to respond to Tusk’s allegation, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov in July denied that Russia was responsible for cyberattacks on Polish energy infrastructure.
Responding to Tusk’s address, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, called the prime minister a “pathological liar” and accused him of setting Poland ablaze while pretending to extinguish the fire. “It’s hard to find a single word, expression, or sentence that would be true, that would reflect the actual or legal reality,” he added.
Tusk’s accusation comes after several Western media outlets, anti-Russia hawks, and Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky propagated the claim that Kiev’s drone strikes, which damaged several data centers operated by Russian technology giant Yandex, crippled alleged Russian bot networks supporting Western right-wing movements, including Germany’s AfD and US President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement.
However, several independent investigations by cybersecurity and research firms quickly debunked the narrative. Experts in particular pointed out that one viral graph supposedly showing a collapse in AfD-related activity was found to contain fabricated or unverifiable figures.
Commenting on the chaos, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev described it as a “constitutional coup.” He suggested that “Brussels’ protégé Tusk” was persecuting PiS conservatives over the latter’s hostility toward Ukrainian Nazi collaborators. Medvedev concluded by sarcastically invoking an old schoolyard joke, saying, “And these are the people who scold my brother and me for picking our noses.”

Yemeni government forces seize strategic positions in al-Jawf
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:08:55 UTC
19:08:55 KST

Yemeni government forces seize strategic positions in al-Jawf
Weapons and ammunition depots are seized after a counteroffensive.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government says its forces have recaptured military positions and strategic heights east of al-Hazm, the capital of the northern governorate of al-Jawf, while fighting continues to deepen the humanitarian crisis in the besieged city of Taiz.
The army’s media centre said in a post on X on Saturday that the 1st Emergency Brigade seized weapons and ammunition depots after wounding, killing and capturing Houthi fighters. It also said the attacks resulted in the destruction of armoured vehicles.
The Houthis, meanwhile, said they had thwarted advances by government forces in al-Jawf and neighbouring Marib.
Al-Jawf borders Saudi Arabia and lies alongside the Houthi-held governorates of Sanaa and Saada, making it a vital strategic front in the government’s campaign to regain territory. The fighting is part of Operation Dawn of Yemen, launched in October to reverse Houthi gains and restore government control over territory held by the group, which seized Sanaa in 2014.
Fighting has also continued around Taiz in southern Yemen with government forces saying they repelled Houthi attacks in al-Aqroudh, southeast of the city, and on the Tur al-Baha front in neighbouring Lahij governorate.
Meanwhile, Houthi-affiliated media reported that two air strikes targeted an oil company facility in Bajil district in Hodeidah governorate.
Aid shortages deepen crisis
The fighting comes as the siege of Taiz strains hospitals and restricts deliveries of food, fuel and medical supplies. Although the Houthis do not control the city, they hold key routes in and out of it, limiting access to essential supplies and making it harder for civilians to leave amid reported sniper fire from the surrounding hillsides.
Videos published by Yemeni media showed what the outlets described as the first shipment of medical aid arriving from Marib to support wounded people, displaced families and other residents. Further shipments were reportedly held up by road closures.
More than 290,000 people have fled their homes since fighting escalated in August, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. The UN Population Fund said nearly 6,100 pregnant women were among those recently displaced, including 600 expected to give birth within two weeks of its briefing on Friday.
The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees warned that more than 65,000 refugees and asylum seekers in Yemen face worsening conditions as services are disrupted and food and fuel prices rise.

US midterm elections 2026: Five key Senate races that could determine control of Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:06:47 UTC
19:06:47 KST

Americans head to the polls on Tuesday for midterm elections.
Ahead of the elections, here are The Jerusalem Post’s key Senate races to watch.
Michigan
The race between Democrat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and MAGA favorite Mike Rogers has been the source of many national headlines.
El-Sayed has hammered his planks of universal healthcare and overall affordability in the state, but has gained significant attention for his criticism of Israel and outreach to Jewish voters.
Rogers’s platform mostly aligns with US President Donald Trump, and has specifically highlighted his plank of bringing manufacturing jobs back to America.
A poll recently released by CBS Detroit has El-Sayed leading by seven percentage points, or 51% to Rogers’s 44%.
Texas
Democrat James Talarico is poised to be the first Democrat to hold statewide office in conservative-stronghold Texas since the 1990s.
He is taking on the state’s Attorney-General Ken Paxton, a MAGA loyalist who has been plagued by scandals for the last decade.
Throughout the course of the campaign, Talarico has framed politics as a struggle between billionaires and working people. His platform includes raising the federal minimum wage, expanding universal childcare, raising public school teacher pay, creating pathways for long-term immigrants and DREAMers to gain US citizenship, and expanding pathways for legal immigration.
Paxton's platform includes Trump-aligned immigration policies, cutting taxes and government spending, America First foreign policy, and supporting crypto growth
Overall, Paxton promised to "carry the torch for Trump's agenda" on his website.
North Carolina
North Carolina could be one of the least competitive races on the ballot.
Though Trump endorsed ex-RNC chair Michael Whately in 2024, he admitted in October that he was “worried” about him.
Whately is running against two-term former governor Roy Cooper.
Whately’s platform is mostly focused on crime, immigration, and tax cuts. He supported Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill and has pledged to push Trump’s policies in the Senate.
Cooper’s “make stuff cost less” platform targets healthcare, child care, utility bills, and the standard cost of living in the state.
He’s pushed for expanded Medicaid access in the state, but has tried to pitch himself as an “independent voice” for voters on both sides of the aisle.
Cooper is currently leading in polls by 10 points, according to MS NOW.
Georgia
Jewish Sen. John Ossoff is defending his seat against GOP Congressman Mike Collins. Notably, Ossoff is the only Democrat in the Senate up for re-election in a state Trump won in the 2024 presidential race.
Ossoff’s platform calls for a ban on stock trading while in federal office, expanding rural broadband access, lowering housing prices, protecting abortion rights, and protecting voting rights. He is a critic of the war in Iran, but describes his support for Israel as “ironclad”, though he voted to block weapons sales in 2025.
Collins’s platform focuses on Trump-aligned immigration policies, rural hospital funding, reducing medicare spending, and other conservative fiscal policies that he claims will help small businesses.
Ossoff is up 52.6% to Collins’s 42.3% in the latest polls released by MS NOW.
Alaska
The race in Alaska has caused a stir after Republicans called for an investigation into a ballot-stacking scheme by Democrats.
Trump and his allies accused Democrat Mary Peltola of recruiting candidates with the same name as her and her opponent, Republican Dan Sullivan, to purposefully confuse voters when they cast their ballots.
Peltola has since denied the accusations and said that she is “not out soliciting more competition.”
“I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters.”
Federal prosecutors are now investigating the matter.
Peltola’s platform includes targeting corruption and influence in Washington, more benefits for Alaskan military families, balancing oil production with environmental protections, and supporting the state’s fishing industry.
Sullivan’s platform includes pieces on energy strategy and environmental standards to support the energy industry.
Peltola is up by two percentage points, 50.2% to Sullivan’s 48.4%, in the race.
Notably, Democrats would need to win seven seats to gain a 51-seat majority in the Senate.
Additionally, the president’s party historically loses House seats in the midterms. The Trump administration and Republicans have stressed to their base for months the importance of voting.

Betting on AI and robotics, Dyson opens Glilot flagship store in Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:06:45 UTC
19:06:45 KST

Dyson has opened a new flagship store at BIG FASHION Glilot, north of Tel Aviv, showcasing its latest developments in artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and personal care technology as the British company looks to push household appliances beyond traditional mechanical engineering.
The store features the company’s newest products, including the Spot+Scrub AI robotic cleaner, Airwrap Co, Airsmooth hot air brush, and CameraJet electric toothbrush. The opening also provided a platform for Dyson to demonstrate how it is incorporating advanced sensing systems, computer vision, and automation into products designed to address everyday household problems.
Guy Turner, a design engineer on Dyson’s robotics team in Singapore, spoke with The Jerusalem Post about the engineering behind the company’s latest developments, describing a shift toward smart machines that can understand their surroundings and respond without requiring constant human intervention.
“We believe solving problems in the home is about sensing and perceiving what you want to clean, and creating products for problems that already exist,” Turner said.
He explained that the company’s philosophy is to look for products and tasks that have not undergone significant change and find ways to rethink them.
“Dyson likes to find new ways to solve problems in products that haven’t seen change in a while,” he said. “The goal is to remove problems, not make new ones.”
That approach has defined Dyson’s development for more than three decades. Its founder, James Dyson, went through 5,126 failed prototypes before developing the company’s first bagless vacuum cleaner, a breakthrough that helped establish the company.
“Since DC01, our first bagless vacuum cleaner, Dyson has spent more than 30 years solving the problems others ignore,” Turner said. “That started with mechanical innovation: bagless cyclonic separation, high-speed digital motors, and bladeless airflow. Today, we’re increasingly combining mechanical engineering with connectivity, sensor systems, and on-product intelligence.”
Teaching robots to understand their surroundings
One of the central challenges in the company’s robotics development is enabling machines to navigate intelligently while cleaning effectively.
The Spot+Scrub AI, one of the products demonstrated at the Glilot opening, combines wet and dry cleaning with AI-powered vision systems designed to identify dirt, debris, and stains.
The robot uses an HD front-facing camera, green LED illumination, LiDAR, and dual-laser sensing to identify objects and navigate indoor environments. According to Dyson, it can recognize nearly 200 household objects, including cables and socks, and adjust its cleaning behavior accordingly. Its ability to identify stains and return to them repeatedly is particularly important. Rather than simply following a predetermined cleaning route, the robot detects dirty areas and continues scrubbing them until they are clean.
“Spot+Scrub AI detects a dirty area and does it persistently until it’s gone,” Turner explained.
Users can schedule cleaning, view home maps, and request targeted cleaning through the MyDyson app.
Bringing intelligence to personal care
Dyson’s interest in applying technology to established product categories also extends to personal care.
The company presented its new CameraJet electric toothbrush, which Turner described as an attempt to address a problem that has remained largely unchanged despite decades of developments in oral-care technology.
“The electric toothbrush has been around for about 30 years,” he said, pointing to the fact that many people still do not floss or spend enough time on dental hygiene as an opportunity for innovation.
The CameraJet combines a camera with water-jet technology, allowing users to see how they brush through a live feed on a connected app. The system is designed to provide dental hygiene guidance and help users improve their brushing technique.
Turner said the camera incorporates a macro lens capable of capturing approximately 100,000 pixels across a one-millimeter-by-one-millimeter area, allowing users to see details that would otherwise be difficult to observe. The toothbrush also has a live feed where users can watch how they brush.
The toothbrush is expected to become available in Israel during the first half of 2027.
Another product on display was the Dyson Airsmooth, a hot air brush designed to dry, smooth, and lift hair in one step, highlighting the company’s continued expansion into beauty technology.
Israel’s technology-minded consumers
Turner said Dyson sees Israel as an attractive market for its products, citing consumers’ strong interest in technology and willingness to adopt innovations.
“There’s a passion for technology in Israel. Consumers here are very tech-savvy,” he said.
Although Dyson has no engineering and development base in Israel, its international operations include its headquarters in Singapore and research and innovation activities in the UK, alongside engineering teams in other countries.
The company, founded in the UK in 1993, employs approximately 14,000 people worldwide, including 6,000 engineers, and sells products in 85 markets.
The new Glilot store is intended to give Israeli consumers an opportunity to experience the company’s latest products through interactive displays and live demonstrations, while offering a glimpse into the direction Dyson believes household technology is heading.

Herzog calls on political leaders to demonstrate flexibility ahead of coalition negotiations

President Isaac Herzog on Sunday called on Israel's political leaders to accept the election results and demonstrate flexibility in coalition negotiations, warning against political entrenchment that could force the country into another election, ahead of consultations at the President’s Residence set to begin on Wednesday.
“The election results are an established fact – they are the reality. And now is the time to tell all the leaders: Stop climbing trees and position yourselves in front of this reality," Herzog said while speaking at the state memorial ceremony for Israel's first president, Chaim Weizmann.
Herzog made the remarks amid the political deadlock in which the election results showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanayhu's bloc and the bloc seeking to oust the premier both fall short of the required 61-seat Knesset majority.
Netanyahu’s bloc maintained its lead, securing 53 seats in the next Knesset, while the opposition bloc won 48. Meanwhile, the Arab parties, Ra'am and the Joint List, won a record-breaking total of 19 seats combined.
The Joint List and Ra'am are expected to recommend Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot for prime minister during consultations with President Isaac Herzog, a senior Joint List official told Walla on Sunday.
Talks at the President's Residence will begin Wednesday, when Eisenkot is expected to be the first candidate to receive the mandate from the president, giving him 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension, to form a coalition.
Along with the 48 seats won by the opposition bloc, the Arab parties' 19 recommendations would give Eisenkot 67 in total, prompting Herzog to grant him the mandate.
The Knesset is expected to be sworn in on November 10, regardless of any government or coalition talks.
By law, the president is required to consult the Knesset factions before deciding who receives the task of forming a government.
Herzog called for cooperation and open minds
Herzog said that this week, at the President’s Residence, "we will try to put up ladders to allow the leaders to position themselves in front of this reality in a measured and careful manner."
Herzog said he would receive the official election results on Wednesday from Central Elections Committee chairman and Supreme Court Deputy President Justice Noam Sohlberg.
"Following that, I will begin consultations at the President's Residence. The President's Residence will be wide open to all factions and parties."
The president emphasized the importance of cooperation among party leaders, urging them to demonstrate a willingness to consider different proposals and reach agreements.
"I have already said that I hope the representatives will come with open minds, and I add that they should come with open hearts, to listen and share ideas and find creative solutions to prevent another election," he said.
On Saturday, Eisenkot laid out four principles for joining his proposed coalition, saying that “any MK” willing to accept them could become a partner in forming the next government.
Eisenkot said he intended to establish the broadest possible Zionist, statesmanlike government, bringing together elected representatives who agree on Israel’s fundamental character, national service obligations, and the need to eliminate Hamas’s military and governing capabilities in the Gaza Strip.
Last week, Democrats party leader Yair Golan called on Wednesday for the opposition to form a coalition with the Arab parties.
Other heads of the opposition parties, Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett (B'Yachad), and Avigdor Liberman (Yisrael Beytenu), had drawn a red line to Arab parties being part of the government, saying they are not viable coalition partners after the October 7 massacre in 2023.
The political deadlock could ultimately lead to another election, although the parties may still reach an agreement through coalition negotiations. Other possible outcomes include a unity government among Netanyahu and members of Eisenkot’s bloc, or the formation of a minority government.
The Arab parties have expressed willingness to cooperate with the oppostion bloc to work toward replacing Netanyahu.
Meanwhile, opposition party leaders have also reportedly agreed that their first move after the new Knesset is sworn in on November 10 would be to oust Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party.
The move would require a majority in a Knesset vote and could be achievable with the support of the Arab parties, bringing the potential backing to 67 seats.
Replacing Ohana would give the opposition bloc greater control over the parliamentary agenda, including votes, legislation, and committee appointments, even if Netanyahu remains in office as head of a caretaker government.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

LISBON – Riot police with dogs stormed protest camps in Lisbon and Porto early on Nov 1, charging demonstrators with batons, arresting 13 people and leaving dozens injured in the latest confrontation over Portugal’s housing crisis.
Clashes quickly broke out as dozens of officers moved in on an encampment in Lisbon’s Rossio Square and a smaller camp in Porto’s Dom Joao I Square at around 4.30am local time.
Protesters shouted “smells like a dictatorship”, while the police said some hurled bottles and paint at officers as they tried to take down the tents.
The police said in a statement that six people were arrested in Lisbon and seven in Porto for refusing orders to disperse. It said 13 police were injured in the process, with eight taken to hospital.
In Porto, the police said three plain-clothes officers monitoring the protesters were assaulted after being spotted by a group.
One of the officers displayed his firearm as a deterrent, police said.
An unspecified number of civilians were also injured during the operation, which was carried out “with rigour, balance and respect for citizens’ rights”, the statement read.
Porto protest organisers said 38 people were injured, including three seriously, while Lisbon organisers reported more than 30 injured.
Activist group Acampada Lisboa said more than 30 protesters were injured, including 10 who required hospital treatment, and called a fresh rally in the capital on the afternoon of Nov 1 to protest against the police operation.
“We will not be silenced,” it said in a statement posted on social media, alongside photographs of protesters with bruises or bleeding from injuries it blamed on “police violence”.
Some protesters carried red carnations, a symbol of Portugal’s 1974 revolution, evoking the peaceful military-led uprising that ended nearly five decades of dictatorship.
Police said they seized 69 tents in Lisbon and 30 in Porto.
The camps had been set up late on Oct 31 after peaceful marches through the two cities against soaring housing costs.
Officers have repeatedly dismantled encampments that have sprung up across Lisbon and Porto in recent weeks.
‘Dark night’
After police cleared protest camps in the two cities last weekend, Amnesty International said it was “deeply concerned by the excessive and disproportionate use of force by police”.
A lawyer representing protesters at Lisbon’s housing camps, Ricardo Sa Fernandes, said on Nov 1 he would file a criminal complaint against Interior Minister Luis Neves and the national police chief for abuse of power.
“This is a dark night in the history of Portuguese democracy. This is absolutely intolerable and has crossed all limits,” he told reporters outside a police station in Lisbon where some of those detained were taken.
Neves has defended the police response to the protests, insisting that the encampments must end and warning that officers will use force when necessary to restore public order.
“I feel deep sadness about what happened again last night. Nobody takes any pleasure in seeing this outcome,” he said on Nov 1.
Protesters want the minority centre-right government to abandon plans to ease evictions and remove rent caps on new leases, warning the measures would push up housing costs and leave tenants more vulnerable.
Prime Minister Luis Montenegro has acknowledged that property prices have doubled in a decade, but blames the crisis on previous left-wing governments for failing to build enough homes and pursuing what he calls an overly permissive migration policy.
Portuguese protesters have taken inspiration from a similar movement in neighbouring Spain, where tents have been set up in central Madrid and other cities for weeks. AFP

From railway tragedy to gov’t change: Serbia’s two-year fight for justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:04:22 UTC
19:04:22 KST

From railway tragedy to gov’t change: Serbia’s two-year fight for justice
A timeline of events since the deadly train station collapse in Novi Sad, which led to a change of government in Serbia.
Sunday marks two years since 16 people were killed when a train station canopy collapsed in the Serbian city of Novi Sad.
The accident prompted student-led protests which swiftly evolved into a wider political campaign that brought the Student List opposition movement to power last week.
Here is a timeline of events from the tragedy in Novi Sad on November 1, 2024, to the elections that led to a change of government in Serbia.
November 1, 2024 – The collapse of a concrete canopy on the renovated Novi Sad railway station building kills 14 people at the scene, with three others taken to hospital in critical condition. Two of them later die of their injuries in November 2024 and March 2025, bringing the total number of victims to 16. The tragedy leads to public outrage, raising questions about the quality of the work, lack of transparency in the spending of public money and endemic corruption.
November 5, 2024 – Just four days after the accident, thousands of protesters gather in Novi Sad to demand accountability for those responsible. The protests escalate into clashes with police, with dozens of protesters arrested and City Hall damaged. Observers point to the swift judicial response to the protesters, while the investigation into the accident itself remains stalled.
November 19, 2024 – Opposition MPs, councillors and citizens block the entrance to the court and prosecutor’s office building in Novi Sad for three consecutive days, demanding the release of those arrested and an accelerated investigation into those responsible for the collapse of the canopy. The blockade is marked by daily confrontations with police in riot gear.
November 21, 2024 – After three weeks of public pressure, the higher public prosecutor’s office in Novi Sad announces that 11 people have been arrested in connection with the deaths at the railway station, including former Construction Minister Goran Vesic and other officials.
November 22-25, 2024 – Students and professors come under attack during a memorial service for the victims of the canopy collapse in front of the faculty of dramatic arts of the University of Arts in Belgrade. The incident marks a turning point, prompting students to launch a university sit-in to demand the prosecution of the attackers, the publication of documentation on the railway station’s reconstruction and the release of all detained protesters.
December 11, 2024 – Under strong pressure from months of protests and university blockades, authorities publish part of the documentation on the reconstruction of the railway station. Eight binders containing 195 documents are presented, but students and others dismiss the move as insufficient, demanding full transparency and criminal accountability for the contractors and supervisory institutions.
December 30, 2024 – Prosecutors in Novi Sad officially file an indictment against 13 people on suspicion of committing serious crimes against public security, improper execution of construction works and abuse of office. But higher courts overturn detention orders for Vesic and Serbia Railways Infrastructure’s acting General Director Jelena Tanaskovic, putting them under house arrest. The transparency of the proceedings is further called into question by a dispute over the jurisdiction of the prosecution offices and the transfer of case files.
January 15, 2025 – In addition to the proceedings in Novi Sad for the canopy collapse, the public prosecutor’s office for organised crime in Belgrade officially launches a separate investigation into potential financial fraud, corruption and money laundering during the reconstruction of the railway station. It involves Vesic, former Trade Minister Tomislav Momirovic and 12 other individuals, including managers of construction and supervision companies.
January 28, 2025 – Public outcry erupts after governing party activists attack and cause serious bodily harm to students of the Academy of Arts in Novi Sad. Serbian Prime Minister Milos Vucevic submits his resignation in the government’s biggest political concession to date. However, protests and blockades continue.
March 11, 2025 – Thirteen activists and students are arrested in Novi Sad on the eve of planned large protests in Belgrade, charged with undermining the constitutional order and violent behaviour. The arrests prompt a strong reaction from civil society organisations and citizens, who denounce them as politically motivated and organise protests and road blockades in Novi Sad.
March 15, 2025 – Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrate in Belgrade.
May 28, 2025 – After months of student-led protests and blockades, Novi Sad’s High Court decides to replace prison detention with house arrest for some of the imprisoned activists and students.
June 25, 2025 – With the prosecutor refusing to withdraw the charges of undermining the constitutional order and security services continuing to exert pressure, some of the accused activists leave Serbia for European Union countries, where they continue to draw attention to the situation.
September 9, 2026 – The informal student-led movement morphs into a political force following the announcement of snap parliamentary elections for October. The Student List-Students Win grouping is formed, bringing together students, professors and legal experts.
September 27, 2026 – Longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic resigns as president of Serbia to lead the Serbian Progressive Party-led electoral list. On his last day as president, he pardons all prosecuted students and activists, ending the proceedings for “undermining the constitutional order” and allowing the safe return of activists from exile. The move is widely seen as an attempt to ease social tensions ahead of the election campaign.
October 25, 2025 – Vucic concedes defeat to the Student List in the elections, which saw voter turnout reach its highest level in more than 30 years. Accountability for the Novi Sad railway station tragedy remains a central issue following the announcement of the results.

Israel issues over 9,500 demolition, stop-work notices in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:03:28 UTC
19:03:28 KST

Israeli authorities have issued 9,518 demolition or stop-work notices against Palestinian structures in the occupied West Bank since the start of 2015, a Palestinian government commission said Saturday, Anadolu reports.
The Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said the notices halted construction and left properties under threat, disrupting the lives of families and limiting ability of communities to build homes, expand services and sustain livelihoods.
The report, obtained by Anadolu, documented 9,174 notices between 2015 and 2025 and another 344 in the first nine months of 2026.
The commission cautioned that its figures did not necessarily capture every notice issued by Israeli authorities. The tally was based on cases documented by the commission and partner legal organizations, including the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center and the Society of St. Yves.
Hebron accounted for the largest share, with 2,697 notices, followed by Bethlehem with 1,310, Ramallah and al-Bireh with 1,118, and Jerusalem with 929.
The annual total peaked at 1,333 in 2023, compared with 701 in 2015.
Separately, data from the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) showed that nearly 12,000 structures were demolished during the same period, including 1,698 funded by donors.
The demolitions displaced more than 18,000 Palestinians and affected approximately 843,000, according to OCHA.
The UN office records demolitions carried out on grounds including the lack of Israeli-issued building permits, as punitive measures or during military operations.

UK police arrest Palestine Action supporters ahead of hearing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:02:33 UTC
19:02:33 KST

Breadcrumb
UK police say 325 people were arrested at Palestine Action demo
British police said Sunday they had arrested 325 people at a London protest in support of Palestine Action the previous day, ahead of a court appeal over the government's contentious ban of the group.
Demonstrators staged a "mass action" outside the US embassy ahead of the Supreme Court holding a two-day hearing from Wednesday on the UK government's July 2025 decision to outlaw Palestine Action under anti-terror legislation.
The United States also designated Palestine Action as "terrorist" in August, as the administration of President Donald Trump intensifies its campaign against left-wing movements.
The British designation puts the group on a blacklist that also includes entities like the Palestinian group Hamas, and makes membership of, or support for, Palestine Action a crime punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
It has resulted in more than 4,000 people, including many senior citizens and Holocaust survivors, being arrested for showing their support for the group, according to campaigners and police tallies.
"In total, 325 people were arrested yesterday," London's Metropolitan Police said in a Sunday update.
"The vast majority of arrests, 320, were for expressing support for a proscribed organisation under the Terrorism Act."
A smaller number of protesters also rallied outside the US consulate in the Scottish capital Edinburgh on Saturday, but no arrests were made there at the time.
"Enquiries are ongoing to identify people seen wearing t-shirts and holding banners showing support for a proscribed organisation," Police Scotland said in a statement shared with AFP on Sunday.
"Evidence is being reviewed and further action will be taken as appropriate."
Many of those arrested, including senior citizens and Holocaust survivors, have displayed signs at rallies reading: "I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action."
In July, hearings related to more than 2,000 of those cases were postponed until later this year.
"It is truly dystopian that there have now been over 4,000 arrests under terror laws for peaceful vigils," Protest organisers Defend Our Juries said in a statement.
The group's co-founder Huda Ammori has legally challenged the ban, arguing it was "disproportionate" and infringed human rights.
The Supreme Court is set to hold a two-day hearing on the high-profile case from Wednesday, after the Court of Appeal ruled in the government's favour in June.
'Losing faith'
Saturday's London protesters held banners bearing slogans such as "How is trying to stop a genocide a crime?" and "We are protesters, not terrorists."
Attendee Angie Zelter, 75, told AFP she had already been charged at least eight times at previous rallies but wanted to protest again ahead of the Supreme Court hearing.
"I am hoping they will come to their senses and agree PA (Palestine Action) should not have been proscribed," she said.
Marji Mansfield, 70, a retired financial adviser, said she had previously been arrested about 10 times.
"I am losing faith in the judicial system," she told AFP.
"If they lift the ban, it would be a way out for the government," Mansfield added, while noting there was currently "no sign" of the ban's reversal.
Bestselling Irish author Sally Rooney has entered the controversy, with her publisher Faber revealing this month it can no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for the group.
Set up in 2020, Palestine Action's stated goal on its website, blocked to UK internet users, is to end "global participation in Israel's genocidal and apartheid regime".
It gained visibility after the outbreak of Israel's genocidal war in October 2023.
Palestine Action has mainly targeted weapons factories in Britain, especially those belonging to the Israel-based defence group Elbit.

Russia’s Baltic Exclave Goes Dark as Major Power Plant Failure Triggers Widespread Blackout

- Category

Russia’s Baltic Exclave Goes Dark as Major Power Plant Failure Triggers Widespread Blackout
A major power outage swept across Russia’s Kaliningrad region overnight on October 30–31, leaving large parts of the Baltic exclave without electricity and disrupting mobile internet services following an emergency shutdown at one of the region’s largest power plants.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Moscow Times on October 31, the blackout was triggered by the activation of an emergency protection system at Kaliningrad’s CHPP-2 thermal power plant, which caused some of its equipment to shut down.
The outage affected multiple districts of Kaliningrad and several surrounding towns, including Guryevsk, Svetlogorsk, Pionersky, Yantarny, Gvardeysk, and Bagrationovsk.
The affected power plant has an installed generating capacity of 900 megawatts, equivalent to approximately 54% of the region’s total installed electricity generation capacity as of 2019.
Mariam Bashkirova, spokesperson for the regional governor, confirmed that emergency protection equipment had activated at the facility. She said electricity demand had been redistributed to other regional power plants while crews worked to restore supplies.
Russian grid operator Rosseti stated that its regional subsidiary, Rosseti Yantar, had experienced no technical failures on its own infrastructure. The company said electricity was being restored in stages and expected all affected customers to be reconnected within an hour.
However, The Moscow Times reported that residents continued experiencing electricity interruptions despite those assurances. Some also complained of disruptions to water supplies and heating, with outages lasting from several minutes to several hours.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave located between Poland and Lithuania, geographically separated from mainland Russia and home to more than one million people.
In February 2025, the Baltic states disconnected their electricity networks from Russia and Belarus and synchronized with the continental European grid. Since then, Kaliningrad has operated its electricity system independently, relying on its own power generation infrastructure to maintain supplies across the region.

====================================================================================================

Call for two attack submarines at sea at all times
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:01:21 GMT
19:01:21 KST

Two of the five Astute class submarines should be fully deployable and operational at all times, one patrolling northern waters or the Channel and a second working alongside the deterrent patrol, according to a briefing paper published by the 878 Institute.
The recommendation appears in the first of a planned series on the condition of the Royal Navy. It reads: “To ensure that two of the five Astute-class submarines are fully deployable and indeed operational at all times: one actively patrolling the North Sea, the Greenland-Iceland-UK (GIUK) Gap, or English Channel to deter increased Russian submarine activity around British waters; a second always patrolling alongside the CASD.”
It follows the paper’s account of the summer, which states: “Despite maintaining a fleet of five vessels, it was reported that not a single Astute-class submarine was operationally deployed through summer 2026, and that all five remained laid-up in British harbours. Only HMS Agamemnon (one of the two planned additions to the five in service) is at sea conducting trials.
“This is deeply concerning, given both the rise in Russian sub-surface activity around British waters, but perhaps more worrying because of the lack of available escorts for Britain’s nuclear deterrent.” The Ministry of Defence does not comment on submarine operations.
A linked recommendation asks for more money for the class, and warns of what follows without it. It reads: “To increase resource allocation for the troubled Astute-class submarines, all of which were in docks for a period from June 2026. Increased resources are needed to alleviate maintenance backlogs, industrial bottlenecks, and dockyard infrastructure limitations. Without this, the Astute-class must be said to be failing, and with it, Britain’s nuclear deterrent risks being left defenceless at sea or dependent upon allies for support, eroding the UK’s ‘sovereign’ nuclear deterrent.”
Setting a standing requirement of two boats available continuously would mean two fifths of the in-service class at sea at any moment. Sustaining that demands considerably more than two hulls, because the conventional planning assumption across submarine operating navies runs at roughly three boats for every one deployed, allowing for deep maintenance, work-up and crew training, so the recommendation implies six or seven available boats against a class of five with two more coming.
The Astute class carries two primary roles, hunting other submarines and protecting the Vanguard boats, and the paper describes both when it says the class exists for “anti-submarine warfare, as well as fleet protection for the nuclear-armed Vanguard-class.”
Devonport holds the only licence in Britain to refit nuclear submarines, and ministers told Parliament this week that the programme rebuilding the submarine berths there is being recovered after design difficulties, with construction still to start. The refit of HMS Vanguard at the same yard ran to seven and a half years against an original plan of three and a half.
Russian activity around British waters has risen, and the paper records that the Royal Navy spent twenty-one days in July alone monitoring Russian ships, and tracking operations rose twenty-five per cent on the previous year. The Defence Committee reported this month that availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines raises questions about whether Britain can meet its commitments in the High North, and that the department has accepted an anti-submarine warfare gap in northern waters.
The 878 Institute published a broader paper on British deterrence gaps in August, which UKDJ reported at the time.

Attack boats stayed in harbour all summer, report warns
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:00:59 GMT
19:00:59 KST

Britain’s attack submarine fleet spent the summer tied up in harbour while Russian activity around British waters increased, and the availability of escorts for the ballistic missile boats that carry the nuclear deterrent is among the consequences raised, according to a briefing paper published by the 878 Institute.
The paper, the first in a planned series on the condition of the Royal Navy, opens by saying: “The Royal Navy is gripped by a critical but needless decline in strategic capacity, as demonstrated by a steep reduction in both mass and readiness.
“This comes at a time of intensifying maritime competition and growing threats to British national interests. These threats are most acute in and around British waters, as Russia’s submarines, warships and even its shadow-fleet carrying illicit Russian oil across the globe, are all increasing their operations off Britain’s coasts.”
It records that the Royal Navy spent twenty-one days in July alone monitoring Russian ships, that operations to track Russian activity rose twenty-five per cent on the previous year, and that Russian warships made repeated voyages through the Dover Strait and the North Sea. Ministers have confirmed that Moscow uses commercial proxies to threaten undersea infrastructure, and the paper cites analysis uncovering five hundred incidents of Russian civilian vessels loitering above cables.
Concerns about the frigate and destroyer fleets are set out alongside the navy’s transition to automation through the hybrid navy concept, before the paper turns to its main subject. It says: “However, it is in the submarine fleet that we see an especially stark vulnerability and where, due to its purposes, creates unique threats to Britain’s security.”
On the Astute class, which numbers five in service with two more being readied, the paper states: “Despite maintaining a fleet of five vessels, it was reported that not a single Astute-class submarine was operationally deployed through summer 2026, and that all five remained laid-up in British harbours. Only HMS Agamemnon (one of the two planned additions to the five in service) is at sea conducting trials.
“This is deeply concerning, given both the rise in Russian sub-surface activity around British waters, but perhaps more worrying because of the lack of available escorts for Britain’s nuclear deterrent.” That finding draws on reporting by Navy Lookout, and the Ministry of Defence does not comment on submarine operations.
Turning to the four Vanguard boats, the paper acknowledges that deployment cycles are not discussed publicly and then sets out what it describes as widely understood. It says: “Due to the nature of their deterrent, HM Government rightly does not comment on their deployment cycles or current state. However, it is widely understood that the fleet has been in a poor state for some years.”
Designed for patrols of three to four months, the boats have run planned patrols of under a hundred days well past that mark. The paper says: “Most SSN- and SSBN-operating navies view 100-day patrols as the sensible maximum; at least the last ten deterrent patrols all exceeded five months in duration, up until April this year, with the last coming in at over 200 days, apparently becoming the new normal.”
On the four Dreadnought boats due in the early 2030s, the paper argues that work on their successor cannot wait, since each is designed for thirty years of service and the build alone takes twenty. The Ministry of Defence accepted the Strategic Defence Review’s recommendation to begin early definition and requirement-setting during this parliamentary term, a pledge affirmed in July, and the paper says: “However, this pledge was only affirmed in July 2026, and there have been no major announcements since; with only two full Parliamentary years left before the next General Election must be called, the Government needs to properly commit to Dreadnought’s successor at the earliest opportunity.”
The sharpest warnings concern SSN-AUKUS, where steel cutting on the first British boat is scheduled at Barrow-in-Furness in 2027. The paper says: “Given the likely concurrent Astute and Dreadnought programmes, the sole UK submarine construction site in Barrow-in-Furness risks facing acute labour shortfalls as soon as SSN-AUKUS begins. In the meantime the site has added only about 500 workers against a required 2,500 to run the parallel Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS build lines.
“The projected build-timeframes for SSN-AUKUS are also deeply concerning. Astute-class boats averaged 128 months to build; SSN-AUKUS are projected to take only 18 months each. This feels unrealistic, and risks cost overruns, delays, supply-chain over-stretch, and potentially an even bigger ‘submarine gap’.”
Describing the programme as Pillar One of AUKUS and saying it must not fail, the paper adds: “However, without guarantees of resource from HM Government that are currently absent, and instead a vague pledge of total vessels built, a lack of political leadership and gaps in the defence-industrial base, Britain risks being the weak link in the partnership.”
Four recommendations follow, covering a firm commitment to twelve SSN-AUKUS boats at the spring Spending Review in 2027, increased resources for the Astute class to clear maintenance backlogs and dockyard constraints, a standing requirement for two of the five Astutes to be deployable and operational at all times, and the commissioning of the Dreadnought successor definition phase by the close of 2027.
The 878 Institute published a broader paper on British deterrence gaps in August, which UKDJ reported at the time, covering land, space and naval capability with a foreword by General the Lord Dannatt. The Defence Committee reported this month that Britain has allowed its under-ice submarine capability to lapse and that the department has accepted an anti-submarine warfare gap in northern waters, and the Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise.

Zheng notes that she never intentionally pursued a conducting career, choosing instead to ‘let everything happen naturally’
China’s first female conductor, Zheng Xiaoying, is 97 years old, but she continues to give outstanding performances to audiences.
In August, the nonagenarian conducted the Chinese-language version of the opera Carmen in Xiamen, in southeastern China’s Fujian province, where she lives. Tickets for the performance were like gold dust, and audiences marvelled, as always, at her elegant, expressive conducting.

But at 19, she decided to flee to the liberated zone in search of “a new world she had never seen.”

Sadiq Khan calls for cap on numbers of robotaxis on London streets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:00:09 UTC
19:00:09 KST

London’s mayor has called for a cap on the numbers of robotaxis on its streets, with the UK government poised to allow fully driverless vehicles to operate in the capital.
Sadiq Khan said politicians had failed to “grasp the pace of change” from the technology, which could threaten jobs and increase congestion in the city, and questioned whether the rules for autonomous cars were fit for purpose.
His comments came after Chinese robotaxis, now being tested in London, were unveiled by Freenow by Lyft, a rival to Uber.
In September Uber started offering limited passenger services in Wayve’s self-driving cars, albeit with a safety driver in the front seat, under licence from Transport for London (TfL).
Freenow by Lyft is hoping to launch fully driverless Baidu robotaxis as early as next year, under a national licensing scheme.
However, the companies, as well as Waymo – which operates robotaxis in San Francisco and other US cities – are primarily focusing on London and Khan said the city needed to be able to limit the rollout.
“What we don’t want is a situation where there’s a big bang without proper regulation in place. We’ve got to make sure the regulation is fit for purpose before we have a mass rollout of things like automated vehicles,” said Khan.
He added: “I think the pace of change when it comes to tech and innovation has not been fully grasped by politicians. There’s got to be incremental movement when it comes to things like robotaxis or automated vehicles.
“We’re lobbying the government for TfL, for London, to have more powers than it currently has on things like automated vehicles.
“There are big questions that haven’t been answered yet: what impact will this have on air quality, on congestion, on those people whose livelihood is being a private hire vehicle driver or a black-taxi driver.”
Drivers’ unions have held protests at the London HQs of Wayve and Waymo in recent weeks, with many Uber drivers fearing for their future.
Khan added: “Is there going to be a cap? At the moment there’s no cap on the number of private hire vehicles or taxis. We’ve lobbied for those powers as well.
“London isn’t San Francisco. We’re a city of almost 10 million, 400 villages, narrow roads, and it’s really important to get this right.”
Under current regulations for fully autonomous vehicles, TfL can only give or refuse consent for their use within London and not manage or license robotaxi services, making the capital’s authorities somewhat less enthusiastic than ministers to accelerate towards the new technology.
However, Freenow by Lyft said the UK’s national framework for driverless cars was an important factor.
Danny O’Gorman, UK and Ireland general manager, said it was “great news for us to really invest in the market. But in terms of how it’s going to be regulated, once the service is up and running, that’s something that still needs to be ironed out.”
O’Gorman said the company was working closely with TfL and “wanted to do things the right way”. About 24 autonomous Baidu Apollo Go vehicles are being tested in the London borough of Brent.
The spacious Chinese cars, which incorporate a massage seat and a built-in touchscreen in the back for passengers, are in fully autonomous service in cities in China and the UAE, and appeared to be handling the streets safely in a test drive in October for the Guardian.
But many test trips still require human intervention, with roadworks proving difficult. For autonomous vehicles (AVs), “an interesting challenge in London is following the rules of the road”, when many drivers ignore them, O’Gorman said: “You get beeped at a lot for following the speed limit.”
Freenow by Lyft is promising a purpose-built AV depot in the UK. O’Gorman said a large proportion of displaced taxi drivers could be employed there in remote operating and servicing jobs.
The company has traditionally worked with black cabs and, he said: “The larger risks to that industry are the driver age profile: two-thirds are over 50 and they’re retiring, and the vehicle’s too expensive.
“AV is not going to be really competing in that space and it’s going to take a long time for us to scale up to vehicle numbers that threaten anything to do with that.”

A Newly Discovered Trail of Cosmic Debris Illustrates How the End of the Solar System Could Look
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Astronomers at the European Southern Observatory (ESO) have discovered a debris disk around a white dwarf, consisting of the remnants of the solar system that once orbited it. For researchers, these structures could offer a clue as to what the end of our solar system will look like once the sun runs out of fuel.
The white dwarf J1328−1450 is located about 1,600 light-years from Earth. Astronomers were already aware of it thanks to star-mapping catalogs, but new observations taken with ESO’s Very Large Telescope (yes, that’s its real name) revealed that it is surrounded by a disk of debris with an unusual structure: Two distinct rings of gas separated by a gap.
According to the observatory, this disk of material is likely the remnant of the planetary system that once orbited J1328−1450. As it passed through a red giant phase and subsequently became a white dwarf, the star may have destroyed some of its planets and left other rocky bodies exposed to an extreme environment. Some of the released material ended up forming a disk of gas and dust around the dead star.
The process that shaped this system could repeat itself in our own. In about 5 billion years, the sun will exhaust its fuel and expand into a red giant. During this phase, it could engulf nearby bodies, like the closest planets. It will then shed its outer layers, leaving behind a white dwarf. Any rocky bodies that survive this transformation could break apart and form a debris disk around the dead star, like the one astronomers are now observing in J1328−1450.
But the white dwarf’s two debris rings hint at another possibility. Their structure appears to be shaped by bodies that astronomers have not yet been able to identify directly. The data suggest that, following the star’s transformation, at least two planetary objects may have survived among the remnants of that system.
Researchers believe these two bodies could be very different in size. The one closest to the white dwarf would measure just a few kilometers in diameter, while the more distant one could be as large as Pluto or even the moon. Their interaction with the surrounding material would explain the formation of the two rings, although it has not yet been confirmed that they exist as separate objects. An alternative possibility is that the structure originates from different parts of a single planet-like body, such as its crust and core.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Dezeen's favourite furniture and homeware from October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Dezeen’s favourite furniture and homeware from October
The first piece of furniture by architecture office Studio Hagen Hall and a pleated cabinet by Didi Ng Wing Yin feature in this roundup of design pieces spotted by Dezeen’s Jane Englefield over the last month.
SHH-001 table by Studio Hagen Hall
Louis Hagen Hall of London-based Studio Hagen Hall has made his first foray into furniture with this sculptural coffee table, delivered as two legs and a weighty glass tabletop that require no mechanical fixings.
Hagen Hall originally designed the asymmetric piece for Pine Heath, a modernist Hampstead renovation with a corner sofa that required a bespoke coffee table to offset the negative space left by the seating.
Cherry veneer legs are paired with recyclable brown smoked glass to create the made-to-order piece, informed by the design philosophy of modernist American architect John Lautner.
Exo 01 vase by Flora Lechner
Austrian, Netherlands-based designer Flora Lechner originally caught the attention of London’s Max Radford Gallery with her alternative aluminium chandeliers that look like ornate robots
Lechner has now translated her distinctive style into an unusual vase, composed of aluminium clips held together by stainless steel bolts. Stems can be slotted into the clips, which are supported by a base that can be filled with water.
“Exo 01 approaches the vase more as a support structure than as a container,” explained Lechner. “Inspired by braces used to hold and align parts of the body, the work applies this principle to flowers.”
Low-relief table by Anne Holtrop
Anne Holtrop is known for his rough-hewn furniture pieces, which conjure images of volcanic craters and mountainous landscapes.
For his inaugrual exhibition with Carpenter’s Workshop Gallery in London, the Dutch architect and designer is showing off his Low-relief collection of tables made from cast glass.
Their unrefined legs were informed by stone reliefs Holtrop visited in Aswan, Egypt.
Pleats Cabinet No 1 by Didi Ng Wing Yin
Helsinki designer Didi Ng Wing Yin is known for his distinctively pleated wooden furniture, which he makes from locally sourced Finnish timber.
Last week, the designer debuted his first cabinet at Paris’s Spazio Nobile Gallery. Made from a mixture of fir and pine, finished with tung oil, the cabinet features a delicately pleated door made using Ng’s combined splitting, brushing and carving technique.
“I wanted to explore the dynamic contrast between form and texture,” Ng told Dezeen.
“The chunky pedestal base is built from straightforward architectural beams that retain their natural knots and raw characteristics, providing a heavy, structural anchor for the light, organic silhouette of the pleated cabinet door.”
OBJ-05 Chair by Manu Bañó
One of many design events in October was PAD London, a collectible fair that takes place annually in Mayfair’s Berkley Square.
Among this year’s exhibitors was Mexico-based Manu Bañó, who showed a duo of striking patinated brass chairs formed from stacked, sculptural slabs of metal.
The chairs are a continuation of Bañó’s existing brass and stainless steel furniture, and were presented as part of the Objects with Narratives exhibition.
Ballon furniture by Seungjin Yang
South Korean designer Seungjin Yang has been making playful furniture shaped like balloons for years, using colourful epoxy resin.
At PAD London, Yang showed his most recent balloon-like creations in the form of a sofa, two armchairs and two stools.
The designer coats real balloons in resin, painstakingly building their strength. Each piece is complete after around two weeks of delicate testing.
Don’t be misled by the intriguingly delicate appearance of Yang’s finished pieces, which are solid enough to be sat on.
