AA Photo
Türkiye and South Korea are looking to deepen cooperation across a range of sectors, including trade, tourism, investment and defense, as the two countries pursue a goal of increasing their bilateral trade volume to $15 billion.
South Korea remains one of the priority countries under Türkiye’s “Distant Countries Strategy,” which aims to strengthen economic ties with key markets around the world.
As part of these efforts, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan is expected to visit South Korea later this month. During the visit, the two sides are anticipated to review bilateral relations comprehensively and discuss steps to enhance cooperation in energy, defense industries, transportation, infrastructure, high technology, culture and tourism.
The free trade agreement between Türkiye and South Korea entered into force in stages. The framework and goods trade agreements became effective on May 1, 2013, while the services trade and investment agreements took effect on Aug. 1, 2018.
Bilateral trade volume stood at $6.9 billion in 2013 and totaled $11.4 billion in 2025.
In the first nine months of 2026, trade volume between the two countries reached $8.7 billion.
Türkiye’s exports to South Korea amounted to $920.3 million during the January-September period. Pharmaceutical products were the leading export category at $321.8 million. Other major exports included ores, slag and ash at $124.2 million; boilers, machinery and mechanical appliances at $101.6 million; electrical machinery and equipment at $34.2 million; and preparations of vegetables and fruits at $33 million.
Tourism has also remained an important area of cooperation. The number of South Korean visitors to Türkiye increased 9.4 percent year-on-year to 226,434 in 2025. In the first nine months of 2026, arrivals from South Korea totaled 133,604.

18:59:53 KST

Istanbul’s consumer prices increased by 2.47 percent month-on-month in October, according to the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce (İTO), which publishes the Istanbul Consumer Price Index, a key indicator of retail price movements in the city.
The monthly inflation rate accelerated from 2.11 percent in September.
Among the main expenditure groups, the largest monthly increase was recorded in clothing and footwear, where prices rose 10.60 percent. This was followed by recreation and culture with a 5.32 percent increase and communication with a 5.05 percent rise.
Prices also increased by 2.58 percent in food and non-alcoholic beverages, 2.24 percent in housing, 1.87 percent in restaurants and hotels, and 0.45 percent in transportation.
On an annual basis, Istanbul’s consumer inflation slowed to 32.47 percent in October, down from 33.55 percent in September.
Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) will unveil the official inflation data on Nov. 3.
Economists surveyed in state-run Anadolu Agency Finans expect Türkiye’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) to increase by 2.2 percent in October.
Based on the average forecast, annual inflation is expected to ease to 29.28 percent in October from 29.73 percent in September.

Greece receives second FDI frigate HS Nearchos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:57:10 UTC
18:57:10 KST

- Naval Group delivered HS Nearchos, Greece’s second FDI frigate, at Lorient on Oct. 30, ten months after the first ship, HS Kimon.
- The third Greek frigate is due by the end of 2026, and a fourth, ordered in November 2025, is scheduled for 2028.
Naval Group handed over HS Nearchos, the second of Greece’s new French-built defense and intervention frigates, to the Hellenic Navy at its shipyard in Lorient, France, on Oct. 30, ten months after Greece received the first ship of the class.
Greek Defense Minister Nikos Dendias and French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin attended the ceremony. The third Greek frigate, HS Formion, is due by the end of 2026, which would give the Hellenic Navy three of the ships within a year, the company said. Naval Group did not say when Nearchos will sail for Greece or enter operational service.
“Only ten months after the delivery of HS Kimon, it is an honour to deliver the second FDI frigate for the Hellenic Navy, HS Nearchos, in the presence of Catherine Vautrin and Nikos Dendias, whom I would like to thank for their renewed trust,” said Pierre Éric Pommellet, chairman and CEO of Naval Group.
The FDI, short for Frégate de Défense et d’Intervention, is a French design of about 4,500 tons and 122 m (400 feet) built for air defense, anti-ship and anti-submarine warfare. Greece’s version, known as the FDI HN or Kimon class, carries a heavier weapons fit than the French Navy’s ships, with Thales Sea Fire radar and up to 32 Aster 30 long-range air defense missiles. Greece is also buying Schiebel CAMCOPTER S-100 drones to fly from Kimon, Nearchos and Formion for surveillance and anti-submarine work.
The first ship, HS Kimon, was delivered on Dec. 18, 2025, and arrived in Greece in January. In March, Greece sent it to Cyprus to help defend the island against Iranian attacks, alongside a Hydra-class frigate and F-16 fighters, its first operational mission. At the time, Kimon was the only Greek warship able to provide long-range air defense, Naval News reported.
Greece agreed in September 2021 to buy three of the frigates, with an option for a fourth, in a package worth about €3 billion including weapons, and the program started in 2022. It exercised the option in November 2025, ordering a fourth ship, HS Themistokles, along with maintenance and upgrades for the whole fleet. That ship is due in 2028.
More than 75 Greek companies are involved in Naval Group’s frigate and submarine programs for Greece, supplying parts ranging from electronic maps to pre-outfitted hull blocks and complex mechanical and electronic systems, the company said. Naval Group has committed to 25% local content on the fourth frigate. It has also won the initial in-service support contract for the Greek FDIs, which it will carry out with its Greek subsidiary, Naval Group Hellas, and local partners.
The Greek ships are part of a larger order book. Thirteen FDIs have now been ordered for three NATO navies, five for France, four for Greece and four for Sweden, and Naval Group says its Lorient yard can now deliver two of the frigates a year.

U.S. F-16s Resume Combat Air Patrols from Eareckson Air Station, Over 1,500 km from Mainland Alaska
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:56:56 UTC
18:56:56 KST

U.S. Air Force F-16 fighter jets carried out a North American defense mission from Eareckson Air Station, located on Shemya Island in the Bering Sea, more than 1,500 km from mainland Alaska.
The North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) said this in a statement.
The aircraft conducted air defense operations from the remote airbase during a deployment from October 18 to 26. On October 25, the fighter jets launched on a North American defense mission, which also involved aircraft from two other bases in Alaska and one Canadian airbase.
After deploying to Eareckson Air Station, the F-16s began carrying out missions as part of Operation NOBLEDEFENDER. The mission was subsequently continued under Operation NOBLE EAGLE, supporting efforts to protect sovereignty in the northern region.
The mission evolved into a coordinated U.S.-Canadian operation involving two F-16 Fighting Falcon fighter jets, F-35 Lightning II aircraft from Eielson Air Force Base, an E-3 Sentry airborne early warning and control aircraft from Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, and Royal Canadian Air Force CF-18 Hornet fighter jets from Cold Lake Air Base in Alberta.
Several KC-135 Stratotanker aircraft and one CC-150 Polaris provided aerial refueling, while an HC-130 Combat King II provided search-and-rescue support and personnel recovery.
Eareckson Air Station is located about 2,600 km from Eielson Air Force Base and 4,200 km from Cold Lake Air Base, highlighting the vast distances over which NORAD coordinated the participating forces.
F-16s deployed to Eareckson Air Station provided coverage over the southern part of the zone, while F-35s and additional F-16s from Eielson operated in the northwest, and Canadian CF-18s covered the northern approaches.
“The joint operation demonstrated NORAD’s ability to rapidly assemble, deploy, and coordinate a combat-ready air force to defend North America,” the command stated.
According to TWZ, regular fighter patrols at Eareckson Air Station ceased in the early 1990s. As a result, the October 2026 deployment marked a significant milestone, representing a return to combat air patrol operations at one of the westernmost U.S. military installations.
The island is also home to the AN/FPS-108 Cobra Dane radar station, located directly opposite Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula and the Kura missile test range.
The powerful phased-array radar plays a critical role in detecting ballistic missiles and tracking their trajectories.

Gallery: AI revives Estonian artist's lost 19th-century masterpiece
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:55:00 UTC
18:55:00 KST

Gallery: AI revives Estonian artist's lost 19th-century masterpiece
A reproduction of a massive long-lost painting by Estonian master Johann Köler is on view in Viljandi, brought back to life using AI and a single black-and-white photograph.
The painting, "Waking from Charmed Sleep" ("Ärkamine nõidusunest"), dates back to 1864 and measures 4.3 by 3.2 meters. Viljandi Museum exhibition curator Kristjan Mändmaa describes it as a politically charged work highlighting native Estonians' lack of land ownership under Baltic German rule.
The painting depicts a German nobleman opening a tomb and reaching for an amulet worn by an Estonian woman representing the people emerging from 700 years of serfdom. The amulet, Mändmaa explained, symbolizes Estonian land, which was largely controlled by Baltic Germans at the time.
"Köler saw this as a tremendous injustice, and this was his way of fighting against it," he added.
The work sparked a major scandal when it was first shown, drawing furious reactions and threats from the Baltic German press.
"Legend has it that the Baltic Germans somehow arranged to have the painting destroyed, which would explain why it disappeared," Mändmaa said.
Anniversary shows draw large crowds
Viljandi Museum program director Signe Susi said three major exhibitions marking the 200th anniversary of the birth of Estonia's first professional artist drew large crowds to Viljandi this year. The Kondas Center welcomed nearly 11,000 visitors, Rüki Gallery 2,500 and the Viljandi Museum itself expects more than 13,000.
Music educator and orchestra conductor Harry Illak, who also took part in events marking Köler's 190th, said his interest in the artist's life and work had only grown since.
"After all these visits, my understanding of Köler and his work has changed considerably from what it was ten years ago," he added.
The AI-restored reproduction of "Waking from Charmed Sleep" remains on view at the Viljandi Museum on Sunday.

A US federal judge permanently dismissed President Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal over its reporting on an alleged sexually suggestive birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein bearing Trump’s name, media reports said Saturday.
US District Judge Darrin P. Gayles ruled that Trump failed to plausibly demonstrate that the newspaper acted with “actual malice” when publishing the story, according to CNN.
The judge rejected Trump’s argument that the newspaper should have withheld publication after he denied writing the letter, saying such a requirement would violate the First Amendment.
“Were that the law, any time a public figure or his team denies an accusation, journalists would be immediately blocked from publishing negative or contradictory press,” Gayles wrote.
The judge previously dismissed the lawsuit in April, allowing Trump to file an amended complaint.
However, Gayles found that the revised complaint failed to address the legal deficiencies and dismissed the case with prejudice, preventing it from being refiled in the same court.
“We’re pleased with the court’s decision,” a spokesperson for Dow Jones, the newspaper’s parent company, said.
Trump’s legal team indicated plans to appeal the ruling.
The president originally filed the $20 billion lawsuit in July 2025 against the newspaper, its parent companies, Rupert Murdoch and two reporters. The amended lawsuit sought at least $10 billion in damages.
Trump has denied writing the letter and accused the newspaper of knowingly publishing false information.

Fire Point confirmed the strike on the Kstovo Refinery, one of Russia’s largest oil refineries

Fire Point confirmed the strike on the Kstovo Refinery, one of Russia’s largest oil refineries
Kyiv • UNN
A fire broke out at the NORSI refinery in Kstovo after a drone attack. The exact extent of the damage and the location of the strike are being determined.
During the night of November 1, the Defense Forces struck the Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez oil refinery in the city of Kstovo, Nizhny Novgorod region—one of Russia’s largest refineries. This was reported on its Telegram channel by the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, the manufacturer of FP-1 long-range attack drones, UNN writes.
Details
The company published the post on Sunday morning, playing on the Halloween phrase "trick or treat."
Kstovo Oil Refinery, trick or treat!
Fire Point had previously reported that the Defense Forces used FP-1 drones in earlier strikes on the Kstovo refinery, including on August 26.
Local residents reported a series of explosions in Kstovo during the night, after which a fire broke out on the plant’s premises—video footage appeared on social media at around 4 a.m. According to a preliminary assessment by the Exilenova+ monitoring channel, the fire may have started in the area of the AVT-5 and AVT-6 primary oil-refining units, the visbreaking unit for fuel oil, or the 35/11-600 unit. The exact strike location and extent of the damage have not yet been established.
Nizhny Novgorod Region Governor Gleb Nikitin said that the region had come under a "massive drone attack" during the night. According to him, an industrial facility in Kstovo District sustained significant damage.
What is known about the Kstovo refinery
"Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez" (NORSI) is Russia’s fourth-largest refinery by processing volume. Its designed capacity is approximately 17 million tonnes of oil per year, or about 340,000 barrels per day; according to the Special Operations Forces, the plant accounts for up to 11% of gasoline production in the Russian Federation. The facility produces gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel, fuel oil, bitumen, and lubricants, and is one of the main fuel suppliers to the Moscow region. According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the plant is involved in meeting the needs of the Russian army.
Additionally
In 2026, the Kstovo refinery has already been attacked more than once. The Defense Forces struck it on May 18 and 20—after which, according to Reuters, the plant shut down its primary refining unit, which accounts for more than half of its capacity. On July 2, the General Staff confirmed that the plant had been struck, preliminarily identifying the AVT-6 unit; as UNN reported, weapons manufactured by Fire Point were used at the time. On August 26, FP-1 drones struck the refinery, and on September 4, the General Staff confirmed that the facility had ceased operations.
A few days ago, Fire Point also reported that FP-1 drones had struck the Novokuibyshevsk refinery in Russia’s Samara region, whose designed capacity is approximately 8.8 million tonnes of oil per year.
We remind you
In September, following strikes by the Defense Forces, the operations of LUKOIL-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez LLC and NOVATEK-Ust-Luga in Russia were halted.

Ticino opens bridge lost in deadly storm
Authorities have opened a new bridge in Visletto, in Ticino’s Maggia Valley, nearly two years after a devastating storm swept away the original structure, restoring a permanent road link to the upper valley.
The bridge is due to open to motor traffic from 4:30 pm on October 31, canton Ticino’s department of spatial planning said. Its opening marks “a decisive step towards the permanent restoration of the road link with the upper Maggia Valley”, according to a press release.
The new bridge has been built slightly further upstream than the previous one in order to improve its protection against erosion. Over 150 metres long, it features a reinforced concrete deck and also houses the necessary infrastructure for water supply, wastewater disposal, electricity and telecommunications.
The construction of the bridge cost CHF10.5 million ($12.7 millon), a sum covered in full by the canton. Its opening marks an important stage in the reconstruction, but “does not bring the region’s restoration programme to a close”, the authorities stressed.
More
Why Alpine debris flows are becoming more intense and unpredictable
Planned works include flood protection measures, facilities for pedestrians and cyclists, and the redevelopment of the hamlet of Visletto. The aim is to sustainably improve safety and infrastructure in this part of the valley.
The old Visletto bridge was swept away by the River Maggia during the night of 29–30 June 2024, following severe storms. Several side valleys were temporarily cut off from the road network at the time.
The storms claimed seven lives in the region. One person is still missing.

Japan’s Economic Diplomacy: A Compass in a Divided World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:52:00 UTC
18:52:00 KST

During the second term of U.S. President Donald Trump, protectionist measures – including unilateral trade actions and reciprocal tariffs – have re-emerged as central pillars of U.S. foreign policy. With this fundamental structure shift in trade policy of the United States, once the preeminent champion of open markets, Japan has arrived at a critical strategic juncture. Tokyo must bolster its economic “strategic autonomy” and diversify its international economic partnerships, even as it maintains its core alliance with Washington.
To be clear, the foundational importance of the U.S.-Japan alliance remains unaltered. Strategic diversification does not imply distancing Tokyo from Washington. Rather, expanding Japan’s economic options and building national resilience alongside this indispensable alliance ultimately fortifies bilateral stability. Simultaneously, Japan must differentiate itself from Washington’s protectionist drift by steadfastly anchoring an international economic order based on predictable, rules-based trade.
Beijing views these shifts in U.S. policy as an opening, positioning itself as a defender of globalization while expanding ties across the Global South. The high-profile U.S.-China summit in late 2026 illustrated this shifting dynamic: while the spectacle drew international headlines, the meeting produced minimal structural adjustments in their underlying economic rivalry, leaving regional partners navigating persistent uncertainty.
In this volatile environment, Japan’s imperative is not to compete with China for regional hegemony. Instead, Tokyo should collaborate with a broad coalition (which includes the European Union, the United Kingdom, Australia, and key Indo-Pacific partners) to co-create an international economic climate that remains open, rules-bound, and inclusive.
CPTPP and the European Connection
The symbolic inflection point of America’s retreat from multilateral trade leadership occurred in 2017 with its withdrawal from the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP). Taking the helm among remaining signatories, Japan led the negotiations that brought the 11-nation Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) into force in 2018. The CPTPP moved beyond conventional tariff elimination, introducing high-standard 21st-century discipline on digital commerce, state-owned enterprises, intellectual property, and service liberalization.
With the formal accession of the United Kingdom, the CPTPP now encompasses roughly 15 percent of global GDP. As additional economies seek entry, upholding the agreement’s rigorous standards, particularly regarding non-market policies and state subsidies, remains vital to preserving the integrity of both the accord and the broader multilateral system.
Concurrently, the institutional architecture underpinning Japan-EU ties has seen significant development. Building on the 2019 Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), the comprehensive Strategic Partnership Agreement (SPA) is now in effect, consolidating broad cooperation rooted in shared norms. Meanwhile, following Brexit, the U.S.-UK CPTPP connection and bilateral EPAs have established a strategic alignment linking Europe and the Indo-Pacific.
This momentum reached a new milestone at the Japan-EU Summit, where both sides established the Japan-EU Competitiveness Alliance. Designed to enhance mutual resilience, this framework deepens cooperation in supply chain security, critical minerals, semiconductors, and emerging technologies, while reinforcing joint leadership to revitalize the World Trade Organization (WTO).
Constructing “Open, Predictable, and Resilient Trade”
A critical conceptual task is to refrain from casting open trade and economic security as mutually exclusive. In today’s interconnected yet fragmented economy, maintaining open markets while mitigating single-source dependencies and fortifying supply chains are complementary objectives. What Japan must advocate is not a simple return to pre-crisis free trade, but the construction of “Open, Predictable, and Resilient Trade.”
While the post-World War II economic architecture developed under American leadership, Washington’s stepping back from its traditional role is accelerating multipolarity and fragmentation. In this emerging landscape, Japan occupies a unique position.
However, Tokyo should not seek to impose its own template. Japan’s principal asset lies in its capacity to connect diverse nations across varying developmental stages, identify overlapping strategic interests, and build practical, durable coalitions.
This approach is indispensable in engaging the Global South. Rigidly demanding compliance with external standards without addressing local realities will not cultivate lasting support for a rules-based order. What is required is a pragmatic strategy that respects national sovereignty, supports tangible development needs, and delivers shared economic benefits.
By sustaining its vital alliance with the United States and preserving pragmatic economic ties with China, while simultaneously deepening multi-layered partnerships across Europe, Asia, and emerging economies, Japan can chart a stable path forward. This multi-layered diplomatic network offers a compelling alternative to stark binary choices, providing a clear compass for navigating an increasingly fractured global economy.

Why Qatar is buying American LNG while expanding its own exports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:50:13 UTC
18:50:13 KST

Qatar is buying American liquefied natural gas while spending billions to expand its own export capacity. That apparent contradiction offers a way to understand Doha’s diplomacy during the Persian Gulf crisis. Buying gas abroad gives QatarEnergy something to sell when tankers cannot leave Ras Laffan. It does far less for a customer whose contract specifies a Qatari loading terminal. My article examines what a peace agreement could restore within a week, what will take engineers years to rebuild, and why the decisions that Asian and European buyers make in the meantime could prove more consequential for Qatar than the immediate loss of revenue.
Qatar’s next LNG cargo depends on Hormuz. So does its next expansion.
In October, Qatar’s energy minister, Saad Sherida al-Kaabi, offered two very different answers to the question of how long his country’s gas industry would take to recover. If Washington and Tehran reached a peace agreement and enough tankers were available, QatarEnergy could restart its undamaged liquefied natural gas facilities within a week. Repairing the two production lines struck by Iranian missiles in March would take about three years. For a government trying to limit its losses in the Persian Gulf crisis, those estimates help explain where diplomacy can make an immediate difference and where even a durable settlement would leave difficult work ahead.
For Qatar’s customers, recovery has a more practical meaning. A utility needs to know whether a cargo will arrive in time to meet demand and, if it will not, when to buy a replacement. A government in Doha weighing the cost of another month of conflict has to consider what happens when that same utility negotiates its next supply contract.
The immediate loss is the revenue from a shipment that never leaves port. The longer-term risk is that a customer still willing to buy Qatari gas decides to buy less of it.
What the strikes cost Qatar
Follow a cargo back from the Strait of Hormuz and the geography of Qatar’s vulnerability comes into focus. The gas comes from the North Field, the offshore reservoir Qatar shares with Iran, where it is known as South Pars. On the Qatari side, it is brought ashore at Ras Laffan, processed and cooled into liquid form for shipment. Concentrating those operations in one industrial city helped Qatar build an export industry on an extraordinary scale. It also means that buyers thousands of miles apart depend on the same facilities and the same maritime passage for their deliveries.
The Iranian missile strikes of 18th and 19th March damaged two liquefaction units at Ras Laffan, Trains 4 and 6. Together, they could produce 12.8 million tonnes of LNG a year, about 17 percent of Qatar’s prewar export capacity.
QatarEnergy estimated in March that the damage could cost roughly $20 billion in annual revenue. The effects extended beyond LNG. Production of condensate and liquefied petroleum gas also suffered, and the strikes damaged the Pearl gas-to-liquids plant that QatarEnergy operates with Shell. A single episode disrupted several businesses that draw on the same industrial complex.
By June, the cost of the wider conflict was visible in QatarEnergy’s accounts. First-half net profit fell to 15 billion Qatari riyals from 48 billion a year earlier, a decline of 69 percent. Revenue fell 35 percent. Those figures measure what happened across the company during the first six months of 2026. The $20 billion figure measures something different: QatarEnergy’s estimate of annual revenue at risk from the damage. The broader national toll is harder to isolate, although the IMF projected an 8.6 percent contraction in Qatar’s real GDP for 2026.
A cable across contested waters: The great sea interconnector’s promise and risks
A new plant can be ready before its customers can receive the gas
One of the clearest illustrations of Doha’s predicament stands at Ras Laffan itself. In early October, people familiar with the North Field East expansion told Reuters that its first new liquefaction train could be technically ready in November. Later that month, al-Kaabi said he expected it to start up in the first quarter of 2027, with production dependent on a US-Iran peace agreement. The distinction matters for a project of this size. Engineers can finish their work, suppliers can deliver the equipment and the plant can pass its tests while the date of its first commercial shipment remains beyond their control.
Qatar has decided to keep building. Before the war, Ras Laffan had annual LNG capacity of about 77 million tonnes. The North Field East, South and West projects are intended to lift that figure to 142 million tonnes. Al-Kaabi said in October that all contracts had been awarded and none of the announced projects had been cancelled. The first new train could help replace some lost output once shipping conditions allow. The later phases carry a larger commercial ambition. Qatar expects buyers to absorb substantially more of its gas for decades, even as those buyers reassess how much of their supply they want moving through Hormuz.
Consider the decision facing a utility that has bought Qatari LNG for years. It may value the relationship, expect the damage to be repaired and still choose a different supplier for its next tranche of gas. A second contract with another exporter gives it access to a different loading port when passage through the Gulf becomes difficult. Qatar could therefore retain a longstanding customer while losing part of that customer’s future business. This is a quieter risk than an outright cancellation. It would show up gradually, in the volumes buyers commit to as each new Qatari train comes onstream.
Why a leading gas exporter is buying American LNG
QatarEnergy’s response suggests that its own traders understand the value of a second loading port. In October, al-Kaabi confirmed that the company was buying long-term LNG supplies from the United States and other producers.
If a future disruption prevents Qatari tankers from sailing just as international prices rise, QatarEnergy could still earn money selling cargoes loaded elsewhere. For its trading business, the attraction is straightforward.
A shipment already available outside the Gulf becomes especially valuable precisely when gas at Ras Laffan is hardest to bring to market.
The limits of that strategy are written into QatarEnergy’s contracts. Al-Kaabi explained that its long-term customer agreements specify the terminal where a cargo must be loaded and the destination where it must be delivered. Under those terms, QatarEnergy cannot simply send an American cargo to fulfil an obligation tied to Ras Laffan. That distinction is easy to overlook when gas is discussed as a globally traded commodity. For the trading desk, access to American supply creates an opportunity to recover some income. For a buyer awaiting delivery under a Qatari contract, the immediate question remains when its scheduled shipment can sail.
What Doha can gain from diplomacy
Qatar’s relationship with Iran gives that question a particular urgency. The two countries draw gas from opposite sides of the same reservoir, and Iran sits alongside the passage Qatar needs to reach its customers. Even after the March strikes, Doha kept a channel open. Al-Kaabi said in October that he had met Iran’s acting petroleum minister twice in recent weeks to discuss possible oil and gas cooperation after the war. For Qatar, there is a practical reason to hold those conversations while the political outcome remains uncertain. Its next phase of gas development will unfold alongside Iran, whatever course relations take after the fighting.
A settlement would give Doha something tangible almost immediately. With safe passage and ships available, the undamaged facilities could bring production back to roughly 83 percent of its prewar level while repairs continue. Customers could begin planning around deliveries again. The first North Field East train would have a clearer route to market. The harder judgment belongs to the utility deciding where to buy its gas for the next twenty years. What will matter to that buyer is whether cargoes keep arriving after the first tanker makes it through. Qatar has good reason to pursue an agreement that outlasts the immediate pressure to reopen the strait.

Mass riots, looting in Germany mar nationwide Gen-Z protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:50:00 UTC
18:50:00 KST

Nationwide youth-led protests in Germany were marred by rioting, looting and attacks on police Saturday as largely peaceful daytime demonstrations gave way to serious unrest in Frankfurt and Cologne that evening.
Rioters smashed shop windows, looted stores, and threw Molotov cocktails at police in central Frankfurt. In Cologne, attackers threw bottles and bicycles at officers near the city's famous cathedral.
Politicians and police blamed the violence on groups of masked, radical left-wing activists.
Unrest followed demonstrations by tens of thousands of young Germans demanding better schools, relief from rising living costs, and greater social justice. Protesters also vented anger at conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Many protests were peaceful.
Participants carried placards with slogans including "Our future is not for sale," "System change, not climate change," "Education, not bombs," and "Eat the rich."
The "Gen Z regelt" (Gen Z Takes Charge) initiative had expected demonstrations in more than 30 German cities, drawing inspiration from weeks of large-scale youth demonstrations in France and elsewhere in Europe. Despite strong interest on social media and widespread media coverage, turnout was more modest than anticipated.
Before the evening's chaos, organizers hailed the protests as a success, reporting more than 100,000 participants nationwide in major cities and smaller centers like Erfurt, Münster, Nuremberg and Karlsruhe.
Nationwide police figures were unavailable, though individual cities released their own turnout tallies.
Frankfurt experienced some of the worst scenes. Rioters smashed shop windows and broke into stores to steal trainers and other goods, dpa journalists observed.
Rioters attacked a specialist firearms shop late Saturday. Police arrested several people and recovered two weapons from the store. Officials did not specify the type of weapons.
Rioters also set trash bins on fire, tore down street signs and smashed shop windows with signs and other objects.
Police reported Molotov cocktails were thrown at officers as violent clashes continued downtown.
At about 10 p.m., officers sealed off a section of the Zeil, one of Germany's busiest shopping streets and urged people to avoid the area.
Authorities deployed special police units (SEK) as unrest continued late into the night. Authorities said more than 1,000 security personnel deployed downtown shortly before midnight. Police reported about 30 people taken into custody.
Earlier, up to 8,000 people joined a largely peaceful demonstration, police said, while organizers estimated turnout at about 9,000.
The protests began in the afternoon on the banks of the Main river near the European Central Bank. The procession moved through central Frankfurt for several kilometers over several hours. Organizers urged participants to remain peaceful.
However, the situation deteriorated hours later when police came under repeated attack with stones, bottles, and firecrackers.
Officers used water cannons and broke up the demonstration in the early evening, but violent groups remained active downtown after many peaceful protesters left.
Hesse state Interior Minister Roman Poseck said several police officers were injured, adding that one officer may have suffered more serious injuries.
Poseck said about 100 suspected left-wing extremists were responsible for the evening violence.
In Cologne, about 200 people, including some rioters, were involved in disturbances around the city's cathedral, next to the main railway station.
Attackers threw bottles and bicycles at police officers during the unrest. One person was injured.
Five people were detained, police said.
In a nearby side street, someone smashed a window with a thrown electric scooter.
After repeated clashes, police dispersed the large crowd outside the cathedral to deescalate the situation. However, smaller groups continued moving downtown, with occasional fireworks set off.
A police spokeswoman said the later incidents appeared linked more to Halloween celebrations than to the earlier youth protests.
Disturbances were also reported in other cities.
In Berlin, police broke up an evening demonstration after officers were attacked with stones and protesters set off fireworks. Police said 27 officers suffered minor injuries and up to 56 demonstrators were temporarily detained.
About 700 people initially gathered at Rosenthaler Platz downtown for a march under the slogan "Gen Z Has Had Enough!" toward Prenzlauer Berg. The crowd grew to as many as 3,500 participants, police said.
Police said the atmosphere was tense from the outset, with many participants dressed in black and wearing masks. Groups on the political left organized the march, and pro-Palestinian activists also took part.
After police ended the demonstration early in coordination with organizers, smaller groups continued moving through nearby streets.
"It's now like a game of cat and mouse," police spokesperson Julia Scholz said. The situation calmed by about 8 p.m.
The evening march was separate from the main "Gen Z regelt" demonstration, where up to 5,000 people gathered peacefully at the Brandenburg Gate earlier in the day.
In Hamburg, a largely peaceful demonstration of about 6,700 people was followed by disturbances near the main railway station.
People dressed in black, some with covered faces, set off fireworks, tore down plastic construction barriers, and set them on fire. Police used water cannons to extinguish the flames and pepper spray to disperse the crowd.
In Bremen, where about 2,800 people demonstrated, isolated incidents included officers being punched and kicked, and at least one trash container set alight.

Man, 84, walks 6 km to escape Kherson
An 84-year-old man from Kherson has walked almost 6 km (nearly 4 miles) to leave the city, where he had been living in isolation for six months because of Russian attacks.
Source: Kherson City Military Administration
Details: Vasyl Zaichenko had lived in Kherson for 60 years. He and his wife built a family home, planted an orchard and grew flowers on their plot of land. But for almost the past six months Vasyl had been living in near-total isolation, existing on humanitarian aid delivered to him by drones.
"The attacks became intense, and there was no heating. In winter the temperature was around +8°C. Everyone was evacuated, but I chose to stay. I lived on what I grew in the garden," Vasyl said.
When he finally decided to evacuate, he had to walk to reach a safer area. He covered about 6 km in an hour and a half, taking only a torch and a phone charger with him.
Volunteers met Vasyl, and his daughter and grandson picked him up from a transit centre. He will now live with his family in Nikopol, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast.
Vasyl will celebrate his 85th birthday on 22 November. He says his greatest wish is for victory and to return home.
"This story once again shows how important it is not to delay evacuation. We urge people living in dangerous areas of Kherson to leave in good time while they still can," the city administration stressed.

NATO turns 5G towers into sensors in Baltic battlefield experiment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:48:48 UTC
18:48:48 KST

- NATO linked a Maven system to a national system in hours using agentic AI and ran a Lithuania-to-Latvia counter-drone engagement during DiBaX 2026.
- The Oct. 19-30 experiment in Latvia also tested military use of commercial 5G networks, jam-resistant communications and 5G-based object detection.
NATO linked a Maven targeting system to a national military system in a matter of hours using agentic artificial intelligence and ran a cross-border counter-drone engagement during a two-week experiment in Latvia, the alliance’s top transformation commander said on Oct. 30.
Adm. Pierre Vandier, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, described the results at Ādaži Military Base near Riga at the close of the Digital Backbone Experimentation, known as DiBaX 2026, which ran from Oct. 19 to 30. He said some tests failed along the way and that the alliance had deliberately accepted that risk.
“We have connected systems that were never designed to communicate with each other, using artificial intelligence to overcome interoperability barriers. It’s the first time that we have, for example, a Maven system that is speaking to a national system, and that has been fixed in hours with Agentic AI,” said Vandier.
NATO bought its own version of Palantir’s AI-enabled Maven Smart System in 2025 to help commanders pull together intelligence and speed up decisions, and has been rolling it out across its headquarters. Vandier did not say which country’s system Maven was connected to. Agentic AI refers to software that can carry out multistep tasks on its own, in this case working out how two systems exchange data.
The counter-drone test crossed a national border. A drone took off in Lithuania, flew into Latvia and was engaged there by a counter-drone system, Vandier said. It was one of several trials under NATO’s Layered Counter-UAS Initiative, which looks at how sensors and weapons from different countries and companies can work together as one layered defense against drones.
“Even if it didn’t work this morning, it has been done this week. So we had a drone taking off from Lithuania, arriving here and being engaged by a counter system,” said Vandier.
DiBaX itself tested three ways to keep NATO forces connected. In the first, organizers set up a private slice of a host country’s commercial 5G network, reserved and secured for military use, so arriving NATO forces could have command and data links from their first day before their own infrastructure arrived. The second tested automatic switching between communication paths when one is jammed, including radio across different frequencies, satellite links such as 5G direct-to-device, and troposcatter, which bounces radio signals off the lower atmosphere to reach beyond the horizon. The third used ordinary 5G cell towers as passive sensors to detect objects moving through their coverage, particularly in cities with dense tower networks. Vandier said a team of medics in the field also sent patient biodata over the network to doctors in the United States.
The scenarios were built around grey-zone incidents below the threshold of NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense clause, such as drone incursions and damage to undersea cables in the Baltic Sea. A third track, Next Generation Targeting, tested AI-enabled decision support to shorten the time between collecting information and acting on it, and Vandier said the targeting process ran noticeably faster by the end of the week than at the start.
“For us, as a NATO member of the Alliance Eastern Flank here in Latvia, we cannot afford to treat technological innovation and adaptation as a distant objective for us,” said Lt. Gen. Kaspars Pudāns, commander of the Latvian National Armed Forces.
Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, the United States, Canada, Finland and other allies took part, along with NATO bodies including the DIANA innovation accelerator and the NATO Communications and Information Agency. More than 60 technology companies joined, among them Ericsson, Nokia, Thales and Portuguese drone maker TEKEVER, with Latvian telecom company LMT acting as technical integrator. This was the fifth year in a row the experiment has been held in Latvia.
The event closed with NATO FUSE on Oct. 29 and 30, which included live field demonstrations. NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, visited Latvia on Oct. 30 and met President Edgars Rinkēvičs. European Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis used the event to announce two pilot European Drone Technology Hubs, one in Latvia and one in the Netherlands, to open in 2027 and speed up development and testing of drone and counter-drone technology in cooperation with NATO.
“The next challenge, and it’s the most difficult, is adoption,” said Vandier.

01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
German police arrested more than 200 people on Saturday night after violent clashes erupted in several cities following largely peaceful Generation Z demonstrations demanding better education funding and social policies.
The unrest broke out in Hamburg, Frankfurt and Berlin after radical groups staged smaller demonstrations, erecting barricades and clashing with police.
The main daytime protests, organized by the Gen Z Regelt initiative in more than 30 cities, drew tens of thousands of young people demanding increased education funding, relief from rising living costs and opposition to plans to revive compulsory military service.
After dark, radical groups staged smaller demonstrations in other parts of the cities, erecting barricades as the situation escalated once police moved to contain them.
Some activists threw stones, bottles and firecrackers at officers, who responded with water cannons and special units in several locations.
 
- Weapons stolen during Frankfurt unrest
In Frankfurt, masked groups not involved in the main Gen Z demonstrations smashed shop windows and looted businesses, including a gun store.
Police said the groups broke the store's windows and stole at least two firearms before officers intervened.
One suspect was arrested, and the stolen weapons were recovered, according to police.
A police vehicle was also damaged, with its windows smashed and tires punctured.
Authorities reported more than 30 provisional arrests and extensive property damage as the unrest continued into early Sunday.
 
- 120 detained, 11 officers injured in Hamburg
In Hamburg, violence erupted after the main demonstration ended around 5 pm local time Saturday, police said.
Authorities took 120 people into custody after black-clad and partially masked protesters erected burning barricades near the central bus station.
The groups threw stones, bottles and pyrotechnics at police officers, injuring 11, according to police.
Smaller fires and disturbances continued overnight in the city's eastern districts.
 
- 56 detained in Berlin clashes
Police in Berlin temporarily detained up to 56 people during an evening demonstration in the Mitte district, separate from the earlier peaceful gathering at the Brandenburg Gate.
Police reported that 27 officers sustained minor injuries as protesters threw stones, bottles, eggs and firecrackers.
Demonstrators also blocked a tram, prompting authorities to halt the march before it reached its planned destination.
In Cologne, police detained at least five people after smaller groups clashed with officers near the city's cathedral, throwing bottles and pyrotechnics.
Cologne Police Chief Johannes Hermanns condemned the violence, saying extremists had disrupted peaceful demonstrations.
"It is sad that young people who wanted to demonstrate peacefully for their future were infiltrated by extremists who had nothing but violence in mind," Hermanns said.
He thanked participants who remained peaceful and distanced themselves from the violence.
By early Sunday, the situation had largely calmed across the affected cities, while police continued investigating the incidents and assessing property damage.

Zelensky Eyes Missile Loans Against 500 US Patriot Deal

President Volodymyr Zelensky plans to negotiate with individual international partners to secure an emergency temporary transfer of 10 to 30 air defense missiles from their stockpiles, with Kyiv guaranteeing repayment from a newly approved US purchase package of 500 interceptors.
Speaking to Ukrainian media during a press briefing in Istanbul on Saturday, Oct. 31, the head of state outlined a queue-swapping mechanism designed to bridge an acute munitions deficit ahead of winter, as deliveries under the American procurement program face multi-year production delays.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Several times during this war, during various dialogues, we executed an operation where you swap queues,” Zelensky explained.
“I will try to do this with certain partners, where against that 500-missile package we could take 10, 20, 30 missiles somewhere, sign appropriate guarantees and contracts stipulating that we will later return them from that American package – with some interest, or perhaps without interest.”
Zelensky noted that such bilateral borrowing arrangements would allow Ukrainian air defense batteries to receive interceptors directly from partner arsenals long before factory-fresh munitions roll off American assembly lines.
Multi-year US delays
The president explained that deliveries under the US proposal are deferred by several years due to industrial manufacturing cycles and Washington’s reluctance to draw down directly from its own strategic military reserves.
Zelensky Arrives in Turkey for Talks With Erdogan on Black Sea Safety
Zelensky emphasized that the sluggish delivery pace cannot provide adequate protection for Ukrainian civilians as Russian standoff bombardments escalate, noting that significant volumes of Western air defense packages have simultaneously been directed toward the Middle East.
“We are grateful to the United States of America. This is a very good proposal. Naturally, money must be gathered for this proposal. I am confident that we will find the financing, thanks above all to our European partners,” Zelensky stated.
The president added that Ukraine will continue aggressively pursuing surface-to-air interceptors through bilateral agreements with European and other allied nations, underscoring that relying solely on American deliveries is insufficient to safeguard national airspace.
Post-2030 timeline
Zelensky’s comments follow the Trump administration’s formal authorization on Friday, Oct. 30, of a possible Foreign Military Sale to Ukraine encompassing 500 Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (PAC-3 MSE) interceptor missiles, spare parts, and support equipment at an estimated cost of $2.1 billion.
However, diplomatic sources cited by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty correspondent Alex Raufoglu revealed that the contracted munitions represent newly manufactured hardware rather than drawdowns from existing American military inventories, with deliveries not expected until after 2030.
“As sources inform me, these are new missiles, with deliveries not expected until after 2030,” Raufoglu reported. “This does virtually nothing to resolve the acute deficit of interceptors in Ukraine ahead of winter.”
Raufoglu noted that bilateral discussions have not yet secured an agreement for joint coproduction of the interceptors within Ukraine, with the Pentagon still engaged in an extended review regarding whether to grant Kyiv domestic manufacturing licenses.
Zelensky initially voiced frustration with the extended timetable late Friday, pointing out that deliveries would only begin in several years and appealing to American and European partners to identify immediate solutions for the impending winter heating season.
Pre-winter infrastructure defense and monthly interceptor needs
The drive to secure immediate missile loans comes amid an intensifying Russian air campaign against Ukraine’s civil life-support networks.
Ukrainian government figures indicate that during the final two weeks of October alone, Russian tactical and strategic forces executed more than 30 coordinated strikes against critical electricity generation and transmission infrastructure.
Zelensky previously stated that Kyiv requires an emergency winter allocation of 100 PAC-3 interceptors per month to establish a reliable defensive shield against Russian ballistic barrages.
Over the preceding 90 days, Ukraine received only 24 Patriot interceptors from the US, despite facing salvos that included more than 20 ballistic missiles fired in a single day on Oct. 22.
The head of state stressed that securing 10 to 30 missiles in the near term from partner inventories would provide critical localized reinforcement for batteries shielding high-density urban areas and regional power grids from catastrophic winter blackouts while multi-year procurement contracts proceed through standard defense-industrial channels.

Bulgaria votes in presidential runoff after tight first round

SOFIA, Nov 1 (Reuters) - Bulgarians went to the polls on Sunday to elect a president after a tight race between the two leading candidates failed to produce an outright winner in last weekend’s first round vote for the largely ceremonial role.
Incumbent president, Iliana Iotova, 61, led over ex-caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, but fell short of the 50% threshold in the first round race of 27 candidates that saw a record-low turnout.
Exit polls will be published after voting ends at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT), with a result likely on Monday as the ballot papers are counted.
The presidential vote comes against the backdrop of a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast in the past month, which have sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine.
About two dozen seafarers are feared dead and the strikes have prompted the government to seek allied assistance to bolster maritime security. On Wednesday a Greek container ship sank after being hit by sea drones.
Both leading presidential candidates have condemned the attacks. Prime Minister Rumen Radev, who backs Iotova, said the strikes’ outcome “benefits the Russian Federation”. They have both called for a diplomatic end to the war.
A victory for Iotova would make her Bulgaria’s first elected female president. She became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter and win a parliamentary race on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine. He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
A host of right-leaning political figures, among them ex-premier Boiko Borisov, have expressed support for Gyurov.
(Reporting by Alex Lefkowitz;Editing by Alison Williams)

China’s Communist Party tightens oversight of officials
Italy
Unknown Publisher

10:45:06 CET
18:45:06 KST

BEIJING, Nov 1 (Reuters) - China’s ruling Communist Party put the demand for loyalty front and centre in an official resolution on toughening internal discipline, and vowed to keep waging its high-pressure anti-corruption campaign to cleanse the party of “impurities and viruses”.
The resolution, adopted during a key party leadership gathering this week and previewed in a shorter communique on Thursday, stressed the need to intensify efforts to instil loyalty to the party within its ranks, vet and promote officials based on their “party spirit” assessed through their day-to-day work, personal conduct and remarks, social contacts and family values, and carry forward its “self-revolution”.
“The party’s ranks are sound overall, but problems of ideological impurity, organisational impurity, and impure work style have not yet been fundamentally resolved,” according to the resolution released by the state-run Xinhua news agency on Sunday.
The detailed document provided an updated framework for the party’s more than decade-long discipline and anti-graft drive, which has ensnared millions within the country’s vast bureaucracy.
It came roughly a year ahead of a leadership reshuffle when its leader, President Xi Jinping, is expected to secure another five-year term.
The party leadership called for closer, career-long oversight of cadres, including tighter checks on officials’ personal disclosures and investigations where family assets or spending appear out of line with legitimate income.
It also called for routine scrutiny of the business activities of officials’ family members.
The anti-corruption drive would take aim at hidden and tech-enabled graft, including proxy shareholdings, and the use of cryptocurrencies, blockchain and cross-border funds to facilitate corruption, the document showed.
Although the party drew attention to collective leadership and said party organisations must not require subordinates at successive levels to uphold the “personal authority” of those ultimately in charge, the provision appeared directed at curbing personalised rule in lower-level party and government bodies, rather than limiting the already consolidated authority within the central leadership.
The document called on party members to resolutely safeguard Xi’s status as the party’s “core” and to remain fully aligned with the top leadership “in thought, politics and action”.
“Only by advancing full and rigorous party self-governance with unwavering persistence, and continually removing the viruses that corrode the party’s healthy body, can the party be ensured never to lose its nature, conviction and character, and can the red country be passed down from generation to generation,” Xi said in a speech explaining the resolution.

====================================================================================================

Zac Brettler posed as an oligarch's son. Then he plunged to his death in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:44:36 UTC
18:44:36 KST

A few weeks after the coronavirus pandemic began in the spring of 2020, a podcast premiered with a question almost nobody had thought to ask: Had the CIA secretly written "Wind of Change," the enormous hit by German rock band Scorpions, as part of a psychological warfare operation intended to accelerate the collapse of the Soviet regime? Released in 1990, shortly after the fall of the Berlin Wall, the song became an unofficial anthem of the end of the Cold War. The idea that the CIA could have produced such a catchy ballad, complete with its unforgettable whistle, sounded almost too ridiculous to qualify as a conspiracy theory. Yet Wind of Change became one of 2020's most acclaimed podcasts and attracted millions of listeners.
Part of its success came from the timing, with much of the world stuck at home during the pandemic. But there was another reason: When investigative journalist Patrick Radden Keefe takes on a mystery, people pay attention. He traveled around the world, interviewed dozens of people and ultimately concluded that while the CIA might know how to bring down governments, writing irresistible pop songs was probably beyond its capabilities.
Six years later, Keefe is sitting in a small cafe in Manhattan's West Village, exhausted by the jet lag that comes with traveling around the world. In 2020, he was already a respected American journalist and author. By 2026, he has become a genuine star in a profession that has relatively few stars left. He has written for The New Yorker for more than 20 years, but over the past decade has reached audiences far beyond the magazine's traditional readership, the kind willing to spend an afternoon reading a 7,000-word article.
Keefe has carved out an almost unique literary niche: exhaustively researched investigative journalism, built entirely on real events and verified facts, that reads like a gripping thriller. His books do more than tell extraordinary true stories. They expose larger truths about power, wealth and society. In at least one case, his reporting helped change the course of events in the United States.
Keefe recalls an encounter on the New York subway some 12 to 15 years ago, when he spotted a woman pulling a copy of The New Yorker from her bag. She began flipping through it until she reached an article he had written. Standing about 10 feet away, he watched excitedly as she started reading and considered introducing himself. But just as he worked up the courage, she finished the first paragraph and turned to the next article. "I'm haunted by that woman," he says. "If I can get you into that first paragraph, I never want to let go of you."
More recently, someone told him that although he loved The New Yorker and had subscribed for years, he now fed 10,000-word articles into ChatGPT and requested 4,000-word summaries. Keefe was unimpressed. "I told him, don't read my stuff. It's not for you," he recalls. "It's not supposed to be boiled down to nuggets. Like, you read it for pleasure." For him, the experience of reading is not simply about extracting information as efficiently as possible.
Perhaps surprisingly, Keefe says he finds the writing process relatively easy, even when the finished result is a 400-page book. He never begins until he has completed his reporting and developed a detailed outline, allowing him to write quickly before revising extensively. "I like velocity when I'm writing because I feel like it goes on the page," he explains. "The faster I write it, the faster you're going to read it." He compares the process to a chef preparing every ingredient before cooking. The extensive preparation allows the final dish to come together relatively quickly.
The books that changed everything
Keefe, 50, grew up in Boston and began reading The New Yorker in high school, an unusual interest for a teenager. He initially imagined becoming a fiction writer but decided he was not particularly good at it. By his third year at Columbia University, he was already pitching ideas to the magazine. One of his professors, historian Simon Schama, was writing for The New Yorker at the time and became something of a mentor. "I thought he was the coolest," Keefe recalls. "That's what I wanted to do."
He soon discovered that even The New Yorker's generous word counts could not always accommodate the stories he wanted to tell. His first two books explored electronic surveillance networks and the criminal underworld of New York's Chinatown. Both largely went unnoticed, and nearly another decade passed before he tried again.
In 2018, Keefe published Say Nothing, an investigation into the 1972 abduction and murder of Jean McConville, a mother of 10, in Northern Ireland. From that killing, he constructed one of the most compelling accounts of the three decades of political violence known as the Troubles. The book became a bestseller in the United States, appeared on numerous lists of the best books of 2019, was ranked 19th on The New York Times' list of the 100 best books of the 21st century and was adapted into an acclaimed television series.
Its success came as a surprise. After the book received little attention following its initial British release, Keefe feared he had wasted years on a project that nobody wanted to read. "I just thought, the juice isn't worth the squeeze," he says. Then it reached American readers and transformed his career. "There's my life before Say Nothing and my life after Say Nothing," he recalls, describing the dramatic turnaround.
By the time Say Nothing became a sensation, Keefe was already deeply immersed in his next project. It began with a 2017 investigation into the role of the billionaire Sackler family in America's devastating opioid crisis. After publishing the article, he accumulated so much additional material that he turned it into Empire of Pain, a disturbing history of a family that built an enormous fortune from addictive prescription painkillers. His reporting helped focus public attention on the people behind the crisis and contributed to pressure for accountability.
The Sacklers faced multibillion-dollar settlements, their reputation was devastated, their name was removed from prominent institutions, and Purdue Pharma, the pharmaceutical company they controlled, eventually ceased operations. Empire of Pain became one of those rare examples of investigative journalism helping bring about tangible change.
Yet Keefe is reluctant to describe himself as an activist. "I'm not an activist, I'm not a lawyer. I'm a journalist," he says. "If I spent too much time thinking, like, what's the consequence of this going to be? I would drive myself crazy." What matters most to him is the permanence of the written record. Once published, the book exists independently of its author and the people it exposes. "I have this book, and it's like a physical artifact, and it's in the world and it's on the Internet, and it's never gonna go away, and it can't be erased."
His motivation, he explains, often comes from the gap between the image people construct of themselves and the reality behind it. "So often when I start out, what motivates me is that there's some slippage between the story that someone's telling about themselves and the truth. And that's what I go for."
The teenager who invented a $270 million fortune
Keefe receives story pitches constantly. His instincts have become finely tuned, and it is increasingly difficult to catch his attention. But when something does, he usually knows immediately. "I wish I could tell you," he says, describing the process. "It's more just. I feel it." That was precisely what happened when someone told him about a British teenager who had died while pretending to be the son of a Russian oligarch. "I was in," Keefe recalls. The story became London Falling, his latest book and, surprisingly, the first of his works to be translated into Hebrew, published in Israel by Penn.
At its center is Zac Brettler, a 19-year-old from a comfortable Jewish family who died after going over the balcony of a luxury apartment building overlooking the River Thames in London in 2019. His body was recovered several days after he was reported missing, and the initial police investigation left his parents struggling to understand what had happened. Matthew and Rachelle Brettler soon discovered that their son had been leading an elaborate secret life. He had presented himself as the son of a Russian billionaire and heir to a fortune supposedly worth approximately $270 million. He had also become involved with two questionable men, including businessman Akbar Shamji, who figures prominently in Keefe's investigation.
A mysterious death, an invented fortune and a young man from a respectable family were compelling ingredients for a book. But what particularly interested Keefe was the opportunity to explore the larger world surrounding Zac's deception: the transformation of London by Russian oligarchs and international wealth. Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, he had written a roughly 4,000-word article for The New Yorker about the city's oligarchs. By the magazine's standards, that counted as a short piece.
Keefe had lived in London 25 years earlier and watched the city change. He was interested not only in the Russians who had settled there, but also in the influence of American finance and the legacy of the British Empire. "The first big invasion is not the Russians, it's the Americans in 1987, it's the bankers," he explains. "So in a way, it's a story about London becoming more American."
For Keefe, however, the way into a complicated subject is almost always through the people involved. He regularly receives proposals about gruesome murders, serial killers and spectacular crimes, but sensational details alone are not enough to sustain his interest. He wants stories that illuminate larger questions about society and human behavior. "There have to be kind of deeper themes," he says. "It has to implicate some larger, some larger universe of issues."
He points to climate change as an example of an enormously important subject he has struggled to approach. The problem is not a lack of interest, but the difficulty of finding a compelling human narrative through which to explore such vast, interconnected systems. "I'm not writing just to write, I'm writing to read. I want people to read what I'm writing," he says.
The Brettlers' story offered exactly the kind of human drama he was looking for. Unlike many of his previous investigations, which involved people who were dead, unwilling to cooperate or threatening legal action, this time he found a family prepared to share its story. He initially met Zac's parents twice, off the record and without making any commitment. "I was bluffing a little bit because I knew I wanted to write it," he admits. The couple, meanwhile, had not read his work and needed time to decide whether they could trust him.
The family had kept Zac's death largely private. Rachelle's father, Hugo Gryn, had been a prominent British rabbi, and the Brettlers belonged to the close-knit community surrounding London's West London Synagogue. Although hundreds attended Zac's funeral, the circumstances of his death had not attracted significant press coverage. Keefe believes the family's instinct to protect its privacy also contributed to a sense of isolation.
The parents had expected the police to investigate thoroughly, but felt that they had failed to obtain satisfactory answers. Keefe describes their growing uncertainty about whether they were demanding too much from the authorities. "They felt a little bit gaslit," he says, explaining that the couple had begun questioning whether their expectations were unreasonable.
At their first meeting, Keefe did not even take out a notebook. He listened for almost two hours as the parents described what they had discovered about their son's life and death. When they eventually showed him the material they had collected, he was shocked by what he saw. His reaction, he believes, helped reassure them that their concerns deserved to be taken seriously.
Still, he was careful not to promise that he would solve the mystery. He knew that the couple might hope for an outcome similar to Say Nothing, in which he identified the person he concluded was responsible for a decades-old murder. "Don't say yes because in the back of your minds you're hoping that I'll solve it," he told them. "It's not fair to either of us."
‘I'm writing for the readers. I'm writing for the truth’
Working with grieving parents posed an obvious challenge for a journalist who insists on factual accuracy and independence. Keefe rejects the idea that objectivity requires emotional distance. "I think you can be objective but not be cold," he says. His writing often contains dramatic twists and unexpected discoveries, but he insists these are not literary devices manufactured to create suspense. They reflect the experience of investigating a story, following clues, challenging assumptions and discovering that things are not always what they initially appear to be.
He wants readers to experience the same emotional journey. When he meets parents who have lost a child, he believes compassion is essential to understanding their experience. But when the time comes to write, he must be able to examine that experience critically. He made this clear to the Brettlers from the beginning. "I'm not writing this book for you. I'm writing for the readers. I'm writing for the truth," he told them.
That meant including uncomfortable details and family secrets, even when the people involved might have preferred to keep them private. Keefe knew that a book examining deception and the stories people tell about themselves would lose its credibility if he selectively protected the family while exposing others. "If I were to tell that story, but then, like, discreetly hold back these things that I learned about Hugo, it would be a cheat," he says. "Nobody should trust that book."
The investigation also forced Keefe to confront a disturbing question about his own family. He has two teenage sons, and the realization of how much Zac's parents had not known about their child's secret life unsettled him. As he spent more time with the Brettlers, he began interpreting ordinary teenage behavior at home through the lens of the tragedy he was investigating. His wife eventually intervened, telling him that it was unfair to their children.
It was not the first time his reporting had followed him home. Years earlier, he covered the trial of Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, one of the perpetrators of the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing, and his defense attorney. A family severely affected by the attack lived near the neighborhood where Keefe had grown up. The testimony about the victims, including children, was devastating. "I don't want to overstate it because there's no special courage in what I do," he says. "I hate it when journalists make themselves the story." Nevertheless, he suffered nightmares for months afterward.
As for Zac's death, Keefe believes he has reached a convincing conclusion, even if some details remain uncertain. He does not think the teenager deliberately took his own life, accidentally fell or was physically pushed from the balcony. Instead, he believes Zac jumped because he feared what would happen if he remained inside the apartment.
"I think Zac didn't jump to kill himself. I don't think he fell. I don't think he was pushed. I think he jumped because he thought if he stayed in that apartment, he was gonna die," Keefe says. This is his interpretation of the evidence, not an established judicial finding. He acknowledges that he cannot know precisely what was said in the apartment immediately before Zac's death, but says he is confident in the conclusion he reached.
The Brettlers remain supportive of the book, and Keefe continues to speak with them regularly. They attended its New York launch at the 92nd Street Y, where he was interviewed on stage by Sarah Jessica Parker. But he recognizes that having their private tragedy transformed into a bestseller has been an emotionally complicated experience. He recalls how Zac's brother Joe encountered a woman who mentioned reading London Falling with her book club. When Joe explained that the book was about his family, the woman burst into tears, and he found himself comforting her.
Keefe sees the encounter as characteristic of the family, but he also understands that their feelings about the book may change over time. He describes the material as emotionally charged and considers it his responsibility to remain in contact with them. For him, the book is a completed investigation. For the Brettlers, it is their life.
‘We're all swimming in a sewer’
Like many American journalists, Keefe is deeply alarmed by what he sees happening to the United States and its news media. He worries about efforts to weaken longstanding legal protections for journalists, including the precedent established by the Supreme Court's landmark New York Times Co. v. Sullivan ruling. He is also troubled by President Donald Trump's attacks on the press, declining literacy, diminishing public trust in news organizations and growing concentration of media ownership. He opposes the prospect of the Ellison family controlling both CNN and CBS, arguing that such consolidation would be harmful to journalism and democracy.
Keefe is equally disturbed by what he sees as the American public's growing indifference to political and institutional abuses. He questions whether the Sacklers would have faced similar accountability if his investigation had emerged in today's political environment. He cites the Trump family's business interests and incidents involving immigration enforcement agents as examples of developments that, in his view, have failed to provoke sustained public outrage.
"The amazing thing is Americans don't care," he says. He compares the muted response he sees in the United States with countries such as France, where attempts to raise the retirement age can trigger mass demonstrations. Growing up, he assumed American democratic institutions were firmly established. He is now troubled by how vulnerable they appear to be.
Yet his pessimism is not absolute. He describes a small group of mostly older people who gather every Saturday morning with handmade protest signs. On one level, the sight of the same few demonstrators week after week might seem discouraging. But Keefe finds something moving in their persistence. They are bearing witness, he says, making clear that they recognize something is wrong and refuse to accept it.
Despite the political climate and the decline of traditional media, Keefe remains convinced that serious long-form journalism has an audience. The New Yorker article that eventually became London Falling was the magazine's most-read article of its year, he says, despite its length and complexity. He acknowledges that readers' attention spans have changed, and that the lengthy descriptive passages once associated with writers such as Truman Capote may be harder to sustain today. But compelling stories still attract readers, including young people in their 20s who approach him at public events.
Nor does he believe The New Yorker is inevitably headed for extinction. Normally pessimistic, he sees a potential opportunity for established news organizations in the growing distrust of digital content. People are increasingly exhausted by their phones, he argues, while artificial intelligence has made it difficult to determine whether online images, videos and even emails are genuine. "I think everybody hates their phones now," he says. "I think we all feel like we've been broken."
For Keefe, that uncertainty could ultimately benefit publications that maintain rigorous reporting and fact-checking standards. "We're all like swimming in a sewer," he says. Readers want information, but they also want to know that the person providing it can be trusted. He compares reliable journalism to buying food with a label confirming that it has been inspected and is safe to consume.
At 50, after decades spent investigating some of the world's darkest stories, Keefe has no intention of slowing down. "I never want to quit. I'll do this forever," he says. He has already identified the subject of his next book, although he is not ready to reveal what it is. He does not consider himself an optimist, but finds consolation in family, friends, music, art, food and writing. Even the poetry of World War I reminds him that "even in the bleakest moments, there's room for beauty."
What Keefe does not expect is to write the investigation that finally changes the minds of Americans who remain committed to Trump. He recognizes the fantasy shared by many journalists that one explosive revelation might suddenly make the public reconsider everything. But he no longer believes such a moment is likely. "I'm not going to be the one who breaks this spell," he says.
At least one mystery from his career has a relatively satisfying resolution. Returning to Wind of Change, Keefe explains that the CIA did not write the Scorpions' Cold War anthem. "They didn't write the song, but they were involved in the promotion of the song," he says.
As for whether his investigation prompted any calls from the CIA asking him to drop the subject, Keefe says he has heard from people who told him the agency was particularly enthusiastic about the podcast. "You know who listens to this podcast more than anybody?" he asks, smiling. "They love it. Absolutely."
