Damp and mould in barracks cleared in three weeks
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:43:17 GMT
18:43:17 KST

Damp and mould reported in Single Living Accommodation takes an average of 20.94 days from the report being made to the work being completed, according to an answer given in Parliament.
James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat member for Lewes, asked what the average time is between damp and mould being reported in Single Living Accommodation and works being completed to rectify it.
Calvin Bailey, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for Veterans and People, said: “As of 23 October 2026, the average time between damp and mould being reported in Single Living Accommodation and works being completed was 20.94 days.”
An average of twenty-one days covers cases cleared within a few days and others that run considerably longer, and the department has told Parliament separately that it cannot supply the longest outstanding waiting time without disproportionate cost. Damp and mould in service accommodation became a political issue after the death of Awaab Ishak in Rochdale in 2020 led to Awaab’s Law, which imposes fixed timescales on social landlords in England for investigating and repairing hazards of this kind.
Service accommodation falls outside that regime because the Ministry of Defence is not a registered social landlord, and the department instead applies the Decent Homes Standard to family housing and a Defence Minimum Standard of its own design to the blocks. The blocks were last assessed against that standard in 2023, when 72 per cent met or exceeded it.
There have been 31,540 urgent reactive call-outs to Single Living Accommodation since the start of January, and forty-three buildings are currently scheduled for refurbishment. Capital spending on the blocks reached £299 million in 2024-25, and the Defence Investment Plan sets aside £1.4 billion for them over this Parliament.
An independent review of Single Living Accommodation and the overseas estate began in January 2026 and is expected to report this autumn.

North Korea tests cluster-bomb warhead for ballistic missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:36:31 UTC
18:36:31 KST

- North Korea tested a “Standard Type 2” cluster-bomb warhead for tactical ballistic missiles on Oct. 31, claiming it can destroy 12 to 13 hectares.
- The Missile Administration said units will be able to use four types of cluster warheads by the end of the year.
North Korea tested a cluster-bomb warhead for its tactical ballistic missiles on Oct. 31 and said it will let its military units choose from four types of cluster warheads by the end of the year, state news agency KCNA reported on Nov. 1.
The Missile Administration, which runs North Korea’s missile development, said the test assessed the warhead’s combat readiness and destructive power. Its Ballistic Missile System Institute and Warhead Institute said they confirmed that the “Standard Type 2” cluster warhead can destroy a target area of 12 to 13 hectares, about 30 to 32 acres. Kim Jong Sik, a member of the ruling Workers’ Party’s Central Military Commission and first vice director of a Central Committee department, oversaw the test. Leader Kim Jong Un was not reported to have attended.
KCNA did not name the missile or give its range, altitude or launch site. The missile was fired at an uninhabited island target in the West Sea, also known as the Yellow Sea, South Korea’s JKN reported, and analysts said it appears to be the first time North Korea has fired a cluster-armed missile from a wheeled mobile launcher.
“We classify the cluster-bomb warheads into four categories according to special and standard purposes. Within this year we will enable units to select and use all those types according to operational aims and specific features of targets,” said the general director of the DPRK Missile Administration.
A cluster warhead opens in the air and scatters dozens or hundreds of small bomblets over a wide area, making it effective against troops, vehicles, artillery positions and airfields rather than a single hardened target. Neither North Korea nor South Korea has joined the international convention banning cluster munitions.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff did not announce the launch on the day it happened, a break from its usual practice of reporting North Korean ballistic missile launches in real time. The military said on Nov. 1 that it had tracked related activity before the launch in close information sharing with the United States and maintained a readiness posture. Because the missile flew a short range at low altitude, the military wanted to complete its analysis before confirming it was a ballistic missile, Financial News reported.
North Korea has tested cluster warheads on its tactical missiles before. In April, it tested a Hwasong-11A short-range ballistic missile with a cluster warhead alongside other new weapons, and later that month Kim Jong Un watched the launch of Hwasong-11 Ra missiles fitted with cluster bomb and fragmentation mine warheads, which state media also claimed could devastate an area of about 13 hectares.
The test came two days after North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area during a firepower demonstration tied to a drone exhibition, where Kim called for “absolute superiority” in drone technology. The Missile Administration described the Oct. 31 launch as part of regular research work to improve the power of its weapon systems.

Russia suffers record troop losses in October, its worst month since full-scale invasion, Ukraine says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:30:23 UTC
18:30:23 KST

Russia suffers record troop losses in October, its worst month since full-scale invasion, Ukraine says
Russia's combat losses were greater in October 2026 than in any other month since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces reported.
According to the data from the General Staff, Russia's estimated losses reached 54,400 soldiers in October. That's 8,170 more than in the previous month.
The figure includes those killed, wounded, and missing in action.
"This is a record for any month of the full-scale war," said President Volodymyr Zelensky on social media.
Zelensky also mentioned that in October, Ukraine liberated more territory than it lost, 96.2 square kilometers (37.1 square miles) vs 85.8 square kilometers (33.1 square miles) occupied by Russia.
In October, our Ukrainian Defence Forces inflicted record losses on the enemy and recaptured more territory than the Russian occupiers were able to seize.
"We thank all our defenders, all our soldiers, every brigade and every unit for this result, which is so important for our country. Russia is losing," Zelensky said.
The General Staff said the high rate matters because it "exceeds the enemy's ability to replenish its units. Every month of the war is costing the Russian army more and more."
The National Guard's 1st Azov Corps said a significant share of Moscow's losses stemmed from Russia's offensive in the direction of the city of Dobropillia, in Donetsk Oblast.
The Corps estimates it has killed, wounded, and captured over 6,800 Russian troops in "one of the key axes of the Russian offensive."
October was also a record month for Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, its commander Robert "Magyar" Brovdi wrote on social media.
Brovdi said that his forces hit a Russian soldier every 159 seconds in October, averaging 542 casualties daily.
The more Russia racks up combat losses, the greater the need for Moscow to increase its own mobilization efforts.
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned in August that Russia plans to mobilize around 300,000 people after its September election is out of the way.
So far, Moscow announced plans to conscript an additional 120,000 people on Oct. 2.
"Ukrainian Defense Forces will continue to inflict losses on the occupiers until the complete cessation of Russia's armed aggression against Ukraine," said the General Staff.
According to the General Staff, Russia has lost 1,590,270 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to have been killed in action.

Russia redirects grain exports to the Arctic due to problems in the Black Sea - FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:29:04 EET
18:29:04 KST

Russia redirects grain exports to the Arctic due to problems in the Black Sea - FT
Kyiv • UNN
Due to disruptions at Black Sea ports, Russia is testing wheat shipments through Murmansk. More expensive logistics are hitting farmers and buyers.
Russia is testing a new grain export route through the Arctic port of Murmansk due to serious disruptions in the operation of Black Sea ports. The alternative logistics increase transportation costs and create problems for farmers and buyers. This is reported by the Financial Times, according to UNN.
Details
Russia is testing grain exports through the Arctic port of Murmansk, located thousands of kilometers from the farms where the grain is grown, as a Ukrainian drone campaign has practically severed its traditional route through the Black Sea. According to the port’s Telegram channel, a bulk carrier in Murmansk began loading 29,500 tonnes of wheat on Wednesday for a trial shipment to buyers in North Africa, adapting equipment normally used to handle fertilizer for grain. This extraordinary detour illustrates how the escalating struggle for control of the Black Sea has upended trade between Russia, the world’s largest wheat exporter, and Ukraine, another major supplier, despite relatively high harvests in both countries
According to the publication, the trial Arctic shipment is the first of its kind, but Moscow is already exporting through ports on the Baltic Sea.
The main issue is not simply whether we can redirect a certain volume. The point is that logistics will cost significantly more than transportation through the Azov–Black Sea basin, and someone will have to cover the difference
According to Rusagrotrans, Russian wheat exports fell by 38% from July to September compared with last year. At the same time, freight rates on some Black Sea routes have more than doubled since mid-July, forcing importers to look for alternatives.
Exporters are turning to increasingly inventive solutions. Some vessels travel inland from the Sea of Azov, up the Don and through the Volga–Don Canal to the Caspian Sea and buyers in Iran. Others use containers to transfer grain from railway cars onto vessels at terminals without traditional bulk-loading facilities. But the alternatives cannot replace the southern ports. Zlochevsky estimated that Baltic terminals could compensate for no more than half of the lost transportation volumes in the Black Sea and Azov regions by the end of the year. According to him, the rush to the north has overloaded the railways, and railcars have accumulated at the terminals
At the same time, the publication writes, logistics problems are also affecting Ukraine. Alternative routes through the Danube and neighboring EU countries can provide only about half of the usual agricultural export volumes. According to Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi, such transportation adds at least $50 to the cost of transporting a tonne of produce. As a result, some Ukrainian farmers are forced to sell their harvest at a loss. Corn prices have fallen by almost 20% in three weeks.
In Russia, producers in the southern regions are also receiving less because of difficult access to ports. According to Andrey Sizov, head of SovEcon, domestic prices, after falling in August and September, remain "tens of percent below production costs."
According to the publication, many farmers cannot afford to hold on to their harvest until prices improve.
We remind you
Ukrainian farmers have harvested 72% of the area and collected 41.7 million tonnes of grain. Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk and Mykolaiv regions lead in terms of acreage.

Zurich and Basel protests turn violent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:27:17 UTC
18:27:17 KST

Zurich and Basel protests turn violent
Several hundred people took part in protests in Zurich and Basel on Saturday night under the banner “On en a marre – en Suisse aussi” [We’ve had enough – in Switzerland too], echoing protests in France.
The two unauthorised demonstrations were marred by violence, requiring the intervention of the police.
In Zurich, hundreds of people, some wearing Halloween masks, gathered at around 10:30 pm on Langstrasse in the city centre. Fireworks and flares were set off as the crowd made its way towards Helvetiaplatz, a few hundred metres from the main station.
The atmosphere changed as soon as the demonstrators reached the square, a Keystone-ATS journalist observed at the scene. The shelter at the local bus stop was damaged and a barricade made of rubbish bins, bicycles and other objects was set alight.
The police intervened with water cannons to disperse the demonstrators. Small groups of rioters set fire to rubbish bins in various locations, according to the municipal police. A car was also set alight and the shop windows of several shops were damaged. The police said they were repeatedly targeted with fireworks, bottles and stones. They replied using tear gas and rubber bullets. The clashes continued until around 1:30 am.
A police patrol, which had responded to a medical emergency, was attacked by a crowd, the police said. Their vehicle was damaged and the officers were forced to withdraw before they could assist a teenager who had suffered serious leg injuries following an accident.
More
Ex-Swiss minister Berset defends young people’s right to demonstrate
In Basel, around 150 people gathered in the city centre at around 9pm, according to a statement from the cantonal police.
After a number of speeches, the procession crossed the Mittlere Rheinbrücke, which spans the Rhine and connects the city centre on the left bank of the river with the Kleinbasel district on the right bank, to reach the Marktplatz, in the heart of the historic centre, before heading north into the St. Johann district. There some demonstrators set fire to barricades made of rubbish bins and metal barriers, prompting the police to intervene.
As in Zurich, the Basel demonstrators drew parallels with the youth protests in France and other European countries. In recent days, unknown individuals have launched a call on social media using the slogan “GenZ regelt!” [Generation Z is in charge!], a phrase used by young demonstrators in Germany.

Kenyan, Ethiopian athletes win 48th Istanbul Marathon as men's course record broken
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:26:33 UTC
18:26:33 KST

Bozhan Memis and Merve Berker
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
Kenya's Philimon Kiptoo Kipchumba broke the men's course record at the 48th Istanbul Marathon on Sunday, while Ethiopia's Kasanesh Ayenew Baze won the women's race.
Kipchumba completed the 42.195-kilometer (26.2-mile) course in 2 hours, 8 minutes and 44 seconds, breaking the previous record of 2 hours, 9 minutes and 44 seconds set by fellow Kenyan Daniel Kibet in 2019.
Ethiopia's Sufaro Woliyi Kebeto finished second in the men's race, while Kenya's Vincent Kipyegon Ronoh took third place.
Organized by Spor Istanbul, a subsidiary of the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality, and sponsored by Türkiye Is Bankasi, the marathon was held for the 48th time.
Known as the world's only intercontinental marathon, the race began 250 meters (820 feet) behind the July 15 Martyrs Bridge on Istanbul's Asian side and finished at Sultanahmet Square.
 
- Ethiopian athletes sweep women's podium
Ethiopia's Kasanesh Ayenew Baze won the women's race with a time of 2 hours, 24 minutes and 40 seconds.
Ethiopian runners claimed all three podium positions, with Azmera Abreha Gdey finishing second in 2 hours, 24 minutes and 47 seconds.
Diribe Hirko Alemu, also from Ethiopia, took third place with a time of 2 hours and 25 minutes.
 
- Turkish athlete Huseyin Can finishes 11th
Among Turkish national athletes competing in the elite men's category, Huseyin Can finished 11th with a time of 2 hours, 17 minutes and 53 seconds.
Can, who finished among the top 10 last year, narrowly missed a top-10 finish this year.
Fellow Turkish athlete Mert Girmalegesse placed 12th in 2 hours, 18 minutes and 47 seconds.
Halil Yasin finished 14th with a time of 2 hours, 19 minutes and 31 seconds, followed by Ahmet Alkanoglu in 15th place with 2 hours, 19 minutes and 38 seconds.
Yavuz Agrali completed the race in 16th place with a time of 2 hours, 21 minutes and 44 seconds.

A slight increase in voter turnout is being observed in the second round of the presidential election, despite participation remaining low, Boryana Dimitrova of Alpha Research told BNR. As of 12:00 p.m., 9.6% of eligible voters had cast their ballots, compared with 8.6% at the same time during the first round. According to the sociologist, turnout in the runoff is expected to be slightly higher than last week.
Voter turnout in Bulgaria’s presidential election stood at 6.8% as of 11:00 a.m.,according to data from the Myara polling agency.
Voter turnout across the country stood at 3% as of 10:00 a.m., according to Alpha Research.
PHOTO Myara polling agency
Voter turnout stood at around 2% as of 9:00 a.m., roughly the same level as at the corresponding time last Sunday, when the first round of the presidential election was held, Genoveva Petrova of Alpha Research told the Bulgarian National Radio.
She added that there were reasons to expect voter turnout to pick up, although this did not necessarily mean it would reach particularly high levels. Voter turnout in the first round was just 22.98%.
Voter turnout in Bulgaria stood at 2.1% as of 9:00 a.m., according to data from the Myara polling agency.
The candidate who receives the highest number of votes will be declared the winner, regardless of voter turnout in the runoff.

‘Deeply shameful’: Tharoor slams UK over colonialism omission in slavery apology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:22:34 UTC
18:22:34 KST

Shashi Tharoor slams UK PM over proposed slavery apology, questions omission of colonialism. (File photo)
NEW DELHI: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor has criticised British prime minister Andy Burnham for considering an apology for Britain's role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade while leaving out its colonial past.The Thiruvananthapuram Lok Sabha MP described the omission as “inexplicable and inexcusable”, arguing that Britain must also acknowledge the suffering caused by its colonial rule.Tharoor's remarks followed Burnham's announcement that his government would consider issuing a formal apology for Britain's involvement in the slave trade as part of efforts to strengthen ties with countries in Africa and the Caribbean.
In an article published in The Guardian on Saturday, Burnham said Britain needed to confront its “complicated history” to protect the future of the Commonwealth, a grouping of 56 independent countries that largely emerged from the former British Empire.Burnham is scheduled to visit Antigua and Barbuda this week for a meeting of Commonwealth leaders.
Tharoor says colonialism cannot be left out
Responding to Burnham's remarks in a post on X on Saturday, Tharoor said he had long maintained that putting a monetary figure on the damage caused by British rule was difficult.
"But moral atonement for the ravages of colonialism is indispensable. I am glad to learn that Prime Minister Burnham is prepared to offer a formal apology on behalf of the British state for the horrors of slavery. But the omission of colonialism from his apology is inexplicable and inexcusable," the MP from Thiruvananthapuram said.
Tharoor's remarks followed Burnham's remark over Britain's involvement in the slave trade.
He also said Britain had never formally apologised for the destruction and exploitation carried out during its colonial rule."It remains deeply shameful that Britain has never said a simple 'sorry' for the loot, pillage, death and destruction perpetrated during the colonial era on millions of innocent victims of British imperialism," he said.
Burnham pitches for 'honest conversation' on slavery
In his article, Burnham said countries affected by the trans-Atlantic slave trade had repeatedly sought an acknowledgement of its lasting consequences.“For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery,” Burnham was quoted as saying by media reports. “By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function.”Tharoor, who has written extensively about British colonial rule, is the author of Inglorious Empire: What the British Did to India. The book examines how British rule led to the systematic exploitation and plunder of India's wealth.

DGCA mandates twin pilot operations from Monday, chopper operators threaten to suspend Char Dam flights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:19:46 UTC
18:19:46 KST

Chopper operators on Char Dham routes have threatened to suspend operations from Monday over DGCA's mandatory twin-pilot rule, citing unviable costs, after a crash killed six people.
NEW DELHI: Chopper operations on Char Dham routes could come to standstill from Monday. Following a chopper crashing soon after take off from Badrinath on Friday (October 30), killing all six people on board — a pilot and five passengers, the DGCA has made it mandatory for choppers operating on Char Dham to be manned by two pilots starting Monday (Nov 2), in a bid to improve safety. However chopper operators have termed the move unviable and threatened to suspend these sorties from Monday “until the matter is reviewed and a mutually workable solution is arrived at.Chopper operators on Saturday sent their “collective objection to the implementation of mandatory twin-pilot operations and intimation of suspension of operations from Nov 2, 2026,” to Directorate General of Civil Aviation chief Vir Vikram Yadav. “… (we) collectively place on record our serious concern and reservation regarding the mandatory requirement of twin-pilot operations for charter services (in) the new operational restrictions communicated by DGCA proposed to be implemented with effect from the first take-off on Nov 2, 2026.”“The mandatory deployment of two pilots on every charter sortie will substantially increase operating costs, crew requirements, accommodation and logistical expenses, and overall operational commitments.
Given the existing commercial structure, prevailing charter rates and limited operational margins, these additional costs cannot be reasonably absorbed by the operators. Nor is it commercially feasible to pass on the entire additional burden to customers,” it says.“… all operators have consistently complied with applicable DGCA regulations and have invested considerable resources in maintaining safe, efficient and reliable operations in the challenging Himalayan terrain…. any additional safety-related measures must be practical, proportionate, commercially sustainable and developed in consultation with the operating stakeholders. Accordingly, after due consideration and mutual consultation, all operators collectively express their inability to accept the mandatory twin-pilot requirement in its present form,” it says.
"In view of the above, we wish to formally convey that all participating operators are proposing to suspend their Char Dham charter operations with effect from Nov 2, 2026, until the matter is reviewed and a mutually workable solution is arrived at by the concerned authorities in consultation with the operators. Under the proposed framework, continuing operations would result in unsustainable financial and operational commitments, leaving the operators with no commercially viable alternative,” it said.Operators have DGCA and Uttarakhand Civil Aviation Development Authority (UCADA) to "reconsider the mandatory twin-pilot requirement, engage with all stakeholders on an urgent basis, and explore an alternative operational framework that adequately addresses safety concerns while ensuring the commercial viability and sustainability of helicopter operations in the region. We remain committed to aviation safety, regulatory compliance and the continued development of helicopter services in Uttarakhand. We hope that the matter will receive urgent consideration and that a constructive resolution can be reached before the proposed implementation date.”

It has resulted in more than 4,000 people, including many senior citizens and Holocaust survivors, being arrested for showing their support for the group, according to campaigners and police tallies.

The UAE is hoping for a breakthrough in negotiations between Iran and the United States while being prepared for the worst, a senior official said on Sunday, following threats of a resumption of the Middle East war.

"It is not the interest of the region to go through another round...But I think we're also, as we've shown before, braced for the worst."
Iran army says any new war with US could be 'longer'
Iran warned on Sunday that any new war with the United States could last longer than the previous conflict and that US President Donald Trump would not be the one to determine its duration.
"A potential future war could last longer than previous conflict, and the American president would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion," said army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia, according to Iranian state television.
Trump says US still has 'one or two targets' in Iran
President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the United States has knocked out much of Iran's military but still has to "take care of" one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked.
Trump maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, which was started by the United States and Israel in February, were "going fine but you know they're not very reliable."
The Republican president said the United States is not in a hurry to take offensive action because it had already decimated Iran's military and nuclear program.
"We've knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes," Trump told reporters at his Florida residence.
"You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly," he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
Iran warns US, Israel against new attacks after Trump
Iran's supreme leader warned the United States and Israel on Saturday of fresh attacks following their threats to resume strikes after crucial elections, as fears increased over a return to fighting.
President Donald Trump suggested he could launch fresh military action after the United States holds its midterm elections early next week.
But US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday: "If there is a diplomatic solution, we would be open to it."
UN says Yemeni staff member dies in Houthi custody
A Yemeni staff member of the UN Human Rights Office has died in Houthi custody after being arbitrarily detained for more than two years, the UN human rights chief said on Saturday, calling for an independent investigation and the release of other detained personnel.
Mohammad el Shami had been held by the Houthi militant group since June 6, 2024, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said in a statement.
His family said they had been informed of his death only recently, more than a month after it occurred, and had received no explanation of the cause or circumstances, Turk said.
A Qatari tanker has been attacked with "unidentified objects" while transiting Gulf waters, the country's state news agency reported Sunday.
The attack on Friday evening struck a liquefied natural gas carrier, Al Mayeda, owned by the Qatar Gas Transport Company, Qatar News Agency said.
Since the Middle East war broke out in February, Iran has been targeting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf in an effort to assert control over shipping.

Drone strike hits power station in northern Sudan as attacks on energy facilities mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:19:15 UTC
18:19:15 KST

A drone strike hit a power station in northern Sudan early on Sunday, sparking a fire and triggering loud explosions, witnesses told Anadolu.
The attack targeted the Abu Hamad power station in River Nile state, about 334 miles (538 kilometres) north of the capital, Khartoum, according to witnesses.
They said loud explosions were heard around the facility as flames engulfed parts of the station.
Videos circulated by activists on social media showed a large fire at the power station.
The latest strike brought to 12 the number of power stations targeted by drone attacks across six Sudanese states since Monday.
The affected states include Khartoum, Gezira, Sennar, Gedaref, River Nile and Red Sea.
There was no immediate comment from Sudanese authorities on the attack or the extent of casualties and damage.
Power infrastructure targeted in series of drone strikes
The latest attack followed another drone strike on Saturday targeting the Hayya power station in Red Sea state, a facility still under construction.
The attacks on power infrastructure come amid the ongoing conflict between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
The two sides have been fighting since April 2023, when disagreements over the integration of the country's military forces escalated into armed conflict.
The war has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, amid a worsening humanitarian and hunger crisis.

====================================================================================================

Are US Supremos Failing to Learn Lessons, or Maybe They’re Oblivious?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:19:00 UTC
18:19:00 KST

Top US officials and envoys are increasingly openly looking on Ukraine and Zelensky as being to blame for current international crises. At the same time, their statements and rhetoric are shifting positively towards Russia. This is not, simply, an anti-Ukrainian or pro-Russian shift. Nor is it necessarily pro-American. Rather, it is pro-establishment and pro-MAGA, ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.
All of this is a serious mistake, regardless of the fact that Trump is not in the strongest position in the polls and the elections are fast approaching. Is American policy towards Ukraine and Russia credible in the eyes of American voters? Not necessarily. It may even seem absurd, but it is not a campaign issue. Do Americans understand the Russian threat at all, or do they simply perceive it differently?
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Over the past weeks and months, the Americans have eased sanctions on Belarus and Russia, including through the latest, much-discussed “Diesel Deal.” Easing sanctions on Russian oil is not a game changer when it comes to America’s fuel situation. At first glance, it looks like part of an initial effort to rebuild relations and establish trust. Yet, in doing so, America is voluntarily giving up the leverage it has over Russia. Can this be interpreted as forcing Ukraine into an unfavorable peace, or even capitulation? Indirectly, yes.
Pressure on President Zelensky to step down, if it were hypothetically successful, could trigger massive political chaos and effectively make it impossible to hold elections in Ukraine. The question is whether this is obvious to the American administration and, if so, whether it has decided to abandon Ukraine – in the event Russia manages to win.
‘Russia Russia Russia’ Was No Hoax
This division of spheres of influence seems increasingly apparent with each new proposal to organize a Trump-Putin-Xi meeting.
Russia consistently pursues its goals
The Kremlin announced its plans long ago, through Putin himself, including in his 2007 Munich speech. The dictator’s proposed new Yalta should come as no surprise. He is consistently pursuing his objectives, enabled by the absence of genuine democratic processes in Russia. Unlike Western countries, he does not have to worry about elections or make any particular effort to win over voters.
The gradual pursuit of goals announced almost two decades ago shows that Moscow operates on a much longer time horizon than the West. This is evident, for example, in the way Washington behaves towards the upcoming US midterm elections and the approaching electoral cycle in Europe.
What are the Americans discussing with the Russians?
Washington-Moscow talks are not solely about Ukraine, and the proposal for a US-China-Russia summit only reinforces this point. The first other subject that comes to mind is Iran and oil –the talks will certainly address these issues as well.
There is undoubtedly also a question of trade and spheres of influence, particularly on NATO’s eastern flank. Russia has long sought to rebuild its influence and reduce the militarization of NATO’s eastern flank. Put bluntly, it wants to return de facto to the situation before 1997, when the alliance began expanding. The militarization of the region is not the result of aggressive plans by these countries, but a direct response to the threat posed by the Kremlin’s neo-imperial policy.
Russia, however, understands that Trump alone cannot force Ukraine into radical concessions or, to put it bluntly, capitulation. Europe stands in the way, having taken on a significant share of the burden of assistance. Diplomatically, the EU and the UK are also capable of steering the US away from ideas about abandoning Ukraine.
At the same time, the Americans are concerned about the future of the situation in Eastern Europe. This was expressed by top diplomat Marco Rubio himself, who said that the war could spread to other countries. This, in turn, could be interpreted as an the US drawing a red line for the Kremlin.
Does this make sense? Paradoxically, yes. The Americans do not view the red line, the purchase of Russian oil and their position on supporting Ukraine as one single package, but rather as several separate issues.
None of this should come as a surprise
Trump provokes strong emotions, particularly because of his pro-Russian shifts and his distinctive style of public appearances. However, if we look at America’s approach to Ukraine and Russia since 1991, we can identify numerous events and twists that ran counter to Ukrainian independence.
The first came even before Ukraine declared independence. On August 1, 1991, George H. W. Bush delivered what became known as the “Chicken Kyiv Speech” in Kyiv. The president simply miscalculated badly and warned Ukraine against independence.
In 2005, Barack Obama, still a senator at the time, personally oversaw the process of disarming Ukraine in Donbas. Later, as president, he failed to respond particularly firmly to Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014 and pursued a policy of warming relations with the Kremlin during his presidency.
As president, Joe Biden did provide substantial support to Ukraine in 2022. However, before the invasion, he spoke of a potential Russian “minor incursion”, triggering a wave of criticism and forcing the then US Secretary of State, Antony Blinken, to explain the remarks.
None of this means that the US was consistently hostile to Ukraine from the very beginning. Biden provided enormous assistance. During his first presidency, Donald Trump supplied Ukraine with Javelin antitank missiles and actively opposed the construction of the two Nord Stream gas pipelines.
One encouraging development in the current situation is that, at the recent Warsaw Security Forum, Alexus Grynkewich, Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) and commander of United States European Command (EUCOM), presented a theory of victory for the region. Its underlying approach is defensive, but unequivocal. The venue where it was announced was not accidental either.
Grynkewich was, of course, not simply expressing his personal views, but presenting a position agreed upon with the Pentagon and the American administration. It is also worth noting that talks are underway on closer security cooperation between the US, Poland and Lithuania. There are no concrete details yet.
The Americans simply continue to regard Russia as an important country, or even as an equal. Yet, given their inconsistency and naivety, it also seems that they do not understand Russia or President Vladimir Putin’s wider agenda.
We can certainly expect continued pressure on Ukraine, although its intensity and dynamics may vary, as they have so far. Russia, in turn, periodically humiliates Trump diplomatically. Around the same time as the US president was saying that the Kremlin was not supporting Iran, the foreign ministers of Iran and Russia were talking about the countries’ very close cooperation. There are plenty of other examples.
The inconsistency of American policy and its frequent shifts against NATO allies and Ukraine certainly do not make the US a credible partner. This is dangerous not only for America’s reputation, but also for the international security situation in at least several regions of the world. Even more concerning is that the administration doesn’t seem to understand these realities.

Malawi cattle farmers travel farther as El Nino worsens drought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:16:24 UTC
18:16:24 KST

Malawi cattle farmers travel farther as El Nino worsens drought
For many families, keeping cattle alive is becoming an increasingly costly struggle.
Mulanje, Malawi – Lawrence Abison walks along the bank of the Likhubula River, stopping every few metres to inspect the grass.
He eventually moves towards a patch of green Napier grass and reeds.
The 25-year-old takes out a sickle. With three friends, he starts cutting. They work through the morning, tying the grass into bundles, carrying them uphill and returning to the river for more.
They left Nsanjama, 27km away, at dawn.
After two hours of cutting, they had gathered enough grass to feed 10 cattle for one day.
Later that afternoon, dozens of other men carrying bundles of grass could be seen around Chitakale in Mulanje district. They had come from different directions, searching for fodder for cattle kept on farms across the district.
“It’s very hard to find the grass these days, that’s why we have travelled this long distance,” Abison told Al Jazeera, sweating. “Even here, the grass is not enough for a week and we need to proceed farther.”
The search for grass
The Likhubula River flows from Mount Mulanje, the 3,002-metre massif rising sharply from the plains of southern Malawi. The mountain is the highest point in tropical southern Africa and an important source of water for communities around it.
People living around the river say they have seen changes in the water and vegetation over the years. In some places, they say, the river has become shallower, while trees and grass along its banks have disappeared.
The changes are being felt by farmers who depend on the river, not only for water, but also for grass to feed their cattle.
Malawi experienced dry spells and high temperatures in parts of the country during the 2023/24 rainfall season, while El Nino affected rainfall patterns across southern Africa.
The Department of Climate Change and Meteorological Services warned then of below-normal rainfall and prolonged dry spells in parts of Malawi, with southern areas among those facing the increased threat of drought.
For farmers in Mulanje, the immediate problem is finding enough feed for their cattle.
A longer journey for cattle feed
Abison and other fodder gatherers say they have started making trips to the rivers earlier than they used to. Previously, they would cycle to the river after October. This year, they had already been making the journey for months.
They are also travelling farther.
That has brought them into competition with people living close to the rivers, who also depend on the vegetation. Reeds are used locally to make mats, while grass is needed to feed livestock.
Macdonald Khandalawo, 54, has kept cattle in Nsanjama, in the area of Traditional Authority Juma, since 2014. He has 10 cattle and sends men such as Abison to the rivers to collect grass.
He says the cost of keeping the animals has risen as the grass becomes harder to find.
“After the rains have stopped, we look for the grass around here but due to the change in climate there has been scarcity of grass. That is why we send these boys to those rivers,” Khandalawo said.
“It’s a long distance and sometimes they take the whole day.”
The lack of feed has affected his cows’ milk production, he said. The animals are eating less and the feed arrives later.
Maize bran, which farmers use to supplement grass, is also scarce and expensive, farmers say. Lower maize harvests have made the bran harder to afford.
Khandalawo also points to another pressure on the rivers: cultivation along their banks.
“Our complaint is that people are cultivating even in riverbanks. Previously, you would find plenty of reeds, plenty of grass, but now you can’t find it because some of our friends who grow vegetables are cultivating even where the water is,” he said.
“Because of that, the water is drying up faster and grass is scarce.”
“If possible, we want it to be like before where people were not allowed to cultivate beyond some metres in the riverbanks. Most of our rivers have no vegetation,” he added.
A changing landscape
Khandalawo is treasurer of the New Thuchira Milk Bulking Group, a cooperative with up to 400 farmers. The group collects milk from members, preserves it and sells it to commercial processors.
It also gives farmers a place to exchange ideas on dealing with feed shortages.
Some collect maize stalks during harvest and keep them for periods when grass is scarce. Others collect the remains of peas and rice to add to the animals’ feed.
But the shortage is eating into farmers’ earnings.
In a normal month, Khandalawo makes more than one million Malawi kwacha ($577) from milk sales. Recently, much of that money has gone back into the farm to pay fodder gatherers and buy maize bran.
He is no longer certain how long he can keep the herd under the current conditions.
Rivers under pressure
Near the Likhubula River, in Supuni Village under Traditional Authority Chikumbu, 57-year-old Batson Kweluza has watched fodder gatherers come and go for years.
He has also watched the landscape change.
Kweluza was weeding in his vegetable garden when he pointed towards the river.
“In the past, it was always dark even during the daytime because of the canopy that was created from the trees here,” he said.
The trees are gone in many places, he said, and the river has become shallow enough for people to cross without removing their shoes.
“Now even rains don’t come as they used to because of those trees that have been cut and people can cross that river without even taking off their shoes.”
In Nkando, 25-year-old Alefa Saulo is watching a similar change on her own farm.
She raises bulls and sells them after about a year. Her three cows, however, are getting thinner.
She pays two boys about MK50,000 each ($29) to help with the work on her farm, but they have not shown up for two days because of illness.
Waiting for it to pour
Saulo is waiting for the rains. She hopes they will come soon enough for the grass to grow and the cattle to regain weight.
She watches them as they feed.
“As a farmer, I always get concerned because when the animals are eating and looking healthy, I am also happy,” Saulo said. “But now I am sad. The animals are hungry but I can’t give them food.”

El Nino, weak monsoon behind Hong Kong’s warmest October since records began

El Nino, weak monsoon behind Hong Kong’s warmest October since records began
All three monthly temperature averages broke October records, with the average high reaching 30.5 degrees Celsius
Hong Kong sweltered through its warmest October on record, as an extremely strong El Nino, a weak northeast monsoon and a persistent anticyclone aloft over southern China combined to drive temperatures to unprecedented levels, the weather forecaster has said.
The Hong Kong Observatory said on Sunday that the mean maximum temperature last month was 30.5 degrees Celsius (86.9 Fahrenheit), the mean temperature 27.6 degrees and the mean minimum 25.8 degrees – all the highest for any October since records began in 1884.
“Aside from the impact of climate warming, we are experiencing an extremely strong El Nino event,” the weather forecaster said.

Russia’s Starlink Dream Goes Up in Flames as Second Satellite Burns Up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:15:02 UTC
18:15:02 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Starlink Dream Goes Up in Flames as Second Satellite Burns Up
Russia’s attempt to build its own alternative to Elon Musk’s Starlink has suffered another setback, with a second Rassvet-3 satellite burning up in Earth’s atmosphere after failing to reach its intended orbit.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on October 30, the satellite, designated Rassvet-3 No. 17 (NORAD 100083), reentered the atmosphere on October 30, just three months and 11 days after its launch aboard a Soyuz-2.1b rocket on July 19.
The spacecraft apparently never activated its propulsion system to raise its orbit, leaving it to gradually lose altitude due to atmospheric drag until it burned up.
This marks the second satellite lost from Russia’s Rassvet constellation, developed by Bureau 1440 as a domestic alternative to SpaceX’s Starlink. The first, Rassvet-3 No. 4, reentered the atmosphere on June 6 after experiencing similar difficulties.
However, Russia managed to rescue another troubled satellite, No. 23, which began raising its orbit on October 20 after descending to approximately 220 kilometers. It has since climbed to around 300 kilometers and continues gaining altitude.
Despite the losses, the overall constellation remains operational in its testing phase. Of the 30 Rassvet-3 satellites still in orbit, 26 have reached approximately 500 kilometers, while another is approaching that altitude.
Although the planned operational altitude is around 800 kilometers, the satellites are currently positioning themselves at 500 kilometers before a coordinated ascent.
Bureau 1440 has also reportedly begun testing satellite internet terminals in remote Russian regions. Separately, equipment resembling satellite communication terminals has been spotted aboard Russian drones used against Ukraine, although its connection to the Rassvet network remains unconfirmed.
The two satellite losses highlight technical challenges in Russia’s efforts to establish an independent satellite internet network, but do not necessarily indicate that the wider project is failing.
Earlier reports indicated that two Rassvet-3 satellites were rapidly losing altitude and risked burning up in Earth’s atmosphere within weeks. One has now been lost, while the other has successfully begun raising its orbit.

His workplace safety proposals include strengthening labor inspections, adding inspectors, subsidizing vehicle replacements, and providing cooling vests for outdoor workers.

Culture Wars bet on themselves with Taipei show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:07:51 UTC
18:07:51 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Austin-based band Culture Wars is scheduled to perform at Taipei's Legacy next Friday.
For Culture Wars frontman Alex Dugan, a good gamble can pay off in more ways than one.
During the pandemic, Duggan and his bandmates discovered that nearly empty Las Vegas casinos were willing to offer free hotel rooms to blackjack players. They took full advantage, spending stretches of time at the Wynn, writing music in their rooms during the day and heading downstairs to gamble at night.
“We would live in Vegas for like two weeks at a time for free, essentially,” Dugan recalled in a conference call with Taiwan News. “We would write all day, go down and gamble, and get everything for free pretty much.”
He estimates he spent six weeks at the hotel across three separate stays. Blackjack eventually gave way to craps and baccarat, but the bigger bet was still to come.
After building an audience through singles, streaming, and social media, Culture Wars is spending the past year proving it can sell tickets without relying on festival slots or support appearances.
The results have been encouraging, selling out medium-capacity rooms not only in their hometown but also in Warsaw and Stockholm despite promoters' initial reservations.
The band also sold out two nights at Los Angeles' historic Troubadour, a venue Duggan had long wanted to play.
“Everything we have been doing this last year is doing our own stuff and proving that we are capable of holding our own and having our own shows,” he said.
That makes the Nov. 13 concert at Taipei's Legacy especially important. It is the band's only headline show during its Asia tour, and Taiwan is one of its biggest markets for both streaming and social media.
Duggan calls the concert a test and “a very big stake in the ground," a chance to show promoters that the band's online following can translate into a live audience.
The band released its debut album “Don't Speak” this year after putting out singles one at a time to build an audience. Duggan said he wanted each song to have its own chance to find listeners before the album arrived.
That patient approach also applies to the music. Culture Wars puts melody and songwriting ahead of a signature sound or a flashy riff. “If we're gonna do this, the songs themselves have to be good,” Duggan said. “Let's not hide behind a sound or a cool riff.”
He wants the band to develop its own songwriting skills rather than depend on outside writers, arguing that strong songs give musicians more freedom to experiment and offer a better path to longevity.
The band's connection with its audience is another part of the plan. Members regularly stay after shows to sign records and shirts and talk with fans, sometimes for as long as two hours. Duggan said those conversations help the band understand how people are discovering its music, whether through Instagram or Spotify.
Touring has also produced its share of mishaps. One crew member was ticketed in Malaysia after packing a giant novelty sex toy intended as a prank for the drummer, apparently unaware the item was prohibited. On another tour, a bus driver failed to secure the trailer properly, and it detached from the bus.
Through it all, the band keeps moving. Duggan, who recently became a father to a baby boy, is already looking ahead to a second album and hopes to set aside several months for writing.
For now, the next wager is Taipei. Culture Wars has seen the numbers online and sold out rooms in Europe and the US. On Nov. 13, the band gets to find out whether that momentum holds on the other side of the world.

How Merz’s five-day Asia trip ended up being mostly about Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01

18:07:45 KST

How Merz’s five-day Asia trip ended up being mostly about Europe
Security concerns are following the German Chancellor to Singapore, Japan and Korea. And his proposal for a new trade alliance is already facing hurdles.
KOREAN DEMILITARIZED ZONE — Friedrich Merz ended his five-day trip to Asia on Friday reflecting on Europe's past.
After visiting the blue barracks where the armistice that ended the Korean War was signed in 1953, in the Joint Security Area where North and South Korean troops stand face-to-face, the German chancellor addressed the obvious parallels between his country's history and Korea's present.
"Thoughts are running through my mind about how grateful we may be that in Germany we haven't had to experience this for 36 years," Merz said.
Advertisement
The remarks concluded a tour of Singapore, Japan and South Korea, where the chancellor was challenged by Asian capitals over security and trade cooperation — and often reminded of how the region's turmoil are intertwined with Europe's precarious moment.
'Collective security'
One only has to look across the border. Shortly before Merz arrived in the demilitarized zone, North Korea fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan. The chancellor's greatest security concerns at home — Russia’s war against Ukraine and Moscow’s threat to Europe — are increasingly becoming problems in the Asia-Pacific region as well.
The fact that Pyongyang is able to launch so many ballistic missiles, testing and expanding its long-range strike capabilities, is directly linked to its cooperation with Russia. North Korea has been sending soldiers to the Russian front in Ukraine for two years and in return benefited from combat experience and technology transfers.
North Korean state television on Thursday showed leader Kim Jong Un with new military drones, including a potential stealth drone, underscoring the great strides the country is also making in drone development. These are serious security issues that other countries in the region, including Japan, cannot ignore.
Besides provocations from Pyongyang, there is China, which is not only becoming increasingly dominant in trade but also casting its eye toward Taiwan, making far-reaching territorial claims in the South China Sea and putting strong pressure on critics such as Japan. And there is Russia, which is forging close military ties with Beijing and carrying out joint bomber flights with the Chinese air force near the Japanese border.
“Russia’s war against Ukraine is ever-present here in the region,” Merz told reporters following his visit to the border. “There is no longer such a thing as unilateral security in the world, only collective security,” he added, underscoring his call to “work closely” with Japan, South Korea and Singapore “on security policy issues” and in the defense industry.
Advertisement
Middle power struggle
This German offer has generated considerable interest. Given Berlin’s position as Ukraine’s largest supporter, German defense companies are highly active in the war-torn country and cooperate with local manufacturers, giving them access to rapid technological developments. This makes them attractive to Asian partners who fear falling behind North Korea and China as they benefit from their cooperation with Russia.
The fact that the chancellor traveled with a large business delegation — the kind previously seen only on visits to China — underscores this focus. Among the companies were several defense firms, including aircraft manufacturer Airbus, air defense manufacturer Diehl Defense and drone specialist Quantum-Systems. Japan welcomed the cooperation, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi speaking of a “premium partnership” with Germany.
Yet Merz's trip was about more than defense deals. The chancellor used his visits to warn against violations of international law by Russia but also increasingly by China and the United States. “We are on the threshold of a new era,” he said in Tokyo. “We are witnessing how the major powers are pursuing a new policy and how international rules are eroding.”
Friedrich Merz arriving in Japan on Oct. 28, 2026. | Hans Von Der Burchard
His words echoed a similar warning issued by German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier during a parallel trip to Beijing. “An order that was never perfect, but at least served as the foundation for international cooperation, is eroding. Lawlessness looms. I see this as a great danger for all of us,” said Steinmeier.
To counter this trend, Merz built on Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's proposal that “middle powers” should team up to better defend themselves in the face of unreliable major powers and toothless international organizations.
In speeches in Tokyo and Seoul, Merz proposed a “global political alliance for rules-based trade.” Medium-sized powers such as the EU, Asian nations, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the South American Mercosur trade bloc should “coordinate” and “act together” if others challenged international rules “or if economic pressure were to be exerted,” said the chancellor.
Advertisement
It's a thinly veiled reference to Chinese threats to restrict access to rare earth metals and the tariff threats made by U.S. President Donald Trump. Merz also said the alliance could strengthen the World Trade Organization and seek to unblock the nomination of judges to the organization's appellate body.
“Considerable concern” over Franco-German car deal
During his trip, however, Merz experienced firsthand just how difficult it is to put such an ambitious proposal into practice when special interests complicate an alliance of small and medium-sized powers.
This became most evident when the Asian countries issued a sharp protest over planned “Made in Europe” rules for the car industry. Under a proposal agreed by Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, Brussels would restrict subsidies for cars to vehicles produced inside the EU, Switzerland and the U.K., putting foreign manufacturers at a disadvantage.
In polite but direct terms, South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung told reporters he had “asked Merz for support so that Korea would be treated like the EU member states.” A similar complaint was voiced in Japan.
“That was, in fact, a topic that surprised me a bit, given the intensity with which it was presented,” Merz told reporters before returning to Germany on Friday evening. He admitted that the Franco-German proposal had “sparked considerable concern in the region — in Singapore, Japan, and Korea — that we may be facing a new wave of protectionism in Europe, that we are closing ourselves off from other countries.”
Merz vowed to take those complaints “very seriously” and raise them at the next EU leaders' summit. Yet they are a sharp reminder of how much industry-specific details can hamper the implementation of his proposed broader alliance.
Advertisement
The chancellor's trip also revealed challenges when it comes to security cooperation: A request for Japan to supply Patriot anti-aircraft missiles to Ukraine fell flat. And it remains unclear whether Tokyo continues to contribute several billions to a new Ukraine loan next year, as Brussels hopes.
A Japanese diplomat, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, posed a different question to the German delegation: “How exactly will you help us if China attacks Taiwan?”

Where are the most expensive midterm races and who is funding them?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:04:44 UTC
18:04:44 KST

Where are the most expensive midterm races and who is funding them?
Senate races in Texas, Michigan and Ohio rank among the most expensive in this year’s midterm cycle.
On Tuesday, voters across the United States will head to the polls to cast a ballot in the 2026 midterm elections.
The race is expected to serve as a referendum on Republican President Donald Trump’s job performance so far, at the halfway mark of his second term.
Maintaining the Republican majority in both chambers of Congress will be key for the success of Trump’s legislative agenda in his final two years.
But control of the US Congress could hinge on a handful of closely contested Senate and House of Representatives races nationwide.
Candidates, political parties and outside groups are pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into the contests, with major political action committees (PACs), including those associated with billionaire tech CEO Elon Musk, fuelling the spending battle.
Which races are costing the most, and who is bankrolling the fight for control of Congress?
What are the most expensive races?
This year’s midterms are projected to break records for the total amount of spending in a political election cycle.
The advertising firm AdImpact estimated that $11.21bn has been spent in total for advertisements and reservations as of October 26, compared with $3.2bn for the 2024 presidential election season.
Among the most expensive individual races are those for toss-up Senate seats. Battles in Texas, Ohio and Michigan rank as the costliest.
The race in Texas, for instance, is projected to shatter spending records for a US Senate race. A Democrat has not won statewide office in Texas since 1994, but Senate hopeful James Talarico aims to break the left-wing party’s losing streak.
Nearly every major poll suggests Talarico has a slim lead over his Republican rival, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. CNN, for instance, projected in late October that Talarico had 49 percent support, compared with Paxton’s 43 percent.
Interest in the race is high. The Texas secretary of state’s office released data indicating that nearly 4.5 million Texans cast their ballots in the first week of early voting alone.
This election cycle, candidate campaigns and outside groups have spent more than $534m on the Texas race.
Talarico has outpaced his opponent in fundraising. The Democrat has raised $146m, compared with Paxton’s roughly $22m. However, Paxton has benefitted from significantly more outside spending, with nearly $300m spent on his behalf, compared with about $80m for Talarico.
Some $37m for Paxton has come from MAGA Inc, a super PAC aligned with President Donald Trump.
Ohio is considered the second-most expensive Senate race this cycle. More than $435m has been spent so far on the contest between Democrat Sherrod Brown and Republican Jon Husted.
Polls are tight in the Buckeye State. A Marist Poll released on October 20 suggested Brown was leading Husted by four points, while other surveys showed the two candidates virtually tied.
So far, roughly $248m has reportedly been spent on the Republican Husted, compared with $187m on the Democrat Brown.
Michigan has also seen record spending in its Senate contest between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
An estimated $333m has been spent on that race. As in Texas, Democrat El-Sayed has led in fundraising but lagged behind his Republican opponent in outside spending.
Rogers has raised about $23m, while El-Sayed has brought in approximately $54m. Outside groups, meanwhile, have spent approximately $169m supporting Rogers and roughly $94m supporting El-Sayed.
A late October poll released by Michigan State University has El-Sayed leading Rogers 48 percent to 45.5, but the race is expected to be tight.
How do fundraising totals compare for Democrats and Republicans?
Republicans have out-raised – and out-spent – Democrats during this year’s midterm cycle.
Candidates and political groups are required to file quarterly reports on campaign donations and spending with the Federal Election Commission (FEC).
According to the FEC’s filings, Republicans have raised more than Democrats since the start of 2025. That cash advantage was noticeable among the committees that lead each party.
For instance, the Democratic National Committee (DNC), which heads the Democratic Party, spent more than it took in. It raised nearly $252.3m but spent about $252.8m.
The Republican National Committee, meanwhile, received about $341m and paid out roughly $303m, as of October 14.
An analysis by the publication Politico, which looked at donors from January 2025 through October, found that Republicans are more reliant on large donors, like Musk, as their small-dollar donor base has grown smaller.
Most donations from everyday people, Politico found, have gone straight to Trump, not the candidates.
But it is unclear whether the Republican Party’s fundraising and spending prowess will be enough to counter Democrats’ enthusiasm. Polls project that the Democratic Party will likely take back the US House and is favoured to control the US Senate as well.
Who are the biggest midterm donors?
The top donors during this campaign have overwhelmingly backed Republicans.
On the right, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk gave $446m, and Elizabeth and Richard Uihlein of the shipping supply chain company Uline donated about $150m.
Jeff Yass, founder of the trading firm Susquehanna International Group, and his wife, Janice, also contributed $110m to right-wing causes in the midterm cycle.
On the left, philanthropist George Soros gave about $102m to left-leaning candidates.
Former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg also pledged $84.2m to Democrats, with an additional $36m added on Friday. Reid Hoffman, the cofounder of LinkedIn, and his wife, Michelle Yee, gave about $41.2m.
But it is the contribution from the world’s richest person that stands out from the rest. Musk has donated nearly as much as the top six donors – on either side of the aisle – combined.
The bulk of the tech billionaire’s donations, more than $150m, has gone to boost Paxton, the Senate hopeful in Texas, in an effort to help Republicans maintain their Senate majority. The contribution amounts to one of the largest political donations in US history.
Big-dollar donors like Musk have increasingly opted to funnel their money towards Senate candidates as the House appears more likely to come under Democratic control.
Among the Republican-aligned groups, the political nonprofit One Nation has spent $133m. The conservative group was founded by allies of former Republican Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.
The American Action Network, a conservative advocacy group, has spent $64.3m, while the American Prosperity Alliance has spent about $51m.
On the Democratic side, Majority Forward has spent $102m, followed by House Majority Forward at about $93.7m and the Economic Opportunity Fund at $41.5m.
