A shot of gold: Curator Marie Shek closes a circle at the Tower of David Museum Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:01:50 UTC
18:01:50 KST

‘For me, Jerusalem is a shot of gold,” said curator Marie Shek. “In my heart it’s close to God, close to what once could have been a dream, and maybe was a dream.”
Shek built a whole exhibition around that idea. Gold: Touches of Gold in Contemporary Israeli Art opened this month at the Tower of David Jerusalem Museum and will run until March 2027. It brings together 16 Israeli artists who work with gold leaf, gold powder, gold thread, and metallic paint, alongside rare archaeological finds in gold, most of them never shown to the public before.
The setting is part of the story. The Citadel’s stones go back more than 2,000 years, through the Hasmoneans, Herod, the Byzantines, the Mamluks, and the Ottomans. The first gold treasure ever found in Jerusalem’s archaeological history, a hoard of Byzantine coins, was excavated right here in the 1980s.
For Shek, the show settles unfinished business. “This is my exhibition number 50 since ’96,” she said. That first exhibition was meant for the Tower of David, and it was a gamble. Shek came to the museum’s director at the time, Adi Semel, with a proposal for a sound art show, long before sound art was in fashion. Her idea was to exchange sounds between East and West through the arrow slits of the Citadel walls.
“The arrow slits were once a place for shooting, for guns, for death, for murder,” she said. “I wanted to carry sound through the ear, from speakers in the western city into the mosque, into the East, and back.” Semel went with it. Eight months into the work, he lost his job, and the people who had worked with him went too.
Shek was left holding a first exhibition and no venue. “You don’t know if you’re worth anything or who you are,” she recalled. She took the project to the Artists’ House in Jerusalem, where Ruti Tzadka agreed on one condition: Shek would bring the funds.
She raised NIS 10,000, the full budget then, and gave each artist, including Gideon Gechtman, Buki Schwartz, Belu-Simion Fainaru, and Philip Rantzer, a room with a sound of his choice. A sound lab produced the catalog. Her son, then in second grade and now 38, still calls it her best show. She brought his whole class to see it, and he remembers.
“That’s how I started my career,” she said. Thirty years and 49 exhibitions later, she has brought the 50th to the Citadel. “I wanted to close the circle at the Tower of David.”
Over three decades, she curated all over the world, but the Citadel stayed with her. “It didn’t sit quietly with me that I hadn’t done something in this spiritual place,” she said. “This place speaks to me. Unlike most Tel Avivians I know, for me Jerusalem goes far beyond religion or politics. First, it’s international. Second, it’s eternal. I’m nothing; we are dust. There were Romans, Ottomans, and Byzantines; Herod lived here, and tomorrow there will be I don’t know what. To be part of the cultural food chain, that’s what I want in this world.”
Shek grew up in Tunis and came to Israel as a child. She studied for her BA in Jerusalem, met her husband there while he served in the Foreign Ministry, and her children were born in the city. She knows how much it has changed. “But didn’t the whole world change?” she asked. “I get on the light rail, I get off at Davidka, I can see the Old City, and I start breathing again.”
'It’s spiritual, it’s the Temple'
GOLD CAME to her almost the moment she knew she would mount a show at the Tower of David. “For me, the place itself is a kind of gold,” she said. “It’s spiritual, it’s the Temple.”
There was a suggestion to call the exhibition “Jerusalem of Gold.” Shek refused. “Absolutely not,” she said. “In my mind, Jerusalem is not of gold. Jerusalem is of wars. Afterward, everyone can build their own movie.”
That is where her own movie begins. It ties back to the child from Tunis. “They told me Israel is a land flowing with milk and honey, and it wasn’t. It all connected,” she said. She recalls her childhood belief that the sidewalks in Israel “were covered with gold,” only to be disappointed upon arrival. “Maybe,” she told me, “maybe this is a way to close the circle.”
She went looking for precedents and found few. “I haven’t seen many exhibitions with gold in the world,” she said. Instead, she spent days in the library of the Pompidou Center in Paris, reading about ancient cultures, the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, and Egypt. She found that gold always belonged to a culture. “It’s a substance that doesn’t oxidize, that doesn’t spoil, whose value is constant and only goes up.”
Her catalog essay follows that thread. Gold has stood for power, holiness, beauty, and eternity, she wrote, from the tombs of the pharaohs through medieval and Renaissance churches to modern art. In the 20th century, it shed its religious ties, and artists such as Gustav Klimt, Yves Klein, Robert Rauschenberg, and Anselm Kiefer used it to probe the relations between matter and spirit, value and memory, and beauty and power.
The Incas, she noted, called it the sweat of the sun, and the ancient Egyptians saw in it the flesh of the gods.
Shek is known for exhibitions that hurt. “All my exhibitions give you a kick in the stomach,” she said. “Even when they’re poetic, they hurt a bit; they remind you, they’re cold. They deal with the harder side of humankind.”
This time she decided otherwise. “I said, I will pamper myself. In such a very, very difficult time, I want people to come in and smile. I want the gold to heal, to be a friend.”
For her, that meant no video. “Video steals the show,” she said. “I didn’t want competition. I wanted the eye of the visitors to stop at every work, look for the gold, and let it fill their souls.”
The result is spare and calm. Every work stands on its own, and the eye moves from one to the next by color and light rather than theme. Shek admitted she chose some pieces purely by sight.
She compared the process of selecting the works to clearing out a closet. “If I took down my wardrobe right now and kept only what I truly love, what I wear, and will keep, I’d keep 20%. Those 20% are this exhibition.”
When I suggested a box of chocolates, she sharpened the image. “Godiva. I went to the Godiva store and chose: the nuts, the orange, not just milk chocolate. That’s what I did for four years.”
Four years, 16 studios
The exhibition took four years to put together, partly because of the war. The delay worked in its favor. It gave Shek and the artists time to find the exact work for each place on the wall, and gave some of them time to create new pieces specially for the show. Several of the works on display date from 2026.
Throughout all four years, a constant question sat in the back of Shek’s mind: How would each artist sit beside the next?
Three generations of one artistic family hang in the show. Moshe Gershuni, one of the most influential artists in the history of Israeli art who died in 2017, is represented by an untitled triptych from 1995. It’s made from acrylic gel and spray on canvas.
In one of its panels, a field of gold is broken by a dark, crusted circle with red at its core, and a thin red drip runs down to the bottom edge. Shek chose the triptych by eye and only learned later, reading on a train, that all three panels dated from 1995.
Facing the triptych hangs his son Aram’s Girl with Golden Hair (2024), which turns the formula around. The ground is black, a young woman stands in profile, and the gold lives only in the mass of curls lit up around her head. Moshe’s granddaughter Alma, born in 1996, made The Man with the Golden Helmet (2026), a clay relief painted in oil after Rembrandt. Here too, the figure is dark, and the gold gathers on the ornate helmet and a few flecks on the shoulder.
Shek often chose the works together with the artists. “What do you love? What do you want it to be?” she would ask. Aram Gershuni, whom she calls a master, offered to paint her a new picture in the classical Renaissance style, with gold. Then, in his studio, she saw a profile he had already painted of his regular model, a young woman with golden hair. The painting, oil on wood, recalls the maidens of Sandro Botticelli. “I saw it and said, that’s it, perfect,” she recalled.
Nelly Agassi, one of Israel’s most important artists, made her piece from scratch. Agassi, who is based in Chicago, kept Shek in the loop through daily phone calls and Zoom sessions, from the first samples of the material she bought in a Chicago store, some 200 fabrics in all, to the filling and every stage after.
“It’s a birth,” Shek said. “I was the doula.” The result, Stronghold (2026), is a gold wall piece of embroidery, silk, and padding that bulges like a living thing.
Joshua Borkovsky has painted for years on the Kaaba, the black cube at the heart of the Great Mosque of Mecca. His Pilgrimage (1986) sets gold leaf against black in a way that recalls the gold-embroidered black curtain that covers the Kaaba.
“His gold is real,” Shek said. “He buys gold. It’s not expensive paint, it’s not just gold leaf, it’s real gold.” When she first visited, Borkovsky told her she should give him the whole exhibition. “He was right, in a way,” she laughed. At the press preview, he lectured at length on the Hajj and on his years of travel in the East.
FOR YIFAT BEZALEL, gold is barely a material at all. In The Window (2023), a large drawing in oil, black gesso, and pastel, it appears only as a thin halo. “But for her the gold is the content,” Shek said. “It’s the Pietà. That’s what’s excellent.” Bezalel draws on Christian iconography and on the Kabbalistic sefirot, and her pencil and gold leaf pull the eye down before the light lifts it again.
The only artist Shek had not known before is Elena Ceretti Stein, who lives and works between Israel and Milan. Shek saw her painting of a delicate, lightly gilded hand, Fuligo Septica after Durer (2025), at the Braverman Gallery and immediately thought of Dafna Shalom. Shalom’s Cast in Sign Language (2026) is a bronze fist cast in a gold hue, one of two hands that together spell the word “we.” Placed together, the two works read as a blessing.
“It’s almost a religious exhibition,” Shek said, then corrected herself. “Not religious, spiritual. As if we received a blessing. Not from the Western Wall. A blessing from above, with the gold, in this place.”
Other artists carry gold into very personal histories. Leor Grady embroiders Psalm verses in gold thread on linen, a technique tied to Yemenite Jewish culture, in Give Thanks to the Lord for He Is Good (2024). The catalog describes his work as an attempt to mend and re-stitch a history full of injustice.
Elham Rokni, who came to Israel from Tehran as a child, built a private dictionary of symbols from Persian carpet culture. Her gilded Hoopoe (2024), Israel’s national bird, graces the catalog cover.
Lilac Sasson’s The Iranian Series (2001-2003) places pages torn from a book on Iranian art and architecture inside iron boxes, partly covered with gold leaf that hides as much as it shows. Yoram Chisin, the third generation of an artistic family whose grandfather decorated a cathedral in eastern France, sometimes buries books under thick impasto.
Miriam Cabessa paints with her body and household objects instead of brushes; at first glance, her painting on aluminum shows a gilded structure that recalls the Temple, and as the viewer moves, the building dissolves into glowing metal. Yoav Brenner’s Beat (2023) also asks visitors to move so the sheen can shift on the surface.
Gabriel Klasmer shows six works on paper in which real gold and imitation gold play off each other, not without irony. At the center of the space sits Mosh Kashi’s Gold Ball (2012), a porcelain sphere in 24-karat gold that reflects the room around it and pulls every gaze toward it.
“THE BOND between Jerusalem and gold runs deep, from the Midrash and Jewish tradition to the city’s very name in song,” said Eilat Lieber, director and chief curator of the Tower of David Jerusalem Museum. “But Gold reaches beyond history. It speaks to something timeless in the human spirit: the yearning for what is pure, true, and eternal, a yearning that grows strongest in times of hardship and uncertainty.
“The works in this exhibition search for light within darkness, for the spark at the heart of things, and it is in the tension between shadow and beauty that they lift us from the everyday toward the sublime.”
“As we open the 60th anniversary year of Jerusalem’s reunification, the Tower of David Jerusalem Museum continues to tell the story of this city through its contrasts: the fleeting and the eternal, creation and preservation,” she said. “Gold adds a vital contemporary layer to that story, one alive with Israeli talent and inspiration. I hope every visitor finds here not only great beauty, but a space to pause, reflect, and connect.”
The Tower of David points visitors beyond the exhibition to more gold in its permanent galleries, among them a hoard of coins minted under the Byzantine emperors Maurice Tiberius and Phocas, found in the Citadel excavations, and a Byzantine gold ring engraved with a seven-branched menorah. On the roof of Phasael Tower, a viewpoint called “Jerusalem of Gold” takes in the city’s golden domes in a full circle.
Down in the galleries, the gold comes in smaller touches: a halo, a thread, a fist, a shining ball. Shek wanted visitors to come in and smile, and they do. Fifty exhibitions into her career, she knows how to give every work its space, and she knows her artists the way a mother knows her children: what each one loves, and who should hang beside whom.
The result is a beautiful show, worth seeing slowly, and more than once. As Shek put it, everyone can build their own movie.
Gold: Touches of Gold in Contemporary Israeli Art will run at the Tower of David Jerusalem Museum until March 2027.
Coins, a queen, and a biscuit tin
The archaeological display, curated by Ravit Nenner-Soriano, ties the show to the city’s ancient past. The items come on loan from the Israel Antiquities Authority and the Staff Officer for Archaeology in Judea and Samaria, and most of them are on public view for the first time.
Two kinds of gold appear here. The first is coinage. “The coin is an object that passes to the merchant on one hand,” Nenner-Soriano says, “and on the other hand, it is a kind of propaganda of the ruler toward his subjects.”
A gold coin of Ptolemy I Soter, the first ruler of the Ptolemaic kingdom after Alexander the Great, comes from the sacred enclosure on Mount Gerizim in Samaria and dates to the early third century BCE. It shows how closely the Egyptian kingdom was tied to the region.
Beside it is a coin of Berenice II, wife of Ptolemy III, dated 246-221 BCE and found in the Givati Parking Lot excavation south of the Temple Mount. The queen appears alone, wearing a diadem and veil. “She was an independent ruler,” Nenner-Soriano says. “She was the queen of the Ptolemaic Empire and minted coins for herself. Berenice II says a lot of things inside this small coin.”
A third find tells a quieter story. Four gold coins turned up in a small jug in an excavation near the Western Wall Plaza. Two date from the late Abbasid period (946-957) and two from the start of Fatimid rule (971-980). Someone hid the savings, meaning to come back for them, and never did. The two pairs of coins also record a change of regime, from Abbasid to Fatimid, in a single hiding place.
The second kind of gold is jewelry: rings, earrings, amulets, and thin gold sheets from Roman and Byzantine tombs, dating from the second to the sixth centuries CE. They belong to the collection of Frances Emily Newton, a British missionary who lived in the country in the early 20th century.
Newton did not dig. She bought from antiquities dealers she knew, and she was choosy. “She told them, give this to the authorities, I’m collecting only gold,” Nenner-Soriano says. She tagged each item with her name and a serial number, kept a diary of where each piece had been found, as the dealers told her, and stored the lot in a safe at her house in Haifa.
When World War I broke out, Newton had to leave for England and gave the key to a neighbor. The Ottoman governor removed the safe and shipped it toward Turkey. The British army intercepted the shipment, and Newton later wrote that the collection came back to her almost whole.
Determined that the public should see it, she packed it into biscuit tins, took it to Jerusalem, and left it on the desk of Prof. John Garstang, director of the Mandatory Department of Antiquities, who was out. The next morning, the tins were gone. Staff turned the offices upside down and searched the trash. The night cleaner, it turned out, had cleared the desk and thrown the tins away. They were rescued from the bin.
When the Rockefeller Museum opened in 1938, a small part of the collection went on display in a case marked as the gift of Frances Newton. What is displayed at the Tower of David now is the part that was never shown.
Newton’s lists have been lost, so the dating rests on comparison. One detail survives from her 1948 book: She loved one medallion so much that she wore it until her last day and asked in her will that it return to the collection. It is on display at the Rockefeller. – N.B.

The water diplomats: How western Negev AgTech and WaterTech are taking root in Colorado
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:01:31 UTC
18:01:31 KST

At Schell Farms outside Sterling, Colorado, the smartest machine on the property never leaves the field. Cameras and ground-penetrating radar, designed in Israel, are bolted to a center pivot and scan the corn and soil on every pass.
"When corn is 10 feet tall in July, you can't see what's happening in the middle of the circle," said Daniel Schell, a fourth-generation grower. "Having the pivot tell my phone, 'Hey, nozzle 14 on span 3 is clogged,' before the crop shows stress, that's huge."
I came to northeastern Colorado as director of Innovation Diplomacy at HaMitbah, the Western Negev Innovation Authority, representing our region's full innovation coalition: Ofakim Municipality, the Eshkol Regional Council , Sapir Academic College's Tech and Innovation Departments, and 17 AgTech and WaterTech companies in our deal flow.
Two food-security engines
Logan County sits in one of the top agricultural regions in the United States, a farm economy worth more than $6 billion, with 1.38 million head of cattle. The Western Negev is Israel's food-security engine, growing 65% of the country's field crops in a desert that gets even less rain.
Our challenges are the same: extreme climate, water scarcity, and labor shortages. The connection began with the BIRD Foundation, the US-Israel Binational Industrial Research and Development Foundation. Trae Miller, executive director of the Logan County Economic Development Corporation (LCEDC), read that Nutrien Ag Solutions had won a BIRD grant with the Israeli smart-spraying start-up GreenEye Technology.
"When I first read the article about Nutrien Ag and their BIRD grant, I was excited to get connected and learn more," Miller said. "After BIRD referred me to Jordan and CO-IL, we began conversations on potential opportunities. That chain of events led to this exploration visit."
The Colorado-Israel Chamber of Commerce (CO-IL), led by co-directors Jordan Kastrinsky and Jeremiah Baronberg, brought in HaMitbah and hosted our delegation.
Autonomous Pivot turns irrigation hardware into a data platform. Its cameras catch clogged nozzles and leaf browning, and its radar reads moisture through the root zone, so growers know whether to irrigate when water allocations run short. The company sells an annual membership instead of a $50,000 hardware package and now runs more than 800 systems across the High Plains.
"His pivot's always there," said Daniel Bridges, the company's US representative, who lived on Kibbutz Kinneret before moving to Kansas. "It doesn't need the weekend off. It doesn't get sick."
Innovation that fits the farmer
Israeli drip irrigation is famous worldwide, yet row-crop farmers here run center pivots and refuse to lay and pull up plastic lines every season.
"They're basically telling you: 'No, I'm not going to put all this in my ground when I'm going to have to pull it up every year,'" Kastrinsky said. "But if I could do something with my pivot where I'm dropping water... that's the thing that works."
Our deal flow fits that reality. Aqueduct Agrotech runs drip at ultra-low gravity pressure, cutting pumping costs. Ness Fertigation plugs into existing irrigation lines to dose fertilizer at the roots.
At NA Timmerman, general manager Ryan Timmerman oversees about 50,000 head of cattle at one of the company's multiple locations.
Asked about his biggest challenge, he pointed to labor with one word: "Help." We presented Cattle Measurement's 3D cameras, which weigh animals without a chute, and RumaFeed, which turns potato and tomato foliage into high-protein feed.
Near Denver, Lioz Aharon of BACCARA USA, a valve maker founded on Kibbutz Geva, offered the hardware backbone young Israeli start-ups need. "Software is great, but at the end of the day, water has to flow through a physical valve that won't fail when hard water or sand gets into the line," he said.
The water diplomats
Logan County Commissioner Jim Yahn, who ran the North Sterling Irrigation District for 34 years, showed us South Platte water rights dating to 1873.
"We use the water seven times," he said. "My return flow, somebody else picks it up downstream."
Colorado's regional basin roundtables bring farmers, cities and state engineers together to settle water disputes before they reach court. Kastrinsky called it social water technology, an innovation Israel can learn from.
The same grassroots ingenuity runs through Graham Electric Planter, where six employees build their own circuit boards to turn old planters into precision machines, and through Northeastern Junior College, whose president, Mike White, welcomed a "twin college" bridge with Sapir College.
What we are building
LCEDC is taking over management of 170 acres beside Sterling's historic 1905 Sugar Factory as a test field for AgTech and WaterTech.
"My game plan as of right now is that the 2027 growing season is really a kickoff," Miller said. "We might have four different water management technologies on one field and be able to compare them."
Bridges committed Autonomous Pivot hardware to the site, and Ofakim set aside land as a reciprocal test site. Lance Gloss of the Colorado Office of Economic Development and International Trade outlined state grant opportunities of up to $500,000.
In March 2027, we will bring Western Negev start-ups to Idea Farming 2.0 in Sterling, and we are exploring a county-to-county partnership.
"County to county," I mentioned to Kastrinsky. "Nobody's done that before in Israel."
At the CO-IL gala in Denver, I told the room: "We come presenting 'Ecosystem as a Service,' exporting field-tested resilience and technologies developed under severe climate and operational stress to help feed a changing world.”
Before I left Sterling, I gave Miller a desert flower from Kibbutz Sa’ad in the Western Negev, sealed in wax, the kind that blooms without water. Next season, on 170 acres of Colorado farmland, we will see what Western Negev innovation can grow.
Noam Bedein, director of Innovation Diplomacy and Strategic Partnerships, HaMitbah, the Western Negev Innovation Authority

Over $6 billion in 20 minutes: FBI accuses North Korea of largest-ever crypto hack against Binance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:01:19 UTC
18:01:19 KST

The FBI accused North Korea of stealing more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance in a cyberattack on Thursday, identifying the perpetrators as a North Korean hacking operation known as TraderTraitor, according to a statement released on Saturday.
The attack, which occurred on October 29, is believed to be the largest cryptocurrency theft in history, surpassing previous cyberattacks targeting digital asset exchanges.
In its official cybersecurity alert, the FBI attributed the theft to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), North Korea's official name, and warned that the hackers had already begun converting the stolen funds into other cryptocurrencies.
Working alongside the US Secret Service and the Internal Revenue Service's Criminal Investigation division, the bureau said investigators had observed TraderTraitor operatives converting stolen digital assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH), one of the world's largest cryptocurrencies.
The agencies warned that the stolen assets were expected to undergo additional laundering through decentralized finance (DeFi) platforms and instant cryptocurrency exchange services, potentially complicating efforts to trace and recover the funds.
The blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs estimated that approximately $6.36 billion was transferred from Binance wallets across 10 blockchain networks during the October 29 attack, with most of the assets moved in roughly 20 minutes. The firm attributed the operation to TraderTraitor with high confidence.
US agencies urge cryptocurrency platforms to block stolen funds
The FBI called on cryptocurrency exchanges, blockchain infrastructure operators, and other digital asset service providers to help prevent the stolen funds from moving further through the financial system.
The appeal specifically targeted THORNode operators, remote procedure call (RPC) node operators, instant exchanges, DeFi services, and blockchain analytics firms.
These organizations were urged to block transactions involving digital wallet addresses identified as being controlled by or closely connected to the North Korean hackers.
The FBI published an extensive list of cryptocurrency addresses associated with the theft, including wallets on the Ethereum, Bitcoin and Solana networks. The bureau said the addresses either currently hold or previously held assets stolen during the attack.
The alert reflects concerns that the hackers could exploit the decentralized nature of cryptocurrency transactions to obscure the origins of the stolen assets and move them beyond the reach of investigators.
Binance said Saturday that it had replenished approximately 90% of the stolen cryptocurrency and set aside about $6.34 billion in company funds to cover the losses. The exchange also said it had been working with blockchain partners to identify and freeze affected assets.
The company suspended withdrawals after the breach and said it was working the restore service on Sunday. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng described the breach as a complex attack involving a compromised laptop and malware designed to erase evidence of the intrusion.
The exchange has pledged to cover customers' losses, drawing on its corporate treasury and financial reserves as it works to restore normal operations.

He was allegedly targeted via an IDF drone while he was on the roof of a displaced people shelter in Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip after receiving a phone call from a Shin Bet officer giving him the choice between having the whole shelter bombed with his family inside or going up to the roof to be targeted alone. ====================================================================================================

The AniNation animation festival marks its first decade of business at the Jerusalem Cinematheque
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:01:14 UTC
18:01:14 KST

If, like me, you are of a certain vintage and you instinctively associate the word “animation” with such industry leaders as Disney or former cartoon trailblazer Hanna-Barbera of Tom and Jerry fame, a visit to this year’s AniNation animation festival, taking place at the Jerusalem Cinematheque between November 3-8, should help to flex your thinking on the filmic field in question.
Artistic director Shlomi Steiner Yosef, now in his fifth stint with the festival, has covered numerous stylistic, genre, cultural, thematic, and philosophical bases in a programmatic roll-out that caters to all kinds of tastes, leanings, and age groups. This year’s edition also closes the festival’s first decade of envelope-pushing entertaining endeavors. Not bad going for any cultural venture here, it must be said.
Steiner Yosef does not just have an educated overview of the wider global animation scene. He is in the thick of the creative action himself, as an independent artist, director, and animator who tends to dip into an eclectic range of disciplines in his work. His curatorial choices were duly fueled by his own overarching professional experience.
The six-day program is a very varied affair. There are choice items from all over the geographic and cultural landscape, including an intriguing satirical French work called Jim Queen, with the somewhat absurd yet thought-provoking storyline focusing on the outbreak of a virus in Paris that turns gay men into heterosexuals. And there is Peleliu: Guernica of Paradise, which is based on a Japanese manga series.
It is set in the dying days of World War II and raises deep questions about the value of life, morality, and how to physically and emotionally survive extreme violence. That, of course, references our own existential circumstances here and should leave viewers with plenty of food for thought. There is also a nod to the power of art and visual presentation.
“Comics are the art of imagining fictional stories,” observes a Japanese officer in the movie and, one may add, of reflecting real life.
Animation evolution
Animated cinematic material has come a long way since the days of Tom and Jerry and Donald Duck. The festival itinerary features several full-length efforts with intriguing, alluring, entertaining content. In addition to the aforementioned, there is something of a psychedelic film by Spanish director Alberto Vázquez called Decorado.
Imagine, if you will, a central character in the shape of an unemployed middle-aged mouse who surveys the world around him as an artificial theater set. Things go comically from bad to worse as he tries to make sense of the catastrophes he encounters en route to finding his own truth. Not exactly Snow White and her seven little pals.
Interestingly, 41-year-old Steiner Yosef’s own pathway into the inner workings of the animation field was sparked by a perennially popular, perfectly delectable classic created long before he was even a twinkle in his parents’ eyes.
“The first animated film I saw was The Jungle Book, when I was nine,” he says, surprising me, and very pleasantly, I may add. That was a high-class introduction. The Walt Disney Productions creation came out in 1967, the last feature produced by Disney himself, and has proven its staying power over the years, despite being crafted using old-school technological means.
Notwithstanding the huge advances made in animation technology in the almost six decades since that iconic Disney movie, there are contemporary animators who opt, at least, to start with a manually fashioned substratum before bringing in the big technological guns. One such project is Letter to A Pig by Tal Kantor, which was a nominee for an Oscar in the Short Animated Film category in 2024.
If you are more than a little dismayed at the way technology is taking over good old human abilities, proffering neat shortcuts to results and nimbly leapfrogging the “bother” of having to actually put some manual and/or mental effort into the venture, you might find Kantor’s creative process encouraging and heartwarming.
The 30-something Jerusalem-born animator and filmmaker used basic paintbrushes and paper to create the baseline for the characters and scenes in the film that referenced the Holocaust, and shone an unforgiving light on our ability to express sympathy and empathy, and how we treat the world around us.
Steiner Yosef is more than happy to trumpet Kantor’s stellar showing, along with the efforts of his compatriot professional counterparts. And that despite the ludicrously petty support they get from the state.
“Each year, I am so proud of what we [in the Israeli animation community] manage to do, and what I am able to show in the AniNation program,” he beams. “It beggars belief that people continue to create such original and meticulous works here.”
Local industry strides
Things are moving along nicely, despite all the hurdles to be navigated.
“Not so many years ago there was no animation industry here; there weren’t all those [academic] departments that teach animation. Many members of the [animation] community are dead-set on promoting the field. The industry has to grapple with lots of difficulties,” he says.
Naturally, that includes the financial aspect, although Steiner Yosef isn’t taking that personally. “It’s the same for most areas of culture here,” he observes.
Regarding his own professional field, he says that is partly down to simple ignorance rather than any ill will, per se. “They [state powers that apportion aid] just don’t know how to relate to animation, including providing support for the festival. It’s not the same as cinema. Yes, animation is also shown on screens, but it is different, and requires a different approach.”
Things ain’t getting easier, either: “I recently attended a meeting with all the [cultural sector] unions at the Knesset when we learned about the budget cuts.” Cuts? There surely isn’t too much left to cut. “Whatever there was will now be reduced,” he notes with commensurate gravitas. “That’s part of it. The cultural pie is small in any case.”
Steiner Yosef and his fellow Israeli artists can only look on with envy at the helping hand their counterparts in other OECD countries get for their creative endeavors. “France, for example, has the CNC (National Centre for Cinema and the Moving Image). The state and, naturally, the public are totally behind it, and the citizens pay a culture tax and are happy to do so. That money is invested in culture, and helps to disseminate French culture around the world.”
Now there’s a thought. Perhaps making greater efforts to spread the Israeli artistic word abroad might pay dividends and make some difference to the way people elsewhere relate to us. In any case, the politicians don’t seem to be making much headway on that score, so why not give our artists a shot?
There is also a misconception about the financial outlay required to bring animated works to full fruition. One might have thought that, in the absence of actual human actors and with the largely technologically-assisted production and directorial process involved, putting a cartoon movie together is logistically a lot simpler and financially more user-friendly.
“Not at all,” Steiner Yosef enlightens me. “There are so many people involved. You only have to look at the length of the credits at the end of an animated film to see that.” I stand corrected.
Recognition from abroad
Happily, the word of Israeli animation is getting out and about beyond our shores and, amazingly in these politically charged times, there are a bunch of professionals flying in to lend some of their knowledge and expertise to the festival.
“There is a group of 14 coming over – 13 from LA and one from Spain,” Steiner Yosef advises. “They are coming to learn more about Israeli animation. They will also serve as jurors for the competition.” That references the shorts competition, with the entries screened on the first day of the program.
Members of the incoming contingent will also present master classes, including one by celebrated Canadian-American voice actress Tara Strong. “She is renowned for her voice work in animation, websites, and video games,” says Steiner Yosef. Strong will enlighten her audience about what went into devising some of her iconic characters from Hello Kitty, The Powerpuff Girls, and My Little Pony.
That warms the cockles. Indeed, any artists or, let’s face it, anyone at all willing to make the trek over here these days, no doubt defying all manner of anonymous or otherwise online fire and brimstone sent their way via social media, are a welcome occurrence.
One thing that appears to set animated offerings apart from movies with actual actors is the capacity of the former to accommodate and thereafter present to viewers all manner of topics and storylines which may be considered a little too close to the bone for the regular format. Steiner Yosef has a left-field take on that.
“Throughout time, animation has provided a means for conveying messages that could be considered subversive,” he laughs. “That is probably because of its ostensibly innocent image.” If one thinks back to the Disney-like persona conjured by beloved characters such as Mickey Mouse, Cinderella, or Pocahontas, that public profile makes perfect sense.
But there are also decidedly non-lily white figures in the art form’s timeline, such as Fritz the Cat, the eponymous feline from the 1972 film who is into drugs, radical politics, and hedonism. That’s about as far away as you can get from the socially acceptable creatures that are more readily identified with cartoon output. That’s not just an American thing. Animation has also made use of its seemingly non-threatening front elsewhere to bypass political or etiquette strictures.
“Under Soviet Union regimes, there were wonderful works that managed to introduce a degree of criticism of repression,” says Steiner Yosef. “They got away with that because the authorities related to the films as being tailored to children. They didn’t take that on board.”
At the end of the day, the festival honcho posits, all filmic output has some kind of subtext to it. “In Hollywood, for example, there is always some kind of message in there, some kind of [societal-moralistic] Christian American value they want to get across. It’s the same with animation, of course, together with the entertainment element.”
Natalie Rissin’s Ve’az Me At (And So, Who Are You?) contribution to AniNation is a case in point. It is an apolitical venture, though it could be construed as political with a small p, which tells the moving documentary-like story of Rissin’s own mother who of Rissin’s own mother who, at the relatively advanced age of 56, dispensed with her traditional homemaker role and became a flight attendant. It is basically a coming-of-age picture, albeit way past the normal game-changing stage of adolescence.
“It’s interesting that as a service provider she finds freedom. She has to wear a uniform, and stick to a routine, but still finds new meaning in her life.”
Offering a different view of the regional conflict
Boh Niftor Et Zeh Echat Uletamid (Let’s Settle This Once and For All), by Shalev Ben Elya and Michael Jacob Buchstav, is another homegrown effort worthy of note. It features in the Short Animation Films competition and runs all of eight minutes. Modest length notwithstanding, Ben Elya and Buchstav make the most of the format and raise the continually burning issue of finding a solution to our regional conflict.
The filmmakers deftly shed light on the eternal quandary by asking young Arabs and Jews how they would resolve the matter. Their replies are presented as moves in a chess game, each of which sparks a countermove as the “players” search for the decisive advantage.
AniNation not only covers an eclectic range of topics, but it also culls works from different cultures around the globe. In addition to films by some of our own promising talents, there are items from Britain, the US, China, France, Japan, and Germany.
The latter includes a 100-year-old film called The Adventures of Prince Achmed, made by Lotte Reiniger. It is a true historical gem and is the oldest surviving feature-length animated film. The screening will be accompanied by a live score performed by DJ-producer Itamar Shlomo Cohen.
The British contribution includes a mouth-watering selection from Aardman Animations, marking the renowned market leaders’ 50th anniversary with a medley of movies made by Oscar-winning Wallace & Gromit creator Nick Park. Anyone over the age of, say, 40 may recall the seminal The Wrong Trousers caper, from 1993, which introduced audiences all over the world to the lovable adventurous pair. It also landed director Nick Park an Oscar for his troubles.
That features in a three-parter of the first Park works released, which also includes A Grand Day Out and A Close Shave. The Aardman medley slot goes by the name of Cinema Stitch and takes place on November 6 in cooperation with the Jerusalem-based The Crafts Club.
The screenings will be preceded by craft workshops and a knitting circle lasting an hour, with patrons encouraged to watch the movies with their knitting, felting, sketchbook, embroidery, or any quiet creative practice, “and settle into the shared rhythm of making while watching the films.”
That hands-on accompaniment to the silver-screen entertainment sounds simply delightful and imbues the berth with an oxymoronic experiential ambiance. In truth, there is an AI/technologically-spawned virtual domain vs tangible reality ebb-and-flow dynamic to the entire festival program, which is packed with fun, compelling and thought-provoking works from right across the stylistic and thematic board.
Ten years after its birth, it would be fair to say that the AniNation festival truly offers something for everyone.
For tickets and more information: jer-cin.org.il/en

Asylum seekers still being sent to France under ‘one in one out’ weeks after scheme ended
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:00:07 UTC
18:00:07 KST

The Home Office is still putting asylum seekers on to planes to France weeks after the controversial scheme to remove them ended, the Guardian has learned.
The “one in, one out” scheme was announced by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the former prime minister Keir Starmer in July 2025. It aimed to deter small boats crossing the Channel to the UK from northern France, with some asylum seekers arriving here forcibly returned to France while a similar number in northern France were brought legally to the UK.
The scheme ended on 1 October, but the Home Office is understood to still be detaining dozens of people. Officials chartered a plane to France on Wednesday for a group of people who are thought to have arrived on small boats in the UK before the scheme ended. A second flight is scheduled for 17 November.
Home Office sources said returns of the remainder of the “one in, one out” cohort were continuing after the deal had ended. According to freedom of information data, almost one-third of the scheme’s deportation flights – seven out of 23 – were cancelled between July and September this year, more than double the total of cancelled deportation flights to France in the first six months of 2026.
Emma Ginn, the director of Medical Justice, said that asylum seekers are still being held in detention centres in preparation for forced removal to France. “Even though the scheme has been abandoned, vulnerable people still held under its powers continue to suffer immensely due to the severe harm known to be caused by immigration detention being compounded by the prospect of imminent return to France, where many have reported experiencing violence and abuse at the hands of smugglers.”
The scheme has been controversial because it does not appear to have had the intended deterrent effect on small boat crossings, and many asylum seekers have reported being left homeless or abused by smugglers. Some were told they would be sent back to other EU countries they passed through on their journeys to the UK. While small boat crossings have reduced by approximately 40% so far this year compared with the same period last year, there has been a similar level of reduction in irregular migration to Europe over the same period.
Home Office data showed that after no crossings for three weeks, 263 people crossed in three boats on Thursday and 671 people in nine boats on Friday.
The Guardian understands that at least seven asylum seekers returned to France have come back to the UK since 1 October, with reports of several more waiting in northern France to cross back to the UK in the next few days when a favourable weather window is forecast.
The Guardian has interviewed two asylum seekers who the UK sent to France during the scheme who have returned to UK since 1 October and are having their asylum claims processed in the UK.
The first is Syrian and the second Iranian. Both returned just days after one in, one out finished.
“At first the Home Office put me back in detention,” said the Syrian man. “They said they were looking for a safe third country to deport me to. But there wasn’t one, so they released me and my asylum claim is now being looked at in the UK. I am very relieved that I am no longer locked up and am safe in the UK.”
The Iranian man said he had been planning to return to the UK for several months as he had been abused by smugglers in France and wanted to escape as soon as he could.
“I was tortured and beaten by the smugglers. I was too afraid to go outside in France. People have no idea how difficult the life is in France for people like us sent back by the UK.”
Maddie Harris of Humans for Rights Network questioned the purpose of the scheme as hundreds gather along the French coast waiting to cross the Channel. “Hundreds of millions of pounds of British taxpayers’ money has been transferred to the French government. Men, women and children are teargassed and beaten on the beaches, after being subjected to repetitive, violent evictions from living sites, yet people still cross to the UK. This money has done nothing but cause harm. Our government fails to acknowledge the most obvious policy to prevent dangerous crossings: accessible safe routes for all to claim asylum in the UK.”
According to evidence the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, gave to a recent session of parliament’s cross-party home affairs committee, removing people to France has cost at least £78m. Some who were sent to France returned to UK and were then returned to France a second time, incurring a further cost.
One asylum seeker who was sent back to France under the scheme and is now in the area known as the “Jungle” in Dunkirk, a camp where asylum seekers pitch tents while waiting to cross the Channel, told the Guardian: “There are at least five or six people from one in, one out waiting in the Jungle at the moment to cross the Channel back to the UK. The place is so full at the moment of people waiting to cross there is no space for people to lie down and sleep. The Home Office has not stopped people reaching the UK, but both the smugglers and the French government have made a lot of money out of this scheme.”
Another, who said he was 17 years old, explained he had been caught by police when trying to board a lorry to cross the Channel a few days ago but would continue to try to reach the UK.
“It is very dangerous to get here but we have no choice. Somehow we will handle it.”

Why Scottish nationalists should see Burnham as a real threat – and an opportunity | Rory Scothorne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:00:07 UTC
18:00:07 KST

Fifty years ago this month, a group of leftwing Scots gathered in the Golden Lion hotel in Stirling for the inaugural conference of a new political party. The “Scottish Labour party” had formally split from Labour at the beginning of 1976, driven by disillusionment over the party’s timid proposals for a new Scottish assembly. They were led by the firebrand MP for South Ayrshire, Jim Sillars, who promised to take Scotland’s Labour tradition back to its roots in both socialism and home rule.
Sillars’ new party was a media sensation in Scotland, and quickly joined by public intellectuals such as Tom Nairn, Hamish Henderson and Neal Ascherson. It offered something new and exciting: a fusion of the two movements that were battling for Scotland’s soul in a decade that had already been defined by electoral clashes between Labour and the Scottish National party.
The party struggled, however, to enthuse the working-class voters on whom Sillars had gambled his future. It did attract a handful of Trotskyist activists from the International Marxist Group, and at the October 1976 conference, Sillars orchestrated a heavy-handed purge of the far left, causing proceedings to degenerate into near-violence. At one point, a member of the party’s national organising committee summoned up Ayrshire’s mining heritage against the “entryist” threat, yelling: “We should get our fucking pit boots on and wade into them!”
Andy Burnham was not quite as forthright earlier this month, when, midway through the SNP’s conference in Aberdeen, he delivered his own speech in Motherwell, offering to cooperate on further devolution within Scotland. The conference itself was far more peaceful, the SNP having already shed its “fundamentalist” wing with the breakaway of Alex Salmond’s Alba party (which Sillars, it’s worth noting, also endorsed). The National Economic Council meeting on Friday between Burnham, John Swinney and the Welsh first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth, emphasised the shared agenda of three governments seeking to combine devolved power with reindustrialisation – precisely what the SLP was calling for in 1976. But the SLP, which never recovered from its public meltdown in Stirling, made another contribution to the cause that matters intensely to the relationship between Burnham and the SNP.
Keen to make national self-determination palatable to socialists, Sillars’ party sought to remove any hint of separatism from its politics by embracing the new European Economic Community, arguing for “independence in Europe”. With goods, people and services moving freely across borders, independence would no longer mean separation, but simply real equality between self-governing, co-dependent nations.
After the SLP’s collapse, Sillars found his way into the SNP, rising through the ranks to become deputy leader in 1991. “Independence in Europe” came with him. The SNP made some of its first breakthroughs in the 1970s as a Eurosceptic party, distinguishing itself from the three pro-EEC Westminster parties by campaigning against membership in 1975 with the slogan “No voice, no entry”. But by the 1990s, it had completely reversed this position, helped by the new European Union’s growing emphasis on the rights of small nations and minority cultures.
The SNP’s newfound Europeanism reflected and reinforced that of the country it came to govern. It was helped, too, by Scotland’s tendency to define itself against English politics, which became more Eurosceptic over the same period. When the SNP’s success produced a referendum on independence, Europe was one of the central issues. An independent Scotland, voters were told, would be a new state, and would therefore have to reapply to join the EU. Scots voted against independence partly to protect their European passports. Two years later, they voted overwhelmingly to remain in that larger union too.
But England, with 10 times Scotland’s population, swung the result the other way. Scotland was thus asked, over the period of just two years and two votes, to choose between its membership of the UK and of the EU – but in the wrong order. Immediately after the Brexit vote, support for independence briefly surged, but then dropped. Scots realised they did not fancy yet another wrenching break-up. It was only with the arrival of Boris Johnson as prime minister, the conclusion of a hard Brexit, and the beginning of the Covid-19 pandemic that “yes” moved into a consistent lead.
Today, yes and no are neck and neck, but many independence campaigners remain concerned about how another referendum campaign might unfold. The fundamental political case for independence has always been that British politics is overwhelmingly Anglocentric, and Scotland’s interests are marginalised. While Brexit has deepened this structural complaint, it has also transformed the economic arguments against independence: if Scotland were to vote for independence and rejoin the EU tomorrow, it would suddenly face a hard border with the rest of the UK, which buys more of Scotland’s exports than every other country in the world put together – including the whole EU.
Some nationalists argue that, under such circumstances, Scotland could be granted the same status as Northern Ireland, which has found a middle ground between European and UK markets. But Northern Ireland has been given special treatment because of the simmering threat of a return to open conflict over the partition of Ireland; Scotland is not a remotely serious candidate for civil war over its borders with England or Europe and would be highly unlikely to be treated with the same sensitivity by the global community.
Scottish nationalism’s problem is also its greatest selling point: it is not motivated by any deep ethnic grievance, and as such its supporters are hard to mobilise into the kind of bloody-minded self-sacrifice that might justify some deeper rupture with England. It is founded, instead, on a modern, peaceful and democratic discontent with Westminster’s gradual abandonment of everything that seemed to make Britain worthwhile: good jobs, functioning public services, international cooperation and a vaguely shared moral compass.
Burnham is therefore a meaningful threat to the SNP, for this is precisely the nostalgic vision of Britain that he promises to restore – with messaging skills that can finally rival the SNP’s and promises of “regional empowerment”. Yet it offers an opportunity as well. It is hard to imagine that Burnham, whether he has three years in power or a decade, will truly be able to resurrect the lost world of dignified work, British industry and social security that he conjures up in his speeches. But it looks increasingly plausible that he may have to rebuild some of Britain’s relationships with Europe as a precondition of his wider agenda. That would repair the one bridge that Scotland truly needs intact for a successful sprint towards independence, should the rest of Burnham’s project falter.
- Rory Scothorne is a historian and writer based in Edinburgh

WHO candidate Budi Sadikin: no country can fight a pandemic alone
Here is episode two of our series in partnership with the Global Health Centre at Geneva's Graduate Institute, bringing you exclusive interviews with the candidates for director general of the World Health Organization (WHO).

Switzerland and the AfD: political, personal and financial ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Switzerland and the AfD: political, personal and financial ties
As the Alternative for Germany (AfD) continues to gain support in its home country, its Swiss connections are also attracting some fresh attention.
Like most countries, Germany is keen to ensure its politics does not come under the influence of foreign meddling, including in the form of donations to political parties. As such, gifts from outside the European Union are capped at €1,000 (CHF918); anonymous donations are also not allowed. Oversight is mainly done by Germany’s parliamentary administration.
But should the country where illicit donations originate also take responsibility? In the Swiss parliament recently, the Green Party’s Andrea de Meuron askedExternal link just this – and referred specifically to the AfD, whose surge in popularity in recent years has sparked debates about the compatibility of its far-right positions with liberal democracy.
De Meuron cited the case of a contested €2 million donation, with alleged Swiss links, which the AfD is appealingExternal link in a Berlin court. The party was also fined in 2020 over a €130,000 donation from a Zurich pharma firm. “Such cases show that Switzerland acts as a ‘hub’ for illicit financing models,” de Meuron claimed. She wants the government to clarify what can be done to prevent them – as well as what they mean for the country’s reputation.
What can be expected? A justice ministry response to her question is likely during the parliamentary session starting November 30. But according to Odile Ammann from the University of Lausanne, Switzerland’s own political finance transparency rules, introduced in 2023, do not address financial flows leaving the country. That said, she adds, one “loophole” in the Swiss regulations – allowing “intermediary structures” to hide the origins of political donations – can also obscure the source of donations being sent abroad.
Due to the loophole, Ammann tells Swissinfo, “it would not surprise me if there were additional examples” – beyond the AfD – of illicit political funding coming out of Switzerland. She has previously recommended tightening the law.
>> How transparent is political funding in Switzerland compared to other European countries?
More
What role does money play in Swiss politics?
Small town life in Schwyz
Yet whatever the government’s answer to de Meuron, the AfD’s links with Switzerland go well beyond the question of financing, and have done for some years.
One of the most visible ties involves the residency status of AfD co-leader Alice Weidel. Though her political career is in Germany, a lot of her private life is centred in Switzerland. She has a home with her wife and children in Einsiedeln, canton Schwyz – a quiet place where she says she can “recharge her batteries”, far from Berlin’s pressures, as she toldExternal link the NZZ am Sonntag newspaper in 2025.
Yet while Weidel still also has a German address and pays her taxes there, her status as a “German abroad” – particularly at the head of a nationalist party – can raise eyebrows. And as the party continues to gain in popularity, scrutiny has intensified, the Blick newspaper recently wroteExternal link, noting that even AfD supporters aren’t overjoyed about their leader living abroad. Switzerland, meanwhile, is rather used to prominent foreign residents – although there have been questions about police security for Weidel. And in 2025, hundreds turned up in Einsiedeln to protest against the AfD.
Fans of the Swiss model
Weidel and her party also seem to have a clear – and often positive – vision of Switzerland. For example, as a place where things work well. In a recent interviewExternal link with the British Economist magazine, Weidel spoke of a “brain drain” from Germany, with people leaving the country due to what she claimed was insecurity, high costs, and a lack of prospects. “[People] rather work in the US, or Switzerland, or somewhere else, but not in Germany anymore,” she said.
More importantly, AfD figures see Switzerland as having successfully pursued goals that they themselves share: maintaining sovereignty in relation to the European Union, preserving a certain cultural homogeneity, or giving citizens more say through direct democracy. “Switzerland is one of our models,” the AfD’s Björn Höcke toldExternal link Blick in 2023. There is also here a “tendency to remove the country’s character, but common sense still prevails”, added Höcke, an AfD regional leader who has been convictedExternal link of using a banned Nazi slogan.
>> Swiss-style referendums and people’s initiatives are particularly appealing to the AfD:
More
Why the AfD is keen on Switzerland’s direct democracy
Parallels with the Swiss People’s Party
Whether or not this “model” aligns with Swiss realities is more complicated. It does however align in parts with the model put forward by the right-wing Swiss People’s Party, the biggest political group in Switzerland for decades. Often seen as a pioneer of right-wing populism in Europe, the People’s Party rose to prominence at the turn of the century with a combination of economic liberalism and sovereigntist demands. As such, it has also frequently drawn comparisons with the AfD – although direct parallels are difficult to make, not least because of the very different Swiss political system, based on consensus and the inclusion of all major parties, including the People’s Party, in governing.
It does seem that the People’s Party has long been on the contact lists of some top AfD politicians. In 2016, before the German party’s recent rise, its then-leader Frauke Petry spoke at an event in canton Bern run by the Campaign for an Independent and Neutral Switzerland, an isolationist group with close ties to the People’s Party. More recently, Weidel has been at People’s Party events in Zurich; former Swiss government minister Ueli Maurer even appeared by video at a 2025 AfD campaign rally. And according to trove of hacked AfD emails leaked in October, and reportedExternal link on by the SonntagsBlick, Weidel floated the phrase in 2017 of “making the AfD into a German version of the Swiss People’s Party”, before her spokesperson advised against it.
As for the People’s Party itself, it has talked down the links. It “maintains no official contact or exchange with foreign parties”, the party’s president Marcel Dettling told the Zofinger Tagblatt last year. And it’s not alone on this: the AfD’s far-right reputation has also led some other right-wing groups in Europe, like the National Rally in France, to keep their distanceExternal link from the AfD.
What is clear is that, comparisons of ideology aside, both the AfD and the Swiss People’s Party are currently reaching voters. As the Neue Zürcher Zeitung wroteExternal link after the AfD’s gains in September regional elections, both have managed to move beyond core themes like immigration to do something centrist parties aren’t managing to: bundle daily concerns like living costs or education into an overarching narrative that resonates with many.

Kärcher CEO warns Europe faces 'perfect storm' as he calls for economic reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:59:35 UTC
17:59:35 KST

Europe and Germany risk deindustrialisation, Kärcher CEO Hartmut Jenner has warned. He is urging major cuts in bureaucracy, incentives for extra work and a firm EU trade policy towards China and the US.
Hartmut Jenner, the CEO of German cleaning equipment manufacturer Kärcher, believes Germany and Europe are facing a "perfect storm" when it comes to the economic situation facing the continent.
"Geopolitical crises are casting a shadow over the European economy. The unpredictable trade policy of the U.S. keeps threatening, without warning, to raise tariffs and erect trade barriers – a toxic scenario for free global trade and export-oriented companies," he wrote in an exclusive opinion piece for Euronews.
US and China are making fair competition 'virtually impossible'
In addition to US trade policy, the executive also pointed to the threat posed by China's tech growth: "China is no longer merely a low-cost manufacturer but has become a highly aggressive technological competitor that, with its tremendous speed, threatens to outpace key European industries in future-oriented fields," he wrote.
China's success is the result of a targeted state industrial policy. The country operates with massive subsidies in strategic key industries and with a "currency policy artificially focused on competitiveness," per Jenner.
Both help contribute to "noticeable market distortions and overcapacity," he went on.
For privately run companies like Kärcher, this creates an imbalance "that makes fair global competition almost impossible," Jenner added.
Germany faces the threat of deindustrialisation
Jenner, 61, has been the head of Kärcher since 2001 and has tripled both staff numbers and turnover in that time.
Now he is warning of a downturn in the German economy: "The loss of tens of thousands of industrial jobs and the decline in production volume show that deindustrialisation is not an abstract threat – it is happening right now."
"When plant closures and production relocations are being negotiated in key German industries such as the automotive and manufacturing sectors, it must be clear even to the most optimistic observer: We are at a critical turning point," he continued.
So far Kärcher has managed to make it through these difficult moments, Jenner said.
The company invests heavily in research and development, setting benchmarks in cleaning robots, battery technologies and the digitalisation of all areas of the business.
According to the company, more than 1,000 employees worldwide work in research and development.
Kärcher was founded in 1935. In 2025, the company generated almost €3.5 billion in turnover. The firm, which is still family owned, earned 86% of that abroad.
Kärcher's portfolio comprises more than 3,000 products related to cleaning and care, with its high-pressure cleaners particularly well known.
The company's headquarters are in Winnenden in the state of Baden Württemberg. It operates in 87 countries and employs 17,000 people around the world.
Business conditions and unfair competition making new jobs uneconomical
Yet even "innovation leaders" as Jenner describes his company cannot always prevail against "increasingly challenging operating conditions."
In view of sharply rising structural and labour costs, new production facilities and additional jobs in Germany and Europe are barely economically viable, he said.
Accordingly, Jenner is taking the German government to task.
Forecasts of 1.3% economic growth in Germany are "cautiously optimistic," but he warned that people should not be fooled by them, arguing it was "borrowed growth" - artificially driven by government debt, defence orders and subsidies.
"A short-term boost fueled by debt is no substitute for a real, self-sustaining recovery in private investments," Jenner wrote for Euronews.
"The causes of the ongoing weakness are largely homegrown: a creeping reform fatigue and a regulatory frenzy on the part of government institutions that hinders rather than facilitates investment," he added. "Instead of promoting entrepreneurship, regulations from Brussels to Berlin are suffocating the courage to embrace change."
Jenner grew up as the youngest child on his parents' farm in Winnenden. He studied business administration and engineering and continued to work on the family farm alongside his studies until he joined Kärcher in 1991 as an assistant. Hard work was instilled in him on the family farm.
"Success doesn’t just fall from the sky; for me, it consists of 97% hard work and dedication, 2% talent, and 1% luck."
His conclusion: "If we want to secure our prosperity and our social standards, we must once again recognize that value creation is the precondition for prosperity – and not the other way around. If you rest, you rust – that applies to people just as much as it does to economies."
Fight against bureaucracy, more work and determined trade policy
The Kärcher boss is therefore calling for "a real fitness programme for Germany."
Above all, rigid rules, excessive bureaucracy, high energy costs and steadily rising non-wage labour costs are poison for Germany as a business location, he argued.
But instead of tackling the problem at its root, a flood of regulations is allowed to continue, tying up valuable working time and costing companies millions, Jenner went on.
"Money and personnel that are needed for core business operations and innovation are being wasted on documentation requirements alone."
Cosmetic corrections are not enough, he said, what is needed is a cultural shift in the administrative apparatus, with authorities acting as service providers for business, pragmatic, fast and supported by AI.
"If other countries are already moving toward eliminating reporting obligations overall, this must send a clear signal to Germany and all Europe."
People should not shy away from necessary labour market debates either, Jenner stressed, adding that "demographic trends require an increase in the overall volume of work in the economy."
"Incentives for overtime, flexible working hours, practical rules regarding continued pay during medical leave, and a noticeable reduction in bureaucracy when employing skilled workers are essential."
Jenner is also calling on the EU to pursue a "resolute trade policy at the European level that guarantees fair competition and consistently punishes rule-breakers – because free trade only works when everyone follows the same rules."
Jenner's conclusion is that Germany's and Europe's future competitiveness can only be secured if they move away from bureaucracy and back to a "can-do mentality."
"Less regulation, more personal responsibility, ambitious investment incentives, reliable framework conditions, and, above all, the courage to tackle issues properly and comprehensively once again. Real change begins in the mind – it’s time to act."

Justice chancellor nominee pledges nonpolitical office, social rights focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:58:00 UTC
17:58:00 KST

Justice chancellor nominee pledges nonpolitical office, social rights focus
Supreme Court Justice Oliver Kask, nominated as Estonia's next chancellor of justice, says he will protect the office's political independence while focusing on social rights.
President and previous justice chancellor Ülle Madise has nominated Kask for the seven-year post, which is appointed by the Riigikogu. Parliamentary groups plan to meet with him before making their decision.
Kask said he took time to consider the offer, given the importance of the issues handled by the office. He plans to focus on social rights, particularly where people struggle to defend their interests or take cases to court, as well as protecting democracy and the rule of law.
"It's important to me that the institution of the Chancellor of Justice not be political," Kask said. Political questions, he added, should be left to the Riigikogu and the government to decide.
Kask has worked at the Ministry of Justice, served as a Tallinn Circuit Court judge and chaired the National Electoral Committee (VVK). He is currently a Supreme Court justice serving on the court's Administrative Law Chamber.
Riigikogu parliamentary groups have outlined several priorities for their meetings with him.
Isamaa MP Lea Danilson-Järg pointed to the state's obligations to citizens, including 2,000 people waiting for special care services. "The state has failed to meet its obligations there," she said.
Danilson-Järg also cited the official status and role of the Estonian language as another party priority.
Transparency and quality
The Social Democrats (SDE) want the justice chancellor to continue working on data protection issues. Party leader Lauri Läänemets said growing volumes of personal data must be protected without obstructing law enforcement.
"We don't need haste here; we need balanced and considered decisions," he said.
Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) MP Anti Poolamets said Kask must demonstrate the office's independence and commitment to fundamental rights — "with conviction, not just as a formality."
He also called for safeguarding the transparency of online voting and the ability to file election complaints.
Reform Party MP Madis Timpson, chair of the Riigikogu's Legal Affairs Committee, said the justice chancellor's focus should be on better laws, not more of them.
"We need better-written legal provisions and a state where everyone can understand they aren't being subjected to unjustified restrictions," Timpson explained.
The parliamentary groups are scheduled to meet with Kask the week after next.

Bulgaria votes in presidential runoff after tight first round
SOFIA, Nov 1 - Bulgarians went to the polls on Sunday to elect a president after a tight race between the two leading candidates failed to produce an outright winner in last weekend's first round vote for the largely ceremonial role.
Incumbent president, Iliana Iotova, 61, led over ex-caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, but fell short of the 50% threshold in the first round race of 27 candidates that saw a record-low turnout.
Exit polls will be published after voting ends at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT), with a result likely on Monday as the ballot papers are counted.
The presidential vote comes against the backdrop of a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast in the past month, which have sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine.
About two dozen seafarers are feared dead and the strikes have prompted the government to seek allied assistance to bolster maritime security. On Wednesday a Greek container ship sank after being hit by sea drones.
Both leading presidential candidates have condemned the attacks. Prime Minister Rumen Radev, who backs Iotova, said the strikes' outcome "benefits the Russian Federation". They have both called for a diplomatic end to the war.
A victory for Iotova would make her Bulgaria's first elected female president. She became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter and win a parliamentary race on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine. He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
A host of right-leaning political figures, among them ex-premier Boiko Borisov, have expressed support for Gyurov. REUTERS

The verified success of the humanitarian operation in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky demonstrates that active hostilities can be halted and can serve as a vital confidence-building measure to advance a broader, permanent peace, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced on Sunday, Nov. 1.
Writing on X, Sybiha confirmed that evacuated civilians had safely crossed the state frontier into Ukraine’s northern Chernihiv region, emphasizing that the operation represents hundreds of innocent lives preserved following months of severe deprivation.

“Ukrainian citizens evacuated from Oleshky have crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv region. This is about saved lives,” the foreign minister stated.

Sybiha’s remarks follow the arrival of the evacuation convoys in Chernihiv region late on Saturday, Oct. 31, concluding an intricate multi-stage transit corridor that began inside occupied Kherson region.
Under the negotiated framework, a humanitarian convoy of 25 buses and specialized ambulances entered Oleshky following de-mining operations around the municipal hospital.
Trapped civilians – prioritizing the elderly, individuals with disabilities, and families with domestic animals – transited overland through Russian-occupied Crimea to the Russian Black Sea port of Anapa.
From Anapa, four charter flights airlifted the evacuees to Gomel in Belarus, where the final aircraft touched down on Saturday afternoon before the group boarded cross-border coaches into northern Ukraine.
At the Chernihiv reception point, Ukrainian authorities, medical detachments, psychologists, and volunteer organizations mobilized emergency warming shelters, hot food distribution, and specialized animal care depots for pets brought by the evacuees.
The humanitarian mission was executed under a strict, localized 87-hour silence regime that took effect at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time on Tuesday, Oct. 27, and was scheduled to remain in force until 10:59 p.m. on Sunday, Nov. 1.
Throughout the designated ceasefire window, Ukrainian and Russian armed forces adhered to commitments suspending drone interdictions, tactical aviation, artillery bombardments, and ground maneuvers across the Oleshky perimeter, recording zero kinetic violations.
The compliance underscored statements delivered on Saturday by Melania Trump, who characterized the Oleshky mission as grounds for hope for a sustainable peace and proof that humanity can rise above war.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also thanked the US First Lady, noting that American mediation enabled life-saving deliveries and civilian evacuations.

Golan said forming a new government as soon as possible was "of utmost importance, as Israel's security and the safety of its citizens are at stake."
The warning came after neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition parties secured enough seats to form a government in last Tuesday's parliamentary elections.
Preliminary results showed Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for Jewish opposition parties and 19 for Palestinian parties.
The results left all blocs short of the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority.
The inconclusive election results have raised several possible scenarios, including a government backed by Palestinian parties, a unity government or another election.
Netanyahu faces corruption trial, ICC warrants
Netanyahu, 76, faces an ongoing corruption trial involving charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, which could result in imprisonment if he is convicted.
He has also been wanted by the International Criminal Court since 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity against Palestinians during Israel's war on Gaza, which began in October 2023.
