US midterms: 2 days to go – what polls say as Trump, El-Sayed hit the trail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:47:19 UTC
17:47:19 KST

US midterms: 2 days to go – Who leads in the polls as Trump rallies
Democrats remain ahead in national polls as Trump and candidates make their final push in the days before polling day.
With two days to the United States midterm elections, Democratic and Republican leaders are making last-ditch efforts to woo voters, with the cost-of-living crisis, exacerbated by the US-Israel war on Iran, becoming one of the key talking points.
According to the latest survey, Democrats are still ahead of the Republicans, but several closely fought Senate races may decide which party ends up in control of the US Congress.
On Sunday, President Donald Trump will be campaigning in Iowa and Kansas, while Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate who has faced an increased wave of Islamophobic attacks, will be holding events in Michigan.
Here is what to know:
What do the latest US midterm polls say?
Democrats continue to lead Republicans by 51.5 percent to 43.1 percent, according to the latest RealClearPolling average.
A national THP/MM survey conducted on October 28 and 29 put Democrats ahead by 54 percent to 41 percent, while an Emerson College poll conducted from October 24 to 26 showed a 10-point Democratic lead.
Natalie Jackson, a political analyst and pollster, told Al Jazeera that the results reflected public dissatisfaction with Trump and the economy.
“Polling shows an environment that is pretty favourable to the Democrats. The president is very unpopular, Americans feel the pinch of high costs, which are partly due to tariffs and the war in Iran, and the general sentiment is that Republicans did not deliver in the last two years.”
In Kansas, a Washington Post-Schar School poll released on Friday suggested Democrat Adam Hamilton was leading against Republican Senator Roger Marshall by 52 percent to 43 percent.
But another Emerson College survey indicated a tighter race, with Hamilton ahead of Marshall by 50 percent to 47percent.
Doug Heye, a Republican strategist and former communications director for the Republican National Committee, questioned the nine-point lead of the Washington Post-Schar School survey.
“I don’t know how it plays out, but, you know, we saw an outlier poll in Iowa just two years ago that caused a lot of damage to the whole polling industry,” Heye said.
He was referring to a Des Moines Register poll published days before the 2024 presidential election that showed Kamala Harris leading Trump by three percentage points in Iowa. Trump went on to win the state by about 13 points, a difference of 16 points from the poll’s margin.
“A lot of Republicans just don’t want to answer calls from pollsters,” he added.
Jackson, the political analyst, also said polling might not accurately reflect the result of individual Senate contests.
“In some individual races – particularly the close Senate races – we could see polling error that shifts the race in one direction or another,” she said.
“Pollsters have reported some potential issues with getting Republicans to answer polls. That might indicate that polls are underestimating Republicans, but we don’t know until the votes are counted.”
What happened on the campaign trail in the past 24 hours?
As the election nears, both parties are focusing their final campaign messages on the economy and the cost of living.
While Democrats have been focusing on affordability issues, Trump has been conducting telephone rallies for Republican candidates in closely contested races.
Heye said Republicans were struggling to convince voters that their economic policies would improve the situation in the country.
Asked whether Republicans had found a convincing closing message, he said: “No, they haven’t. That’s a big part of their challenge.”
The Republican strategist said candidates should focus on issues voters were raising, particularly the cost of energy, healthcare, groceries and other everyday expenses.
“Families are making very real economic decisions; you have to address to them what you’re going to do to solve those problems,” Heye said.
Celinda Lake, a Democratic strategist and pollster working with El-Sayed’s campaign in Michigan, said Democrats were also facing questions about what they would deliver if they controlled Congress.
“The feelings about the Democrats are negative, too, which is very different from, say, 2018, when Democrats were positively perceived,” she said.
Lake said while many voters were seeking change, they were still unsure what either of the parties would do.
Where will Trump, El-Sayed and other candidates campaign today?
Trump is scheduled to hold rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday. The president had initially cancelled both appearances before reversing his decision on Friday.
In Iowa, in one of the contested Senate races, Trump will campaign with Republican US Representative Ashley, who faces Democrat Josh Turek. In Kansas, Senator Marshall is also looking for re-election against Democrat Adam Hamilton in a tight contest.
This state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, but rising farming costs and opposition to Trump’s immigration crackdown have made this race unexpectedly competitive.
Heye said Trump should not have cancelled the appearances in the first place.
“They never should have been cancelled to begin with,” he said. “Whether they help or not, they certainly help Trump to show that I’m out there trying to do the things to get my people over the line.”
Meanwhile, El-Sayed is scheduled to campaign in Detroit and Southfield, Michigan, as he seeks to defeat Republican Mike Rogers in the Senate race.
Lake, who is working with El-Sayed’s campaign, said the candidate had made affordability key to his message.
“He’s very clear. He says, ‘Money out of politics, money in your pockets, and healthcare for all.'”
She said the Michigan race would depend heavily on voter turnout.
“I think the race is going to be really close. What we’re looking at is turnout,” she said.
How many Americans have already voted?
More than 51 million Americans have already voted, according to reports. Both parties have encouraged voters to cast their ballots using the mail-in system or make plans to vote on Tuesday.
But early-voting numbers do not show which party will win, because they do not establish how those voters voted.
Lake, the Democratic strategist, said turnout would be one of the most important factors in the elections.
“Did Trump really rally the Republicans? Did the Democrats come out in record numbers?” she asked.
She also identified young voters and the gender gap as important indicators to follow during the election.
Jackson, the political analyst, said the final two days will probably not bring major changes to the national political environment.
“It’s unlikely that anything really shifts in the national environment. We could see some local developments in some of these races, but by now things are pretty locked in.”
Can Democrats take control of Congress?
A total of 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats are up for grabs.
Democrats need a net gain of three House seats and four Senate seats to win the majority in both chambers.
While polling suggests Democrats are ahead, control of the Senate will depend on individual contests, including races in Michigan, Texas, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Alaska.
Jackson said the polling provided a clearer picture of the national political environment than the likely outcome of individual Senate races.
“We can be fairly confident that Democrats will win the House majority, but the Senate picture is unclear,” she told Al Jazeera.
Heye, the Republican strategist, also pointed to the differences between the House and Senate contests.
“The Senate is so campaign-, state- and candidate-specific. It’s a much harder read,” he said.
What happens next?
Candidates have Sunday and Monday to make their final appeals to voters before they head to the polls on Tuesday.
Polling stations will begin closing on Tuesday evening, with the first results expected shortly afterwards. However, some of the closely fought races might take longer.
Heye said he would be watching the first results in Indiana and Kentucky for indications of how the election might unfold.
“Yeah, I start with the two states that close earliest, which are Indiana and Kentucky,” he said.
But Jackson cautioned that the results in individual Senate races could differ from what the final polls suggest.
“That is always possible with polling,” she said, adding that the scale and direction of any polling errors would become clear once the votes were counted.

48th Istanbul Marathon begins with nearly 46,000 participants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:47:00 UTC
17:47:00 KST

AA Photo
The 48th Istanbul Marathon reaffirmed its status as a global athletic landmark on Nov. 1, welcoming 45,679 registered participants from 143 nations for the world’s only cross-continental marathon.
Organized by the Istanbul Municipality’s department of youth and sports services and its subsidiary Spor Istanbul, the Türkiye İş Bankası 48th Istanbul Marathon started at 9 a.m. local time near the metrobus stop on the Asian side of the July 15 Martyrs Bridge.
The event, which holds Gold Label status from World Athletics, featured 42-kilometer and 15.5-kilometer races, corporate and public runs, as well as wheelchair competitions.
A total of 43 elite athletes, including 16 women and 27 men, competed in the marathon. Among the prominent names in the men’s field were 2024 champion Dejene Debela, Amdework Walelegn and Sufaro Woliyi. The women’s competition featured defending champion Bizuager Aderra, alongside Judith Korir and Veronicah Maina.
Road closures were introduced across the race route and connecting roads ahead of the event.
The 42-kilometer race took runners across the July 15 Martyrs Bridge from Asia to Europe, before passing through Beşiktaş and Galata Bridge toward Istanbul’s historic peninsula. Athletes then followed Kennedy Street toward Bakırköy before turning back along the coastal road and finishing at Sultanahmet Square.
The 15.5-kilometer race followed the same initial route as the marathon before reaching Yenikapı, while participants in the corporate and public runs crossed the bridge and continued along Barbaros Boulevard toward Dolmabahçe.
The marathon also serves as the 2026 Şevki Koru Turkish Marathon Championships, with domestic athletes competing for national titles.
The men’s and women’s winners of the 42-kilometer race will each receive $50,000, with an additional $5,000 available for breaking the course record. A total of 12 million Turkish Liras ($240,000) in prize money will be distributed across all categories.

France taps strategic diesel reserves, diesel prices fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:46:06 UTC
17:46:06 KST

Several fuel retailers announce lower pump prices after drawing on strategic reserves. Prices will still track markets but volumes from these reserves will help offset rises.
On average in France, diesel was selling on Saturday 31 October at around 2.37 euros per litre.
TotalEnergies' Access stations were already below that average, with the price reduced to 2.15 euros per litre, 10 cents less than in the group's other stations.
The multinational explained that it had decided on a price cut "without waiting for the physical delivery of strategic diesel stocks and in order to allow its customers to benefit from access to these stocks at their historic cost".
The E. Leclerc supermarket chain is following suit and has announced a reduction of 21 cents per litre of diesel sold at its roughly 742 service stations in France.
According to E. Leclerc, the 21-cent reduction will be deducted from the price every day, and that price will continue to fluctuate in line with market prices.
The other major retail group Coopérative U will be offering an identical cut.
In mid-October the government announced the release of ten million barrels of diesel from strategic stocks. These volumes had been bought before the war in the Middle East and are being sold at 0.28 euro per litre, compared with 1.1 euro per litre on average in mid-October.

Türkiye implements social media age restrictions for minors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:46:00 UTC
17:46:00 KST

AA Photo
Türkiye has begun enforcing a ban on social media accounts for children under 15, requiring users to verify their age through e-Devlet, the Turkish e-government gateway.
The regulation, which entered into force on Nov. 1, introduces different requirements for three age groups. However, existing accounts will not be subject to immediate mass suspensions, as platforms have until March 31, 2027, to complete age verification for current users.
Under the new rules, children under 15 will be prohibited from creating new social media accounts. Those who already have accounts will be subject to age checks during the transition period. Platforms suspecting that an account belongs to a child below the age threshold may temporarily suspend it and request verification through e-Devlet. Accounts confirmed to belong to under-15s will be closed.
Teens aged 15 to 18 can still join social platforms, but under tighter controls. Accounts will automatically default to private, DMs will be restricted to followed users, follower lists will stay hidden and read receipts will be turned off. The age group will also face restrictions on certain features, including livestreaming and continuous scrolling through short-form videos such as Instagram Reels. They will not be served personalized advertisements.
Adults aged 18 and older must also verify their age via e-Devlet when creating new accounts, while existing users have until March 31, 2027, to complete verification.
The verification system is designed to prevent social media companies from accessing users’ personal identification details. Instead of receiving names, surnames or Turkish identification numbers, platforms will only be provided with a digital code confirming whether a user has reached the age of 18.
Social media companies will be responsible for monitoring accounts and implementing age verification, rather than the government directly overseeing individual users. Platforms will be able to use artificial intelligence-assisted technologies and other methods to estimate users’ ages. These may include examining account activity, shared content, interactions and visual indicators. However, the regulation does not mandate the use of any particular AI technology.
Authorities have also provided an appeal mechanism for users whose accounts are mistakenly suspended or closed following incorrect age assessments. Appeals cannot be evaluated solely by automated systems; human review will also be required.
Users have also been warned about potential phishing attempts exploiting the new verification requirements. They are advised not to click on age-verification links sent through text messages, emails or social media, and not to share their e-Devlet passwords or SMS verification codes.

designboom radar: exhibitions to see around the world this november

designboom radar: exhibitions to see around the world this november
explore our monthly round up of must-see art, design, and architecture exhibitions to check out around the world.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
november exhibitions from DESIGNBOOM RADAR
November’s designboom exhibition radar begins with an unlikely reunion in Paris, where two Alexander Calder mobiles return to public view after decades. In Zurich, 125 familiar lamps become a walk-through tunnel, while a new gallery in Hong Kong transfers the grain of wood into cast aluminum. Elsewhere, a house lost to Mexico City’s architectural history returns through an imagined botanical setting, and a new museum in Western Sydney opens with exhibitions on flight and water.
Some of the exhibitions highlighted in earlier radars and listings on our dedicated events guide remain on view, giving designboom readers more time to encounter them around the globe.
mariko mori: all that shines
Visitors can enter Mariko Mori‘s Wave UFO, an interactive work that incorporates brainwave feedback, as part of All That Shines at Tokyo’s Mori Art Museum. Developed between 1999 and 2002, the large, futuristic installation connects neurological activity with visual experience. It appears in a retrospective of approximately 40 works spanning more than three decades of the Japanese artist’s practice.
The exhibition begins with Mori’s early performance-based photography and science-fiction-inspired imagery, including her experiments with cyborg identities in the 1990s. Later works turn toward Buddhist concepts of consciousness and questions about the cosmos, using sculpture and technology to approach subjects that resist direct representation. Together, the installations and moving-image works trace Mori’s changing ideas about the relationship between human perception and technological experience.
name: Mariko Mori: All That Shines
artist: Mariko Mori
museum: Mori Art Museum
location: Tokyo, Japan
dates: October 31st, 2026 — March 28th, 2027
hella jongerius: whispering things
More than 400 objects trace the experimental practice of Dutch designer Hella Jongerius at the Museum für Kunst und Gewerbe Hamburg. Whispering Things, organized by the Vitra Design Museum, brings together furniture, textiles, ceramics, and early prototypes to examine how she has approached the making of objects over three decades.
The exhibition moves from commercially produced designs for companies such as Vitra and IKEA to more sculptural investigations of material and color. Sketches, collages, and films reveal the processes behind the finished work, including experiments that resist the predictability of industrial production. Throughout her career, Jongerius has returned to the relationship between craftsmanship and manufacturing, considering how objects can retain the irregularities and physical traces of their making.
name: Hella Jongerius: Whispering Things
designer: Hella Jongerius
museum: Museum für Kunst und Gewerbe Hamburg
location: Hamburg, Germany
dates: October 23rd, 2026 — June 13th, 2027
charlotte perriand: free to rethink the world
A reconstruction of Charlotte Perriand‘s 1929 domestic prototype, Équipement intérieur d’une habitation, appears at Barcelona’s Fundació Joan Miró in Free to Rethink the World. Produced by Cassina in collaboration with Perriand’s daughter, architect Pernette Perriand-Barsac, the installation revisits a project developed with Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret during Perriand’s early career.
The exhibition follows four decades of work through ten sections, extending from her Parisian interiors to her encounters with Japanese craftsmanship. Photographs and archival documents reveal her interest in creating spaces around the changing needs of their occupants. The presentation also revisits her friendship with architect Josep Lluís Sert, whose building for the Fundació Joan Miró opened in 1975, with Perriand attending its inauguration the following year.
name: Charlotte Perriand: Free to Rethink the World
designer, architect: Charlotte Perriand
museum: Fundació Joan Miró
location: Barcelona, Spain
dates: October 9th, 2026 — February 28th, 2027
no ordinary light: akari at 75
A monumental paper lantern measuring roughly two meters across takes its place at the Noguchi Museum in New York for No Ordinary Light: Akari at 75. The exhibition traces the development of Isamu Noguchi‘s Akari light sculptures, first conceived in Gifu, Japan, in 1951. Over the following decades, Noguchi developed more than 200 variations of the familiar illuminated forms.
Among the works identified for the presentation is the large-scale 200D, created around 1985, alongside archival sketchbooks and examples of Noguchi’s sculpture in other materials. The exhibition revisits Akari’s appearance at the home of Charles and Ray Eames in 1951 and its later presentation at the 1986 Venice Biennale, following the movement of these paper forms between sculpture and the domestic interior.
name: No Ordinary Light: Akari at 75
artist, designer: Isamu Noguchi
museum: The Noguchi Museum
location: New York, USA
dates: November 4th, 2026 — September 5th, 2027
sabine marcelis: light and color
At the Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, 125 circular IKEA lamps form an eleven-meter-long tunnel in Sabine Marcelis: Light and Color. A mirrored wall with a color gradient extends the installation visually, turning a familiar household object into an illuminated passage. The Dutch designer’s first museum exhibition brings together recent projects and new works conceived for the museum’s Toni-Areal location.
Another room contains eight Mathmos lava lamps, each nearly three meters tall, multiplied through surrounding mirrors. In Sunbeam Captured, developed with Boris Acket, mechanical waves move across a thin layer of water as a shifting light source follows the path of the sun. Material studies accompany the installations, revealing how Sabine Marcelis works with transparency and reflection.
name: Sabine Marcelis—Light and Color
designer: Sabine Marcelis
museum: Museum für Gestaltung Zürich
location: Zurich, Switzerland
dates: October 30th, 2026 — April 4th, 2027
misha kahn: all intensive purposes
A sprawling cast-metal dining table, complete with a sculpted torn napkin and scraps of food, appears among the new works in Misha Kahn‘s All Intensive Purposes at Friedman Benda in New York. Its glass-and-stone surface introduces a surprising degree of order to an object assembled from seemingly accidental gestures. Elsewhere, an onyx table adopts the appearance of a far more roughly constructed piece.
The exhibition marks ten years of collaboration between Kahn and the gallery, following his interest in the unpredictable paths of making. New upholstered furniture incorporates exaggerated forms and graphic surfaces, while multilayered plywood becomes the basis for sculptural objects. The title deliberately alters the familiar phrase ‘all intents and purposes,’ placing the emphasis on experimentation itself.
name: Misha Kahn: All Intensive Purposes
designer: Misha Kahn
gallery: Friedman Benda
location: New York, USA
dates: October 29th, 2026 — December 12th, 2026
calder: françois premier
Two major Alexander Calder mobiles return to public view at Hauser & Wirth Paris in Calder: François Premier, an exhibition devoted to the artist’s years in France during the early 1950s. The presentation brings together Les Granettes (1953), a large standing mobile exhibited for the first time in 72 years, and The Putney Mobile (1954), making its public European debut.
The show takes its name from a seventeenth-century stone house in Saché, where Calder lived and worked after returning to France in 1953. Ink and gouache paintings from this period accompany the sculptures, tracing a particularly productive chapter in his career. There is a geographical coincidence, too: the Paris gallery occupies a historic building on rue François Premier.
name: Calder: François Premier
artist: Alexander Calder
gallery: Hauser & Wirth
location: Paris, France
dates: October 19th, 2026 — December 19th, 2026
dan flavin: some light
Green fluorescent tubes stretch across several meters in Dan Flavin‘s greens crossing greens (to Piet Mondrian who lacked green), one of the works presented in Some Light at the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao. Made in 1966, the installation arranges ordinary industrial fixtures into two illuminated sections, bringing color directly into the surrounding architecture.
The exhibition draws on the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum‘s holdings, with works dating from the 1960s through the 1980s and particular attention to Flavin’s early experiments. Beginning in 1963, the American artist used commercially available fluorescent lights to construct corners, barriers, and corridors. Their arrangement changes the appearance of the gallery itself, allowing visitors to experience color through the spaces the light occupies.
name: Dan Flavin: Some Light
artist: Dan Flavin
museum: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
location: Bilbao, Spain
dates: November 11th, 2026 — April 4th, 2027
powerhouse parramatta
With architecture by Moreau Kusunoki, Powerhouse Parramatta opens in Western Sydney on November 7th with five inaugural exhibitions devoted to art, design, science, and technology. Among them is Task Eternal, an ambitious exploration of aviation and space designed by OPEN Architecture. Its more than 850 objects include drawings of flying machines by Leonardo da Vinci and a NASA Moon rock, alongside a new light installation by James Turrell.
Elsewhere, Overflow brings together seven Aboriginal organizations to examine the living systems of Water Country. The Mall, developed with OMA/AMO, investigates the shopping mall as an architectural and cultural form, while Es Devlin presents five immersive installations in The Turning. A fifth exhibition, The Dark, creates an imaginative environment for children. Together, they introduce the museum’s extensive new program.
museum: Powerhouse Parramatta
participants: multiple artists, designers, architects, and First Nations organizations

tai shani: m.i.a.s.m.a.
British artist Tai Shani brings M.I.A.S.M.A. to Jupiter Artland outside Edinburgh, transforming the gallery through sculpture and sound. The exhibition revisits the ancient Greek tragedy Antigone, asking how mourning becomes a form of resistance and whose lives are allowed to be remembered. Its expanded title, Moral Injury in the Apocalyptic Sunsets of Modernity disAssociation, gives some indication of the political and emotional territory Shani is exploring.
Developed as an international co-commission, the project was first presented at Kunsthalle Bern earlier this year. Jupiter Artland’s presentation combines imagery with architectural elements to construct an environment shaped by feminist mythology. Visitors can also encounter Shani’s separate installation The Spell or The Dream in the sculpture park’s orchard, where its setting changes with the approaching winter.
name: Tai Shani: M.I.A.S.M.A.
artist: Tai Shani
gallery: Jupiter Artland

paul r. williams: architect for living
Previously unexhibited drawings and photographs offer a closer look at the career of Paul R. Williams in Architect for Living at LACMA in Los Angeles. Working from the 1920s through the early 1970s, Williams designed buildings across Southern California during a period of extraordinary urban expansion. His commissions ranged from private residences to major civic projects.
The exhibition explores this breadth through archival material, tracing a practice that moved between different architectural languages and types of clients. Williams became particularly well known for his houses for Hollywood figures, while his larger body of work included public housing and hotels. Presented alongside related exhibitions at the Getty Research Institute and USC Fisher Museum of Art, the LACMA survey places his architecture within the wider development of Los Angeles.
name: Paul R. Williams: Architect for Living
architect: Paul R. Williams
museum: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
location: Los Angeles, USA
dates: November 15th, 2026 — May 31st, 2027
sophie calle: matrimoni, rotture e funerali inclusi
An attempt to capture her mother’s final breath is among the personal investigations revisited in Sophie Calle’s Matrimoni, Rotture e Funerali inclusi at MAXXI in Rome. Bringing together eight projects made between 1978 and 2026, the exhibition follows the French artist’s longstanding interest in the rituals people invent around intimacy and loss.
Photographs and written accounts guide visitors through experiences shaped by separation, absence, and the passage of time. Calle’s projects often begin with a self-imposed rule, whether documenting the end of a relationship or recording encounters with people seeing the sea for the first time. The presentation extends beyond the museum with a new permanent installation at Rome’s Non-Catholic Cemetery for Foreigners, adding another setting to her exploration of how personal histories are remembered.
name: Sophie Calle: Matrimoni, Rotture e Funerali inclusi
artist: Sophie Calle
museum: MAXXI

dates: October 16th, 2026 — February 7th, 2027
álvaro urbano: helen
A vanished house in Mexico City becomes the starting point for Álvaro Urbano’s Helen at Museo Jumex. The exhibition revisits Casa Cueva, the home and garden created by architect Juan O’Gorman and inhabited with his wife, artist and botanically minded writer Helen Fowler O’Gorman. Built in the rocky landscape of Pedregal de San Ángel, the house brought architecture into close contact with its surroundings.
Urbano draws on Fowler O’Gorman’s 1961 book Mexican Flowering Trees and Plants, imagining the botanical world that once occupied the property. References to Juan O’Gorman’s stone murals and later interventions by artist Helen Escobedo add further layers to the presentation. Through an atmospheric architectural reconstruction, Urbano considers how a building’s history can survive through fragments, images, and the people who lived there.
name: Álvaro Urbano: Helen
artist: Álvaro Urbano
museum: Museo Jumex

dates: October 16th, 2026 — February 7th, 2027
jeonghwa seo: precise play
Wood grain appears on the surface of cast aluminum in Precise Play, an exhibition by South Korean designer Jeonghwa Seo at Carwan Gallery‘s new Hong Kong space. Seo uses sand casting to transfer the texture of wood into metal, producing objects that retain traces of the organic material used in their making. The exhibition inaugurates the gallery’s new location.
Bringing together established pieces and newly commissioned works, the presentation moves between sculptural furniture and lighting. Seo also works with resin and natural rush, combining materials with different physical qualities in precisely constructed forms. His objects invite a second look at the relationship between surface and structure, particularly when a metallic piece appears to preserve the grain of timber or a functional object adopts an unexpected sculptural form.
name: Jeonghwa Seo: Precise Play
designer: Jeonghwa Seo
gallery: Carwan Gallery
location: Hong Kong, China
dates: November 20th, 2026 – February 20th, 2027
yu nishimura: towards a sea
A sea glimpsed through a train window or partially hidden behind trees runs through Yu Nishimura’s Towards a Sea at Lafayette Anticipations in Paris. The Japanese painter’s first institutional solo exhibition in France brings together approximately 50 works from the past decade, including new pieces made for the presentation.
Working in oil and tempera, Nishimura moves between landscape and portraiture, allowing familiar subjects to become blurred or partially obscured. A bicycle wheel might appear alongside a human face, while the boundary between water and sky remains difficult to locate. The exhibition follows the artist’s interest in how places are recalled through imperfect images. His compositions borrow from the language of photography and cinema, and give ordinary scenes the elusive quality of something remembered.
name: Yu Nishimura: Towards a Sea
artist: Yu Nishimura
museum: Lafayette Anticipations

giuseppe penone: the inner flow of life
Trees and other natural forms enter the architecture of the National Museum of Qatar in Giuseppe Penone: The Inner Flow of Life. Installed across the museum’s Baraha and Old Palace, the exhibition brings together sculptures and architectural interventions by the Italian artist, whose practice has explored the physical relationship between human bodies and the natural world for more than five decades.
The presentation moves between early works and recent pieces, including Rovesciare i propri occhi from 1970 and Vene di bronzo from 2026. Penone uses materials such as wood and bronze to investigate the forces that shape living matter, often bringing the traces of touch or growth into sculpture. A newly installed public artwork, Idee di Pietra, extends the project to Doha Old Port.
name: Giuseppe Penone: The Inner Flow of Life

Rashid Johnson: A Poem for Deep Thinkers
More than 70 works spanning nearly three decades of Rashid Johnson’s practice come together at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago in A Poem for Deep Thinkers. The survey brings together photographs, large-scale installations, and films, including his black-soap Cosmic Slops paintings and the expressive faces of the Anxious Men and Broken Men series.
Throughout his career, Johnson has drawn on Black intellectual culture and art history to explore questions of identity, anxiety, and freedom. His 2024 film Sanguine turns toward his own family, examining relationships with his father, brother, and son, and incorporating a poem by writer and activist Amiri Baraka.
name: Rashid Johnson: A Poem for Deep Thinkers
artist: Rashid Johnson
museum: Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago

dates: November 7th, 2026 — April 25th, 2027
global antiquity
An ancient Indian ivory statuette discovered in Pompeii offers a glimpse into the far-reaching connections explored in Global Antiquity at Fondazione Prada in Milan. Bringing together more than 150 artworks and artifacts, the exhibition examines cultural exchange across Afro-Eurasia between approximately 600 BCE and 1000 CE. The presentation occupies the foundation’s Podium building, with exhibition design by Rem Koolhaas and AMO/OMA.
Curated by Salvatore Settis, Anna Anguissola, and Chiara Ballestrazzi, the exhibition considers how objects traveled through systems of trade and political contact long before the modern idea of globalization. Their places of discovery become as revealing as their origins. Together, the artifacts trace connections between distant societies across 1,700 years.

Police dismantle protesters' tent camp in Lisbon - Reuters

Portuguese police dispersed the camp following a march against the housing rental bill. A similar camp was also dismantled in Porto.
On Sunday, police entered Rossio Square in Lisbon and dismantled a tent camp that protesters had set up after a march attended by thousands. The demonstrators demanded that the Portuguese government withdraw a housing rental bill which, in their view, would deepen the housing crisis. Reuters reports, as reported by UNN.
Details
According to the publication, on Saturday, after marching through central Lisbon, protesters set up more than 50 tents in Rossio Square. At around 4:30 a.m., dozens of police officers, some accompanied by service dogs, entered the camp. Before that, police commander Yuri Rodrigues warned the protesters three times that the tents would be dismantled if they did not remove them. He also said that those who resisted could be charged with disobedience.
Hundreds of protesters defending the tent camp were dispersed by police using shields and several baton charges. Separately, police dismantled a similar, though smaller, tent camp in Dom João I Square in Porto
According to available information, the demonstrations are taking place against the backdrop of Portugal's housing crisis.
Portugal is grappling with one of the worst housing crises in Europe, with young people among those most affected. Housing prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents under new rental agreements have nearly doubled. Since 2017, housing prices have more than doubled, while rents under new agreements have almost doubled. Young people are feeling the problem particularly acutely. Protests over the rapid rise in housing prices have intensified in Portugal in recent weeks, reflecting similar unrest that has swept Spain, France, Germany and other European countries
We remind you
Mass protests have erupted in a number of European countries over the rising cost of living, high energy prices, unaffordable housing and insufficient funding for public services. Some demonstrations escalated into clashes with police, while trade unions have already announced new strikes for November.

Rachel Reeves says UK’s future is in EU as she backs Andy Burnham on Brexit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:37:34 UTC
17:37:34 KST

The former chancellor Rachel Reeves has argued Britain’s future should be back in the European Union, saying Brexit has made the UK “poorer, weaker and less secure”.
In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury when Andy Burnham took office, she said those forging a path back towards EU membership had to make compelling arguments to the public.
Reeves, who was sacked as chancellor by Burnham, said in an article for the Sunday Times that no one who worked with her in the Treasury could be in doubt about her pro-European instincts. “I am proud of the progress we have already made in strengthening our relationship with the European Union. Brexit has made us poorer, weaker and less secure,” she said.
“There is a debate to be had about our future relationship with Europe, and I welcome Andy Burnham’s leadership in facing up to this. No one in the Treasury ever doubted where my instincts were.”
The current focus for British negotiations is the EU summit later this month to seal an agreement to ease some trading restrictions and a youth mobility deal. But the prime minister has made it clear he wants to see a long-term and stable relationship with the bloc.
Burnham has said he believes there should be “honest discussion” about freedom of movement and that rejoining the single market could be done without the need for another referendum, if Labour put it in its manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll.
In her article, Reeves said it was “incumbent on supporters of our re-entry to make the argument, demonstrate tangible benefits and to get the next steps right”.
At his last cabinet meeting, Burnham warned individual ministers not to express their opinions about how the government should approach Brexit, but said the Conservatives’ deal with Brussels had been more extreme than that promised in the 2016 referendum.
It follows reports that some ministers, including Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, have worries about the possibility of a revised deal and its impact on migration.
Burnham has set out a two-stage approach to reforming Brexit, beginning with any initial changes that will be within the scope of Labour’s 2024 manifesto – which committed to remaining outside the EU’s customs union and single market, and not reinstating freedom of movement. The process will formally kick off when the prime minister attends the European summit.
Anything more substantial would need to wait until after the next election, with Burnham saying he wanted a discussion on what this might entail.
As chancellor, Reeves was one of the first senior ministers to articulate that Brexit had damaged the British economy and its ability to grow. In her Mais lecture in March this year she said Brexit had “created profound uncertainty, raised new barriers to trade, and leaves Britain facing an additional danger today … The risk that we find ourselves stranded between powerful trading blocs, as globalisation retreats.”

When money replaces the will of people in the United States
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:30:03 UTC
17:30:03 KST

It is for years that the United States has imposed tough restrictions and sanctions on some countries, and justifying its own foreign policy under the banner of spreading democracy, claiming to be the champion of freedom and popular sovereignty. Yet, an examination of the US electoral structure reveals that, even within the United States itself, there exists a significant gap between the formal equality of citizens and their actual power to influence policy.
In the United States, every citizen has one vote, yet not all citizens possess equal power to shape the electoral landscape. While millions of people head to the polls to elect their representatives, billionaires, large corporations, and economic groups, by injecting billions of dollars into political contests, play a pivotal role in setting the electoral agenda, managing advertising, and elevating specific candidates. The issue goes beyond mere high campaign costs; it concerns how wealth is converted into political power and the extent to which this can undermine the principle of equal sovereignty among the people.
Billionaires: The Key Players Behind the Scenes of US Elections
The 2026 US midterm elections serve as a clear example of this situation. According to an October 27 report by the American organization "Public Citizen," more than 500 donors, each contributing at least $1 million to Super PACs (Independent expenditure-only political action committees), have collectively allocated approximately $4.2 billion to these committees; a figure that accounts for over 70 percent of the funds raised by them.
In the same report, Elon Musk’s financial contributions to super PACs for the 2026 election cycle are estimated at approximately $445 million. Thus, a single billionaire possesses vast financial resources to support his preferred candidates and political movements—a capacity that is essentially unimaginable for an ordinary citizen.
The significance of these figures lies not merely in their magnitude. Vast financial resources can be used to establish advertising networks, disseminate campaign messages on a massive scale, and boost the visibility of candidates backed by the wealthy. Under such circumstances, while citizens’ votes are still counted on the election day, the wealthy have already spent months shaping the environment in which voters make their decisions.
This influence is not limited to a single party. According to an analysis by the Brennan Center for Justice, the 40 largest donors to the 2026 midterm elections had contributed over $2.4 billion to political contests by mid-October. This figure alone is more than 50 percent higher—even after adjusting for inflation—than the combined contributions from the largest financial backers during the entire 2022 midterm election cycle. Thus, the issue is not merely the financial support of Republicans or Democrats; rather, it is the structural influence wielded by holders of capital on both sides of the political divide.
Large-scale Corporations: Investing for Political Influence
Other dimensions of this problem are revealed in the spending of large companies. According to an Oct. 29 report by Public Citizen, registered contributions from for-profit corporations to super PACS and political committees related to the 2026 federal election totaled about $737.3 million; A figure that is 60% more than what the companies spent in the 2024 presidential election.
Among economic sectors, companies operating in the fields of cryptocurrency, online betting, and Big Tech—particularly those involved in artificial intelligence and data centers—have collectively contributed approximately $391 million to election campaigns. A single Super PAC aligned with the Trump political movement has received about $141 million of these recorded corporate contributions.
These figures indicate that corporations are not merely passive observers of the election. Decisions made by the administration and Congress regarding taxes, technology regulations, the cryptocurrency market, energy, and government contracts can directly impact their economic interests. Consequently, the significant presence of corporate funds in the election should be viewed as an effort to influence public policy.
Super PACs: The Legal Mechanism for Converting Wealth into Influence
One of the most significant instruments in this process is the type of committee known as a "Super PAC." Under US Federal Election Commission regulations, these committees may accept unlimited contributions from individuals, corporations, and unions, and spend these funds on independent advertising to support or oppose candidates—provided that such expenditures are not coordinated with the candidate or their campaign.
The expansion of this mechanism traces back to the 2010 US Supreme Court ruling in the *Citizens United* case—a decision that struck down previous restrictions on independent spending by corporations and unions in connection with federal elections. Subsequently, the "Super PAC" mechanism paved the way for the infusion of vast financial resources into political contests.
The impact of this trend is also evident in election advertising expenditures. According to data from the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, the total value of advertisements purchased and reserved for the 2025 and 2026 election cycles had surpassed $11.21 billion as of October 27—a figure that exceeds the total advertising spend for the 2024 presidential election cycle. This amount pertains exclusively to advertising and does not encompass costs such as field organizing, staff salaries, or other campaign-related activities.
Democracy for Others, Challenges at Home
The primary contradiction becomes apparent when this situation is viewed alongside US foreign policy. Washington has frequently invoked democracy, human rights, and political freedoms as a basis for evaluating other governments; in some instances, it has employed targeted sanctions and other forms of economic pressure, citing these very justifications. Iran, Cuba, Nicaragua, and several other nations are subject to US sanctions regimes—measures that are, in part, predicated on political and human rights-related concerns.
Of course, not all US sanctions are imposed in the name of democracy; Washington also cites other reasons for them, such as national security, nuclear issues, or the fight against terrorism. Nevertheless, democracy and human rights remain key instruments within the discourse of U.S. foreign policy.
But can a country where economic power exerts such extensive influence over political competition evaluate others by democratic standards, without first examining its own internal problems?
This question gains even greater significance when international reports also point to democratic challenges within the United States. According to a 2026 report by Freedom House, the US score on the global freedom index has declined from 84 the previous year to 81 out of 100. The report identifies factors such as deepening political polarization, the growing influence of money in politics, and functional issues within government institutions as key challenges facing American democracy.
Furthermore, in an April 2026 report—which examined indicators from Freedom House, the V-Dem Institute, and the Economist Intelligence Unit—the Pew Research Center stated that all three assessments point to a weakening of the state of democracy in the United States in 2025. According to V-Dem data, the US score on the Liberal Democracy Index has reached 0.57 out of 1, marking its lowest level since 1965. Additionally, the Economist Intelligence Unit has categorized the United States as a "flawed democracy" in its 2025 Democracy Index.
Conclusion
The core issue in critiquing American democracy is not that citizens lack the right to vote or that elections are not held; rather, it concerns the inequality in actual power to influence the political process. When an ordinary citizen participates in an election with a single vote, while a billionaire can spend hundreds of millions of dollars on advertising and supporting candidates, one cannot claim that political equality exists simply because the ballot box is present.
Democracy is not merely about holding elections; it also depends on citizens having equal opportunities to participate in shaping their political destiny. From this perspective, the American electoral structure faces serious questions regarding the role of the wealthy, the influence of corporations, and the accountability of decision-makers.
Washington cannot, on the one hand, make democracy a benchmark for evaluating other nations while, on the other hand, ignoring the structural challenges within its own political system. Before calling upon others to uphold democratic standards, the United States must address this question: in a country where billions of dollars in capital shape electoral contests, to what extent is the equal will of citizens the true basis for political decision-making?

Residents in Kstovo began circulating footage of major blazes lighting up the skyline around 4:00 a.m. local time, reporting repeated loud detonations and low-flying drone engine sounds over the municipal industrial zone.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Open-source intelligence monitors, including Ukrainian OSINT channel Exilenova+, reported that incoming unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) penetrated dense local air defenses, causing simultaneous large fires in several operational sections of the facility.
Monitoring group Crimean Wind corroborated the strikes, confirming that blazes engulfed sections of the refinery.
The enterprise, operated by Russian oil major Lukoil, functions as one of the largest petroleum refining facilities in Russia, boasting an annual design crude throughput capacity of approximately 17 million metric tons – equivalent to roughly 340,000 barrels per day.
Nationally, the Kstovo facility ranks fourth among Russian refineries by total processing volume and stands as the country’s second-largest producer of commercial motor gasoline.
The installation manufactures high-octane automotive gasoline, diesel fuel, jet propulsion kerosene, bitumen, and specialized petroleum fractions utilized directly by Russian military logistics and heavy mechanized equipment.

Situated directly within the Kstovo industrial belt, the Novogorkovskaya CHP serves as the primary regional energy backbone supplying high-pressure steam and electricity to surrounding heavy petrochemical complexes, including the Lukoil refinery.
Deepening asymmetric campaign against Russian refining nodes
Overnight Oct. 30-31, Ukrainian long-range strike drones struck the northern industrial hub of Ufa in the Republic of Bashkortostan, located 1,400 kilometers east of Ukraine.
Open-source intelligence analysis confirmed that the Ufa strike ignited the critical L-35 catalytic reforming unit at the Bashneft-Novoil refinery and damaged facilities at the adjacent Bashneft-UNPZ plant, disrupting high-octane gasoline output across the 23.5-million-ton Ufa refining cluster.
That raid followed an attack 24 hours earlier, overnight into Friday, Oct. 30, against Rosneft’s 8.8-million-ton Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery in Samara region, which produces specialized aviation fuel for the Russian Aerospace Forces, struck alongside an enterprise supplying military combat food rations.
Combined strikes on defense-industrial and propellant supply chains
The sequential targeting of major refineries coincides with synchronized precision interdiction against Russian military-industrial supply chains and tactical logistics.
Overnight Oct. 30-31, the Ukrainian Navy and unmanned aerial units launched a combined strike utilizing domestically manufactured Neptune cruise missiles in a land-attack role and long-range drones against the “Kamensky” chemical plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Rostov region.
The strike ignited a warehouse storing finished solid rocket propellant and damaged four production workshops at an enterprise producing propulsive charges for 220mm Uragan, 300mm Smerch, and 300mm Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, as well as tactical guided missiles.
Concurrently, Ukrainian precision strikes destroyed four Russian material-technical logistics supply depots across occupied Ukrainian territories near Khartsyzk, Dokuchaievsk, Novovasylivka, and Novoaidar.
These operations build upon earlier deep-rear strikes against critical single-source defense suppliers, including the Avisma titanium and magnesium complex in Perm region, the Omsky Kauchuk rocket propellant and polymer plant in Siberia, the Tolyattikauchuk synthetic rubber facility in Samara, and the Energiya defense accumulator plant in Yelets.

Russia’s War Losses in Ukraine Exceed 2 Million, Independent Estimate Finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:24:17 UTC

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s War Losses in Ukraine Exceed 2 Million, Independent Estimate Finds
Russia’s mounting battlefield losses are reaching a staggering scale, with new estimates revealing how heavily Moscow has paid for its prolonged war against Ukraine.
Russia may have suffered between 1.4 million and 2.1 million military casualties, including as many as 770,000 soldiers killed, since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Economist on October 30, an updated statistical assessment estimates Russian military deaths at between 374,000 and 770,000, with the remaining casualties consisting of wounded personnel.
The figures represent a substantial increase from the publication’s previous estimates. In July 2025, The Economist assessed Russia’s total casualties at 900,000 to 1.3 million, including 190,000 to 350,000 deaths. By May 2026, those estimates had risen to 1.1–1.5 million casualties and 280,000–518,000 deaths.
The Economist’s calculations combine Western intelligence assessments, defense ministry data, independent research, and battlefield tracking. Russia does not publish comprehensive official casualty figures, making independent verification difficult.
Despite these losses, Moscow continues its military operations. The Economist also reported that Ukrainian forces had recaptured approximately 73 square kilometers of territory over the previous three months.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 31 that Russian forces had suffered another 1,670 personnel losses over the previous 24 hours, bringing Ukraine’s cumulative estimate to approximately 1,588,170 since February 2022.
The Ukrainian military also reported the loss of two Russian air defense systems and 206 vehicles and fuel tankers during the same period.

Cambodia sees rise in drug arrests, drop in seizures in first 10 months of 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:22:35 CST
17:22:35 KST

PHNOM PENH, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia reported a rise in drug-related arrests but a drop in overall narcotics seizures during the first 10 months of 2026, according to an Anti-Drug Department (ADP) report released on Sunday.
The Southeast Asian nation detained 25,360 drug suspects during the January-October period, a 16.3 percent increase compared to 21,800 during the same period last year. Foreign nationals made up 1,248 of the detainees, representing 25 different nationalities.
Of the total suspects, 48.3 percent were classified as drug traffickers, manufacturers, possessors, or transporters, while 51.7 percent were recorded as drug users.
"Authorities confiscated 4.26 tons of illicit drugs and 537 kilograms of dry cannabis between Jan. 1 and Oct. 31, 2026," the report said, adding that this marked a decrease from the 5.48 tons of narcotics and 516 kilograms of dry marijuana seized during the same timeframe in 2025.
Other seized evidence included 73 pistols and 27 homemade rifles, the report said, adding that the confiscated narcotics largely consisted of ketamine, ecstasy, heroin, crystal methamphetamine, methamphetamine pills, cocaine, and cathinone.
Cambodia does not impose the death penalty for drug offenses. Under national law, individuals convicted of trafficking more than 80 grams of illicit drugs can face life imprisonment. ■

Protocol upgrading China-Peru FTA takes effect
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:22:31 CST
17:22:31 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- The protocol upgrading the China-Peru free trade agreement (FTA) took effect on Sunday, according to China's Ministry of Commerce (MOC).
China and Peru launched negotiations on the upgrade in November 2018 and signed the protocol on Nov. 14, 2024. The original FTA was signed in 2009 and took effect in 2010.
The protocol improves seven existing chapters of the original FTA, covering rules of origin, customs procedures and trade facilitation, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, intellectual property rights, trade in services, temporary entry of business personnel, and investment, the MOC said in an online statement.
The protocol also adds five new chapters on standards and conformity assessment cooperation, competition policy, e-commerce, global supply chains, and environment and trade.
The two sides also set out future provisions for negotiations on negative lists for trade in services and investment, aimed at further raising openness in these areas, according to the statement.
The China-Peru FTA was the first comprehensive free trade agreement China signed with a Latin American country.
China is Peru's largest trading partner, largest export market and largest source of imports, while Peru is China's fourth-largest trading partner in Latin America and an important investment destination, said an MOC official.
Under the protocol, the new chapter on global supply chains encourages multimodal transport and the development of foreign trade logistics corridors and infrastructure, an innovative arrangement that signals the two countries' commitment to keeping supply chains stable and unimpeded.
The chapter on standards and conformity assessment cooperation establishes a dedicated cooperation mechanism and sets out an intended cooperation list, creating a platform for mutual recognition of standards that is expected to reduce trade costs for enterprises.
The two sides agreed to launch negotiations on negative lists for trade in services and investment within two years after the protocol takes effect, in a bid to further raise the level of openness in these areas and continue to tap the potential of bilateral trade and investment, the official added.
Since the original FTA came into force in 2010, it has played an important role in promoting bilateral economic and trade cooperation. Two-way trade rose from 6.4 billion U.S. dollars in 2009 to 50.4 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, an increase of nearly seven times, official data show.
The protocol is expected to help tap further opportunities for bilateral trade and investment cooperation, provide a better business environment for enterprises of both countries and inject new vitality into bilateral economic and trade relations, the MOC said. ■

Chinese research ships map Taiwan’s undersea infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:22:25 UTC
17:22:25 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — China has ramped up undersea mapping operations in waters east and south of Taiwan to advance its ability to seize it, according to a Wall Street Journal report.
Chinese research vessels are surveying the subsurface landscape to help its submarines and underwater drones, which could be used to blockade or halt US intervention, Bryan Clark, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, said.
Surveying around Taiwan increased following an announcement by Japan and the Philippines in May of plans to hold discussions on overlapping maritime boundaries in waters east of Taiwan. The two countries have stepped up defense cooperation in response to what they see as threats from Beijing.
“China is capitalizing on the boundary talks as a pretext for what it likely wanted to do anyway: that is, to ratchet up the pressure on Taiwan,” said Allen Zhang, a Heritage Foundation research assistant. “Beijing has long sought legal cover for its gray-zone tactics—coercive activities short of lethal force—and research vessels fit that mold quite well,” Zhang added.
Su Chih-chieh (蘇志杰), an associate professor at National Taiwan University’s Institute of Oceanography, said, “They are launching research ships as fast as dropping dumplings into a pot. Taiwan is having a really hard time catching up right now.”
Taiwan has only five ships actively carrying out its own maritime research. It added two ships in August.
Chen Chung-ling (陳璋玲), president of the National Academy of Marine Research in Kaohsiung, said Taiwanese research efforts demonstrate Taiwan’s commitment to security, WSJ reported. “The more you understand the ocean, the more you can get from it,” she said.
However, Liao Te-yu (陳璋玲), director general of the Taiwan Ocean Research Institute, warned that Taiwan’s research ships are more academically focused and do not necessarily align with defense needs. “We actually understand very little about the waters surrounding us,” Liao said.
China also uses research vessels to locate telecommunications cables, which are another target in a conflict, WSJ cited analysts as saying.
“They’re trying to see what the undersea infrastructure looks like, because they probably want the ability to cut off Taiwan from outside communications if they can as part of a coercion campaign,” Clark said.
WSJ cited a Center for Strategic and International Studies report as saying China-linked research vessels “spent a disproportionately large share of their observed time near critical infrastructure compared with research vessels from 47 other countries.”

"He had a big problem with Haiti. They killed some of his people. And I said, you're running your country, you have to do what you have to do," he added.
The remarks appeared to suggest that at least some of the four missing Salvadoran technicians had died, although their deaths have not been officially confirmed.
Asked whether Washington was considering providing assistance, Trump said: "He doesn't need help. He's in pretty good shape."
El Salvador deploys over 2,000 troops to Haiti
El Salvador announced Wednesday that it was deploying more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti to search for four Salvadoran aviation technicians who disappeared following a gang ambush near Port-au-Prince on Oct. 18.
The four technicians were serving with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, which supports Haitian authorities in combating armed criminal groups.
Bukele later confirmed on US social media platform X that he spoke with Trump.
The Salvadoran president had previously rejected reports that bodies recovered in Haiti belonged to the missing technicians.
Meanwhile, the office of Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime confirmed Wednesday that the Salvadoran and Haitian governments agreed to strengthen coordination on rescue operations and security.

FBI blames North Korea for $6.3 billion Binance crypto hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:15:37 UTC
17:15:37 KST

According to the CISA, TraderTraitor is a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group that has been associated with cryptocurrency thefts and cyberattack tactics since at least 2020.
The US' Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has accused North Korea of being behind a major hack targeting the Binance cryptocurrency exchange earlier this week.
Binance suffered what its co-CEO Richard Teng described as a "complex attack" that saw hackers gain access to its hot wallets and steal $6.3 billion in digital assets.
"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the FBI said in a statement on Saturday.
"The FBI refers to this specific North Korean malicious cyber activity as 'TraderTraitor,'" it continued, adding that it had observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets into Ethereum and that it expected these to be "further laundered by converting them using DeFi and instant swap services."
According to the US' Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), TraderTraitor is a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group that has been associated with cryptocurrency thefts and cyberattack tactics since at least 2020.
It is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which the CISA says has carried out attacks against a variety of blockchain and cryptocurrency industry targets using spearphishing campaigns and malware.
Following the Binance attack, the exchange announced that it had suspended deposits and withdrawals as its team carried out security checks, froze funds and worked with law enforcement operatives to investigate the incident.
The company said that it has now covered around 90% of the impacted amount stolen in the hack and that withdrawals were resuming "in phases."
Binance said the remaining 10% of tokens were "less liquid," meaning they could take longer to buy.
In a video statement posted on social media, Teng said the company was "committed to covering all hacked losses through our company funds."
"Your assets are safe," he added.

Bangladesh forms wage board as garment workers protest
Demonstrations held in industrial cities as workers demand wage increase as cost of living rises.
Bangladesh has formed a new wage board to review the minimum wage for garment workers as it tries to quell a protest movement that has disrupted key industrial hubs.
Despite the announcement on Sunday, thousands of workers demanding higher wages continued protesting around the capital, Dhaka. Clashes were reported with police, who fired tear gas and sound grenades.
The garment sector is the backbone of Bangladesh’s export-driven economy, employing millions of workers and generating the bulk of the country’s foreign earnings.
Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($242), more than double the current wage of 12,500 taka ($101). They said the rising costs of food, housing, transport and healthcare have sharply eroded their purchasing power.
The six-member board is to include representatives of the government, workers and factory owners and is tasked with determining a new minimum wage.
“The issue of forming the wage board has been resolved. There will be no more problems now,” Ministry of Labour and Employment adviser M Sakhawat Hossain Chowdhury told reporters.
“The workers should return to work and work smoothly,” he added.
Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury warned that prolonged factory closures and production disruptions could delay export shipments and payments from international buyers, creating further difficulties for manufacturers and workers alike.
The protests began on Saturday and prompted about 30 garment factories on the outskirts of Dhaka to declare holidays, according to Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of the Ashulia Industrial Police.
Clashes between workers and police in Ashulia injured several people, including police officers, police said.
Bangladesh’s garment industry is the world’s largest after China’s, contributing about 10 percent of gross domestic product.
Manufacturers, however, said the sector is facing mounting challenges, including rising production costs, periodic gas and electricity shortages, and uncertainty in energy markets linked to tensions in the Middle East during the United States-Israel war on Iran.

Donald Trump loses allies after elections in Serbia and Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:11:00 UTC
17:11:00 KST

Donald Trump loses allies after elections in Serbia and Brazil
November 1, 2026
The midterm elections in the United States are just around the corner: On Tuesday, November 3, American voters will choose their representatives to the US Congress. The right-wing-conservative Republican party of President Donald Trump currently has a majority in both chambers.
But in other parts of the world election results are already in. The majority of voters in both Serbia and Brazil cast their ballots for left-wing parties. Those results will not influence the midterms in the US, but the victories of the Student List in Serbia and the incumbent president, Luiz Inacio "Lula" da Silva, in Brazil are bad news for Trump all the same.
In Serbia, he has lost an important European ally in outgoing president Aleksandar Vucic. And in Brazil, the Trump camp had been hoping Flavio Bolsonaro would triumph.
"Trump was a strong supporter of both Jair Bolsonaro, the Trump-like figure who served as president before Lula defeated him in 2022, and of his son Flavio," says Lawrence J. Haas, a senior fellow for US foreign policy at the American Foreign Policy Council, who was communications director for Al Gore, Bill Clinton's vice president, in the 1990s. "Trump wasn't happy about the defeat of either Bolsonaro," he continues, "and he doesn't feel warmly toward Lula. So relations will remain cool at best."
Trump declared Brazilian election looked "rigged"
Flavio Bolsonaro is under investigation in Brazil for alleged corruption and money laundering. After losing the election, he fled the country for Florida. The US State Department granted him and his family entry visas in spite of the pending legal action.
Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat. Instead, he claims there were irregularities in the vote. This is very reminiscent of Trump, who continues to claim – falsely – that Joe Biden and the Democratic Party "stole" the US election in 2020. Trump's comments on Bolsonaro's defeat sounded very familiar. "It looked like another rigged election, frankly," the US president said on Monday. "Elections have to be indisputable – and it looked very bad to me."
Good relations with Putin ally Vucic
Aleksandar Vucic had ruled Serbia as president with an iron fist since 2017. He resigned just before these elections in order to stand as prime minister, a role he previously held from 2014 to 2017. Vucic has commented in the past that he and President Trump are like-minded people. Trump's eldest son, Donald Jr., visited Vucic in Belgrade shortly before the US presidential elections in November 2024, and again a few months later.
The US Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), which is closely connected with Trump's MAGA ("Make America Great Again") movement, recently announced that it was organizing a meeting in Belgrade in November, at which Vucic was to be a keynote speaker. It is unclear whether this is still the case.
Another thing Vucic and Trump have in common is that the soon-to-be-ex-president of Serbia has a much more positive attitude toward Russian president Vladimir Putin than do most other European heads of state. Vucic did not join EU countries in imposing sanctions on Russia after it launched its war of aggression against Ukraine. Belgrade still buys Russian raw materials, and Serbian state media under Vucic presented a more positive image of Russia than of the EU.
Trump also seems increasingly inclined toward Moscow. His special envoy Steve Witkoff recently described Putin as a "humanitarian," while, in an interview, Trump himself openly admitted that he got on better with Putin than with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The end of the Vucic government now means that Trump has lost one of his few allies in Europe who takes a similar view.
Israel: Outcome still unclear
There's still a chance of an outcome in the Israeli elections that might be to Trump's liking. With more than 96% of votes counted, the right-wing bloc led by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu is in the lead. However, Trump ally Netanyahu has lost his majority, and the coalition negotiations will be very difficult.
Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies since well before February this year, when they joined forces to launch a war against Iran. In 2018, during his first term in office, Trump moved the US embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. This was controversial, because both Israel and Palestinians claim Jerusalem as their capital. Netanyahu's camp welcomed the decision.
Today, the United States is still by far Israel's most important partner, while Israel is an important regional ally for the US. It is not clear what their relationship would be like with a different Israeli government. If Netanyahu remains in power, little, if anything, will change.
No rosy prospects for Trump in the midterms
With Vucic's defeat, Trump has lost a loyal ally. And Lula's victory means, for him, that a disagreeable president remains in power. None of this is good for Trump, but foreign policy analyst Haas said it won't influence the important midterm elections in his country. "Americans will be voting [...] on the basis of issues that affect them, and how they feel about the party in power."
But this doesn't bode well for Trump, either. "Trump has the lowest approval rating of any president on the eve of a mid-term election since Harry Truman in 1946," Haas explained. "Americans are very concerned about issues of affordability, [and] they strongly oppose the US-Iran war."
Benjamin Alvarez Gruber in Miami contributed to this report, which was originally written in German.

Judge rules on Trump’s $10 billion WSJ-Epstein lawsuit
A federal judge has permanently dismissed US President Donald Trump’s $10 billion amended defamation case against the Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a report about his letter to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
In July 2025, the WSJ published an article describing a sexually suggestive note, which Trump allegedly presented to the disgraced financier for his 50th birthday in 2003. It reportedly appeared in a book of congratulatory letters put together by Ghislaine Maxwell, who is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence for her participation in Epstein’s sex-trafficking scheme.
The note, which, among other things, said: “Happy Birthday – and may every day be another wonderful secret,” contained several lines of typed text framed by a hand-drawn outline of what looks to be a nude woman. A signature resembling the one used by Trump appeared in the area where the figure’s pelvic region might be.
Following the publication, the US president vigorously denied the authorship of the raunchy birthday card, claiming: “This is not me. This is a fake thing. I never wrote a picture in my life. I don’t draw pictures of women.”
Trump’s initial defamation case against the Wall Street Journal and Murdoch’s News Corp., which owns the outlet, was rejected by US District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami in April. However, he allowed the president’s team to fix the legal defects that he had identified and file another complaint.
On Saturday, the same judge threw out Trump’s second attempt to sue the WSJ and Murdoch, saying that “as with his first attempt, he has failed” to prove that the defendants acted with actual malice when they reported on the birthday card.
Gayles disagreed with Trump’s lawyers, who argued that the outlet should have dropped the story as soon as the president denied his involvement with Epstein. “That is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment,” he wrote in a 20-page ruling.
The judge dismissed the case “with prejudice,” meaning that it cannot be refiled again.
A spokesperson for the WSJ’s publisher, Dow Jones & Co., said in a statement that it’s “pleased with the court’s decision.”
The representative of Trump’s legal team insisted that “the president will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions.” A source told CBS News that the ruling by Gayles will likely be appealed.
Trump has repeatedly denied having been friendly with Epstein, who died in a New York jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges. However, the US president’s name is mentioned on at least 3,000 occasions in a massive trove of files related to the investigation of Epstein’s case, which had been released by the US Department of Justice last year.
