Israel’s war on homes: From Hebron to Gaza and southern Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:34:55 UTC
16:34:55 KST

“Around 12:30 at night, the Israeli army vehicles were at al-Jalda Square,” one Hebron resident told Al Jazeera. “They told us to leave our homes. We asked until when, and they said until further notice. We left with the clothes on our backs.”
Hours earlier on October 23, two Israeli soldiers had been killed by armed Palestinian men at a checkpoint near the city. Hebron, the occupied West Bank’s largest city, has been under Israeli siege ever since, with restrictions extending across a governorate of about 800,000 Palestinians.
A black X now marks the homes from which families have been forcibly expelled. Soldiers have moved into others, turning them into military outposts.
In just over a week, nearly 5,000 Palestinians have been displaced, according to UNRWA, the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, which called the measures collective punishment in violation of international law.
The current operation builds on years of demolitions. From 2009 up until the siege began on October 23, Israeli forces demolished 2,491 buildings and displaced 3,534 Palestinians in the Hebron governorate, according to the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). Across Area C and occupied East Jerusalem, the monthly average of demolitions since 2024 has been at least double that of the preceding 15 years.
Many demolitions are linked to Israel’s restrictive permit system. Palestinians struggle to obtain Israeli-issued building permits, leaving structures built without them vulnerable to demolition.
In Masafer Yatta, a cluster of 13 communities in the South Hebron Hills, Israeli authorities have demolished about 400 structures in 15 years, displacing 969 Palestinians. Nearly half were demolished since January 2025.
UNRWA’s West Bank director, Roland Friedrich, said the scenes in Hebron carry “alarming echoes” of the mass displacement in the northern occupied West Bank in early 2025, when Israeli military operations emptied the Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams refugee camps.
More than 34,000 Palestinian refugees from the Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams camps remain displaced, according to UNRWA, more than a year after Israel’s “Iron Wall” operation began in January 2025. The operation destroyed more than half of the camps’ residential buildings.
OCHA’s demolition records capture only a fraction of that destruction. Between 2009 and October 2026, the agency recorded 1,399 buildings demolished in the Jenin and Tulkarem governorates, displacing 4,139 people. Those records mainly track demolitions carried out for lack of permits or as punishment, not buildings destroyed during military raids.
An investigation by the research group Forensic Architecture found evidence of deliberate, systematic destruction. Researchers verified more than 200 incidents involving the destruction of buildings and streets across four refugee camps, using armoured bulldozers, controlled demolitions and air attacks. They found that roads were widened through homes and gardens to create routes for military vehicles. The group concluded that Israel was applying tactics in the occupied West Bank similar to those it had used in Gaza.
In February 2025, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said Tulkarem and Jenin would come to resemble Jabalia and Shujayea, two of Gaza’s most devastated areas.
The raids have not stopped. Last week, Israeli forces detained four Palestinians in Tulkarem, and in the village of Burin, south of Nablus, troops converted several homes into military barracks, as they have in Hebron.
Near Jenin, the army has ordered the residents of an entire village to leave permanently. “I have sheep and cows. Our entire lives are tied to this land,” said farmer Jabri Yahya. “Last year they uprooted our olive trees, and this year they want to force us to leave. We don’t know where to go.”
In Gaza, the destruction is on a far larger scale. By June 16, 2026, an estimated 201,290 structures had been damaged or destroyed, about 82 percent of all structures in the Strip, according to the UN Satellite Centre (UNOSAT).
Many families now shelter in tents, makeshift structures or damaged buildings, often without reliable water or sanitation.
Another winter brings new risks. Mohammed al-Jamal, 60, has been displaced several times since he fled his home in Gaza City’s Shujayea neighbourhood. He now shares a worn-out tent on the beach with about 30 members of his extended family, patching it before every storm because they cannot afford a new tarpaulin. “We are living in the street, not in houses that protect us,” he said.
Across the Strip, the neighbourhoods families fled have been reduced to rubble. Google Maps satellite imagery updated in September shows the scale of the destruction across the besieged Gaza Strip, more than three years into Israel’s genocidal war.
Drag the sliders below to compare neighbourhoods before and after.
In southern Lebanon, a July 2026 assessment by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), based on satellite imagery from June 16, identified 31,259 buildings damaged or destroyed, mainly south of the Litani River.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) recorded displacement of 333,144 people across Lebanon as of September 9.
Despite the ceasefire between Israel and Lebanon, Israeli forces continue to occupy parts of the south, and demolitions have left many residents unsure whether they can return.
Across Hebron, Jenin, Gaza and southern Lebanon, the destruction does more than displace people. It leaves them nothing to return to.
In Hebron, UN human rights chief Volker Turk warned that “threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods” raise "serious concerns of ethnic cleansing", and called for all those displaced to be allowed home.
For many families, the question is no longer when they will go home, but whether there will be a home to go back to.

====================================================================================================

India is running out of time on fifth-generation fighter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:33:59 UTC
16:33:59 KST

India is running out of time on fifth-generation fighter
Despite India’s increased defense spending, robust government support for domestic arms and military technology manufacturers, and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s personal focus on the development of the military-industrial complex, experts warn that the Indian Air Force faces a critical squadron decline that may influence its ability to counter potential adversaries.
This paradox stems from India’s procurement policies, which do not prioritize the acquisition of advanced aircraft for the air force. Apparently, segments of India’s business elite and military leadership, possibly influenced by Western companies, are lobbying for contracts that offer questionable benefits to the country’s armed forces.
While India’s geopolitical and military rivals (China and Pakistan) invest in cutting-edge technology – such as the fifth-generation J-20 and J-35 multi-role fighters – India continues to acquire fourth-generation aircraft like the Rafale and Tejas fighters. However, such aircraft cannot address modern combat challenges or threats effectively.
The situation looks even more dire considering that the Rafale and Tejas fighters are not superior to the Su-30MKI, the primary fighter in service with the Indian Air Force, and may even fall short when it comes to certain tactical specifications. The Su-30MKI boasts significant advantages in speed, maneuverability, payload capacity, and operational range.
This raises a crucial question: why are substantial financial resources from the Indian budget allocated for the purchase of expensive aircraft (Rafale fighters cost about €160 million each) directly from the French private firm Dassault Aviation, when the state-owned Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) offers the option to procure Su-30MKI aircraft assembled under license from Russia at a considerably lower cost?
Real threats
Clearly, the rivalry between Pakistan (and China, which stands behind it) and India is not going to fade anytime soon. In fact, competition will likely intensify in the foreseeable future. A critical factor in preventing the most dangerous scenarios lies in maintaining a balance of military capabilities and defense potential between the opposing sides. So, what does the power balance look like today?
Islamabad and Beijing are heavily investing in fifth-generation multirole fighters. By 2030, Pakistan is expected to field no fewer than 40 J-35AE fighters, while the Chinese Air Force could deploy up to 500 J-20s and J-35 fighters. Additionally, the Chinese Navy may have over 50 carrier-based J-35s. In total, this amounts to about 600 fifth-generation fighters – each one of them superior to any fourth-generation aircraft.
Armed with highly effective long-range air-to-air weapons, Pakistan and China’s stealthy fifth-generation fighters will be able to launch missile attacks without being detected by Indian Air Force radar systems. Under such circumstances, India’s military aviation could face a devastating defeat, leading to humiliation and a prolonged recovery process. This is inevitable, since fifth-generation fighters surpass fourth-generation aircraft.
The strategy of overwhelming the enemy with sheer numbers and concentrating an extensive air force over specific combat zones, is fundamentally flawed: no number of Rafale or Tejas fighters can match the combat capabilities of J-20 and J-35 aircraft.
The air forces of Pakistan and China possess cutting-edge technologies like stealth capabilities, advanced radar systems capable of covertly tracking opponents, and long-range missiles that significantly outdistance those in the arsenals of Rafale and Tejas fighters.
However, if the Indian Air Force were to acquire Su-57E fighters, equipped with stealth technology, the modern N-036 Byelka radar, long-range RVV-BD missiles, and other state-of-the-art munitions, India’s ability to confront its neighbors in the above-mentioned scenarios would change dramatically.
Why Russia?
For over 70 years, Soviet and Russian aviation technology has been in service with the Indian military, demonstrating remarkable efficiency and reliability. Russia has proven to be a dependable partner in military-technical cooperation.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has praised the quality and effectiveness of Russian weapons, particularly highlighting their successful deployment during Operation Sindoor in May 2025. Moscow is eager to continue the mutually beneficial collaboration with New Delhi in the defense sector. This includes maintaining the joint Su-30MKI program and potentially organizing licensed assembly of the fifth-generation Su-57E fighter at facilities operated by India’s HAL.
The ongoing modernization of the Pakistani Air Force and the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Air Force with advanced aircraft has prompted India to take decisive actions to restore parity and the balance of power. Given the current circumstances, a swift acquisition of 50 Su-57E fighters from Russia under a fast-track mechanism, along with plans for licensed production of an additional 450 units in India, seems like the most prudent course of action. This could involve the latest two-seat variant, the Su-57D. Over the next few decades, such a project would effectively address the challenges and threats that India faces.
More than just a prototype
The Su-57 fighter jet has already entered service with the Russian Air Force and has participated in combat operations.
India contributed to the development of the fighter that served as the basis for the Su-57. In 2010, the Indian Ministry of Defense initiated the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) program to create an indigenous fifth-generation fighter. However, after more than 15 years, this program has yet to reach the flight testing stage. Serial production is not likely to commence before 2035.
Alexander Mikheev, head of Rosoboronexport, and Vadim Badekha, head of the United Aircraft Corporation (UAC), confirmed that the Su-57 aircraft – specifically its export version, the Su-57E – is already being delivered abroad. The Su-57E is available for friendly countries collaborating with Russia on defense projects. If India approaches Moscow regarding the supply of this combat aircraft, Russia would likely respond in a positive manner.
Moreover, advanced Russian technologies transferred to India under a licensing agreement will assist Indian specialists in refining and successfully implementing several national projects, including the AMCA.
Unlike American F-35s – which have struggled to maintain supersonic speeds in sustained cruise mode – the Su-57 meets all the criteria expected of a fifth-generation fighter.
For New Delhi, the Su-57 offers multiple advantages, especially since it was designed at the same bureau that developed the Su-30MKI – the Indian Air Force’s primary combat aircraft as of 2026. This continuity provides valuable benefits in terms of operational procedures, maintenance, repair, and logistical support, leveraging existing airfield, storage, and training infrastructures.
Indigenous programs
Prime Minister Narendra Modi highly supports India’s national defense industry initiatives. He made history as the first prime minister of India to fly in the cockpit of a supersonic fighter jet.
Professional pilots who have flown the Tejas aircraft praise its performance, noting it surpasses the MiG-21, which the Tejas was designed to replace under the Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) program that began in 1983. However, the mission was not fulfilled; the project has faced significant delays, and by the time the Tejas was deployed in 2015, the vast majority of the 874 MiG-21s acquired by the Indian Air Force between 1963 and 1987 had already been retired due to wear and tear. Instead of 20 squadrons of MiG aircraft, by 2026, the Indian Air Force had just two Tejas squadrons consisting of 30 single-seat and six two-seat models. Field tests are being conducted to identify and rectify issues on aircraft from the initial production batch.
The 18th Squadron, formed in 2020, has already lost two Tejas planes in accidents – one in March 2024 and another in November 2025. The latter incident involved a fatal failure during a demonstration flight at an airshow in Dubai. The initial variant (Mark I) will no longer be produced, as it proved unreliable and technically inadequate.
Like many Indian projects, Tejas is plagued by delays which result in technological obsolescence by the time of production. Consequently, the substantial financial investments in such programs fail to deliver the expected returns or strengthen India’s defense capabilities.
Indian manufacturers also developed a naval version of the Tejas. Testing began in 2020 aboard the INS Vikramaditya aircraft carrier (built by Russia under Project 11430) and continued three years later on the indigenously constructed INS Vikrant. The compact design of the Tejas offers advantages for hangar storage; however, with a standard combat load, it can only operate within a few hundred miles. During combat operations, the carrier would need to approach the target closer, increasing the risk of retaliatory strikes from the enemy.
After conducting evaluations, the Indian Navy concluded that such an aircraft was not suitable for carrier operations. The official reason for rejecting the LCA-Navy was its low thrust-to-weight ratio, which prevented full utilization of the aircraft’s potential when taking off from an aircraft carrier. In response to requests from Indian industry, further tests were conducted on an upgraded version, but its performance still fell short of naval requirements.
Coming to terms with the LCA-Navy’s inability to meet expectations, Indian aerospace engineers proposed a completely new aircraft – the Twin Engine Deck Based Fighter (TEDBF), which bears a striking resemblance to the French Rafale-M. This move signifies a concession by the creators and advocates of the Tejas, acknowledging their defeat in the competition for carrier aviation. Work on the TEDBF began in 2020. The prototype’s first flight is scheduled for 2032 and serial production is anticipated in 2038.
Meanwhile, last year, the People’s Liberation Army Navy received its third aircraft carrier, the Fujian, equipped with fifth-generation J-35 fighters. Construction has also begun on the fourth Type 004 aircraft carrier. It will likely have a displacement of around 100,000 tons and accommodate an air wing of 100 aircraft, including the J-35.
Dependence on the US
In coordination with the main contractor, Indian industry continues Tejas Mark IA testing, which started in spring 2022. Without waiting for these trials to conclude, the Indian Air Force has placed two successive orders totaling 141 single-seat and 41 two-seat aircraft, scheduled for delivery between 2027 and 2032. Production will take place at two facilities in Bangalore and Nasik.
Following this, production of the Tejas Mark II is expected to commence. The first test flight has faced multiple delays and is now expected no earlier than 2028. While no firm order has been placed for this new model, the Air Force leadership hopes to eventually have 18 squadrons of Tejas aircraft, including 10 Mark II variant squadrons.
The idea to direct resources into producing fourth-generation fighters for the next decade seems imprudent, given that China has mastered mass production of fifth-generation aircraft and is set to begin transitioning to sixth-generation models in the coming years. Deliveries of Chinese J-35 fifth-generation fighters to Pakistan are underway, while existing JF-17s are being upgraded with systems and munitions developed for the J-35.
However, a far more pressing issue is the potential deepening dependence on the United States. Throughout the practical implementation of the LCA program, the technical specifications of the aircraft have been repeatedly adjusted, primarily by replacing certain Indian components with foreign ones, which gradually increases the foreign share in the cost of mass-produced products. Among the imported items, the most expensive was the US engine, which had to replace the GTX-35VS Kaveri engine which faced challenges in meeting technical criteria.
Negotiations for a licensed production agreement for the F414 engine have been challenging, largely because Washington is reluctant to share advanced General Electric technologies developed with Pentagon funding. The US is only willing to share some of the technology, omitting the most sensitive components.
The reluctance to fully share F414 engine technology can be explained by one factor: Washington seeks to maintain leverage over New Delhi by controlling the pace of the licensed production of engines for India’s frontline air force.
The second most costly imported component is the onboard radar system. Development of an indigenous MMR radar was halted due to unsatisfactory test results, leading to a preference for foreign alternatives. The prototype aircraft utilized the Ericsson-Ferranti PS-05 radar, originally designed for the Swedish JAS-39 Gripen. Delays in the LCA program rendered the PS-05 obsolete, resulting in its discontinuation. It has since been replaced by the EL/M-2032, which now equips Mark I variants.
It’s worth noting that Elta’s product is also outdated; it was developed in the 1980s for the Israeli Lavi fighter jet (canceled in 1987). The obsolescence is particularly evident in its use of mechanical beam scanning, while the Russian N-011M radar on the Su-30MKI, which was introduced into the Indian Air Force in 2002, boasts more advanced electronic scanning technology.
Recently, Elta proposed the EL/M-2052 with an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar configuration. The manufacturer promises to refine it by the time Mark IA aircraft (formed in 2015) are delivered to the air force, projected for late this year or early next year. Various publications have diligently presented Israeli radars as a “temporary solution” for the Tejas program, but as seen with General Electric engines, “temporary” solutions often end up being used much longer than expected.
Strategic decision-making
The practical implementation of the LCA program has resulted in yet another fourth-generation supersonic fighter jet emerging on the global stage. However, the Tejas does not surpass its foreign counterparts. Technically, the Tejas Mark I barely matches the Chinese FC-1, which was adopted by the Pakistan Air Force as the JF-17 in 2007. At best, the Tejas Mark II might reach the level of the JF-17 Block III (with AESA, operational since 2023) and the J-10CE, which Pakistani pilots effectively utilized to fend off an Indian airstrike in May 2025.
With the Indian Air Force already operating a substantial fleet of over 300 Su-30MKIs and Rafale aircraft, which are far better suited for the interception of aerial threats and air superiority missions, the Tejas Mark I may only serve effectively in ground attack operations and pilot training. Fortunately, being a lightweight, single-engine aircraft means it has low fuel consumption. Nevertheless, its limited thrust-to-weight ratio, outdated radar, reduced payload capacity, and narrow selection of munitions (lacking long-range air-to-air missiles), along with the absence of critical stealth technologies naturally confine the aircraft to its own niche. The Su-57E is in a different class altogether.
Consequently, the Tejas cannot be viewed as a viable alternative to the Su-57E. Continuing the LCA program in its current form hampers the decision-making process, since the program competes for budget resources. Moreover, there’s another contender for state funding – the AMCA, with its first flight planned for 2034 and serial production slated for 2036.
In selecting a fifth-generation fighter program, decision-makers in India will need to consider numerous factors and criteria that can sometimes be conflicting and contradictory. Among these is the inherent bias towards domestic projects (i.e. AMCA, LCA, etc.), even if they may not be technically or technologically superior compared to the best foreign alternatives.
The desire to produce everything domestically is understandable, but there are many compelling arguments in favor of purchasing the best foreign technologies or producing them under license. The advanced Su-57E, a premier frontline fighter, is one of such example. For India, Russia remains a reliable partner as decades of effective military-technical collaboration have proven.

The opposition bloc has agreed on its first move in the new Knesset - replacing Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana of the Likud - despite the fact that it has not yet been decided who will form the next government, according to local news reports.

The speaker is elected in an open vote, one of a new Knesset’s first orders of business. To oust Ohana, the opposition bloc will need a majority of the Knesset’s 120 members behind a single candidate, possibly with support from the Arab parties. No agreement on the next government is required.
Possible candidates for speaker include Chili Tropper, Matan Kahana, and Elazar Stern of Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party; Merav Ben-Ari and Eitan Ginzburg of Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad party; Efrat Rayten of the Democrats; and Oded Forer of Yisrael Beytenu.
On Wednesday, KAN News reported that the bloc leaders were considering Yair Lapid for speaker.
Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman predicted this week that some outgoing coalition lawmakers would also back replacing Ohana, estimating that as many as a third could vote against him.
Eisenkot lays out top intentions, top issues, in process of forming a gov't
This comes as Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot announced on Saturday that he intended to negotiate his way to a parliamentary majority, establish an October 7 Commission of Inquiry, implement compulsory military service for all, and repeal the judicial reform laws.
"Every Knesset member who is willing to sign on to these principles is a potential partner on the path to establishing a new and better government for Israel," Eisenkot wrote on X. “We are ready and prepared to pave the way for ousting the Netanyahu government. Change goes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a real and equal partnership. Nothing less than that, and nothing more than that,” Joint List chairman Prof. Yousef Jabareen said.
Ofer Cassif, a Knesset member who is No. 5 on the Joint List’s slate, also addressed the opposition bloc parties.
“This is now or never: the removal of the malicious government and the beginning of repair, or the continuation of the horrors of the last four years. We are committed to repair; will the opposition bloc rise to the occasion? The ball is in their court,” he said.
Joint List leader MK Ahmad Tibi said that his party will not join the coalition in a "Meet the Press" interview on Saturday.
"We will not be a part of the government," he said, noting that he and his fellow party members want to make the coalition process "easier, not harder."

London's Metropolitan Police arrested 139 people during a demonstration outside the US Embassy in the British capital on Saturday after protesters expressed support for Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian group that has been outlawed in the UK and designated a terrorist organization.
The Metropolitan Police said most of those detained were arrested for expressing support for a banned organization and that officers continued making arrests at the scene.
According to a report by the Associated Press, many of the demonstrators were pensioners carrying signs reading, "I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action." One protester also climbed a tree near the embassy and held up a sign calling for support for the organization.
The demonstration was organized by the activist group Defend Our Juries, which is campaigning against the British government's decision to outlaw Palestine Action.
According to the organizers, more than 4,000 people have been arrested since July 2025 for violating the ban on supporting the organization. The organizers condemned the arrests, arguing that detaining people for participating in peaceful demonstrations constituted a serious violation of civil rights and freedom of expression.
Palestine Action activists broke into and vandalized Elbit facilities
The British government banned Palestine Action in 2025 following a series of operations carried out by its members against defense facilities, particularly those belonging to Israeli defense company Elbit Systems.
Under British law, membership in or support for an organization designated as a terrorist group can carry a prison sentence of up to 14 years.
Palestine Action, founded in 2020, campaigns against what it describes as British military assistance to Israel. Its members say they seek to disrupt the operations of companies that support Israel's defense industry.
In 2024, activists from the organization broke into a British factory belonging to Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems and vandalized equipment using sledgehammers and crowbars.
In June 2025, activists broke into a British Royal Air Force base, sprayed red paint into the engines of two refueling aircraft, and caused additional damage using crowbars.
The US also took action against the organization, announcing sanctions against it in August and designating it a terrorist organization.
Alongside the London demonstration, a protest in support of Palestine Action was held outside the US Consulate in Edinburgh, Scotland.
No arrests were reported there, but Police Scotland announced that it was examining evidence to identify participants who wore shirts and carried signs expressing support for the banned organization. Police said further enforcement action could follow.
The demonstrations took place ahead of a hearing scheduled for Wednesday at the UK's Supreme Court, concerning an appeal against the authorities' decision to designate Palestine Action a terrorist organization.
Supporters of the group argue that the ban infringes on freedom of expression and the right to political protest.

Israeli President Herzog to begin coalition consultations on Wednesday in hopes to form new goverment

Unknown Publisher

Israeli President Herzog to begin coalition consultations on Wednesday in hopes to form new gov't
Herzog has urged political leaders to enter the discussions with “an open mind,” emphasizing the need to avoid a fresh vote
Israeli President Isaac Herzog will begin consultations with Knesset parties on Wednesday, November 4, launching the process of forming a government after parliamentary elections left neither major bloc with a majority.
The meetings will take place at the presidential residence in Jerusalem after Central Elections Committee chair Justice Noam Sohlberg formally presents the results. The consultations are expected to be broadcast live.
The October 27 election gave Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, compared with 48 for Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc. Arab parties won the remaining 19 seats. A governing coalition generally requires the support of at least 61 lawmakers.
During the consultations, each party will be able to recommend a candidate to form the next government. Herzog will then assign the task to the lawmaker he believes has the best chance of assembling a coalition. The mandate does not automatically go to the leader of the largest party.
The selected candidate will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension. If that attempt fails, Herzog may assign the task to another lawmaker. Failure to secure a government could ultimately trigger another election.
Herzog has urged political leaders to enter the discussions with “an open mind,” emphasizing the need to avoid a fresh vote.
Netanyahu will remain prime minister, leading a caretaker government, until a new government takes office.

Rubio Doubts Ukraine Peace Deal Before Spring 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:31:00 UTC
16:31:00 KST

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio does not believe Russian President Vladimir Putin will agree to any negotiated settlement regarding Ukraine before the spring of 2027, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty correspondent Alex Raufoglu reported, citing three senior European officials.
According to European diplomats briefed on transatlantic discussions, Rubio also characterized near-term Ukrainian accession to NATO as unrealistic as a security guarantee mechanism, expressing conviction that Moscow would never consent to Kyiv’s membership in the alliance.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Speaking at the Group of 20 (G20) foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, the top US diplomat adopted a sober tone regarding the prospects of an imminent diplomatic breakthrough, pushing back against assumptions that an accord is close at hand.
“I don’t know if negotiated peace is achievable in Ukraine. That’s what we’re trying to find out,” Rubio stated during a press briefing. “I don’t think anyone here is claiming that we are on the verge of a negotiated settlement.”
Rubio explained that the Trump administration’s immediate diplomatic efforts are focused on probing the belligerents’ positions to establish whether common ground exists, rather than prematurely declaring the conflict near its conclusion.
Miami G20 summit invitations and Putin skepticism
Rubio expressed skepticism that Putin will travel to the US to attend the G20 leaders’ summit scheduled for Dec. 14-15 in Miami, Florida, despite an official invitation extended to the Russian leader by the White House.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 31, 2026
However, both Rubio and US President Donald Trump signaled that President Volodymyr Zelensky could be formally invited to participate in the Miami summit alongside world leaders.
Speaking to journalists during Halloween celebrations at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, Trump was asked whether he plans to invite Zelensky to the summit given that Putin has already received an invitation.
“Yes, no problem,” Trump replied to reporters, confirming his willingness to include the Ukrainian head of state in the gathering.
Rubio noted that leader-level attendance remains an executive presidential prerogative, while indicating openness to the idea if it advances diplomatic progress.
“This is a leader-level meeting. The decision on that has to be made by the president,” Rubio said at a press conference. “I wouldn’t rule out that possibility. Especially if something positive could happen as a result of his participation, but today I have no announcements to make on that front.”
The Kremlin previously stated that Putin’s attendance at the Miami G20 summit depends directly on the outcomes of an anticipated trilateral meeting involving Trump, Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, scheduled for Nov. 18-19.
Territorial framing and diplomatic mediation
Rubio’s cautious timeline follows remarks delivered on Oct. 22, in which he framed the armed conflict as an impasse fundamentally centered on the Donbas region.
“People keep talking about it’s a war in Ukraine. That war is about Donbas. It’s about one region of the country,” Rubio said during a prior briefing.
“At its core, it’s about 11 percent of one part of that country that Russia wants and cannot take militarily and that Ukraine is unwilling to give up. And they have good reasons why they don’t want to do that – for sovereignty and their own security long term.”
The secretary of state reiterated that neither side can achieve an absolute military victory, insisting that an enduring armistice will require mutual accommodations brokered through direct diplomacy.
“This war is not going to be solved militarily. This war is only going to end diplomatically,” Rubio explained, outlining Washington’s desired role as an honest broker.
“Can you arrive at an outcome in which both sides receive something of benefit but also give concessions and bring this to an end? As hard as it is, it is impossible to do unless both sides are at the table talking, and we’re happy to play the mediating role in that regard.”
President Zelensky previously stated that Ukraine is prepared to freeze combat operations along existing front lines to bring a swift end to active fighting, but emphasized that Kyiv will never legally recognize occupied territories as Russian sovereign soil.
Zelensky noted that Russian forces currently occupy 19.3 percent of Ukraine, dismissing suggestions that Ukraine cede the remainder of the Donbas.

SOFIA, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Bulgarians go to the polls on Sunday to vote in the second round of the country's elections for president and vice president.
Nearly 6.6 million voters are eligible to choose between incumbent President Iliana Iotova, running with Kiril Valchev as her vice-presidential candidate, and Andrey Gurov, who is seeking the presidency with Georgi Kandev as his running mate.
The Iotova-Valchev ticket, backed by the ruling Progressive Bulgaria party and the Bulgarian Socialist Party, among others, came on top in the first round on Oct. 25 with 34.76 percent of the votes.
The Gurov-Kandev ticket, supported by the parties We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria, came second among the 27 candidate pairs with 31.95 percent.
The first exit polls are expected to be released at 8:00 p.m. (1800 GMT), immediately after the close of the polls. Official results are due no later than Wednesday.
The Bulgarian president and vice president are elected directly by voters for a five-year term. Iotova's term is set to expire at the end of January 2027.
Iotova, 62, was elected vice president twice, in 2016 and 2021, serving alongside President Rumen Radev. In accordance with the country's Constitution, she succeeded Radev as head of state after he resigned in January this year. Before that, she served on the National Council of the Bulgarian Socialist Party from 2000 to 2016, as well as in the Bulgarian National Assembly and the European Parliament.
Valchev is director general of the Bulgarian News Agency.
Gurov, an adjunct professor of finance at the American University in Bulgaria, has less political experience than Iotova. He served as Bulgaria's caretaker prime minister for 78 days in the first half of this year and chaired the parliamentary group of We Continue the Change in two legislatures from December 2021 to February 2023.
Kandev is a former career police officer who served as acting secretary general at the Ministry of Interior for several months this year. ■

World Insights: Yerevan Pathway charts course for biodiversity action, but challenges remain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:25:46 CST
16:25:46 KST

YEREVAN, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- The 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) concluded in Yerevan on Saturday after negotiators secured agreement on the conference's main decisions, including the Yerevan Pathway aimed at accelerating global biodiversity action.
This encouraging outcome came at a critical time for global biodiversity protection. Halfway between the adoption of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and its 2030 deadline, countries face a widening gap between their commitments to protect nature and the action to fulfill them. Whether the Yerevan Pathway can help close that gap will depend on financing, national policies and sustained international cooperation.
A PATHWAY TO ACCELERATE ACTION
The conference's main task was to conduct the first global review of collective progress in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which sets out 23 targets for 2030.
The assessment presented governments with a clear warning: Without a rapid acceleration of implementation, the framework's 2030 targets and mission would not be achieved, putting its longer-term goals for 2050 at risk.
The Yerevan Pathway is part of the response to that assessment. Rather than setting new targets, it focuses on how countries can step up efforts to meet those already agreed upon.
Embedded in the global review decision, the pathway identifies several priorities for the period through 2030: accelerating implementation, broadening the coverage of national targets, strengthening financial and other support, engaging governments and societies more widely, and improving monitoring and knowledge.
Negotiators also adopted decisions covering protected areas and forest biodiversity, sustainable wildlife management, invasive alien species, marine and coastal biodiversity, synthetic biology and other areas.
Alongside the negotiations, nearly 2 billion U.S. dollars in new biodiversity funding was announced, according to the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). This included 560 million dollars under the ninth replenishment of the Global Environment Facility and its Global Biodiversity Framework Fund, 500 million dollars through the Species Recovery Alliance, and more than 330 million dollars through the Value Nature Fund.
Together, the decisions and funding announcements provide a basis for further action. However, the effectiveness of the pathway will depend on whether international agreements lead to changes in national priorities and concrete action on the ground.
FINANCE DIVIDE TESTS DELIVERY
Finance remains one of the main obstacles to implementation, both in terms of how much funding is available and how the responsibility for providing it is shared.
The global report found that developed countries had failed to meet their commitment to provide at least 20 billion dollars annually in biodiversity finance to developing countries by 2025. This shortfall was a major point of contention in negotiations over funding for the next stage of implementation.
Some developed countries called for broadening the contributor base, bringing into focus a longstanding dispute over the relationship between countries' financial capacity and their obligations under the CBD.
Article 20 of the convention requires developed-country parties to provide new and additional financial resources, while allowing other parties to assume such obligations voluntarily.
The new funding announcements offered some encouragement, but the broader challenge of securing predictable support on the scale needed remains. For developing countries, efforts to strengthen conservation, restore ecosystems and monitor progress continue to depend heavily on access to finance and technical assistance.
Nor did the conference resolve every issue. Negotiations on cooperation and strategic review, along with two items under the Nagoya Protocol, remained unfinished and were deferred to the next ordinary meetings.
"Every diluted clause, every deferred target, is a step towards irreversible loss," Guido Broekhoven, interim global director of multilateral policy at the World Wide Fund for Nature International, told a press conference before the closing session.
His remarks underscored a central challenge facing the negotiations: while consensus is essential to international cooperation, biodiversity loss continues as governments work to reach agreement.
CHINA'S ROLE IN ADVANCING IMPLEMENTATION
Turning commitments into concrete results was also a key theme in discussions of China's contribution, including its support for the global review, sharing experience in domestic conservation and financing for biodiversity projects in developing countries.
The global review decision specifically thanked China for hosting the Kunming dialogue to support preparations for the review. It also acknowledged financial support provided through the China Trust Fund via the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP).
In an interview with Xinhua during the conference, COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan said China had made important contributions to advancing the talks, from preparatory work to the formal negotiations.
Such cooperation has practical relevance as countries seek ways to overcome implementation barriers, Matevosyan said, adding that national experiences can help identify approaches that others may adapt to their own circumstances.
Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the secretariat of the CBD, said the progress reflected in China's seventh national report was encouraging and highlighted its ecological conservation red lines as an example of how biodiversity protection could be incorporated into national planning and development.
Financial support is another important part of turning the framework into action.
Inger Andersen, executive director of the UNEP, recognized China's continued leadership through the establishment of the Kunming Biodiversity Fund following its COP15 presidency. She emphasized the importance of helping developing countries access the financing needed to implement the agreement.
These contributions point to the task now facing all parties: ensuring that international cooperation is backed by the funding, institutions and policies needed to deliver results.
The Yerevan conference preserved a common direction at a difficult moment for biodiversity protection. The next four years will determine whether governments can turn their commitments into measurable progress before the 2030 deadline.
As Schomaker put it: "Ultimately, the test is not what governments agreed in Yerevan, but what they change when they return home." ■

Economic Watch: New Zealand firms seek to deepen China market engagement via import expo
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:25:41 CST
16:25:41 KST

WELLINGTON, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- From established exhibitors who were present for many consecutive years to innovative businesses making their debut with independent booths this year, New Zealand companies are participating in the China International Import Expo (CIIE) in increasingly diverse ways.
The CIIE is the world's first national-level exhibition dedicated to imports, and its ninth edition will take place in Shanghai from Nov. 5 to 10. For many New Zealand companies, this annual event has become an important gateway to the Chinese market.
GATEWAY TO HUGE CHINESE MARKET
For Sanchia Yonge, chief executive of New Zealand Trade and Enterprise, the international business development agency of the New Zealand government, China is an important market for New Zealand exporters.
The CIIE provides New Zealand exporters a valuable opportunity to showcase their products to buyers and consumers, understand the evolving Chinese market, strengthen brand awareness, and connect with customers, commercial and government partners who can support their long-term growth in China, Yonge stressed.
"We perceive CIIE as the most important exhibition or event for foreign companies to enter the Chinese market," said Roy Van Den Hurk, CEO of Milk New Zealand Dairy Ltd.
"It's a central point where all the buyers come to see you," he added.
For many years, Van Den Hurk personally traveled to Shanghai for the expo almost every year. From a very small booth when the company first joined it to its current independent 200-square-meter exhibition space, the company has achieved tangible business growth through the platform.
Blis Technologies, a New Zealand biotechnology company, is experiencing a new milestone this year, as it will have its own independent booth at the Shanghai expo. In just two years, sales of its oral probiotics products in China have exceeded 100,000 orders.
"First and foremost, China is a very large market. You've got to be very targeted in what you do," said Scott Johnson, CEO of Blis Technologies. "We also believe that the Chinese consumer is taking a more proactive approach to their health."
"TASTE OF NEW ZEALAND"
Sanchia Yonge said that more than 80 New Zealand exporters will be showcasing a diverse range of New Zealand products and services at the CIIE this year. Products and services on display will include food and beverages, dairy, fruit, meat, wine, honey, wool, pet food, consumer goods, health supplements, healthcare and technology.
Some New Zealand companies are participating collectively under the organization of business associations. The China Chamber of Commerce in New Zealand, in cooperation with New Zealand Trade and Enterprise, has taken the lead in organizing the "Taste of New Zealand" exhibition group. This year, it has brought 35 New Zealand exhibitors to the CIIE, with the exhibition group covering an area of 1,170 square meters.
The New Zealand Pavilion will bring together distinctive exhibitors to present a more complete tapestry of New Zealand products. These include king salmon from mountains and glacial waters on the South Island, manuka honey associated with native plants and Maori culture, avocado oil from the Bay of Plenty on the North Island, Hawke's Bay wines, as well as dairy products, ice cream and nutritional supplements.
Together, the exhibitors will showcase different aspects of the industries, from planting and farming to food processing.
Throughout the week, the New Zealand Trade and Enterprise team in China will connect exporters with buyers, partners and media, support customer meetings and networking, livestreaming, product launches and stand by as business agreements are signed.
"We want to help New Zealand exporters turn conversations at CIIE into lasting commercial partnerships in China to support their ongoing growth," said Yonge.
TARGETING SHIFTING CONSUMER DEMANDS
For New Zealand exhibitors, the CIIE is not only a platform for bringing products into the Chinese market, but also an opportunity to gain a closer understanding of the market and consumer demand.
"Going up there each year for the CIIE, you can actually feel how it changes. It's quite big changes actually that you notice," said Van Den Hurk.
To attract Chinese consumers, companies must keep up with the pace of the Chinese market, the CEO stressed, adding that they must come to China in person and engage face-to-face with consumers, the market and distribution channels.
For this reason, the company also introduces new products at the CIIE every year.
"We try to bring new products every year. And I think overall it's very successful," Van Den Hurk said, adding that the company will bring new formulations again for milk powder products, which are going to help the elderly.
He noted that his company's products, packaging and promotional channels are all being updated in response to changing Chinese consumer demand, and the CIIE is an important channel for the company to keep up with the pace of the Chinese market.
"It's the opportunity for businesses like Blis and other New Zealand companies and other global companies to showcase their products in China, with a whole lot of people coming together at one event," Scott Johnson said, adding that it also helps get feedback and understand more about the Chinese consumer and the market up there, so that "we can actually get better and improve our offering because it's always evolving".
"It's even more important to be up there on a regular basis because it's changing so quickly," he added. ■

Gaza doctors struggle with bereavement, overwork, trauma amid genocidal war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:24:20 UTC
16:24:20 KST

Gaza doctors struggle with bereavement, overwork, trauma amid genocidal war
Doctors and nurses struggle to cope with the horrors they endured during the height of the Gaza war.
Deir el-Balah, Gaza – Manar Fayyad, 29, an anaesthesiologist at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, has suffered severe psychological trauma since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.
The turning point came when he discovered that a man lying before him in the operating room was his own brother Shadi, who was killed in an Israeli air strike on December 27, 2023.
He recalled the moment he was summoned into the operating room to administer anaesthesia to a critically injured man before emergency surgery.
“He died before I could reach him,” he said. “When I arrived in the operating room, I recognised the man’s clothes. I had a strange feeling, so I approached him and uncovered his face. To my shock, he was my brother Shadi, who was 34.”
Since then, the hospital has become inseparable from the traumatic memory, and he has been unable to continue to work, ultimately bringing his professional career to a premature end.
He continues to struggle with the psychological effects of the experience, trying to cope with it on his own without professional help. He has withdrawn from social life and avoids people and noise as he searches for peace since his brother died.
Sitting by the sea and writing offers him some solace, helping him express his pain and process what has happened. Yet he remains preoccupied with the idea of leaving Gaza, hoping that distance might free him from the reminders of that day.
Having lost his brother, his profession and much of his social life, Fayyad now faces a different battle: one against trauma that he is trying to confront alone.
Khaled Raafat, 29, a nurse in the emergency department at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, stepped away from work for an extended period after losing his wife, children, mother and several siblings in an Israeli air strike on his family home on October 18, 2023. He was at the hospital at the time, trying to save their lives of others injured that day.
“Learning that I had lost my family marked a painful turning point in my life,” Khaled told Al Jazeera. “I could no longer do my job in the same way. The hospital, once associated in my mind with my humanitarian duty, became a reminder of personal pain that was beyond what I could bear. It deeply affected my ability to continue my professional and social life.”
Raafat said he eventually decided to rebuild his life.
“I realised that life could not stop at the tragedy and that I had to find a way to carry on. I decided to work towards my psychological recovery, got married and started a new family in an attempt to regain stability and hope,” he said. “I then returned to work at the hospital.”
At least 1,700 medical personnel have been killed in Israeli attacks during the war while 83 healthcare workers remain in Israeli detention, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.
These figures do not reveal the deep psychological burden borne by medical workers who have lost family, friends and colleagues and witnessed horrific injuries and death on a daily basis. They have also faced continued displacement, relentless pressure and have been overworked for years.
A study found that 41 percent reported losing family members and 46 percent had experienced both personal bereavement and displacement from their workplaces, according to a report on the strain on medical workers in Gaza published in the Public Library of Science.
At least 78 percent of healthcare workers in Gaza lacked access to mental health services, showing the gap between the trauma healthcare workers endure and their access to psychological care. It has meant that Gaza’s health system is struggling to retain its remaining staff and prevent them from leaving the medical field.
Although it is difficult to assess how many doctors, nurses and other medical workers have left Gaza and their jobs, official reports have acknowledged a “loss of human resources” and “diminished capacity in the healthcare system”.
To help halt this brain drain and protect healthcare workers who have experienced psychological trauma – probably most of those in Gaza, they need psychological and social support.
“They are caught between their professional duty to save lives and the pain of losing the people closest to them,” Munir al-Bursh, director general of Gaza’s Ministry of Health, told Al Jazeera. “They find themselves treating others’ wounds while struggling to heal their own.”
Working under constant pressure without adequate support or rest deepens exhaustion and threatens healthcare workers’ ability to continue, he said.
“Protecting medical personnel is not just about securing medicines and equipment. It also means safeguarding their mental health and giving them time to rest and recover. Those who save others also need someone to reach out and help them.”
The acute shortage of medical staff after the killings, detentions and injuries of many healthcare workers makes it difficult to give those who remain enough time to recover, he added. This is compounded by the continuing arrival of patients and wounded people, shortages of equipment and a lack of replacement staff.
The experiences of these doctors and nurses reveal the psychological toll of war on Gaza’s healthcare system. Those accustomed to confronting death and saving the wounded have sometimes found themselves facing it as bereaved family members rather than medical professionals. Caught between their duty to save others and their own grief, some have paid a profound psychological price with consequences for both their professional and personal lives.
Nurse Hiba al-Tawil, 39, witnessed her brother’s death in the intensive care unit at the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, where she worked.
“Losing my brother at my workplace was a difficult experience that had a profound psychological impact on me,” she told Al Jazeera. “Being in the intensive care unit afterwards reminded me of what had happened and made it harder to cope with the loss.”
She later transferred to another department. which helped ease the psychological pressure she was experiencing and allowed her to distance herself from the place where her brother died.
The psychological clinic at the hospital treats doctors and nurses struggling with trauma caused by bereavement and their experiences during the war. In some cases, these experiences can develop into severe psychological disorders that affect their everyday lives and ability to work.
Reham Abu Rokba, a psychologist at the complex, said treatment begins with assessing the patient’s psychological condition, diagnosing symptoms and determining their impact before developing a treatment plan.
For patients with post-traumatic stress disorder, treatment may include cognitive behavioural therapy, which helps them understand their psychological responses to traumatic events and regain their ability to cope.
Depending on the patient’s needs, treatment may involve about 12 individual sessions and, when necessary, medication.
Reham said that continued psychological support, appropriate treatment and adherence to the treatment plan can help ease symptoms and lead to improvements.
“Recovery requires time and ongoing participation in psychological support sessions,” she told Al Jazeera. “Providing the appropriate treatment and ensuring adherence to it can help alleviate symptoms and lead to tangible improvements in an individual’s mental wellbeing.”

The world according to Ellen von Unwerth: Glamour, sensuality and photography
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:17:01 UTC
16:17:01 KST

Euronews Culture sat down with the renowned German photographer Ellen von Unwerth to discuss her contribution to Maurizio Cattelan and Pierpaolo Ferrari's 2027 Toiletpaper calendar, her unique approach to fashion photography and the stories behind some of her most iconic images.
If you have ever seen a fashion photo where the woman looks like she is getting away with something — running in heels, laughing in lingerie, stealing a car in a ballgown — you have very probably seen an Ellen von Unwerth picture. You just might not have known it was her.
For more than four decades, the German photographer has made her name with portraits that are sensual, provocative and playful.
From luxury brand commercials to fashion magazines, she's been immeasurably influential over the years, having perfected a shooting style that's often been imitated. In short, von Unwerth hasn't just captured fashion, she's created it.
She's developed what's widely recognised as the 'female gaze' and changed who gets to be sexy, and crucially, who gets to decide.
Perhaps, it's because of the ten years she spent as a fashion model herself, and knowing all too well what it felt like to be told to "stand still and look pretty".
In this edition of European Lens, von Unwerth talks about her life and times, when she first picked up a camera, getting laughs on set and slipping into something comfortable with celebrities.
We also took the opportunity to have a sneak a peek at her one of her latest projects, a collaboration with Toiletpaper, the contemporary arts magazine set up by Maurizio Cattelan and Pierpaolo Ferrari.
You’re a former model, and you made your name through your particular eye and, most notably, the gaze through which you photographed women and the power you gave them in your pictures. How did you come up with that?
Ellen von Unwerth: Well, I think the biggest inspiration was actually being a model for ten years and being quite frustrated, because I always wanted to express myself in front of the camera, move, be silly and show my personality. Photographers were always saying, “No, no, no, don’t move. Look to the left, to the right, and just pose.”
I never felt really great about it. I always saw my model friends living their lives and being so beautiful. After ten years of modelling, my boyfriend at the time gave me a camera and said, “There’s a plus, a circle and a minus. When the circle lights up, you push the button.” It was my crash course.
Then I started to photograph my model friends. I dressed them up in my clothes. I always had fun clothes, like vintage pieces from the flea market. I dressed them up and did their makeup. Quickly, I noticed that we had a great connection, and they behaved differently. They felt free and were playful. I became very passionate about it very quickly. We had a darkroom in our tiny apartment, and my boyfriend taught me how to print pictures. I started printing my pictures and got obsessed. I worked all night and stuck them to the walls in my little bathroom. That’s how I started.
Do you still surprise yourself? How has your approach has changed over the years?
It hasn’t really changed. Of course, I’ve had an amazing career since then, and I’ve been very, very lucky. I’ve met so many wonderful people. But I still love capturing life and those moments that are real and spontaneous. It’s such a great connection that I reach with people in that way.
The recent story about Sydney Sweeney's ad campaign came to my mind as you spoke. In terms of objectifying women, do you think things have improved, or have they regressed?
Well, I never objectified women. That was my subject. I think Sydney Sweeney decides what she wants to do, and that’s what she wants to do. She doesn’t care, and I kind of think that's great. Of course, not everybody is happy about it, but she lives her life, and that’s how it should be.
I wanted to ask you about the techniques involved, especially technology and how that has evolved in photography. How do you use modern tools now? So many people now have high-powered cameras in their pockets. Does that affect your vision?
Well, mostly, everybody has a phone. People don’t even have cameras. It's actually rare to see people with cameras. Yes, of course, it has affected things enormously. I was maybe one of the last people to switch to digital because I loved film. I still love it, and I’m actually shooting more and more with film again.
With film, you have a certain grain and a certain quality. You can’t really change that afterwards, but with digital you have the RAW files and all the possibilities in the world to do what you want with them. It’s great, but it’s also more difficult to find your style. I had my style from before, and I’ve kept it, but there are lots of possibilities.
As I say, it’s more difficult to find your style. And, of course, there’s the iPhone. I love the iPhone, too. It’s incredible, with all the possibilities and options. You can film, edit and do so many things, and then you have Instagram as a direct outlet. But at the same time, there are so many images. There’s an overload of images, and people just scroll, scroll, scroll. Sometimes you spend so much time creating an image with a big team, and you think, "Wow, now it’s out," and two seconds later it’s gone.
Do you feel that this has affected your process when you take pictures? Do you think, "Okay, this may be thrown away tomorrow"? Do you spend the same amount of time trying to compose and get the right shot?
Yes, because what I love about photography, first of all, is the teamwork. I love choosing the team: the people for the hair, makeup, styling and set design. I love it. I always say that if I wasn't a photographer, I’d be a circus director. It’s a little bit like that: you choose the team. You want them to be creative, but you also want to have a good time with them. For me, the fun is in creating. It’s not about thinking what’s going to happen tomorrow.
Then there’s the talent, of course. There has to be a connection with the person, whether it’s a model, a singer or an actress. I love the process, so I don’t think of it as throwaway, because fortunately I can make books and exhibitions. You think, "Oh, maybe one day that’s going to be on a wall and somebody will buy it" or whatever.
Let's talk about your relationship with the "talent", because so many of your photos are iconic. It always makes me think: how did you get them to do that?
That’s what I mentioned at the beginning. I think there’s something about me and my camera that makes people feel free in front of it. I don’t know; there's something special about the lens. Even animals start to behave weirdly.
Of course, I have my tricks. I always have music. I love disco music, something everybody can relax to. I see all my teams having fun and dancing in the background. Before I go on a shoot, I have to know that I can connect with those people. With some people, I know I won’t take great pictures. It’s something in their eyes, something in the way they are. It's more about their personality, really.
Looking back at your career, who stands out in your portfolio? Are there any pictures where you think, "Yeah, if I had to choose my top five, these are the ones I’m most proud of," or where there’s a backstory that makes you think, "I never thought we’d achieve that, considering how we started"?
Of course, at the beginning of my career, Claudia Schiffer was one of my favourites. Not just the picture, but, of course, that one picture of her wearing the corset. It’s very famous and maybe the most famous picture I’ve done. It was such a fun time, actually meeting this girl and saying, "Hey, look, she looks like Brigitte Bardot. Let’s give her the hair and makeup to make her look like Brigitte Bardot."
Then I started working for Guess, and I said to Paul Marciano, “Look at this girl,” because he always loved that cinematic ’50s and ’60s vibe, the French and Italian cinema. He said, "Yeah, let’s try it." We photographed her overnight, and when the pictures came out, everybody was talking about them. There was no Instagram at the time, of course. So this was really the beginning of my career, and it's very important to me.
Then there are so many others. I did Naomi Campbell, and I took so many pictures with Naomi, including the ones with Coke cans in her hair. I worked with David Bowie, Sophia Loren and Drew Barrymore too. Drew Barrymore was one of my favourites. I remember being at an awards after-party and seeing this girl, with a huge queue of people lining up in front of the toilet. I thought, "Who’s this little girl, looking so ’20s and so charming?" I went up to her and asked her, and we did a lot of shoots together.
And, of course, some of my favourite pictures are of my daughter.
I also wanted to ask you about something we touched on earlier: artificial intelligence. Are you tempted by it? Do you see it as a help or a hindrance to what you do?
Well, it definitely helps sometimes with retouching. The other day, we had a picture by the river, and there was this really ugly boat that was very distracting. I said to my retoucher, "Can we do something?". He circled it, and it was gone. I was like, "Amazing!". Of course, it helps with things like that. Sometimes we also animate my pictures, and it’s crazy how easy it is. It takes a little bit of skill, and I have fun with it.
I always get a lot of very bad comments: "Ellen, you’re an artist. Why do you use artificial intelligence?". And I’m like, "Yeah, it’s there. It’s a tool. You have to jump on the bandwagon or you’re going to be left behind."
That said, I really love the process of taking pictures, the connection with people, the creative process, having ideas and sitting in my room thinking. That’s my thing, not just sitting in my room and doing everything with AI. And, of course, you know what it's doing: it’s getting a lot of people out of jobs. Even models are now creating their own AI versions. I think it’s like a big monster coming towards humanity, and I find it quite scary, actually.
You’re not alone in that. Tell me something now about Toiletpaper. How did this collaboration begin?
Well, I was in Berlin, and I had an event at Fotografiska, where they (co-founders Maurizio Cattelan and Pierpaolo Ferrari) had an exhibition. It was a really fun exhibition, with a big pool - you know, those pools filled with plastic bananas. You could roll around in it, and the pictures were sliced open so you could walk through them. It was a super-fun experience.
I posted lots of pictures from it on Instagram, and they contacted me. They were like, "Hey, Ellen, I hope you had fun at our exhibition." I said, "My God, I loved it!".
From there, we started a collaboration. I love that very pop, loud, flamboyant style, and part of my work is also very loud, flamboyant and pop. We talked, and I was very proud that they approached me, because I’m a big admirer of what they do. I was very proud, and we started the collaboration.
It was very hard to choose, because there are only six pictures each. We had so many, and narrowing them down to six was very hard.
I can see how there was a meeting of minds there. But how did the collaboration actually work? Did you have complete free rein? I’m interested in how it went.
Yeah, I had complete free rein. But after so many years of working, you know the style of each publication or brand. When you work for Vogue it’s one thing, when you work for i-D it’s another, when you work for Dior, it’s something else. You learn their style.
Then you get to know people's styles, too. My team and I looked through my archive and chose pictures that fitted the style, because they said we'd do an opposition: one picture would be mine and one would be theirs. We chose pictures that had something in similarity, so we could make a game of asking people what the similarities were.
It was fun. It was a very fun project, and I’m super proud and happy that it’s just come out.
Looking forward, Ellen, what else are you preparing at the moment? You spoke to me about the show in St Tropez. How often are you exhibiting now? How are you filling your days?
Well, I'm having a big exhibition in Maastricht. It's called My Circus because, before I was even a model, I was working in the circus in Germany. I saw the circus and it was so magical. After the show, I asked the director if I could work in the circus.
He said, "Oh, you look like a circus girl. You can start tomorrow." I wasn't a juggler or anything, but I was an assistant to the juggler. It was a very, very fun period, which actually inspired me a lot. In my pictures, there's always glitter, dishevelled glamour and magic. So, at the museum in Maastricht, the theme is My Circus. There are around 130 pictures inspired by the circus, featuring actors and actresses, as well as my fashion stories for Italian Vogue and American Vogue.
Then I have a little exhibition in St Tropez called Not Your Angel. Obviously, beautiful women look like angels, but don't get them wrong.
I'm also working on new books. I have a couple of new book projects. I'm planning to make a movie based on one of my books. It's called Revenge. We were already talking about it years ago, but then COVID came along. We were also supposed to film in Ukraine, which unfortunately fell through. Now we're starting to talk about it again, and I'm also creating a perfume. That's my big, big project this year.
ToiletEllen von PaperUnwerth Calendar 2027 is published by Damiani Books and is available now.
