Jews don't bomb buses: RFK Jr. doubles down on Arab remarks and praises Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:14:15 UTC
16:14:15 KST

U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is refusing to retract his controversial remarks about Arabs, which sparked an uproar across the United States last week. Instead of apologizing, he has published a lengthy manifesto praising Israel and the Jewish people while launching a sweeping attack on the Muslim Brotherhood and Arab countries. 
In an unusually long post on X on Friday, spanning approximately 3,700 words, Kennedy accused Iran and Gulf states of financing an anti-Israel propaganda machine whose power he compared to that of Nazi Germany. He also claimed that Jews have contributed more to humanity than any other ethnic or religious group.
"My speech was not a critique of Arabs or Islam, but of Islamism," Kennedy wrote at the beginning of his response, describing the ideology as a dangerous distortion of Islam promoted by the Muslim Brotherhood. He accused major news organizations of omitting critical context from their coverage, suggesting they had done so to lend credibility to allegations that his remarks were racist and Islamophobic. "Criticizing Islamism is neither Islamophobic nor racist," he added.
Much of Kennedy's response focused on Israel and the war in Gaza. He argued that the Muslim Brotherhood had spent decades developing a global propaganda network designed to incite hatred against Jews and portray Israel as an enemy of humanity. He further claimed that the Nazis were the movement's principal financiers during the 1930s and that "Joseph Goebbels and an army of Nazi and ex-Nazi propagandists built the Muslim Brotherhood’s powerful propaganda machine in the 1930s, ’40s, and ’50s."
"The massive influx of money from Iran and the Gulf States starting in the 1990s turned this operation into an amplifier of unmatched power that makes Goebbels look like a piker," Kennedy wrote. He claimed the resulting global propaganda campaign had convinced Western supporters of Hamas that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, while diverting attention from what he described as atrocities committed by Islamist movements. These were Kennedy's allegations, not independently established findings about the organizations or governments he named.
Kennedy also rejected accusations of genocide in Gaza by citing what he said were CIA figures showing that the territory's population had increased since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel. However, previous fact-checks have found that the widely circulated CIA World Factbook population-growth figures were based on projections prepared before the war, rather than measurements of population changes during the conflict.
Four times the Marshall Plan
Kennedy urged readers to compare the Gaza Strip with Israel. "Palestinians have received over 4X per capita in international aid than Europeans received under the Marshall Plan," he claimed, referring to the U.S.-funded program that helped rebuild Europe after World War II. "Europe used its money to rebuild 17 nations. Palestinians couldn’t build themselves even one."
According to Kennedy, Hamas diverted international assistance toward weapons, payments to its leaders and an extensive network of underground tunnels and bunkers intended for its fighters rather than civilians. He described Gaza as a society suffering under authoritarian rule, alleging that Hamas had squandered opportunities for economic and political development.
By contrast, Kennedy portrayed Israel in glowing terms. He described it as "a tiny sliver of swamp and desert 1/600th the size of its Arab neighbors" that had become "an agricultural juggernaut and a global economic and technological superpower."
According to Kennedy, the Jewish people transformed an arid landscape into a thriving, pluralistic democracy where Jews and Arabs can vote, practice their religions and participate in public institutions. He held Israel up as an example of economic development, technological innovation and democratic government in the Middle East.
"Women and gays in Israel have all the rights of men, and Israel’s biggest annual celebration is the Pride parade in Tel Aviv," Kennedy wrote, offering a sweeping characterization of Israeli civil rights and public life. He went on to describe Israel as "a robust and heroic outpost for freedom and Western values."
Kennedy's praise extended beyond Israel to the Jewish people as a whole. "There is no ethnic or religious group that has contributed more than Jews to the welfare of humanity or to the advancement of liberal democracy," he declared.
He noted that Jews account for approximately 0.2% of the world's population but have received, by his calculation, about 22% of all Nobel Prizes awarded since 1901. "Relative to their proportion of the population, the astonishing contributions by Jews have been breathtaking," he wrote.
What Jews ‘don't do’
Kennedy, who has been one of the most prominent voices in the American anti-vaccine movement, notably praised Jewish scientists responsible for developing polio vaccines, including Jonas Salk and Albert Sabin. He also listed medical pioneers Paul Ehrlich, Selman Waksman and Ernst Chain among those whose achievements helped transform modern medicine.
His list extended to physicists Albert Einstein and Niels Bohr, as well as Jewish founders and executives associated with major technology companies, including Google, Meta and Oracle. He also credited Jews with playing a foundational role in creating Hollywood and shaping the American entertainment industry.
"In a rational universe, wouldn’t non-Jews be expected to celebrate these contributions with gratitude?" he asked.
Kennedy then presented a lengthy list of acts he asserted Jews do not commit. It included suicide bombings, beheadings, attacks on gay people, forced child marriages, violence against women, hijacking passenger planes and flying them into buildings, as well as bombing buses and crowded restaurants. He also mentioned acid attacks, slave markets and calls for global jihad.
"These are the gifts that Islamism has bestowed on the world, along with closed minds, poverty, starvation, ignorance, oppression, and violence," Kennedy wrote, using the list to draw a broad contrast between Jewish contributions to society and the violence he associated with Islamist extremism.
He then posed the question: "Why does the world hate Jews and embrace Islamists?" His answer was that a sophisticated propaganda campaign had distorted public perceptions of Israel and its adversaries by ignoring evidence and reversing the roles of victim and aggressor.
From the Michigan rally to the deleted post
Kennedy's manifesto followed the controversy surrounding his remarks last Monday at a campaign rally in Grand Rapids, Michigan, where he appeared in support of Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers.
"There's 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don't produce science," Kennedy said at the event. He also asserted that Arabs do not win Nobel Prizes, Fields Medals or Wolf Prizes and no longer produce significant literature.
The remarks drew condemnation from scientists, physicians and civil rights organizations, which pointed to numerous Arab achievements that directly contradicted his claims. Among those cited were Egyptian American chemist Ahmed Zewail, who won the 1999 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; Egyptian author Naguib Mahfouz, who received the 1988 Nobel Prize in Literature; and Jordanian American chemist Omar Yaghi, a recipient of the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Kennedy's sister, Kerry Kennedy, also condemned his statements. "Today, I am deeply ashamed of him," she wrote, recalling earlier remarks in which her brother had warned against politicians exploiting prejudice and xenophobia. She described his latest comments as false, cruel and derogatory.
Rogers is running in Tuesday's November 3 midterm elections against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, an Egyptian American Muslim physician and former public health official. Rogers, President Donald Trump and Kennedy have sought to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, allegations the Democratic candidate has rejected.
Kennedy devoted the final portion of his lengthy post to demanding that El-Sayed explicitly distance himself from the organization and its ideology, even though the candidate has already publicly disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood. Kennedy questioned whether El-Sayed had sufficiently condemned the movement and portrayed the issue as a test of his commitment to American democratic values.
This was also not the first time Kennedy had invoked Nazi propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels in attacking what he described as an anti-Israel information campaign. On October 7, the third anniversary of the Hamas attack, he posted on X that a global Muslim Brotherhood propaganda operation funded by Qatar made Goebbels look like an amateur.
That post also dismissed allegations of genocide against Israel, but Kennedy deleted it shortly afterward, when it had already accumulated approximately 336,000 views. Neither he nor his department offered an explanation for its removal.
In his new manifesto, Kennedy returned to the same argument about an alleged global propaganda operation, but with one notable change: Where his deleted post had singled out Qatar, the latest version accused Iran and Gulf states more broadly of providing the money.

Police storm Portugal housing protest camps

Police storm Portugal housing protest camp
Dozens of officers, some accompanied by police dogs, moved into Rossio Square in Lisbon early on Sunday.
Police have used shields and batons to disperse housing protesters from a tent camp in Portugal’s capital, Lisbon, a week after similar operations drew criticism from protesters and rights groups.
Dozens of officers, some accompanied by police dogs, moved into Rossio Square at about 4:30am (04:30 GMT) on Sunday, a day after thousands marched demanding the government withdraw a rental bill they say would deepen the country’s housing crisis.
Protesters had erected more than 50 tents following Saturday’s march through Lisbon. Police commander Iuri Rodrigues issued three warnings to remove the tents, saying they had been erected illegally and that anyone resisting their removal could face disobedience charges.
Hundreds of demonstrators shielding the camp were dispersed, while police also dismantled a smaller encampment in Porto’s Dom Joao I square.
Earlier, lawmaker Pedro Delgado Alves said Rossio Square was peaceful and that nothing justified “a police intervention involving force, physical violence or baton charges, the kind of scenes we witnessed last week”.
The intervention followed operations in the same squares the previous Sunday, when police arrested 25 people in Lisbon and six in Porto. Housing campaign group Casa para Viver said 60 people were injured across those operations, which police described as “proportionate”.
Rising housing costs
The protests reflect growing anger over housing costs across Europe, including demonstrations in Spain and opposition to government economic policies in France, Germany and Albania.
Portugal faces one of Europe’s severest housing affordability crises, with young people among the hardest hit. House prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents on new leases have almost doubled.
The Bank of Portugal estimates a nationwide shortage of 300,000 homes, equivalent to Lisbon’s entire housing stock.
Demonstrators want the minority centre-right government to scrap legislation that would make evictions easier and remove rent caps on new leases, saying it would worsen affordability and leave tenants more exposed.

Bulgaria votes in presidential runoff amid political instability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:05:28 UTC
16:05:28 KST

Bulgarians return to the polls on Sunday to elect their president in a runoff between acting President Iliana Yotova and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov after neither candidate secured a majority in the first round.
Yotova and her running mate, Kiril Valchev, received 34.8 percent of the vote, while Gyurov and Georgi Kandev secured 32 percent, according to the Central Election Commission.
Turnout in the October 25 vote stood at around 22.5 percent, the lowest recorded in the country's post-communist history.
A total of 27 candidates contested the first round.
A candidate must receive more than half of the valid votes, with turnout exceeding 50 percent of registered voters, to win in the first round under electoral rules. If those conditions are not met, the two leading candidates advance to a runoff.
The vote comes amid political instability in Bulgaria, which has held eight parliamentary elections since April 2021, including seven early elections.
Disagreements
The repeated parliamentary votes followed difficulties among political parties in securing the support needed to form stable governments.
Disagreements over coalition arrangements led to the collapse of successive attempts to establish regular governments, resulting in caretaker Cabinets and further early elections.
The latest parliamentary election, held in April, saw Progressive Bulgaria, led by former President Rumen Radev, win 131 of the National Assembly's 240 seats, giving the party an outright majority.
Yotova, who served as Radev's vice president, assumed the presidency after he resigned in January. Backed by Radev's Progressive Bulgaria party, she is seeking a full presidential mandate.
A victory would make Yotova Bulgaria's first elected female president, whose duties include representing the country, serving as commander-in-chief of the armed forces and exercising a veto on legislation.
Gyurov, an economist and former deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, served as caretaker prime minister before the parliamentary elections in April. He is backed by opposition parties.
The campaign has included debate about Bulgaria's foreign policy and its relations with Russia, Ukraine and Western allies.
Polling stations are scheduled to open at 7 am (0500GMT) and close at 8 pm (1800GMT).

Tusk, Nawrocki Double Down as Poland Court Crisis Deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:04:00 UTC
16:04:00 KST

Both Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and President Karol Nawrocki on Saturday doubled down on their respective sides of the dispute over the leadership of Constitutional Tribunal, which has been in crisis since Friday evening.
The long-running political dispute over the Tribunal, dating back to 2015, has effectively paralyzed the institution, with the pro-European government and the nationalist president refusing to recognize appointees put forward by the other side.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Late on Friday, the Constitutional Tribunal said its longest-serving judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska had suspended Bogdan Święczkowski, the tribunal’s president and an appointee of Tusk’s hard-right predecessor, and was now in charge of the court.
On Saturday evening, Tusk justified Friday’s events by saying he and the ruling coalition had tried to reach a compromise with the president in recent months, but it had been rejected.
“We proposed resolutions and laws to all political forces and both presidents that would enable the joint restoration of the rule of law,” he said in a televised address to the nation. “All to no avail.”
He added the Tribunal’s judges had been lawfully elected and that no politician, not even the president, had the right to obstruct their work.
“The rule of law differs from the law of the jungle,” the prime minister said, adding that in some matters, “there can be no compromise.”
Poland’s Nawrocki Convenes Crisis Talks Over Constitutional Court
Earlier on Saturday, Nawrocki met with right wing political parties the Polish People’s Party, Poland 2050, Razem, Konfederacja and PiS to discuss the situation. The parties, which do not see eye-to-eye, have found common ground over the Tribunal issue.
The president previously described Friday’s actions as a “breach of public order” and “a forcible takeover of a constitutional body.”
Long-running dispute
The confrontation has brought a long-running dispute between Poland’s government and president to a head and raised new questions about who is ultimately in charge.
The current impasse is the latest phase of a dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal, its appointments and its leadership. It centers on whether a president can prevent parliament’s elected judges from taking up their duties by declining to swear them in.
Earlier this year, Nawrocki – who is supported by Poland’s right-wing opposition— failed to administer the oaths of office of five judges elected by the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament. The judges gave their oaths before parliament instead.
The Venice Commission, the Council of Europe’s independent advisory body on constitutional law, has described the president’s role in the procedure as ceremonial. It said he should administer the oath without delay and should not claim the power to review parliament’s election of judges.
The president is now seeking to contain a crisis in which his own refusal to administer the five judges’ oaths remains a central unresolved issue.
The latest escalation began on Friday when Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska issued an order suspending Święczkowski and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, from their duties for one month.
The move prompted protests involving right-wing politicians and supporters.
Nawrocki turned his flight to Senegal around mid-air as the situation unfolded and went to the Tribunal, where footage showed him pushing past judges standing at the entrance to get into the building.
The court remains the casualty
TVP World’s political analyst Stuart Dowell said the biggest casualty of the dispute is Tribunal itself, which can only do its work effectively if the “government, the president and the courts are prepared to accept its rulings.”
He also pointed out that, even if a compromise is found, next year’s elections may not improve the situation.
“If the right returns to power, it could attempt to reverse whatever changes are made now, setting off yet another round of constitutional warfare,” Dowell wrote on Saturday.
“Eleven years after the original dispute began, Poland could still be arguing over who gets to run the court that is supposed to settle such arguments.”

A Gulf non-aggression pact could be the path forward
Oman is in a unique position to mediate talks on a security arrangement that could stabilise the region.
Proposing a non-aggression pact amid regional hostilities may seem premature. Yet agreements to stop war matter most when distrust is the deepest. The key question is whether regional governments can agree on rules that make their disagreements less destructive.
In a recent lecture at Cambridge University in the UK, Oman’s Foreign Minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, called for a non-aggression pact among all eight Gulf littoral states: the six members of the Gulf Cooperation Council along with Iraq and Iran. He described it as the essential prerequisite for an inclusive regional security architecture.
Could such a pact work? As Albusaidi conceded, it would be hard to achieve. But as another major escalation looms between Iran and the United States, the region urgently needs a diplomatic path forward.
Indeed, the ongoing conflict has proved so hard to resolve because the region’s security arrangements have remained underdeveloped, relying for too long on external powers. The way forward then can be an inclusive agreement.
Reviving the promise of 1976
The Omani proposal is anchored in a historic precedent. In November 1976, the foreign ministers of all eight Gulf littoral states met in Muscat to pursue collective security after Britain’s withdrawal from the region.
It remains the only time all eight have sat at one table. The Iranian Revolution, the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iran–Iraq war then pushed the region towards defensive arrangements that later hardened into exclusion.
For decades, Iran, in particular, was seen as a threat to the rest of the region. Yet, given that the country holds roughly half the Gulf coastline, any security architecture without it is structurally unsound.
It was not until 2019 that the idea of a regional security arrangement was revived. In May of that year, then Iranian Foreign Minister Javad Zarif proposed a regional non-aggression pact with Gulf neighbours during a visit to Baghdad, which Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov endorsed.
That September, Iranian President Hassan Rouhani launched the Hormuz Peace Endeavour (HOPE) at the UN General Assembly, envisaging a non-aggression pact among Hormuz states. Gulf reactions were largely dismissive, citing Iranian support for armed groups threatening regional stability.
The US-Israeli war on Iran has revived the idea on the Arab side. In May, the Financial Times reported that Saudi Arabia was discussing a non-aggression framework with Iran, reportedly modelled on the Helsinki process between the US and Russia during the Cold War.
This month, Qatar’s defence minister called for GCC–Iran dialogue, joined by Turkiye and Pakistan, towards a non-aggression agreement.
Oman’s proposal comes as the latest iteration of this regional shift. Muscat is in a unique position to mediate given its history of acting as a mediator and its recent record of hosting US-Iran talks in 2025 and February 2026. It has access that few others have.
Concluding a pact that works
The strongest objection against a Gulf pact with Iran is simple: Why trust a state whose conduct has threatened the region’s security? Gulf concerns about Iranian actions are not misunderstandings. Oman itself formally protested to Iran after drone attacks targeting Musandam and Al Wusta in July.
Reassurance is therefore insufficient. Inclusion must mean obligation. Membership in a regional pact would have to bind Iran as much as any other signatory, providing a means to constrain threatening behaviour and address legitimate grievances.
A pact must rest on observable conduct, reciprocal restraint and consequences for violations. At minimum, it would need commitments against the threat or use of force, interference in internal affairs, attacks on civilian infrastructure and support for armed groups conducting cross-border attacks, alongside protection of navigation.
To reach a workable agreement, negotiations can adopt a gradual approach. Consultations among the eight countries could first identify minimum shared interests: territorial security, functioning ports, reliable energy exports, civilian protection and uninterrupted trade. Oman can facilitate, but each state would represent itself; Muscat’s channel to Tehran confers no mandate to negotiate for its neighbours.
Initial talks should yield limited, reciprocal measures: military hotlines, rules for maritime encounters, notification of exercises and rapid communication after attacks. An understanding about protecting energy facilities, desalination plants and commercial shipping would offer an early test of compliance.
Hormuz is the obvious starting point, though progress could be hard. Oman-Iran talks have already outlined a temporary navigation arrangement. However, as Albusaidi conceded, it cannot be implemented unless Washington and Tehran compromise, including by reversing wartime actions that halted maritime traffic. Any wider framework must respect international navigation rights.
Armed groups would be the hardest issue to resolve. Governments should undertake neither to direct nor materially support cross-border attacks by such actors, and demonstrate compliance through verifiable steps. Where control is contested, the pact would need procedures for establishing evidence and requiring corrective action.
Compliance with initial measures could open cooperation on maritime safety, environmental protection and emergency response. Serious violations should trigger investigation, urgent consultation and agreed diplomatic consequences, while the right of self-defence would remain intact.
A regional pact would not settle every conflict touching the Gulf. The United States and Israel, both parties to this year’s war on Iran, would remain outside it and Yemen’s war involves actors whose agendas a Gulf arrangement could not easily bind. But a framework need not end every war to be worth having. It need only make it harder for any of them to become a war among its signatories.
The pact’s credibility will depend on whether it changes conduct. Fewer or no attacks, functioning crisis channels and demonstrable respect for sovereignty will matter more than signatures.
Present hostilities make the task difficult, but they also expose the cost of postponing it. The first achievement would be modest but consequential: establishing that disagreement entitles no state to endanger another’s security.

Binance said Sunday that it had resumed withdrawals after a major hack that affected more than $6 billion in funds.
Binance, which is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes, had suspended user withdrawals after the attack.
Read moreHow the record-breaking $6.3 billion heist in crypto history unfolded
"First batch network now opened in phase one of withdrawals is $BTC bitcoin network," Binance said on X.
The company said in an earlier update that it was preparing to resume the first phase of withdrawals between 0600 and 0900 GMT on Sunday.
"We are taking a phased approach by prioritizing tokens based on the past week data of user demand, so that each network and asset pair can be restored carefully, with stability and security checks completed before access is reopened," it said.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Binance said Saturday that it has set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds to cover losses in the hack, which is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist.
"User funds remain safe. Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users," it said on X.
FBI says North Korea behind $6 billion crypto theft
The FBI accused North Korea of being behind the attack on Saturday, confirming earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a Pyongyang-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack.
"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the statement said.
The FBI added that it had observed "TraderTraitor actors" converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralized finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."
US President Donald Trump, however, cast doubt on the North Korea's involvement in the hack.
"I'm not concerned. We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea," Trump told reporters at his residence in Florida late Saturday.
The president often reflects with pride on summits he held with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his first term.
The hack is the latest in a string of high-profile cyber thefts linked to North Korea, which has built a formidable hacking operation, generating funds believed to help finance its weapons program.
News of the cyberattack caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday.

A gift to scammers: why you should probably keep your birthday a secret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:00:05 UTC
16:00:05 KST

You get a call from your bank saying there has been suspicious activity on your account. They read out your name, address and date of birth so you are happy it is a legitimate caller.
But you are talking to criminals who have used your date of birth as part of a web of verifying information to convince you they are someone else.
People’s DOBs are often held in online accounts after being entered as part of a sign-up process for a retailer, loyalty scheme, newsletter or online competition. In a recent hack of the online retailer Asos customers’ dates of birth were among the details taken by scammers.
Now cybersecurity professionals have warned people to resist entering a date of birth, or to put in a fake one, to limit the amount of personal data that is online, frustrating criminals’ attempts to “jigsaw” together personal profiles.
Jake Moore, an adviser for the cybersecurity company ESET, says information gathered during hacks can be sold on and used by scammers, either to trick people into trusting them, or to impersonate them.
“A date of birth alone is not particularly valuable to criminals, but combined with other information, such as names and phone numbers, it can help criminals … commit identity fraud,” he says.
Alexandre François, who investigates scams for the intelligence company WhoisXML API, found that eight out of 14 retailers he surveyed recently asked for a date of birth on sign-up. “Retailers may also have little incentive to remove this field, as the full date gives them the customer’s age, which is useful for marketing and targeting,” he says.
What it looks like
You may hear about a hack either in the news, or in an email from an organisation telling you that your data has been compromised. How the scam manifests itself will depend on what happens to the information that has been stolen.
If a retailer is hacked, and the details end up on the dark web, they can be used to make phishing emails look more authentic, says Serpil Hall, a security expert from Datos Insights. Hackers can also use them to try to convince company help desks that they are talking to the victim. But it may not all happen straight after a security breach.
“The process typically runs like this: a retail breach provides a name, date of birth, email and address,” she says. “Other leaked data adds credentials, phone numbers and identifiers. Public information such as social profiles, employment details and relatives adds more context. The result is an enriched identity profile with more identifiers and greater confidence when matching records.”
What to do
Be wary of anyone who contacts you out of the blue, even if they seem to have a lot of information.
“Using a different birthday on low-risk websites can reduce exposure, but it is even better to not enter any personal fields that aren’t mandatory,” says Moore. “It is even worth using a separate email address for shopping online, too, so you can bin the email if it gets caught up in a breach and you can start again.”
François says shops only need your payment card details and a delivery address. (You will, however, need to verify your age in some cases if you are buying age-restricted items, such as knives.)
François says: “Strictly speaking, you only need to give your real date of birth, and your real name, where they are checked against official records and used to prove who you are: your bank or any lender, the tax office, the driving licence and passport agencies, right-to-work checks, a police notice. In those systems the date of birth works as a key. A shop is not one of them.”
Leaving a birthday field blank is best, he says. “If this is not an option, use the same date across all retailers, possibly the first day of your birth month, so that you do not forget it.”

It’s snow time: the best winter activity holidays in Europe for non-skiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:00:04 UTC
16:00:04 KST

Arctic thrills and survival skills in Finnish Lapland
At Ruka, the first skiers of the year slalomed down the slopes on 2 October. Just inside the Arctic Circle, Ruka’s long snow-sure season and cosy village atmosphere make it a popular ski resort with Finnish families. The long polar nights mean there are only a few hours of dim twilight each day, but the slopes here are floodlit, so that never stops play.
The Narnia-like setting offers just as much action off the runs as on them, and in December the resort launches Ruka Guides, guided adventures from a dedicated activity centre. Spend the morning e-fatbiking through snowy forests (from €90) or cutting a hole in a frozen lake to catch fish (from €89), before learning Arctic survival skills (from €85) or snowshoeing in the evening darkness on the hunt for the northern lights (from €89).
Other, more offbeat diversions include floating in a thermal suit down the freezing Kiveskoski river in meditative silence (from €135), whizzing down an alpine coaster at up to 25mph (from €11.88) and practising your sun salutation in the forest surrounded by grazing reindeer (from €45).
Dasher and Dancer are a clue to the other reason Ruka is such a hit with children: the main merry man himself. Father Christmas, Mrs Claus and the elves live at Santa’s Cottage, about 30 minutes’ drive from Ruka, where they test how good little helpers are at gingerbread baking and Christmas card making, before those wannabe elves sing Santa’s favourite carol to him in Finnish, post cards at the post office and sledge down the hillside outside (from €105).
 
All activities at ruka.fi. Rukariutta Superior apartments sleep up to six from €362 a night (rukapalvelu.fi). Lumo Lakeside Lodges sleep up to two adults and two children from €215 (rukasafaris.fi)
Stargazing in the Cairngorms
In the depths of winter, the sun sets just a shade after 3.30pm in the Cairngorms national park and doesn’t rise again until about 8.50 the following morning. Those long hours of darkness combined with low levels of light pollution (the area around Tomintoul and Glenlivet is an International Dark Sky Park) makes it the perfect place for stargazing.
While it’s easy to be dazzled by the Milky Way without even reaching for a telescope, the Discovery Centre in the village of Tomintoul lends out stargazing kits (pre-booking required) to help visitors delve deeper into the cosmos at one of their recommended viewing sites, such as the nearby Tomintoul Field of Hope, with its purpose-built Skyhide pavilion.
The centre is also the meeting point for astronomy events (there is a close-up look at the moon on 18 November and an evening of meteor spotting when the Geminids shower is at its peak around mid-December (suggested donation £7, cairngormsdarkskypark.org).
A short drive away, just north of Aviemore, storyteller Sarah Hobbs leads monthly Stargazing Storywalks. The 1½-mile after-dark amble weaves in Gaelic and Pictish tales of the night sky from thousands of years ago, from warrior queens to one-eyed giants, and ends with a cup of foraged wild tea (£20pp, Oct-March). For something a little more strenuous, Hillgoers organises regular three-mile night walks with certified star rangers, spotting glowing planets and nocturnal wildlife (£40pp, maximum of eight in a group).
The Lazy Duck continues the dark-sky theme with a clutch of off-grid huts among the pines of the Abernethy Forest with stargazing windows above the beds (from £187 a night in December).
There are plenty of winter activities in daylight hours too, from driving the SnowRoads route, which winds along the highest public roads in Britain, to meeting the country’s only free-roaming reindeer herd (guided hill trips run Feb-Dec from £29.40pp, cairngormreindeer.co.uk).
Toboggans and glaciers in Chamonix
At the foot of Mont Blanc, Chamonix is famous among skiers for its gnarly off-piste terrain and intense black runs. But that dramatic landscape makes it prime territory for action off the slopes too. One of Responsible Travel’s new trips this season is a four-night self-guided snowshoeing holiday in the Chamonix valley.
Using the traditional mountain spa town of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains as its base, the itinerary ventures deep into the snow-covered Vallorcine valley, hiking through larch meadows and pine forests, heading up the Flégère gondola to walk along a balcony trail facing Mont Blanc, and taking in the views from the summit of Mont d’Arbois at 1,833 metres.
The Mont Blanc massif is one of the most densely glaciated areas in the Alps, and while the ice is receding due to the climate crisis, taking the dinky red Montenvers cog train up to the Mer de Glace is still an impressive experience. This huge river of ice winds some 5 miles between the mountains, and at the top a cable car followed by around 200 steps descends into the Grotte de Glace, a blue tunnel carved into the glacier (€49.70 for the train, gondola and ice cave visit).
A more intrepid ice-spotting option is Les Contamines-Montjoie circular snowshoeing route, which climbs through pine forests to the Plateau du Truc, with its views of the d’Armancette, Miage and Covagnet glaciers.
Back in Chamonix, the Mont-Blanc Museum opened in July, tracing the valley’s history and Alpine exploits from the ice age to today, showcasing objects that include memorabilia from the first Winter Olympic Games (held in Chamonix in 1924) and the walking stick of Jacques Balmat, half of the two-man team that made the first ascent of Mont Blanc in 1786. That climb is only for serious mountaineers, but the cable car from Chamonix town centre is a shortcut to Aiguille du Midi’s almost-as-impressive 3,842-metre peak (€43 round trip) – leaving plenty of energy to hit the nearby La Luge toboggan run (€23 for the pedestrian lift pass and one descent; ski-saintgervais.com).
 
A four-night self-guided snowshoeing trip in Chamonix from £790pp with Responsible Travel, including B&B accommodation, route maps, smartphone navigation app, GPS trackers and 24/7 phone support
 
Snowshoeing and bear spotting in Transylvania
Hiking along narrow trails in the Piatra raiului national park, you’re more likely to come across bear or wolf tracks than other walkers’ footprints. The Carpathian mountains are one of Europe’s last bastions for large predators – there are thought to be more than 10,000 brown bears and around 2,500 grey wolves in Romania alone.
A week-long guided trip with Exodus makes tracks into Transylvania’s dramatic karst landscape, and is an atmospheric introduction to snowshoes and crampons. Base camp is the family-run Villa Hermani guesthouse, over 1,000 metres above sea level in the village of Magura, where there’s always a warming glass of homemade pălincă (fruit brandy) waiting.
Hikes climb up to the high ridge of Dealul Măgurice or to the plateau between the Piatra Craiului and Bucegi mountains, where the only thing that might break the silence is the howling of a wolf. One of the most spectacular walks heads along the Zărnești Gorge, its vertical limestone walls rising 200 metres above the icy canyon floor.
When not snowshoeing through Christmas-card scenes, take in medieval churches, the cobbled old town of Brașov and the Libearty bear sanctuary, which has rescued over 120 brown bears from the cruelty of captivity. And while Bram Stoker never set foot in Romania, let alone Bran Castle (often said to be the inspiration for Dracula’s lair), you can. With its frosty turrets and towers set against the Carpathians, it looks more gothic than ever, and even better without the bloodthirsty summer crowds.
 
Exodus’s seven-night Transylvania winter walk and snowshoe trip from £1,459pp, including all accommodation, meals, transport and activities, tour guide, snowshoes and poles
Igloos and Christmas markets in Innsbruck
Innsbruck is ringed by the Austrian Alps, meaning wherever you wander in the city – among the medieval alleys of the Altstadt or past the colourful houses along the River Inn – snow-covered mountains are the constant backdrop. Those jagged peaks are home to 12 ski areas within 15 to 75 minutes of the city by public transport, and some are worth the trip for the snow-plough-averse too.
Zaha Hadid’s swooping, modernist Bergisel ski jump is a dominant sight above the town and the vertiginous view is even better from its observation deck. The architect also designed four of the Nordpark Cable Railway stations that feature fluid glass canopies mimicking natural ice formations and glaciers. They take skiers and non-skiers up to the Nordkette mountains for a bird’s eye view of the Tirolean capital.
There’s plenty more to get pulses racing without clipping on a pair of skis, from bobsleighing down the 1,399-metre Olympic track at Igls at speeds of up to 115km/h (from €45 for bobrafting, €119 for piloted race bobsleighing) to night sledding at Rangger Köpfl (€25). For more icy fun, there are igloos to spend the night in at Iglu-Dorf in Kühtai, Austria’s highest ski resort (from €537 for up to three people, including cheese fondue, community sauna and breakfast).
Back down in Innsbruck, Christmas market season kicks off in November, and there are seven dotted around the streets and squares, from the historic old town market to the lofty Hungerburg – be sure to try kiachl, a doughnut-like pastry served either savoury with hot sauerkraut, or sweet topped with wild cranberry jam.
New skating experience Ice Magic also launches this winter, with illuminated ice paths connecting different parts of the city, alongside light installations and projections, ice disco nights and DJs (from €8).
Nordic ice-skating in Sweden
While Scandinavians started using animal bones to make primitive ice skates thousands of years ago, wild, or Nordic, skating as we know it (long-distance skating outdoors on natural ice for sport rather than utility) evolved in Sweden in the 1900s. Stockholm’s Skridskoseglarklubb (“Skate Sailing Club”) was formed in 1901 and today has more than 10,000 members, who share the latest ice information online to find the ideal skating locations.
Nordic skates have long blades attached only at the front of the boot, used to make long, rhythmic glides; other specialist safety kit includes long, pointy poles to assess ice thickness and a backpack that doubles as a flotation device.
Wild is the operative word here, and it is prudent as a beginner to skate with a pro. Stockholm-based Ice Guide runs a number of trips, from one-day introductions to multi-day tours, which head out on to Lake Mälaren or the Baltic Sea in the Stockholm archipelago (from £143 including all gear, transport and lunch). Hellasgården, less than half an hour outside Stockholm, is another popular skate spot with ploughed tracks on Lake Källtorpssjön, and there are holes cut in the ice for the bravest swimmers (and a sauna for after).
While in the city centre, get your frozen kicks at the ice rink at Kungsträdgården (skate rental about £7.50 an hour) or by joining the boisterous crowd at a Djurgården IF ice hockey match at the Hovet stadium.
 
Ruby Frida opened this summer and has doubles from £70 room-only
A foodie walk in the Dolomites, northern Italy
Hearty Tirolean food is made for winter: Knödel dumplings smothered in melted butter and parmesan, the ricotta- and spinach-filled pasta pockets of Schlutzkrapfen, the cast-iron skillet hash of Bauerngröstl. Hiking through the slopes and valleys of the Dolomites’ Drei Zinnen (Three Peaks) nature park on a week-long trip with self-guided walking holiday specialists Inntravel is a good way to work up an appetite.
From the charmingly traditional Hotel Drei Zinnen in the village of Sesto near the Austrian border, a network of 100km of well-groomed, partially cleared paths (meaning no snowshoes required) branches out through the Fischleintal valley and beyond into the nature park.
Mountain huts (rifugios) are dotted along routes for a warming lunch: Talschlusshütte serves mountain pine and porcini mushroom risotto and classic comforting Gerstensuppe (barley soup) along the Fischleintal valley walk; while the 100-year-old Dreischusterhütte among the fir trees in the nearby Innerfeldtel valley is much loved for its Kaiserschmarrn (shredded pancake) and homemade Apfelkiachl (fried apple rings).
Other routes start with a cable car ride and cut across the snowglobe landscapes of the Kreuzbergpass (stopping for a drink on the terrace at the Klammbach hut, of course) or loop around the banks of the frozen Lake Toblach.
Hotel Drei Zinnen has welcomed a fair few winter explorers through its doors since it opened in 1930. One regular guest – the mountaineer and author of Seven Years in Tibet Heinrich Harrer – inspired the hotel’s original owner Hans Watschinger to transform the establishment and the village of Sesto (Sexten in German) into a winter destination. It’s still run by the Watschinger family, and today there’s daily afternoon cake and a Finnish sauna to ease walk-weary muscles, and four-course nightly feasts of Italian favourites and local South Tirolean specialities to fuel up for another day in the mountains.
 
A seven-night Italian Dolomites Winter Walking trip from £1,076, including half-board accommodation, local bus pass and transfers (inntravel.co.uk)
Husky sledding, reindeer and the northern lights in Norway
For as long as the lights of the aurora borealis have danced across the sky, the people living beneath them have told stories explaining the mysterious, spectral glow – are they omens or gods, communication from spirits or threat of war? For some Sámi communities in northern Scandinavia, they were the souls of the dead, souls that were not to be disturbed by looking, talking, waving or pointing at them, in case the ghostly veil snatched you into the sky or cut off your head.
At 217 miles (350km) above the Arctic Circle, Tromsø is the ideal destination for northern lights chasers and learning about the indigenous Sámi people – many of whom still herd reindeer across the vast wilderness.
The Oskal family have lived a way of life shaped by reindeer for generations, and their herd spends winter around the camp near Tromsø and summer roaming free in the mountains. The family now share that traditional way of life through Tromsø Arctic Reindeer, opening up their camp to visitors to sled ride, feed the herd and join the family around the fire in the lavvu (tent), for joik (traditional Sámi song) and perhaps glimpses of the aurora overhead (experiences start at 990 kroner/£75 for reindeer feeding).
At the gateway to Norway’s frozen far north, Tromsø is the launchpad for numerous activities – ice fishing and fjord cruising, husky sledding and snowmobile safaris – and the lively university town is interesting in itself. It was once the departure point for expeditions to the north pole – a history captured at the Polar Museum on the harbour front – and today also draws cultural travellers for concerts in the angular Arctic Cathedral and the international film festival in January.
 
Three-night trip to Tromsø from £767pp, including B&B and an aurora-chasing trip, with Discover the World

Bulgarians vote in highly polarized presidential runoff overshadowed by Ukraine war

Bulgaria votes in closely contested presidential runoff
November 1, 2026
Bulgarians on Sunday began voting in a highly contested presidential runoff following a tight race between the two main contenders last weekend.
The November 1 runoff pits two competing visions of Bulgaria against each other. Moscow-friendly incumbent Iliana Yotova opposes military aid to Ukraine, while former caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov is backed by the pro-Western opposition.
In last Sunday's first round, which saw voter turnout fall to a historic low, Yotova won with 34.76% of the vote, less than three percentage points ahead of Gyurov with 31.95%.
Although Bulgaria's presidency has largely ceremonial duties, the president can appoint interim governments during political crises, serve as commander-in-chief of the armed forces, and veto legislation.
Ukraine war divides Bulgaria
The war in Ukraine has become a central issue in the election, with voters heading to the polls amid growing security concerns in the Black Sea, which borders Bulgaria, following a rise in drone attacks targeting commercial vessels.
Yotova has presented herself as a "president of peace" who favors dialogue with Moscow.
In a TV debate before the runoff, Gyurov accused Yotova of avoiding direct criticism of Russia over the Black Sea attacks.
"Russia must stop its aggression so that the next steps can be taken. Let us name the country from which the threats are coming," he said.
In response, Yotova argued that "peace can come only through negotiations," and maintained that continued aid for Ukraine "leads only to more destruction and the deaths of many people on both sides."
Yotova vs Gyurov: Between Russia and the West
If elected, Yotova is expected to pursue a similar approach to Prime Minister Rumen Radev — keeping Bulgaria on its European path while seeking closer ties with Russia and advocating the lifting of sanctions.
Her opponent Gyurov previously served as deputy governor of Bulgaria's central bank and as caretaker prime minister, leading the country in early 2026.
He has repeatedly voiced strong support for Ukraine and signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his premiership.
After the first round of voting, Gyurov said that Bulgaria faced a choice "between two personalities, two directions, and two ways of exercising presidential powers."

Ukrainian drone forces commander reports monthly record: one target hit every 41 seconds
In October, units from the Unmanned Systems Forces hit a Russian asset every 41 seconds on average and a Russian soldier every 159 seconds. The month set a record for the number of Russian personnel losses inflicted by the grouping.
Source: Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, Commander of Unmanned Systems Forces, on Telegram
Details: Brovdi said that in October, units from the Unmanned Systems Forces hit 64,807 targets, and Russian military personnel losses inflicted by them amounted to 16,796.
The figure for Russian personnel losses was a record for the Unmanned Systems Forces since the start of the full-scale war – 52.55% higher than in August and 24.71% higher than in September.
The daily average was 542 Russian soldiers. The highest daily figure, 701, was recorded on 24 October.
In total over the month, the group's units carried out 255,605 combat missions, of which around 151,500 were strike missions and 104,000 reconnaissance missions.
Around 69.5% of Russian personnel losses were recorded on the Dobropillia-Pokrovsk, Oleksandrivka and Huliaipole fronts.
Brovdi stressed that these figures relate solely to units from the Unmanned Systems Forces and did not include data from other components of Ukraine's defence forces. He said all the results had been verified in the Delta situational awareness system.

MOSCOW, November 1. /TASS/. Ukraine’s economic losses resulting from explosions from January through October 2026 amounted to nearly 1.9% of its nominal GDP, or about $4.28 billion, excluding the metallurgical sector, according to TASS calculations based on the Ukrainian government’s reports.
Over the past few months, explosions have occurred in warehouses and at facilities in the military-industrial and energy sectors, as well as at port infrastructure sites and data centers serving the Ukrainian armed forces.
As a result, instead of the 1.5-2.5% annual GDP growth projected for early 2026, Ukraine’s GDP is currently showing zero growth. A recession was observed in the second and third quarters, and the National Bank expects a 0.4% decline by the end of the year.
The metallurgy sector could see the largest GDP losses in the coming months. Following a series of explosions in August and September, all of the country’s metallurgical enterprises ceased operations. If these companies do not resume operations, annual GDP losses could reach 7% compared to the same period last year.

Slender-billed nutcracker spotted by amateur photographer in Landen: “Rare phenomenon underway”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:44:00 UTC
15:44:00 KST

In Landen (Flemish Brabant), amateur photographer Eddy Koninckx managed to photograph a slender-billed nutcracker. The little bird is rare and has been in the area for several days now. It has also been spotted in nearby Heverlee (Flemish Brabant) and Averbode (Flemish Brabant).
Slender-billed nutcracker spotted by amateur photographer in Landen: “Rare phenomenon underway”
“The bird was remarkably easy to spot and certainly not shy. At one point, it came within a good 5 metres,” says Eddy.
The thin-billed nutcracker is related to the crow. It has dark brown plumage with distinctive white markings. Its sturdy beak is also striking. The bird is a rare sight in Belgium. It is mainly found in Scandinavia and Eastern Europe.
Invasion of nutcrackers
According to environmental organisation Natuurpunt, a rare phenomenon is currently taking place: an invasion of nutcrackers. “Since October, they have been appearing in unusual numbers across Flanders, whereas they are normally seen here only extremely rarely. These are birds that have undertaken an enormous journey from the taiga, the forested region in the far north-east of Europe. We have to go back decades to find a comparable, large-scale invasion.”
Not enough seeds
The birds are probably looking for food. “They mainly eat pine seeds. But some years, the trees produce few seeds, forcing the birds to seek alternative sources. That was the case this year in the north-eastern breeding grounds. These nutcrackers are then forced to move to temperate regions where they can find sufficient food. In many cases, that means Western Europe,” says Natuurpunt.
And so, the thin-billed nutcracker has also ended up in Landen, though it has already been spotted in Heverlee, Averbode and Merksplas (Antwerp Province), amongst other places. In Landen, it is already attracting many birdwatchers.
“Armed with binoculars and large cameras, they’re trying to catch a glimpse of the bird. The locals are quite pleased about it too, and some just pop round for a chat and even call it ‘their bird’. It’s lovely, isn’t it?”, says Eddy.

Venezuela's army attacked Colombian rebels camped on its side of the border, leaving several people dead, an NGO said on Saturday.
Friday's attack marked the first time that Venezuela, ruled by socialists for decades until Nicolas Maduro was ousted by US forces in January, has attacked National Liberation Army (ELN) forces camped inside Venezuela, said Javier Tarazona, director of an NGO called Fundaredes.
The NGO shared a video which showed bodies lying on the ground, trees knocked down and the ruins of what appeared to be a camp site in a rural area of Venezuela's Apure state.
A Fundaredes staff member counted at least nine bodies, Tarazona said.
The Venezuelan government did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.
The ELN has been the most powerful rebel group in Latin America since the FARC guerrilla army signed a peace accord with the Bogota government in 2016.
Colombia and Venezuela share a more than 2,000-kilometre (1,240-mile) border where other rebel groups also operate, such as FARC holdout factions that rejected the peace accord and are now fighting each other to control cocaine trafficking and illegal mining operations.
For many years, the Bogota government accused leftist Venezuela of granting safe haven to Colombian rebels.
But now Venezuela is governed under the close watch and control of the US administration after the abduction of Maduro, as the United States seeks to cash in on Venezuela's vast oil wealth and other natural resources.
Local people in Apure reported Friday's army attack and said there could be another 10 ELN fighters dead, said Rocio San Miguel, a human rights activist who specialises in military affairs.

Separately, Trump, who had previously called Brazil’s election “rigged”, voiced sympathy for Bolsonaro and said he could stay in the US indefinitely.
“I think he got treated very shabbily, very shabbily, so he can stay here as long as he wants,” the president told reporters at his Florida residence on Saturday.
The Reuters news agency reported that Bolsonaro was admitted to the US under humanitarian parole, a status that typically lasts for one year.
Trump’s comments suggested relations between the Western Hemisphere’s two largest democracies may remain strained for some time.
After Bolsonaro’s run-off loss, he fled Brazil to the US via Argentina and Ecuador on a journey that some US media outlets reported was partly arranged with the help of Jason Miller, a White House official.
Bolsonaro has refused to concede the Brazilian election and called the results fraudulent without providing evidence.
Since arriving in the US, he has claimed to be the true “leader” of Brazil and said he left the country because he was a victim of “persecution”.

From silent cinema to 1970s New York: Astana Opera unveils new romantic ballet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:37:08 UTC
00:37:08 KST

From silent cinema to 1970s New York: Astana Opera unveils new romantic ballet
Astana Opera has presented Charlie and Irene, a new romantic ballet-comedy inspired by 1970s New York and the visual language of silent cinema, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The world premiere was scheduled for October 31 and November 1, featuring original music by composer Alexey Kestner, choreography by Kirill Radev, and costumes designed by fashion designer Igor Chapurin.
The two-act production tells an unconventional love story between Charlie, a kindhearted homeless man living in New York’s Central Park, and Irene, a young woman from a wealthy and influential family.
Their romance faces opposition from Irene's father, who disapproves of their relationship. However, an unexpected encounter with a mysterious postman changes Charlie’s life when he receives a letter revealing an inheritance.
Despite his sudden wealth, Charlie remains faithful to his principles of kindness and generosity, while the story explores whether love can overcome social divisions.
The production draws inspiration from silent cinema, combining neoclassical choreography with humor, romance and cinematic storytelling.
Although the central character shares his first name with Charlie Chaplin, the ballet is not based on the legendary silent-film actor. Instead, it tells an original story in which movement and physical expression play a central role.
Speaking at a press conference ahead of the premiere, choreographer Kirill Radev said the creative team wanted the dancers to feel free onstage and embrace the production's playful atmosphere.
“We worked with the artists for a long time, looking for ways to help them enjoy themselves onstage, let go, be themselves and, above all, not be afraid to laugh at themselves,” he said.
Valery Kopeikin, the ballet’s librettist and founder and general producer of Mosaic Del Arte, explained that the idea emerged from a desire to create a more accessible and uplifting theatrical experience.
He said Charlie and Irene marks the company’s third ballet production in Kazakhstan. Unlike its previous works, which explored more serious dramatic themes, the new production was conceived as a lighthearted romantic comedy.
“We wanted to try something light and cheerful, so that people would leave the ballet with a smile,” Kopeikin said.
He also stressed that the story was created from scratch rather than adapted from an existing literary work.
Original music and new opportunities for dancers
The ballet features an original score composed specifically for the production by Alexey Kestner.
Radev said he worked closely with the composer throughout the creative process, discussing musical passages and making adjustments to ensure the score complemented the choreography.
Altynai Assylmuratova, artistic director of the Astana Opera ballet company and People’s Artist of Russia, welcomed the production as an opportunity to expand the theater’s repertoire with an original work.
She emphasized the importance of creating choreography specifically for the dancers rather than transferring an existing production to a new company.
“The most valuable thing is when a production is created specifically for you, rather than transferred, and you are not stepping into roles originally created for someone else,” Assylmuratova said.
She also highlighted the potential of young dancer Doskhan Zaidin, one of the performers cast as Charlie. Shugyla Adepkan is among the dancers cast as Irene.
Bringing 1970s New York to the stage
The visual concept of Charlie and Irene draws on the fashion and cultural atmosphere of New York in the 1960s and 1970s.
Costume designer Igor Chapurin said he wanted the characters’ clothing to reflect their personalities and emotional lives rather than simply reproduce recognizable fashion trends of the period.
The designer explored different styles associated with the era, from hippie influences to French avant-garde fashion.
Scenographers Anastasia Kapustina and Natalia Shakhmatova developed a stage environment inspired by New York’s Central Park.
The designers studied films, paintings, posters, furniture and architectural details to recreate the atmosphere of the period without overwhelming the performance.
Kapustina explained that the stage design combines different worlds, including the contrasting lives of Charlie and Irene, while incorporating subtle visual references that audiences may discover over multiple viewings.
Shakhmatova said the team paid particular attention to furniture, props and everyday objects to create a convincing sense of place.
The production was developed in collaboration with the creative team of Mosaic Del Arte, with support from Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Culture and Information.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that Astana Opera was set to present Beethoven – Immortal – Love, a ballet exploring the life and inner world of the legendary composer, under the artistic direction of Altynai Assylmuratova.

Protocol upgrading China-Peru FTA takes effect
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:32:33 CST
15:32:33 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- The protocol upgrading the China-Peru free trade agreement (FTA) took effect on Sunday, according to China's Ministry of Commerce (MOC).
China and Peru launched negotiations on the upgrade in November 2018 and signed the protocol on Nov. 14, 2024. The original FTA was signed in 2009 and took effect in 2010.
The protocol improves seven existing chapters of the original FTA, covering rules of origin, customs procedures and trade facilitation, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, intellectual property rights, trade in services, temporary entry of business personnel, and investment, the MOC said in an online statement.
The protocol also adds five new chapters on standards and conformity assessment cooperation, competition policy, e-commerce, global supply chains, and environment and trade.
The two sides also set out future provisions for negotiations on negative lists for trade in services and investment, aimed at further raising openness in these areas, according to the statement.
Since the original FTA came into force in 2010, it has played an important role in promoting bilateral economic and trade cooperation. Two-way trade rose from 6.4 billion U.S. dollars in 2009 to 50.4 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, an increase of nearly seven times, official data show.
The protocol is expected to help tap further opportunities for bilateral trade and investment cooperation, provide a better business environment for enterprises of both countries and inject new vitality into bilateral economic and trade relations, the MOC said. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: China's resident-led renewal efforts give old neighborhoods new life
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:32:27 CST
15:32:27 KST

HANGZHOU, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Amid the ongoing urban renewal drive in China, residents in an east China neighborhood have spearheaded a new model by raising funds for rebuilding their dilapidated residential block.
Unlike the government-led model that typically offers residents new apartments and cash compensation, this project saw its 548 homeowner households raise 499 million yuan (about 74.32 million U.S. dollars), more than 80 percent of the reconstruction bill, with the government covering the rest.
The compound with 13 previously run-down buildings, known as Zhegong Xincun, sits in the downtown Gongshu District of Hangzhou, capital of the affluent Zhejiang Province. These six-story walk-ups were transformed into seven mid-rise buildings, surrounded by green spaces and shared facilities, in February last year.
Hangzhou was an early adopter of this approach. It is among initiatives piloted across Chinese cities, from Harbin in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province to Shenzhen in south China's Guangdong Province, to avoid large-scale land acquisition and heavy investment from developers.
Such pilot projects address long-standing hurdles for urban regeneration in China. Small scattered plots often deliver slim returns for commercial developers, and matching residents' compensation expectations has frequently stalled renewal plans, said Wu Songtao, professor at the School of Architecture and Design of Harbin Institute of Technology.
According to a State Council executive meeting held in May, China is shifting from the stage of large-scale incremental expansion to a stage focused on improving the quality and efficiency of existing urban stock.
"Instead of large-scale demolition, the goal now is to revitalize existing buildings, factories, neighborhoods and public spaces," said Zheng Degao, vice president of the China Academy of Urban Planning and Design.
Zheng added that all beneficiaries, namely government, businesses and property owners alike, should share both the costs and the benefits.
But translating this vision into practice was no easy task. Renewing old neighborhoods involves many interests and is prone to disputes, said Li Yin, an official with Gongshu District.
Previous attempts to renew Zhegong Xincun all failed due to residents seeing only limited benefits and strains on public finances.
Built in the 1980s and 1990s as faculty housing for Zhejiang University of Technology, the compound sits in a prime location in central Hangzhou, surrounded by shopping areas, metro stations and a large hospital.
However, over the years, safety hazards mounted. Stiff windows were difficult to close, and building settlement warped door frames and locks, sometimes forcing residents to climb over walls to enter their homes.
"The plaster crumbled at the slightest touch. We lived in fear every day," said a resident surnamed Yu.
The university once carried out reinforcement work, but the effect was limited. Because the buildings continued to tilt and crack due to ongoing building settlement, such measures offered only temporary relief.
A previous housing-relocation plan failed to win broad support. According to residents, a 2014 survey on demolition and reconstruction, and another attempt in 2018, both came to nothing.
"The old idea was that the government should cover everything, from relocation to renovation," one resident said. "But as previous plans kept falling through, we realized we had to do it ourselves."
The turning point came in April 2023, when the subdistrict community office reached out to residents for their opinions on starting a resident-led renewal project.
With support from local policies on renovating old urban neighborhoods, Gongshu District developed and adopted a resident-led renewal model for the compound. The initial stage of the renewal project was launched in mid-2022. The district set up a special task force to coordinate departments, study relevant policies and win public support via explanations.
Local officials said that the harder part was reaching a consensus. "The core of the entire project lies in community engagement, shifting residents' mindset from being asked to renovate to wanting to renovate," Li said.
A voluntary committee of 13 representatives was formed. After consulting all households, it submitted an application and entrusted local authorities to coordinate and initiate the renewal.
By late August 2023, all but one of the compound's 548 homeowner households had signed agreements, bringing the signing rate to 99.82 percent, thus paving the way for the renewal plan to move forward.
In May 2024, the last household came forward to sign before delivery. "This last resident later told me, 'I watched for a long time, and I could see the project is fair,'" Li said.
Yu calculated that her original 76-square-meter apartment, plus an additional 19 square meters and a parking space, brought her total payment to nearly 980,000 yuan.
"I originally bought the apartment for 1.51 million yuan. Even with this expense, my total cost remains below the market price, and I have more living space. I am also a beneficiary," she said.
The project, though, has benefited from the community's demographics. Experts noted that although Zhegong Xincun is an aging community, its residents, mostly Zhejiang University of Technology faculty members and their families, are relatively better off, a factor that helped the project move forward.
When the project was launched, the community also had a large elderly population, with 208 residents aged 80 or above and 36 aged 90 or above. Some feared a long construction period might keep them from returning, while others with children overseas faced the daunting task of relocating alone.
To address these concerns, the working group provided comprehensive support. Ambulances were arranged to escort several residents over 90 on the moving day. Transitional housing was secured and rented to elderly residents, refurbished with age-friendly features such as shower seats and toilet grab bars.
The compound was handed over last year, with about 70 percent of households having moved in, and they have begun renovating their new homes.
The approach of Zhegong Xincun aligns with China's grand roadmap to advance urban renewal as the country endeavors to create safer, greener and more comfortable cities, while fostering new growth momentum.
Under the urban renewal plan during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China aims to renovate 500,000 units of dilapidated urban housing and 115,000 old urban residential communities. It supports resident-led renewal and on-site demolition and reconstruction of old housing, while exploring sustainable operation models.
"This resident-led renewal model has opened a new path for urban renewal in China," said Xu Lin, a professor at Zhejiang University, noting that as China's urbanization enters a new phase, cities are no longer expanding through large-scale demolition and construction, but focusing on improving living conditions for residents.
"At the end of the day, it's about giving people a better life," said Xu. ■

Researchers discover first fully marine stem amphibian in Late Triassic fossils
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:32:23 CST
15:32:23 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- A group of international researchers has reported the first fully marine species of stem amphibian, Gerrothorax maritimus, in a recent research article published in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution.
Based on two nearly complete skeletons measuring at least 737 millimeters from the Late Triassic (about 237 million years ago) discovered in southwest China's Guizhou Province, the researchers reconstructed the appearance of Gerrothorax maritimus: a flattened body covered with heavy bony armor, a broad and flat head, a wide mouth, and sturdy, well-developed gill arches, according to a report by China Science Daily.
More than 8,000 amphibian species exist today, but none of them lives entirely in the sea. Amphibian skin is permeable, which aids respiration but causes water loss in seawater, where high salinity adds physiological challenges.
Some living amphibians can tolerate brackish habitats where freshwater meets seawater, and fossils of ancient species have been found in coastal sediments. But previous evidence was insufficient to confirm that any amphibian ever had a fully marine lifestyle.
Gerrothorax maritimus is therefore recognized as the first stem amphibian known to date to have lived entirely in a marine environment, said Jiang Dayong, the article's corresponding author.
The researchers suggested that Gerrothorax maritimus's flattened body suited life on the seafloor, allowing it to hide in sediments.
The species' heavy bony armor helped prevent water loss through the skin, while adults retained their gills and could breathe underwater, possibly without needing to surface to breathe air with their lungs.
The researchers of this study come from the Geological Museum of Guizhou, Peking University, and the University of California, Davis. ■
