Scrapped marine rope recast as stools that rock like buoys
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Scrapped marine rope recast as stools that rock like buoys
Rotterdam studio The New Raw has used discarded rope salvaged from the city’s harbour to create a series of 3D-printed public seating for its waterfront.
Called Buoy, the urban furniture project is shortlisted for a 2026 Dezeen Award in the sustainable design category.
To create the stools, The New Raw founder Foteini Setaki collected a series of plastic ropes from Rotterdam harbour, which were formerly used for managing boats and would’ve otherwise gone to waste.
The ropes were then transported to Maastricht, in the south of the Netherlands, where they were cleaned, shredded and mechanically recycled into pellets.
After returning to The New Raw’s Rotterdam studio, the recycled plastic pellets were melted and 3D-printed to create the stools, layer by layer.
“The material fuses as it is deposited, so no separate binder is needed,” Setaki told Dezeen.
Setaki explained that marine ropes are challenging to recycle because they contain a cocktail of materials that accumulate various residues over time.
Careful selection is essential to determine the ropes with the highest polypropylene content to be transformed into recycled plastic pellets, she explained.
While no virgin plastic is used in the creation of the stools, a small percentage of additives support the furniture’s long-term outdoor use, including UV protection.
“These additives are compatible with recycling the material again,” said Setaki.
Each seat features a subtly different hue, which is determined by the colour of the original rope rather than additional pigments or coatings.
The stools were also designed with spinning top-style pointed bases, so that they rock when the user sits down.
This gentle rocking motion was chosen to mimic real buoys bobbing along on the water.
“We wanted the seats to carry a recognisable link to their maritime origin, through both their shape and the slow movement of floating buoys,” explained Setaki.
“Borrowing that movement brings a playful quality to sitting, and the connection to the harbour becomes something you can feel.”
Each unique stool was engraved with its batch and production number, and then placed by Rotterdam harbour.
The project was created as an example of how designers can seek out local, surplus resources in an effort to contextualise their practice with the place that they work.
“Working with a local waste stream is a way of strengthening the relationship between the city and its harbour,” said Setaki.
“The material’s journey and the experience of sitting make that relationship tangible. This approach could also be adapted to other harbour cities, starting with their own discarded materials and local networks.”
Founded in 2016, The New Raw is run by Setaki and Panos Sakkas. The studio 3D prints locally sourced plastic waste to create furniture.
Buoy is nominated alongside a vibrant shortlist of sustainable design projects, including a cement-free architectural material made of waste date pits and lighting for an Australia bookshop made of its own faulty publications rejected due to printing errors.

India news: Opposition holds major rally in Delhi over voter roll revisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01

14:56:00 KST

India opposition holds major rally against voter roll revisions
Published November 1, 2026last updated November 1, 2026
What you need to know
This blog is closed. Here is our coverage from India on Sunday, November 1:
- India's opposition parties are marching to Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi to seek the resignation of the election chief over alleged voter roll manipulation
- Rahul Gandhi tells protesters that India's election chief 'will go to jail'
- Pollution curbs have kicked-in in the Indian capital
Thank you for reading!
That's all for today. We will be back with more news from India tomorrow.
Rahul Gandhi says India's election chief 'will go to jail'
Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar would be removed from office and jailed, accusing him of facilitating electoral fraud.
Speaking at a rally organized by the opposition INDIA alliance in New Delhi, Gandhi alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah owed their positions to Kumar.
"Gyanesh Kumar will be removed from the post of Chief Election Commissioner. Gyanesh Kumar will go to jail," Gandhi told supporters.
The Congress leader also accused authorities of manipulating elections through electronic voting machines and changes to electoral rolls.
"For years, vote theft has been happening in this country," Gandhi said, citing several state elections and the 2024 parliamentary vote.
He further claimed that 15% of India's voters had been removed from electoral rolls following the 2024 election. The allegations have not been independently verified.
Gandhi also criticized economic inequality and the treatment of farmers, young people and workers.
"The farmer is not getting his rights. The youth are not getting employment. The laborer is not getting his rights, and the entire wealth has gone into the hands of two or three people," he said.
Home Minister Amit Shah denounces opposition rally
Union Home Minister Amit Shah took aim at opposition leader Rahul Gandhi from an event in Punjab state's Chandigarh on Sunday as the opposition alliance reached Ramlila Maidan for its rally.
He slammed the Congress for calling the opposition rally on the anniversary of the 1984 anti-Sikh riots, which Shah said were "incited" by the main opposition party,
"Our party held a press conference requesting that they not hold the event on November 1, 2, 3 — the very days the anti-Sikh riots took place — as it would deeply hurt the sentiments of the Sikh community, including mothers, sisters, and children. But they remained adamant," Shah said.
The senior minister of the Modi government highlighted that he was speaking from Punjab, which he went on to say was the "land of the (Sikh) Gurus."
"I strongly condemn this vile attempt. India and Punjab will never be able to forget this," he said, referring to the opposition rally.
Congress and the opposition have accused Shah and Modi of "vote theft" amid allegations of electoral irregularities.
On Saturday, Shah challenged Gandhi and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav to discuss the "vote theft" row in a special session of the parliament. He has accused the opposition of evading parliamentary debate and making baseless allegations against India's poll body.
INDIA bloc leaders arrive at Ramlila Maidan
India's opposition leaders, led by Congress' Rahul Gandhi, have reached Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi — the ground-zero of their rally against a sweeping review of voter lists and their demand for the resignation of the chief election commissioner.
The rally is November's first public display of dissent, following near-daily protests in October by opposition parties, India's 'Cockroach' movement, student organizations and civil society groups over the Special Intensive Revision of voter rolls in the world's largest democracy.
Gandhi, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's political arch-rival, rode through an almost 1.5 kilometer-long (0.9 mile-long) stretch in New Delhi in an open-top jeep, with leaders of India's opposition parties seated behind him.
Thousands of people, including supporters and cadres of the opposition from different states, began gathering at Ramlila Maidan from Sunday morning, waving the national flag and party flags as they awaited the arrival of the opposition convoy.
Visuals on Indian news channels showed the opposition leaders taking their seats on a stage set up at the historic square.
Gandhi is expected to address the rally shortly.
Opposition leaders set off for Ramlila Maidan
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has shared visuals of the opposition INDIA alliance's rally headed toward Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi.
A split screen showed a large crowd of supporters gathered at the rally site as promient opposition lawmakers seated onboard an open-top vehicle made their way to the Ramlila Maidan through Delhi's roads.
"Come to Connaught Place, let's march together. Or meet directly at Ramlila Maidan - but you must come," Gandhi wrote on X earlier at noon local time as he called for the march to "Save the Vote, Save the Nation."
Delhi enforces winter pollution plan
With winter on the horizon in New Delhi, dread of the annual smog that season brings with it has also set in.
Starting today, the Indian capital is imposing strict and sweeping pollution curbs to tackle the toxic winter smog.
The restrictions include a ban on older vehicles registered outside the city, a suspension of dust-generating demolition activities and outdoor civil construction activities, doubling of parking fees to discourage the use of private vehicles and reduction of physical attendance in government and private-sector offices to 50%.
Agencies including the Delhi Pollution Control Committee, the Municipal Corporation, the city's transport department and traffic police have been tasked with ensuring a stringent enforcement of the winter pollution rules.
The measures will be implemeted for varying time frames, with some lasting until February 28.
"Delhi's Winter Action Plan 2026-27 comes into effect with stricter pollution controls, stronger enforcement and 24×7 monitoring. We humbly request all Delhiites to follow the guidelines and contribute towards making Delhi's air cleaner and healthier," Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta's office said.
How has Modi's BJP reacted to the opposition stir?
The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of Prime Minister Narendra Modi is staging a rally of its own in New Delhi, setting the stage for a battle of marches.
The BJP march will take place in West Delhi in remembrance of the 1984 anti-Sikh riots, with the ruling party accusing the Congress of staging a political rally on the anniversary of the violence.
The deadly riots took place following the assassination of the then prime minister, Congress'Indira Gandhi— opposition leader Rahul Gandhi's paternal grandmother — by two Sikh bodyguards on October 31, 1984.
"The sobs of the 1984 riot victims cannot be drowned out by the noise of rallies!" the BJP wrote on X.
"The wounds of 1984 are still raw today. Congress cannot bury them under the din of its theatrics!" the party added.
The BJP also shared videos from different states in the country of rallies held over the weekend under its campaign named "Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy" to counter the Congress and the opposition.
The BJP deems the opposition protests over alleged voter roll manipulations as attempts to "create anarchy."
INDIA bloc holds big rally against electoral irregularities, election chief
India's political opposition is carrying out a major march in New Delhi to protest the nationwide revision of electoral rolls that they say benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
They are also seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The 'Chalo Dilli' march, heralded by the main opposition Congress party, will begin from Central Delhi's Connaught Place Minto Road Junction to reach Ramlila Maidan.
Top faces of the opposition alliance — called the INDIA bloc — are among those expected to participate. These include Congress' Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee, Samajwadi Party supremo Akhilesh Yadav and Rashtriya Janata Dal's Tejashwi Yadav.
India's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which carried out its own demonstrations against Kumar last month, has also backed the opposition rally.
What is India's electoral roll controversy?
Under a contentious nationwide voter-verification exercise, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), around 130 million names have been purged from electoral rolls.
The opposition and critics say that those struck off the voter lists include a large number of minority voters and accuse Modi's BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains. BJP denied the allegations.
The outcry against election chief Kumar began in September after an investigative report by an Indian daily said that there were divisions in the country's poll body — the Election Commission of India (ECI) — over the revision of voter lists, which it oversees.
Concerns emerged over the ECI's independence.
The ECI has maintained the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and helps prevent the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
Opposition stages symbolic impeachment of election chief
On Saturday evening, the INDIA bloc staged a mock impeachment of the chief election commissioner. The symbolic proceedings saw opposition members reenacting a parliamentary session in a garden at Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge's residence.
"I don't think anything like this has ever happened in history. The entire opposition sitting in a garden to discuss the impeachment of the CEC, it is absurd," leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi said.
He added that the opposition lawmakers had to hold the mock exercise — which even featured furniture, seating arrangements and carpeting resembling the Lok Sabha (lower house of the Indian parliament) — because they "have nowhere else to go."
"We have no other option. Every single institution ... is closed for us," Gandhi said.
Meanwhile on Sunday, the opposition expects thousands of supporters to descend upon Ramlila Maidan.
It is the first major demonstration to be held at the famous ground, located between Old and New Delhi, since it was labeled as one of the three designated protest sites in the capital last month.
Early visuals showed supporters beginning to gather at Ramlila Maidan and posters of the 'Chalo Dilli' march propped up in the capital.
The Delhi Police said that around 200 to 250 CCTV cameras have been set up at the site as part of the security arrangements.
News agency ANI reported that around 4,000 security personnel have been deployed at Ramlila Maidan.
"The organizers have set up various enclosures, and we have police personnel stationed within them. There are also pathways between these enclosures, where our police personnel are deployed to ensure the area remains secure,” deputy commissioner of police (Central District) Rohit Rajbir Singh told ANI.
The capital's traffic police announced curbs and diversions in Central Delhi ahead of the rally.

Rioters smash, loot storefronts amid cost of living protests in Germany
Masked rioters smashed storefronts and looted goods late Saturday in Frankfurt, Germany amid a protest against the rising cost of living.
The largely peaceful demonstrations were led by a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" - roughly translated to "Gen Z's got this" - rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.
Tensions peaked in the evening as some groups of protesters refused to disperse, sparking clashes and violence in major cities including Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg.
in Frankfurt's financial hub, masked protesters hurled stones, fireworks and pepper bombs, according to police.
Authorities also said looters stole weapons from a gun store, which were later retrieved. Some rioters also threw Molotov cocktails at police after pummeling them with stones and bottles earlier in the day, Frankfurt police said on X.
In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police responded by using water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds.
Earlier in the day, demonstrations had been largely peaceful. In Berlin, young protesters gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.
"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection - in short, in our future - because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.
Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.
"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.

Bulgaria returns to polls in presidential runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:51:39 UTC
14:51:39 KST

AA Photo
Bulgarians return to the polls on Nov. 1 to choose between acting President Iliana Yotova and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov after a first round marked by record-low turnout produced no outright winner.
Yotova and her running mate, Kiril Valchev, won 34.8 percent of the vote on Oct. 25, ahead of Gyurov and Georgi Kandev on 32 percent, according to the Central Election Commission. Only about 22.5 percent of eligible voters cast ballots, the lowest turnout in Bulgaria’s post-communist history.
Polling stations are scheduled to open at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT) and close at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT). The campaign has featured competing views on Bulgaria’s foreign policy and its relations with Russia, Ukraine and Western allies.
Yotova is seeking a full presidential mandate with the backing of Progressive Bulgaria, the party led by former President Rumen Radev. She served as his vice president and assumed the presidency after he resigned in January.
A victory would make her Bulgaria’s first elected female president. The office’s responsibilities include representing the country, serving as commander-in-chief of the armed forces and vetoing legislation.
Gyurov, an economist and former deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, is backed by opposition parties. He led a caretaker government before April’s parliamentary election.
A total of 27 candidates contested the first round. Electoral rules require a candidate to win more than half the valid votes, with participation exceeding 50 percent of registered voters, to secure a first-round victory. Otherwise, the two leading candidates advance to a runoff.
The presidential contest follows years of political instability. Bulgaria has held eight parliamentary elections since April 2021, including seven early votes, as parties repeatedly struggled to assemble stable governing coalitions. Failed coalition negotiations led to caretaker Cabinets and further elections.
In the latest parliamentary vote in April, Radev’s Progressive Bulgaria won 131 of the National Assembly’s 240 seats, securing an outright majority.

Bulgaria еlects its seventh President and Vice President
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:51:11 UTC
14:51:11 KST

Sunday 1 November 2026 07:05
Sunday, 1 November 2026, 07:05
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Voting in Bulgaria's presidential and vice-presidential runoff begins at 7 a.m. on November 1, with Bulgarian citizens at home and abroad casting their ballots. The two tickets vying for voters' support are Iliana Iotova–Kiril Valchev and Andrey Gyurov–Georgi Kandev, who finished first and second, respectively, among the 27 candidate tickets in the first round held on October 25.
Campaigning and the publication of opinion poll results related to the election are prohibited until voting officially ends at 8 p.m.
According to the Central Election Commission, more than 6.58 million Bulgarians are eligible to vote. If voters are still queuing outside polling stations at 8 p.m., voting may be extended until 9 p.m. The same rule applies to Bulgarians voting abroad, according to local time.
Voting is taking place on 11,902 machines in more than three-quarters of all polling stations. Paper ballots are being used in polling stations with fewer than 300 registered voters.
A total of 613 polling stations have been set up for Bulgarians abroad in 60 countries. The largest numbers are in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, with 82, followed by Türkiye with 78 and Germany with 70.
Voting machines are available at 242 polling stations abroad.
A different set of voting machines, placed in storage before the first round, has been sent for use in the November 1 runoff, Central Election Commission (CEC) spokesperson Stoyanka Balova-Tsvetkova explained. The reason is that there is not enough time during the week between the two rounds to install the new software on the devices and send them abroad again.
To ensure transparency in the voting process, video surveillance has been provided during the counting of ballots and the completion of election protocols. The "Elections 360°" application offers an interactive map of polling stations, information about the candidates and the option to follow the election results.
The presidential ticket receiving the highest number of votes cast is declared the winner of the runoff, regardless of voter turnout.
The President is the head of state of the Republic of Bulgaria and Supreme Commander-in-Chief of the country's armed forces. The President is assisted by a Vice President in exercising these powers. The President and Vice President are directly elected by Bulgarian citizens for a five-year term.

Bulgaria's National Music Academy: 105 years of artistic excellence and spirit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:50:55 UTC
14:50:55 KST

Author
Tsvetana Toncheva
Article
Bulgaria's National Music Academy: 105 years of artistic excellence and spirit
Sunday 1 November 2026 07:05
Sunday, 1 November 2026, 07:05
PHOTO BTA
Font size
In 2026, the National Academy of Music “Prof. Pancho Vladigerov”, Bulgaria’s first institution of higher music education, marks its 105th anniversary with an extensive programme of concerts, academic forums and cultural initiatives. The institution was established under the name State Academy of Music by a decree of Tsar Boris III on 21 July 1921, in response to the pressing need for trained singing teachers in Bulgarian schools and highly qualified musicians for the country’s concert and operatic stages.
The Academy’s first rector was Dimitar Hadjigeorgiev, a composer and educator who had graduated from the Prague Conservatory. As early as 1904, he had been among the founders of Sofia’s first secondary music school, becoming its director in 1912. 
Bringing secondary and higher music education together under one roof in two separate divisions, the newly established Academy soon attracted an ever-growing number of pupils and students. Its teaching staff included some of Bulgaria’s most distinguished musicians: the eminent opera singer Ivan Vulpe; virtuoso flautist Nikola Stefanov; the celebrated brothers Todor and Ivan Torchanov, a violinist and pianist respectively; the great composer and pioneer of Bulgarian music Dobri Hristov; Nikola Atanasov, composer of Bulgaria’s first symphony; the legendary folklorist Vasil Stoin; and the distinguished Czech musicians Henrich Wisner, pianist and conductor, and Ivan Cibulka, cellist.
Composer Pancho Vladigerov
PHOTO Archives State Agency
“The Academy has become a platform for presenting outstanding, high-quality cultural content, of the kind that only the country’s most distinguished institutions can boast,” Rector Prof. Dr Sava Dimitrov recently told the media on the occasion of the anniversary. In a special interview with Radio Bulgaria, he described the significance of these 105 years:
Prof. Sava Dimitrov, rector of the National Music Academy
PHOTO Facebook /National Music Academy "Prof. Pancho Vladigerov"
“105 years of tradition, 105 years of statehood, I would say! The establishment of the Academy as an institution of higher music education in 1921 was a deliberate act of state policy. It gives us every reason to look back at the generations who came before us and to recognise the enthusiasm and energy with which they built what is now one of the most highly respected institutions, not only in Bulgaria and much of Europe, but, I can confidently say, throughout the world.
Our educational offering stands out in the academic landscape as a product of considerable substance and value. That is the fashionable way of putting it nowadays, although we know that education is, in fact, a mission of much broader significance. In many respects, it is education that safeguards our national tradition, strength and spirituality. It is through education that we are able to recognise progress and understand the skills required for life in the modern world.
In this sense, 105 years is both a long time and a short one. I would venture to say that these are the first five years of the Academy’s new century, marking the beginning of a new and different era. Just five years ago, the devastating COVID-19 pandemic brought the world to a standstill, and this is precisely how the first five years of the Academy’s new century began. I hope that all the years ahead will prove far more fruitful for its development than the period of stagnation we experienced. With considerable optimism, I would say that new generations and emerging trends in education are setting new standards, standards that the Academy both follows and helps to shape through its educational process.”
PHOTO Facebook /National Music Academy "Prof. Pancho Vladigerov"
Among the Academy’s earliest graduates were some of Bulgaria’s most renowned composers: Lyubomir Pipkov, Asen Karastoyanov, Veselin Stoyanov, Svetoslav Obretenov, Philip Koutev, Marin Goleminov and Georgi Zlatev-Cherkin. Its alumni also include legendary pianists and piano pedagogues such as Dimitar Nenov, Panka Pelishek, Lyuba Encheva and Tamara Yankova, as well as violinists Vasil Lolov and Vasil Chernaev.
From the outset, alongside the classical musical heritage, the Academy made Bulgarian musical creativity one of its priorities. At the end of its first academic year, its leadership issued an appeal to Bulgarian composers to submit their works for performance at public concerts. The first scholarly studies also began to emerge at this time, primarily in the field of musical folklore research.
In the 1930s, an exceptional generation of musicians joined the Academy’s teaching staff. They included composers Pancho Vladigerov, Veselin Stoyanov, Marin Goleminov and Asen Karastoyanov; violinists Nikola Abadzhiev, Vladimir Avramov and Hristo Obreshkov; pianists Dimitar Nenov, Panka Pelishek and Tamara Yankova; cellists Konstantin Popov and Konstantin Kugijski; oboist Vasil Spasov; bassoonist Atanas Gardev; singers Hristo Brambarov and Lyudmila Prokopova; and musicologists Stoyan Brashovanov and Stoyan Dzhudzhev. 
In 1936, the higher education programme was extended from three to four years and divided into two streams: one for the training of music teachers and the other for instrumentalists and singers.
Professors from the theoretical, composers' and conducting faculty
PHOTO Facebook /Museum for the History of Radio in Bulgaria "Prof. D-r Veselin Dimitrov"
In 1954, the State Academy of Music was renamed the Bulgarian State Conservatoire and restructured into three faculties: Theory, Composition and Conducting; Instrumental Music; and Vocal Music. Shortly afterwards, a permanent choir and symphony orchestra were established to support conducting studies.
An Opera Studio was also founded within the Faculty of Vocal Music, becoming the Educational Opera Theatre in 1964.
In 1995, the Conservatoire regained its status as the State Academy of Music and was named after the eminent Bulgarian composer Prof. Pancho Vladigerov. In 2006, it became the National Academy of Music.
PHOTO Facebook /National Music Academy "Prof. Pancho Vladigerov"
Speaking to Radio Bulgaria, Prof. Sava Dimitrov emphasised that the 105th anniversary would be a true celebration of music, reflecting the full breadth of activity across the musical community. The Academy’s major ensembles will take to its stage, including its professional Academic Symphony Orchestra, which has been part of the institution since 1928, its Chamber Choir and its student ensembles.
The National Academy of Music works in partnership with all of Bulgaria’s major musical institutions, from the Sofia Philharmonic and the Sofia Soloists Chamber Ensemble to the orchestras in Ruse, Varna and Burgas, the Vratsa and Vidin Symphony Orchestras, and the ensembles of the country’s opera houses.
The Music Academy is a comprehensive higher education institution offering the full range of specialisations in music and music education, including the essential theoretical disciplines that develop the body of scholarly knowledge relating to Bulgaria’s musical heritage. This is why the anniversary programme also features numerous conferences and academic events, many of them open to the public.
The rector also highlighted the wide range of support available to doctoral students, who represent the third cycle of higher education and are being prepared to become the next generation of academic colleagues and teachers.
“As you know, the law has made a doctoral degree a prerequisite for advancement within the academic hierarchy. I therefore firmly believe that, in this respect, the Academy is exceptionally vibrant and currently ranks among the strongest higher education institutions in the country. I would confidently extend that assessment to Europe as well.”
PHOTO Facebook /National Music Academy "Prof. Pancho Vladigerov"
Today, the Academy’s teaching staff comprises distinguished musicians and researchers whose professional standing is reflected in their presence on the international stage and their active participation in scholarly exchange. Students are given regular opportunities to perform in concerts and stage productions, take part in academic forums and publish their work in the Academy’s print and online publications. Alongside the regular curriculum, numerous masterclasses and special lecture series are organised, led by prominent Bulgarian and international musicians and musicologists.
PHOTO Facebook /National Music Academy "Prof. Pancho Vladigerov"
Asked whether he considers the Academy competitive with other European institutions of higher music education, Prof. Dimitrov replies:
“I believe that we often set an example and offer innovation, combining traditional and modern approaches to education. Naturally, the Music Academy meets all the requirements laid down, first and foremost, by our national legislation. The fact that this legislation is harmonised with European standards is further proof that we operate at the highest standards available.”
Prof. Dimitrov has no doubts about the high quality of education provided by the National Academy of Music:
“You know, we have been talking quite a lot lately about Bulgaria’s concertmasters. A respected colleague of mine, a professor and conductor, took the trouble to calculate that there are as many as 72 Bulgarian concertmasters working in orchestras in the so-called ‘Category A’ group, regarded as the world’s leading professional ensembles. This is not an assessment we are making of ourselves; it is one made by the world. So I can say that, at present, we offer an exceptionally high standard of education, one whose quality is firmly established.”
PHOTO Facebook /National Music Academy "Prof. Pancho Vladigerov"
Today, the Academy’s reputation is carried around the world by musicians such as Pavel Balev, Vesko Eschkenazy, Penka Kouneva and Plamena Mangova. In earlier decades, Bulgaria’s most prestigious higher music institution introduced the world to brilliant opera stars including Todor Mazarov, Hristo Brambarov, Dimitar Uzunov, Nicolai Ghiaurov, Lyubomir Bodurov, Yulia Wiener, Ghena Dimitrova, Raina Kabaivanska, Anna Tomowa-Sintow, Stefka Evstatieva, Kaludi Kaludov, Valeri Popova and Kamen Chanev.
The Academy has also educated generation after generation of Bulgarian composers, among them Filip Kutev, Marin Goleminov, Veselin Stoyanov, Svetoslav Obretenov, Parashkev Hadzhiev, Konstantin Iliev, Lazar Nikolov, Krasimir Kyurkchiyski, Vasil Kazandjiev, Todor Popov, Aleksandar Raichev, Aleksandar Yosifov, Nikolai Kaufman, Aleksandar Vladigerov, Stefan Dragostinov, Simeon Pironkov and Georgi Arnaoudov.
Its distinguished alumni also include conductors Atanas Margaritov, Ivan Marinov, Georgi Robev, Vasil Arnaudov, Georgi Dimitrov, Georgi Notev and Emil Tabakov. Among the leading Bulgarian pianists who graduated from the Academy are Anton Dikov, Nikolai Evrov and Ludmil Angelov, while its outstanding violinist alumni include Petar Hristoskov, Boyan Lechev, Georgi Badev and Mincho Minchev.
We are bringing you our interview with Prof. Sava Dimitrov on 1 November, the Day of the National Enlighteners. What message would the rector of the National Academy of Music like to share with Bulgarians at home and around the world?
“My wish is that they listen to the national spirit as expressed through music, and work to strengthen and promote our national identity around the world.”

Bulgarians vote in presidential runoff amid security tensions in the Black Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:47:51 UTC
14:47:51 KST

Bulgarians vote in presidential runoff amid security tensions in the Black Sea
Bulgarians voted Sunday in a presidential runoff between two candidates with opposing views on the Ukraine war and relations with Russia as tensions mount in the Black Sea. Incumbent President Iliana Iotova, who favours dialogue with Moscow, faces off against Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition.
Bulgarians voted Sunday in a presidential runoff between two candidates with contrasting visions on the war in Ukraine, following a series of drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea.
The race pits President Iliana Iotova, who favours dialogue with Moscow and opposes military aid to Ukraine, against Andrey Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition, in the race for the largely ceremonial post.
Read moreBulgaria searches for missing crew as drones hit two Black Sea ships
Iotova won 35 percent of the vote in the first round last week, with Gyurov on 32 percent – a much narrower gap than the 20-point lead for Iotova predicted by opinion polls.
The first round recorded turnout of 23 percent, and election officials were expecting higher participation in the runoff.
Political analyst Teodor Slavev told AFP that voters were giving their verdict on "Iotova's unconvincing response regarding Russian threats in the Black Sea".
Several vessels were struck in the Black Sea off Bulgaria in October, leaving 21 people missing, in suspected spillover from the Russia-Ukraine war.
Read moreNATO to address drone attacks in the Black Sea after seven missing off Romania
While centre-left Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said the attacks appeared to serve Russian interests and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government insists there is so far no evidence directly linking them to Moscow.
'Lesser evil'
At a polling station in Sofia, 64-year-old teacher Krassimira Kostova said she voted despite dissatisfaction with both candidates.
"I don't like either of the two candidates, but I don't like the return of communism we've been seeing in recent years either. That's why I came to vote," she said.
Petar Doitchinov, a 67-year-old retired engineer, said he had skipped the first round because he expected a runoff. He said he voted for "the lesser evil", as neither candidate matched his "vision of democracy".
In rainy, windy weather across much of the country, turnout stood at 6.1 percent at 11:00am local time (0900 GMT), compared with 5.8 percent at the same time in the first round, according to the Bulgarian electoral commission.
Polls opened at 7:00am and will close at 8:00pm, with exit polls shortly after that expected to give an indication of the winner.
'Strong Bulgaria'
After voting in Sofia, Iotova, 62, said she wanted "Bulgaria to be strong in a strong Europe" and remaining "sovereign in its decisions".
A longtime ally of Radev, she supports Bulgaria's EU and NATO membership while arguing that peace in Ukraine can be achieved only through negotiations.
Gyurov, 50, said after voting in Blagoevgrad that he had voted for a "secure, stable and European Bulgaria".
In a television debate before the runoff, Gyurov criticised Iotova for not explicitly blaming Russia for the Black Sea attacks.
"Russia must stop its aggression so that the next steps can be taken," said Gyurov, a former deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank.
Iotova maintained that "peace can come only through negotiations".
Read more'It is clear that sooner or later we will have European casualties', Romanian MEP
Radev has also argued that a ceasefire and peace talks offer the best chance of preventing further attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
He has presented Iotova as a pair of "safe hands".
A former journalist and member of the European Parliament, Iotova was elected vice-president alongside Radev in 2016 and 2021.
She took over as president this year when Radev stepped down to run in parliamentary elections.
If successful in the runoff, she would become the first woman president in the country of 6.4 million people.
Historically close to Russia, Bulgaria remains deeply divided over its relationship with Moscow.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

German students rally against cuts and conscription
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:44:20 UTC
14:44:20 KST

AA Photo
More than 100,000 school and university students rallied across Germany on Oct. 31 against government spending cuts and plans to revive military conscription, demanding greater investment in education and public services.
The demonstrations remained largely peaceful through the afternoon. In Berlin, police recorded up to 5,000 participants outside the Brandenburg Gate, half the turnout announced by organizers from the Gen Z Regelt movement.
Students accused the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz of prioritizing military expansion and big business while cutting welfare and social spending. They said years of cuts had left classrooms underfunded and public services strained.
Banners called for Merz to resign and carried messages including “Your austerity policy is costing our future,” “No to cuts and war budgets” and “Invest in people, not war.” Other signs demanded support for education, urged politicians to listen to Gen Z and declared: “Berlin is saving, the rich are laughing.”
Student representatives also criticized the government’s proposed health and pension reforms and its handling of the climate crisis. Demonstrators opposed a new military service law requiring compulsory medical examinations, which they said could pave the way for mandatory conscription.
“We want to show solidarity with France, we want to reclaim our future, we want to fight for educational justice,” university student Michelle told Anadolu Agency.
She said cuts were affecting public services needed to secure a fairer future and called for education funding to take priority over military spending.
Anastasia, 17, said students felt politicians were not listening to them. She opposed compulsory military service and rejected further militarization as a response to conflicts.
“I just don't think that we should send young kids into wars,” she told Anadolu Agency.
Sophie, a 16-year-old student, described teacher shortages, inadequate education budgets and poor school infrastructure. Inspired by demonstrations in France, she said she hoped similar action could bring change in Germany.
“More budget for schools, for example, because our school is very bad, the windows can't even close,” she said.
Several demonstrators wore keffiyehs, while others carried Palestinian flags in support of people in Gaza. Speakers expressed solidarity with student groups worldwide.
Participant Jean-Michel opposed higher defense spending while education remained underfunded. He also expressed solidarity with students in Lebanon, Syria and Palestine whose schools had been bombed, alleging Germany had provided financial, moral and political support for the destruction.
Before the rallies, media reports questioned the movement’s organization and security officials raised concerns about possible violence. Berlin organizers said they were committed to peaceful protest and were directing their criticism at political parties.
“The police are not our focus; we’re here because the political parties are all failing us,” one organizer said.
Berlin police said the Brandenburg Gate rally ended without any serious incident. Participation fell short of expectations in the capital and several other cities after some organizations withdrew their initial support.
The BSK, the largest student organization, and the Jusos, the youth wing of the center-left Social Democratic Party, cited a lack of transparency. They described the movement as a loose online coalition whose organizers were difficult to reach and whose leadership remained unclear. The Greens and the socialist Left Party supported the protests.
The demonstrations followed similar student actions in France, Belgium and Italy. Many participants cited the French protests as an inspiration, arguing large street demonstrations could push politicians to respond.

How do you score 171 out of 170 in a Harvard Exam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:38:04 UTC
14:38:04 KST

In a recent conversation with 
The Times of India
, Impact Catalyst Aruna Lohia Goenka unveiled YASHA
, her five-pillar framework for Viksit Bharat 2047: Yuva, Anna, Shiksha, Hunar and Abundance, shaped by nearly 30 years of engagement in national development.
The 
knowledge series
, under the overarching theme of Viksit Bharat 2047, now takes that conversation further. Across five interviews, Sanjiv Kaura, CEO-CSR, The Times of India, explores the experiences, convictions and ideas behind each pillar of the YASHA framework.
We begin with 
S for Shiksha
.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 As we approach a world in which machines may become more intelligent than human beings, what is the greatest danger facing our children?
Aruna Goenka:
 The danger is not that machines will become more intelligent. It is that humans may stop thinking and become like robots: programmed to respond, but forgetting how to feel, empathise and connect.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 Can you share an example of an educational intervention that reflects this philosophy?
Aruna Goenka:
 In the tribal district of Bastar, Chhattisgarh, we taught children 
how to think, rather than 
what to think. That was in the 1990s. The greatest moment is not when a child says, "I know the answer." It is when the child asks, "But why?" Today, 30 years later, I feel blessed to be associated with the AM/NS India Times Critical Thinking Championship, which reaches 1 million children each year across 28 states and 8 Union Territories in 14 languages. The scale has changed enormously, but the underlying conviction remains the same.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 If AI can become a personal tutor to every child, will we still need teachers?
Aruna Goenka:
 More than ever! AI may explain Einstein’s and Newton's laws, but can it recognise the child who has stopped believing in herself? A machine can deliver a lesson, but a great teacher can change a life. AI should be our children's co-pilot, not their autopilot.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 Are we sometimes confusing marks with intelligence?
Aruna Goenka:
 (Laughs) We give children marks for answering questions correctly. Perhaps we should reward them much more for asking questions nobody else thought of! And who says 100% is the ceiling? Let me tell you a fascinating story. In December 2018, an IIT alum and IAS officer, Ankur Garg, studying at Harvard Kennedy School, scored 171 marks out of 170 in a macroeconomics examination conducted by the world-renowned economist Professor Jeffrey Frankel. Yes, you heard that correctly. 171 out of 170! Now, isn't that wonderful?
For me, that is a beautiful metaphor for education and life. Never allow someone else's definition of the maximum to become the limit of your potential. And why restrict this philosophy to examinations? Whether it is knowledge, kindness, compassion or service, give more than is expected of you. After all, a
100% cent may be the examiner's limit. It need not be the limit of human potential.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 Socrates famously argued that the unexamined life is not worth living. Are we losing sight of that larger purpose of education?
Aruna Goenka:
 Absolutely, Socrates was reminding us that a meaningful life must be examined, not merely lived. For him, the pursuit of wisdom was inseparable from virtue. Compassion, honesty, courage, self-discipline and consciousness are not optional extras in education. They are at its very heart.
And education is not confined to degrees. Think of the extraordinary wisdom ancient Bharat produced: the 
Upanishads
, 
Tirukkural, Yoga Sutras
, 
Charaka Samhita
, and 
Panchatantra
. Consider Gautam Buddha's teachings on compassion and mindfulness; Lord Mahavira's Anekantavada, which reminds us that truth has many facets and no single viewpoint captures its entirety; Kabir's fearless questioning of dogma; Guru Nanak's message of equality and service; Tulsidas's 
Ramcharitmanas
, with its timeless reflections on duty and devotion, and Kahlil Gibran's timeless wisdom on love, self-discovery and nurturing of independent minds across centuries and civilisations, these extraordinary minds explored not merely how much we can know, but how wisely we can live. Their insights continue to inspire humanity even today. I believe we must cultivate the awareness to discover the possibilities present in the Universe; otherwise, surrounded by information and technology, we risk becoming intellectual zombies!
Sanjiv Kaura:
 You come from a family blessed with Lakshmi (prosperity), yet your affection for Saraswati (knowledge) seems just as profound!
Aruna Goenka
: (With a twinkle in her eyes) I come from a family of geniuses and wizards! My elder brother has one of the world's largest collections of handwritten books/manuscripts. Imagine the centuries of knowledge, imagination and wisdom preserved in those pages. I have never seen 
Lakshmi
 and 
Saraswati as rivals but as two complementary forces within us. 
Lakshmi
 symbolises the subconscious mind, where dreams are born, while 
Saraswati represents the conscious mind, which gives direction to the dreams. And remember, 
Lakshmi
 does not stay where 
Saraswati is neglected. Wealth without wisdom never creates lasting abundance.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 We sometimes celebrate the 
silver spoon
. But listening to you, I wonder whether a 
Silva Mind
 is the greater inheritance.
Aruna Goenka:
 (Laughs) Interestingly, I have seen the Silva Mind technique being used by my elder brother for decades – I saw him reading a book about it when he was just fourteen! The power of visualisation fascinated me. I believe it helped him envision extraordinary possibilities and turn them into reality, including the remarkable library he eventually built. But I like your comparison. A silver spoon may feed the body, but a silver mind feeds curiosity. And I must say, there is something wonderful about knowledge. It is perhaps the only inheritance that becomes richer the more you give it away.
Sanjiv Kaura: Which are some of your favourite books?
Aruna Goenka: Oh, Sanjiv, that's like asking a mother to choose her favourite child! (Laughs) But a few have stayed with me. 
Autobiography of a Yogi
 opens our minds to spirituality, consciousness and life's infinite possibilities. Then there is Thoreau's 
Walden
, which reminds us that a rich life need not be a complicated one. And I love Ralph Waldo Emerson's essay 
Self-Reliance
, with its powerful message about trusting one's own judgment rather than blindly following the crowd. Another favourite is 
Critical Thinking
 by Richard Paul. And here's a lovely coincidence! Only recently, I discovered that my younger brother has been reading it since the early 1990s! Imagine - all these years, we have been travelling along similar intellectual paths without even realising it.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 Aruna ji, your closing thoughts?
Aruna Goenka:
 Literacy teaches us to read, education teaches us to understand, and wisdom teaches us to question. Literacy opens the book. Education opens the mind. Wisdom opens the heart. And above all, dream big! But why confine your dreams to the night? Dream during the day, with your eyes wide open, and work to turn those dreams into reality. Imagine 1.4 billion people, each with a dream for Bharat, and each determined to make it happen! When 1.4 billion dreams become 1.4 billion actions, Viksit Bharat 2047 will not be just a vision. It will be our reality!
Disclaimer: This article has been produced on behalf of Aruna Goenka for Times Foundation as part of the Knowledge Sharing Series and published by Times Internet's Spotlight team.

Fat-dissolving claims land FatX Solution in regulatory trouble; CDSCO cancels registration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:37:54 UTC
14:37:54 KST

CDSCO finds over 160 drug samples as 'not of standard quality' for December
NEW DELHI: Promising to dissolve fat cells may sound like an attractive pitch for a slimming product, but it has landed FatX Solution in trouble with the country's drug regulator. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has cancelled the product's registration after finding that it was being promoted with claims that are not permitted for cosmetics.In an order dated October 28, CDSCO said Delhi-based importer Tekno Midas Aesthetics was marketing FatX Solution on its website as a product that could dissolve fat cells and reduce their size. The regulator said these were drug-related claims and did not fit the definition of a cosmetic under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.The action followed a scrutiny of the company's application and website, during which CDSCO found differences between the claims being made online and those mentioned on the approved product label.Under the Cosmetics Rules, 2020, cosmetic products cannot make false or misleading claims. The rules define cosmetics as products meant for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering appearance.
Claims to dissolve fat cells go beyond this definition, the regulator said.CDSCO had issued a show-cause notice to the company on August 10, citing violations of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and the Cosmetics Rules. The company submitted its response on September 1, but the regulator found it inconclusive and unsatisfactory. The firm also requested that its registration certificate be voluntarily surrendered.
Rajan Bhatnagar of Tekno Midas Aesthetics told TOI that the product had been registered as a cosmetic more than four years ago. "At that time, the licence was granted because the product was registered as a cosmetic. The authorities have now changed their interpretation of the category under which the product falls. Earlier, it was considered a cosmetic, but now they say it falls under another category," he said.He said the company had decided not to contest the matter after receiving the notice. "We did not want to get into any dispute or challenge the notification. We voluntarily requested the surrender of the licence, and the authorities cancelled it," he said.The Central Licensing Authority subsequently cancelled the registration certificate, RC/COS-003300, which was issued in July 2022 and was valid until July 14, 2027. The cancellation took effect from October 28.

She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

North Korea tests cluster warhead for tactical ballistic missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:36:51 UTC
14:36:51 KST

North Korea conducted a test of a cluster warhead for a tactical ballistic missile to assess its combat applicability and destructive power, state media reported on Sunday.
The Missile Administration carried out the test on Saturday, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
The test was overseen by General Kim Jong-sik, a member of the Central Military Commission of the ruling Workers' Party of Korea and first deputy director of a department of the party's Central Committee.
North Korea's Ballistic Missile Systems Research Institute and Warhead Research Institute said the test confirmed that the country's "Type-2 standard cluster warhead" could devastate a target area of about 12 to 13 hectares (29 to 32 acres) at what they described as an "ultra-high density."
The head of the Missile Administration said North Korea classifies its cluster warheads into four categories, including special-purpose and standard types.
He said Pyongyang plans to make all four types available to military units by the end of this year, allowing them to select warheads according to operational objectives and the characteristics of targets.
The Missile Administration described the test as part of regular scientific research aimed at increasing the destructive power of its weapons systems.

Two Palestinian babies die in Gaza tent fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:35:57 UTC
14:35:57 KST

Two Palestinian infants have died of severe burns after a fire tears through a displacement tent in Al Mawasi, west of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, as families cook over open flames amid shortages under Israel’s blockade.
Habiba Mohammed Zanoun, two months old, and Aseel Abu Suhayban, seven months old, died on Saturday morning at Nasser Medical Complex, which identifies them. Both are admitted to intensive care after flames break out on Friday afternoon while relatives are gathered at the tent.
Habiba was due for her two-month vaccinations on the day she dies.
Sources tell Anadolu the fire started while food is being cooked inside the tent. They said severe shortages of cooking gas and basic supplies force displaced families to prepare meals over open fires.
Aseel’s mother rushed to save her daughter and suffers burns. She was also taken to hospital.
‘Why is all this happening to us?’
The girls’ grandmother told Anadolu that her daughter had come to visit the family when the fire erupted. Habiba was her daughter’s baby, she said, and neither infant could withstand the severity of her injuries.
“Why is all this happening to us?” she asked. “Every day there are accidents, bombings and fires, and people are dying in so many ways.”
“For three years, we have been living like this, amid displacement, anguish and pain,” she added.
Cooking without safe alternatives
Sources said the blaze is one of three fires reported on Friday in displacement tents in central and southern Gaza.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned in June that cooking inside tents is a leading cause of fires. It said blankets, old fabric, cardboard and plastic sheeting used to reinforce shelters let flames spread rapidly and make fires harder to control.
OCHA also reported that Israeli authorities denied entry on August 26 and September 2 to a previously approved shipment through the Egyptian corridor. The shipment contained 36,960 pieces of timber and 660 emergency shelter kits.
The Gaza Government Media Office previously said more than 800,000 displaced Palestinians live in tents unfit for human habitation. It estimates that 162,000 of Gaza’s 270,000 displacement tents need immediate replacement.

Interview: Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building provides key insights for political parties worldwide, says Tajik expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:35:44 CST
14:35:44 KST

DUSHANBE, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building provides important guidance for political parties in different countries to strengthen their organizational foundations and enhance their governance capacity, a Tajik expert has said.
"Political parties in various countries are facing new risks and challenges in today's world," said Suhrob Raufzoda, editor-in-chief of "People's Tribune," the newspaper of Tajikistan's ruling People's Democratic Party, in an interview with Xinhua.
In his view, steadily strengthening organizational foundations and enhancing governance capacity are important guarantees for a country's long-term stability and development, and the Communist Party of China's (CPC) experience in advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance provides useful guidance for political parties in other countries.
Raufzoda attaches particular importance to China's efforts in personnel training. He said that modern state governance requires high-caliber officials with firm political conviction, professional expertise and a strong sense of responsibility. Therefore, cultivating officials and building such a cadre represent important investments in China's long-term development, he added.
In Raufzoda's view, strengthening the Party's organizational system, advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance, and cultivating high-caliber officials characterized by loyalty, integrity and a sense of responsibility are interconnected and mutually reinforcing.
The Tajik expert believes that an important objective of Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building is to further strengthen the CPC so that it always remains a vibrant Marxist governing party and the strong leadership core of the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
"The experience of the Communist Party of China has attracted the attention of many countries, as it demonstrates practical experience in continuously improving institutional development, strategic planning, the training of highly qualified personnel and mechanisms of state governance," Raufzoda said.
He stressed that every country has its own historical traditions, political system and development path. At the same time, continuously enhancing governance capacity, strengthening institutional development, cultivating highly qualified personnel and building public trust are common tasks facing many countries, he said.
Raufzoda also noted that China's achievements in areas such as poverty alleviation, personnel training, state governance, scientific and technological innovation, and modernization can provide useful guidance for countries of the Global South as they seek development paths suited to their national conditions.
"A deeper study of China's concrete practices can help provide a more objective and comprehensive understanding of the CPC's ideas on state governance and its experience in governance," he said. ■

‘Like Kashmir’: How a toxic marble dump yard became a tourist spot in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:25:32 UTC
14:25:32 KST

‘Like Kashmir’: How a toxic marble dump yard became a tourist spot in India
The vast ‘snow yard’ in otherwise arid Rajasthan state attracts hundreds of tourists daily, but residents face severe health risks.
Kishangarh, India – As Bagharam Gurjar kneels to pull weeds from his maize field in western India’s Rajasthan state, the sound of his wife coughing nearby makes him restless.
“Everything gets ruined when dust settles on the soil,” says Gurjar, 53, barely looking up.
“May God make everything right,” replies his wife between bouts of chronic cough. “Otherwise, it becomes difficult to grow crops.”
The Gurjars are among nearly 5,000 people living in the vicinity of what has turned out to be one of the most unusual tourist destinations in India.
Their village, Bhogiyawas, is just 6km (4 miles) from Kishangarh, where a 300-acre (121-hectare) marble slurry dumping yard resembles a snow-clad landscape, attracting hundreds of tourists every day in an otherwise arid state.
Locally known as a “Snow Yard”, the landfill in Rajasthan’s Ajmer district is the largest of its kind in Asia. Its pristine white hills and slopes with water-filled pits provide a surreal backdrop for visitors, who get free entry to the site.
Newlyweds pose against the snowy backdrop or the blue artificial lake, while couples soon to get married organise pre-wedding photoshoots. Social media influencers throng the landfill to make reels. Music videos and movies are also frequently shot here.
“Everyone, right from my five-year-old niece to my mother, loves it very much. Their first impression was that this looks like Kashmir,” Salim Shahzada, a businessman from Uttar Pradesh state, told Al Jazeera, referring to Indian-administered Kashmir.
Shahzada said he had visited the place a couple of times and decided to bring his family along this time. But he had no idea about the health and environmental problems linked to the dumping yard.
“I do not have much knowledge about this place or its ill effects. I only know that this is where marble cutting waste is dumped and that the hill itself is made of this waste,” he said.
Kishangarh, a marble and granite hub, is home to nearly 1,200 processing units, with the total daily business estimated at more than 160 million rupees ($1.7m), providing jobs to about 25,000 people, according to the Federation of Indian Granite and Stone Industry.
Every day, nearly 1,000 tankers carry slurry from those units and empty roughly 5,500 tonnes of waste on the government-allotted dump site, which, for the people living nearby, has turned into a health hazard.
Gurjar said the yard has affected residents in at least six villages. “How many problems can I even tell you about? If there were just one or two, we could deal with them,” he said.
“But here, almost everything is going wrong because of the dumping yard. People like me are suffering from chest infections, dental problems and skin allergies. It does not matter whether they are children or elderly people; everyone is suffering.”
Gurjar said he and his wife are forced to take regular medicines for chest infections or skin problems.
Aditi Goyal, a general physician at Ajmer’s Ganga Narayan Hospital, said the residents of Kishangarh face several health risks, mainly respiratory and skin problems. She said the workers in the marble processing units are more vulnerable to chronic illnesses because of prolonged exposure to toxic dust.
“Over the last couple of years, cases of respiratory problems have increased significantly in this area because people are exposed to dust from the dumping yard,” Goyal told Al Jazeera.
“However, dust from industrial waste is not the only issue. People in Kishangarh, who are mostly farmers, also suffer from infections caused by dust coming from the soil,” she said, advising people to wear masks to protect themselves from dust.
The same dust settles on the fields, hardening the soil and making it difficult to grow crops.
A study led by Laxmi Kant Sharma, professor in the department of environmental science at the Central University of Rajasthan, found that the concentration of lead silicate in Kishangarh’s soil was several times higher than normal, indicating extreme contamination.
“Since the waste particles are smaller than 75 micrometres, they can spread far and wide, making the soil infertile,” the study said.
The study also found that the concentration of PM2.5 exceeds the limit of ambient air quality standards. “Several people may be suffering from silicosis. The government needs to take immediate action to prevent the situation from getting out of hand,” it said.
Ugam Singh, another resident of Bhogiyawas, remembers when things were different. The continuous dumping of slurry slowly changed the landscape and the lives of people in Kishangarh, says the 65-year-old.
“Nowadays, the situation has worsened to such an extent that even the groundwater is no longer fit for consumption,” Singh said.
“The fluoride levels in the water are so high that it tastes salty. My teeth have started decaying and my bones have become weak,” he added, pointing to his teeth, which appeared pale, pitted and worn.
Singh said the residents of villages surrounding the dump yard have complained to the authorities, including officials of the Rajasthan State Pollution Control Board (RSPCB). But their requests fell on deaf ears.
“What I have come to understand is that it does not matter which government is in power. No one listens to the poor. To make the rich richer, the government sacrifices the interests of people like us. It feels as though our lives have no value,” Singh said.
“Even today all we want is for this marble slurry dumping to stop so that we can breathe freely again and our fields can become green and productive once again.”
Singh also claims that if residents of all the villages around the dumping yard were properly examined, almost every household would have someone suffering from respiratory problems such as asthma.
Last year, local environmentalist Drupad Malik filed a case before the National Green Tribunal over the harmful health and environmental effects of the Kishangarh dumping yard. The tribunal observed that unregulated dumping of marble slurry was contaminating groundwater and air. It directed the RSPCB to enforce monitoring, conduct sample inspections and penalise the marble processing units violating environmental norms.
Al Jazeera reached out to a senior official at the RSPCB’s regional office in Kishangarh, but she refused to speak on the matter.
Central University’s Sharma said the areas surrounding the Kishangarh dumping yard are unfit for human settlement. He said his research was shared with state authorities, but nothing was done to improve the environmental conditions in the area.
“There is a dire need to shift the dumping yard to another place where there is no human contact. This area has become extremely toxic and vulnerable to severe diseases. I am surprised that people are allowed to visit the site without masks and even have food there,” Sharma told Al Jazeera.
“I have forwarded several suggestions, including installing tile units, as [marble] slurry is used in tile manufacturing. This could, to some extent, help reduce pollution in Kishangarh,” he added.
Meanwhile, Ram Lal, a resident of Tokra village, about a 15-minute drive from Bhogiyawas, appealed to the government to find an alternative site for dumping the marble slurry.
“Kishangarh is full of slurry, and it is time to shift the dumping yard out of here to some other place where no one will suffer for at least two to three decades,” Lal told Al Jazeera.
“We also demand that free medical camps be set up to assess people whose health has declined because of the fine dust particles that have been flying in the air and settling here for years,” he said.
“No one from our village can afford it if someone develops a disease that costs thousands of rupees to treat.”

Israel ready for renewed Iran conflict: Report

AA Photo
Israel has completed preparations for renewed fighting with Iran, but no decision to resume attacks has been made, Yedioth Ahronoth reported on Oct. 31 as diplomatic contacts continued.
The Israeli military has finalized offensive and defensive preparations, while U.S. Central Command chief Brad Cooper has presented President Donald Trump with options for further strikes, according to the newspaper, cited by Anadolu Agency.
Citing unnamed political sources, the newspaper said the decision rests with Trump as he weighs an agreement with Tehran against renewed attacks coordinated with Israel. Israeli political and military leaders do not control whether another round of fighting begins, the report said.
Preparations have moved beyond planning. The Israeli air force has repeatedly flown dozens of fighter jets and refueling aircraft through Syrian and Iraqi airspace toward Iran’s borders to rehearse potential attack routes, according to the newspaper.
Cooper presented the military options at a meeting attended by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine. The newspaper said no decision to resume combat emerged from the meeting.
Citing media reports, it said 10 U.S. military transport aircraft had arrived at Israeli air bases in recent days, delivering equipment as Washington reinforced its forces in the region and prepared for possible military operations.
The unnamed sources questioned whether Washington had clear strategic objectives for another operation. Strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities, missile systems and other military capabilities would not necessarily bring down its government or change its policies, they said.
The sources suggested Washington could use the threat of force to secure an agreement on more favorable terms. They said any settlement failing to address Israeli concerns about Iran’s nuclear program, missile systems and armament would leave unresolved the threats Israel says it faces.
Another round of fighting could spread to Lebanon if Hezbollah joined, as it had previously, the sources said. Such an escalation could prolong the conflict and put further pressure on Israeli air defenses and stocks of interceptor missiles.
Alongside the military preparations, the newspaper cited reports of progress in indirect contacts between Washington and Tehran through Qatari mediation, aimed at opening direct negotiations.
Those talks would cover Iran’s nuclear program, the Strait of Hormuz and economic incentives for Tehran, with China and Russia potentially acting as guarantors of an agreement, according to the report.
The newspaper argued Israel’s challenge was to ensure any military action served its long-term security interests, with clear objectives, intended outcomes and conditions for ending hostilities.
The war began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28. An April ceasefire halted the fighting before hostilities between Washington and Tehran resumed in July as negotiations stalled.

Lebanese artist turns Israeli war remnants into ‘silent witnesses’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:14:21 UTC
14:14:21 KST

AA Photo
A Lebanese visual artist is transforming shrapnel, metal and other debris collected from buildings hit by Israeli attacks into sculptures and art objects, preserving the remnants as silent witnesses to the destruction and displacement caused by war.
Lina Jouni began working with the materials after returning home following Israel’s 2024 attacks on Lebanon. While sorting through the rubble around her home, including broken glass, stones, metal and cables, she realized the debris carried traces of a period that should not be forgotten.
After initially experimenting with glass, she turned to shrapnel, preserving its rust, curves and marks while making minimal alterations. The fragments have since become her artistic tools, taking the shape of faces, hands and abstract figures.
Some of the materials are collected by Jouni herself, while others are brought to her by people in the community. Through her work, she documents the destruction caused by Israeli attacks and preserve the memory of events, including the killings in Nabatieh, the 2024 pager explosions and attacks on vehicles. “I approached shrapnel as something capable of carrying history,” Jouni said. “I turned these pieces, which symbolize destruction, into instruments of life that tell the story of our survival.”
She said collecting the materials remained difficult, as some areas hit during the 2024 war were still inaccessible due to security risks and the presence of drones.
Describing reconstruction and the restoration of life as the central themes of her work, she said: “We experienced war and displacement, and we suffered. We need life again. Rebuilding means bringing life back.”
“We have materials, land and labor. We can build a new life and reconstruct at a lower cost,” she added.

Bulgaria heads to presidential runoff amid political instability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:11:22 UTC
14:11:22 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
Bulgarians will return to the polls Sunday to elect their president in a runoff between acting President Iliana Yotova and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov after neither candidate secured a majority in the first round.
Yotova and her running mate, Kiril Valchev, received 34.8% of the vote, while Gyurov and Georgi Kandev secured 32%, according to the Central Election Commission.
Turnout in the Oct. 25 vote stood at around 22.5%, the lowest recorded in the country's post-communist history.
A total of 27 candidates contested the first round.
A candidate must receive more than half of the valid votes, with turnout exceeding 50% of registered voters, to win in the first round under electoral rules. If those conditions are not met, the two leading candidates advance to a runoff.
The vote comes amid political instability in Bulgaria, which has held eight parliamentary elections since April 2021, including seven early elections.
The repeated parliamentary votes followed difficulties among political parties in securing the support needed to form stable governments.
Disagreements over coalition arrangements led to the collapse of successive attempts to establish regular governments, resulting in caretaker Cabinets and further early elections.
The latest parliamentary election, held in April, saw Progressive Bulgaria, led by former President Rumen Radev, win 131 of the National Assembly's 240 seats, giving the party an outright majority.
Yotova, who served as Radev's vice president, assumed the presidency after he resigned in January. Backed by Radev's Progressive Bulgaria party, she is seeking a full presidential mandate.
A victory would make Yotova Bulgaria's first elected female president, whose duties include representing the country, serving as commander-in-chief of the armed forces and exercising a veto on legislation.
Gyurov, an economist and former deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, served as caretaker prime minister before the parliamentary elections in April. He is backed by opposition parties.
The campaign has included debate about Bulgaria's foreign policy and its relations with Russia, Ukraine and Western allies.
Polling stations are scheduled to open at 7 am (0500GMT) and close at 8 pm (1800GMT).
