Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start Sunday, including G20 foreign ministers concluding their Atlanta meeting with a focus on energy security, supply chains and geopolitical tensions; clashes during nationwide protests in France; the Yemeni army’s capture of a strategic mountain range from the Houthis; and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying he agreed with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to work on establishing a new Black Sea grain corridor.
G20 foreign ministers concluded two days of discussions in the US city of Atlanta focusing on energy security, global supply chain resilience and geopolitical tensions affecting international trade and economic stability, according to a statement by the US presidency.
The meeting, held Oct. 30 - 31 during the 250th anniversary year of US independence, was part of Washington's effort to refocus the G20 on its core mission of addressing global economic challenges and promoting prosperity.
In the chair's statement, the US presidency said the foreign ministers held "candid discussions" on Washington's priorities, including disruptions affecting strategic maritime routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Energy security emerged as a central theme, with the statement emphasizing the importance of affordable, abundant, and reliable energy supplies for economic growth and improved living standards.
Clashes between protesters and police were reported in several French cities during nationwide demonstrations, with police using tear gas in Lyon and Grenoble, as 15,000 people took part in 65 actions in France, according to media reports.
In Lyon, tensions emerged after some demonstrators tried to leave the authorized route and move toward the city center near Place Jean Mace, prompting police to use tear gas, broadcaster France info reported.
In Grenoble, southeastern France, police also used tear gas after initial tensions near Place Gustave Rivet, where a march was split into two.
In the port city of Marseille, clashes broke out at the front of an unauthorized march, with protesters throwing paving stones at riot police blocking Boulevard Chave. Officers responded by charging the crowd, while the march continued toward Saint-Charles train station.
Scuffles between protesters and police were also reported in Toulouse, Rennes, and Nantes.
The Yemeni army has completed its capture of a strategic mountain range in the northern province of Al-Jawf following battles with Houthi forces, according to a field commander.
Col. Rabie al-Qurashi, an army field commander in Al-Jawf, told Anadolu that government forces secured the entire Huwayshian mountain range east of Al-Hazm, the provincial capital.
He said the advance followed fighting with the Houthis and was backed by warplanes that destroyed dozens of vehicles belonging to the group. The military operation remains underway, he added.
The mountains form the first line of defense for Al-Hazm, which remains under Houthi control, said al-Qurashi.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had agreed with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to work on establishing a new Black Sea grain corridor.
“Today, I reached an agreement with President Erdogan to work on the Black Sea grain corridor,” he said during a joint news conference in Istanbul, following talks with Erdogan.
Zelenskyy said Türkiye supports efforts to ensure safe navigation in the Black Sea and restore normal living conditions.
The Golden State Valkyries defeated the Atlanta Dream 68-63 to win their first Women's National Basketball Association (WNBA) championship in their second season.
French international Gabby Williams led Golden State with 30 points in the decisive Game 7 at Chase Center in San Francisco, helping the team secure a 4-3 victory in the best-of-seven Finals series.
Williams scored 28 of her points in the second half, including a crucial 3-pointer with just over two minutes remaining that put Golden State ahead for good.
Atlanta led 30-24 at halftime, but the Valkyries rallied in the third quarter, outscoring the Dream 21-14 to take a narrow lead into the final period.
Kiah Stokes contributed 13 rebounds for Golden State, while Veronica Burton made two late free throws to seal the victory.
The game marked the first Game 7 in WNBA Finals history, with the championship series expanded to a best-of-seven format in 2025.

Morgan Rogers opened the scoring early in the second half before Cole Palmer doubled Chelsea’s advantage from the penalty spot after United defender Lisandro Martinez was sent off for a second yellow card.
The defeat increased pressure on United head coach Michael Carrick, whose side entered the match in 16th place with seven points in eight league matches, one point above the relegation zone.
US rapper Macklemore performed to a sold-out crowd at London’s OVO Arena Wembley, bringing his three-city European “Free Palestine Tour” to a close with a lineup of musicians, activists and speakers expressing solidarity with Palestinians.
The concert, which followed stops in Dublin and Paris, featured performances by British singer Paloma Faith, alternative hip-hop group Cure for Paranoia, political hip-hop duo Dead Prez and Palestinian and Arab artists Nemahsis, Lina Makoul, Shadia Mansour and Dana Salah.
Aja Monet and DJ Habibeat also joined the lineup.
The event combined musical performances with political speeches and messages of solidarity, featuring Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, Holocaust survivor Stephen Kapos and Palestinian activist Arab Barghouthi.
Salem, a British-Palestinian concertgoer whose parents were displaced during the 1948 Nakba, said: “He’s done a fantastic job for the Palestinians. […] But people like Macklemore give us a bit of hope, give us a glimmer of hope that we can change things around a bit.”
The evening also included a screening of a short film by Palestinian journalist Bisan Owda and contributions from Nadia Greenspan.

Users can choose whether to enable the integration and what information to share. Alibaba said it would not use user requests and generated responses to train its AI models.

‘People are dying in so many ways’: Tent fire kills 2 infant girls in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
04:20:53 UTC
13:20:53 KST

Ramzi Mahmud and Tarek Chouiref
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
Habiba was due for her two-month vaccinations on Saturday. Instead, her family mourned her death alongside that of seven-month-old Aseel after a fire tore through the tent where their relatives had gathered in the southern Gaza Strip.
The family’s visit in al-Mawasi, west of Khan Younis, ended in a desperate attempt to save the two infants when flames broke out Friday afternoon.
Both suffered severe burns and were admitted to intensive care. They died Saturday morning.
Nasser Medical Complex identified them as Habiba Mohammed Zanoun, two months old, and Aseel Abu Suhayban, seven months old.
Sources told Anadolu that the fire started while food was being cooked inside the tent. Severe shortages of cooking gas and basic supplies under Israel’s blockade have forced displaced families to prepare meals over open flames, they said.
'Why is all this happening to us?'
The girls’ grandmother, who did not give her name, told Anadolu that her daughter had come to visit the family at their tent when the fire suddenly broke out.
Habiba was her daughter’s baby, she said. The infant died on the day she was supposed to receive her two-month vaccinations.
Aseel’s mother rushed to rescue her daughter and suffered burns. She, too, was taken to hospital.
The grandmother said neither infant could withstand the severity of her injuries.
“Why is all this happening to us?” she asked. “Every day there are accidents, bombings and fires, and people are dying in so many ways.”
“For three years, we have been living like this, amid displacement, anguish and pain.”
Cooking without safe alternatives
The blaze was one of three fires reported Friday in displacement tents in central and southern Gaza, according to sources.
With cooking gas scarce, families have resorted to makeshift fires to prepare food. Inside crowded shelters built from flammable materials, an everyday necessity can put lives at risk.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned in June that cooking inside displacement tents was a leading cause of fires.
Blankets, old fabric, cardboard and plastic sheeting used to reinforce shelters allow flames to spread rapidly and make fires harder to control, it said.
Fire is one of several dangers facing families in deteriorating tents that offer little protection from the weather.
OCHA also reported that Israeli authorities denied entry on Aug. 26 and Sept. 2 to a previously approved shipment through the Egyptian corridor containing 36,960 pieces of timber and 660 emergency shelter kits.
The Gaza Government Media Office previously reported that more than 800,000 displaced Palestinians were living in tents unfit for human habitation. It estimated that 162,000 of Gaza’s 270,000 displacement tents needed immediate replacement.
The grandmother, mourning the loss of two grandchildren, appealed to the world to pay attention to Gaza’s displaced families and help end their suffering.

WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump said on Oct 31 that the United States has knocked out much of Iran’s military but still has to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked.
He maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, which was started by the US and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable”.
He said the US is not in a hurry to take offensive action because it had already decimated Iran’s military and nuclear programme.
“We’ve knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” he told reporters at his Florida residence.
“You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly,” he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
The Iranian government denied any nuclear work is carried out there.
Earlier on Oct 31, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump had not made a decision about fresh strikes on Iran and that the US would be open to a diplomatic solution.
Iran’s supreme leader on Oct 31 warned the US and Israel against launching a new offensive, following threats that they could resume strikes after crucial elections in both countries.
Trump had previously warned an attack could come after the US midterms this week, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke of a “historic, one-time opportunity” to topple the Iranian government.
The elections in both countries could determine the direction of the conflict, with Israel having voted in a general election on Oct 27 but yet to form a new government.
“Any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response,” Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei told top military commanders, according to a statement.
Khamenei also ordered commanders to update Iran’s target list to include “all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy”.
This was the first reported meeting between Khamenei and the military’s top brass.
He has not been seen publicly since before he took the helm in March, after the killing of his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in US-Israeli strikes.
Rubio warned that “we can achieve military objectives if we seek to”, adding that Trump had not made a decision on any fresh strikes.
Oil price spike
Since the recent outbreak of the war, Tehran has restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries around one-fifth of global oil consumption.
Iran has previously warned that it would also consider severing undersea cables in the Strait of Hormuz.
A ship traversing the strait struck a mine and caught fire, Iranian state television reported on Oct 31.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Oct 30 that three oil tankers had been halted after encountering unspecified “incidents” or hitting mines.
The blockade has caused a spike in global energy prices, making the war unpopular among the US public ahead of the upcoming polls.
Gains for the opposition Democrats could restrict, to an extent, Trump’s ability to enact policy.
Voting in Israel has left Netanyahu’s political camp with the most seats in Parliament but short of a majority, leaving the make-up of the next administration unclear.
‘Flames of war’
Fresh diplomatic efforts are under way to avert any resumption of fighting.
Qatari mediators landed in Tehran on Oct 30, and US Vice-President J.D. Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei.
“I read the letter,” said Rezaei, in a video broadcast on Iranian television. “I haven’t yet responded. Their tone has completely changed,” he added, describing that as “a good sign”, without going into more detail.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there were currently no plans for meetings with US officials.
“Iran’s conditions are clear and consultations regarding them are ongoing among mediators,” he said in an interview with Al Jazeera, according to the state news agency IRNA.
Rezaei insisted Iran would continue to blockade the Strait of Hormuz until its conditions, including releasing frozen assets, were met.
Qatar and Pakistan have been mediating between the warring parties, but the talks have yet to produce a lasting agreement.
Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said any resumption of hostilities would only expand the scope of the war.
“The flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area,” he said on social media.
Araghchi warned on X that there would no longer be any “red lines”. AFP

Poland's Tusk vows Constitutional Tribunal independence as Nawrocki alleges forcible court takeover

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk sought to offer assurances that the country's Constitutional Tribunal will operate in accordance with the law, after President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of the previous hard-right government, accused him of staging a forced takeover of the court.
Late on Friday, the Constitutional Tribunal said its longest-serving judge, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, had suspended Bogdan Swieczkowski, the tribunal's president and an appointee of Tusk's nationalist predecessor, and was now in charge of the court.
The move escalated a battle between Nawrocki and Tusk's pro-European government over control of the judiciary.
"I am certain that the Constitutional Tribunal will function as it should. Also, independently of me and in line with the constitution," Tusk said in a televised speech.
"The task of the executive branch, and therefore mine, is to ensure its safety and working conditions, and I intend to fulfill my duty."
Nawrocki calls off flight mid-air
In a dramatic move, Nawrocki turned back his plane, which he was heading to Senegal on, late on Friday and headed for the court headquarters in central Warsaw, following Swieczkowski's suspension.
Riot police have been guarding the court since Friday afternoon, with several hundred protesters gathered to demand Swieczkowski's reinstatement.
"Tonight, there was a breach of public order in the Republic of Poland and a forcible takeover of a constitutional body," Nawrocki said in a statement read by an aide outside the court early on Saturday.
Nawrocki held political consultations throughout Saturday.
Tusk, writing on X, said his government was seeking to restore the rule of law, which the European Union had accused his predecessors - the Law and Justice Party - of subverting.
"This process is difficult, at times even painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way," he said.
Long-running political dispute
A long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralyzed the institution, with the pro-European government and the nationalist president refusing to recognize appointees put forward by the other side.
The dispute dates back to 2015, when Law and Justice sought to appoint judges to seats already filled by the previous government.
Its nominees gained a majority on the Constitutional Tribunal, while critics at home and abroad said the court no longer met the standards of an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.
After Tusk's coalition took office in 2023, it pledged to restore the rule of law and reform the court, but Law and Justice ally Nawrocki has acted to thwart those efforts since his election as president in 2025.
Earlier this year, Nawrocki refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, while Swieczkowski, a former deputy justice minister in the Law and Justice administration, declined to seat judges elected by the current parliamentary majority.
Last month, parliament appointed Tusk ally Maciej Berek to the tribunal, which critics said undermined the government's stated goal of restoring checks and balances.

Israel needs a bold, fresh approach and unity government in wake of election stalemate - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
04:17:56 UTC
13:17:56 KST

The strong showing of the Arab parties in last week’s election was one of the only bright lights to emerge from the frustrating stalemate that the results produced.
According to the final results, the Joint List received 11 seats and Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, got eight, marking a historic record of 19 seats (up from 10 in the current Knesset) going to parties made up of mostly Arab voters.
Even if the investigation into suspected foreign interference in the election finds evidence of bribery to influence voting in the Arab sector, the extent will likely be marginal, and its impact would be unlikely to affect the results.
The Arab parties’ strong showing has thrown the outcome of the election into murky waters, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc (with 53) nor the opposition bloc, led by Yashar’s Gadi Eisenkot (with 48), having enough support to form a coalition on their own.
There are only slim options available to break the deadlock and prevent another round of elections – a minority opposition government or a centrist unity government.
Arab parties can not be lumped together as monolith
The movement calling for the opposition parties to push for a minority government with its 48 seats, propped up from the outside by the Arab parties’ 19 seats, is highly problematic. What that push doesn’t acknowledge is that just like all the Jewish parties can’t be lumped together, neither can the Arab ones.
Ra’am, which was already part of a government coalition in 2021 and features a Jewish member, Yoav Segalovitz, in its second slot, argues that Arab citizens can use political participation and coalition negotiations to improve their communities and combat the horrific crime level.
The Joint List – consisting of Balad, Ta’al and Hadash – includes anti-Israel extremists, with the parties themselves focused on Palestinian nationalism and calling for a democratic bi-national state to replace Israel. They should never be part of an Israeli government, on the inside or from the outside.
Even if Golan could convince Eisenkot and, somehow, B’Yahad’s Naftali Bennet and Yisrael Beiteinu’s Avigdor Liberman – who have adamantly stated they would not form a coalition with the Arab parties – to agree to bringing in Ra’am, it would only raise the numbers to 56: clearly a non-starter.
Ra’am’s time may come, but in the current constellation, there’s not a place for that party in the government.
That leaves the specter of a unity government. Intense pressure is going to be placed on Netanyahu, Eisenkot, and B’Yahad’s Bennett and Yair Lapid (with 12 seats) to join forces and form a coalition that can agree on most issues.
It would be a bitter pill to swallow for all involved, albeit one that the country desperately needs to prevent another election.
They would be supported from the outside by Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beteinu (with seven seats), creating a stable 67-seat coalition.
There are plenty of obstacles. Netanyahu may think that another election round would tip in his favor, with a smaller turnout and fewer expatriate votes.
Unity government would force Netanyahu to sever alliances with haredi, far-right parties
A unity government would also mean that Netanyahu would have to sever his alliances with the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties and with the far-right parties of Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, whom he last week pledged to keep in a future coalition. He would also have to accept the formation of a state commission of inquiry into October 7.
For their part, Eisenkot and Bennett would have to break campaign promises not to sit with Netanyahu and, for the good of the country, concede that unity is the only way to move forward. Their natural distrust of Netanyahu is warranted, but an arrangement could be worked out that plays to all of the members’ strengths.
Netanyahu, as prime minister, could continue to focus on Israel’s security and the threats emanating from Iran, Hamas, and Hezbollah, and be in charge of foreign policy. There’s not much daylight between any of the parties in regard to that.
Eisenkot and Bennett, in turn, would receive the other vital ministries – Justice, Education, Interior, Internal Security – and begin restoring order to the chaos swirling in the country.
Now is the time for fresh thinking and bold moves. The voters have spoken and given Netanyahu, Eisenkot, and Bennett 60 seats. For the greater good, these leaders must put personalities and egos aside to lead the country into a stable future.

Bolivia declares state of emergency over El Nino weather pattern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
04:04:40 UTC
13:04:40 KST

Bolivia declares state of emergency over El Nino weather pattern
Drought is affecting 78,000 families, and has led to the loss of more than 75,000 cattle, as El Nino is due to peak in late 2026.
Bolivia has declared a nationwide state of emergency to free up resources to deal with the effects of the El Nino weather phenomenon.
Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz signed the decree on Saturday, which also called for further deployments of rescue teams in areas of the country hard hit by flooding and drought.
El Nino will have “very severe impacts in terms of drought and floods”, Paz said, adding that Bolivia needs “the cooperation of all institutions”.
Drought is now affecting 78,000 families in six of Bolivia’s nine departments and has led to the loss of more than 75,000 cattle, according to a government report this week.
Bolivia is also prone to flooding. In December 2025, floods in the Santa Cruz region killed dozens of people.
Neighbouring Chile’s capital, Santiago, recorded the rainiest October ever, while wildfires in Peru killed at least 12 people last month.
El Nino, a global climate phenomenon that occurs roughly every two to seven years, is part of the planet’s natural weather cycle.
During this climate event, warming in the Pacific Ocean brings worldwide changes in winds, pressure, and rainfall patterns, often causing extreme weather.
El Nino’s intensity varies, and its impact changes based on geographic location, but this cycle could be the strongest in recorded history. It is due to peak at the end of 2026, but its impacts could continue well into 2027.
Scientists predict El Nino could cause more than 450,000 deaths globally, with the poorest countries worst impacted.
In early September, the World Meteorological Organization reported a nearly 100 percent likelihood that El Nino will continue through February 2027.

Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport has reclaimed its position as China’s busiest airport, handling more than 67 million passenger trips in the first nine months of 2026 following a major expansion last year, the municipal government announced.

The expansion took half a decade to complete and includes a new third terminal and fifth runway. Authorities projected it would handle 90 million passenger trips this year.

The three agreed to meet to discuss ways to cooperate, according to the report.
Court releases two Arab party activists arrested on suspicion of election bribery
The Be'er Sheva Magistrate's Court rejected a police request to keep a United Arab List activist under house arrest, ruling that he could be released subject only to periodic reporting to authorities. The judge also criticized the lack of progress in the investigation.
A second UAL activist was released to house arrest.
In his ruling, the Judge said no new evidence had emerged since the previous hearing and that the material presented did not justify continued restrictive conditions.
"Several days have passed, and the investigation remains exactly where it was. I also did not receive answers to the questions I asked. The indications do not relate to the respondent and are based solely on a search of his phone. Accordingly, the strength of the suspicion has diminished compared with the first detention extension hearing," he wrote.
The investigation was launched after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's chief of staff passed information to the Police that activists possessed envelopes of cash intended to bribe voters.
Joint List lawmaker tells Jordanian media party seeks cooperation with opposition
Israeli lawmaker Ahmad Tibi, chairman of the Ta'al faction in the Arab-led Joint List party, said in an interview with Jordanian media that the party wants to cooperate with any force working to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Tibi said the party is offering a political safety net to advance the urgent needs of Arab society, including combating illegal weapons and crime organizations, preventing murders, halting demolitions and addressing longstanding infrastructure problems.
The lawmaker said the next Israeli government would not be ideal nor a government of peace, but would be less harmful than the government of Benjamin Netanyahu, Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Meanwhile, Balad MK-elect Bakhar Awawdeh, who is also part of the Joint List, criticized Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot, saying the Joint List "categorically rejects the four principles Eisenkot presented during his election campaign regarding the Palestinian issue" and refuses to accept them as a basis for reaching agreements.
Eisenkot previously said the four principles for joining his coalition are: recognizing Israel as a Jewish, democratic, liberal state; committing to the values of Israel's Declaration of Independence; requiring all citizens to perform military, national or civilian service; and recognizing Hamas as a terrorist group.
Man indicted on incitement charges over calls to kill Netanyahu, public officials
The State Prosecutor's Office filed an indictment and a request to keep the defendant in custody until the end of proceedings at the Petah Tikva Magistrate's Court against a 49-year-old resident of Ein Hahoresh.
The suspect is accused of posting 21 inciting messages on X ahead of the 26th Knesset election, calling for the murder of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, ministers, lawmakers and their supporters. He is also accused of possessing a firearm until recently.
The indictment charges him with 10 counts of incitement to terrorism and 18 counts of incitement to violence.
Israeli Police seek Arab party activists' arrest extended over alleged voter bribery
Israeli police will ask a Be'er Sheva court on Sunday to extend the detention of some of three United Arab Party activists arrested last week on suspicion of attempting to bribe voters, after investigators discovered new evidence on the suspects' phones over the weekend, sources told Haaretz.
Police had initially planned to release the activists to house arrest but changed course following the development in the investigation, a police source said.
The investigation was launched after Ido Norden, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's chief of staff, passed information to Police Commissioner Danny Levy. According to the complaint, the activists possessed envelopes of cash intended to bribe voters in southern Israel to cast their ballots for the party.
Eisenkot bloc parties aim to get a mandate from the president to form a coalition
The four leaders of a bloc of parties led by former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot are set to meet early this week for the first time since Election Day to coordinate their strategy and next steps, chief among them whether to seek the first mandate from President Isaac Herzog to form a government.
Under Israeli law, the president must consult with representatives of the parties elected to the Knesset before assigning a lawmaker the task of forming a government.
Haaretz has learned that over the past few days, one-on-one meetings have taken place between opposition leaders Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett and Yair Golan, but none involving Avigdor Lieberman or all four together.
The assessment among senior sources within the so-called bloc of change is that they will prefer to receive the mandate before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in order to gain control over legislative proceedings in the Knesset.
Herzog calls on party leaders to offer 'creative solutions' to avert another election
Israeli President Isaac Herzog reiterated his call for party leaders to arrive at consultations, set to begin this week at the President's Residence, with "creative solutions to prevent another round of elections."
He made the remarks during a state memorial ceremony for Israel's first president, Chaim Weizmann.
Arab parties open to help replace Knesset speaker, blame Lieberman for gridlock
Following an unprecedented electoral success in last week's election, Israel's Arab parties are weighing their options and signalling their willingness to help Gadi Eisenkot's bloc in replacing Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana while being trepidatious about the prospects of replacing the current government.
With the possibility of repeat elections, United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas fears the party would be unable to recreate its high voter turnout in this election cycle and, according to party sources, sees Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman as the main obstacle to forming a new government.
The leadership of the Joint List is also currently discussing the political options available to them. According to senior officials in the list, the discussions revolve around electing a new Knesset Speaker.

AI-designed virus given to a human patient for the first time
Unknown

AI-designed virus given to a human patient for the first time
The viruses, known as bacteriophages, infect and kill bacteria. Unlike antibiotics, they can target specific bacteria while leaving beneficial bacteria largely untouched.
The treatment was developed by Radical Numerics, a company that uses AI to study and design biological systems. Its AI model, Omnii-1, helped create virus variants selected to target the bacteria causing the patient's infection.
Laboratory tests showed that a mixture of the AI-designed viruses eliminated the patient's bacteria. Doctors then administered the experimental treatment under a special permission process for patients with serious conditions who have no satisfactory treatment alternatives.
The company has not disclosed the patient's condition after treatment or other clinical details to protect their privacy. It also stressed that the treatment has not been approved for wider medical use and that one patient's case cannot establish its safety or effectiveness.
The approach could offer another option for patients whose infections no longer respond to antibiotics. However, researchers must still develop reliable ways to design and test treatments for individual infections before the method can become more widely available.

HANOI, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Vietnam has reduced the special consumption tax on all types of gasoline to zero percent from Sunday through March 31, 2027, under a new government resolution issued on Saturday, local daily VnExpress reported.
Under the special consumption tax law, which took effect on July 1 this year, the tax rates are set at 10 percent for regular gasoline, 8 percent for E5 biofuel and 7 percent for E10 biofuel.
The tax was previously reduced to zero percent from late March to June 2026 to help stabilize the domestic market.
Meanwhile, the environmental protection tax on gasoline and oil products remains at zero Vietnamese dong per liter.
These products are also exempt from value-added tax declaration and payment under a policy extended through the end of 2026, the report said. ■

Bolivia declares state of emergency over El Nino

11:45:16 CST
12:45:16 KST

LIMA, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz signed a decree Saturday declaring a national state of emergency to address the impacts of El Nino.
Paz said he signed the decree to tackle drought affecting several regions of the country and prepare for potential flooding in the coming months.
The president said the measure aims to mobilize financial and human resources, strengthen coordination among government agencies and seek international cooperation to assist affected families and mitigate the impact of climate-related disasters on people's lives and economic activities.
Paz said 63 communities in Bolivia have already been affected by drought, while the livestock sector is also struggling with shortages of animal feed.
Bolivia's Vice Ministry of Civil Defense said Wednesday that nearly 80,000 families across six of the country's nine departments had been affected by water shortages, with drought killing more than 75,000 head of livestock.
El Nino is a climate phenomenon characterized by unusually warm surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, often causing abnormal weather patterns in many parts of the world. ■

Three Chinese-language newspapers in Hong Kong have raised their retail prices by HK$3 (40 US cents) this month, marking the first sector-wide adjustment in two years.
Ming Pao’s increase took effect on Sunday, raising its single-copy price from HK$12 to HK$15, up 25 per cent.
Two financial broadsheets will follow suit on Monday. The Hong Kong Economic Times (HKET) will raise its price from HK$12 to HK$15, while the Hong Kong Economic Journal (HKEJ) will increase its price by 20 per cent from HK$15 to HK$18.

Ukrainian evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky reunite with family
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
03:37:23 UTC
12:37:23 KST

Ukrainian evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky reunite with family
Starved and exhausted residents of Oleshky arrive in Ukraine after months of isolation, but some stay behind.
Starved and exhausted residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky have crossed into Ukraine in a major evacuation operation of civilians, under the first humanitarian truce of its kind in more than four years of Moscow’s war.
The six-day ceasefire covering the town was reached with mediation efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump and help from Pope Leo XIV. It is the longest local pause in fighting since Russia’s full-scale invasion of its neighbour in 2022.
“Ukrainian citizens from Oleshky have crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv region. All of them will receive the assistance they need,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X, thanking the United States and the first lady for mediating.
“Further steps toward de-escalation and real progress toward peace are also needed,” he added.
Evacuees wrapped in blue and yellow Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border and reunited with family members.
Ukrainian officials met the evacuees with posters reading “You’re not alone” and “We embrace with our hearts”, while residents from nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and flashlights to greet them.
Forced to eat grass
Supply routes to Oleshky had been disrupted by fighting and drones. According to some residents, food deliveries were stopped in May, pushing hundreds of people into starvation.
One evacuee, an elderly man in a wheelchair, told the Reuters news agency that he had lost 20kg (44lbs) over the past year, becoming so weak he required hospital treatment.
Another evacuee, Svitlana Yermakova, told Reuters they had to eat grass to survive.
“We chopped grass and squash… just to hold on,” she said, adding that she risked riding by bicycle through minefields to a nearby village to get food for herself and her dog.
To reach Ukrainian-held territory, Oleshky residents had to take a complicated route to leave the devastated town just a few kilometres from the front line.
They first crossed Crimea by bus to the Russian town of Anapa before flying to Belarus, from where they crossed into Ukraine.
Ambulances lined the street, and several large military tents were erected, where hot meals, tea and medical aid were provided.
Russian and Ukrainian officials say the ceasefire in Oleshky has held since Tuesday, allowing them to de-mine the roads and bring food, medicines and other supplies into the town again.
The truce is due to end on Sunday evening.
Some stay behind
Some residents have decided to remain in Oleshky, despite the ongoing lack of gas, electricity and running water.
Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said living conditions in the occupied Oleshky remained difficult, pledging she would continue to work with her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmytro Lubinets, to help those who stayed.
“The mission has come to an end,” she said on Telegram. “We have agreed to carry out regular humanitarian missions, which is a very important step.”
Oleshky had a pre-war population of about 24,000, which plunged to an estimated 1,700 before the evacuation.
Ukrainian officials have not said exactly how many residents were evacuated or how many remained.
Despite the ceasefire in Oleshky, fighting rages on in other parts of the front, with Russia and Ukraine keeping up drone attacks against each other.

Rugby League World Cup: Tonga beats Samoa after Lebanon steals one from France in extra time
Tonga has held on for a 20-18 victory over Samoa in a the Rugby League World Cup contest that more than lived up to the hype.
The clash between Pacific rivals was ultimately decided by goal-kicking as Samoa scored four tries to Tonga's three, but Isaya Katoa's boot (3/3 conversions, 1/1 penalty goal) got the Mate Ma'a over the line and into the semifinals for just the second time.
Tonga will face New Zealand in the first men's semifinal at Newcastle's Hunter Stadium on Saturday, before the Kangaroos take on Samoa in Sydney on Sunday.
Both sides will fancy their chances in the final four after producing a scintillating Test brimming with as much skill as it was physicality.
The teams were deadlocked until some brilliance from Haumole Olakau'atu and Rob Toia saw Tonga strike first after 26 minutes, with Katoa adding a penalty goal soon after.
But, just before half-time, Samoa stayed in the contest with winger Brian To'o's first try off a brilliant Stephen Crichton offload.
Tonga looked the better team to start the second half and got the rewards when Jojo Fifita dove in after a Samoan error, but then came Samoa's reply.
To'o got his second off another brilliant pass, this time from Chanel Harris-Tavita, but it proved to be the five-eighth's last impact on the game as he left the field after grabbing at his hamstring immediately after missing the conversion.
Samoa kept pressing and added tries to Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow and Harris-Tavita's replacement, Ronald Volkman, who potted Samoa's only successful conversion of the match to make it 18-14 heading into the final 10 minutes.
But prop Addin Fonua-Blake was the hero for Tonga as he skipped through a tired Spencer Leniu tackle to score soon after and Katoa's final conversion gave Tonga the decisive lead.
Samoa thought Sua Fa'alogo had pinched the win in the shadows of full-time, but replays showed him just stepping on the touchline before he crossed.
The two-point thriller came after a chaotic golden-point win for Lebanon against France as a group stage littered with enormous blowouts wrapped up with two of the tournament's most exciting showdowns at Western Sydney Stadium.
The two men's games were in stark contrast to the first game of the Parramatta triple header, when the Jillaroos scored a record-breaking 124-6 victory over Wales.
The Australian women will meet Fiji in the semis on Sunday, with New Zealand and Samoa playing the first semifinal on Saturday evening in Newcastle.

Key Event
Kiwis to be without Mulitalo after nasty high tackle
— reporting by AAP
New Zealand have been dealt a blow ahead of their do-or-die Rugby League World Cup semifinal, with Ronaldo Mulitalo handed a one-game ban.
The Kiwis' 78-0 thumping of Fiji on Saturday on the Gold Coast came at a cost, with the star winger sent off for a shoulder charge on Ronald Philitoga in the 52nd minute.
It led to a melee between Fiji and New Zealand players, which culminated in halfback Brandon Wakeham punching Mulitalo in the head. The action earned the Fijian his marching orders as well.
On Sunday, the judiciary deemed Mulitalo's tackle careless and charged him with a grade-two offence.
But much to his relief he was only given a one-game suspension if he takes an early plea, meaning the winger would be eligible to return for the grand final if New Zealand win their semi next Saturday in Newcastle.
Multialo's ban will hurt the Kiwis, because he has scored three tries and been typically busy under the high ball.
New Zealand face a challenge to qualify for the final, playing either Samoa or Tonga.
Wakeham also avoided a heavy ban, handed a one-game suspension, although that won't matter because Fiji have been eliminated from the global showpiece.

Key Event
REPORT: Jillaroos thrash Wales in record-breaking World Cup win
— reporting by AAP
Australia have broken the record for the biggest victory in women's rugby league by scoring 21 tries in a 124-6 thumping of Wales.
Both Jess Sergis and Jaime Chapman, who scored a double-hat-trick at Western Sydney Stadium on Sunday, recorded more running metres than the entire Welsh side.
Winger Chapman's six-try haul equalled the record for most tries in a game for the Jillaroos, who will face Fiji in a semifinal next Sunday at the Sydney Football Stadium.
The one-sided result surpassed France's 116-0 win over Serbia in 2023 as the heaviest victory in the history of the international women's game.
Australian five-eighth Jesse Southwell was almost perfect on the kicking tee, slotting 20 conversions from 21 attempts.
Coupled with a try, the five-eighth's 44 individual points are a new Jillaroos record.
A clunky opening for the Aussies was put to bed when Olivia Kernick crossed for the first points of the afternoon before Chapman burned Wales on the outside for the next two tries — all three scored without Wales touching the ball.
The Welsh did not have another possession for the entire first half as Australia cruised to a 60-0 half-time lead.
Whilst suffering a historic defeat, the Welsh also put on the first points scored against the Jillaroos all tournament.
Wales got themselves on the board in the 59th minute when Tayla Preston grubbered through to Paige Travis for a much-celebrated try.
Sergis had four tries, while Keilee Joseph, Abbi Church and Tamika Upton crossed for doubles.
Kernick, Southwell, Kezie Apps, Sariah Paki, and Keeley Nizza had a try each.
Ruthless Jillaroos dissect dismantling
Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner and captain Isabelle Kelly have spoken to the media after their thumping win over Wales.
Skinner said despite the lopsided nature of the Jillaroos' pool games, there are positive signs for the future of the game.
"I love women's international rugby league, and I think our Pasifika crew are really building nicely to that.
It would be really great to get some investment there in the Northern Hemisphere.
We know what it took Wales to get here and the work that they've done. Our jersey was there not too long ago as well.
So a way that we did that was our [Pacific Championships] concept. We built NRLW as well. That was probably the biggest one for us.
So it'd be really good to see even the Super League to get a little bit more investment and stronger support over there. And I think that'll help that region a lot.
And not taking anything away. This is a World Cup, and Wales has done the work to be here. They've qualified to be here unfortunate result for them today. But we're playing every game to to put our best foot forward to win this thing."
Kelly had similar sentiments.
"I've been really impressed with Samoa this year. I think what they're doing and girls going back and pledging their allegiance to their nations has been incredible.
I think they're leading that, and I think how well they're doing is only going to inspire other girls to do so.
We don't go out there and say that we want to put a certain amount of points on team.
We go out there to be competitive and play the best footy that we can. So I think it's going to take time, but it's definitely starting to happen now."
Key Event
The records which the Jillaroos set today
Highest score in an international match men or women: 124
- The previous high score was a men's Test in 2003, when France defeated Serbia 120-0.
Highest score in a Rugby League World Cup match men or women:124
Previous records were:
- Men's: Australia 110-4 Russia in 2000
- Women's: Australia 92-0 France in 2022, and New Zealand 92-0 France 2026
Largest margin in a women's international: 118
- The previous record was France's 116-0 win over Serbia in 2023
Most tries scored in a women's international: 21
- The previous record was 20 during France's 116-0 win over Serbia in 2023
Most goals kicked in a women's international: 20
- The previous record was 18 during France's 116-0 win over Serbia in 2023
Most individual goals kicked in rugby league international men or women: 20 (Jesse Southwell)
- The previous record was 18 by Ryan Girdler during Australia's 110-4 win over Russia in 2000
Most individual tries in a women's international: 6 (Jamie Chapman)
- Equals the record with Fuarosa Time (New Zealand, 2003), Honey Hireme (New Zealand, 2017), and Julia Robinson (Australia, 2024)
The Cedars fans are here
While most of the build up to this day has focused on Samoa v Tonga, shortly Lebanon and France will face off in the second match of this triple header.
And some of Sydney's huge Lebanese community has turned out on a beautiful afternoon in Parramatta to cheer on the Cedars.
I joined several hundred fans on their march to the stadium, with drummers leading the way, Lebanese music blaring, and lots of dancing and revelry.
It's been great to see how Australia's multicultural communities have embraced this tournament and been able to celebrate their culture through rugby league.

What is celebrated on November 1 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:32:29 EET
12:32:29 KST

What is celebrated on November 1 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On November 1, Ukraine celebrates Social Services Worker’s Day. Around the world, Vegan Day, Eco-Labeling Day, and Ballet Day are observed.
On November 1, Ukraine celebrates Social Worker’s Day, while around the world, under the auspices of international organizations, World Vegan Day, World Ecolabel Day, and World Ballet Day are observed. In the church calendar, according to the new style, Saints Cosmas and Damian of Asia, the Unmercenary Physicians and Wonderworkers, are commemorated, while according to the old style, Saint Joel the Prophet and Saint John of Rila are remembered, UNN reports.
World Vegan Day
A global environmental observance established in 1994 by Louise Wallis, head of The Vegan Society, to mark the 50th anniversary of the organization’s founding in the United Kingdom and the introduction of the term "vegan".
The event opens International Vegan Month and aims to promote a plant-based lifestyle, highlight issues of ethical treatment of animals, minimize the negative impact of livestock farming on climate change, and promote the health benefits of a complete plant-based diet.
World Ecolabel Day
An international environmental observance established by the Global Ecolabelling Network.
The day is intended to raise consumer and business awareness of the importance of ecolabelling, which confirms the environmental safety of products throughout their entire life cycle - from the extraction of raw materials to disposal. The event encourages responsible consumption and the production of goods that do not harm the environment.
World Ballet Day
A global arts celebration established at the initiative of leading opera and ballet theaters around the world, including the Royal Ballet in London.
On this day, leading ballet companies around the world hold hours-long live broadcasts, showing viewers the process of morning barre training, rehearsals for premiere performances, backstage life, and master classes by renowned choreographers, thereby popularizing classical and contemporary ballet.
Social Worker’s Day in Ukraine
An official professional holiday established by a Decree of the President of Ukraine in 1999, observed annually on the first Sunday of November.
The event honors the dedicated work of specialists in social protection authorities, pension services, employment centers, and social services, who provide daily support to low-income groups, people with disabilities, veterans, pensioners, and internally displaced persons.
All Saints' Day
A major holiday in the Western Christian calendar that is an official public holiday in many countries of Europe and Latin America.
Established in the eighth century by Pope Gregory III, the holiday is dedicated to commemorating all canonized saints, as well as martyrs and righteous people whose names have remained unknown to the general public.
Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Saints Cosmas and Damian of Asia, the Unmercenary Physicians and Wonderworkers, and their mother, Saint Theodota. The physician brothers studied the art of medicine and received from God the gracious gift of healing spiritual and bodily ailments through prayer.
They accepted no payment from the sick for their work, following Christ’s command, which is why they were called the Unmercenary Physicians.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate Saint Joel the Prophet - one of the 12 Minor Prophets of the Old Testament, who foretold the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles.
They also remember Saint Martyr Huar and Saint John of Rila - a prominent Bulgarian ascetic and founder of the renowned Rila Monastery.

Hezbollah unlikely to attack Israel in case of US-Iran war unless regime under threat - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
03:24:31 UTC
12:24:31 KST

Hezbollah is not likely to join in if the United States and Iran renew military operations against each other unless Iran’s leadership faces an existential threat, according to a Saturday report from United Arab Emirates state-owned news outlet, The National.
Hezbollah would, according to a senior Lebanese official, join the fight despite its weakened military capacity if the Iranian regime's survival was found to be at stake.
The official said that an explicit red line was crossed in the previous bout, when the Khamenei was killed in a joint US-Israeli strike on February 28.
“We knew earlier this year, when the war in the region first broke out, that Hezbollah would join the fighting if [late Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali] Khamenei were killed,” said the anonymous official. “We even informed the Americans about it.”
KAN news reported last month that Hezbollah terror operatives have maintained their presence in southern Lebanon's pilot zones, gathering intelligence and recuperating their fighting ability.
Hezbollah rearming with Iranian funds
Hezbollah has spent at least three months preparing for a resumption of hostilities with Israel, after receiving an infusion of cash from Iran, according to Lebanese security personnel briefed on its activities.
The terror organization remains committed to attacking Israel and has used a lull in hostilities since June to rearm, with a focus on procuring explosives and producing drones that can be flown into the security zone, two Lebanese security sources told Reuters.
One of the sources, and another close to Hezbollah, said the group had received tens of millions of dollars from Iran to help boost its military capabilities. That is in addition to around $200 million that the terror group previously received from Tehran, which Reuters reported earlier this month.
The group has been restoring command-and-control structures that broke down in key battles, according to one of those sources and three other security officials familiar with the group's operations.
In response to questions from Reuters, Hezbollah's media office rejected the suggestion that its command-and-control systems had broken down.
A US State Department spokesman said Washington would keep strangling Hezbollah's finances through sanctions and other measures. A US Treasury spokesperson said Iran was running out of money and ways to move money.
Trump pulling for Lebanese peace, Israeli withdrawal
US President Donald Trump pledged to secure a full Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon if Beirut agrees to join the Abraham Accords, a senior Gulf diplomatic source told the Lebanese newspaper Ad-Diyar.
The claim was published in an article by Lebanese journalist Nour Naameh amid ongoing diplomatic efforts and concerns in Lebanon over the potential consequences of another military confrontation between the US and Iran.
According to the report, the source described the American promises as official commitments. However, the newspaper provided no documents supporting the claims, did not identify the diplomat or the country he represents, and offered no confirmation from the White House.
The report also did not specify when the commitments were made, who they were communicated to, or whether a timetable had been set for their implementation.
Senior Israeli officials responded to the report by insisting that Israel would not withdraw its forces before Hezbollah was disarmed.
Anna Barsky and Reuters contributed to this report.

Binance’s US$6b crypto heist: Five things to know about North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
03:23:00 UTC
12:23:00 KST

Binance’s US$6b crypto heist: Five things to know about North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers
- North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers are blamed for a record US$6 billion Binance crypto theft. US authorities say the group is linked to Lazarus and Pyongyang’s cyber warfare programme.
- TraderTraitor uses fake job offers and malware to steal data and digital assets. The FBI says hackers have also hit DMM Bitcoin, Atomic Wallet, Alphapo, CoinsPaid and Bybit.
- Stolen crypto is laundered through mixing services and private exchanges, then used for weapons research and procurement. Analysts say cybercrime gives North Korea fast money despite sanctions.
AI generated
SEOUL – North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking group has been blamed by the US authorities for stealing more than US$6 billion (S$7.7 billion) in virtual assets from Binance, in what is believed to be the largest crypto heist in history.
The Oct 29 attack is the latest in a string of high-profile cyberthefts linked to Pyongyang, which has built a formidable hacking operation, generating funds believed to help finance its weapons programme.
Here are five things to know about the group and its place in North Korea’s cyberwarfare programme:
Who are they?
TraderTraitor is the name given to a North Korean hacking operation linked to the broader Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it hacked Sony Pictures in retaliation for The Interview, a satirical film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Pyongyang has invested heavily in developing its cybercapabilities since at least the mid-1990s, building a force that South Korean intelligence estimated in 2024 comprised around 8,400 personnel.
“North Korea has built a capable cyberforce, funnelling many of the country’s top students into computer science and IT training,” the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on its website.
Much of the hacking activity is known to have been directed by Pyongyang’s Reconnaissance General Bureau, its primary foreign intelligence agency.
“The top two students in my class were recruited to the hacking unit,” South Korean MP Park Choong-kwon, who studied at the North’s elite National Defense University before his defection, told AFP in a 2024 interview.
How do they operate?
TraderTraitor actors have been known to pose as recruiters offering lucrative jobs to trick victims into downloading malicious software.
The malware can allow hackers to infiltrate victims’ computer systems and steal sensitive information and digital assets.
In a 2024 heist involving the theft of US$308 million from Japanese cryptocurrency exchange DMM Bitcoin, a North Korean hacker posing as a recruiter on LinkedIn contacted an employee of a separate virtual currency wallet software company.
They sent the employee what appeared to be a pre-employment test, which actually contained a malicious line of code.
That allowed the hacker to compromise their system and impersonate the employee, the FBI said.
What have North Korean hackers done?
High-profile cyberattacks attributed to North Korean hackers include the theft of US$81 million from Bangladesh’s central bank in 2016 and the WannaCry ransomware attack that disrupted computers worldwide in 2017.
In 2022, the US authorities blamed Lazarus-linked hackers for stealing some US$620 million from the Ronin blockchain network.
The FBI subsequently attributed three more cryptocurrency heists in 2023 to TraderTraitor actors, involving the theft of nearly US$200 million from Atomic Wallet, AlphaPo and Coinspaid.
The scale of the thefts increased dramatically in February 2025, when the FBI blamed TraderTraitor for stealing around US$1.5 billion in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit.
“TraderTraitor actors are proceeding rapidly and have converted some of the stolen assets,” the FBI said at the time.
How does North Korea use stolen funds?
The North Korean regime launders stolen cryptocurrency and converts it into cash “through mixing services or private exchanges”, Lim Eul-chul, a professor at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, told AFP.
“The proceeds are then channelled directly into military research, the illicit procurement of weapons components and the defence industry,” he added.
A 2024 United Nations report said proceeds from North Korean cyberattacks “reportedly helped to fund the country’s development of weapons of mass destruction”.
Why cybercrime?
Analysts say Pyongyang’s illicit cyberactivity is driven by its ability to obtain vast sums of money quickly and at “minimal cost”.
“While international sanctions severely restrict North Korea’s ability to earn foreign currency through conventional trade, cybertheft allows it to acquire billions of dollars with minimal personnel and resources,” said Lim.
“Hacking offers Pyongyang a way to obtain funds outside conventional banking channels, taking advantage of the pseudonymous and borderless nature of digital assets to bypass financial restrictions,” he added. 
AFP

Earlier on Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that Trump has not finalised any decision regarding fresh strikes on Iran and emphasised that the United States remains receptive to a diplomatic resolution.
Concurrently, Iran's supreme leader warned Washington and Tel Aviv against initiating fresh bombardments following rhetoric threatening to resume hostilities post-elections.

Kazakhstan established diplomatic relations with all UN member states
Kazakhstan and Nauru have established diplomatic relations, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the press service of the Kazakh Foreign Ministry.
The Joint Communiqué on the Establishment of Diplomatic Relations between the two countries was signed by Kazakhstan's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Kairat Umarov, and the Permanent Representative of the Republic of Nauru to the United Nations, Lara Erab Daniel.
Nauru became the 194th country with which Kazakhstan has established diplomatic ties.
Thus, Kazakhstan has completed the process of establishing diplomatic relations with all United Nations member states, including Nauru, as well as the two Observer States at the Organization. This marks an important milestone in the history of Kazakhstan’s diplomacy.
The signing of the document laid the foundation for the development of bilateral cooperation based on the principles of the UN Charter and international law, including mutual respect for national sovereignty and territorial integrity, equality of States, and non-interference in each other’s internal affairs.
During the meeting, the two sides discussed prospects for developing political dialogue and expanding trade, economic and humanitarian ties. Trade, sustainable development, digitalization and human capital development were highlighted as potential areas of cooperation.
Particular attention was paid to strengthening cooperation within the United Nations and other multilateral forums. The two sides emphasized the importance of maintaining regular dialogue on current issues on the international agenda and developing partnerships between Kazakhstan and countries of the Pacific region.
The establishment of diplomatic relations with Nauru reflects Kazakhstan’s consistent policy of expanding international cooperation, strengthening friendly ties and fostering constructive dialogue with countries around the world.
Earlier, Kazakhstan proposed closer coordination among 5 nuclear-weapon-free zones and Mongolia at the forum on “Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zones: From the Comprehensive Study to Practical Cooperation" at the United Nations.

Economic Watch: China's "super seller" role expands, benefiting more consumers, businesses
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:48:50 CST
11:48:50 KST

GUANGZHOU, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese-made heat pump that could save European households hundreds of euros a year. Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered teaching tools reaching classrooms in Vietnam. Industrial machinery helping developing countries expand production.
The 140th China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, is offering a window into how China's exports are giving consumers more choices and businesses access to technology and equipment.
When Gree Electric Appliances first attended the Canton Fair 31 years ago, it mainly exported household air conditioners. This year, the Zhuhai-based company is showcasing low-carbon energy solutions covering home appliances, industrial equipment, energy storage and cold-chain technologies.
One heat pump system designed for the European market can cut annual electricity use by about 50 percent. At an average European Union electricity price of 0.3 euros per kilowatt-hour, it could save a household in a 150-square-meter home around 800 euros a year, or more than 1,000 euros in countries such as Germany, according to Gree.
The company's products now reach more than 200 countries and regions, serving around 600 million consumers.
"For Gree, the story of going global is very simple," said Zhu Lei, Gree's vice president and chief marketing officer. "We have one fundamental goal -- to meet consumers' needs and provide them with the best products and services."
The potential savings for European households illustrate what Chinese Premier Li Qiang described as the benefits of China's role as a "super seller."
"As a 'super seller,' China brings benefits to its trading partners," Li said at the Canton Fair's opening ceremony.
He said quality and affordable Chinese goods had raised consumers' actual purchasing power, improved their quality of life, and helped countries strengthen their capacity for industrial development.
China exported 23.2 trillion yuan (about 3.46 trillion U.S. dollars) worth of goods in the first nine months of 2026, up 16.4 percent from a year earlier, according to the General Administration of Customs.
Its exports range from 300,000-tonne oil tankers and industrial robots to miniature ice makers and portable filming equipment. China's manufacturing supply chains allow businesses to turn ideas into customized products.
From 2012 to 2025, China exported about 39 billion U.S. dollars' worth of textile machinery to developing countries, helping some countries in Southeast and South Asia become major textile producers and exporters, according to Chinese industry figures.
Marking its 70th anniversary this year, the Canton Fair reflects how China's exports have evolved, offering a wider range of products and technologies to consumers and businesses worldwide.
At the first fair in 1957, agricultural products and handicrafts, including silk, tea and porcelain, accounted for 63.9 percent of export transactions by value. Machinery and electronic products became the largest product category in 1999. Today, consumer electronics, AI-powered devices and energy storage equipment are among the products on display.
More than 32,000 Chinese and overseas companies are participating in this year's fair, held in three phases in Guangzhou from Oct. 15 to Nov. 4. The first phase drew a record 189,000 overseas buyers from 214 countries and regions.
About 64 percent of exhibitors have adopted technologies such as the industrial internet and AI. New products account for 23.2 percent of exhibits and green products for 26 percent, both record shares.
At the fair's new energy vehicle exhibition area, GAC Group showcased models that included the AION i60, aimed at overseas consumers concerned about travel costs and driving range.
Wei Haigang, president of GAC International, said the company is expanding overseas while building charging and energy storage networks to support local customers.
Chinese companies are also bringing technology and services to overseas schools. At the booth of Guangzhou-based CVTE, AI-powered displays turn abstract lessons into visual presentations. Another AI system helps teachers prepare lesson plans, slides and classroom activities.
Xiao Hang, president of CVTE's overseas business group, recalled a project in Vietnam in 2024. Rather than simply installing equipment, the company sent a seven-member team to work with local users for three days.
"When the children came out of their classrooms, they gathered around us, greeting us in English, Vietnamese and even imperfect Chinese, eager to give us high-fives," Xiao said. "At that moment, we realized this was not just a business, but also a responsibility."
Pascal Lamy, former director-general of the World Trade Organization, said the Canton Fair had become a major meeting point for Chinese producers and businesses worldwide, connecting "supply and demand, producers and consumers, ideas and markets."
Lamy said China had been one of the greatest beneficiaries of the opening of the world economy over recent decades, while also contributing to the global economy through production, innovation, investment and trade. ■

Government will not promise net savings in budget update, despite inflation pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
02:48:18 UTC
11:48:18 KST

Government will not promise net savings in budget update, even as rate rise looms
In short:
The finance minister and treasurer have refused to confirm December's budget update will contain more savings than new spending, even as pressure mounts on the federal government to tighten its belt.
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher told ABC Insiders pressures on the budget were growing, and decisions were still being made for the mid-year update.
What's next?
The mid-year economic and fiscal outlook will be delivered in December.
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says growing pressures on the federal budget mean the government cannot promise it will find overall savings in its December update, even as Australians brace for another interest rate rise amid ongoing high inflation.
On Wednesday Treasurer Jim Chalmers also refused to commit to net savings in the mid-year budget update following a worse-than-expected inflation figure of 4.3 per cent over the year to September, which lifted expectations of another rate hike when the Reserve Bank meets on Tuesday.
The finance minister told ABC Insiders despite pressure being put on the government to rein in its spending, she would not pre-commit to overall savings.
"I can't, I don't want to pre-empt the [Expenditure Review Committee] process. We will go through that ... but there is enormous effort being placed, particularly by Jim and myself on the savings side," Senator Gallgher said.
"We are doing a lot of work on the savings side but I can’t get ahead of decisions that haven’t been made yet."
The minister rejected suggestions the pressure to find savings was causing tension inside cabinet, saying it was healthy for ministers to have "robust" debate and bring different perspectives.
Senator Gallagher added that the government's record in each of its previous budgets and mid-year updates had been to deliver overall improvements to the budget, and that in recent budgets its policy decisions had also found more savings than new spending.
The Reserve Bank's chief economist said last week that government spending remained a contributor to ongoing inflation, even if the government points to the war in Iran as the "primary driver".
The treasurer has previously warned that the cost of borrowing would add billions of dollars in additional costs to the budget, as long-term expectations that global interest rates would remain higher for longer were priced into bonds.
Senator Gallagher said other pressures on the budget were also growing, including in health and aged care.
She said the government's spending measures in those pressure areas were necessary to rescue a Medicare system "in freefall" and clear processing backlogs for veterans.
"If you go back to … the Howard era, you know, they were not dealing with AUKUS, they were not dealing with aged care," Senator Gallagher said.
"They weren't dealing with Medicare falling over there, all of these pressures that are coming. So there has to be some acknowledgement of that. We are living in a different world."
The government maintains that the budget is helping to tackle inflation.
However ahead of his departure to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese acknowledged that the Reserve Bank only had a single "blunt instrument" in the inflation fight.
The remaining levers to reduce demand in the economy rest with federal and state governments.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor told radio station 2GB that the government could do more to avert further rate rises.
"The government can commit tomorrow to take pressure off interest rates and inflation, that would send a strong signal to the Reserve Bank [that] they don't need to raise," Mr Taylor said.
"But they won't do it."
The Reserve Bank's chief economist Sarah Hunter said last week that state and federal government spending was "definitely" contributing to demand pressures in the economy, before adding that it was not the RBA's place to advice government on its spending.
Frontbench minister Murray Watt told News24 demand growth in the economy tripled in the private sector last financial year, while government demand growth halved.
"The substantial portion of the growth in spending in the economy is happening in the private sector rather than in the public sector. Now, I'm not being critical of people who are spending money, going to restaurants, buying a car, whatever it is that they're they're spending money on. But that's where most of the spending [growth] is happening," Senator Watt said.
"And that, of course, is contributing to inflation, as is fuel prices."

Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
02:44:28 UTC
11:44:28 KST

Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
- Date:
- October 31, 2026
- Source:
- INRAE - National Research Institute for Agriculture, Food and Environment
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.
- Share:
Trees have a remarkable ability to sense their own shape and adjust their growth to stay upright. This awareness of body position, known as proprioception, was once thought to exist only in animals. However, in 2012, researchers working with INRAE demonstrated that plants also possess this ability (Bastien R. et al., PNAS).
This internal sense allows plants to monitor their posture and make adjustments that help them grow as straight as possible (Moulia et al., Science). Although scientists had established that plants could detect their own shape, the biological processes responsible for turning that information into physical movement remained a mystery.
How Scientists Isolated Trees' Hidden Sense
Plants use several kinds of information to guide their growth. They respond to gravity, detect the direction of sunlight, and monitor the shape and position of their own stems. To understand how this internal sense works independently, researchers needed to eliminate the directional signals provided by gravity and light.
They developed an unusual experimental system designed to isolate proprioception. Young trees were placed on a horizontal platform that rotated around its axis inside a sphere illuminated equally from every direction. The rotating platform prevented the trees from receiving a consistent directional signal from gravity, while the surrounding light eliminated cues about which way they should grow.
This arrangement allowed the researchers to investigate how trees respond to their own shape without relying on the usual environmental signals that influence their growth.
The Muscle-Like Wood That Helps Trees Straighten Themselves
The experiment began with young poplar trees positioned horizontally. As the trees grew, their stems gradually curved upward, bringing their tops back toward a vertical position.
This response depends on a specialized type of wood called tension wood. Unlike ordinary wood, tension wood can generate pulling forces as it develops. When it forms along the upper side of a stem, it acts much like a contracting muscle, pulling the stem upward and causing it to bend.
After approximately ten days, once the trees had developed a noticeable curve, researchers moved them into the experimental apparatus. Over the following weeks, something remarkable happened. Instead of maintaining their curved shapes, the stems slowly straightened until they became nearly straight again.
To determine what caused this change, the team examined the structure of the wood that developed during the straightening process.
They found that the original tension wood, which had formed along the upper side of the stems and pulled them upward, stopped developing once the experimental system was activated. At the same time, identical tension wood began forming on the opposite side.
This newly formed wood appeared to act like an opposing muscle, producing a pulling force in the other direction. As the forces worked against each other, the curved stems gradually returned to a straight shape.
The production of tension wood involves a complex sequence of biological events controlled at the cellular level. The findings indicate that a tree's internal sense of its own shape helps regulate this process, determining where tension wood develops to correct its posture.
A Surprising Discovery About How Trees Control Their Shape
Previously, scientists believed that tension wood formed only on the upper side of stems, where it helped pull them upward. This is particularly noticeable near the bases of trees growing on mountain slopes, where trunks often need to curve to maintain an upright position.
The new research reveals that tension wood has a more versatile role. It can develop on opposing sides of a stem and generate forces in different directions, functioning much like the opposing muscle groups animals use to maintain posture and control movement.
This discovery suggests that trees possess a sophisticated system for coordinating their growth. They combine information about their surroundings (such as light and gravity) with an internal awareness of their own shape. By processing these signals, they can regulate where tension wood develops and adjust their posture accordingly.
Why This Discovery Matters for Forests and Agriculture
The ability to sense and correct their own shape is especially important when trees encounter environmental disturbances. Powerful storms, landslides, and other extreme events can bend or displace trees, making the capacity to regain an appropriate posture essential for their resilience.
Understanding this mechanism could become increasingly valuable as climate change exposes forests to more extreme conditions.
The findings also have practical implications for forestry and agriculture. By identifying plants with particularly effective proprioception, scientists may be able to select varieties that grow straighter, maintain better posture, and produce higher-quality wood.
In agriculture, the same knowledge could help researchers develop cereal crops that are less likely to fall over before harvest. This problem, known as lodging, can cause significant yield losses when crops collapse toward the end of the growing season.
The discovery could also improve timber quality. Poorly coordinated tension wood formation can create excessive internal stresses in trees, potentially affecting the properties of the wood they produce.
Bruno Moulia, INRAE research director, explained:
"What we have uncovered is a genuine sensorimotor loop operating in the woody parts of trees! Poor coordination in the successive activation of tension wood results in excessive internal tension, which can affect wood quality. These findings therefore reshape more applied research aimed at improving wood quality... and at obtaining trees that are as straight and as relaxed as possible, whatever life throws at them!"
The research also highlights the importance of combining expertise from different scientific fields to understand the complex ways plants interact with their environment.
Félix Hartman, INRAE research engineer, emphasized the collaborative effort behind the discovery:
"Revealing the remarkable capabilities of trees requires a great deal of ingenuity. In this project, we achieved it by bringing together researchers from different disciplines, with complementary skills and perspectives. This requires time and perseverance, but these interdisciplinary discoveries show that the effort is worthwhile."
Story Source:
Materials provided by INRAE - National Research Institute for Agriculture, Food and Environment. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Alexandre Caulus, Félix P. Hartmann, Éric Badel, Stéphane Ploquin, Nicole Brunel‐Michac, Julien Ruelle, Mélanie Decourteix, Bruno Moulia. Proprioception drives tension wood formation for autotropic straightening and postural control in trees. New Phytologist, 2026; DOI: 10.1111/nph.71238
