Binance says 90% of losses from $6.3bn hack covered as FBI says North Korea behind attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
02:41:34 UTC
11:41:34 KST

The cryptocurrency exchange Binance has started to allow its customers to withdraw their funds from the platform, as it recovers from a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack.
The exchange was hit by the theft on Thursday, which has since been described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.
Binance initially froze withdrawals as it investigated the breach, but on Sunday announced that it had began a phased reopening after 2pm Singapore time.
The first phase will allow people who hold the ethereum, USDT and USDC tokens on the ethereum blockchain to withdraw their funds, as well as some others held on the BNB Smart Chain blockchain.
The platform said it had replenished 90% of the amount stolen. The remaining 10% of tokens were less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, the company said in a post on X on Saturday.
Richard Teng, Binance’s co-chief executive, said separately that the company was “committed to covering the remaining 10%” and that users would not bear the financial impact of the hack.
It came as the FBI on Saturday confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
“The Federal Bureau of Investigation is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6bn in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29,” the law enforcement agency said in a statement.
The FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralised finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors” were “using to launder these stolen assets”.
Teng said on Friday that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate.
Binance said it had set aside about $6.34bn of company funds to cover the losses. “Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said.
The money spent rebuying tokens came from using part of its $1bn Secure Asset Fund for Users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company’s own corporate treasury, it said on X.
The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.
Bitcoin plunged nearly 5% after the news of the hack, while ethereum dropped nearly 6% and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%.
The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea – which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programmes – to find illicit means to capture revenue.

Is the bra the new T-shirt? The fashion trend taking over runways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
02:33:45 UTC
11:33:45 KST

Would you leave the house wearing nothing but a bra on top? I imagine the answer is no, but in the fashion world, our everyday habits — such as wearing a shirt — aren't always what dictate the trends. In other words, bras have been a hot fashion trend for several seasons now. So hot, in fact, that the bra has gone from a hidden undergarment to a legitimate piece of outerwear in its own right.
For proof, look no further than the proliferation of bras at the latest international fashion month, where designers unveiled their spring 2027 collections. At Prada, for example, more than a third of the women's looks on the runway consisted of a skirt and bra. At Miu Miu, designed by the same woman, Miuccia Prada, tiny sports bras served as tops. The trend was also prominent at Simone Rocha, Fendi, Tom Ford, Erdem and seemingly everywhere else, as well as on various celebrities walking the red carpet.
British Vogue recently devoted an article to the phenomenon under the headline "Bras are the new T-shirts." The article suggested that, as with almost everything else, the Kardashian-Jenner sisters are partly to blame, along with stars such as Dakota Johnson. They have made revealing outfits so commonplace that the look has filtered down to fashion designers.
Still, there's a difference between how a bra looks on celebrities and models and how it looks on an ordinary woman. Or, as Vogue put it: "Can anyone who isn't Gigi Hadid wear this?" The magazine therefore recommends embracing the trend with some restraint, such as wearing a bra under a sheer shirt or blazer.
The trend has also taken hold in Israel, where it repeatedly makes headlines and draws disapproving comments online. For example, model Yael Shelbia attended actress Omer Nudelman's wedding wearing a bra-like top, singer Agam Buhbut performed in a bra-inspired dress and Inbal Eldan, a contestant on the Israeli version of "Big Brother," filmed herself walking around a shopping mall wearing a bra. More recently, a music video featuring Anna Zak and Eden Golan embracing while wearing bras surfaced online. And these are just a few examples.
As far as I'm concerned, every woman should do what feels right for her. I have no problem with bras, nor do I have a problem with ultra-modest clothing. Every woman is entitled to her own worldview and sense of style.
Let's put it this way: I much prefer the women wearing bras to those attacking them on social media. The problem begins precisely when people try to tell us what we should wear and how we should look.
We live in a time when we have choices, including, in my view, the freedom to make our own decisions about our bodies, what we wear and how we live our lives.

Cost of countering aerial threats should be proportionate to threat – defense industry representative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
02:32:00 UTC
11:32:00 KST

Cost of countering aerial threats should be proportionate to threat – defense industry representative
CEO of Ukrainian defense-tech company UNWAVE Taras Bublyk said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“One of the main challenges is the price imbalance between the threat and the means of countering it. If an expensive missile is used every time to destroy a relatively inexpensive drone, maintaining such protection over the long term will be difficult. The cost of countering a threat should be proportionate to the cost of the threat itself… Countermeasures must be affordable, produced in sufficient quantities, and operate as a single system,” Bublyk stressed.
He sees the solution in a multi-layered defense system combining detection, electronic warfare, interceptor drones, physical protection measures, and conventional air defense. This approach makes it possible to select an effective and economically viable way of countering a specific threat. At the same time, different means should complement one another so that where electronic suppression or a cheaper interceptor is sufficient, there is no need to expend an expensive missile.
The Ukrainian defense industry representative believes that for Europe, this means the need to invest both in the technologies themselves and in their integration and scaling up of production. The mere availability of advanced weapons does not in itself guarantee readiness to use them effectively, he noted. Increased European defense budgets are a positive step, but there is a risk that a significant share of these funds will be directed toward solutions developed without taking into account the experience of the current Russian-Ukrainian war.
“Because of this, there is a risk of investing in expensive systems that may prove insufficiently effective… European countries need to learn how to integrate drones, electronic warfare systems, and other technologies into specific combat missions, taking into account Ukraine’s experience,” Bublyk said.
He noted that a significant portion of critical infrastructure in Europe is currently insufficiently prepared to respond to modern drone threats. Even at facilities where certain protection systems have already been installed, they have often been developed without taking into account the practical experience of using such technologies in combat conditions. Ukraine, which already has practical experience in deploying such solutions in combat, is ready to help European countries incorporate this experience into the development of their own protection systems.
“European countries should make use of Ukraine’s experience in protecting critical infrastructure and move from planning to the creation and deployment of relevant systems now,” Bublyk said.
At the same time, he drew attention to shortcomings in Europe’s regulatory framework. Today, many European countries have restrictions on the use of electronic warfare systems, including their operation in certain frequency bands. Rules governing the use of such systems in the event of a real threat need to be established, while the responsible agencies should have clear powers and rapid-response mechanisms so that valuable time is not lost obtaining permits after a threat has already been detected.
As reported, in early October, Ukraine and Germany signed an agreement to deepen cooperation in countering drones, under which Germany is to make greater use of Ukraine’s experience.

FBI blames North Korea for record $6.3bn crypto heist from Binance
Crypto firm Binance says it has covered 90 percent of losses from the multibillion-dollar hack.
The FBI has linked North Korea to the theft of a record $6.3bn in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance.
Malicious actors from North Korea were observed laundering the stolen assets by converting them primarily into the cryptocurrency Ethereum, the FBI said in a statement on Saturday.
The US agency blamed the operation specifically on a group called TraderTraitor, the same group blamed for a $1.5bn theft from the Bybit platform in February last year.
According to the statement, the assets are expected to be “further laundered” in stages.
The FBI called on virtual asset service providers to block transactions being used in the latest laundering operation, providing the suspected digital addresses to watch for.
In a separate statement on Saturday, Binance said it has replaced 90 percent of the amount stolen by using company money to buy new tokens.
The remaining 10 percent consists of less liquid tokens, meaning they may take longer to buy, it added.
“We will continue to buy the remaining relevant token assets… until the covered amount reaches 100 [percent] for all tokens. Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users,” the company said on X.
The money spent re-buying tokens came from a $1bn Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a Bitcoin reserve fund Binance holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund and the company’s corporate treasury.
Crypto prices fell on Friday, as Binance, which runs the world’s largest crypto exchange, sought to reassure customers their funds were safe.
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on Friday that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it hard to trace and investigate.
After the hack, the exchange stopped allowing customers to withdraw their funds.
Binance said later on Saturday that it was on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday.
Binance also announced the publication of a new proof-of-reserves snapshot, allowing users to independently verify that their assets were backed at a minimum 1:1 ratio.

From fridges to nuclear power plants, hackers are gaining control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
02:13:34 UTC
11:13:34 KST

In an unstable world super-charged by AI, hacking is the new war front
In the year 2000, on the sleepy banks of the Maroochy River on Queensland's Sunshine Coast, a new water treatment facility was experiencing technical difficulties.
Radio communications to wastewater pumps were not working, and the alarms designed to alert staff were not sounding.
Over a three-month period, more than 800,000 litres of untreated sewage was released into local waterways.
At first, council staff attributed the pump malfunctions to growing pains at the new plant.
But the real culprit? A hacker.
In the same year Australia cemented itself on the global stage hosting the first Olympics of the new millennia, it also secured its spot in the world of cybersecurity as the home of the first attributable case of operational technology hacking, becoming a case study used by engineers, academics and governments to this day.
Cyber-retribution a new war front
Operational technology (OT) is the hardware and software that monitors and controls physical machines.
OT is everywhere and is used to operate critical infrastructure such as power plants, conveyor belts, traffic lights, air traffic control systems and water treatment plants.
The Maroochy incident was 26 years ago, but OT hacking is now on the rise and will likely be supercharged by AI.
Last month, hackers remotely raised fridge and freezer temperatures across hundreds of French supermarkets.
In July, 30 water systems across the United States were attacked, consistent with methods used by an Iranian-backed hacking group the CyberAv3ngers.
In June, a cyber security incident brought Australia's second-largest raw sugar producer to a halt, shutting down milling and cane haulage. A Russian-speaking group called The Gentleman claimed responsibility.
In March, the Handala Hack group, also said to be operating under the Iranian government, claimed responsibility for cyber attacks against medical equipment supplier Stryker.
Since US President Donald Trump launched the war in Iran, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has issued warnings regarding "ongoing Iranian-affiliated cyber targeting".
In other words: cyber-retribution.
Hacking has become targeted, a new war front for enemies across the globe to attack each other.
The Stryker hack was in retribution for the bombing of an elementary school in southern Iran.
Although the hackers targeted a US company, the attack put Australian hospitals on alert because it remotely wiped associated devices around the world.
Such attacks have obvious financial impacts, but as the technology powering them becomes more sophisticated, the scope and severity of the risks increase.
And as the world destabilises, incentives for hackers to cause harm, including the risk to human life, also increases.
Hacking goes nuclear
In 2025, hackers sponsored by China breached more than 400 agencies across the globe via Microsoft's SharePoint.
One of the agencies was the US National Nuclear Security Administration, the organisation responsible for managing the United States's nuclear stockpile, as well as the nuclear power plants on warships and submarines.
Although an IT hack, not an OT attack, Raji Rajagopalan, a senior fellow at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, explained that such breaches could be used to conduct an OT hack later.
"They get into a system, lie dormant for a very long time and when there is an opportunity, get into sensitive areas," Dr Rajagopalan said.
"That could create lots of different nuclear incidents that could be really disastrous from a humanitarian perspective."
One protection that nuclear facilities use to prevent such a disaster is an air gap, meaning that administrative systems are largely disconnected from operating systems.
However, Dr Rajagopalan said the assumption that these separations were watertight was not entirely true.
"There are digital upgrades, remote monitoring. All of these always compromise that air gap," she said.
A hacker remotely triggering a nuclear meltdown may sound like the work of Hollywood, but one known incident proved it is closer to reality than fiction.
Stuxnet is a highly sophisticated computer worm.
It was designed as part of Operation Olympic Games, a secret US-Israeli joint cyber-sabotage campaign — although the US government has never publicly taken responsibility.
Stuxnet was unleashed on the Natanz Iranian nuclear facility, where it lay undetected between 2009-2010.
The worm targeted the centrifuges used to enrich uranium, causing them to spin out of control until they broke. It was also sophisticated enough to hide what it was doing.
Stuxnet destroyed at least 1,000 centrifuges at Natanz and set Iran's nuclear program back by about a year.
Such attacks make global headlines when they are discovered, causing policymakers to make sweeping statements at press conferences.
But, Dr Rajagopalan said, political momentum was often lost after the fact.
"Somehow it seems all very theoretical, sounds very futuristic,"
she said.
"You don't want to scare people away, but at the same time, people need to understand that there are consequences to these attacks, that these attacks are real."
Critical infrastructure a sitting duck
Why is OT so vulnerable? How is it that the most critical infrastructure in the world is so at risk of being hacked?
UQ cyber security expert Ryan Ko said the main issue with OT was that much of it had been installed 20 to 30 years ago before existing knowledge of the latest cyber threats.
The old legacy systems were increasingly connected to the internet, he said, and every piece of critical infrastructure connected with OT was at risk.
And with the rise of AI, the scope of cyber-attacks had "changed drastically".
"It is now easier for an adversary to automatically detect a previously unknown vulnerability," Professor Ko said.
OpenAI's rogue agent Medicare data portal hack raised significant alarms for the Australian government.
Although not an OT attack, the incident highlighted how AI can efficiently find weaknesses that in other circumstances could be leveraged by bad faith actors.
Domestically, the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) provides frameworks for governments and businesses to boost their cyber-defences against what it has described as "increasingly complex and persistent threats".
"Critical infrastructure and operational technology are attractive targets for state-sponsored cyber actors, cyber criminals and hacktivists," an ASD spokesperson said.
Can we stop OT spiralling out of control?
Dr Rajagopalan said as OT hacking incidents increased, the possibility of inadvertent incidents spiralling out of control also increased.
It is a scenario where neither side may want to engage in "big open-ended conflict, but things going out of control".
In a fracturing world, not only does the current geopolitical climate increase the incentive for enemies to attack one other, but it also limits the ability for allies to work with each other.
"We don't see the major powers coming together, discussing and debating these issues in full earnest,"
she said.
One solution for Australia, Dr Rajagopalan said, could be partnering with multilateral organisations such as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations over major powers.
"Bring together smaller groupings of countries who have similar or like-minded interests and who have a certain amount of appeal to international law," she said.

When someone does something terribly wrong, we are outraged. We want to express our disapproval, our…
Unknown

When someone does something terribly wrong, we are outraged. We want to express our disapproval, our displeasure, and perhaps even our anger. We want everyone to know that we condemn these actions. We want them to understand that we will not stand for what has been done, as it was entirely unacceptable.
At the same time, there are others who disagree with our judgment. They see what was done not as wrong, but as correct and good. These others also become targets of our ire. We cannot understand how they could think that wrongdoing is actually rightdoing, which outrages us further. Two camps then form, each deeply opposed to the other. There is no trust between the groups, for each side feels their values are superior. Both sides think that the other is deluded by their beliefs.

Rick Sanchez reports from Alyoshki Russia-Ukraine truce zone (VIDEO)
RT’s Rick Sanchez has traveled to the frontline town of Alyoshki in Kherson Region to witness firsthand a rare local ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine aimed at evacuating civilians and delivering humanitarian aid to residents.
An estimated 1,500 to 2,000 people had been trapped in the town on the left bank of the Dnieper River, opposite the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, amid Kiev’s repeated drone strikes and the airdropping of mines on supply roads.
More than 750 civilians have since been evacuated under the six-day truce around Alyoshki, arranged with the assistance of US First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV. The ceasefire is set to expire on Sunday evening.
Officials from both sides oversaw the evacuations, with civilians offered the choice of relocating to another city in Russia or traveling to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus. Evacuees and Russian officials interviewed by RT described months of shortages and the hardships of living under shelling they attributed to Ukrainian forces.
The host of Sanchez Effect compared the town’s destruction to that seen during World War II, pointing to what he described as an extraordinarily high concentration of mines of various types scattered throughout the area.
However, Sanchez expressed cautious optimism as he watched Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova work alongside her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmitry Lubinets.
“Could the deal that they worked out for the town of Alyoshki end up being the very thing that sparks some kind of a hopeful sign that maybe both sides can come together in a bigger way?” Sanchez said. He added that some observers believe the truce could pave the way for a broader peace agreement.
Sanchez also suggested that Russia’s drone capabilities may have made Ukraine more willing to “sit down with the Russians.”
Lantratova said she and Lubinets had appealed to Melania Trump to help coordinate further humanitarian missions. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said earlier that, if successful, the Alyoshki truce could serve as a precedent for future agreements.

Protesters at Saturday’s rally told the AFP news agency this may be the “last chance for real change” and that Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, is a “great manipulator”.
Main opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has previously ruled out forming a coalition with Israel’s Arab parties, but a deadlock in Tuesday’s elections means siding with the parties could help him form a government.
“People really want this vote for change to work out, and they believe that… Gadi Eisenkot and other leaders of the Jewish-Israeli parties need to listen to their voice,” Al Jazeera correspondent Nour Odeh said from Ramallah on Saturday.
Counter-protesters also showed up to Saturday’s demonstrations, with Netanyahu supporters seen shouting their own demands that “Israel should not have a government with so-called terrorists”, Odeh said.
Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday’s elections, while Eisenkot’s won 48, meaning neither side can form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament alone.
Israel’s three Arab-led parties won 19 seats, having made significant gains in Tuesday’s election.
Nearly 840,000 people voted for Ra’am and the Joint List, a coalition of three Arab-led parties, a 64 percent increase from the last elections in 2022, according to the Central Election Committee.
The Arab electoral success means a coalition with Eisenkot would provide a comfortable majority of 67. However, for many in Israel, the idea of siding with Arabs is politically unpalatable.
Netanyahu has accused Palestinian-Israeli parties of “stealing” the polls and accepting funding from Qatar to do it. Qatar has rejected the allegations, calling it a disinformation campaign.
Odeh said that Israeli right-wing circles have described “the historic turnout of Palestinian Israelis as electoral terrorism, equating it to the October 7th attack”, when Hamas-led fighters stormed southern Israel, killing more than 1,200 people and taking hundreds captive.
“Palestinian-Israeli votes and voices” are under attack because they have a “prominent position” in deciding whether Eisenkot can form a government, she added.

Sri Lanka's major blackout triggered by sudden power plant trip: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:00:38 CST
11:00:38 KST

COLOMBO, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka's island-wide power outage on Oct. 17 followed the sudden disconnection of 187 megawatts (MW) of generation capacity at the Norochcholai Lakvijaya Power Plant, according to a preliminary investigation report submitted by the National System Operator (NSO), the country's national grid operator.
According to the report submitted to the Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka, the national power grid collapsed within 4.1 seconds of the initial disturbance, despite the activation of all five stages of the Under Frequency Load Shedding system designed to prevent widespread outages.
The protection mechanism disconnected 449.2 MW of electricity supply, equivalent to 39.6 percent of the 1,135 MW being generated immediately before the incident. However, the measures failed to stabilize the grid.
The disruption began at approximately 11:43 a.m. local time, when 187 MW of electricity generated by the first unit of the Norochcholai plant was disconnected within 450 milliseconds, causing the system frequency to fall to 48.75 hertz.
Protection systems subsequently shut down additional generating units at Norochcholai and several hydropower plants, including Victoria, Kotmale, Randenigala, Samanalawewa and Laxapana.
The NSO said restoration operations began immediately after the collapse, with electricity supplies gradually restored through four main networks covering the Mahaweli, Laxapana, Samanalawewa/Southern and Colombo systems.
The restoration process involved the Kotmale, Victoria, New Laxapana, Wimalasurendra, Samanalawewa, Kukuleganga and Kelanitissa power plants. All major substations were restored by 4:58 p.m., approximately five hours and 15 minutes after the outage began. ■

Taiwan says China harassing shipping with east coast patrol
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
03:00:27 CET
11:00:27 KST

TAIPEI, Nov 1 (Reuters) - China’s Coast Guard is harassing shipping with its latest patrol off Taiwan’s east coast and trying to exert a fictional jurisdiction, the Taiwanese Coast Guard said, adding it had sent its own ships to keep watch.
China, which views Taiwan as its own territory, has stepped up activity off the island’s east coast since June with regular coast guard patrols. Officials in Taiwan, which rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims, say they believe China is practising for a potential maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets.
Taipei regards the area off its east coast as critical to wartime supply routes from allies in the event of a blockade or conflict. China recognises no claims of sovereignty by Taiwan.
Responding late Saturday to China’s announcement of its latest east coast patrol, Taiwan’s Coast Guard said two Chinese ships were involved and it had sent its own forces to monitor.
Chinese state media showed video of one of its ships broadcasting a radio message that it was carrying out law enforcement and offering help should any be needed.
It did not say who the message was broadcast at, but showed footage of an unidentified fishing trawler.
Taiwan’s Coast Guard said China’s “attempts to harass ships at sea through radio communications are a clear expansion of power that violate international law, undermine regional peace and stability, and deviate from reality”.
“Our country holds sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the exclusive economic zone east of Taiwan, and China has absolutely no jurisdiction over any of Taiwan’s waters,” it added.
China on Saturday also sent another Coast Guard ship close to the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands, which are strategically located at the top of the South China Sea, Taiwan’s Coast Guard said separately.
Taiwan has so far this year “expelled” Chinese Coast Guard vessels from Pratas waters 13 times, it added.
The Pratas have no permanent civilian population and lie roughly between southern Taiwan and Hong Kong. Security experts see them as vulnerable to Chinese attack due to their distance — more than 400 km (250 miles) — from Taiwan.
(Reporting by Ben Blanchard; editing by Lincoln Feast.)

Shops looted as German cost of living protests turn violent
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
01:59:57 GMT
10:59:57 KST

Shops looted as German cost-of-living protests turn violent
- Published
Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.
Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters who were targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.
Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.
The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.
On Sunday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild newspaper that overnight police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris" in recent weeks and called for "harsh punishments" for rioters and looters.
Overnight, a large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.
Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.
Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".
She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."
- Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them? 
  - Published3 days ago
On Saturday night Frankfurt police said "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre and that special police units had been deployed.
The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said.
Officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect. People also broke into other shops, stealing items like trainers.
Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended.
"We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard."
Police said the situation calmed down overnight into Sunday in the city.
Similar instances took place in other German cities, following largely peaceful demonstrations.
In Cologne, police said officers were attacked near the main train station, with bottles thrown and a bicycle launched.
Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was "deeply saddening that young people who wanted to peacefully demonstrate for their future were infiltrated today by extremists who had nothing but violence in mind".
A smaller demonstration in the evening in Berlin - following larger protests in the day - resulted in 27 police officers being injured, and up to 56 people temporarily detained, Berlin police said.
In Hamburg, people dressed in black set off fireworks and set barricades on fire, with public broadcaster NDR reporting that 120 people were arrested.
The protests in Germany took place on the same day as other large-scale demonstrations in Europe.
In France, more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful protests in cities across the country, demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially in the education sector.
Thousands of police officers were deployed across the country, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests across France during the demonstrations on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said a police officer had been injured by a molotov cocktail and French prosecutors later launched an attempted murder probe.
Police in Paris said several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles.
French protest organisers, the Gilet Jaune, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".
France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported, external that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.
Protests also took place in Italy, with some clashes between police and demonstrators in Rome and Turin.
In Portugal, police moved to clear a new tent camp that had been assembled after thousands marched to protest against a rental bill that they argue could worsen a housing crisis in the country, where house prices have more than doubled over the past decade.
Mostly young protesters have recently taken to the streets in a swathe of European nations: France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania.
While the specific demands vary from country to country, the protesters have largely focused on cost-of-living issues, such as access to housing, the quality of education and cuts to public services.

Trump says Flavio Bolsonaro can stay in US as long as he wants
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
02:59:53 CET
10:59:53 KST

By Gram Slattery and Andrea Shalal
PALM BEACH, Florida, Oct 31 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Saturday evening that defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro can stay in the United States indefinitely.
The comments, made to reporters during a Halloween party at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club in Florida, suggest that relations between the Western Hemisphere’s two largest democracies may remain strained for some time, even as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Brazil’s top diplomat earlier in the day.
“He can stay here as long as he wants,” Trump said of Bolsonaro, who left Brazil after losing the election to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, despite leading in most opinion polls. “In my opinion, the election was a disgrace.”
The Brazilian embassy in Washington did not immediately return a request for comment.
Outside observers described the election as free and fair. Bolsonaro’s decision to go to the US followed a ruling by a Brazilian Supreme Court justice to revoke his passport shortly after his loss, as the candidate faces a pair of federal money-laundering probes in Brazil and police there considered him a flight risk.
He was admitted to the United States under humanitarian parole, Reuters has previously reported, a status that typically only lasts for one year.
Rubio had said earlier on Saturday that he spoke with Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira at a Group of 20 meeting in Atlanta, and that they would see each other again in a few weeks.
In comments that had pointed to a potential rapprochement, Rubio told journalists that he and Vieira were expected to see each other again in France at a G7 foreign ministers’ summit that will take place next month. Brazil is expected to attend the meeting as an observer, he noted.
A US official and a person familiar with the matter have told Reuters that Trump has no current plans to support the political ambitions of Bolsonaro — who has described himself as Brazil’s rightful leader — despite allowing the Brazilian politician into the US. Trump on Saturday said he has no plans to meet with Bolsonaro.
Rubio said on Saturday that the US government “was not involved directly in any of the moves” that led to Bolsonaro’s departure from Brazil earlier this week. EU’s new levy on parcels kicks in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
01:57:00 UTC
10:57:00 KST

EU’s new levy on parcels kicks in
- The EU introduced a €2 handling fee on parcels from outside the bloc to curb the flood of cheap imports, especially from China, before the holiday shopping rush.
- The fee applies to each item type in a parcel and adds to the €3 duty on small packages. The EU says consumers should not pay extra, but BEUC fears platforms may pass on costs.
- Officials say nearly six billion small parcels entered the EU in 2025, with 93% from China. The fee is permanent, while the €3 duty lasts until July 1, 2028.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – The European Union slapped a €2 (S$2.90) handling fee on packages from outside the 27-nation bloc on Nov 1 in a bid to curb the influx from China.
The new levy – coming just weeks before the Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and the Christmas season shopping rush – will be on top of the EU’s €3 fee on small parcels.
How will it work?
The fee will apply to each type of item in a package sent directly to consumers from outside the EU, regardless of the value.
For example, if there are 10 T-shirts in a package, the handling fee will be €2. But if a package contains two hats and 10 T-shirts, the fee will be €4.
The handling fee comes on top of the €3 duty imposed in July on small packages worth less than €150.
European consumers are not expected to pay the handling fee, the EU insists, but online retailers and sellers can add a €2 charge before a sale.
The European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) said it was “concerned that some platforms may try to pass these new costs onto consumers at the final stages of the purchase”.
It added: “That would be illegal under EU law, which requires the full price to be shown upfront.”
Why is the EU introducing the fee?
Nearly six billion small packages entered the EU in 2025, according to official data.
Some 93% of the cheap packages that arrived in Europe came from China, usually via popular Asian platforms such as AliExpress and Temu.
Brussels says this is putting increasing strain on Customs authorities, thereby raising their costs too. The handling fee will compensate their efforts.
Since the EU imposed the €3 duty on small parcels in July, imports have fallen by around 64% – although officials warn that it is too early to draw firm conclusions.
Europe has expressed concern about “unsafe” non-EU products such as toys that violate the bloc’s rules arriving via Chinese e-commerce platforms.
“For years, Customs have been asked to take on illegal imports with limited resources while small parcels have multiplied out of control,” said BEUC’s Agustin Reyna.
What’s next?
The €2 handling fee is a permanent levy, but the €3 duty on low-value packages is a temporary measure until July 1, 2028.
From that date onwards, standard, product-specific customs tariffs will apply.
The EU will have to assess the handling fee’s amount every two years to ensure it remains proportional to the cost of Customs operations in the bloc. AFP

FBI says North Korea behind $6 billion Binance crypto theft
Published November 1, 2026last updated November 1, 2026
The FBI said Saturday that North Korea was behind the theft of more than $6 billion (€5.36 billion) in virtual assets from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance.
"The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the US law enforcement agency said in a statement.
The theft, which happened within a matter of minutes, is believed to be the biggest cryptocurrency heist in history.
The stolen assets included bitcoin, ethereum and stablecoins such as tether and USD Coin, whose values are pegged to traditional currencies.
News of the cyberattack caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to slump on Friday.
On Sunday, Binance resumed withdrawals, saying the process would be completed in phases, with the first covering 15 cryptocurrencies, including bitcoin, ether, XRP and dogecoin.
The company had suspended withdrawals after the hack.
What did the FBI say?
The FBI said the theft was tied to "malicious cyber activity" by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.
The agency said it had "observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets" primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum.
"It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi [decentralized finance] and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages," it added.
The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to ensure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins.
What did Binance say about the heist?
Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes.
The exchange said on Saturday it was using company funds worth over $6.34 billion to buy tokens to replenish about 90% of the assets stolen in the attack.
The remaining 10% consisted of tokens that were less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy back, the company said.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the company said on X.
The heist came amid growing worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

The governor maintained that California's existing chain-of-custody protocols and statutory retention mandates already guarantee that any potential ballot-related evidence is securely preserved, arguing that there is "no legitimate law enforcement reason" to confiscate equipment or materials indispensable to processing and tallying votes.
"The stakes for democracy and the rule of law are too high to consider any such application without additional scrutiny," Newsom emphasised in the correspondence.
To assist the courts, Newsom provided judges with legal guidance formulated by the UC Berkeley Edley Center on Law & Democracy regarding the evaluation of search warrants for election infrastructure, urging bench vigilance ahead of California's official certification deadline on December 11.

Inside the U.K. movement to pardon women executed for witchcraft centuries ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
01:35:50 UTC
10:35:50 KST

Inside the U.K. movement to pardon women executed for witchcraft centuries ago
Just outside of London sits Maidstone, a quiet country town in a peaceful corner of southern England.
But around 400 years ago, Maidstone was the scene of witch hunts in the literal sense of the phrase.
Records show that more than 20 women convicted of witchcraft were hanged in Maidstone. Witch hunts reached their peak in England in the 1600s.
In total across England and Scotland, around 5,000 women convicted of witchcraft were executed, some by hanging and some by burning.
"They were usually single women, spinsters, or widows, usually without a man to stick up for them," Claire Kehily, a member of the Maidstone Borough Council, told CBS News. "... They were easier to target."
Inside Maidstone's town hall, Kehily showed CBS News a prison cell, reconstructed from an earlier medieval building where accused witches were held before trial.
Now Kehily and her fellow councilors are lobbying the U.K. government and planning to petition King Charles III for an official pardon for all of Maidstone's convicted witches.
"It matters because it was a miscarriage of justice," Kehily said. "The crimes they were accused of they couldn't have been guilty of. And they had no way of being found innocent in many of the cases. This is 400 years ago. But there are still miscarriages of justice. There are still, to these days, people being scapegoated for things."
America's most famous witch trials were in the 1690s in Salem, Massachusetts. Their memory was revived by Arthur Miller's play "The Crucible," an allegory for the political witch hunts led by Sen. Joseph McCarthy in the 1950s.
All of the falsely accused witches in Salem have since been pardoned. But in the U.K., not a single convicted witch has been exonerated.
Samantha Harris, the collections manager at Maidstone Museum, showed CBS News the official record of a witch trial in the town in 1652.
"There had to always be someone to blame," Harris explained, saying that natural disasters or illnesses were often blamed on these women.
"Death of pigs, cattle," Harris said. "... We were scapegoating and blaming people that were often quite vulnerable."
Harris said that for her, getting the women pardoned is personal.
"Being single, being independent, these are things that would have been seen as threatening," Harris said. "I probably would've been targeted absolutely as a witch at the time … If we don't learn from the past, what's to say things won't be recurring again in the future? There's a lot to learn from history."

How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
00:55:06 GMT
09:55:06 KST

How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán
- Published
When they met in northern Serbia last November, Serbian President Aleksandar Vučiċ and Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán could hardly have guessed they would both be out of power within a year.
Both were ousted by popular movements - Orbán fell first, in April, defeated by Péter Magyar's Tisza party. Then last Sunday a student movement less than two years old won Serbia's parliamentary elections by a landslide.
The Tisza party in Hungary and the Student List in Serbia look very different - Tisza is centred on the personality and energy of its leader, while the students in Serbia insist they have no leadership.
But the huge turnout - 79% in Hungary and 69% in Serbia, was driven by tech-savvy young people in both countries. They used AI tools to crunch numbers, identify threats to the vote, and mobilise tens of thousands of election monitors to prevent intimidation and electoral fraud by the governing parties.
Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.
Last weekend, the DE civic action group in Hungary sent 70 election monitors to Serbia, to work with students' movement representatives, visiting polling stations in the northern Serbian province of Vojvodina.
During the summer, even before the election was called, they held workshops to share their experience and methods from the Hungarian election with the Serbian students.
A key technique was to identify "infected" polling districts in advance - places where the surprisingly high number of votes for the governing party at previous elections suggested that voter intimidation or "chain voting" techniques were used.
"From around 16:00 on election day, we noticed groups of masked hooligans - Vučiċ supporters - gathering near voting stations," Péter Klemm, a student activist from Subotica, told the BBC. "So we sent mobile teams, and started filming everything."
Combined with the "stationary" monitors already in place, 20 to 30 volunteers at each threatened polling station acted as a strong deterrent, he believes, and prevented intimidation or fraud.
Orbán in Hungary, Vučiċ in Serbia, both looked invincible. Both were powerful leaders, in office for 16 and 14 years, who had taken over state institutions and established business empires overlapping the two countries.
Orban chose cheese, Vučiċ meat, when they sat down to a quick lunch of traditional burek pastries at a small, popular town centre bakery in Subotica almost a year ago.
They continued to a local winery, to talk about oil and other business deals - the planned Hungarian purchase of a controlling stake in Serbia's NIS oil company. The two nationalist leaders found much in common, in business and politics, not least their friendship with Vladimir Putin in Russia and Chinese President Xi Jinping, and their strong support for Milorad Dodik, the separatist leader of the Bosnian Serbs.
A high-speed railway between Belgrade and Budapest is being built with Chinese finance and know-how.
The parallels between the fall from power of the two men are extraordinary. Aleksandar Vučiċ admitted defeat at exactly 21:30 on Sunday evening, just as Viktor Orbán did on 12 April. Few observers expected either leader to concede peacefully.
There has been speculation this week that Vučiċ spoke to Orbán twice on Sunday night to ask his advice - once before he conceded, and again at 23:15. And that Orbán convinced his Serbian ally not to use force.
Vučiċ denies that he spoke to Orbán before he made his announcement, but acknowledges the later conversation. Viktor Orbán, contacted by the BBC, declined to comment.
An hour before polls closed in Serbia, masked and hooded vigilantes took up position in central Belgrade. During voting, similar groups were photographed at many polling stations, and blocked by election monitors.
There is another strange numerical similarity. The Student List will have 140 seats in the 250-seat Serbian parliament, the same number Péter Magyar's Tisza party won in the 199-seat Hungarian parliament.
Magyar was the only European leader to ring the students directly to congratulate them that evening - and probably the only one who had their number.
"It is always good to hear that the story of Tisza could provide an inspiration for other nations," the Hungarian prime minister told the BBC.
"The result of the Hungarian election clearly showed us that what we are doing here is right," the head of the Student List, Ilija Srdanoviċ, said on the eve of the vote.
Srdanoviċ was one of those Péter Magyar spoke to that Sunday evening.
Orbán, 63, and Vučiċ, 56, may now both face prosecution for corruption and abuse of power.
The judicial machinery in both countries is similar. Serbia's special prosecution service for organised crime, JTOK, and Hungary's brand new special prosecutors, known as NVVH, have similar powers. They could prove useful to each other.
Hungarian companies close to Orbán were also involved in the Novi Sad railway station construction project. The collapse of the station's canopy on 1 November 2024 - blamed on corruption, as well as negligence - killed 16 people, and acted as the catalyst for the Serbian student movement.
"There was a perception in Europe that the longer the Orbán and Vučiċ regimes stayed in office, the stronger they got," Áron Timar, founder of the DE civic action group in Hungary told the BBC.
"In fact they got weaker. And once society found its voice and rose up, there was no way of stopping it."

WASHINGTON, November 1. /TASS/. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has accused the North Korean authorities of a massive hacker attack on the Binance cryptocurrency exchange that could have led to losses of $6.3 bln, the FBI press service said.
The FBI said that North Korea is responsible for the theft of virtual assets worth over $6 bln from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange committed on or about October 29, 2026. The Binance cryptocurrency exchange will allocate 50% of the funds from its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) to compensate for the losses caused by the hacker attack. The platform said earlier that it reimbursed 90% of the amount stolen during the attack.

Trump speaks with Netanyahu shortly after discussing military operations with senior commanders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
00:42:54 UTC
09:42:54 KST

US President Donald Trump addressed overnight on Sunday the possibility of an additional military strike in Iran, claiming the United States is capable of hitting what remains of the Iranian nuclear program "in just ten minutes."
"There are 'one or two sites' left that need to be dealt with, including Pickaxe Mountain. We can do it in ten minutes. We have a plan for it, and we can execute it very quickly," the president said.
Referring to negotiations with Iran, Trump later said, "They want to reach an agreement, and we will see what happens. Things are moving along fine, but they are not really reliable. They reach an agreement and then back out. They want to reach an agreement, and we will see if they actually sign it."
Hours earlier, Trump spoke by phone with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as the United States prepares to resume strikes on Iran, according to a report in the Wall Street Journal.
The call took place after Trump discussed options for resuming military operations with senior military commanders, including a meeting with CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine.
US, Israel posture for strikes, but war unlikely to occur before midterm elections
According to previous reports, the Pentagon reinforced air defense systems, ammunition, and military equipment in the Middle East in recent weeks, while simultaneously repositioning forces from bases that could be vulnerable to an Iranian retaliatory attack.
The timing is particularly sensitive politically. Trump is in the final stretch of the campaign for the congressional midterm elections, which will take place this Tuesday, November 3.
The war with Iran and rising fuel prices in the United States weigh heavily on Republicans, and the president seeks to bolster support for his party in the final days of the campaign.
As such, the United States has reportedly been pushing back the timeline for war with Iran, with the latter itself reportedly deliberately prolonging negotiations ahead of the US midterm elections.
Defense officials assess that despite preparations by CENTCOM and Israel for a strike on Iran, the White House will not order an operation against the Islamic regime before the elections take place unless it detects preparations for a surprise attack.
Israel's defense establishment has remained ambiguous regarding preparations for a possible escalation with Iran, as the White House attempted to offer the Iranian regime another opportunity to return to negotiations, according to Israeli defense assessments.
Defense officials assess that the Iranians, who are facing an economic crisis that is worsening from week to week, will not sign an agreement requiring them to completely abandon their nuclear program, and certainly will not agree to stop producing ballistic missiles that now also threaten Europe.
US Air Force aircrafts arrive at IAF bases
Last week, ten US Air Force (USAF) transport aircraft arrived at IAF bases in southern Israel as part of a larger Middle East air convoy transferring military equipment across the region, KAN News reported.
The aircraft, which came from Texas' Fort Bliss base, are likely stocked with air defense systems intended to protect regional assets amid reported US warnings earlier this week of a potential "short, focused war with Iran," according to KAN.
Other aircraft in the air convoy landed in Jordan, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia, with the KAN report coming after an earlier report that the US had transferred an additional Patriot system to the region pending a potential escalation with Iran.
An Israeli source told KAN that the US and Israel are closely coordinating on Iran, with reports that an additional US naval aircraft carrier will join American forces in the region, alongside an additional Marine unit.\
Two weeks ago, dozens of Israel Air Force fighter jets flew "as far as the Iranian border" before turning around and returning to Israel in a practice sortie, according to an Axios report citing US and Israeli officials.
Tehran: Ready for negotiations, but also for war
Alongside diplomatic signals, Iran recently escalated its threats toward the United States and Israel.
According to an announcement published in Tehran, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered military commanders to prepare for an immediate and powerful response, without geographical limits, in the event of an additional attack.
Iranian Chief of Staff General Ali Abdollahi warned that his country has expanded its list of potential targets and that another American attack would be met with a broad response. According to him, Iran will be the one to determine the end date of any new war.
Conversely, the US administration continues to stress that it prefers a diplomatic agreement over a strike. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said today that if Trump wanted to act militarily, he would have done so weeks or months ago, though he clarified that the United States possesses all necessary capabilities for a successful operation.
At this stage, talks with Iran and military preparations are proceeding in parallel. The report of the phone call between Trump and Netanyahu underscores coordination between Washington and Jerusalem, though it remains unclear whether diplomatic contacts will yield an agreement or if the American president will choose to resume strikes following the elections.

Early US midterm voting shatters record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
00:37:05 UTC
09:37:05 KST

Early US midterm voting shatters record
More than 51 million Americans have cast ballots ahead of the US midterm elections, surpassing the previous early voting record set in 2022.
The November 3 elections, held halfway through a president’s four-year term, will determine control of Congress, with all 435 House seats and roughly a third of the Senate at stake. Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers.
By Saturday, early voting had surpassed 51.3 million ballots, well above the previous record of 45.9 million set in 2022, according to data from the University of Florida Election Lab.
Across 27 states that track voters’ party registration, Democrats accounted for 43.1% of early ballots, compared with 31.8% for Republicans. The figures reflect voters’ party affiliations rather than their choice of candidates.
Pennsylvania recorded one of the widest gaps, with registered Democrats accounting for 65% of early ballots, compared with 25% for Republicans. In traditionally Republican Iowa, Kansas, and Nebraska, Democrats were nearly matching or exceeding GOP early turnout despite being outnumbered among registered voters.
Florida, Michigan, and Texas showed signs of renewed Republican participation in early and absentee voting. In Florida, Republicans had overtaken Democrats by three percentage points, compared with a 6.4-point advantage in 2022.
In Texas, Republicans accounted for 45% of early voters despite making up only 36% of the electorate, according to voter data firm L2. Its figures for Michigan showed that 30% of registered Republicans had voted early, compared with 23% of Democrats.
The Cook Political Report shifted its ratings for 12 House contests toward Democrats on Friday. The forecaster classified 18 House races and seven Senate contests as toss-ups.
“We know that early voters are going to be more Democratic. That’s been a feature of elections for a while now,” University of Florida Election Lab director Michael McDonald told Bloomberg.
“On Election Day, the electorate shifts very much in the red direction. So Democrats have to build up an advantage in the early vote just to withstand what’s going to happen on Election Day,” he added.
Early voting was once a bipartisan practice, but voting patterns shifted during the Covid-19 pandemic. While many Democrats opted to vote by mail as a precaution in 2020, Republicans favored casting ballots in person on Election Day. That trend is now beginning to reverse, according to TargetSmart senior adviser Tom Bonier, cited by Bloomberg.
Trump has blamed mail-in voting for his 2020 defeat to Joe Biden, alleging widespread electoral fraud. In March, he signed an executive order directing the US Postal Service to introduce new requirements for handling mail ballots, including voter lists and tracking measures. On September 14, the Supreme Court declined to lift a lower court injunction blocking the Postal Service from enforcing the new rules ahead of the midterms. The president has softened his stance in recent weeks, urging supporters to vote early or by mail if they prefer.
The elections come amid low approval ratings for Trump, against the backdrop of the unpopular war in Iran and his administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown.
Trump is scheduled to hold rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday after initially canceling the trips. The appearances were rearranged to accommodate additional tele-rallies, AP reported, citing a person familiar with the plans.

Demonstrators have rallied across several Israeli cities to demand the formation of a government incorporating Arab parties, whilst right-wing activists staged counter-demonstrations opposing their inclusion and calling for fresh elections.
Israeli daily Haaretz reported that thousands gathered at Habima Square in central Tel Aviv, calling for a governing alliance alongside the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra'am).
Demonstrators held signs reading: "Through partnership and equality, we change the government" and "The people gave you their support — form a government now", before marching towards Rabin Square.
Similar demonstrations unfolded at Paris Square in Jerusalem, the auditorium plaza in Haifa, across Beersheba, and at the Ras Amer junction near Tira and Tayibe.
Protesters in Tel Aviv and Haifa carried signs displaying the numbers "67" and "53", illustrating the parliamentary distribution following Tuesday's national poll.
Factions opposing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured 67 seats in the 120-member Knesset—comprising 48 seats for Jewish parties in the change bloc and 19 for Arab parties—against 53 seats for Netanyahu's right-wing alliance.
Right-wing counter-protest
Concurrently, hundreds of right-wing demonstrators gathered at Habima Square to reject any inclusion of Arab parties.
Counter-protesters chanted "Bibi is king of Israel", "The people want election integrity", and "The people demand new elections".
Although police designated a separate perimeter, dozens of right-wing activists entered the zone allocated to the pro-partnership demonstration.
Despite commanding a combined 67-seat majority, most Zionist opposition party leaders have refused to construct a governing coalition dependent on Arab lists, according to The Times of Israel.
This stance leaves the Jewish opposition factions with 48 seats—five behind Netanyahu's camp and short of the 61 required for an absolute majority.
Consequently, neither Netanyahu nor his Zionist rivals can build an administration without Arab party votes or cross-bloc defections.
Ra'am has reiterated its willingness to enter government, whilst Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen affirmed his party is ready to facilitate the removal of Netanyahu's administration.

Cryptocurrency platform Binance has said it has used company money to buy tokens to replenish 90 percent of $6.3 billion stolen in a huge hacking attack, as the FBI links the theft to North Korea.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the company said on X.

The attack on Binance came as many observers expressed worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

Polish president holds crisis talks in court standoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
00:30:59 UTC
09:30:59 KST

Polish president holds crisis talks in court standoff
A dispute over the politicisation of Poland’s constitutional court is deepening, with no side appearing to back down.
The Polish president has held crisis talks with political leaders as a dispute over the independence of the country’s top constitutional court deepens.
Representatives of nationalist, far-right, and some governing coalition parties attended President Karol Nawrocki’s talks at the presidential palace on Saturday, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s governing centrist party, Civic Coalition, stayed away.
Nawrocki said in a statement that he convened the “urgent” consultations “due to the threat to Poland’s internal security” presented by the sudden suspension on Friday of the Constitutional Tribunal’s chief judge, Bogdan Swieczkowski.
No breakthrough had emerged by Saturday afternoon.
Meanwhile, in a Saturday evening speech addressing the ongoing crisis, Tusk accused conservative nationalist opposition leaders of wanting to “destroy democracy and rule of law”.
“Let’s call things by their name,” he said. “For years in Poland there exist organisations and politicians who wish to destroy democracy and rule of law.”
Followers of the opposition right-wing Law and Justice party (PiS) gathered outside the court on Saturday, extending protests that have been running for weeks in support of PiS-friendly judges.
Constitutional crisis
The Constitutional Tribunal is Poland’s top court for deciding constitutional matters. It has been at the centre of a years-long political saga related to the politicisation of Polish courts, which Tusk says began under the right-wing PiS government.
Swieczkowski, whom the PiS appointed during its 2015-2023 government, was accused of using his powers as head of the court to block parliament from electing new judges.
Tusk argued that the court’s judges were not politically neutral and that Swieczkowski’s removal was a “painful” but necessary decision to restore the rule of law in Poland after years of erosion under PiS rule.
The court’s official X account on Friday described the government’s move as a “coup d’etat”.
Nawrocki, himself a right-wing figure, has also blocked nominations to the court under his administration.
A key complaint brought by Tusk and his pro-European party was that the court’s PiS-aligned judges frequently ruled in favour of Polish legislation over EU law.
The European Commission on Saturday urged Nawrocki to accept the nomination of new judges at the centre of the country’s constitutional crisis, the AFP news agency reported.
US Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose called for calm on all sides.
“The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse,” Rose wrote in a post on X.

Binance says it covered 90% of losses in cyberattack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
00:24:40 UTC
09:24:40 KST

01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance announced that it had covered 90% of the losses from a cyberattack and was continuing purchases through market and over-the-counter (OTC) channels to cover the remaining amount.
In a statement, Binance noted that it had allocated more than $6.34 billion in company funds to compensate users affected by the attack.
Noting that approximately 80% of the affected amount had previously been covered, the statement said: “The coverage rate has now reached 90%.”
It said that losses involving Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Tether (USDT), BNB, Solana (SOL), USD Coin (USDC), XRP, USD1, RLUSD and Zcash (ZEC) had been fully covered.
It added that the remaining 10% consisted of lower-liquidity tokens other than these 10 assets.
Binance said it would continue purchasing the affected tokens through market and over-the-counter channels until the coverage rate reached 100% for all tokens.
“Binance, not our users, will bear the financial burden of the stolen funds,” the statement said.
The company emphasized that its next priority was to resume users' withdrawal services, adding that it remained on track to reopen withdrawals on Nov. 1, in line with a previously announced schedule.
The statement also announced the publication of a new proof-of-reserves snapshot, enabling users to independently verify that their assets were backed at a minimum 1:1 ratio after a zero-knowledge proof was generated.
On Thursday, Binance said it was investigating reports of a potential security issue and assured users their funds were safe.
In a statement on Saturday, the company said the estimated scale of the security breach was $6.3 billion, adding that about $3 billion in assets had been frozen.

Salvadoran families demand fair trials, mourn prison dead on Day of the Dead

By Wilfredo Pineda
SAN SALVADOR, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Relatives of people detained under El Salvador’s controversial state of exception gathered at the San Salvador metropolitan cathedral on Saturday to leave offerings for inmates who have died behind bars, demanding justice.
Participants arrived carrying yellow and red flowers, banners and photographs of jailed family members. Inside the capital’s cathedral, they knelt in prayer around the tomb of Archbishop Oscar Arnulfo Romero, a saint, and placed flowers there.
On the cathedral steps, the group held a rally honoring the dead and remembering relatives still in custody. Many of those present have had no contact with their detained relatives since their arrest, and - in some cases - do not know whether their relatives are still alive.
Natalia Funes, 61, a farmer from Puerto El Triunfo in the eastern province of Usulutan, attended in hopes of seeking answers about her jailed son. Her son, Oscar Orlando Rodriguez, was arrested in July 2022 and has been held incommunicado since.
“I am a distraught mother, a mother who has never seen my son. I am a mother who has never seen their face or heard from them,” Funes said.
El Salvador’s state of exception, imposed by President Nayib Bukele four years ago, has allowed security forces to detain more than 90,000 people.
Cristosal, a prominent human rights organization, has documented 454 deaths in Salvadoran prisons among people detained under the state of exception.
Many relatives of those still detained fear their loved ones will become an unwanted addition to the statistic.
Protesters used the Day of the Dead, observed on November 1 and 2 across several Latin American countries, to remember those who died behind bars, and also called for fair trials for detainees who remain jailed.
Liliana Urias, 44, spokeswoman for the Mothers for Freedom movement, said some members of the movement had lost a son, a brother or the father of their children.
“We are here in memory of all the innocent people who have died under the state of exception,” Urias said.

Jaishankar speaks at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, calling for diversified supply chains and the de-politicisation of energy markets
External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Saturday called for reducing political interference in energy markets and diversifying global supply chains, saying disruptions were placing a disproportionate burden on developing countries.Speaking about the message he delivered at G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Jaishankar said the discussions covered geopolitical conflicts, energy and food security, and resilient supply chains.“Look, there are big conflicts today, two major conflicts which are having global ramifications,” ANI quoted him as saying. He added that “there are no military solutions; we have to find a diplomatic pathway.”
On energy security, Jaishankar warned against disruptions in fuel distribution and their impact on developing economies. “This distortion of the energy markets, the politicisation of energy flows, this is something which is very harmful,” he said, adding that “the Global South was bearing the brunt of the energy shortages and that something needs to be done.”He also flagged risks to food security, citing disruptions to grain shipments through the Black Sea and fertiliser shortages linked to tensions in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea regions.
At the meeting's concluding session on supply chains, Jaishankar called for wider diversification of manufacturing and production across countries. “Today we need more diversified supply chains,” he said, advocating “more globalised, you know, more diversified production, more diversified manufacturing.”In a post on X after the session, he said securing supply chains was central to the global economy's well-being and called on the G20 to promote “the right to industrialise” and resist “predatory practices”.“Diversification and de-risking, including in connectivity, is the key to supply chain resilience, threatened by pandemics, conflicts, climate events and mishaps,” he said.
Jaishankar also urged the grouping to work towards the “de-politicisation of markets” and prevent the concentration of production and resources in a few geographies.US secretary of state Marco Rubio, who hosted the meeting, also stressed the need to secure critical trade routes, including the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb, and strengthen supply chains for critical minerals.On the sidelines, Jaishankar attended a Quad foreign ministers' meeting with Rubio and his Japanese and Australian counterparts. He also met Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov, with discussions covering the Ukraine conflict, the Gulf situation and multilateral issues.

Flavio Bolsonaro fled Brazil accompanied by former Mossad agent: Report

2026-11-01
00:00:13 UTC

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
01 November 2026•Update: 01 November 2026
Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro left Brazil for the US in an operation involving two vans, a private jet and a former agent of Israel's Mossad intelligence agency who reportedly accompanied him, according to an investigation published by CNN Brasil.
Bolsonaro, his wife Fernanda and their two daughters crossed into Argentina by road Tuesday through the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, connecting Foz do Iguacu in southern Brazil with Puerto Iguazu in Argentina, CNN Brasil reported Friday.
Security camera footage identified two vans and their drivers. One driver was a former councilman for the city of Foz do Iguacu. The other was his son.
A former Israeli intelligence officer who had worked for Mossad reportedly accompanied Bolsonaro from Brasilia to Argentina, according to the investigation.
The agent arrived in Brazil on Oct. 19 and later traveled in the same van as the senator, according to the report. It did not establish what role, if any, he played in organizing the operation.
The family boarded a Gulfstream G400 private jet in Puerto Iguazu. The aircraft, operated by Argentine charter company Baires Fly, stopped in Guayaquil, Ecuador, to refuel before arriving at Opa-locka Executive Airport in Miami early Wednesday.
CNN Brasil said the operation was internally referred to as "Operation Alba" and had been planned before the presidential election campaign ended.
Brazilian investigators were examining possible logistical support from contacts linked to the governments of Argentine President Javier Milei and US President Donald Trump, said the report.
No direct involvement by either government in the operation has been confirmed.
Brazil's Federal Police said Wednesday it found no records of Bolsonaro passing through Brazilian immigration checkpoints when leaving the country.
His departure came after Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered him to surrender his personal and diplomatic passports and prohibited him from leaving Brazil.
The Federal Police is investigating the circumstances of his departure and may ask the Supreme Court to block his assets, including bank accounts, according to CNN Brasil.

Southeast Asia’s EV boom sidelines local car parts suppliers
Suppliers in Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia grapple with falling demand, as Chinese carmakers favour their own networks
Local manufacturers across Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia are facing a double squeeze: demand is weakening for parts used in petrol and diesel cars, collectively known as internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, while steep barriers to entry also keep them out of EV supply chains.
Analysts say repair and servicing work plus hybrids, which pair a petrol engine with an electric motor, could offer a lifeline, but without stronger government support and better access to Chinese manufacturers, the EV transition threatens to hollow out the region’s established supply base.
Chinese EV investments have so far generated minimal business for established local component makers, according to Indonesian economist Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara.
